en: Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
In the Nyāyavārtika,
the first chapter.
That Akṣapāda, the most eminent of sages,
proclaimed this treatise for the sake of the world’s tranquility,
as a means to eliminate the ignorance of fallacious logicians.
I shall compose a commentary on it.

"From the knowledge of the reality of categories such as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) follows the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa)"—this is the opening aphorism (sūtra) of this treatise. Its introductory statement is "The comprehension of an object through the means of valid cognition," and so forth.
The connective statement for that [opening aphorism] is that the treatise is a communicator of the human good (puruṣa-śreyaḥ). The treatise...

Furthermore, a collection of words denoting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, distinguished by its arrangement, is a "word-group" (*pada*). A word, moreover, is a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*). A collection of words is a treatise (*śāstra*); a collection of aphorisms (*sūtra*) is a topical section (*prakaraṇa*); a collection of topical sections is a daily lesson (*āhnika*); a collection of daily lessons is a chapter (*adhyāya*); and a work consisting of five chapters is a treatise. Its categories (*padārtha*) are the means of valid cognition and the rest. Of that [treatise]...

002.02 The meanings of the words of the treatise consist of sixteen entities, beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That treatise [002.03] declares the supreme good (*śreyas*) for persons. A treatise is the authoritative exposition of the reality of things not yet apprehended through perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
[002.04] Dharma is its subject matter; it is the reality of internal things not yet apprehended through perception or inference.

002.05 A student is one endowed with the perfection of capacity. Furthermore, a person is divided into four types: the one who has understood (*pratipanna*), the one who has not understood (*apratipanna*), 002.06 the doubtful (*sandigdha*), and the mistaken (*viparyasta*). Among these, the one who has understood is the instructor (*pratipādayitṛ*).

002.07 The others, being dependent [on others], are those to be instructed (*pratipādya*). They are so called when they depend upon the contact between the sense faculty and its object (*indriya-artha-sannikarśa*).

When it depends upon the perception of a mark (*liṅga*) and recollection (*smṛti*), then it functions as inference (*anumāna*). When it further depends upon instruction (*upadeśa*), then the scripture (*śāstra*) operates. Well-being (*śreyaḥ*), moreover, consists of happiness and the cessation of what is harmful. That well-being, being divided, is established as twofold by way of the distinction between the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). The seen...

002.11 Happiness is the non-perception [of suffering]; it is the cessation of the harmful. Furthermore, the cessation of the harmful is both absolute and non-absolute. 002.12 Non-absolute [cessation] occurs through the avoidance of the means of suffering, such as thorns and the like. Absolute [cessation] occurs, moreover, through the abandonment of suffering divided into twenty-one varieties. 002.13 Furthermore, suffering is divided into twenty-one varieties.

002.14 The body, the six sense-faculties, the six objects, the six cognitions, pleasure, and pain. 002.15 The body is suffering because it is the locus of suffering. The sense-faculties, the objects, and the cognitions are [suffering] because they serve as its instruments.
002.16 Pleasure is [considered] suffering because it is accompanied by suffering; [pain] is suffering by its very nature. The cessation of that [suffering] is Dharma.

By abandoning the means for unrighteousness (*adharma*), by the non-arising of both righteousness (*dharma*) and unrighteousness when they have not yet arisen, and by the exhaustion [of those] through experience when they have already arisen—thus [it is said]. Persons are either possessed of passion and so forth, or free from passion.
In this context, passion is characterized by attachment to sense objects; those who possess it are "possessed of passion and so forth."

Detachment (*vairāgya*), moreover, is characterized by the absence of attachment to enjoyments; those who possess this are "free from passion" (*vīta-rāga*). Activity (*pravṛtti*) is twofold because it conforms to the differences among persons. The activities of those persons, conforming to the distinctions between individuals, are of two kinds: the activity of one free from passion, and [the activity of one still possessed by passion].

003.02. Of one kind. In that regard, the activity of those who are free from passion (*vīta-rāga*) is indeed of a single form; it has the purpose of avoiding the undesirable, and they engage [in action] solely with the thought, "We shall abandon what is undesirable. Furthermore, they have no attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) toward anything whatsoever. However, the activity of those possessed of passion and the like is of two forms. But as for those who possess passion and the like—

003.05 Their mental activities (*manas*) are of two kinds: those for the sake of attaining desired objects and those for the sake of avoiding undesired objects. One who is attached proceeds [in action] with the thought, "I shall obtain what is desired. One turns away out of aversion with the thought, "I shall abandon what is undesired. Furthermore, the activity of one possessed of passion and so forth is also twofold, being either capable...
[This is] due to the distinction between the capable and the incapable. Indeed, that activity which possesses passion and so forth is both capable and incapable.
When one who acts with the thought "I shall obtain what is desired" actually obtains it, then [the activity] is capable.
When one who acts with the thought "I shall abandon what is undesired" actually abandons it, then [the activity] is capable; when...

In the opposite case, they are incapable. Consequently, there is again a twofold activity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), due to its being either purposeful or purposeless. First, a means of valid cognition is that which determines an object; because it shares the common characteristics of a means of valid cognition, even a counterfeit of a means of valid cognition is metaphorically designated as a "means of valid cognition. What, then, is this common characteristic of a means of valid cognition?

003.14 The capacity to determine a general object belongs to both valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and pseudo-cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*); for a general object is determined by valid cognition as well as by pseudo-cognition. 003.15 When this cognizer proceeds after having ascertained [the object] by means of valid cognition, then his activity becomes effective; however, when [he proceeds] by means of pseudo-cognition...

003.17 When one acts after having ascertained the object, then its capacity for that [action] is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as being possessed of an object. 003.18 [This refers to] the introductory commentary beginning with "the comprehension of the object" (*arthapratipattau*). If it is argued that both are unestablished because they are mutually dependent, 003.19 [we reply:
No, because [this process] is beginningless (*anāditvāt*). If there is the capacity for action upon the comprehension of the object through valid cognition, and if...

003.20 Or rather, it must be stated whether the comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs first, or whether the capacity for purposeful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*) occurs first. 003.21 If, first of all, the comprehension of the object occurs prior to the means of valid cognition, then why does one comprehend it without the capacity for purposeful action? 003.22 Alternatively, if one acts toward an object without having previously ascertained the capacity for purposeful action...

Why does [this cycle] proceed? Because it proceeds from valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or because there is the apprehension of an object; thus, the relation of prior and subsequent is not conceivable. But that is not so. Why? Because it is beginningless. We shall demonstrate in the preceding sūtra that this saṃsāra is beginningless. And if saṃsāra were to have a beginning...

004.04 Is this fault [the case] when first there is the apprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or rather when there is the efficacy of purposeful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*)?

004.05 Thus, in the desire to know the relative strength or weakness of the means of valid cognition and purposeful action, for the sake of demonstrating the efficacy of both, people in the world, indeed proceeding with a statement, act after having ascertained the object through a means of valid cognition; and that... 004.06 [is the case].
Proceeding in such a manner, one obtains the result. In this regard, the following is considered:

Is the comprehension of the object capable [of leading to action], or is it the activity? Both are capable, because that result is invariably concomitant with it. This sentence is for the purpose of demonstrating this meaning.

004.10 Thus, all worldly discourse is a restatement of how people act: having ascertained an object by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one who acts obtains a result; this worldly practice is restated by that statement. 004.11–004.12 Because of the distinction between that which is to be abandoned (*heya*), the means of abandoning it (*hānopāya*), and that which is to be attained (*adhigantavya*), there are four categories of meaning (*arthapada*): suffering (*duḥkha*) is that which is to be abandoned, as is its cause (*hetu*).

004.13 Suffering has been described; its causes are ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). Abandonment is the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*). 004.14 Furthermore, that [knowledge] is the realization of the objects of experience as they truly exist; and that is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The means is the treatise (*śāstra*). 004.15 That too has been stated: liberation (*apavarga*) is that which is to be realized; moreover, it is the absolute cessation of suffering.

And [the phrase] "in this group of four" is for the purpose of demonstrating the primacy of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But how, by this sentence, is the group of four beginning with the means of valid cognition demonstrated? The attainment of the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) are understood through scripture (*śruti*), because the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is inseparable from them; for indeed, without a cognizer, [they do not exist].

004.19 This statement, for which a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible, is explained by setting forth its constituent parts. In that context, the suffix *-tas* in *pramāṇataḥ* is intended to demonstrate both the pervasion of the expression and the pervasion of the case ending. This [use of] *pramāṇataḥ* is a fifth case (ablative) expressing the cause (*nimitta-pañcamī*). Its mention is for the purpose of demonstrating the pervasion of the expression and the pervasion of the case ending.
But how is the suffix *tasi* obtained outside of the fifth case? He says: it is obtained by means of an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the rule for "the beginning of the beginning" (*ādy-ādau*).
What, then, is established by this? Through the pervasiveness of the statement, there is both convergence (*saṃplava*) and restriction (*vyavasthā*).
Convergence is understood in cases such as *pramāṇena*, *pramāṇābhyām*, and *pramāṇaiḥ*; whereas restriction is understood in cases such as *pramāṇenaiva*.

005.03. The distinction [of the means] is established through its pervasion by the various grammatical case-roles (*vibhakti*); it possesses the nature of being both a cause (*hetu*) and an instrument (*karaṇa*). From the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the apprehension of the object occurs. 005.04.

Thus, its status as a cause consists in its establishing the object by means of the *pramāṇa*; and because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*), it has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). 005.05.
If it is argued that the convergence [of multiple means of knowledge] is untenable because they have distinct objects, we say: no, for that is not admitted.

It might be thought that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have distinct objects: perception (*pratyakṣa*) has a particular (*viśeṣa*) as its object, while inference (*anumāna*) has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. This, however, must be understood: there is no such thing as a universal that is not also a particular, nor is there ever a perception whose object is a universal, nor an inference whose object is a particular.

005.09 And this is not so, because it is not accepted. First of all, we do not admit two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), nor two objects, nor even their non-confusion. What is the reason? There are four means of valid cognition;

the object is threefold, due to the distinction between the universal (sāmānya), the particular (viśeṣa), and that which possesses them (tadvat). Furthermore, confusion would occur if a single [object] were [cognized] by all the means of valid cognition.

005.12 [Objection: "Cognition is like a sense-faculty (*indriya*). Indeed, a sense-faculty is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it illuminates the object. 005.13 Regarding its determination and confusion: there is determination with respect to odors and so forth, and confusion with respect to earth and so forth, because they are perceivable by two sense-faculties.

With respect to existence (*sattā*) and quality-ness (*guṇatva*), there is cognition through all the sense-faculties; this is because they have already been cognized. 005.14 [Response: Because it has already been cognized.
If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] are redundant, we say no; for there would be no apprehension of that object otherwise.
It may be thought: "If the means of knowledge were to overlap, then when an object has already been apprehended by one means of knowledge, a second means of knowledge would become redundant;
and a means of knowledge that causes the apprehension of an object already apprehended is like grinding what is already ground."

[The opponent says: It would be [like] ground flour. [Reply: No, because the apprehension is otherwise. We do not say that the object is apprehended by means of inference and so forth in the same way it is apprehended by perception. For [in perception], the object is connected with the sense faculty;
[in inference], it is connected with the sense faculty [via a mark]; [in comparison], there is the comprehension of the relationship between a name and the named; [in verbal testimony], the word...

006.01 [It is established] by way of mention and by means of scripture, and because a fixed determination is observed regarding other objects. Furthermore, there is no overlap (*saṃplava*) with respect to every object; therefore, it is not redundant. Consequently, it is established that the suffix *-tasi* is for the purpose of making known the pervasion of the case endings (*vibhakti*). Thus, the definition of the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be determined. But what, then...
006.04. Furthermore, what has been said regarding the validity of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It was stated that "the means of valid cognition is the cause of apprehension.

006.05. Validity is the state of being a cause of apprehension; that which is the instrumental cause of apprehension is the means of valid cognition. 006.06. If it is argued that this is not a definition because it is too broad—if the cause of apprehension is the means of valid cognition, then would not the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) also [be means of valid cognition]?
006.07 Because it is the cause of apprehension, it would follow that [the means of knowledge] possesses the status of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); or else, a distinction must be stated.

This is the distinction: in the case of the means of knowledge, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) have already achieved their purpose; thus, both the cognizer and the object of cognition have achieved their purpose, whereas the means of knowledge has not yet achieved its purpose. Therefore, that alone is the instrument for apprehension.

006.10 If it is argued that the production of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is without an instrument (*akaraṇa*), [we reply: if the instrument is produced by the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), then it follows that the production of the instrument itself would be without an instrument. No; because the contact between the sense faculty and the object (*indriya-artha-sannikarṣa*) serves as the instrument, the production of the instrument is not without an instrument. In the production of the instrument, the sense faculty— 006.12 —[is the instrument].

006.13–006.14: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is produced by the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*), which depend upon the contact between the object and the sense organ (*artha-sannikarṣa*). [Objection: In that case, it would follow that there is no production of a means of valid cognition in the absence of an instrument (*akaraṇa*). [Response: If, then, the cognizer and the object of cognition depend upon the contact between the sense organ and the object for the production of the means of valid cognition, then, in the production of that contact between the sense organ and the object—
"What does it depend upon? [The answer is: "Even in that case, it depends upon the sense faculty (*indriya*). Thus, the relationship between agent and instrument is beginningless (*anādi*).

Whatever comes later depends upon what precedes it; therefore, the relationship between agent and instrument should be understood as beginningless. If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is produced by the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), both of which already exist, then...

Since the relationship between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the status of being a knower and the status of being an object of knowledge are untenable. How then is there a means of valid cognition? Just as this word "agent" (*kāraka*) [requires an action], so too are "knower" and "object of knowledge. Furthermore, words denoting agents do not acquire their own meaning without an action.

Thus, it is neither the substance alone that is the agent (*kāraka*), nor is it the action alone. For a word denoting an agent functions by referring to the means of accomplishing an action (*kriyā-sādhana*) as connected with a specific action.
Furthermore, the words "knower" (*pramātṛ*) and "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) are words denoting agents; they could not function without an action.

007.05 No; because, like words such as "cook" (*pācaka*), they have the three times as their object. We do not say that agentive terms (*kāraka-śabda*) function solely through a connection with an action. Rather, these have the three times as their object.
If they were caused by a connection with an action, they would not function in the absence of a connection with an action.

But how can they function without a connection to an action? What, then, is that capacity (*sāmarthya*) which exists in all three times? Therefore, it is logical that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is produced by the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*);
thus, it is the instrument for the apprehension [of the object]. Alternatively, because it is the most effective cause (*sādhakatamatva*), there is no such undesirable consequence.
And this undesirable consequence does not apply [to us], because the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) are the causes (*nimitta*) of the apprehension (*upalabdhi*).

[If you argue that] "it follows that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [would be the apprehension]," why? Because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*); the means of valid cognition is that which is the most effective instrument.

But this [status of being the most effective] does not belong to the knower or the object of knowledge. What, indeed, is the meaning of "the most effective instrument"? It is that which is the means of valid cognition.

007.14 Only the sentence is being expressed, not the meaning. 007.15 The possession of that [validity] by both existence and non-existence does not occur when there is neither a knower nor an object of knowledge; rather, it occurs when they exist.
007.16 Furthermore, when the means of knowledge exists, validity certainly arises; this is the distinction.

The state of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) is now explained. That which possesses it cognizes; what does it possess? It possesses a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When the means of valid cognition exists, one cognizes, not when it is absent.
Or else, there is the non-agency of that which exists [as the cause], because of whose absence the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) do not exist.
007.20 They both produce valid cognition (*pramā*); that excellence (*atiśaya*) is like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or it is posteriority (*carama-bhāvitā*).

Just as 007.21 conjunction, which occurs later, becomes the capacity (*śakti*) of the substance, so too valid cognition, occurring later, becomes the capacity for valid cognition of the cognizer and the object of cognition. Posteriority is the excellence; it is the immediate succession of the apprehension.
Or rather, it is the excellence consisting in the production of cognitions immediately following the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Or else, it is the status of being the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇa-kāraṇatā*) [of cognition]. For, first of all, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is a common cause for all cognitions, and the object of cognition (*prameya*) is likewise [common] because it is shared by all persons; however, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is uncommon.

Because it is the cause, it is the primary factor (*pradhāna*); and because of its primacy, it is designated as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). Thus, either it is the specific characterizer of the conjunction that is the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), or it is the conjunction itself which is the cause of valid cognition. That which exists for the sake of assisting that [conjunction]—the instrument of valid cognition—is what is expressed by the term "excellence" (*atiśaya*). The mention of the "object" (*artha*) is for the purpose of [defining] the instrument of valid cognition.

008.07–008.09. This is for the purpose of negating the apprehension of an object, because the apprehension of the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) does not impel a person toward action; rather, when one apprehends the existence of an object as it truly is, one then proceeds to act. [This excludes] objects that are to be disregarded.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of negation; for the cognition of an object as something to be disregarded does not impel a person toward action. Rather, when one perceives that an object possesses the nature of being a cause of pleasure or pain, one then engages with it. Thus, the non-apprehension by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is understood [as the cause of inaction].
If it is argued that [the word "pramāṇa" is superfluous] because of this, we say no; for its purpose is to indicate a specific kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

When it is stated that "there is efficacy in the activity toward the apprehension of the object," it is already understood that this occurs by means of a *pramāṇa*; for no apprehension whatsoever occurs without a *pramāṇa*. And yet, it is not in this way [that the word indicates] a specific kind of *pramāṇa*...

Because it serves the purpose of making something known, this word "pramāṇa" exists when applied to a valid means of cognition, and it also exists by virtue of its commonality even with what is a semblance of a means of cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). Thus, in this context, comprehension through a means of cognition demonstrates the efficacy of purposeful action; it is the [valid] means of cognition, and not anything else. Nor is it the case that the means of cognition—

The mention of the fifth [case-ending] is obtained even without the explicit mention of "grasping" (grahaṇa). There is a purpose for this, and therefore the term "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) was employed. By the inclusion of the term "object" (artha), there is a comprehensive inclusion of everything by way of being a cause of pleasure and pain; for everything is being cognized because it is being sought after. Every object, beginning with the means of valid cognition, is a cause of pleasure and pain, and all of it is sought after as it is being cognized.

[The claim that] "the object (*artha*) [is so called] because it is beneficial" is not tenable, because it involves a contradiction and because it is not what is intended to be said. Every object, such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, is a cause of pleasure and pain; thus, for one who says this, the four categories of objects—beginning with that which is to be abandoned (*heya*)—would be contradicted.
Furthermore, it is impossible to abandon the means of valid cognition and the like, nor is their abandonment intended to be asserted.

Therefore, this is not an explanation; rather, those things which are subsumed under the categories of pleasure and pain, and their causes, are what are being designated here by virtue of the context. Consciousness (*saṃvit*) is not included because it does not fall within that context.
Since it is not an object of action (*akarmatva*), consciousness is not to be abandoned; nor is it sought after, because it is neither pleasure nor pain, and is not the cause thereof.
009.07 Because it is a result, this object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-artha*) is incalculable; one cannot say, "This is the extent of the scope of valid cognition.
009.08 It is impossible to enumerate it because of its infinity, nor because both [pleasure and pain] have been fully enumerated.
009.09 This object of valid cognition is just this much: namely, pleasure and pain, along with their causes; and both of these have been fully enumerated.

Therefore, it is not correct [to say] that because of infinity, it is impossible to enumerate [them], since the diversity of living beings is incalculable; thus, the statement that "the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇārtha*) is incalculable" is incoherent. This is not so, because the word *artha* denotes "purpose" (*prayojana*); thus, "the purpose of the means of valid cognition is incalculable" means that the purpose regarding the means of valid cognition is incalculable.

"Immeasurable" (aparisaṃkhyeya) is the meaning of this sentence. How is it that the very same object becomes a cause of pleasure for some and a cause of suffering for others? Furthermore, when a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) possesses its object and is capable [of producing knowledge], the other [factors] are also said to possess their objects and be capable. From the context, the sense of "most effective" (sādhakatama) should be understood as the sense of "one among many" (anyatamatva).

For it is described that in the fourfold group [of treatises], the *prakaraṇa* (systematic exposition) is the primary authority (*pramāṇa*). If, however, the scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*) were to be meaningful [independently], what would be the purpose of describing the capacity of the authority? Therefore, it is as stated: "the system" (*nyāya*).
The knower (*pramātṛ*) is independent; but what is this independence? It is being the enjoyer of the fruit of the causal factors (*kāraka*).

009.19 Because you [hold that] this [agent] is connected with the fruit of the causal factors (*kāraka*), there is either an inherence (*samavāya*) in them, or else the person (*puruṣa*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the action produced by all the causal factors. 009.20–21 This constitutes his status as the instigator (*prayoktṛtva*), or else his non-dependence on others; or else, the causal factors whose capacities are observed—

009.22 One employs the wheels, yet one is not employed by them. The completion of reality is the fitness for application (viniyoga-yogyatā), or rather, it is the state of being disregarded. That non-contradiction regarding the determined object is the fitness for application—knowing that "this object is a means to happiness" or "this object is a means to suffering," one applies oneself accordingly. 010.01–010.02 [The fitness for application consists in knowing: "This object is a means to happiness, or this object is a means to suffering. Having known this, one applies oneself.

010.03 Completion [is] the attainment of that and the negation of that; or, that which is neither a means to pleasure nor a means to pain—this is equanimity (*upekṣā*). Furthermore, what is that "being" (*sat*) and "non-being" (*asat*)? Its state is its "reality" (*tattva*).

In this regard, it must be stated: of which thing is there the state? It is "being" and "non-being," because they are the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), according to the context.

It has been established that "existent" and "non-existent" are the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, "that which is existent and non-existent" refers to their state of being so.

Existence and non-existence (*sadasattva*) consist in the fact that the existent and the non-existent are the objects of the means of valid cognition, as well as the negation thereof. Indeed, the state of these two—the existent and the non-existent—is twofold: being affirmed and being negated. That which is affirmed in one instance [is the object of the means of valid cognition].
That [distinction] is denied elsewhere, as for example: "Earth possesses fragrance; water is odorless.

If it is argued that there must be a distinction between existence and non-existence because they are objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no, because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
In this regard, the thought might occur: if existence and non-existence are apprehended by means of a valid cognition, then from that [apprehension], the [status of being] a valid cognition—

Because both are objects of cognition, it follows that there is no distinction between them; however, this is not so, because of the lack of exclusivity (*anaikāntāt*). All these things, such as cows and jars, constitute a collection of substances accessible through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and are characterized by difference; therefore, this [argument] is inconclusive (*anekāntaḥ*). Furthermore, there is a distinction based on the existence or non-existence of the causes for perception and non-perception, for that which exists is indeed the objective support (*ālambana*) of a valid means of knowledge.

The independent [nature] exists, whereas the dependent [nature], being non-existent, is understood by way of negation, like a lamp. Just as a lamp makes manifest objects such as jars situated in a room or elsewhere, in that same way, it makes manifest even what is non-existent; for no other means is employed for the cognition of the non-existent.

For when an object such as a jar is being perceived, if there were another perceptible object of the same class as this one, it would be seen just like this one; yet it is not seen. Therefore, due to the absence of perception, it is understood that it does not exist.

In the same way, even when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself being cognized, if there were another object of cognition (*prameya*) of the same class as this one, [it would likewise be perceived].

"If it existed, it would be perceived just like this; however, it is not so perceived. Therefore, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [it does not exist]. Thus, a means of valid cognition that reveals an existing thing also reveals what is non-existent.
In that regard, the various types of non-existence are not said to be unmanifested independently, because they are not included within the fourfold category [of existence]."

Just as the proliferation of existence (*bhāva-prapañca*) has been taught, so too should the proliferation of non-existence (*abhāva-prapañca*) be understood to have been taught. Since the teaching on non-existence follows from the teaching on existence, it is for this reason that they are not explicitly stated.

[1-1-1] The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the members of a syllogism (*avayava*), reasoning (*tarka*),...

011.06 Determination, discussion, debate, cavil, fallacies of the reason, quibble, futility, and points of defeat—011.07 from the knowledge of the truth regarding these, the attainment of the supreme good [occurs].
011.08 In this regard, it will indeed be taught as arranged in sixteen ways; "arrangement" (vyūha) means a concise summary. These...
"011.09 These are the six categories (sat-bhedaḥ)"—this is the aphorism. A compound (samāsa) in which all the word-meanings are primary is a copulative compound (dvandva).

011.10 What is being stated? That all these, beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), are to be known. Otherwise, because they would be included among the immediately preceding [categories] and thus function as qualifiers, the means of valid cognition and the others would not be objects of knowledge (avijñeya). 011.11"

011.12 There may be an analysis [of the compound] according to the literal expression; whatever purpose there was in employing a different wording in the original exposition, that same purpose should be seen here as well. 011.13 In the phrase "the reality (tattva) of the means of valid cognition and so forth," the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śaiṣikī*); for what, then, is a "residual relation" (*śeṣa*)? It is the non-intentionality regarding the grammatical factors (*kāraka*s); where neither a *kāraka* nor the meaning of a *kāraka* is intended. 011.14–15 [Objection: But in this case, since the word "reality" (*tattva*) denotes a substance (*dravya*), it ought to be connected with the means of valid cognition and so forth through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Therefore, the genitive case should be understood as expressing identity. [Response: That is not so, because the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a quality (*guṇa*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is black," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the quality of being black. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the qualities of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a specific property (*dharma*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her capacity to carry loads," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the specific property of being capable of carrying loads. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the specific properties of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Alternatively, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of an essential nature (*svarūpa*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her own self-nature," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the essential nature of the cow. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the essential natures of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of an object (*viṣaya*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is the object of his cognition," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the object of cognition. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the objects of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a state (*avasthā*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her state of being a cow," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the state of being a cow. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the states of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is the cause of her milk," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the cause of the milk. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the causes of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a result (*phala*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is the result of her milking," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the result of the milking. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the results of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a connection (*sambandha*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her connection with Devadatta," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the connection with Devadatta. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the connections of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a collection (*samudāya*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is the collection of her horns, hooves, and so forth," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the collection of parts. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the collections of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a distinction (*bheda*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her distinction from other cows," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the distinction. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the distinctions of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a universal (*sāmānya*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is the universal 'cowness'," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the universal. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the universals of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a particular (*viśeṣa*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her particularity," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the particularity. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the particulars of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a function (*vṛtti*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her function of carrying loads," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the function. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the functions of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a transformation (*pariṇāma*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her transformation into a calf," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the transformation. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the transformations of the means of valid cognition and so forth, such as their respective definitions and characteristics. Therefore, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation. Furthermore, the word "reality" (*tattva*) is used here in the sense of a manifestation (*abhivyakti*). For example, when one says, "The reality of Devadatta’s cow is her manifestation," the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses the manifestation. Similarly, in this context, the word "reality" (*tattva*) expresses

Or, when [the relationship] is intended to be expressed, that is the *śeṣa* (remainder), as in the example: "The water-pot of the Brahmin. Regarding the reality (*tattva*) [of the categories], there is a fault in its being either different from or non-different from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. If, first of all, reality were distinct from the means of valid cognition and the rest, it would follow that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) does not result from the comprehension of the means of valid cognition and the rest. What is the reason?

Because it is employed as a qualifier of reality (*tattva*), like the action of "bringing the king’s man. Now, if there is non-difference [between reality and the means of knowledge], the mention of "reality" is redundant; for if you do not admit a reality distinct from the means of knowledge and so forth, then the mention of "reality" becomes purposeless. Some say that this is not a fault in either case. If, first of all—

Reality would be distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, because those [means] are not independent; for the means of valid cognition and the rest are understood [as dependent], just as in the case of the existence of jujube fruits in a bowl—just as one says "the existence of jujube fruits in a bowl.
When the state of being (*bhāva*) is taught, since that state is not independent, it is said that "the jujube fruits exist in the bowl."

Likewise, here too, the attainment of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*); thus, there is the mention of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. Because an entity (*bhāva*) is not independent, even though there is no difference [in essence], the negation of its existence is like the case of an arrow remaining [in flight].

It is not that "another object" (*artha-antara*) is being stated, but rather that "another object" is being negated; it is not merely the means of valid cognition and so forth that are being mentioned.

Just as the "stationing" of an arrow is not merely the arrow itself, but rather a distinct entity possessing motion; [it is] not so [in this case]. This is not correct, because it is established that there is no distinct entity [between the self and the qualities], and because the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of reality (*tattva*).
Thus, reality, when known, becomes the object of action, and the supreme good, when being attained, is realized.
"It arises from karma. But what, then, is reality (*tattva*), or what is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)?
Reality is the state of things being the cause for the arising of cognitions corresponding to their actual mode of existence;
that is, whatever object exists in a certain way, it becomes the cause for the arising of a cognition of that very nature. This is that [reality].

Reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is twofold, distinguished by the seen and the unseen. Among these, the seen supreme good arises from the knowledge of the reality of the categories (*padārtha*), beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For there is no category whatsoever that, when known, does not become a cause for the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference. And having established this, all categories—
They are introduced as objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). However, supreme beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*) arises from the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) concerning the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

The visible [result] comes from the thorough knowledge of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, whereas the invisible [result] comes from the thorough knowledge of the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), such as the self and so forth.
There is no means of valid cognition; it is not that there is none, because the object exists as it is—it is simply this object that exists in such a state.

012.17 When the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is attained through the knowledge of the reality of the objects of cognition (*prameya*), such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth; for when this [person]—012.18 having determined the objects of cognition, beginning with the self, through error—does not transcend cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). We shall establish this point in the second aphorism. Furthermore, if...
Supreme bliss results from the knowledge of the true nature of categories such as the means of valid cognition; those seeking liberation would not strive for liberation [if this were not so].

For it is not the case that anyone lacks knowledge of the true nature of anything whatsoever. Therefore, the self and so forth must be known as the objects of valid cognition by one desiring liberation. Furthermore, because they are taught separately, if the objects of valid cognition were merely the means of valid cognition and so forth [and nothing else], [the separate teaching of the self would be redundant].

And from the thorough knowledge of that [soul], the supreme good would arise. It would not be the case that the object of cognition, such as the soul and so forth, is presented separately [from the categories].

Furthermore, since the object of cognition is already established by the first aphorism within the subsequent system of aphorisms intended for the determination of the objects of cognition, the author of the aphorisms would be unskilled if he were to do so again. And this...

The commentary states that it is restated by the subsequent sūtra. Because of the distinction between that which is to be abandoned (*heya*), the abandonment (*hāna*), the means (*upāya*), and that which is to be attained (*adhigantavya*), there are four subject-matter points (*artha-pada*).
Having correctly understood these, one attains the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). That which is to be abandoned is suffering;
its causes are ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). Abandonment is the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*); the means to that [abandonment] is...

The treatise [states]: "Liberation is to be attained. These four categories of objects are described by all teachers in all branches of inner knowledge (*adhyātma-vidyā*). If it is argued that doubt and the others are not mentioned separately because they do not exist as distinct objects of cognition (*prameya*), we say no; for [they are mentioned] in order to indicate the different systems of knowledge (*vidyā-prasthāna-bheda*). Doubt and the others...

[Objection: Since they are included within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), they should not be mentioned separately. [Response: No, because it is for the purpose of making known the different systems of knowledge (*vidyā-prasthāna*). These four sciences exist, and they have distinct systems:

the *trayī* (the three Vedas) has as its system the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth; *vārttā* (economics) has as its system the plow, the cart, and so forth; and *svāmya-* [has as its system...]
The science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) follows upon the division of subjects; the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*) follows upon the division of doubt and so forth.

If this [science of inquiry] were merely the knowledge of the self (*ātmavidyāmātra*) without having doubt and so forth as its starting point, what would follow? Because it would be merely the knowledge of the inner self, it would be included within the Triple Veda (*trayī*), just like the Upaniṣadic knowledge.
Thus, the fourfold nature ceases; therefore, they are apprehended separately.

In that regard, doubt (*saṃśaya*) is first of all a cognition (*pratyaya*) characterized by the non-determination of the true nature of an object. And [the claim] that "it is a cognition" while being "characterized by non-determination" is contradictory. It is not a contradiction, because its own nature is determined; for its nature is this: [non-determination].

013.21 It is determined [only] that "I have a state of doubt-knowledge"; however, the actual nature of the object is not delimited by this. 014.01 Thus, it is both non-determinative in nature and a cognition; how then can it be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of reasoning (*nyāya*)? Because reasoning does not proceed with respect to what is unperceived or what is not yet ascertained. [Only] when perceived...
And to say "it is unascertained" is contradictory. If it has been apprehended, it is not unascertained; if it is unascertained, it has not been apprehended.

To say "it has been apprehended and yet is unascertained" is contradictory. It is not contradictory, because it has been apprehended in a general way but remains unascertained in its specific details. Even so, it is just as [previously] apprehended.
Likewise, "not determined" implies that the contradiction has not ceased; it is not a case of non-cessation in the sense of "as it is.
Because of this designation, if [the object] were determined in every respect, then the statement "it is perceived as it was determined" would be redundant.
Therefore, it is perceived in its general form but not determined in its specific details. And this is...

Doubt, being of such a nature, is already included within the object of knowledge (*prameya*); nevertheless, it is mentioned separately for this specific purpose. Now, as for the purpose (*prayojana*): what indeed is the purpose? That by which one is impelled to act is the purpose;
this is a worldly matter. By what is one impelled? Some say: by virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation (*dharma-artha-kāma-mokṣa*).

We, however, observe that [the conscious being] is impelled by the attainment and avoidance of pleasure and pain. Since all objects serve as the means for achieving pleasure and pain, they impel the conscious being; this, then, is the "purpose" (prayojana).
As for the "basis" (āśraya) of the Nyāya system: what is the meaning of "basis"? It does not mean a physical support (ādhāra); rather, it means the state of being a benefactor (upakārakatva).

The basis [of the treatise] is its purpose, because the method of investigation is rooted in it; for when there is a purpose, an investigation is undertaken. Thus, the purpose impels the investigation. What, then, is this investigation? And what is this *nyāya* (reasoning)? Investigation is the examination of an object by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). What is being stated? That which consists of the totality—

The realization of an object through the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is *nyāya*. It is not each individual means of valid cognition that is called *nyāya* by virtue of being the cause for the determination of an object; rather, it is all of them taken together. We shall explain that this is the supreme *nyāya* because it brings about the understanding of a person who is in error. [This applies to] perception...

Inference based on scripture (*āgama-āśritam anumānam*) is that which relies upon both perception and scripture; if it is not in contradiction with perception and scripture, then the object apprehended through inference is further corroborated by perception and scripture, whereby the cognition becomes even more distinct. However, in cases where these means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are not mutually corroborated, [the result is otherwise].

These [fallacious arguments] are employed; this subversion of logic (*nyāya-viplava*) is described as a discourse resembling the true path (*tīrtha-pratirūpaka*), propounded by those desiring gain, honor, and fame. Furthermore, that inference which contradicts perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*) is called a semblance of logic (*nyāyābhāsa*).
First, an example contradicting perception is: "Fire is not hot, because it is produced, like a pot."

What, then, is the contradiction of this inference? It is its application to a domain that is not the object of inference. This is not an application within the domain of inference; for that domain to which this [inference] is applied is sublated by perception. Others, however, [assert]: "Sound is non-audible."

They describe this as a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*); however, by them, neither the object of direct perception nor the object of inference has been understood. What is the reason? Because the functions of the sense organs (*indriya-vṛtti*) are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
Furthermore, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is a function of the sense organ; how could that be directly perceived? [To claim it is] pure is contradicted by scripture (*āgama-viruddha*).
[The opponent argues: "A human head-bowl [is pure] because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell or mother-of-pearl. How is this not contradicted by scripture?
By one who asserts that "the human head-bowl is pure," the meaning of "purity" must be stated. What is being said? Regarding "pure":
if it means the absence of transgression for the toucher, then it must be stated for whom [this absence occurs]. If it is for the self (ātman),...
015.14 One should say this because it stands as being intent upon the practice of the meaning of that scripture; thus it is so.
015.15 Now, if one should say "of those who know the Threefold Veda," then it must be stated that there is a contradiction because of their acceptance of the Threefold Veda.
015.16 What is the meaning of "the skull of a human head is pure"? This is a specific injunction; it is a specific [rule].

For a restrictive rule (*vidhāna*) has as its scope the exclusion of the remainder; thus, if it is said that "the human skull is pure," one must state what is impure. Alternatively, if it is argued that "everything is indeed pure," there is no corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because everything has been included within the subject (*pakṣīkṛtatvāt*). Furthermore, if it is [claimed to be] contradicted by inference (*anumānaviruddha*), why does it not constitute a valid inference?

015.20 There is no contradiction, because it is impossible for two inferences to coexist in a single [subject]. For two inferences—endowed with positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—do not coexist regarding a single object; therefore, it is not contradicted by inference. 016.01 But then, would it not also follow that there is no contradiction by perception? It is not the case that there is no such contradiction; for [perception] does contradict that which is endowed with positive and negative concomitance.

Because it is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Now, why is it not contradicted by analogy (*upamāna*)? It is not contradicted by analogy because [analogy] follows upon the contradiction with a prior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Analogy is a cognition of similarity that depends upon the recollection of impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by scripture (*āgama*), which itself follows upon a prior means of valid cognition.

Thus we shall explain. It was stated that [the treatise] exists because of the contradiction between perception and scripture. Regarding that, the *bhāṣya* states: "The *vāda* (debate) and *jalpa* (disputation) possess a purpose. From what does this arise? By means of this purpose, all living beings, all actions, and all branches of knowledge are pervaded. In that regard:

It is appropriate to investigate what the purpose of *vāda* (formal debate) and *jalpa* (wrangling) is; thus he says that both *vāda* and *jalpa* possess a purpose. Regarding that, [it is said] "in that case, there is the semblance of reasoning" (*nyāyābhāsa*). Now, *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is examined as to whether it possesses a purpose or lacks a purpose. First, some describe it as being without a purpose.

Because it consists merely of refutation. And that is not so; it is not merely refutation that constitutes *vaitaṇḍikā*, but rather one who, having accepted a position (*pakṣa*), does not establish it is called a *vaitaṇḍika*. Now, if he were not even to undertake a position, he would be like a madman and should be disregarded. Or, [if you say it is] the making known of the refutation of the opponent's position...

"Regarding the purpose (*prayojana*): this is exactly like that. If one does not establish even this fourfold set (*catur-varga*), then that fourfold set is his position (*pakṣa*) as stated in the Bhāṣya. But if one does not establish it, then, as before, it is to be disregarded. And a statement that lacks the establishment of a counter-position (*pratipakṣa-sthāpana*) is called *vitaṇḍā*. Of that..."

If one understands the meaning, that constitutes his position; if one does not understand it, the fault is as stated previously. Thus, the purpose has been explained. An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is an object within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). What is meant by this?
It is the cause for the non-obstruction of the views of both worldly people and investigators. And in this way, there is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

016.20 Thus, when the example is being described as the cause for the non-obstruction of perception, [the property] is pervaded by the self (*ātman*) and so forth. 016.21 And when [the example] is the object of perception and so forth, the self and so forth are excluded. Consequently, the rule for the illustrative instance (*udāharaṇa-sūtra*) would be contradicted. This very example, because it is an object of apprehension, is an object of valid cognition (*prameya*). 016.22–23. [The opponent argues: "In that case, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is not established that the subject (*pakṣa*) possesses the property of being an object of apprehension. [Reply: No, for the subject is indeed established as possessing the property of being an object of apprehension. Why? Because it is an object of inference (*anumāna*). For the subject is the locus (*dharmin*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). And since it is accepted that the locus of the property to be proven is the object of inference, it follows that the subject is an object of apprehension. Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive. Furthermore, the reason is not contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). Nor is it unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is established in the subject. Thus, the reason is valid. 016.24–25. Alternatively, this is stated as a proof by means of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*): If the self and so forth were not objects of apprehension, then they would not be objects of inference either; and if they were not objects of inference, then the subject would not exist. But since the subject does exist, the self and so forth must be objects of apprehension. Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive. 016.26. Or rather, let us state the reason in another way: "Because it is an object of cognition (*vijñeya*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of cognition. 016.27. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of knowledge. 016.28. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of awareness (*buddhiviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of awareness. 016.29. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of conceptualization (*vikalpaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of conceptualization. 016.30. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of verbal designation (*abhidhānaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of verbal designation. 016.31. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of linguistic convention (*vyavahāraviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of linguistic convention. 016.32. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of worldly discourse (*lokaprasiddhatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of worldly discourse. 016.33. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of common experience (*prasiddhatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of common experience. 016.34. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the world (*lokaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the world. 016.35. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the people (*janaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the people. 016.36. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the multitude (*pṛthagjanaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the multitude. 016.37. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the masses (*mahājanaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the masses. 016.38. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the community (*saṃghaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the community. 016.39. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the assembly (*parṣadviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the assembly. 016.40. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the congregation (*gaṇaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the congregation. 016.41. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the group (*vargaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the group. 016.42. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the host (*gaṇaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the host. 016.43. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the crowd (*samūhaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the crowd. 016.44. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the multitude (*nikāyaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the multitude. 016.45. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the assembly (*parṣadviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the assembly. 016.46. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the gathering (*samāgaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the gathering. 016.47. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the congregation (*samavāyaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the congregation. 016.48. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the collection (*saṃghātavīṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the collection. 016.49. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it is an object of the aggregate (*saṃcayaviṣayatva*). In this case, there is no fault regarding the subject. Why? Because it is accepted that the subject is an object of the aggregate. 016.50. Or again, let us state it thus: "Because it
The separate teaching [of inference] is because it is rooted in that [perception]; for when that exists, inference and scripture may exist, but when it does not, they would not.

Thus, one infers an object previously perceived by direct perception, and one explains to another an object previously known. Furthermore, there is a contradiction for the nihilist (nāstika), whether he accepts [the existence of such objects] or does not accept them.

Thus it is said in the Bhāṣya: "A tenet (siddhānta) is a formal determination of what is accepted. Acceptance means "this is such-and-such" or "it is thus. "This" refers to it in a general sense, while "such-and-such" refers to it in a specific sense.

Its formal determination is "this [is accepted] among the Sāṃkhyas" and "this [is accepted] among the Yogas. In that case, there would be no such thing as a "tenet common to all systems" (sarvatantrasiddhānta).

The established tenet (*siddhānta*) is [defined] as "due to non-establishment," for this [tenet] does not remain fixed anywhere. And that which is accepted by all— namely, that such is the established order— is mentioned separately because it is included within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*),
since debates (*vāda*) and the like proceed based on the distinctions among established tenets.

017.10 Now, the members (*avayava*) are parts of a sentence. But what, then, is a sentence? It is the cognition of the final word, which depends upon the recollection of the preceding words and, through the assistance of that recollection, being reconnected, serves as the cause for the comprehension of the specific meaning; this is the sentence.
Its portions are the parts. How many are there? As many as are required for the completion of the proof.

017.13 Thus [it is asked]: what, then, is this "accomplishment" (siddhi) of a category-meaning (padārtha)? It is suchness (tathatā); it is the completion [of the meaning]. 017.14 The specific cognitions—such as the proposition (pratijñā) and so forth—are designated by those words of technical designation; this is the traditional authority (āgama) in that regard.

017.15 However, it is not logical to call them a "proposition" (pratijñā), because the traditional authority functions to exclude what is not the reality, whereas the object of the proposition does not do so.

Because that which is understood through scripture is what is to be established, and because scripture is what is to be established, there is no fault in saying that "scripture is the proposition" (*pratijñā*). Whatever meaning has been understood through scripture, one explains that very same thing to another; thus, scripture is called the "proposition. Likewise, because the term "reason" (*hetu*) is applied metaphorically to the mere perception of a mark (*liṅga*), inference (*anumāna*) is called the "reason."

However, the second observation of the mark (liṅga) is called the "reason" (hetu) because it serves as the cause for manifesting the recollection of the relationship [between the mark and the probandum]. It is the "example" (udāharaṇa) because it presents again through perception that which was previously experienced as the object of recollection; for one remembers the object, and having remembered it, one takes that remembered object as the example. Thus, by means of the previous experience—
That which conforms to what is well-known is "like perception," as if it were perception itself. What, then, is the meaning of the term *upamāna* (analogy) here?
It is non-disagreement; just as one does not disagree regarding perception, so too regarding the example.
Because the word *upamāna* is applied metaphorically to a part of the analogy—namely, the phrase "as... so"—the application (*upanaya*) is called *upamāna*.
Indeed, analogy (*upamāna*) consists in the instruction "as is [the model], so is [the object]" when it is employed for the purpose of teaching; it is preceded by perception, scripture, and memory.
In this context, the cognition of similarity (*sārūpya-jñāna*) is called "analogy," and they apply the term "analogy" metaphorically to that single part of it.

The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the demonstration of the capacity [of the reason] when all [the members of the syllogism] converge upon a single object. But what, then, [is the definition of the conclusion]?

Co-inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) and the superimposition upon a single sentence (*ekavākyādhyāropa*): what, then, is their capacity (*sāmarthya*)? It is the state of depending on the meaning mutually communicated. And we shall explain this later. By means of this, it is concluded that the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the other members are connected with a single purpose. This, then, is the supreme method (*paramo nyāya*).

018.10 What, then, is the ultimate [purpose]? It is the capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to individually establish a person who is in error. 018.11 When they function individually, they do not establish a person who is in error once they have attained the state of a sentence (*vākya*).
018.12 Furthermore, they establish one who is in error; therefore, this is the ultimate. But are the members (*avayava*) of the syllogism another means of valid cognition, or...
"They are included within those. What follows from this? If there were another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), an exhaustive enumeration would be improper;

or else, [if they are not distinct], the separate mention of the members (*avayava*) would be purposeless. We say that it is not a separate means of valid cognition. These [members], when combined and dependent upon the sentence (*vākya*), serve for those who are in disagreement...

They are mentioned separately because they serve to establish the person [who argues]. These very members, existing separately, become the causes for the engagement in discussion (*vāda*), debate (*jalpa*), and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*), and they become the basis for the determination of reality (*tattva*). What is the meaning of "basis"? It is the state of establishing specific distinctions. Reasoning (*tarka*) is not...

That which is subsumed under a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not another means of valid cognition, because it does not perform the function of determination; a means of valid cognition is that which determines.
It is not reasoning (*tarka*); therefore, for this very reason, it is neither a means of valid cognition nor another means of valid cognition.

However, due to the distinction between the objects of the means of valid cognition, it is an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition—that which pertains to the objects of the means of valid cognition.

He analyzes that [point]: what, then, is the analysis? It is the investigation of what is appropriate and what is inappropriate—namely, "this is appropriate" and "this is inappropriate. Whatever therein is appropriate, he grants permission for it, but he does not definitively determine it. Because of this lack of definitive determination, it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). An example of this is found in the Bhāṣya regarding action (*karman*).
"Birth has its cause. But how is birth caused by karma? Because it possesses differentiation.
What, then, is this differentiation? It is good rebirth and bad rebirth. Within good rebirth, there is the god and the human;
within humanity, there is the male and the other [female]; within masculinity, there is the Brahmin and the other [non-Brahmin]; and within being a Brahmin, there is one with sharp faculties.
Regarding "one of dull faculties" [is spoken] in contrast to having sharp faculties; regarding "of high birth" [is spoken] in contrast to low birth;
regarding "complete" [is spoken] in contrast to incomplete; regarding "the learned" [is spoken] in contrast to the fool; regarding "the wise" [is spoken] in contrast to the unwise;

regarding "one who finds consolation" [is spoken] in contrast to one who is terrified; regarding "consolation" [is spoken] in contrast to fear; and regarding "one who has mastery" [is spoken] in contrast to one who is dependent on others.

"Thus, even in the miserable destinies, there is the distinction between animals and hell-beings; and even within the state of being a hell-being, there is the distinction between the iron cauldron and the *kuṭa-śālmalī* tree.

Among animals, there is the distinction between a cow and others. This variety, which exists as manifold and established, would not be possible without a cause that is impermanent, composed of multiple substances, and restricted to each individual. For what reason?"

Since earth and the other elements are common to all persons, and because there is no cause for the restriction [of qualities] residing in earth and the others, it would follow that everything consists of the nature of everything. Yet, a distinction in restriction is observed; therefore, karma is the regulator. This reasoning, being thus established, is within the scope of perception.

The object of cognition (*prameya*), the final determination (*nirṇaya*), and the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) are the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But when is this final determination the fruit of the means of valid cognition?

It is when it is not employed as the cause for the delimitation of another entity; at that time it is the fruit. When one delimits [an object] by means of it, then it is established as the means of valid cognition.

The relationship between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) will be explained hereafter. Furthermore, it is stated in this sūtra that "the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*) is like the validity of a scale (*tulā-prāmāṇya*)," because a single entity, through the convergence of two characteristics, is denoted by two words. Having understood that these two—reasoning (*tarka*) and ascertainment (*nirṇaya*)—sustain the course of worldly life (*loka-yātrā*).

Having understood [the truth], the world, proceeding by means of reasoning and definitive conclusion, abandons what is to be discarded and adopts what is to be accepted. Furthermore, when this [result] is included within the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), it is then the object of knowledge;
when one determines [an object] by means of it, it is then the instrument of knowledge. Thus is the discussion among various proponents.

Thus, because it conforms to the various differences in philosophical tenets (*siddhānta-bheda*), it has multiple speakers; this is what is meant by "proving with respect to each topic" (*pratyadhikaraṇa-sādhana*).
It concludes with the determination of one or the other topic. Regarding the phrase "with respect to each topic" (*pratyadhikaraṇam*):
what is stated by saying that its proof is "with respect to each topic"? It means that the proof is provided by both [parties].

"It must be stated": the determination occurs in one of the two positions; and this we shall explain. What is the nature of this *vāda* (debate)? It is a collection of sentences. Now, it is heard [in the definition] that it consists of "the establishment by means of proof (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), and the refutation [of the opponent]" (*sādhanopālambha*). And the proofs consist of cognitions, such as those arising from the sense organs and their objects...

By such a method as "knowledge produced from sense-contact" (*sannikarṣa-utpanna-jñāna*) and so forth, it has been stated that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consist of knowledge. Furthermore, reasoning (*tarka*) is deliberation (*ūha*), and since that deliberation consists of knowledge itself, it is incorrect to say that a collection of sentences is debate (*vāda*).
This is not so, because the definition of debate—as "the employment of means of valid cognition and reasoning for proof and refutation"—is explained otherwise.
And we shall explain that sūtra as follows: "The two specific types [of vāda] are jalpa and vitaṇḍā.

What, then, is the distinction? It is the addition of members and the omission of members. Jalpa is superior because it employs *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna*; however, *vitaṇḍā* lacks the establishment of a counter-position to this extent.
