Thus, inference is described as being [based] on perception; yet, through a succession of steps, it is ultimately established as being nothing other than perception itself.

In this way, its status as "having that as its antecedent" (*tatpūrvakatva*) has been stated. Furthermore, when it is said that "those two are prior to it," meaning those two perceptions are prior to the perception [in question], then this perception is called "having that as its antecedent. And those two...

There are two types of perception: the first is the perception of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*); the second is the perception of the mark itself.
For one who desires to know, following the manifestation of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) after the second perception of the mark, there arises a memory;
and immediately after that memory, there occurs once again the perception of the mark, such as "this is smoke. This is the final [perception].
Inference is of the nature of reflective deliberation (*parāmarśa*), supported by the two preceding perceptions and by memory.

What, then, is the meaning of "inference" (*anumāna*)? It has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), in the sense that "by means of this, something is inferred. What, then, is its fruit? It is the cognition whose object is fire. But how can an instrument whose object is one thing [produce] another [result]?
One performs an action upon an object; for instance, [the action] of threshing takes rice and the like as its object, while the instrument is the pestle and the like.

In the case of *śyāmāka* grain, there is the act of striking. It is not because of a lack of restriction that it is said: "The action has the same object as the instrument"; for there is no such rule. Indeed, it is observed that in the case of cutting trees and the like, the action [occurs] upon the parts [of the object].

Regarding "action" (*kriyā*): in the case of "the tree is being cut," the action resides in the part [of the tree]. Furthermore, in some instances, the action has the same object as the instrument (*karaṇa*); for example, "the rice grains are being cooked"—the cooking occurs in those very [grains]. Again, in some cases, the self itself becomes the agent, the instrument, and the action; for example, "the tree stands."

A tree stands by itself. What is meant by "by itself"? It is because it does not employ any other instrument for its own maintenance. Thus, there is an action belonging to one object by means of an instrument belonging to another object. However, in some cases, the action belongs to the same object as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when that very same thing [is both].

"It is cognized. But what is cognized of it, since it has already been cognized? It is "cognized" [in the sense that] it is understood as something to be abandoned (*heya*), something to be accepted (*upādeya*), or something to be regarded with indifference (*upekṣaṇīya*). That is not so, because one does not admit a difference in the object between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*). Furthermore, when that [result] is preceded by this [means], it is called "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvaka*).

Thus, because the distinction [between the two types of inference] was not intended to be expressed at that time, immediately after the observation of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), the consideration of the mark (liṅga-parāmarśa) is distinguished by the observation of the mark and the recollection of the relationship, since it is preceded by those. What, then, is inferred by them? It is the "remaining object" (śeṣārtha). Regarding this term "inference" (anumāna), what [is its meaning]?

The instrument (*kāraka*) is either the action (*bhāva*) or the means (*karaṇa*). When it is the action, then the cognitions of "abandoning" and so forth are the result. When it is the means, then the determination of the remaining object is the result. There is a doubt as to whether [the cause] is the recollection of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), or the perception of the mark itself. Some, for their part, describe [it as] the mark and the bearer of the mark...

047.12: "Inference is the recollection of the relationship [between the sign and the signified]," being assisted by other factors such as the observation of the relationship between the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*).

047.13: Others, however, maintain that "inference is the consideration of the sign" (*liṅga-parāmarśa*). We, for our part, 047.14: see that all inference is [the means of] inferential cognition (*anumiti*), because [the former] is inseparable from the latter; [this distinction is made] according to what is primary or secondary.
The principle is that there must be a consideration of the logical mark (*liṅga-parāmarśa*) when one intends to express those [remaining objects]. But what is the principle here?

It is the understanding of immediate succession; because it is immediately after the consideration of the logical mark that the understanding of the remaining objects occurs, therefore the consideration of the logical mark is the principle. Why is memory not the primary factor? Because it is immediately after memory [that the consideration of the mark occurs].
[This is] due to non-apprehension. For it does not occur that one would say, "Where I saw smoke, there I saw fire.
Immediately following this recollection, it is logical to say that there is the apprehension of the remaining object (the probandum) in the form, "Therefore, there is fire.
Therefore, the consideration of the mark (liṅgaparāmarśa), when assisted by recollection, becomes the means for establishing the intended object.
And thus, the application (upanaya) possesses purposefulness if this consideration of the mark (liṅgaparāmarśa), supported by memory, constitutes inference.

This being the case, the application is meaningful; and in this way, it is stated that the application is a constituent part of the syllogism. Therefore, this is established: inference is preceded by that [perception].

048.03 Thus: if inference is preceded by perception, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it applies to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and to ascertainment (*nirṇaya*). 048.04 [Objection: Since the impression called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), which is the cause of memory, and ascertainment are both preceded by perception, it follows that they must be inference; this is not a fault, because the subject under discussion is cognition (*vijñāna*). [And] sense-object...

Since the section concerning cognition begins with the statement "cognition produced by contact," there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). However, regarding ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), it is both in two ways: sometimes it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and sometimes it is the result (*phala*).
It is the result because it delimits its own object; it is the means of valid cognition because it delimits the remaining [objects].

It is of three kinds: the positive (anvayin), the negative (vyatirekin), and the positive-negative (anvayavyatirekin). Among these, the positive-negative [reason] is that which occurs in the intended subject and its similar class, but does not occur in the dissimilar class; for example: "Sound is impermanent, because, while possessing generality and particularity, it is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves, like a jar."
Thus: [A reason] that possesses positive concomitance (*anvayin*) is one that, while occurring in the intended class of similar instances (*tajjātīya*), is devoid of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

For example, for those who maintain that all things are impermanent, the argument "sound is impermanent because it is produced" has no dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, [a reason] that possesses negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*) is one that, while pervading the intended [similar instances], is absent from the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and [present] in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
048.15 Non-occurrence [of the probans]: for example, "this living body is not soulless, because that would entail the consequence of its being devoid of breath and so forth.
048.16 Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, it is of three kinds, as previously stated: *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.

048.17 That which possesses pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to the previously established probandum (*sādhya*) is *pūrvavat*. The "remainder" (*śeṣa*) consists of that which belongs to the same class as the probandum.

That which possesses [the probandum] is "that which has a remainder" (*śeṣavat*). That which is named "that which has what precedes it" (*pūrvavat*) is that which pervades the probandum; thus, "that which has a remainder" is similar [to this]. It exists, and it is unobserved in general. By the word "and," it is also [understood to be] not contradicted by perception or scripture;
such is inference with four characteristics or five characteristics. Alternatively, it is of three kinds: "that which has what precedes it" (*pūrvavat*), etc.

[The types of inference are] *śeṣavat* and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. Among these, that which is called *pūrvavat* is where the effect is inferred from the cause; such is the *Bhāṣya*. But what is meant by this statement, "the effect is inferred from the cause"? If the meaning is that the existence of the effect [is known] from the perception of the cause—

That "he undertakes [the effect]" is not the case; for no one, having grasped the cause while remaining in a healthy state of mind, undertakes the effect. Thus, it becomes contradictory. Furthermore, if it is again inferred that "where there is a cause, there is an effect," this too is not the case.

Because the effect and the cause occupy different locations: the threads [reside] in their own parts, the filaments, while the cloth [resides] in the threads. Thus, one who asserts that "the effect is inferred from the perception of the cause" breaks the seal of inference.
What, then, is this seal of inference? It is not a principle [to be applied] to what is unperceived or what is not yet determined.

[The opponent says: "It proceeds. [The author replies: If an inference regarding an unperceived object were to proceed from the observation of a cause, then it would follow that the *nyāya* (logical method) proceeds; and thus there would be a contradiction. [The opponent says: "No, because we do not accept that. [The author asks: Who says that one understands the existence of an effect from the observation of a cause?

049.11 Who says that the effect exists where there is a cause? Rather, the meaning of the sūtra is that the effect—which has been employed as a qualification of the cause and is thus subordinate—is inferred. Thus, there is no contradiction with the [analogy of] the seal and its impression. This should be understood in the same way regarding the *śeṣavat* inference and others; here too, the cause...

"It is the effect that is inferred as being a constituent part [of the cause]. But how, then, is the effect denoted by the word *śeṣa*? Since both [cause and effect] have been presented as having the nature of inference, the effect is "the remainder" (*anupayukta*) because it has not yet been employed [as the means of proof]; thus, the effect is what is expressed by the word *śeṣa*. An example is: "There will be rain, because of the rising of the clouds."

"Rain" is an inference of the effect from the cause. How, then, is its formal application (*prayoga*)? These clouds possess rain, because they are deep-sounding, possess many cranes, possess recent flashes of lightning, and are towering—just like a cloud that has rained. [Likewise for] rivers...

The example of the "remainder" (*śeṣavat*) is [the inference of] fullness. But how does this swelling of a river, occurring on the river itself, lead to the inference of a region that has rained upstream? It is not the case that there is an inference of a region that has rained upstream based on the river's swelling, because they have different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Rather, it is the river itself that possesses a connection with a region that has rained upstream.

050.01 It is inferred by means of the characteristics of a river: "The river current is connected to a region where it has rained upstream, because, while being rapid, it carries full fruits, logs, and so forth, and because it is full, like a river that has received full rain. This is stated without intending to specify the time [of the rain], whether it will be or has been. As for that which...

A certain time [of practice] is to be adopted. That which is called "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is that where the subject (*dharmin*) is understood as being qualified by a qualifier that is neither effect nor cause, but is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*); that is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. For example, the inference of water from a crane (*balākā*). But how, indeed, is there an inference of water from a crane?

The inference of water from a crane is as follows: having included within the scope of the inference that region where the presence of the crane is well-established by its non-deviating concomitance (*ajahat-vṛtti-tva*), one establishes the object—such as a tree or other feature—as the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of its being possessed of a crane. Others, however, maintain that the inference of the sun’s motion is an example of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

[The opponent says: "Thus [it is]. We do not understand that. How is it inferred? If, first of all, the sun possesses motion (gatimān), then by what is its motion inferred? For there is no mark (liṅga) related to the sun's motion; nor can an unrelated object be inferred."

"Everything would have to be inferred from everything. Now, if it is argued that reaching another location (*deśāntaraprāpti*) is the inferential mark (*liṅga*), that is not so, because it is unperceived (*adṛṣṭatvāt*). For no one perceives the sun’s reaching of another location; for "another location" must be either a place such as space (*ākāśa*) or a region of the directions (*diś*). And both of these are imperceptible (*apratyakṣa*). Nor is there any other [mode of] motion.

It exists. Therefore, the observation of its arrival at another location is untenable; for everywhere one perceives only the orb of the sun, and it is not logical to infer [motion] from the mere perception of an object.
Moreover, in some manner, the movement of the sun could be perceived through observation.

Because it has attained its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the attainment of another location (*deśāntaraprāpti*) is not eternal, because it is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). For conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which functions as both perceptible and imperceptible, is never itself perceived [as such]. Now, the inference of the motion of the sun based on the observation of Devadatta’s attainment of another location is an inference from general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
050.22 You think that this applies not only to the sun; for you yourself also [infer] the movement of all objects.

051.01 Why, then, is it not inferred in this way: "it goes"? This inference of the sun's movement is certainly not direct (sākṣāt). 051.02 What then? Having inferred its arrival at another location, one infers the movement by means of that; thus there is no fault.
The sun possesses movement to other locations because, while being a substance, it is not an object of the notions of waning and waxing,
and while being perceived by one facing east, it becomes an object of those same notions for one who has not moved his feet but has turned toward a location connected to that [sun],
just like a gem or similar objects; for all these qualities exist in the case of a gem or the like.

The sun possesses the attainment of another location; therefore, because it possesses the attainment of another location, its motion is inferred by means of this inferred attainment of another location. Alternatively, the inference regarding the possession of the attainment of another location is as follows: the sun possesses the attainment of another location, because for one whose vision is stationary, there is no obstruction [of its appearance].
051.09–10: Furthermore, because that which has been seen cannot be the object of seeing again, it is like Devadatta;

thus some first state an inference regarding the perceptibility of the directions: "The direction is perceptible because it can be designated by a finger, like the moon. But that is not so, because it lacks form (*arūpin*); how could a direction, being formless, be external?

051.12 How, then, can there be a designation by means of a finger when [the object] is directly perceived? 051.13 Because of the designation of direction in relation to trees and the like connected with directions and places. Those trees and so forth which are connected with directions and places, they metaphorically designate as "direction. 051.14 This word "east" arises from perception together with the sun; it is a connection with the sun.
It exists in a distinguished direction and location. Together with that initial perception of the sun, one perceives trees and other objects;

these are metaphorically designated as "eastern," and having so designated them, one points them out with a finger. Alternatively, it is threefold—thus he states the well-known existence and non-ambiguity of the mark (*liṅga*), [the phrase] "well-known" (*prasiddham*) being the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*).
"Existing" (*sat*) means it exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*); "without doubt" (*asandigdham*) means it is invariably concomitant with the similar class (*sajātīyāvinābhāvin*).

Alternatively, the phrase "of three kinds" (*trividham*) is for the sake of restriction; it shows the restriction that the variously divided types of inference are subsumed under the three types beginning with *pūrvavat*. How is it divided into many kinds?

The positive-concomitant (anvayin) is of two kinds: that which exists only among similar instances (sajātīya), and that which exists both among similar and dissimilar instances. The negative-concomitant (vyatirekin) is likewise of two kinds.

Thus, the negative-concomitant is of a single form because of the absence of similar instances (sapakṣa). This inference, divided into five types, becomes fifteenfold through the distinction of time; furthermore, it follows the distinctions of persons.

052.02 Its internal subdivisions, however, are infinite. This very variety of inference is thus subsumed by the statement "it is of three kinds. Therefore, the mention of "three kinds" is for the purpose of restriction.
When it was said "pūrvavat" (based on what precedes), what then is meant here by "pūrvavat"? Is it the cause, or rather...

If it is argued that "it is called 'prior' because its cause exists prior to it," then the effect would necessarily be "prior" [to its cause], which results in a contradiction, since one infers the effect from the cause. When we say "it is prior because its cause exists prior to it," we do not mean the effect itself; rather, we mean that the object of cognition is prior to the cognition.

"This is 'pūrvavat' (as before)," by which it is meant that there is an inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*). In the same way, for "śeṣavat" and the others as well, it is stated that these are cognitions whose objects are such [as previously perceived]. Alternatively, this suffix *-vat* in "pūrvavat" functions as follows:
just as an object was previously seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too does one comprehend that very same object through inference.
052.11 Thus it is seen as before. Others, however, describe it otherwise: "Just as one apprehends fire by means of that very smoke. But what is it that is apprehended by this smoke?
Is it fire, or the location, or existence, or the location possessing fire? In that regard, it is certainly not fire.

It is established [that fire is not the probandum] because the relationship between property and property-possessor (dharma-dharmin) is untenable. Fire is not a property of smoke, nor is smoke a property of fire, because fire is already perceived. Furthermore, since fire is already perceived, it cannot be an object of inference. By this, existence (sattā) and place (deśa) are also explained;
for both the existence of fire and the place are already perceived. If it is argued that "the place possesses fire" [is the object of inference], [it is not so].

052.17 It is not [the case that smoke is the probans] because smoke does not have that as its property (*ataddharmatvāt*). Now, it might be argued: "A location possessing fire is inferred by means of smoke.

052.18 But that is not so. Why? Because it does not have that as its property (*ataddharmatvāt*); for smoke is not a property of the location possessing fire. Nor is the connection of fire with the mere location perceived [in the form]: "This [location] possesses fire. 052.19 [Therefore, smoke is not the probans.]

If [it is argued that] it is so, [we reply: no, because that [particularity] is not perceived. It is a particular place (*deśa-viśeṣa*) that is inferred as being possessed of fire, not the mere place (*deśa-mātra*), because that [mere place] is not perceived. For this person does not perceive the particular place;
he merely utters an empty expression, saying, "This place possesses fire," and he does not perceive the mere smoke either.
053.01 He perceives either the indicator of fire or merely smoke; therefore, a specific location is not to be inferred.

053.02 If it is argued that [fire] is indicated by way of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), then this might be the case: there is an invariable concomitance between fire and smoke, and thus one understands fire from the perception of smoke. That is not so, because the alternative options (*vikalpa*) are untenable.

053.04 What is the meaning of "the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between fire and smoke"? Is it the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), or is it inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*)? Or let it be merely that connection; first, suppose it were the relation of cause and effect.
That is not so, because they do not reside in one another. For smoke does not reside in fire, nor does fire reside in smoke.

Because they reside in their own causes, there is no relation of cause and effect [between them], nor is there inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*), since nothing other than those two is produced. Indeed, a substance is not produced from things of different classes.
Furthermore, it has been stated that those two do not reside elsewhere because they reside in their own causes; thus, there is merely a connection (*sambandhamātra*).

Regarding the statement "it exists therein," that too cannot be inferred. How so? First, if one were to say, "There is a connection between fire and smoke," that is not correct, because it is unperceived.
Since smoke is observed even in the absence of fire, there is no inference of a [necessary] connection; rather, there is merely a concomitance (sāhacarya), like that between color and touch.
It will not be so; because both [premises] are fallacious. Smoke has been seen without fire, and fire has been seen without smoke;

thus, both are fallacious. Therefore, there is no necessary concomitance (*sāhacarya*). This has already been refuted by the statement that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. And since there is no other way [to establish the relationship], it follows that it is not [the case].

Fire is inferred from smoke. If it is argued that this contradicts common worldly experience (*loka-virodha*), [we reply: if there were indeed an inference of fire from smoke, would that not contradict the world? No, there is no contradiction, because it is a specific kind of smoke that establishes a specific kind of fire. But how is this fire [known]?

Smoke becomes a qualifier when it is subordinate [to another term]. For example, in the inference "this smoke possesses fire," it is inferred by means of smoke as a unique (asādhāraṇa) qualifier. For in that case, both are perceived:
the smoke itself and the properties inherent in it, such as its continuous nature, its compactness, and its upward movement.

053.22 And these properties of smoke, which function as smoke, cause one to infer a property of smoke that is not yet established. For every object to be inferred, there must be a property belonging to the subject (*dharmin*) that is already established, such as—054.01 for example—the existence of sound itself is established, and its property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is also established, whereas the property characterized by impermanence (*anityatva-lakṣaṇa*) is not yet established. 054.02–03. Just as, for example, the property of being produced is a property of smoke. This is the

054.03 Thus, this [object] is inferred by means of its specific qualification; this is called *seṣavat*, which is *pariśeṣa* (residual inference). 054.04 The commentary states: "The word 'action' (*karman*) is not [the cause], because it is the cause of another word"; thus, through the exclusion of both [alternatives], it is not an uncommon [reason].
054.05 For the property of being the cause of another word exists in action (*karman*), but not in non-action (*akarman*). It is not [uncommon] because of having another meaning; for the word—
The meaning of "being an internal cause" (*antar-hetu-tva*) is that it initiates something of its own kind; thus, there is no fault.

Regarding the definition in the *Bhāṣya*: "That which is called 'inference from generality' (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is where the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is imperceptible.
Does this mean that the relationship between the mark and the possessor of the mark is imperceptible at the very time it is being inferred?
[Objection: Is it never perceived? If it is not perceived at the time it is inferred, then all inference would be of this nature;

thus, the qualification [“not perceived”] is redundant. Alternatively, if it is never perceived, how then does inference operate here? Furthermore, it contradicts [your own principle] that “inference does not proceed regarding what is unperceived or undetermined.”

054.12 Because that which serves as a qualifier is never an object of inference when it is imperceptible; rather, that which establishes the cognition of a subject (dharmin) through the observation of another property is "inference based on general correlation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa), as in the case of the self (ātman) [inferred] from desire and so forth. 054.13–14 Indeed, desire and so forth are properties of the subject, and the self is its qualifier, existing as a subordinate factor (guṇabhūta).

Thus, the quality-status (*guṇatva*) of desire and the rest is an established property (*dharma*). By means of that property, one infers desire and the rest as being specifically qualified by the qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇa-viśiṣṭa*).
Desire and the rest are dependent on another (*paratantra*), because they are qualities, like color (*rūpa*); this is the realization of their dependence derived from this inference.
But how is their independence from the self established? Their independence from the self is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).

054.18 Because they are self-cognizable and because they are not perceptible by external instruments, [the qualities] in earth and the others—054.19 the qualities of earth and so forth—are perceptible to oneself and to others, and are perceptible by external instruments; whereas the self is [perceptible] without being perceptible by external instruments, as are desire and the like. Therefore, [these qualities] do not exist in earth and the others, up to and including space.

054.21–054.22: Because their qualities, like those [qualities], are supersensible (*atīndriya*) in the case of space, time, and the mind; nor does another substance remain—[it is] the self (*ātman*) that remains. Therefore, it is dependent upon that [self]. And the commentary states: "Perception has an existent object (*sat-viṣaya*), while inference has both existent and non-existent objects (*asat-viṣaya*). Now, with reference to what is this distinction made? Is it with reference to the substratum (*dharmin*)?
Or [is it] "the property" (dharma)? If you mean the substratum (dharmin), then inference is never devoid of an existent object;

for it has been stated that inference does not proceed with respect to an object whose universal (sāmānya) has not been perceived. Furthermore, there is no perception of a universal belonging to a non-existent thing. If, on the other hand, you speak with reference to the property (dharma), then properties also...

They are of three kinds: those being affirmed, those being negated, and those that are independent. Among these, the property being affirmed is "possessing odor" in the case of earth; the property being negated is "possessing odor" in the case of what is not earth; and the independent one is "inherence in inherent causes. But how, then, is it independent?
Inherence does not [require] another inherence, because there is no further inherence. For whatever exists in something does so by means of a mode of existence (*vṛtti*);

however, there is no other inherence that serves as the mode of existence for inherence. If there were another inherence for inherence, then in postulating yet another inherence for that too, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, there were a definitive limit (*vyavasthā*), [then inherence would exist without requiring another inherence].

055.11 Is this established in the very first [category]? Should one who has faith accept that inherence (*samavāya*) is non-dependent (*anāśrita*), or is there indeed a logical justification (*nyāya*) for it? There is no doubt; there is indeed a logical justification, because it is the object of the term "occurrence" (*vṛtti*) among the five categories (*padārtha*). Like an atom (*paramāṇu*), inherence is non-dependent.

The logical argument is as follows: [Inherence] must be pervasive, because it is the cause for the cognition of "here," just like the self (*ātman*). Furthermore, if inherence were dependent [on a substrate], what would follow? The effect would be without a substratum.
How so? First, the effect acquires its own nature, and only afterwards does it exist through inherence in the causes.
If it is said that [inherence] "subsists," then prior to its subsistence, it would follow that it is unattached. Furthermore, it is said that inherence "subsists" between cause and effect;
thus, its mode of subsistence (vṛtti) must be stated, for nothing that is currently subsisting is ever observed to be without a basis of subsistence.
If it is argued that it "subsists" because it is a form of reaching (prāpti), like conjunction (saṃyoga), we say no, because that would involve a contradiction: conjunction is indeed reaching.

"It functions"—is this a property of attainment (*prāpti-dharma*) or a property of the effect (*kārya-dharma*)? We, for our part, say it is a property of the effect, not a property of attainment. Likewise, other effects also possess attainment; for if this functioning were a property of attainment, there would also be an attainment of attainment.

If there were an interval [between them], there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā-doṣa*), because the existence of the operation of "attainment" (*prāpti*) [would require another attainment]. Nor can anyone establish this infinite regress, due to the lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, one who asserts that inherence (*samavāya*) exists without another inherence contradicts the treatise; its reality has already been explained by the discussion on "existence" (*bhāva*).

056.04 Thus, there is no proof that a relation persists when the related entities have ceased to exist. 056.05 It is not the case that [the relation] does not exist because the causes of its manifestation have ceased; rather, it is the causes of its manifestation for him that cease.
056.06 Nor is it inherence (*samavāya*), because it is uncreated (*akṛtaka*); and since inherence is uncreated, it would follow that it is like the substratum of an effect.

[The cause] is inferred by its very nature. If this [cause] were produced (*kṛtaka*), then because it would arise together with the effect from its material cause (*upādāna*), the effect would be without a support (*anāśrita*).
Or, if it exists prior to the effect, then it must be stated for what [it is a cause]. Or, if it exists later, the fault of the effect being without a substratum (*anādhāra*) remains as it was.

Therefore, it is established that inherence is independent. In this regard, the inference which has for its object a property being negated has a non-existent object; it does not, however, have for its object an independently existent property that is being affirmed.
If it is argued that "non-existent" (*asat*) means "it comes into being" (*bhavati jāyate*), [we reply: no, for that which is being born...
Because the object is not admitted [as existing], it is said that "it exists" [only as a conceptual construct]. Thus, for now, this is established.

This is inference preceded by that [perception]. Others, however, say: "Inference for one who knows that [object] is the perception of an object that is inseparable [from another]. The meaning of this is: when a certain object does not exist without another object...
It is "invariably concomitant" (*nāntarīyaka*); and since it is both invariably concomitant and an object (*artha*), it is called an "invariably concomitant object" (*nāntarīyakārtha*).

The perception of that [object] by one who knows it constitutes inference—namely, for one who knows, "This is invariably concomitant with that. In this context, the inclusion of the term "object" (*artha*) is superfluous; for there is no such thing as an "invariably concomitant" that is not also an "object"—hence, [it is simply called] *nāntarīyaka*.

The term *artha* (meaning/purpose) is a compound word. In that regard, if it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), then [the meaning is]: the "meaning" (*artha*) of the "inseparable" (*nāntarīyaka*)—that is, producedness (*kṛtakatva*)—is its property (*dharma*) or its purpose (*prayojana*).
If it is a property, then the "meaning" of producedness is the inference of existence (*sattva*), knowability (*meyatva*), nameability (*abhidheyatva*), and so forth.

[The compound] is obtained. Now, the purpose [of the compound] is that which serves as the cause for the realization of impermanence; thus, it is obtained as a *bahuvrīhi*. In the case of the phrase "that for which there is an object that is inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*)," the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is what is inseparable; that [property] is the reason (*hetu*). This property of being produced belongs either to the jar and so forth, or to the sound's impermanence, if [the impermanence] belongs to the jar and so forth.

057.03 The reason [would then] become a jar or the like; [the argument would be]: "Sound is impermanent because of a jar. Alternatively, if sound itself were the reason for sound: "Sound is impermanent because of sound. Furthermore, if "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) were the property serving as the means of proof for impermanence, then it would follow that "sound is impermanent because of impermanence"—which is the meaning of impermanence [itself].
"Being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). In every respect, being produced is the reason for impermanence. Now, regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*):

even if it is [defined] as "that which is necessarily concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) and is an object (*artha*)," the compound is still incapable [of expressing the intended meaning], because there is no restriction between the qualifier and the qualified. When both terms deviate from one another, they are coreferential.

It is like the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*); because the word "blue" (*nīla*) has multiple referents and the word "lotus" (*utpala*) likewise has multiple referents, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, in this case [of the definition], there is no such necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyaka*).
Thus some say that there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since the term "referent" (*artha*) would be meaningful only if it were distinguished from "non-referent" (*anartha*).
057.12 Even when there is deviation regarding only one term, co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed, as in "earth is a substance" (057.13).
Here too, there is deviation regarding both terms due to the distinction between the primary and the subordinate: by the word "substance," "substance-ness" is expressed;
and by the word "earth," when the intention is to express the primary and the subordinate, "substance" is expressed. (057.14)

"Earth" and "earthness"—because both terms are subject to deviation [from one another], it is rightly said that "earth is a substance. However, this further statement—that "the perception of an invariably concomitant object" [is the definition]—is not correct. Why? Because the purpose of the application [of words] is the communication of meaning; for they maintain that the employment of words is intended for the communication of meaning.

Some say that the meaning "invariably concomitant" (nāntarīyaka) is understood [from the word *artha*]; therefore, the word *artha* is not appropriate [in this context]. Furthermore, the phrase "by those who know it" (*tad-vidaḥ*) is also not appropriate, because it is not the case that for anyone else there is an invariably concomitant [relationship]. For indeed, among the inhabitants of Nārikela Island, upon seeing smoke, there is no cognition that it is "invariably concomitant. Therefore, [the term] refers to "those who know it."

Even this should not be said. By this, the statement that "the reason (hetu) is the demonstration of a property (dharma) that is invariably concomitant (avinābhāvin) with such [a probandum]" is refuted. What is the meaning of the extension (atideśa)? Just as it is improper to mention the object (artha) when the object is already implied by the fact of its inseparable connection (nāntarīyaka), so too is it improper to mention the property (dharma). An example, however, is: "smoke [is] of fire. And this...

"It does not exist" has been described in many ways. However, others think that inference consists in the presence [of the mark] in the object of inference and in what is similar to it, and its non-existence where it is absent; since this definition would also include those [marks] that reside in only one part of the object of inference, it is not a valid definition—for example, "atoms are impermanent because they possess odor."

[Objection: There is no such over-extension [of the definition], because it is stated that [the reason] must exist in the object of inference (*anumeya*) like a jar. [Reply: It is not the case that there is no over-extension, because [the reason] subsists in only a part [of the subject], since it is a property of that [subject], just like [a reason] that subsists in only a part of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Just as that which subsists in only a part of the counter-example does not [necessarily] exist in the entire counter-example, so too that which subsists in only a part of the subject (*pakṣa*) does not [necessarily] exist in the entire subject; this is what is being excluded.
Effort must be made [to resolve this]. It need not be done because of the restriction [implied by the word "eva"]. Regarding the presence [of the reason] in the inferable (anumeya):

if there are two restrictions, is it that the presence is only in the inferable, or is it that the presence is only in the inferable? Furthermore, what is excluded by the first restriction—is impossibility excluded, or is possibility excluded?

It is made known in both ways; however, there is no purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), even without that comprehension. Even without the restriction, this meaning is understood: [the reason's] existence or non-existence in the object of inference (*anumeya*). Furthermore, since "subsisting in only a part" (*ekadeśavṛtti*) has already been refuted, the restriction is redundant; moreover, it would contradict the subsequent term. Now, the reply:
Restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is understood; its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the meaning. Nevertheless, the object of inference is restricted by means of that pervasion.

Since the property (*dharma*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the restriction applies elsewhere than that. And by means of the pervasion of possibility (*sambhava-vyāpti*), the object of inference is determined. Possibility extends through both pervasion and over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*); it consists of two groups.
058.17 When the two [alternatives] are being taught, that which is similar to it and its opposite are [implied]; therein, by the phrase "non-existence when it is absent," the opposite is [excluded].
058.18 [Objection: Let the existence [of the probans] in that which is similar to it be established; for what purpose is this begun? For nothing unobtained is obtained by this. 058.19 [Response:
Nothing is obtained [by this], but in that which is similar to it, mere possibility (sambhavamātra) is intended to be expressed. It is mere possibility.

And [the definition] is obtained through non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*), and indeterminate occurrence (*aniyata-sambhava*). Now, "existence in that which is similar to it" (*tattulye sadbhāvaḥ*)—this too is undertaken for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). What, then, is restricted here?

Is it "only in that which is similar to it," or "in that which is similar to it, there is existence only"? If it were "only in that which is similar to it," [there would be the fault of non-pervasion].

When the existence [of the reason] is ascertained, then both the preceding and following terms are sublated; for it is not the case that one says, "Feed Devadatta and likewise Yajñadatta. Here too, the existence [of the reason] is to be inferred in exactly those similar cases.
And the phrase "and" is like the speech of a madman. Now, if existence exists only in those similar cases, then it would reside only in a portion of those similar cases.

059.04 That which is a non-reason (*ahetu*) is that which, being of the same class [as a reason], subsists in only one part [of the subject], such as "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*). By that, he [the opponent] has reached the conclusion that it is a reason.
059.05 Thus, without having properly considered the statement "non-existence [occurs] when there is no [existence]," he has declared that what is non-existent is simply its own nature.
059.06 That is not so; for there can be no substratum (*ādhāra*) for a non-existent thing from which its negation could arise. This too is a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*).

059.07 This is undertaken for the sake of meaning: what is being determined—is it non-existence itself, or [existence] in the case of that which is non-existent? If, first of all, it is "non-existence itself in the case of the non-existent," then it is redundant, because that is understood even without it being stated; for even without it being stated, this is understood: "in the non-existent, there is no [existence]. But if, on the other hand, it is "only in the non-existent is there non-existence of the cow, because of its having horns"—this is...

059.10 It follows, then, that there is a cause. For it is not the case that [the cause] does not exist simply because it is non-existent; rather, it is not the case that it is absolutely non-existent.
Furthermore, although a set of seven [possibilities] is possible through the exclusion of two terms, after stating the negation of six, the cause is said to possess three characteristics.
This too is because the two terms associated with the positive concomitance (*anvayin*) function as the cause. Of that which is associated with two terms...

And because a single [reason] possessing negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*) is the probans, it is incorrect [to say that both are required]. For one who does not accept the position of permanence, the two properties—being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and being necessarily concomitant with effort (*prayatnanāntarīyakatva*)—become probanses even when joined by only two terms, since there is an absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Even though they are negative concomitants, because a similar instance (*tad-tulya*) is impossible, they constitute a probans joined by two terms. For example, this is not...
The living body would be soulless, because it would follow that it lacks breath; therefore, because it is not all-pervasive, this is not a defining characteristic.
By this [argument], the definition—"inference is the establishment of the remainder from one perceived connection"—is refuted. How so? For inference does not arise from a single perception.

Furthermore, as for the claim that [inference arises] from a single perception of a relation (*sambandha*), this too is not the case; for at the time one infers, one does not perceive that relation. If it is argued that it was perceived previously, then it would follow that there could be inference even for one who has not perceived the logical mark (*liṅga*), and there is no other possibility. Moreover, by means of form (*rūpa*)...

059.22 In the inference from touch, there is a contradiction of one's own view; for this person does not perceive a relation between color and touch. 060.01 Now, if it is argued that the relation is "inherence in a single object," that too is untenable because it contradicts one's own doctrine.
060.02 For color and touch do not both subsist in a single object such that "wherever there is color, there is touch. This also...
If it is argued that neither form nor touch exists anywhere in the relation of support and supported (*ādhāra-ādheya*), [we reply:

even if there were such a relation of support and supported, it would not be the case that "form is in touch" or "touch is in form. By this, the sevenfold relation is refuted; for [the relations of] cause and effect and so forth do not [apply here].

Since it is logical that among the relations between color and touch, one relation [serves as] the basis for inferring touch by means of color, it is therefore certain that inference is not a definition, because it is non-pervasive (avyāpaka). //060.07// Inference is thus determined [to be invalid].
060.08 Now, analogy (*upamāna*). Analogy is the means of establishing that which is to be established (*sādhya*) through well-known similarity (*prasiddha-sādharmya*).
060.09 [1-1-6] "Analogy is the means of establishing that which is to be established through well-known similarity.
060.10 The meaning of the sūtra is as before. Regarding the phrase "through well-known similarity": it refers to that whose similarity is well-known.

Or, that which possesses similarity with what is well-known is "that which has similarity with the well-known," namely the gavaya; therefore, the meaning of comparison (*upamāna*) is the comprehension of the relationship between a name and its referent, expressed as "the means of proving the probandum. What has been stated? Comparison is the cognition of similarity that depends upon the recollection of impressions deposited by authoritative testimony (*āgama*). When—

For when it has been heard by him that "as is a cow, so is a gavaya," and the similarity between the cow and the gavaya is well known, then for one who again perceives the similarity with the cow, there arises the cognition of the connection with the designation: "This is a gavaya. Thus, analogy is not distinct from perception and verbal testimony. How so? When—

When one perceives both that cow and the gavaya through direct perception, one then understands through perception that "this [gavaya] is similar to that [cow]. Furthermore, when one hears that "the gavaya is just like the cow," even while merely hearing this, a cognition arises for him that certain properties of the cow are observed to be present in the gavaya.
Some [hold that] it is a distinct [means of knowledge], for otherwise there would not even be such expressions as "in this way" or "in that way.

Furthermore, one perceives the similarity of the *gavaya* to the cow in this manner; therefore, it is not [merely] comparison (*upamāna*), as it differs from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*). One perceives the similarity of the *gavaya* to the cow.

"Or [it is] existence"? Oh, how well-versed in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) the Venerable One is! For the meaning of the Sūtra is this: through the cognition of the similarity between a cow and a gavaya, one comes to understand the relationship between a name and the named object.
Therefore, whatever is said without having fully understood the meaning of the Sūtra is merely arbitrary.
061.04 Now, as for verbal testimony: verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*).
061.05 [1-1-6] Verbal testimony (*śabda*) is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*).
061.06 The meaning of the aphorism is that it is not mere sound. A reliable person (*āpta*) is indeed one who has directly perceived (*sākṣāt-kṛta*) the Dharma.

061.07 Direct perception of an object is "attainment" (*āpti*); one who possesses this is a reliable person (*āpta*). This applies to such things as heaven, the unseen force (*apūrva*), and the deities (*devatā*).

[Objection: Instruction is not possible because [the object] is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*). If "attainment" (*āpti*) means the direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of an object, then since no one perceives heaven, the unseen merit (*apūrva*), deities, and so forth, there would be no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) to communicate them.

[Response: Therefore, it is not correct to say that "instruction is by one who has attained [the truth]" (*āptopadeśa*), because there is no instruction by one who has [directly perceived] the [unseen]. This is not a fault.

061.11 We do not say that heaven and so forth are perceptible to people like us; rather, we say that they are taught by one for whom they are perceptible. 061.12 But what is the reasoning here [that] heaven and so forth are perceptible to someone?
061.13 We reply: because they possess both general and specific characteristics and because they are dependent [on something], they are perceptible to someone.

061.14 Thus: that which is dependent is perceptible to someone, because it exists for the sake of another (parārthatvāt). That which exists for the sake of another is also perceptible to someone, because it is a real entity (vastutvāt) and because it is an object of scripture (āgamaviṣayatvāt). Whatever is a real entity and whatever is spoken of becomes perceptible to someone, just like a jar and so forth. Because of impermanence (anityatvāt), to whom [is it perceptible]? 061.15–16. To someone. To whom? To the person who possesses the cognition of that [object]. Why? Because it is established by means of inference (anumānataḥ). For example, when one says, "There is fire here," it is established by means of inference that there is smoke. Therefore, since the subject under discussion (pakṣadharmatvāt) is established by means of inference, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is an object of scripture, it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a self," it is established by means of scripture that there is an agent of action. Therefore, since it is an object of scripture, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is a real entity, it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "The self exists," it is established by means of inference that there is an agent of action. Therefore, since it is a real entity, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is dependent, it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is dependent on its cause. Therefore, since it is dependent, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is an effect, it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is an effect of its causes. Therefore, since it is an effect, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is a composite (samghātatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is a composite of atoms. Therefore, since it is a composite, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is a whole (avayavitvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is a whole possessing parts. Therefore, since it is a whole, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is a substance (dravyatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is a substance. Therefore, since it is a substance, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is a quality (guṇatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is color," it is established by means of inference that it is a quality of a substance. Therefore, since it is a quality, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is an action (karmatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is going," it is established by means of inference that it is an action of a substance. Therefore, since it is an action, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is a universal (sāmānyatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is existence," it is established by means of inference that it is a universal of substances, qualities, and actions. Therefore, since it is a universal, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is a particularity (viśeṣatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "This is an earth atom," it is established by means of inference that it is a particularity of eternal substances. Therefore, since it is a particularity, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is inherence (samavāyatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is inherence," it is established by means of inference that it is the relation between a whole and its parts, a quality and its substrate, and so forth. Therefore, since it is inherence, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is an absence (abhāvatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is the absence of a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is the negation of a jar. Therefore, since it is an absence, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is an object of knowledge (jñeyatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is an object of knowledge. Therefore, since it is an object of knowledge, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is an object of speech (abhidheyatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is an object of speech. Therefore, since it is an object of speech, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it is an object of mind (cittaviṣayatvāt), it is not non-existent. For example, when one says, "There is a jar," it is established by means of inference that it is an object of the mind. Therefore, since it is an object of the mind, it is not non-existent. [The opponent claims: "Consciousness is directly perceived. [We reply: The impermanence of the *apūrva* (unseen force) is not unestablished; it is not so, because death would otherwise be impossible.

If merit and demerit were eternal, through whose exhaustion would there be death? Furthermore, if they are impermanent, then upon their exhaustion through the experience of the results while they are ripening, that which is ripening—
Because there is no other latent disposition of karma (*karmāśaya*), there is a falling away from the previous body and an attainment of the subsequent body by the mind;
thus, birth and death exist. Therefore, [the self] is not eternal. Or, if it were eternal, a new [entity] would have to be postulated.
Its commonality or its uniqueness must be stated. If it were common...
There would be prosperity common to all living beings, or else there would be no other regulator; thus, there is the loss of ritual action (*kriyā-lopa*).

If [the Veda] is eternal, then because of the difference in its manifesters (*vyañjaka-bheda*), neither of these two faults occurs—namely, that prosperity is common [to all] or that there is a loss of ritual action. Why? Because of the manifesters.
Because it is manifested through differentiation, the result belongs to that which manifests the eternal *apūrva*; thus, the action is for the purpose of manifestation.

Therefore, there is no lapse of the action. It is observed that whatever is manifested by someone, the fruit of that belongs to that very person; it is not otherwise observed, for it is not the case that Yajñadatta [receives the fruit] of a jar manifested by Devadatta.

He does not see it. What is the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of that which is eternal or previously non-existent? Is it perception (*upalabdhi*), or rather the capacity for the production of a result (*phala-pradhāna-sāmarthya*), or the removal of an obstruction (*āvaraṇa-apagama*)? If it were perception, that does not exist; for this [eternal entity] never perceives anything previously unperceived, because it is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). Now, if it were the capacity for the production of a result...

062.10 [The question is: Is "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) manifestation, or is it the capacity predominant in the fruit? Is it the *apūrva* itself, or is it a property (*dharma*) of the *apūrva*? 062.11 If it is the *apūrva*, nothing has been produced. If it is a property of the *apūrva*, what is the proof for the claim that there is some other *apūrva* distinct from that [property]? 062.12 We, however, observe that whatever [entity] from which the fruit arises, that is the *apūrva*. Now, as for the [view regarding] the obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), etc.—

One must state what its obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is—whether it be disappearance or manifestation—for objects that transcend the senses (*atīndriya*), the possibility or impossibility of obscuration cannot be considered. By this, the permanence [of sound] for each individual person is refuted.
This should be understood. How so? Because in that case too, there would be the fault of the cessation of activity on the part of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
And [the argument] that there is a lack of capacity is [invalid], for the activity of one who is eternal for the sake of improvement is illogical because of its indivisibility.
If it is argued that "there is differentiation because it conforms to the differences among the manifestors," no; for such differentiation is not observed in the case of a single [entity].
Furthermore, it might be thought: even a single *apūrva* appears as if differentiated by conforming to the differences among the manifestors, and [this appearance occurs] due to those differences.
062.19 That there are increase and decrease [of the manifestation]—this also does not exist, because it is not observed in a single [entity].

062.20 For no single thing is ever seen to conform to the differences in its manifestors, such that this could be the case. But is it not observed that the face appears different due to the difference in the sword and so forth, since it conforms to them? We reply: it is not so observed.

Furthermore, if that [object] is not seen, we say that it is a false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*). It is as if distinct, yet it is not actually distinct, because it is impossible for anything to possess multiple forms. Indeed, a single thing cannot possibly possess multiple forms.
Therefore, one must either abandon the unity of the unprecedented [entity], or its status as the cause of increase and decrease.

[Is it] manifold for each person, or eternal? Now, if this position is adopted—that for each person the *apūrva* is either manifold or eternal—the contradiction remains unremoved; the fault of the impossibility of death and the consequence of the abolition of action do not cease. [If you argue that] manifestation, however, bestows the fruit—
Does it give its fruit at the time of manifestation, or at a time subsequent to the completion of the action?

If it gives its fruit at the time of manifestation, that is not observed; for the attainment of heaven does not occur immediately after the performance of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). If, on the other hand, it occurs at a later time, then the action would no longer exist at the time of its manifestation.
And if it is granted that [the cause] gives while being assisted by that [assistance], this is merely a wonder; for nothing new has been manifested.

Thus, everything would be a giver of fruit at all times. Furthermore, even if you were to maintain the eternality of action out of a desire to protect your own position, even so, the contradiction regarding action remains unresolved.

"Such as the loss [of the original] and so forth"— thus, in whatever way the eternality of that which is unprecedented is asserted, it cannot withstand logical scrutiny. Regarding "the instruction of a reliable person" (āptopadeśa),
is it the non-deceptiveness of the reliable persons that is being established, or rather the fact that the object is exactly as it is?

If it is argued that the non-deceptiveness of authoritative persons (*āpta*) is established through inference, or that the existence of an object in such a state is established through perception— since when one perceives an object through direct perception, one then establishes the object's existence in that state— that is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra.

This is not the meaning of the Sūtra: that "verbal testimony" (śabda) is the instruction of a reliable person (āpta). Rather, the meaning of scripture (āgama) is that cognition which occurs with the mention of words regarding objects, whether they are in contact with the sense faculties or not. Therefore, this conceptual construction (vikalpa) is irrelevant.
063.21 [1-1-8] It is of two kinds, because it is either perceived or unperceived.

063.22 "It is of two kinds" is for the purpose of restriction; for scripture (āgama), though divided into many ways, is restricted to being the object of only perception and inference. Or else, its twofold nature is according to the difference of the speaker—perceived or...

Because it is spoken by one who has not perceived the object [by other means]. An object perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is an "object perceived" (*dṛṣṭārtha*); an object perceived through inference (*anumāna*) is an "unperceived object" (*adṛṣṭārtha*). This definition is common to sages (*ṛṣi*), Aryans, and barbarians (*mleccha*), because we observe that all of them conduct their worldly affairs by means of scripture (*āgama*). Thus, these are the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By means of these, the linguistic conventions of gods, humans, and animals are established. Thus ends the *Pramāṇavārttika*.
064.07 Now, the object of cognition (prameya).
064.08 [1-1-9] The objects of valid cognition (prameya), however, are the self, the body, the sense organs, the objects, intellect, the mind, activity, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation.

064.10. "But what kind of object is to be cognized by this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?"—this is the commentary [of the opponent]. This question is untenable, because the object of the means of valid cognition is understood through their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). Indeed, these means of valid cognition have not been discussed here as being devoid of objects, such that this question—"What kind of object is to be cognized by this means of valid cognition?"—could even arise. It is not improper [to ask], however, because it concerns a specific object; for this is not a specific instance of the cognizable (*prameya*), but rather concerns the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) in relation to the cognizable in general.

Because it has been awakened by way of a general indication (*uddeśa*). However, its purpose must be the ascertainment of the specific objects of knowledge (*prameya-viśeṣa-avadhāraṇa*). What is that object of knowledge?
It is that which, when thoroughly understood as it truly is, leads to liberation (*apavarga*), but which, when not thoroughly understood, is this very self (*ātman*).
For the sake of illuminating this meaning, there is the aphorism beginning with "the self" (*ātma-ādi-sūtra*). And this indeed is the meaning of the aphorism; in this regard also—

And when the members have the same referent, a *dvandva* compound is formed according to the rule for analysis (*vigraha*). If there is the possibility of restricting both [members], it is a fault to restrict only one. What, then, is being restricted? Is it that "the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists only of the self (*ātman*) and so forth," or is it that "the object of knowledge is the self and so forth"?

If it were the case that the object of knowledge consists only of the self and so forth, this would be stated too narrowly, as it would exclude the directions (*diś*), universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).

Because it is not mentioned in the Sūtra, [the definition] is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Furthermore, if the object of cognition (*prameya*) itself—such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth—is likewise [defined], there is a contradiction, for it would be both the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*), like the validity of a scale (*tulā-prāmāṇya*). In that case, because it is the means of establishing the determination of substances such as gold, and because it is itself that which is to be determined, it is expressible by the terms "means of cognition" and "object of cognition."

065.02 Furthermore, there is a contradiction with common worldly usage because a single thing is expressed by multiple terms for its factors [of action], as in "the tree stands. Just as in that case, 065.03 a single entity called a "tree" is expressed by various words for its factors due to the convergence of their respective causes; 065.04 so too [is the expression] "the object of cognition" (*prameya*) and "the means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*). This is not due to a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra.

The meaning of this sūtra is that the self and so forth alone, when correctly determined as the object of knowledge (*prameya*), lead to liberation; it is not intended to exclude other objects of knowledge. There is no fault in stating that the object of knowledge is precisely the self and so forth. What is being said is that one who seeks liberation must understand that the object of knowledge is indeed the self and so forth.
065.08 Neither is its status as an object of knowledge (prameyatva) being enjoined, nor is the status of other things as objects of knowledge being negated;

rather, 065.09 it is restated that this very thing must be understood by one seeking liberation (mumukṣu). Therefore, both [the affirmation and the exclusion] are determined. And thus, there is no fault as previously stated. 065.10 Even granting [your point], we say that even the directions and so forth are obtained right here by the force of logical reasoning (upapatti-sāmarthya); why? Because...

Furthermore, rebirth is the manifestation [of existence] through twenty varieties; even though these constitute its formative factors (*saṃskāra*), categories such as direction and so forth are not [included].

Generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) are also [to be understood]; and the self (*ātman*) and so forth are taught as being objects of cognition (*vijñeya*) by way of the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*). And among those, generality and particularity exist through their state of mutual exclusion (*itaretara-vyavaccheda*).

"In the Sūtra, inherence (samavāya) has been made a qualifier; however, this Sūtra is not for the purpose of defining the objects of cognition (prameya), nor is it for the purpose of defining specific objects of cognition, but rather for the purpose of defining the mere object of cognition (prameya-mātra). If [the Sūtra] were intended for the former, the author of the Sūtra would be unskilled in his formulation, as he would be prescribing what was already established by the first Sūtra regarding the object of cognition."

Because it is prescribed again after having already been prescribed, this would be like the speech of a madman; and desiring to make this meaning known, why did the author of the Sūtras use the word "tu" (but)? [He says: "There is another object of knowledge (*prameya*), from the knowledge of whose true nature comes the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
By the word "tu," he makes known that this is indeed an object of knowledge. But why is pleasure (*sukha*) not mentioned here?

It has not been stated [whether it is] due to non-existence or due to perception by another. First, it is not due to non-existence, because it is to be personally experienced (*pratyātma-vedanīyatvāt*).

When pleasure is being perceived precisely as something to be personally experienced, it is impossible to say that it does not exist. Nor is there perception by another; for this very reason, there is no mention [of it], which serves to indicate dispassion (*vairāgya*).
066.02 How is it that this person, while being liberated, does not contemplate all suffering as suffering?
For one who contemplates suffering, there is the teaching of the "smallness" of pleasure; for one contemplating all as suffering, there arises the perception of lack of delight in the three worlds.
And for one who relies upon that [perception], craving for the objects of the three worlds is severed. Craving—

Furthermore, for one who contemplates that "this desire for rebirth is all suffering," such desire does not arise; for no one indeed seeks suffering. Because craving has been abandoned, one does not grasp at those means that bring about rebirth.
Due to that non-grasping, future merit and demerit do not come into being, nor do those which have already arisen [persist].
Those two also go to destruction through enjoyment. This very [process] is the cutting off of the seed of saṃsāra, characterized by merit and demerit;
for the purpose of demonstrating this meaning—that one is liberated and is not born again—there is no mention of "pleasure.
Thus it is said.

066.11 This sūtra is for the purpose of distinguishing the self from things of similar and dissimilar classes. [1-1-10] Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (liṅga) of the self.

Whether for the purpose of correlating scripture with inference, or because the self has been established by scripture, [one seeks] its correlation through inference; or else, for the purpose of illustrating the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-saṃplava*), we have stated that "the means of valid cognition converge. This is the scope of that [convergence], regarding the nature of which— 066.14–066.16: For the sake of connecting scripture with inference, or because the self has been understood through scripture, [one seeks] its connection through inference;

or for the sake of providing an example of the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-saṃplava*), that which we have stated as "the means of valid cognition converge"—this is its object, concerning the class of things to which it applies.

"Because of the contact with the object," so says the Bhāṣya. In that regard, the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of desire and the other [mental states] is the proof for the existence of the self (*ātman*). Here, this is investigated: how does desire and the rest, which are not themselves perceived, indicate the self? [They do so] because they share a single object with memory; for it is by means of memory that desire and the others [are connected].

They possess a single object; therefore, they establish that they have a single agent. For there is no synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of those [cognitions] that have different agents, different objects, and different causes.
Indeed, the cognitions of color, taste, smell, and touch are not synthesized; for it does not occur that...
"It is not that one thinks, 'The form which I saw is this very touch,' nor does one think, 'The touch which I felt, that is the form I see now.
Nor is it observed that what was seen by Devadatta is identified by Yajñadatta; for it does not occur that Yajñadatta thinks, 'I saw that which Devadatta saw. What is the reason?"

Because distinct cognitions have specific objects, those who maintain the doctrine of selflessness (nairātmyavādin) cannot hold that these specific objects—which consist of mutual exclusions—undergo synthesis; therefore, that which performs the synthesis is the self (ātman). [Objection: Synthesis occurs due to the causal relationship between cause and effect.

If you should further think: "Recognition does not occur because of having a single agent; rather, it occurs because of the relationship of cause and effect, whereby each subsequent cognition arises from each preceding specific cognition, following the potentiality (*śakti*) of the prior cognition, and thus arises endowed with the entire collection of deposited potencies (*śakti-kalāpa*). Therefore, [recognition occurs] even though cognitions are distinct."

067.12 Connection [of rebirth] occurs due to the relationship of cause and effect, as in the case of a seed and so forth. For example, immediately after a grain of rice (śāli-guṭikā), a sprout appears; its conformity to the potentiality of the rice is established by virtue of being preceded by that [grain]. Immediately thereafter, being assisted by the primary elements (mahābhūta), it produces a subsequent rice seed, and not—

Just as a barley seed [is not the cause] because it is not preceded by that [barley], so too here, although there is a causal relationship among the cognitions belonging to a single continuum, the reconnection [of consciousness] is not due to being preceded by that, for it does not occur from the cognitions of another continuum;
rather, this reconnection is not due to having a single agent, since such is not observed. This, then, is the reconnection.
067.18 Otherwise, one would be unable to establish the existence of the self, because diversity is not sublated.
067.19 By asserting that the reconnection [of births] occurs through the relation of cause and effect, does one not sublate diversity?
067.20 What is the reason? Because the relation of cause and effect is based upon diversity; indeed, the relation of cause and effect [presupposes] diversity.
Furthermore, when there is a diversity of substrates, no recognition is observed even when both parties agree upon that diversity.
Why? Because what is experienced by one cannot be remembered by another, and one who does not remember is unable to recognize.

We do not say that recognition occurs because of a cause-and-effect relationship; rather, we say it is impossible in the absence of such a relationship. It is only when a cause-and-effect relationship exists that recognition is observed.

Moreover, it has been stated that because [the relationship] is not observed in the absence of a causal relation (*akārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*), it is "not preceded by that" (*atad-pūrvakatvāt*). Therefore, this objection is unfounded. This is incorrect, because there is no exclusion of the grounds for dispute (*vivāda-kāraṇa-avyatirekāt*).
By speaking thus, you do not go beyond what I have stated: that [the relationship] is not observed in cases of diversity (*nānātve*).

Thus, you do not say that [the reason] is not a cause for dispute because it is not observed in cases of plurality due to the absence of a causal relationship; for since this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), it does not exceed the grounds for dispute. By your own statement that "it is not observed in cases of plurality," you have likewise discarded the grounds for dispute, as you yourself accept [plurality].
By saying that [the self] is "supreme" and "equal," you have effectively admitted [its existence], for it is not [established] by means of non-existence.
[The opponent says: "Reconnection is established not through the relation of cause and effect, but rather in another way. [The reply is:
"Then the fault of the reason (hetu) being unproven (asiddha-arthatā) is stated. [We say: No, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason.
068.12 You have not specifically understood the nature of the reason; rather, based merely on the generality of the reason, it is otherwise.
068.13 Thus, there is a fault in the reason for one who asserts this. Furthermore, this synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) is qualified by being together with memory (*smṛti*).
068.14 Synthesis consists in the state of having a single object for preceding and succeeding cognitions, and that memory is untenable in your position.

Why? Because one person does not remember what was experienced by another; for indeed, one person does not remember what was experienced by another. Since there is memory, and since memory is possible in this position through the process of recognition (*pratisandhāna*), you [oppose us] by claiming that memory is untenable.
068.18–19. It is not the case that memory is impossible in our position; for how so? Because of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). 068.19–20.

Thus, that continuum of body and mind in which memory or experience arises is itself the rememberer and the experiencer. It is not [the case that memory is impossible] because cognitions are unstable, for [only] what is stable...
