From a specific volition (*cetanā*) that arises simultaneously [with it], a mind distinguished by a prior capacity (*śakti*) is produced; this production of a mind distinguished by capacity is called "latency" (*vāsanā*). Regarding this, it has been said: "Because of instability and because of the lack of connection with that which perfumes (*vāsaka*).
Furthermore, that specific volition which co-exists with the preceding mind does not [reside] in the present mind either.
It does not provide assistance even in the future; how so? First, that which is present is unmodifiable:
just as it arises in a certain state, it perishes in that very same state. Furthermore, it is not connected with the future, nor does it perfume that which is unconnected.
Therefore, memory [does not arise] from the causal relationship between effect and cause.

"Or [it is] untrained regarding the latent impression (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, for you, memory cannot belong to an entity (*bhāva*), because every entity depends upon an agent (*bhavitṛ*). The movement [of memory] belongs to Devadatta as the agent; it does not belong to the object, because even that which is non-existent can occur [as an object]. When one remembers something that exists, then memory would result in being without a substratum (*anādhārā*).
If, on the other hand, it has the agent as its substratum, then this is applicable to our position, but why is it not so for your position? For [in your view], there is no agent.
Because you do not accept that memory has an agent as its object, memory is indeed without a substratum (*anādhārā*).

When this position is held—that memory is without a substratum—there is no inference [of an agent], because an effect is never observed to be without a substratum. Every effect is seen to possess a substratum, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; and memory is an effect.

Therefore, the conventional usage of "the existent" (bhāva) and "the agent of existence" (bhavitṛ) regarding cause and effect is based on a substratum: the moment of the effect is the existent, and the moment of the cause is the agent of existence. And thus, what is the use of postulating another [separate] agent of existence?
Furthermore, that is not so, because of the difference in time; since cause and effect belong to different times, the relationship of support and supported (āśrayāśritabhāva) is untenable.

Why? Because it has been stated that a "becoming" depends upon an agent of becoming. Therefore, in your position, [memory] cannot be the "becoming" in any way whatsoever.

Memory is possible; since there is no recognition without memory, and this recognition does exist, that which is its agent is a distinct, single entity called the self (*ātman*). Alternatively, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): the cognitions of form, taste, and touch belonging to Devadatta are [the effects of] one...

070.18 Just as things are connected because they possess unity, so too here, various objects will be connected because their cause possesses unity; that which is this cause is the self (*ātman*). Alternatively, they describe it otherwise: desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (*liṅga*) of the self. Desire and the others are qualities (*guṇa*).

The principle is that qualities (guṇas) are dependent on something else; therefore, by the method of elimination, their status as a quality [is established], because they are not universals (sāmānya), particulars (viśeṣa), or inherence (samavāya), due to their being non-eternal. Nor are they substance (dravya) or action (karman), because they inhere in a pervasive substance, like sound, and so forth. This constitutes the inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). By this—
071.02 It has been stated that desire and the like possess dependence because they are impermanent and because they are effects, just like form and so forth.

071.03 By virtue of not persisting as long as the substance exists, their status as qualities of the body is negated; and by the negation of that [status], their being qualities of the self [is established].
071.04 Thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the self is proven to exist.
071.05 [1-1-11] The body is the substratum of movement, the sense faculties, and objects.

071.06 Regarding the statement "the body is the substratum of movement, the sense faculties, and objects": what, then, is this "movement"? It is vibration for the purpose of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful; it is that which belongs to one impelled by the desire for that [attainment] upon perceiving the means to happiness.

071.08 It is understood that vibration (*parispanda*) is that [specific] activity (*ceṣṭā*). Likewise, upon perceiving the means to suffering, there is vibration characterized by the performance of the practice of desiring to abandon it. How is the body the substratum (*āśraya*) of the sense-faculties?
Because those sense-faculties which are effects function through their own causes, and because [others] do not so function. As for those sense-faculties which are effects...
071.11 That which does not function as an effect of its own causes does not function [as such]; this applies to the sense organs beginning with the nose and ending with the skin.
071.12 The ear and the mind, however, are not effects; furthermore, the sense organ does not extend from the nose to the mind.
071.13 Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the body is the locus of the sense organs, since they do not function in accordance with the body. 071.14 [Objection: They do follow the body.

071.14 We say that [the sense-faculties] have the body as their support (āśraya), but it is not by way of a relationship between container and contained (ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva) that the sense-faculties exist in the body. 071.15 Thus, rather, the meaning of "having the body as their support" is that they conform to the impairment of the body; they are benefited by the benefit of the body and impaired when it is impaired—this is the meaning of "support. Therefore...
071.17 “Rejection that is contrary to the fact”—by this, it should be understood that the meaning of the "basis" (*āśraya*) of objects has been stated. What is the reason?

For objects such as odors do not themselves function as the body; rather, their effect is the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain. Since that [experience] does not occur in the absence of a body, they are said to have the body as their basis.

It is said: "Just as villagers are said to have taken refuge in the village headman. But how is it that these [words], being general terms (*sāmānya-śabda*), come to function with reference to a particular (*viśeṣa-vṛtti*)? Regarding the particular application of general terms, it occurs through implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Implication arises from context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, as in the command: "Feed the Brahmins."

072.01 Thus, because it is impossible to feed every single Brāhmaṇa, that which is being specifically brought forward—namely, the specific Brāhmaṇa who has entered the context—is mentioned. In this same way, by virtue of their semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), words such as "movement" (*ceṣṭā*) and so forth also abide in a specific sense. And this semantic capacity is understood either from common worldly usage or through the impossibility of [any other] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

072.04 First, according to common usage, people do not employ the word "ceṣṭā" (volitional effort) for mere action in general, but rather for a specific kind [of action]. 072.05 Just as in the cases of "it throbbs," "it crawls," or "it runs"— where these words such as "throbbing" and so on,
while being denoters of action, are restricted to specific types of action— so too is this word "ceṣṭā," even though it denotes action in general.

Because of the impossibility of [such] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it applies to a specific action and not to a mere substratum of action; thus, the body cannot possibly be the cause for the manifestation of an individual. And in this way, there is no over-extension (*aprasaṅga*) to jars and the like. Even those who raise the objection that there is no over-extension to jars and the like when words such as "first" (*ādya*) and so forth are employed here, [their point] is also addressed by this explanation.

This has been answered: even when the term "entirety" is employed, the objection regarding atoms is not thereby refuted; however, according to our explanation, [the self] does not exist anywhere other than within the body.
072.13 [1-1-12] The sense-faculties—the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear—arise from the elements (bhūtāni).
072.14 The aphorism (sūtra) is: "The nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear are the sense-faculties arising from the elements. This is the definition (lakṣaṇa).
072.15 The meaning of all aphorisms is that they serve to distinguish [the subject] from both similar and dissimilar classes. This is the purpose of the aphorism.

It is to be seen as follows: because of the commonality of the enumeration (*uddeśa*), the statement of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is merely the naming of the categories (*padārtha*) by their respective names;
thus, the definition of an "enumeration" has been stated. And since this [definition of the senses] is of such a nature, it is not a definition [of the senses].
This is not so, because they function as instruments (*karaṇa*); for the senses have the characteristic of grasping their own respective objects, and thus they are instruments.

The sense faculties have their own intrinsic natures; thus, it should be understood that those supersensible faculties are characterized by the apprehension of their respective objects, which is their "definition as the apprehension of their own objects.
Regarding the phrase "because of being uncommon," the teaching that they arise from the primary elements (*bhūta*)—namely earth and so forth—is for the purpose of establishing a restriction.
072.22 But what is this restriction? That the capacity to apprehend the specific qualities of the elements belongs only to certain sense-faculties, and not to every sense-faculty.
073.01 It does not apprehend the specific quality of every element; rather, whatever kind of sense-faculty it is, [it apprehends] that which is its [corresponding] specific quality.
073.02 That specific quality—such as odor and so forth—which is the cause for the mutual differentiation between the elements, is apprehended by that very sense-faculty.
This is the rule [that objects are perceived]. However, this rule would not hold if there were a single self;

for if the sense organs were of a single nature and had a single cause, then, due to their conformity with the nature of that cause and because of their unitary nature, there would be no fixed determination of objects—either everything would have all things as its object, or the single [organ] would have all things as its object.
073.06 If it is argued that there may be a difference in intrinsic nature even among things that have a single cause, as in the case of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
073.07 if you should think: "A difference in intrinsic nature is observed among color-form and other qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) which have a single cause"—[we reply:
what, then, is that single cause of color-form and the rest? It is the conjunction with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*). This is not established according to our tenet (*siddhānta*).

073.09. We do not say that color and the other qualities arise from a single conjunction with fire; rather, [we say they arise] in dependence upon the specific prior qualities. When a substance is being cooked by conjunction with fire, the conjunction with fire, depending upon the specific internal quality belonging to those prior qualities of that substance, produces the subsequent [qualities].
It initiates specific [qualities] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. And having established this, there is a distinction among atoms, such as being more or less cooked (*pakvatara-tama*).

Therefore, color-form and the rest do not have a single cause; thus, no effect whatsoever is seen to have a single cause. For every effect, when it manifests, [arises from] inherent (*samavāyin*) and non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) causes.
[It arises] from efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). [Objection: One action is observed to be the cause of conjunction and disjunction.

[Response: If this is argued, it is not so, because we do not accept it. It might be thought: "Is it not observed that action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction? No, because we do not accept it; we do not accept that action is independent.

"It is the cause of conjunction and disjunction. If, then, action (*karman*) also produces conjunction and disjunction while being dependent [on other factors], there is a loss of the definition of action; for it has been stated that "action is that which is independent and is the cause of conjunction and disjunction. That [definition] would be abandoned due to this loss of its characteristic, and therefore it would not be action, and consequently, there would be no conjunction and disjunction.
"Preceded by karma"—this is not a fault. We do not say that karma is the cause independently; nor do we say that it depends on nothing at all.

Rather, the meaning of "independent" here is that it does not depend on any other final causal condition (*nimitta*). For example, [it is like] a collection of substances and their conjunction with substances of the same kind, which is the final [condition].

A substance initiates [an action] by depending on a future cause; however, an action of this kind does not depend on a future cause. Rather, being an action, it initiates conjunction and disjunction. Therefore, there is no loss of the definition of action, nor is it the case that conjunction and disjunction are preceded by a single [cause].
074.05 [1-1-13] Earth, water, fire, air, and space are the primary elements (*bhūta*).
074.06 [1-1-14] Odor, taste, form, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the other elements; these are the objects (*artha*).
074.07 This is the aphorism: "Odor, taste, form, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the other elements; these are the objects."

Regarding the term *pṛthivy-ādi-guṇāḥ*, several types of compound (*samāsa*) are possible. How so? *Pṛthivy-ādīnām guṇāḥ* (the qualities of earth and so forth) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). *Pṛthivy-ādīni ca guṇāś ca* (earth and so forth, and qualities) is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). *Pṛthivy-ādyo guṇā yeṣām* (those whose qualities have earth and so forth as their beginning) is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). Thus, there is the possibility of various compounds.

There is a doubt: what is the truth in this matter? The truth is that it is a *dvandva* compound. It cannot be a *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) compound, because that would entail the consequence that earth and the other [elements] are not objects of the senses. If it were a *ṣaṣṭhī* compound meaning "the qualities of earth and the others," then [earth and the others] would have qualities such as odor and so forth.
Those things employed as qualifiers would not possess the status of sense objects (*indriyārtha*), and there would be the fault of the qualifier being redundant.
For when it is said, "smell, taste, color, touch, and sound," the qualities of earth and so forth are understood;
consequently, the mention of "earth and so forth" would be useless, since smell and the others do not belong to two distinct categories.

Since the qualification "being a quality of earth and so forth" and "being a quality of something else" would otherwise be purposeless, it cannot [be understood] as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Because a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is not established, it cannot be a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*): [namely,] "those for whom earth and so forth are the qualities"—who are those possessors of qualities?
For whom earth and so forth are the qualities; and it is impossible for earth and so forth to have the status of being qualities.

And this bahuvrīhi compound cannot be established by any other means; for this [type of] bahuvrīhi is generally preceded by a term in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "the one with variegated cows" (*citraguḥ*).

This bahuvrīhi is well-established when the possession of cows is already known and the connection with the variegated quality is understood—namely, "the one with variegated cows"—but here, the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is not established.

Furthermore, it is not established that earth and the other elements possess the nature of qualities (*guṇatva*). [If one were to argue] that "earth and the others are qualities because they are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*)," then in this conceptualization, everything would necessarily be a quality.

For in this case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that anything could be either a qualifier or a qualified (*viśeṣya*) for anything else, and thus everything would be a quality.
Therefore, it cannot be a *bahuvrīhi* either. Because both [the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and the *bahuvrīhi*] are prohibited, and because no other compound is possible, it must be a *dvandva*.

Since the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and the *bahuvrīhi* have been ruled out and no other type of compound can occur, the *dvandva* remains as the only remaining possibility; therefore, it is a *dvandva* compound. It is not a *dvandva* compound.

075.08 Because of the absence of both scripture and reasoning, if this were a *dvandva* compound, then either scripture or reasoning would have to be stated as the sense-object (*indriyārtha*) of earth and so forth; [but it is not], because neither of the two is established.
075.10 Both scripture and reasoning are possible regarding earth and so forth being sense-objects. As for scripture: [it says]...
"Because there is the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching. There is also a logical argument (*yukti*) regarding seeing and touching:

the unification (*pratisandhāna*) based on a single object, such as "I touch that which I saw," is the argument concerning the objects of sight and touch. Furthermore, a scriptural authority (*śāstra*) is also possible in this position, because [the object] is described as being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*).

And because it is a universal, therefore it is established that "earth and so forth" and "qualities" form a *dvandva* compound. By the mention of "earth and so forth," earth, water, and fire—which are graspable by the external sense organs—are indicated; and by the mention of "qualities," every quality that is dependent [on a substance] is indicated, such as number and so on.

075.17–18. Dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, viscidity, speed, action, generality, and particularity are non-dependent, as is inherence; because they possess those properties, they are qualities (*guṇa*). In that case, odor, taste, color, touch, and sound should not be mentioned separately, since they are already included by the term "quality. They are the qualities of earth and the other elements, and thus have those [elements] as their objects.
It should be stated in the Sūtra: "And it is thus concise," for that very meaning will be established; therefore, [the detailed list] need not be made.

The separate mention of odor, taste, visible form, touch, and sound is for the purpose of making known the restriction of the specific sense faculties; the sense faculties [operate] upon odors, tastes, visible forms, touches, and sounds, as well as their respective generalities (*sāmānya*).
076.01 Some [substances] are determinate, while others are indeterminate. Among them, earth, water, and fire are perceptible by two sense organs.

076.02 The remaining aggregate of qualities, as well as existence (*sattā*) and quality-ness (*guṇatva*), are perceptible by all the sense organs; so too are inherence (*samavāya*) and non-existence (*abhāva*).
076.03 Thus, the opponent, unable to tolerate the argument that "because a single object is grasped through both seeing and touching," says:
"Grasping touch is by means of the sense of touch, and grasping form is by means of the eye"—this [position] must be questioned.

Now, how is it understood that both form and touch are grasped by the eye and the sense of touch? Because a cognition characterized by those [objects] arises through the eye and the sense of touch. In that case, the negation [of the opponent's view] is not without foundation.
076.07 Since a cognition qualified by that [form] is observed even in the case of a jar and so forth, one perceives the object—the jar and so forth—through both seeing and touching.

076.08 And perceiving it, one understands the object as a jar and so forth qualified by those [qualities]. Therefore, the negation is not established. The cognition of a "jar" and so forth arises from color-form and the other [sensory qualities] when they are arranged in such a manner.
If you say this—that one perceives this jar through both seeing and touching—it is false. It is simply forms and so forth that are arranged in various ways;
the perceiver, apprehending them as having those particular forms, conceives of them as "a jar," but [there is no jar apart from them].

Furthermore, [the claim that] pots and the like are distinct from form and so forth is not tenable, because the meaning of "form" (ākāra) has not been stated. The referent of the word "form" is a commonality between that which is not as it appears and that which is as it appears; for example, when one says "a man with the form of a post," the form of the post—which is not a man—is [perceived] by means of the man.
That which is the commonality is the meaning of the word "aspect" (ākāra), which occurs when there is the conventional recognition of it as either a post or a person.

However, for you [the Yogācārins], there is no seed whatsoever for the aspect of a jar within form and so forth, such that one could say, "form and so forth have the aspect of a jar. Therefore, this claim that "form and so forth have the aspect of a jar" is quite trivial.

Furthermore, for one for whom the pot and so forth are merely color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, there would be no cognition of "pot" and so forth with respect to mere color-form and the rest, because those [factors] are common to all [objects]. These cognitions— such as "cow," "horse," and "pot"— would not arise,
because there is no specific cause consisting of a restriction of cognition residing in the color-form and the rest.

[It is] because of non-existence. If it is argued that the cognition of difference arises from a difference in configuration (*saṃsthāna*), [we reply: by means of some particular configuration, form and the other [sensory objects], while remaining as they are, become the causes for cognitions such as "a jar" because they conform to a difference in configuration. This is not so; because if the configuration were not distinct [from the object], there would be a mere difference in designation, and thus the expression would be useless.
Furthermore, as a consequence, if shape (*saṃsthāna*) were a distinct substance from color and the other [sensory qualities], it would be a mere difference in terminology;

if, on the other hand, it were not distinct, then since the perception of a jar and so forth follows the specific configuration of color and the others, the designation [of "jar"] is redundant. Thus, the cognitions of jars and the like are false cognitions.
If he should think that cognitions such as those of a jar are correct cognitions,

rather than [thinking] that they are false cognitions arising through the power of verbal predispositions (*śabda-vāsanā*), that is incorrect; for wherever those false cognitions occur in the world, they always imitate correct cognitions.

They conform to correct cognitions; however, there is no seed for those cognitions of jars and so forth which are imagined to be false cognitions, nor do these arise without a seed. Therefore, they are not false cognitions. And as for the claim that "these are false cognitions," this is a proof of non-distinction.

Even if [the existence of the universal] were granted, it would not be established; furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that demonstrates its non-difference [from the particular].

It is not the case that [the universal does not exist], because when that [particular] is not apprehended, the cognition of it [the universal] is absent. For whenever something is not a distinct entity from another, it is observed that when the latter is not apprehended, the former is also not apprehended—as, for example, in the case of soup or a row [of ants]. And whenever something is a distinct entity from another, when that [other] is not apprehended...

The apprehension of that [earth] has been observed, just as there is the apprehension of "child" when [the qualities such as] form and so forth are not apprehended. This is not a valid reason because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, in the case of earth and the other elements which have attained the state of being a jar and so forth, when the earth is being apprehended, there is a non-apprehension of water and the others which are distinct entities (*arthāntara*); yet, they are nonetheless distinct entities.

Since the primary elements (*bhūta*), being intangible, do not become objects of visual perception, [your argument] is inconclusive (*anekānta*). Furthermore, if your position is that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are so arranged [as to constitute form], even so, the statement that "form consists of the four great elements" is contradicted. If you say, "For us, there are no [elements] distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities],"...

077.21 Even if [the term] "beginning with earth" (*pṛthivy-ādya*) is used, the meaning of this statement becomes "beginning with form" (*rūp-ādya*). 077.22 Consequently, the claim that "an atom in the desire realm consists of eight substances" (*aṣṭa-dravyaka*) would be contradicted. Alternatively, if [it refers to] earth and the others...
078.01 ...then the conventional usage of "form" and so forth applies merely to an aggregate; nevertheless, in reality, form is not [identical to] earth and the others.

[They] exist. How so? [If it is argued that] the aggregate of earth and so forth is form, and earth and so forth are the aggregate of form and so forth—then, because that which is being aggregated does not exist, no aggregate exists at all. Since every aggregate is seen to depend upon that which is being aggregated, one is in no way released from contradiction if that [aggregate] is not apprehended.

"Because of the absence of that cognition" means that when following the referent of the word "that," the meaning is incoherent. When the referent of the word "that" is followed, it follows that if "that" is not apprehended, its [the cognition's] very apprehension is absent; and that is incoherent. For when earth and so forth are established as being qualified by color and so forth, then, in the absence of the apprehension of that [qualifier], there is an absence of the cognition of it.
Thus, the meaning of the reason [in the argument] "because there is an absence of the cognition of earth and so forth when earth and so forth are not apprehended" follows.
What is the reason? Because the qualifiers of earth and so forth—namely, color and the rest—are not connected by that term [‘earth’].
By this, the [objections concerning] color and the rest as qualifiers of earth and so forth are refuted; for here too, in the non-apprehension of color and the rest...

The meaning of the reason [in the argument] becomes "due to the absence of the cognition of form and so forth," because that word [“earth”] is connected primarily with those [qualities]. Thus, there follows the same undesirable consequence as before: that earth is merely form and so forth, and form and so forth are merely earth;
that earth itself is form and so forth, and form and so forth themselves are earth—this applies in all cases.
There is a contradiction between the proposition and its constituent terms due to a difference in number: "earth" is in the singular, while "form and so forth" is in the plural.

Where there is a conformity to a difference in number, there must be a difference in meaning; for example, as in the cases of "the stars" and "the moon. And here too there is a difference in number; therefore, there must also be a difference in meaning here.

"But is it not observed that there is a difference in expression regarding a single object, as for example: 'the four stages of life' (*catvāra āśramāḥ*) and 'the system of the four stages of life' (*cāturāśramyam*)? No, because this is not admitted. This difference in expression is not observed anywhere in the case of actual identity.
By the term *cāturāśramyam*, what is expressed is the commonality of the four stages of life in being the means for accomplishing Dharma.

By this, it is refuted that there are only six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), or that a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is itself the "particularizer" (*viśeṣika*). Furthermore, the reason [stated by the opponent], "because the cognition of that [substance] does not occur when those [qualities] are not apprehended," is unestablished (*asiddha*). How is it unestablished? Because [the substance] is apprehended even when color and so forth are not apprehended; for instance, in the case of a crystal gem which conforms to the differences of the adjuncts such as blue and so forth.

079.01 The cognition "this is crystal" is observed even when form is not perceived; as for this example [of yours], that it is like broth (yūṣa) or like a row (paṅkti)—you have not understood either the broth or the row. For what is called "broth" is [a state] of substances in which the qualities produced by cooking have arisen, when they are favored by a particular time and are mixed with other substances.
The conjunction that arises from cooking is called *yūṣa* (broth), and that [conjunction] is like a distinct entity (*arthāntara*).
Thus, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*). By this, [the cases of] *kāñcika* (sour gruel) produced by cooking, *viveka* (separation), *avakṣāra* (alkali), and so forth, are refuted.
Furthermore, a row (*paṅkti*) is also [a conjunction] among things connected in one direction and place, which are assisted by mutual proximity, whether they are perceived or not perceived.

The number "plurality" (bahutva-saṃkhyā) is said to reside in these substrates, whether they are of different or non-different kinds, and whose extent is either determined or undetermined. Likewise, the number "plurality" resides in elephants, horses, and chariots that are related to indefinite directions and locations, which are assisted by mutual proximity and whose extent is either ascertained or not.

It is called an "army" (*senā*). Likewise, an assembly (*parṣad*) is so called when it functions by gathering individuals distinguished by their birth; a "community" (*saṅgha*) is so called when it functions by gathering specific types of renunciants. In this way, the terms *pūga*, *vana*, *yūtha*, and *brāhmaṇagaṇa* should also be understood according to their respective occurrences. Thus, regarding those [groups] connected to indefinite directions and locations, which are beginningless—

079.13 Existing within those [parts] that are empty of a middle, it is merely the number "many" [that constitutes] a coil (*kuṇḍalaka*). Therefore, the argument that "a row (*paṅkti*) is not a different entity" is unestablished. Now, if it is a different entity, what is the proof for this?
079.14–15 It is the designation of the object of perception by means of all its perceivable qualities; for example, when this sandalwood is perceived, its whiteness [is also perceived].

"Color, bitter taste, pungent smell, and cold touch"— this designation of perception by means of perception is observed in the case of distinct entities, such as "the water-pot of the Brahmin. Indeed,
it is not understood in this way that this white color [belongs] to those tastes, smells, and touches which are being inferred.

If it is argued that an army or a forest is mentioned as something distinct from its constituent parts, and therefore those [parts] are non-existent; even so, one might conceive it thus:
first of all, number itself does not exist—how then can there be the state of being a distinct object?
For by one who says that number does not exist at all, the occurrence of the cognitions of "one" and "many"—whether they be affirmed or negated—is denied.
The cause must be accepted. Why? Because single and multiple cognitions cannot be rejected.
Furthermore, since these cognitions are specific, they cannot exist by means of rejecting a cause.
For what reason? Because a cognition of a jar that has a cause other than [the jar itself] would be a single or multiple cognition distinct from the cognition of the jar.

Because [the cognition] is like the cognition of blue, therefore that which is the cause of that cognition is number. Since there is no production of a distinct cognition qualified by that [number] apart from the cause that is the object of that cognition, another cause must be required; that which is the cause of the object of the cognition—
It is observed that when a cognition arises apart from its [usual] conditions, it requires another cause.
In this case, the cognitions of cloth, leather, or woolen blankets remain the same;
however, the additional cognition that "this is blue" is seen to arise from another cause, and so it is here as well.

080.12 Even in the case of jars and the like, the cognitions of "one" and so forth occur there as distinct from the causes that have the jar as their object. 080.13 Therefore, those [cognitions] must also arise from a different cause; that which is their cause is number and the rest. 080.14 Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "large" and "flowering," it is not number, nor is it an army or a forest.
It must be so. If it is argued that when a number reaches a great army or a great forest in bloom, there is no "greatness" of the number itself nor any connection with flowers, this is not a fault.
What is meant by "a great army"? It refers to those very elephants and so forth, whose quantity has been determined or not yet determined.

When there is an accumulation of constituent parts (*sthāni-aṅga*) to a certain extent, people designate it as "a great army. In that context, among those things designated by the word "great" (*mahat*), the number "many" (*bahutva-saṃkhyā*) is said to be "great" because of the presence of an accumulation of equipment (*upacaya-upakaraṇāt*).

Likewise, regarding the term "in bloom" (*puṣpita*), even though it refers to trees associated with flowers, through the connection with the flowers, [the tree] is designated as one—[namely, "in bloom"].

When experiencing the inherence of an object, it is the number "plurality" itself that is expressed, as in the cases: "sweet taste" and "bitter molasses. Precisely because of this designation, numbers and the like also exist as distinct entities [from the substance].

It is not a valid reason [to claim they are not distinct] because they are not seen when [the substance] is absent; for example, a pit is not [merely] a hole, nor is it [defined] by a lack of cognition.

Indeed, space is that which is characterized by having form and so forth, produced as an effect from parts, empty in the middle, and endowed with specific configurations. By this, the notion of a "cavity" is explained. Since it is perceived even in a single object, it is not logical to claim there is no distinct entity [of space], just as one says, "the post of the khadira tree."

Or [the term is used] because it is seen applied to many things that are not connected, as in "a row of palaces. Or it is seen applied to connected things of different kinds, as in "the separation of the triad of earth, water, and fire.
As for the claim that it is because it is seen applied even to a single thing, that is incorrect; for the word *khadira* [denotes] a genus (*jāti*).

Because it denotes a specific substance, the word *khadira* expresses a substance qualified by its genus (*jāti*). Likewise, by the word *sthāṇu*, a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) is denoted; and this particular configuration is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) known as accumulation (*pracaya*).
And that [conjunction] is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). By this [same reasoning], [the cases of] a coiled snake, the body of a statue, and gold [are explained].
It has been stated that [expressions] such as "the ring is the body of the stone statue" are indicative of difference (*bheda*).

A row of palaces is to be viewed like a line; this is what was meant by the statement regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and separation (*viveka*), because [the whole] is not perceived apart from the collection of qualities (*guṇa-samudāya*). If you should grant this—that if form (*rūpa*) and so forth...

If substance were distinct [from its qualities], it would be perceived separately from color and the rest; however, it is not so perceived. Therefore, because non-perception has two possible causes, there is no inconclusiveness [in the argument]. What is this "non-perception"? Is it due to the absence of the object to be grasped, or is it due to the absence of the cause for grasping? This is what is being doubted. If you say it is due to the absence of the object to be grasped...
If it is argued that the reason is untenable because it is not apprehended—since the meaning of the reason is implied by the meaning of the thesis—[we reply:

the fault of the reason, namely "the negation of the absence [of the reason] when [the subject] is not apprehended," should be seen to apply to this [thesis] as well. Thus, this doctrine of non-difference is scrutinized more and more.

At each instance, it clearly demonstrates the distinctness [of the means of valid cognition] based on their occurrence in one case and their non-occurrence in another. Therefore, it is established that "earth and so forth" and "qualities" form a *dvandva* compound.
082.03 Now follows the aphorism concerning cognition (*buddhi*), which has reached its proper occasion, by way of defining its characteristics.
082.04 [1-1-15] *Buddhi*, apprehension (*upalabdhi*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not different in meaning.

082.05 Regarding "intellect" (*buddhi*), "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*), and so forth: that category of reality (*padārtha*) which is denoted by these synonymous terms is what is called "intellect. How are these synonymous terms a definition? Because they serve as the cause for delimitation; for everything...

A definition (lakṣaṇa) is that which excludes other categories of objects; furthermore, no other category of object is denoted by these synonymous terms (paryāya-śabda). Thus, because it is unique (asādhāraṇatva), it is a definition, owing to its logical consistency and its expression through synonymous terms. [This concludes] the refutation of the activity of cognition (buddhi-vṛtti). As for those who say that the activity of cognition is the perception (upalabdhi) of the self (ātman):

Regarding the term "function" (*vṛtti*): in order to refute that [notion], it is said that "these words have the same meaning. Thus, the function of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) is refuted separately. What, then, is the reasoning here?
One who says "the self perceives" or "the intellect knows" would be attributing consciousness (*caitanya*) to both of them.

If both were conscious, there would be an inference based on the distinction between cognitions. If the intellect (*buddhi*) were the conscious self (*ātman*), then the conscious one would not perceive objects determined by the intellect as being non-self; for what reason?
Because there is no perception of another conscious perceiver, yet there is indeed such perception; therefore, the conscious one is one.
When the activity of the knower is conceived as non-different from the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*), the true nature of the self (*ātman*) must be stated.

If it is argued that "the intellect determines" while "the self cognizes," then this might be the case: just as the intellect determines objects, so too does the self perceive place and time. [Thus,] it determines.

"Apprehends" (*upalabhate*) and [the other term] are synonymous words (*paryāya-śabda*); and it is not logical that there should be a difference in the referent (*padārtha*) because of synonymous words, just as in the case of "sound" (*dhvani*) and "noise" (*nāda*). Otherwise, there would have to be a difference even between "sound" and "noise. Furthermore, if it is argued that the self (*ātman*) perceives and the intellect (*buddhi*) makes known, then [it must be admitted] that by means of the intellect...
The person knows, not the intellect; rather, it is the intellect that makes known—thus, the intellect is the instrument of cognition.
"Recollection, inference, scripture, doubt, intuition, dream-cognition, and deliberation"—this is the commentary.
These, beginning with recollection, are the marks of the mind. Are these alone [the marks]? Rather, this non-simultaneity of cognitions is also a mark of the mind.
083.04 [1-1-16] The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind (manas).

083.05 Because, even when there is contact between the sense organs and their objects, cognitions do not occur simultaneously; therefore, it is understood that there exists another, non-pervasive auxiliary cause conjoined with those sense organs, whose— 083.06 —[absence results in the non-arising of cognition].
The arising and non-arising of cognition occur in accordance with the presence or absence [of the object];

for what reason? Because when the cause is deficient, the effect is obstructed—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. But how then [do they serve as] the marks of the mind? They are not the first [moments] of recollection; we do not say that the first moments of recollection exist here [as the marks].

Because it is a function of the mind, the mind is indeed indicated by its own activity; however, provided that this activity is distinct from the activities of odor and so forth, [the following applies]:

because it is an activity, it necessitates another instrument. That activity which is distinct from odor and the rest is seen to be performed by another instrument, just like the activity of a chariot and so forth; and this [activity in question] is such an activity.

Therefore, this [cognition] consisting of memory and so forth also necessitates another instrument (*karaṇa*). Pleasure and the rest, being objects while being distinct from attachment (*rāga*), necessitate another instrument distinct from the eye and other [senses], just like a chariot and so forth.
That is to say, just as a chariot and the like, being objects, [necessitate] an instrument distinct from the eye and other [senses].

The sense objects, such as pleasure and so forth, cause one to employ [the senses] with the thought, "Let there be a cutting tool. Therefore, by means of these [objects], an internal instrument must also be employed. Now, if the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is a property of cognition, how does that become the mark (liṅga) of the mind? Furthermore, if even something unrelated is accepted as a mark, then everything would be a mark for everything.
One might say, "The self exists because the crow is black," yet this is not the case;

therefore, a sign that is unrelated [to the probandum] is not a valid reason. Some, however, maintain that even an unrelated thing can serve as a sign, as for example: the sight of a freshly made clay bowl leads one to infer the presence of a potter, and the appearance of a spinning wheel leads one to infer the potter's activity.

And as for the phrase "and [its] perception": it should not be understood here that the presence of a potter is what is to be inferred; rather, it is the location itself that is to be established as being "not far from a potter. Its property (*dharma*) is its state of having a newly made *śarāva* [pot], even though it possesses a rotating wheel. Thus, the location is established as being "not far from a potter" by means of its state of possessing a rotating wheel. Therefore, this inference is not incoherent.

"In some cases" [is said]. Then, how can the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions (*yugapaj-jñānānutpatti*) be a mark (*liṅga*) [of the mind] if it is not connected with the mind? Because the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions itself is made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣakaraṇāt*), how could it be unconnected?
[The inference is: The apprehensions of form and so forth, being distinct from the eyes and other [senses], depend upon another governing agent because they do not arise simultaneously.
084.06 [This is] due to their arising. For example, just as one who is proficient in many arts does not simultaneously perform many actions such as carpentry and so forth;

084.07 or just as the hand and other organs, though present together, do not—depending on a presiding agent—simultaneously carry out many actions such as driving a chariot and so forth; or just as the eye and other senses do not produce many cognitions simultaneously; therefore, that [is the case].
Furthermore, it must be stated whether the sense-faculties themselves are taken as the subject [of the proposition] that they require another sustainer. How so? [The argument is:

"The sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, depend upon another sustainer employed by a self, because they do not function simultaneously, like an axe or similar tools. If, then, the sense-faculties such as the eye depend upon the mind and its contact (manas-sannidhāna), [then...]

Regarding those objects that are apprehended by a single sense-faculty and are not apprehended simultaneously—how is it that they are not apprehended at once? For it is not the case that the mind (*manas*) is absent there. If you say it is because of the difference in their correlates (*sambandhi*), then [we ask]:
how can there be non-simultaneous apprehension due to the difference in correlates in the case of distinct things such as blue and so forth? Now, as for those [objects] which...

How is it that the cognitions "the white cow is walking" are connected simultaneously? Some say that they are not apprehended simultaneously because of a difference in the desire to know (*bubhutsā*). They claim that even though an object is connected [to the senses], it is not apprehended if there is no desire to know it. That is not so, because it would entail the involvement of the mind (*manas*). If that were the case, then the mind—

084.18 If it is to be abandoned because of the distinction in the desire to know (*bubhutsā*), then there would be non-simultaneous apprehensions [of objects]. Elsewhere, 084.19 since the absence of the desire to know is not prevented by a staff, the mind (*manas*) is now useless and should be abandoned.
084.20 And when the desire to know exists, another principle must be determined regarding non-simultaneous apprehension; therefore, [it is] other—

"The reason for the non-simultaneous apprehension [of objects] is what, then? It is the nature of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*). Just as this property of an instrument is such that an instrument operates when presided over by various [agents], so too, even for that which is connected [to the agent], there is no performance of multiple actions; for an instrument, even while connected, does not perform many [actions] at once."

One is able to perform distinct actions; however, if the self alone were the controller, since it is not denied that the self can be simultaneously connected with multiple sense organs, another principle must be determined regarding the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions. And since that [principle] cannot exist without the mind, the existence of the mind is established.
085.05 [1-1-17] Activity (*pravṛtti*) is the undertaking of speech, mind, and body.
085.06 "Activity is the undertaking of speech, mind, and body" means by means of the body, the mind, and speech.
085.07 This activity is each of ten kinds, being both meritorious and sinful. Meritorious [activity] is by means of the body...
Protection, service, and giving; by way of speech, truthfulness, benefit, and pleasantness;
and by way of mind, compassion, desire for the welfare of others, and faith. By their opposites, there are likewise ten kinds of evil.
Because activity is momentary, it is untenable for it to be the cause of birth; yet this very activity is momentary.
It is logical that [the result] being present is not the cause of activity; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the second aphorism.
Furthermore, the fruit of activity is designated as "activity" because it is metaphorically identified with its cause. In this aphorism, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are called "activity.
Why? Because they are the means of accomplishing it. As it is said: "Food is indeed the life-breath of living beings."

085.14 [1-1-18] Defilements (*doṣa*) are characterized by instigation (*pravartanā*). 085.15 Defilements are characterized by instigation. But what is this instigation, by which one is impelled involuntarily?
085.16 It is that by which passion (*rāga*) and the other defilements cause one who is being impelled to proceed. This [instigation], because it is the cause of activity (*pravṛtti*), [is so called].
It is called "activation" (*pravartanā*), just as [the term] "causing to take away" (*hāraṇā*) is used for a cause. Furthermore, how is this activation understood?

It is directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*) within one's own person, whereas in another's body it is inferential (*ānumānikī*), just like the self (*ātman*). For example, just as the self is directly perceived within one's own person by way of being the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*), so too is this [activation]. Indeed, this...

The cognition of the "I" (ahaṅkāra) is inferential; it is not based on scripture. How is it not inferential? Because there is no logical mark (liṅga). How is it not based on instruction? Because there is an understanding of an object that has not been taught. Therefore, like color and so forth, the self is directly perceived within oneself. However, in the case of another's body, it is to be inferred from activity and cessation [of movement].

086.03 [1-1-19] Rebirth is pretyabhāva. 086.04 Rebirth is the transition to another body following the abandonment of the previously acquired body and so forth; that is pretyabhāva. The inclusion of the word "again" (punar) is for the purpose of making known that saṃsāra is beginningless.

086.06 For this reason, [the text] shows that saṃsāra is beginningless by stating that "birth and death occur again and again. What, then, is this saṃsāra? Saṃsāra is the state of cause and effect among [the factors] beginning with suffering and ending with false knowledge, occurring without interruption. And it is beginningless because there is no restriction regarding a prior or subsequent time.

086.09 If suffering existed previously, it would not be tenable without that birth. If birth existed previously, then it would not be tenable without merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). If merit and demerit existed previously, they too would not be tenable without passion and aversion (*rāga-dveṣa*). If passion and aversion existed previously, they could not exist without false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*).
"Manifestation" [is the beginning]. If that were so, false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) would be the beginning; however, even that is not tenable without the body and so forth.

This causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) among suffering and the rest, culminating in false knowledge, is the uninterrupted cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). It is designated as "the state of being worn out again and again," "the state of coming and going," and so on. This is it.

Is cyclic existence (saṃsāra) of the self (ātman) or of the mind (manas)? If it is spoken of with reference to action (kriyā), then it belongs to the mind, for that is what transmigrates. But if it is spoken of with reference to experience (upabhoga), then it belongs to the self, for it is the self that experiences pleasure and pain.
086.18 [1-1-20] The object produced by activity and defects is the fruit (phala).

086.19 The object produced by activity and defects is the fruit. Everything produced by prosperity (śrī) and so forth is a fruit because it is prompted by merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma); in the conceptualization of pleasure, the experience of pleasure and pain alone constitutes its conclusion. 086.20 Because it is prompted by merit and demerit; in the conceptualization of pleasure, the experience of pleasure and pain alone constitutes its conclusion.

Because the experience of pleasure and pain resulting from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) is the final fruit, yet that [fruit] does not arise without the body and so forth; therefore, having established that merit and demerit originate the body and other [factors], they bring about the experience of pleasure and pain. Thus, this word "fruit" refers to the experience of pleasure and pain.
The primary [self] is in the body; the secondary [self] is elsewhere.

087.04 [1-1-21] Suffering is characterized by affliction (bādhanā). 087.05 Suffering is characterized by affliction; this very body and so forth are called suffering because they are accompanied by affliction. 087.06 However, in its intrinsic nature, suffering is simply suffering. The word "characterized" (lakṣaṇa) has the sense of "accompanied by. All of this—

"087.07 The body and so forth are accompanied by suffering. In this context, "accompanied" (*anuṣaṅga*) has the sense of being a cause (*nimitta*); thus, the body is the cause of suffering. The sense organs, objects, and cognitions are the means (*sādhana*), and "accompanied" here has the sense of being the means. Furthermore, pleasure is inseparable from suffering; here too, "inseparability" (*avinābhāva*) is what is meant by "accompanied. However, in terms of its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), [pleasure is distinct].

087.10 Some [maintain] that "suffering, suffering" means everything is suffering by its very nature. This is not so, because it contradicts direct perception (pratyakṣa). For it is impossible to deny pleasure through direct perception. 087.11–12 If it is argued that this is merely a conceptual construction of suffering—that pleasure is nothing but a conceptual construction of suffering—it is not so.

It does not exist by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), because there is no employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) with respect to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Nor is it [non-existent] through conceptual construction; for the negative particle is not observed to apply to a specific instance of a Brahmin, as in "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇaḥ*). Likewise, "non-suffering" (*aduḥkha*) would not apply to a specific instance of suffering. Furthermore, if the self (*sva*) did not exist, the teachings on the factors of existence (*dharma*) would be rendered purposeless.
What is the reason? [The opponent argues: "Dharma is the means for achieving happiness; since happiness does not exist, Dharma is useless. [We reply:

It is not tenable that its fruit is the negation of suffering, because it would follow that Dharma has non-existence as its fruit. Furthermore, in the world, two types of activity are observed; those would not exist if Dharma had non-existence as its fruit.
One person engages [in action] thinking, "I shall attain what is beneficial," while another engages thinking, "I shall avoid what is undesirable.

Since there would be no such thing as the beneficial, this duality of engagement would not exist, nor would there be the instruction on the cultivation of suffering, because its opposite would be absent.
For that non-existence means that no one at all would be attached to suffering; therefore, [the view of non-existence] is not primary.
All is suffering; and by means of the instruction on the cultivation of suffering, it is called "suffering."
088.01 [1-1-22] Liberation (*apavarga*) is the absolute release from that.

088.02 "Liberation is the absolute release from that" means the absolute separation from that suffering consisting of the body and so forth. Some say it is the absolute manifestation of happiness; others, however, [say it is] the absolute...

088.04 They claim that liberation is the manifestation of pleasure; that is not so, because there is no means of valid cognition [for it]. There is no means of valid cognition for the claim that the liberated self possesses eternal pleasure. If it is argued that it is not the case that there is no such thing because there is a regulating factor, [we reply: the inherence of pleasure—which is produced by multiple causes—in the self is not tenable without a regulating factor.

Therefore, if it is argued that there is eternal happiness in the self, because this [transient] happiness, being regulated, depends upon the self—[we reply: no, for it would follow that everything which has an origin must likewise exist eternally in the self, just as happiness does; and thus suffering, desire, and so forth would also have to be postulated as eternal. Alternatively, [the argument fails] due to the lack of certainty regarding manifestation.
And because it does not express a [corresponding] object: if it is argued that "eternal pleasure is manifested," what is the meaning of "manifestation"?

If one says it is "cognition," then the conceptualization of it as either eternal or non-eternal is untenable. If it is said to be non-eternal, then its cause must be stated. Is the cause the conjunction of the self and the mind, or is there dependence upon something else?

The cause must be stated. If you think that the conjunction of the self and the mind is the cause of cognition, then its dependent cause must be stated; for conjunction is not the independent cause when substances, qualities, and actions are being produced. If it is argued that the conjunction of the self and the mind depends upon pleasure, [we reply: no.

Because it contradicts liberation (*kaivalya*). Now, if you think that the conjunction of the self and the mind, being eternally established in the self, becomes the cause of knowledge while awaiting pleasure—that is not tenable, because it contradicts liberation. Just as this conjunction of the self and the mind, while awaiting merely an object, serves as a causal condition...

Independent of anything else, it produces the cognition of pleasure; likewise, with respect to objects such as form and so forth, it would produce cognitions of those objects while depending on them, and consequently, isolation (*kaivalya*) would be precluded.

Furthermore, because this self would obtain all objects, there would be the undesirable consequence of constant perception (*nityopalabdhi-prasaṅga*). [This is refuted by] that which is born of yoga (*yogaja*-)...

If it is argued that knowledge will arise in that which is eternal and blissful when assisted by *dharma*, this is not tenable. Since that [knowledge] is absent upon the destruction of that [dharma], one must state what assists it when the *dharma* born of yoga has perished. If it is argued that the *dharma* born of yoga does not perish, this is also not tenable.
Because everything subject to origination is impermanent by nature, it is observed that everything subject to origination is impermanent.

If it is argued that this dharma produced through yoga and meditative concentration (*yoga-samādhi*) is eternal—since it is both born of yoga and born of concentration—and yet is eternal, this is a contradiction.
If it is further argued that knowledge is eternal, we say no; for [the claim of its eternity] lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like [the claim of] pleasure.

Because of the non-existence [of a permanent self], there would follow the consequence that there is no distinction between one who is liberated and one who remains in saṃsāra. Furthermore, there would be no alternation in the experience of pleasure and pain;

this person would always perceive pleasure, and consequently, the effort for the sake of liberation would be useless. Moreover, this person would not desire to abandon pleasure, because it is impossible to abandon the discernment [of the self] while [still perceiving] suffering.

One who desires to abandon [suffering] also desires to abandon pleasure; yet this [self] never experiences suffering. If it is argued that there is no logical consequence (aprasaṅga) regarding the cessation [of suffering] because of the continuity of the body and so forth, [we reply: there is no such consequence, because the body and so forth do not perceive eternal pleasure.
They are not obstructors, because the body and so forth exist for the purpose of experience; nor does it follow that the body and so forth must be eternal.

Just as eternal bliss is postulated for the liberated one, so too the body and so forth would have to be postulated as eternal. In this way, his isolation (*kaivalya*) would be rendered more perfect through their absence.

If it is argued that it is impossible to postulate the eternity of the body and so forth because it contradicts what is observed, then it cannot be said that it is impossible to postulate the impermanence of pleasure for beings such as ourselves, even though it contradicts what is observed.
It was previously stated that this [postulation] lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but that is not the case; why? Because it serves the purpose of attaining a desired goal.
In this world, as it proceeds, people act for the sake of attaining what is desired, and those seeking liberation likewise act.

For them too, there must be activity for the sake of attaining what is desired; this activity is meaningful only if directed toward eternal happiness, and not otherwise. This is not so, because two kinds of activity are observed; there are indeed two types of activity.

In the world, when something is perceived, it is for the sake of attaining what is desired and for the sake of abandoning what is undesired. In this regard, there is doubt as to whether this state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is for the sake of attaining the desired or for the sake of abandoning the undesired. If it is argued that this is known from scripture (āgama), [the reply is:
from scripture it is understood that the liberated self possesses eternal happiness; thus, the liberated one becomes happy.

090.06 It is heard [in scripture]. Even such scriptural authority (*āgama*) must be investigated in this way: does it speak of a union with eternal happiness, or does it speak of an absolute separation from suffering? For it is observed in many ways in the world that the word "happiness" (*sukha*) is employed even in the absence of suffering. And thus, when common people explain their recovery from fever and other ailments, [they use the term "happiness"].

They think, "We have become happy. However, if this one who observes [the path] were to proceed out of an attachment to pleasure, thinking that there is eternal happiness in liberation, why would he not be liberated?
For attachment is designated as a bond; since attachment is designated as a bond, even if it were [to arise] from aversion...
One proceeds with the thought, "I shall abandon suffering," yet even so, one is not liberated because hatred is recognized as a bond.
Thus, since passion and hatred are bonds, it is not by way of aversion [that liberation occurs]. It is not contrary;
rather, there is the abandonment of suffering. Furthermore, this person does not hate suffering; and not hating it, he proceeds.

One attains the cessation of suffering, which is contrary [to defilements]; thus others [hold] that the mind is liberated from passion (*rāga*) and the rest by virtue of their capacity therein. For the mind, under the influence of passion and so forth, arises with respect to other objects and other states;
however, passion and the rest have no such capacity regarding the self (*ātman*). No, for they are established without effort in the path. Those who...
090.18–090.20: For those who desire liberation as the non-arising or the cessation of the mind, liberation is established effortlessly on their own path.

Why? Because birth has the purpose of destruction; since that which is born must perish, it is established that liberation is attained without effort on that path. [Objection: If liberation is the non-arising of the continuum (*saṃtati*), [we reply: no, because that is impossible for a continuum.
091.01 Arising cannot be produced, because the causal relationship exists as a continuous stream (santati).

091.02 If it is argued that "the non-arising of the future is produced," since the non-arising of the future already exists, what is produced? In every way, the liberation of the mind is not established; for whom [then] could it be?

In that case, regarding liberation (*apavarga*): what is it that is liberated? Is it the self (*ātman*)? And what is this liberation? It is the dissociation from suffering and the other [afflictions].

091.06 Immediately after the object of knowledge (*prameya*), there is the attainment (*prāpti*) of doubt which possesses a locus; this is the statement of its definition. 091.07 That which follows immediately after the object of knowledge in the sequence is now being described.

091.08 [1-1-23] Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a deliberation (*vimarśa*) that depends upon a specific distinction, arising from the perception of common or multiple properties, from conflicting opinions, from the perception of what is apprehended and unapprehended, and from the lack of a fixed determination.
091.09–10 Regarding the aphorism "arising from the perception of common or multiple properties": therein, "common property" (*samāna-dharma*) refers to...

091.11 Doubt arises from the appearance of common properties (*dharma*), from conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*), and from uncertainty (*saṃśaya*). Doubt is indeed threefold because of the qualification of the other terms; such is the meaning of the Sūtra. 091.12 In this context, doubt is a cognition (*pratyaya*) characterized by the non-determination of the true nature of an object, produced from such causes as the perception of common properties. That which does not determine the specific distinction of an object is called "doubt. It is a cognition that lacks determination.

And [to say] that it consists of itself (*ātmaka*) is contradictory, just as this [cognition] has the nature of determining its object; yet this does not determine the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the object.

If it were to determine the intrinsic nature of the object, its status as a cognition (*pratyayatva*) would be contradicted, for it is not from the communication of its own nature that its status as a cognition is contradicted.
Its own nature is indeed perceived, but it does not determine the intrinsic nature of the object; and therefore—
091.17 Doubt is called "cognition" (*pratyaya*) because it is perceived. The word *samāna* has the meaning of "common" (*sādhāraṇa*).
091.18 [The phrase] "from the occurrence of a common property" means "of that which is common. But what here is common?
Is it a quality (*guṇa*) or a universal (*sāmānya*)? If it were a quality, it would not be common.
091.20 Why? Because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) subsists in a single substance, and dimension (*parimāṇa*) likewise subsists in a single substance;

how then could it be common [to many]? Thus, even the claim that it is a universal (*sāmānya*) is not tenable, because it does not subsist in a substance. 092.01 For verticality (*ūrdhvatva*) does not reside in a substance, but rather in a quality (*guṇa*); for verticality does not operate within dimension.

092.02 A universal (sāmānya) ought to produce doubt regarding a substance; why? Because the quality has been ascertained. Since that which resides [in it] is the universal, and it has been ascertained as such, this is not because the meaning of "common" (sādhāraṇa) is explained otherwise. We do not say that the quality is common, nor even that the universal is so; rather, it is in the sense of similarity (sādṛśya).

092.05 As long as I previously perceived the two objects, the property (*artha*) of those two exists as a property (*dharma*) characterized by upwardness; by that property, 092.06 this similar property is apprehended. Thus, its "arising" (*upapatti*) is its determination (*adhyavasāya*).
