Furthermore, since it is not stated "because of the perception of a common property," [the objection] is also untenable.
Why? Because the designation of that which is being traversed (*gamyamāna*) is understood [as redundant]. By what, then, is this understood?
It is understood by the statement "dependent on a particular" (*viśeṣāpekṣa*). How is there dependence on a particular? It is the expectation or desire for it; and that [particular] is not perceived.

It is connected with the particular (*viśeṣa*). And if this [cognition] does not perceive the particular, because of the non-perception of the particular (092.12), it is understood that it thus perceives the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, if it were to perceive neither the universal nor the particular (092.13), then the statement "it depends on the particular" would be meaningless; it is understood by implication through this [fact].

"One perceives the universal. Now, if the word "upapatti" (logical proof/establishment) is indeed a synonym for "upalabdhi" (perception), then "upapatti" is the state of being accessible through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that is "upalabdhi. Furthermore, a property (*dharma*) whose existence is not being perceived is as if it were non-existent. But what is the similarity between that which exists and that which does not exist?

Because it lacks a basis for valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even that which is non-existent cannot independently serve as the basis of a valid cognition. Since that too has reached the characteristic of being unperceived, [the author] refers to the subject by means of the word "object" (*viṣaya*), or alternatively, he states that the cognition of the subject is established by the expression "arising of a common property. This is the worldly [convention].
Or rather, one blocks the logical principle by means of this statement, as speakers do in the world:

"Fire is inferred from smoke. Now, the word "seeing" (*darśana*) is not heard in the sentence; however, because it conveys the meaning, one does not require the word "seeing" in the sentence, for having seen the smoke, the object—fire—is inferred.

093.03 Thus, it should be stated that [the cause of doubt] is "the non-exclusion [of alternatives]. As for this phrase, "the occurrence of a common property" (samāna-dharma-upapatti), 093.04 this term is not itself the cause of exclusion; rather, it should be stated as "the occurrence of a common property.
093.05 For the mere occurrence of a common property is not the cause of doubt; otherwise, [doubt would arise] from [properties such as] being produced (kṛtakatva) and so forth.

[Objection: "There might still be doubt, because 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) is common to all impermanent things; thus, it cannot be a reason for exclusion (vyavaccheda-hetu). [Response: No, because the meaning of "common" has not been properly understood. It is logical that a property which is common [to the subject and the dissimilar class] can be a reason for exclusion, provided it is intended as belonging to that specific class [of the similar class].

That which, while being a property [of the subject], occurs in what is of a different class is the cause of exclusion; and for that, there is no commonality with the object. For a common property is one which, while occurring in that intended class, also occurs in another class; therefore, it should not be said that such a thing is not a cause of exclusion.

This common property (sādhāraṇa-dharma), being perceived, is a cause of doubt—is it [the cause] alone? No, it is not alone; rather, it is [the cause of doubt] because of the non-settlement of both perception and non-perception. And if perception and non-perception are not settled, is this much alone the proof?

It is said: "No. If there is a desire for a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*), one perceives a common property (*samāna-dharma*). Perception and non-perception do not remain fixed [as such]. However, as long as there is a desire for a specific distinction in terms of "this-ness" (*idantayā*), there arises doubt regarding the object. Is this the complete cause?

We say that it is either non-composite or composite. If it is merely stated as "the occurrence of a common property," then even for one who has apprehended an object, there would be doubt because there is a general apprehension of it. Furthermore, if doubt were merely the lack of determination between apprehension and non-apprehension, [then doubt would arise even in such cases].

093.21 Thus, if it were said merely that there is an "undetermined state" regarding perception and non-perception even for that whose universal has not been perceived, 093.22 there would be doubt as to whether it exists. And if it were said merely that [the cause] "requires a particular," 094.01 there would be doubt as to whether there is a recollection of a particular even for that whose universal has not been perceived. In this way, the case is the same.

And regarding the two terms "non-establishment of the apprehension and non-apprehension of the property" (*dharma-upalabdhi-anupalabdhi-avyavasthiti*), for one situated on a moving boat or similar vehicle, no doubt arises. Thus, because there is a lack of determination between apprehension and non-apprehension, [the definition] requires a qualification (*viśeṣa-apekṣa*).
If these two terms were applied elsewhere as well, there would be doubt regarding the object of non-apprehension, due to the occurrence of common characteristics (*samāna-dharma-upapatti*).
And when it is said that [the cause of doubt] is "dependence upon a particularity," even when there is the perception of a commonality, if there is a desire for a particularity,

a doubt arises because of the establishment of perception and non-perception. When this observer previously perceives something possessing both a generality and a particularity, and therein perception and non-perception are established, this is [the case].

When the observer departs from that state, then, due to his departure and the resulting distance, the specific particulars of limited scope do not appear; rather, the universal of great scope appears. Furthermore, perception and non-perception become established, there is recollection of the particulars, and no doubt arises.

Therefore, the complete definition is stated by excluding one or two terms. Because of the occurrence of common properties (*samāna-dharma*), and because of the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception, as well as the requirement for specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*), the exclusion of a single term is made. [This occurs] through the perception of common properties and the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception, which constitute the occurrence of common properties.

And regarding the phrase "dependent upon a distinguishing feature" (*viśeṣāpekṣaḥ*), it is because of the lack of determination between perception and non-perception that one is dependent upon a distinguishing feature.

Thus, the exclusion of two terms has been made; for by the inclusion of the compound term, doubt is a deliberation dependent upon a distinguishing feature, arising from the perception of common properties and from the lack of determination between perception and non-perception.

Thus he says; by this, he makes it known that this is the complete definition. "Vimarśa" (deliberation) means the discernment of multiple objects. It is called *saṃśaya* (doubt) because it, as it were, touches upon both objects;
it is a derivation based on the state (*bhāva-sādhana*) or a derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). By means of this, the self is made to doubt, as if it were asleep.

What is the purpose of a comparison? The purpose of a comparison is the non-determination of the object. By this, [the cases of] the occurrence of multiple properties and of conflicting views are explained. What is the purpose of an extension (*atideśa*)? Just as in the first word, by the inclusion of three words, the abandonment of two words was made in a single word; so too it is for the first and the subsequent ones.

"It is to be seen. [Objection: "Doubt arises from the occurrence of multiple properties (*aneka-dharma*). [Response: If it is argued that "multiple" refers to the property of many things (*anekasya aneka-dharmaḥ*), then the property of many things—characterized as substance, quality, and action—is their being produced by conjunction (*saṃyogajatva*). Furthermore, the property of many things consists of being produced by conjunction, being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), being devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*), and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
095.05. If it is argued that, in the case of sound, there is thus doubt because of the occurrence of multiple properties (*aneka-dharma*), that is incorrect.

095.06. This is because the purpose has already been fulfilled by the phrase "from the occurrence of common properties" (*samāna-dharma-upapatti*). By the very expression "from the occurrence of common properties," 095.07.
that which exists in one and many—that is, that which exists in many—is already obtained; therefore, [the former reason] has fulfilled its purpose. It is not [necessary].
Furthermore, there is a purpose for the designation of "multiple properties" (*aneka-dharma*). Now, what is the meaning of the term "multiple properties"?

How, moreover, is a "unique property" (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) designated by this common term "multiple properties"? [It is so called] because it distinguishes [the object] from both similar and dissimilar classes. It is "common" (*samāna*)—...

And because it is of a different class and manifold, the property (dharma) that distinguishes it from the manifold is called "the manifold property" (*aneka-dharma*). Alternatively, it is the property of those many [individuals], or it is the property belonging to each of them individually; thus it is "the manifold property. Or, the property is called "the manifold property" because it is the cause of the cognition of both the one and the many, since by means of it there arises the cognition: "This is one."

Regarding "the manifold" (*aneka*): therein, non-difference (*abheda*) is the cause of a single cognition (*eka-pratyaya*); a property (*dharma*) that is a particular (*viśeṣa*) is the cause of a manifold cognition (*aneka-pratyaya*).

For example, sound has the quality of being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajatva*). [Sound] is distinguished from generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) by its particularity, such as existence (*sat*) and so forth; however, within that [category of sound], it is distinguished as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*karman*) because it is produced by disjunction.

There is doubt. For it is not observed that any one among substances, qualities, or actions arises from disjunction (*vibhāga*), because [arising from disjunction] is impossible in all cases; thus, the fact of being produced by disjunction creates doubt due to its exclusion from everything else. But surely, there exists the quality of disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*)? It has not been accepted...

This is the case for the disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*). However, for one who does not accept a disjunction produced by disjunction, this is the probans for the determination: "Sound is a quality because it is produced by disjunction, like a disjunction produced by disjunction.
Or, let it be that [sound] also has a disjunction produced by disjunction as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*).

Sound has as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa) the disjunction produced by disjunction (vibhāgaja-vibhāga), and it is not any other category of entity. Thus, being "produced by disjunction" means having "the disjunction produced by disjunction" as its non-inherent cause; this does not occur except for sound.
Therefore, this reason, being excluded from all [other] things, is a cause of doubt because it lacks a distinguishing feature among those things of the same class that are distinct entities.

"Because it is observed in both ways. Or, through the application of a common property (*samāna-dharma*), there arises a non-common [property] (*asamāna*) among many properties. Alternatively, since both the common property and the non-common [property] are presented as causes for doubt, the non-common [property] is that which is not applied when the common property is applied; it is the object of the term "many" (*aneka*).
Regarding the term "viśeṣe" (in the particular): why, then, is it not simply stated as "the occurrence of similar and dissimilar properties"?

It is not possible to state it thus, because the analysis [of the compound] as "that property which is excluded from many" cannot be maintained; nor is there any purpose for brevity, since brevity is achieved by the reduction of even a single syllable.

Or, the designation is based on its purpose. If it means "having multiple properties" or "having a unique property," and if that unique property is a cause for doubt—such as [the argument] "this living body is not soulless, because it would follow that it has a beginning"—then this too, due to its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*), results in being a cause for doubt; yet this is not a fault.

Just as a common property (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*) is a cause of doubt, so too, when a positive concomitant (*anvayin*) possesses commonality, it does not become a cause of doubt because of its deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*). Likewise, for a negative concomitant (*vyatirekin*), even when it possesses uncommonality (*asādhāraṇatva*), both deviation and non-deviation are the causes of doubt and certainty respectively; that which is deviant is [the cause of doubt].

If it is argued that "that which is non-deviant (avyabhicārī) is the cause of certainty (nirṇaya-hetu)," then, since both [the similar and dissimilar properties] are deviant, they would both be causes of doubt. But surely this is already covered by the [definition of the cause of doubt as] "the occurrence of a common property" (*asamāna-dharma-upapatti*); since the meaning is already established by that, this [cause of doubt] should not be mentioned separately as a cause of doubt. True; however, it cannot be [defined] otherwise than through its deviance.

096.19 It is not a cause for doubt; rather, when there is deviation (*vyabhicāritā*), there is deviation in what is being affirmed (096.20), and there is the exclusion of deviation in what is being negated—this is the distinction. By the phrase "because of the occurrence of a common property" (096.21), the deviation in what is being affirmed is taught; by the phrase "because of being produced from division" (*vibhāgajatvāt*), the exclusion of deviation is [taught].
Thus, there is a separate mention for this much [reason], because the negative particle (*nañ*) has *paryudāsa* (exclusion) as its scope.

Some say that "multiple properties" (*aneka-dharma*) refers to the occurrence of two non-deviant properties (*avyabhicāri-dharma*). Others, however, explain it differently: "multiple properties" means different from one [property]; and thus, [it applies to] the non-deviant contradictory (*viruddha-avyabhicārin*).

The conjunction of two properties (*dharma-dvaya-upanipāta*) with respect to which one speaks of "reasoning" (*tarka*) is the cause of doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*), as in the case of audibility and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) in regard to sound. That is incorrect, because it is impossible.
For two non-deviant, contradictory properties cannot possibly exist in a single object, that is, in a real entity (*vastu*).
Because two forms are impossible, if both were non-deviant, a single entity would have to be dual-natured;
but this is not the case, therefore neither of them is non-deviant. Furthermore, this formal argument is not tenable.
Why? Because if he employs it in the manner in which we [Buddhists] employ our reason (*hetu*), [it would be valid].
"In the same way, this [case] also [is so]. It is established that designations are made by means of what is well-known; thus, everything is devoid of a cause.
Because the subsequent [response] is sublated by the apprehension of a contradictory meaning, it is not stated. Or rather, it is formulated as follows:
"Just as the second inference does not exist, so too the preceding one does not exist"—thus it is understood.

The second inference is not a proof here because [it is argued that] two contradictory properties cannot coexist in one place. [We reply: they can coexist; therefore, they are not contradictory. And what is the meaning of "contradictory"? Is it non-coexistence, or is it the proving of contradictory objects, or is it their essential nature? If it means non-coexistence, that does not exist, because they are observed [together].

097.15 Now, if contradiction (*virodha*) consists in the establishment of contradictory properties, that too is not tenable, because it is impossible for a single entity to possess a dual nature. 097.16 If these two properties were to establish contradictory objects, a single entity would result in having a dual nature. Alternatively, if their essential natures (*svarūpa*) are contradictory, nothing is sublated.
Since being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not the same as being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*), nor is being audible the same as being produced, therefore there is no doubt.

Or, even granting that there is a contradiction, if a doubt regarding sound were created by two contradictory properties—being produced and being audible—by the perception of what [would cause it], would that doubt be removed? By the perception of what specific characteristic would it cease?

For when a specific characteristic is perceived, there is no further desire for a specific characteristic, just as there is no desire for a specific characteristic once a general property has been apprehended. If it is argued that [doubt] will be removed by perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no;
that doubt regarding an object which arises from two conflicting means of inference (*anumāna*) will be removed by perception.
This is not tenable, because it is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This matter is not within the scope of direct perception.
[The question remains: "Is sound impermanent? If you say that this will be resolved through scripture (*āgama*), no;
for scripture itself is what is being investigated. This very scripture is being examined: "Is sound..."

"Is it eternal or non-eternal? This is neither an object of perception nor an object of scripture; it cannot be determined by means of the two [other] forms of inference. Thus, this unavoidable doubt has arisen. Let it be so. What is contradicted for us? How is it not contradicted? When inference is that which determines another entity...
For example, [the argument] "cognition is impermanent because it is produced" (kṛtakatvāt) is as follows:

this very property of being produced (kṛtakatva) is observed in sound, yet its nature remains undetermined as to whether it is permanent or impermanent. Since this property of being produced is perceived there [in sound], but elsewhere—in cognition and so forth—it is a cause for doubt, all inference [is thus characterized].

098.11 There would be no proof of impermanence, and this logic would subvert all inference; [this is the objection]. 098.12 This logic, which cuts away the very root of inference, is not fit to be subverted, because permanence is impossible.
098.13 This logic does not subvert [the position] of one for whom nothing is permanent; for such a person, there is no contradiction.
[The opponent claims: "It is non-deviant [for us]. But in our position, nothing at all is eternal. [Reply: No.

Because you have not fully understood the sublation (*bādha*), you have not perceived the actual object of sublation; rather, you merely state a fault in the opposing position by saying, "In our view, nothing is eternal," yet this applies to you as well.
In this case, the "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) [reason] finds its scope;

for instance: "Consciousness is with resistance (sapratigha), because it exists, like form," says one; another says, "Consciousness is without resistance (apratigha), because it has its own nature (svarūpa), like sensation (vedanā).
Thus, due to the occurrence of these two non-erroneous properties, it would be established as neither with nor without resistance. Therefore—
098.20 This is an improper argument; because of the conjunction of two contradictory properties, there is doubt regarding sound.

098.21 Because the two properties are constant, the expression [of them as alternating] is untenable; this sound is never perceived as lacking those properties. 098.22 Rather, it is constantly possessed of those properties, being both audible and produced.

There would be no such expression as "it is eternal" or "it is impermanent. For this observer could never, at any time, perceive both the properties of a post and a person in a single object and yet be able to say, "It is either a post or a person; it will not be thus"—this is a contradictory statement. But surely you yourself assert this?
"It is eternal," so I also declare; why then is it not described as "impermanent"?

This logic of the "non-deviating contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin), when examined, subverts inference in every respect. Enough of this! Now, suppose that "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and "audibility" (śrāvaṇatva) together constitute the reason.
Nevertheless, even when taken together, producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) do not differ from "arising from disjunction" (*vaibhāgajatva*);
for just as arising from disjunction is a cause of doubt regarding sound because it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), being excluded from other things,
so too producedness and audibility are causes of doubt because they reside in sound and are impossible elsewhere.
This [property] is indeed unique and not a separate property; it is subsumed by that very apprehension. Therefore, one must say that a property other than one is a "multiple property.
Furthermore, when two such properties belong to a single entity, then, having perceived it, what [is there] of that entity?
Therefore, when the capacity of those two properties is to be understood, effort must be made to comprehend that capacity— namely,
which of these two is the proof (*sādhana*) and which is not the proof (*asādhana*). And when such effort is exerted, it remains focused precisely upon those things that prove impermanence.
Why? Because eternality is sublated by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and we shall explain that further below.
Thus, it is established that doubt arises from a unique property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) due to the occurrence of multiple properties.
Therefore, the claim that "doubt arises from conflicting opinions" (*vipratipatti*) is a discourse with a contradictory meaning; for [the term] "conflicting opinion"—

099.19 For one who perceives that the meaning of a word is the object of a conflicting discourse regarding its referent, there arises—given the presence or absence of perception—099.20 a state of non-settlement; and when there is recollection of the specific meanings contained therein, doubt occurs.
099.21 In this regard, the common and multiple properties reside in the object of knowledge, whereas perception and non-perception reside in the knower.

[This is] the commentary. In that regard, perception and non-perception do not individually constitute causes for doubt; this has already been discussed. Furthermore, we do not understand how it can be said that "the property of the object of knowledge is both common and manifold. Is it the property (*dharma*) here that is the cause of doubt, or is it the cognition (*jñāna*)? It is not the property.

100.03 It has been established in many ways that [the cause of doubt] is the cause of uncertainty (*saṃśaya*). However, the cognition of common or multiple properties (*samāna-aneka-dharma-jñāna*) is the cause of doubt, and since that resides in the knower (*jñātṛ*), there is no difference [in substance]. As for the separate mention of "common" and "multiple" properties, the purpose for their separate mention has already been stated: it is due to the distinction between the property being affirmed and the property being negated.
100.06. Thus: "Divergence of opinion" (*vipratipatti*) is this cause of doubt residing in the speaker. [The question arises: "Who among these have understood correctly? 100.07.
"Who have erred?"—it is by means of such a distinction that the listener experiences doubt; therefore, it is mentioned separately. 100.08.

If it is argued that "this very thing is the common property (*samāna-dharma*)," [we reply] that the perception of a common property depends upon the expectation of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣa*).

100.09. Since both "investigation" (*vimarśa*) and "apprehension" (*pratipatti*) are already included within this very term "common property" (*samāna-dharma*), it would be redundant [to mention them separately].

100.10. Furthermore, there is no purpose in mentioning "the occurrence of distinct and multiple properties" (*pṛthag-aneka-dharma-upapatti*) and "conflicting opinions" (*vipratipatti*), because they are already subsumed therein.
100.11. Therefore, it should be stated as follows: "Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is an investigation characterized by a desire for distinction, arising from the occurrence of a common property."

100.12 This is not taught because of a lack of thorough knowledge of the meaning of the Sūtras; for, without thoroughly knowing the meaning of the Sūtras, this is taught. And as for the distinction [between types of doubt], it has been described as arising from the occurrence of common and multiple properties, and from conflicting opinions (100.13). Others, however, describe five distinct types of doubt by means of the terms "occurrence of common properties" and so forth (100.14).
100.15–16: "Doubt is a deliberation that depends upon a particularity [and arises] from the occurrence of common properties"—this applies to the remaining terms as well.
100.16–17: That is not correct, because the non-establishment of perception and non-perception is a qualifier of the preceding term;
for when there is the occurrence of common properties and the non-establishment of perception and non-perception, [the mind] depends upon a particularity.

The meaning of the sūtra is that "deliberation" (vimarśa) is doubt (saṃśaya). Thus, it should be stated [as the cause of doubt] as "the occurrence of multiple properties and conflicting opinions. Therefore, the non-establishment of perception and non-perception is not a separate cause of doubt.
Doubt arising from the duality of perception and non-perception is not logical, because it contradicts common worldly experience.
101.01. One who asserts that doubt arises because of the twofold nature of apprehension and non-apprehension contradicts common experience.

101.02. How so? Whatever this person perceives, he would have doubt regarding everything; yet one ought not to be in a state of constant doubt. 101.03. For what reason? Because that which is being perceived is of two kinds. But [the opponent] says it is because of the twofold nature of apprehension...

101.04. "Doubt arises; from what is its cessation? It ceases through the perception of a specific characteristic (viśeṣa)," if [you say this], then regarding those very specific characteristics that are perceived, one might ask: "Are these existent or non-existent? 101.05–06.
As long as there is doubt due to the twofold nature of perception, the doubt is unavoidable. Thus it is with non-perception (anupalabdhi).
Even if this twofold nature were stated, there would be no confidence in him anywhere.

When he perceives a snake or the like in a room or similar place, there arises the doubt: "Is that house like one containing a snake, or like one without a snake? This doubt, too, would be entirely irremovable; thus, there would be no confidence in any matter whatsoever. And for those who...

101.10 The meaning of the sūtra is that doubt is fivefold; by them [the opponents], its distinction based on causes must be stated, 101.11 or else its distinction based on intrinsic nature (svabhāva). If it is caused by external factors, then it follows that doubt is not fivefold but rather manifold in form. 101.12 Alternatively, if it were due to a difference in intrinsic nature, that is impossible, because there can be no difference in intrinsic nature; thus, it would be uniform in form.
101.13 "Doubt" (*saṃśaya*) means uncertainty. Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is not that doubt is fivefold.

101.14 Doubt does not arise from the perception of a common property (*samāna-dharma*), because [doubt] has the locus of properties (*dharmin*) as its object. As for this statement that "doubt arises from the occurrence of a common property," that is incorrect; because it has the locus of properties as its object, for [the common property] is not... in the same [locus].

101.16 When the property (*dharma*) has been apprehended, doubt regarding the substratum (*dharmin*) is not tenable, because of the distinction between the property and the substratum. For when a cow is seen, there is no doubt regarding a horse [as the substratum]; and since the substratum has not been seen, [there can be no doubt]. Furthermore, it is a contradiction to say that there is doubt regarding what has not been apprehended or determined. Some maintain that doubt arises from the relationship between the property and the substratum.

101.19 Some first offer this rebuttal: "When the property (*dharma*) is perceived, there is doubt regarding the substratum (*dharmī*). 101.20 [They argue that] because the state of being a substratum is not established [for the perceived], the diversity [of the two] does not cease through the relation of property and substratum. Now, 102.01 if it is argued that the rule governing the relation of property and substratum is the Sūtra beginning with "desire" (*icchā-ādi*), then how is that [Sūtra] contradicted?

102.02 The meaning of the Sūtra is that desire and the rest lead to the inference of a self because of their reconnection (*pratisandhāna*). Regarding this, the opponent has objected: "Because of reconnection [which arises] from the relation of cause and effect, [the inference] does not establish plurality. By the statement "because it is not sublated" (*abādhanāt*), this objection is refuted. Here, however, you have stated [the reason] as "because of the relation of property and property-possessor" (*dharma-dharmi-bhāvāt*).

Furthermore, it is said that for those who speak [of the relationship], the very distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*)—as characterized by their specific relation—is the regulator.
An opponent might also be able to say that the causal relationship (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*) is the regulator; therefore, this is a misinterpretation.
This doubt arises from the relationship between the property and the substratum. Now, [the doubt] arises from the perception of a common property (*samāna-dharma*).

102.08: "If doubt arises regarding another subject (*dharmin*) that has been apprehended, what is the resolution? 102.09: This is the resolution: because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the term "subject" (*dharmin*) is expressed [by the compound]; thus, by the phrase "due to the occurrence of properties" (*dharmopapatti*), it is the subject itself that is designated within the *bahuvrīhi* compound. How so? [It is explained as follows: 102.10: [The compound means] "that which has the occurrence of properties. In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is the subject (*dharmin*) alone that is being referred to. How? [By the following: "That which possesses the occurrence of properties is the subject. Therefore, since the subject is indicated by the word "occurrence of properties," there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word "property" (*dharma*) here refers to the property of being a cause (*kāraṇadharma*). Because the occurrence of such a property is possible, the subject is established; therefore, there is no fault. Alternatively, the word "property" (*dharma*) here refers to the property of being an effect (*kāryadharma*). Because the occurrence of such a property is possible, the subject is established; therefore, there is no fault. Or else, the word "property" (*dharma*) here refers to the property of being a logical mark (*liṅgadharma*). Because the occurrence of such a property is possible, the subject is established; therefore, there is no fault. Thus, the meaning is that when the subject is apprehended through the occurrence of its properties, there is no room for doubt. Consequently, the statement that "doubt arises regarding another apprehended subject" is not a valid objection. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the word "property" (*dharma*) here refers to the property of being a logical mark (*liṅgadharma*). Because the occurrence of such a property is possible, the subject is established; therefore, there is no fault. Thus, the meaning is that when the subject is apprehended through the occurrence of its properties, there is no room for doubt. Consequently, the statement that "doubt arises regarding another apprehended subject" is not a valid objection. This is the intended meaning. Moreover, the word "property" (*dharma*) here refers to the property of being a logical mark (*liṅgadharma*). Because the occurrence of such a property is possible, the subject is established; therefore, there is no fault. Thus, the meaning is that when the subject is apprehended through the occurrence of its properties, there is no room for doubt. Consequently, the statement that "doubt arises regarding another apprehended subject" is not a valid objection. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the word "property" (*dharma*) here refers to the property of being a logical mark (*liṅgadharma*). Because the occurrence of such a property is possible, the subject is established; therefore, there is no fault. 102.11 One whose property (*dharma*) is common [to two things] is "one of common property" (*samāna-dharman*); the arising of such a person is "the arising of one of common property" (*samāna-dharma-upapatti*). 102.12 What is meant by this? It means from the perception of a subject (*dharmī*) possessing common properties. 102.13 Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a deliberation that depends on specific distinctions; "depending on specific distinctions" means depending on the recollection of specific [features].
102.14 “With regard to ‘dependence’: now, is that recollection of specific features (viśeṣa-smṛti) directed toward those specific features themselves, or is it directed toward something else?

102.15–16 “Does one recollect those specific features of the very object of doubt which one perceives as possessing common characteristics, or does one recollect those of something else? If it were the former, that would not be logical, because [the specific features] of that [object]...”

In some cases, because of non-experience, that object—having previously perceived its specific qualities—recalls those qualities belonging to it. (102.18) Thus, it is logical [that there is recollection] because those specific qualities have been experienced; however, when this [object] is being perceived as a generality (*sāmānya*) whose specific qualities were not previously perceived, doubt arises. In that case, how can there be a recollection of those specific qualities? (102.19)

"Because it has been experienced"—no, because it is a general statement. [The phrase] "dependent on a particular" means that when the particulars contained therein—whether of that [object] or of something else—are intended to be determined by this general statement, then there is a recollection of the particulars previously experienced; however, when they have not been perceived...
103.03 First, there is doubt; then, due to similarity, one desires to recall the specific qualities residing in other [objects].
Thus, 103.04 when [the process] is established, doubt is threefold. And by this definition of doubt, those other contradictory [cases] are also included, such as that which belongs to the Kāśyapīyas.
103.06. Doubt arises from the perception of a commonality, the non-perception of specific qualities, and the recollection of those specific qualities. The meaning of this is as follows:

103.07. "From the perception of a commonality" means from the perception of that which possesses commonalities; "non-perception of specific qualities" (103.08) means that the specific qualities are not fixed—that is, their specific qualities are not determined—and thus doubt arises from the recollection of those specific qualities.

103.09 Thus it is the same. But how, then, is the uncommon [reason] obtained by means of this sūtra? 103.10 It is obtained because of deviation; for that which deviates is common, and since deviation exists even in the case of the uncommon, it is thereby obtained. In that case, the occurrence of multiple properties is not separate.

103.12 They should be recited separately when there is a desire to express the distinction between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, [they are stated] with the desire to express the distinction between the causes of doubt (103.13). As for those who describe a redundancy (*paunaruktya*) in the two terms "because of the non-perception of the particular" (*viśeṣāpratyakṣāt*) and "because of the non-recollection of the particular" (*viśeṣāsmṛteḥ*), [the response is that] when it is stated that "doubt arises from the perception of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the recollection of the particular," [the meaning is already established].

103.15 It is said that this [object] is cognized because its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are not perceived; for no one remembers specific qualities that have never been perceived. That is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra. This is not the meaning of the Sūtra:
that there is a non-perception of specific qualities. Rather, it means that there is a lack of perception of specific qualities belonging to an indeterminate [object].
"Therefore, this is not a fault. Others, however, explain the definition of doubt differently:

"Doubt is a deliberation by one who, having observed a commonality, desires to apprehend the specific difference. Even by them, since the commonality has already been ascertained, the object of the doubt must be stated. If it is argued that it is the locus (dharmin), then has that not already been mentioned as the object of doubt?

104.01. It has been stated that the subject (*dharmin*) is the object; however, this is not tenable. How is it not tenable? If, first of all, one accepts a subject distinct from its properties (*dharma*), there is a contradiction. For if one accepts the difference between property and subject, since the property is already determined [by other means], the subject would remain unperceived; indeed, when one thing is perceived, another is not.

104.04 Otherwise, there would be doubt. Furthermore, if by the expression "similarity" (*sādharmya*) it were meant that the subject (*dharmin*) itself is being stated according to our own position, 104.05 that would not be correct. For "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is the state of having similar properties (*sadharma-bhāva*);

thus, by the expression for a state (*bhāva*), 104.06 it is the property (*dharma*) that is denoted, not the subject (*dharmin*). Nor is it logical [to claim the subject is denoted], because since another [property] is observed, there would be no doubt regarding anything else.
104.07. Furthermore, even if one does not admit the existence of another object, since similarity has already been ascertained, where is there any doubt?
104.08. Thus, if this [person] does not perceive the substratum (dharmin), of what would he seek to perceive a particularity?
104.09. For particularities cannot exist apart from similarity. Or, if they are particularities belonging to that which possesses the universal...

104.10 Thus, it has been stated that "it is not so, because it is unperceived. [The opponent argues: "There are no universals (sāmānya) or particulars (viśeṣa). 104.11 By one who says that "particulars belong to that which possesses a universal," a distinction between the universal, the particular, and the possessor of these is admitted; and the statement is redundant, for there are no particulars belonging to the possessor of the universal. 104.12 [The opponent continues: "Particulars belong to that which possesses a universal"—by speaking thus, a distinction between the universal, the particular, and their possessor is conceded, and the designation is useless, since there are no particulars distinct from the possessor of the universal.

104.13 Thus. And when there is a determination of apprehension and non-apprehension, even though a similarity is observed, [if] there is a desire to know the specific [characteristic], 104.14 doubt does not arise; therefore, it must be stated that [the cause of doubt is] "the lack of determination regarding apprehension and non-apprehension" (upalabdhy-anupalabdhy-avyavasthānam).

And as for the phrase "from the observation of multiple properties" (aneka-dharma-darśanāt), it means "from the occurrence of common and multiple properties" (samānāneka-dharma-upapattiḥ); thus [it is said].

104.16 The opening statement concerning the definition of doubt is now examined: first of all, is this an instruction regarding the causes [of doubt], or is it a determination of the essential nature of doubt? If it is an indication of the causes, then this is too limited.
104.17–18 It is replied: because of "common and multiple properties" and so forth, there are other causes of doubt as well.
104.19 These [categories] are to be enumerated: for instance, the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*) is the internal contact of the self and the mind;

104.20 the contact of the sense organ and the object (*indriya-artha-sannikarṣa*) is the external [contact]. Now, as for the determination of its essential nature, the definition [of doubt] is stated: 104.21 "Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a state of wavering (*saṃśīti*)," which would otherwise be meaningless. Now, first, regarding the cause—

104.22: [Objection: Has it not been stated that this is a restrictive definition (*avadhāraṇa*), and that other causes must also be enumerated? [Response: No, this is not for the sake of restriction; rather, this is an indication of the specific cause (*asādhāraṇa-kāraṇa*). Therefore, there is no over-extension (*aprasaṅga*) to the contact between sense-faculty and object (*indriya-artha-sannikarṣa*) and so forth, because those are common to all forms of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Or, let it be an indication of its essential nature (*svarūpa-nirdeśa*).

105.03 This very nature [of doubt] arises from common characteristics (*sādharmya*) and so forth; thus, this kind of doubt (105.04) is employed as a constituent factor (*aṅga*) of inquiry (*vicāra*). Like doubt, error (*viparyaya*) is also a constituent factor of inquiry;
it too (105.05) must be stated as a category (*padārtha*). It is true that it is a category, but it is not a constituent factor of inquiry; therefore—

105.06–105.07: How is it that what is not the subject of inquiry is not a factor for investigation? Just as one who is in doubt strives toward the comprehension of its specific nature, one who is mistaken does not; thus, because it is not a constituent of the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*), it is not stated here.
105.08 [1-1-24] That object aiming at which one acts is the purpose (*prayojana*).
105.09 "That object aiming at which one acts is the purpose. Regarding the phrase "aiming at which object":
105.10 "Aiming at" (*adhikāra*) means resolve (*vyavasāya*). Of what is there the resolve? It is the resolve regarding the means for achieving pleasure and pain. This...
105.11 Knowing that this is a means to happiness, one strives for the attainment of happiness, thinking, "This is a means to happiness.

105.12 And [one strives] for the realization of the abandonment of suffering; for by the attainment of happiness and the abandonment of suffering, this world is driven forward. 105.13 Thus, the purpose is the attainment and abandonment of happiness and suffering. And by means of this purpose...

105.14 All meanings are thus subsumed. Furthermore, when another person is challenged regarding the meaning of a single sūtra with the intent of exposing a fault, there arises a worldly conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that cannot be avoided; this is the "purpose" (*prayojana*), because by means of this [usage], the meaning is established. And by this, nothing [contradictory] occurs to the principle (*nyāya*).
105.17–18. As for the claim that "it is being done" implies there is no status as a constituent of logic (*nyāya-aṅga-bhāva*), this is merely a worldly matter;

That [purpose] is not a constituent part of the reasoning itself; rather, it is the purpose that is the primary constituent of the method of investigation, because the method of investigation has that as its root.
(1-1-25) That object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts is [the subject matter].

106.10 That which is the object of both worldly people and investigators is the *dṛṣṭānta* (example). Therefore, non-worldly objects such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth would not be *dṛṣṭāntas*.

However, because it is stated by way of illustration that [an example] is the object of worldly people and investigators, it does not mean [the definition applies] only to worldly people and investigators. This is that very [point].

106.13 An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) may be for the purpose of explaining similarity (*sārūpya*), or it may be for the purpose of establishing what is unestablished (*asiddha-sādhana*). If, first of all, it is for the purpose of explaining similarity, then it does not differ from analogy (*upamāna*); if it is for the purpose of establishing what is unestablished, then it does not differ from the instance (*udāharaṇa*). If analogy is included within [the category of] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the instance is a member of the syllogism (*avayava*).
106.16 There is no separate example (*dṛṣṭānta*). We see that this response is irreparable.

106.17 Why? Because even the three [components] are not cognized. By speaking thus, neither the example nor the illustration (*udāharaṇa*) is understood; first of all, the analogy (*upamāna*) does not serve to produce an understanding of similarity (*sārūpya*).
106.19 It has been described. An example (dṛṣṭānta) is for the purpose of establishing similarity or for the purpose of proving what is not yet established; such is the example.
106.20 We shall explain that there is no need for an illustration when one is describing an illustration for the sake of providing an example.

[The term] *tantra* refers to the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*).

"We shall explain [this]. Regarding the statement "the indication of the probandum" (*sādhya-nirdeśa*) in the context of the proposition (*pratijñā*), there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to the case of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because the word "probandum" (*sādhya*) is a qualifier of the tenet (*siddhānta*). This word "probandum" qualifies the tenet; it does not refer to the mere object of proof (*sādhya-mātra*). Therefore, what over-extension could there be?

115.01. The term *siddhānta* (established tenet) qualifies the word *sādhya* (the probandum) by virtue of its immediate mention following the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). 115.02. Since the *siddhānta* has been determined immediately prior, if the *siddhānta* is the qualifier due to its immediate mention, then the statement of that [probandum] constitutes the *pratijñā* (thesis); it is not for the purpose of excluding a *sarvatantre-siddhānta* (a tenet established in all systems). 115.03. Therefore, its formulation is the *pratijñā*. It is not intended to exclude a tenet common to all systems.

115.04. If it is said that the "indication of that" (*tad-nirdeśa*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*), then because it is the subject under discussion, the tenet established by all schools (*sarva-tantra-siddhānta*) would also be drawn in by the word "that" (*tad*). Consequently, the indication of that would also be the thesis; therefore, by the inclusion of the term "to be proven" (*sādhya*), the tenet to be proven is connected [as the thesis], and not the tenet established by all schools—this follows by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).

115.07. "The refutation of the tenets common to all systems" (*sarva-tantra-siddhānta-nirākaraṇam*). Although this is a general term, and its specific designation is "proposition" (*pratijñā*), nevertheless, by implication, the tenet common to all systems is what is being refuted.

This is because a tenet common to all systems cannot be established [as a subject], whereas other types, such as those belonging to a particular system (*pratitantra*) and so forth, are possible at certain stages.

"Because it is that which is to be established (*sādhya*). For example, in the command "Feed the Brahmins," since it is impossible to feed every single Brahmin, a restriction (*niyama*) is understood by implication (*sāmarthya*). If one relies on such implication, then the statement "The formulation of that [probandum] is the thesis (*pratijñā*)"—which implies that the entirety [of the subject] is not explicitly denoted—should also not be made as a definition of the thesis.

115.13 It must be said: since you have not stated that the restriction is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*), how is our position not undermined? 115.14 How is it not undermined? That which was accepted is being set aside; for [the opponent] maintains that "the statement of that [which is to be proven] is the proposition" (*pratijñā*).

115.15 There is no such undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) because of the qualification by "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) and so forth; [the definition is]: "The statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the proposition," qualified by "desire to know" and so on.

115.16 Or, because of this qualification, the [unwanted] consequence does not follow: "The statement of the probandum is the thesis (*pratijñā*)," [defined] by means of inquiry (*jijñāsā*) and so forth.
115.17 This sentence—"the statement of the probandum is the thesis"—is qualified by the members (*avayava*) that initiate the discussion (*prakaraṇa*).
115.18 That object regarding which there is inquiry and so forth is the "probandum" (*sādhya*); the statement of that is the thesis.
115.19 Furthermore, what relevance would there be for the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here? Or, why should the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) be used in the sense of "deserving"?

115.20 [The opponent says: "The statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*"; here the gerundive suffix is used in the sense of "deserving," as in: that which deserves proof is the *sādhya*. 115.21] The statement of that is the thesis; however, the reason and the example do not deserve to be the means of proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, this [objection] does not apply.

115.22 Because of the difference in properties between the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), the property of being an object is one thing and the property of being an instrument is another; thus, [the agent]—116.01 [is established]. "That which is most desired to be reached is the object" is a property of the object, and it is not possible for the property of one thing to become the property of another. 116.02 Thus, this designation of the object is a designation of the goal (*sādhya*), which is the proposition (*pratijñā*); and the designation of the instrument is "visual" (*cākṣuṣa*).
116.03 Because of this, there is no such contingency. Alternatively, due to the distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the unestablished (*asiddha*), the probandum is something else.

116.04 One thing is established and another is unestablished; thus, the probandum is that which is established for one party but not for the other. 116.05 That which is employed as the object of action (*karman*) and is not agreed upon by both parties is "unestablished" (*asiddha*); that which is agreed upon by both parties is [the probandum].

116.06. By that [statement] "it is established" (*siddham*), there is the consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even what is unestablished (*asiddha*) would be the probandum (*sādhya*) because it was stated as "established.

116.07. Likewise, by the statement "it is the probandum" (*sādhyam*), there is the consequence that even what is established (*siddha*) would be unestablished. Now, if even that which does not follow [logically] is pointed out [as a fault]: 116.08. Then all objects (*artha*), even those already established, would have to be presented as the thesis (*pratijñā*). Or else, [if this were not so,]...

116.09. "The thesis (pratijñā) is the statement of the probandum (sādhya)"—this refers to the subject matter of the members [of the syllogism] such as the thesis. That which is the object of the members beginning with the thesis, namely the locus (dharmin) qualified by a well-known property, is the "probandum" (sādhya), because it is established as the substratum for another property; this does not apply in the same way to the reason (hetu) and the example (dṛṣṭānta). If this [objection] is raised:

116.12 There is a logical consequence [of this]; therefore, the inclusion of the word "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is useless, according to the view that "the statement of the probandum is the thesis" (*pratijñā*).

116.13 Because the probandum is not distinguished by the inclusion of the word "intended," there would be the consequence that the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are also [theses], since they too are probanda. 116.14 Thinking thus, some have formulated the definitions of the thesis (*pakṣa*) otherwise, as follows: "The thesis is that which..."

"Intended to be proven" (sādhayitum iṣṭaḥ). Here, first of all, the inclusion of the word "intended" (iṣṭa) is redundant, because fallacious reasons and fallacious examples have already been excluded by the term "to be proven" (sādhya). It is therefore incorrect to say that the inclusion of "intended" is for the purpose of excluding those [fallacies]. Furthermore, since the term "object" (karman) has been used, this [meaning] is already obtained; "intended" (iṣṭa) and "desired" (īpsita) are not different in meaning. Moreover, even if it were "unintended" (aniṣṭa)—

116.18 The term "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is employed for the purpose of excluding [unwanted] positions; indeed, it is by implication that what is contradicted by one's own words and so forth is not intended by him. 116.19 Just as it is said, "words are denoters," the non-denotative nature of words is thus rejected.
116.20 Furthermore, it is asserted that words themselves are uttered for the sake of communicating meaning.

116.21 Thus, [the statements] "fire is not hot" and "sound is not audible" are contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*). 116.22 Some describe this as a contradiction with perception; that is incorrect, because the functions of the sense organs (*indriya-vṛtti*) are themselves beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyatva*).
117.01 The functions of the sense organs are beyond the reach of the senses; it is not the case that one can say, "this is grasped by this sense organ, but this is not grasped by that."

117.02 Someone might argue: "It is perceived by someone; however, because it conforms to the presence and absence of that [perception], the functions of the sense organs are inferred from the cognition of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Therefore, this is not a valid example.
But rather, 'fire is not hot' would be a proper example. [To this we reply: For the Vaiśeṣika, the claim that "sound is eternal" contradicts scripture (*āgama*).

117.05 Thus, we see that this too is not contradicted by scripture (*āgama*). For the Vaiśeṣika has not accepted the impermanence of sound from scripture; rather, [he accepts it] through inference based on its causes and its specific context. 117.07 Since such is the case, that [position] is indeed contradicted by inference. Now, [if it is argued that it is accepted] because of the words of the author of the Sūtras—
If [you say] "it is established," that contradicts scripture (*āgama*). But surely the statement "the jar is eternal" is also a contradiction of scripture?
Therefore, [the claim] "liquor may be drunk by a Brahmin" is a contradiction of scripture; however, [the following] contradicts common consensus (*prasiddhi*):
we do not understand what this "contradiction of common consensus" is. Common consensus consists of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of valid cognition].

The comprehension of an object through one of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is, for example, "the moon is the hare-marked one" (*śaśin*). Therefore, [this] is included within the contradiction of a prior means of valid cognition (*pūrva-pramāṇa-virodha*); thus, we see no purpose in mentioning "contradiction of what is well-known" (*prasiddhi-virodha*) as something distinct. However, it is possible to understand that all of this is indeed a contradiction of what is well-known.

117.14 Thus, they recite the inclusion of the term "intended" (*iṣṭa*) for the purpose of excluding that [fault]. However, we see that all of this is not tenable. 117.15 How so? Because it is accepted that faults such as the subversion of one's own position (*svārthāpavāda*) constitute faults of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*).
117.16 Therefore, all these faults, beginning with the subversion of one's own position, are possible as faults of the proposition by virtue of being so accepted.
117.17 Thus, since the state of the matter remains as it was, how can there be a fault in the position?

117.18 For the object (*artha*) being expressed is exactly as it is even when not being expressed; thus, even the statement [itself]—117.19 "then it is just like this"—would not incur these faults. True, these are not faults of the object (*artha*), nor...

117.20–21. However, the defects of speech are actually the defects of the person; for those which are defects of the agent are manifested by means of the action (*kriyā*). Thus, by metaphorically attributing the defect of the agent to the action, it is said that "the action is defective. 118.01. In the same way, by metaphorically attributing the defects of the speaker to the speech, it is said that "the speech is defective"; yet in reality, [it is the speaker who is at fault].
118.02. The fault lies neither in the object nor in the expression; for since an object possesses the capacity for action, every object is capable of its own [specific] 118.03.
action. However, when that [object], which is capable of its own action, is employed in another action apart from its own, 118.04.
it reveals only the lack of skill on the part of the agent. In the same way, an expression also [is incapable] regarding its own meaning.

118.05 However, when employed with respect to another object, it reveals the speaker’s intention. Regarding the thesis (*pratijñā*): since the thesis has the subject (*pakṣa*) as its object, it is said that "faults of the thesis" are "faults of the subject. This is not correct, because it would follow that faults of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth would also be faults of the subject. If this were the case, then the reason and the others [would likewise be faults of the subject].
118.08. Since they are specific types of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the defects of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth also become defects of the thesis.

Consequently, 118.09, it should be stated that "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*) is a defect of the thesis, and not that refutations—such as those consisting of deficiency (*nyūnatā*), defects of the members (*avayava*), or defects of the rejoinder (*uttara*)—are [defects of the thesis] by way of being objections (*ākṣepa*). Alternatively, there will be a restriction based on the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*).

118.11 It is not correct [to say] "not by way of the relationship between the probandum and the probans," because there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*). 118.12 The thesis (*pakṣa*) stands as the object of the proof; and since it is the object of the statement, there is therein a restriction of the relationship between the expressed and the expresser (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*).
118.13 Let the defects of the statement reside in the thesis, but let them not arise from the relationship between the probandum and the probans. Proof...

118.14. There is no authority for the statement that "faults" (doṣāḥ) are "faults of the thesis" (pakṣa-doṣāḥ), and yet [you claim] faults of the statement (vacana-doṣāḥ) are metaphorically attributed (upacaryante) to the thesis.
118.15. For a metaphorical attribution is not possible when [the primary sense] is applicable, as in the case of "the cots are crying.
118.16. Since the action of crying is impossible in the cot itself, those situated on the cots are [meant] by one who is describing a common worldly expression.

118.17 Thus, in the case of persons who are the substrates [of the action], the metaphorical usage "the beds cry out" (mañcāḥ krośanti) is not applied by superimposing the word "beds" upon them, because [such] a means of valid cognition is impossible. 118.18 Nor do defects such as those pertaining to the thesis (pratijñā-doṣa) apply to the thesis, since they are impossible therein; for being impossible there, they must necessarily be established as belonging to the [opponent's] position (pakṣe).

118.20–21. Regarding the statement that [the word] should be used figuratively (*upacaryeran*), and that one who effects an accidental deviation from the primary meaning (*mukhya-artha-vyatikrama*)—as stated by the Naiyāyika—that [principle] would be contradicted, for it has been said: "When a reason is negated, an accidental deviation from the primary meaning is not obtained. 119.01. Alternatively, if by the term *iṣṭa* (intended) the worldly [usage] is meant—whereby "intended" (*iṣṭa*) means "accepted" (*abhipreta*)—then [the objection does not apply].
119.02 This point also is understood from the very act of proving [the goal], for no one proves what is undesirable (*aniṣṭa*).
119.03 Even for one who, out of fear, pursues what is undesirable, the cessation of that undesirability is itself desired; thus, it is not undesirable.
119.04 Therefore, the inclusion of the term "desired" (*iṣṭa*) is redundant. When analyzed in this way, the object is indeed "desired."

119.05. Regarding the term "proposition" (*pakṣa*), here too the inclusion of the word "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is useless. Furthermore, what kind of deliberation (*vicāraṇā*) is this? If it concerns the employment of proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), then when multiple things are present there, it is not known how that which is intended is to be understood—whether as the probandum (*sādhya*), as the means of proof (*sādhana*), or as the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). Or, is deliberation simply doubt (*saṃśaya*)?

119.08 Just as, for example, in the investigation of the existence or non-existence of a self (*ātman*), [it is said] "of the self's existence or non-existence" (119.09). As long as it is stated that there is doubt (*saṃśaya*), so long must it be stated that there is doubt regarding the investigation of the existence or non-existence of the self; this is not the meaning of the word "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*). 119.10 It is not [the case that]...

119.11. Investigation (*vicāraṇā*) is the examination of the locus of doubt; for what is called investigation occurs subsequent to doubt. 119.12. Consisting in the application of proof and refutation, it culminates in a definitive determination regarding one of the two positions; it is not itself doubt. 119.13. Thus, doubt is not a cognition characterized by ascertainment (*avadharaṇa*); therefore, there is no doubt in formal debate (*vāda*).
119.14 Because those two are [already] ascertained, for it is only those who are certain that engage in dispute.

119.15 Therefore, it has been refuted that "the thesis (pakṣa) is that which is intended to be proven. Since the inclusion of the term "intended" (īpsita) is for the purpose of excluding what is undesired, one need not state "not excluded by a contradictory object"; [this is already established by the definition of] the thesis.

119.17 Regarding the phrase "that which is intended to be established" (*yaḥ sadhayitum iṣṭaḥ*), by the inclusion of the word *iṣṭa* (intended), the undesirable position (*aniṣṭa-pakṣa*) is excluded here as well; because of the inclusion of the term "desired" (*īpsita*), the undesirable position is rejected. Thus, the second half of the subsequent verse need not be stated: "not contradicted by a contradictory object" (*viruddha-artha-anirākṛtaḥ*). Now, by this [phrase] "not contradicted by a contradictory object," the undesirable [positions]—

119.20. The faults of the thesis (*pakṣa-doṣa*) are being refuted; in that case, the inclusion of the term "intended" (*īpsita*) is redundant. Or, if both [the term "intended" and the term "not refuted by a contradictory object"] are used—119.21.

The inclusion of the term "intended" and [the phrase] "not refuted by a contradictory object" serve to refute the faults of the thesis. 119.22. Even in the statement, "That which is desired to be proven is the thesis," there is [the requirement of] "not being refuted by a contradictory object."

120.01 Thus it should be done. In every way, when these characteristics of the thesis (*pakṣa*) are examined, one [definition] reveals a deficiency and the other an excess. Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "himself" (*svayam*) in the phrase "that which is intended by himself as the probandum" (*sādhya-tvena īpsitaḥ*) is unnecessary. What is the reason? Because an object of action (*karman*) depends upon an agent (*kartṛ*); just as, for example, [one says] "the agent [cuts] the tree."

When it is said, "he cuts," it is understood that he does so himself; for one person does not cut what is to be cut by another. Likewise, when it is said, "one who has a goal is the accomplisher," it is understood that he accomplishes it himself. This [opponent], however, is confused regarding the application of his own words, failing to distinguish the fault of redundancy (*akṣarādhikya*). Furthermore, as for the *vādavidhāna*...
120.07. In the commentary, [the author] establishes this because the word "proves" (*sādhayati*) is identical whether used by oneself or by another. 120.08.

It is said that the qualification "by oneself" applies to this word "proves" because it has the same form when employed by the one who acts (*prayojya*) and the one who causes the action (*prayoktṛ*). 120.09. This is true; this word has the same form, yet it is not...

120.10 We see the purpose for employing the common formulation [of the definition]. Therefore, it should be stated thus: "The thesis is that which is intended to be proven. And because there is agreement regarding the actual state of things (*tattva*) between the proponent and the opponent, even though this word is identical in form to the case where there is no such agreement, it is indeed possible to employ it.
120.13 [The suffix] *tumun* is used in the sense of "to accomplish" (*sādhayati*) because it applies figuratively to the agent (*prayoktṛ*) and directly to the one who is made to act (*prayojya*).

120.14 Furthermore, due to the rule that *tumun* occurs when there is a common agent (*samāna-kartṛka*), this usage of *tumun* as in "in order to accomplish" (*sādhayitum*) is observed only in cases where there is a common agent; for example, "I go to bathe" (*snātum gacchāmi*), but not otherwise—for instance, a sane person would not say [something like "I go to bathe for another"].
120.15 This very [usage] is seen only when there is a common agent. For example, "I go to bathe," but a sane person would certainly not say [otherwise].

120.16 One might say, "I go myself to bathe," and so it is here as well. Even though the word *sādhayati* (accomplishes) is of a similar form [to *sādhya*], nevertheless, because it is specified by the suffix *tumun*, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the agent. Furthermore, it has already been stated that by the word *svayam* (himself), he shows an undertaking that does not depend on a treatise (*śāstra*). What was stated? [It was stated that] the word *svayam* indicates that the undertaking is made independently of any formal treatise.
120.19 Because it is improper to despise others, and so forth—what then is this "treatise" (śāstra) with reference to which there is an acceptance that is either dependent or independent?

120.20 By stating, "Indeed, he shows that the treatise is an accepted scripture (āgama) not contradicted by perception or [other] scriptures; therefore, the acceptance is independent of it," one says that he accepts an object based on a single non-authoritative means of knowledge, just as [one might accept something] without any authoritative basis.
121.01 This admission is neither fit to be accepted by one who is sound in mind, nor is it fit to be established [as a proof].

121.02 As for what has been stated in the rules of debate—that the statement of the probandum is the "thesis" (*pratijñā*)—that definition of the thesis is also not tenable because of two faults. How so? If...

121.04. First, with reference to the previously stated position, it is said that "the statement of the probandum is the thesis" (*pratijñā*). In that case, the mention of the term "probandum" (*sādhya*) is redundant; for the "position" (*pakṣa*) under discussion will be connected by that very word, and thus one should simply say, "the statement of that is the thesis. Alternatively, if this definition is independent and does not depend on the "position," even so—

121.07 The fault that was stated regarding the Naiyāyika’s proposition is applicable here as well. One should not say, "The very same rebuttal that you employ there shall also serve as my rebuttal," because I have not accepted it while you have accepted it—just as, for example, someone might [say] to another: [text fragment].

If one were to say of your mother, "She is an unchaste woman because she is a woman," he should reply to him: "Womanhood is not the cause of unchastity; rather, it is the connection with another man apart from her own husband.
Thus, for one who asserts that being a woman entails being unchaste, the unchastity of his mother would be unavoidable. Now, if—
121.13 One might [object]: "If one were to accept that the connection with another man is the reason, then because she is a woman, her being an unchaste woman would be contradicted.
121.14 [The response is: For you as well, there is a contradiction; the statement of the two things to be proven—the reason and the example—would result in it being a thesis (*pratijñā*).
121.15 Therefore, this statement—"the thesis is the statement of that which is to be proven"—is free from all defects.
121.16 [1-1-35] The reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) through similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa*).
121.17 This sūtra, "similarity with the example," is stated by way of defining the reason as it has reached its proper occasion.
121.18 Similarity with the example is "similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*). But what, then, is the example?

121.19–20. "Similarity" (*sādharmya*) is the state of having common properties (*samāna-dharmatā*). It is that property which exists in the subject to be proven (*sādhya*) and likewise exists in the example (*udāharaṇa*); it is not, however, that very same [property], because a property belonging to one thing cannot reside in another. For a property of one thing does not exist elsewhere; rather, it is said to be "that very same [property]" in the sense that it is similar to it. If...

122.02 If it were stated merely that "similarity (sādharmya) is the reason (hetu)," the intended meaning would indeed be established. 122.03 However, there would be no exclusion of what is undesirable; similarity alone would be the reason. Therefore, for the purpose of excluding what is undesirable, the mention of an example (udāharaṇa) is made; because of the mention of similarity with the example, [it follows] that similarity with what is not an example [is excluded].
122.05. It is either excluded by implication or it is excluded by the restriction [of the term], or indeed by the example itself.

122.06. There is similarity (*sādharmya*), but not even by the absence of an example; furthermore, there is dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) as well. Of what, then, would there be similarity by way of the example? Of nothing else but the probandum (*sādhya*), because that is the subject under discussion.
And because of proximity: that which is under discussion is the subject at hand, and the "probandum" (sādhya) is what is proximate; therefore, the similarity of the example is to the probandum.
Furthermore, by the phrase "similarity with the probandum," it is restricted to mean "similarity alone. What, then, is obtained by this restriction?
It is obtained that a reason which subsists in only a part of the probandum is not a valid reason. This is the [proper] reason.
122.11–12. What, then, is this "conjunction" (*pratisaṃdhāna*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*)?

It is the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) [of the reason] in the probandum and its non-occurrence (*asambhava*) in the example. In this way, the reason is obtained as having two characteristics or three characteristics.

122.13–14. By stating that "similarity (*sādharmya*) is established by the example alone," it follows that even for one who has not admitted a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), [the reason is established] by the example alone.

It has been stated that a reason (hetu) possesses two characteristics, namely "similarity" (sādharmya). Furthermore, when it also approaches the counter-example (vipakṣa), it is then established by the example alone through similarity, and not without an example; thus it is said to possess those [two] characteristics. In this way, both positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) belong to the Vaiśeṣika, such as [the argument that sound is] impermanent.

122.17–18: "Sound is produced because it is a product," or "because it is perceptible by the external sense organs of people like us"—these two are positive (anvayin) reasons, as for example, for one who maintains that everything is impermanent: "Sound is impermanent because it is knowable" and "because it is incorporeal.
122.18–19: Thus, it has been stated that the reason, which possesses the distinction of being both positive and negative (anvaya-vyatirekin), as well as purely positive (anvayin), is of four types.

122.20 Thus, by the determination of the nature of the reason (*hetu*), fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are excluded. Among these, by the example [stated as] "only similarity" (*sādharmyam eva*), there is the exclusion of the contradictory reason (*viparyaya-hetu*) and the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*). 123.01 By this restriction, "only similarity with the example," that which does not reside in the probandum (*sādhya*) and that which resides in only a portion of the probandum are excluded.

123.02. Regarding the statement "it is refuted": first, in that context, the reason for error is [the following]: "A horse is not a horned animal because it has horns," which is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it does not apply to the probandum (*sādhya*). "Sound is impermanent because it is visible" is [inconclusive] because it does not apply to the probandum. "Atoms are impermanent because they possess odor" is [inconclusive] because it applies only to a portion of the probandum. Thus, in its own nature, it is inconclusive.

123.05 The inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) need not be made. If, by means of this definition of a logical reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), when it is thus cultivated, fallacious reasons (*anaikāntika-hetu*) and so forth are excluded, [one might ask]: "Is not the 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*) that which deviates from itself, i.e., 'with deviation' (*savyabhicāra*)? Thus, there would be no need to begin the initial sūtra. [The answer is: No, because the restriction is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*atiprasakta*). Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are of many kinds.

123.08–123.10: "They are distinct"—it is for the purpose of making this restriction known that the terms *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) and so forth are mentioned. Some [hold] that there is no means of proving the probandum (*sādhya*) other than through similarity to the example (*udāharaṇa*). Indeed, they claim that there is no means of proving the probandum apart from similarity to the example; therefore, it must be formulated in this way: similarity to the example [is the proof] by itself.

123.11 "The reason (hetu)" [is stated]. Furthermore, since the terms "probandum" (sādhya) and "probans" (sādhana) have already been employed as qualifiers for the similarity to the example (udāharaṇa-sādharmya), 123.12 even so, the mention of the ablative case (pañcamī-apadeśa) is purposeless. For it is not the case that [one says] "the blue lotus from [the lotus]" (nīlād utpalam). Others, however, explain the purposelessness of the mention of the ablative case differently: [regarding] the object—
123.14 “Because it is seen in the interval” is redundant. It is said that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is indeed seen in the sense of a distinct category (*arthāntara*), as in:

Since he states in the definition of the function that "the property belongs to the subject (*pakṣa*)," by this [specification], properties such as "being visible" (*cākṣuṣatva*), which cannot exist in the subject, are excluded. But how is it that [a property] residing in only a part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) is not [excluded]?

129.17 For this [reason] it is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), nor does it subsist in a portion of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣaikadeśavṛtti*), because it is not a property of the subject.
129.18 Therefore, an effort should not be made to refute it otherwise; for by the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), its exclusion is already established.
129.19 By the restriction, subsistence in a portion [of the dissimilar instance] will be excluded. But what exactly is being restricted? Is it that "it is only a property" (*dharma eva*)?

129.20–22: “Is it the property of one side or indeed of both sides? First of all, the entity is simply the property of the side; why then [is this said]? What is the force of this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)? Is possibility (*sambhava*) made known by it, or is impossibility (*asambhava*) excluded? In either case, there is no force in the restriction, because [the exclusion of] possibility and [the affirmation of] impossibility—
