130.01 Furthermore, since comprehension occurs even without the restriction of exclusion (*nivṛtti*), and since existence in only a portion [of the subject] is not being refuted, 130.02 the restriction is redundant. Now, if the meaning of this restriction is pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, that "the property (*dharma*) alone [belongs] to the subject (*pakṣa*)"—130.03 and not "even a non-property (*adharma*)," then that which exists only in a portion of the subject is indeed a non-property; however, by this [restriction], the portion...
130.04–05: Even in this case, while one [objection] is being resolved, another falls away:

"Let the refutation of partial occurrence be granted; for what purpose is this term 'established in the similar class' (sapakṣe siddhaḥ) undertaken? 130.06: Why, then, should this not be undertaken? Because its purpose has already been fulfilled by the restriction intended to express pervasion (vyāpti).

130.07–130.09: "The property alone is the subject" means that the subject is fixed while the property is not fixed; [this refers to] the pervasion of that non-eternal [property]. Through [the presence of the reason] in the similar class and its absence from the dissimilar class, there is the understanding of the similar class (sapakṣa); since it does not exist in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), it is established in the similar class—this is the meaning of the phrase.
Let this not be so. Now, however, if this restriction is formulated differently as "only of the subject," then in this way...

130.10–11. Since both [the requirements]—that it is established in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and that it is absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—are already proven and [any contrary] sublation has been refuted, how could there be [any further need for restriction]?

130.11–12. As for the statement "it is established in the similar class," this restriction is refuted by the fact that a property belonging to the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is what is established in the similar class.
Indeed, such types of sentences do not occur in common usage, such as: "Devadatta alone... [is fat].
130.13 Feed Yajñadatta as well; however, the "northern" position is not to be performed because it is understood that [the reason] does not exist in the counter-example (vipakṣa).

130.14 By the phrase "by what is it understood?", through this restriction, it is understood that the property belongs to the subject (pakṣa) itself and not to the generality. 130.15 Thus, the statement "it does not exist in the counter-example" need not be made; nor is a property that subsists in only a portion of the subject (pakṣa-ekadeśavṛtti) being excluded.

130.16 Thus, that very purpose for which the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) was intended is lost. Furthermore, 130.17 the phrase "established in the similar class" (*sapakṣe siddhaḥ*) is also begun with the purpose of restriction, namely: "established only in the similar class" (*sapakṣe eva siddhaḥ*).
130.18 Or, "established in the similar class alone" (*siddha eva sapakṣe*). What, then, is obtained by this word through such a restriction? If...

130.19 Even if its presence [in the subject] is not ascertained, it is understood to be established in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). If, however, pervasion (*vyāpti*) [is required] for that which belongs to that same class, 130.20 it follows that a reason (*hetu*) that exists only in one part [of the similar class] would not be a valid reason. If, on the other hand, it is established only in the similar class, even so, 130.21 the preceding and following statements become contradictory; for there is the restriction that "it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and does not exist in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)."

131.01 Because it is contradicted by the facts, the former [position] is not to be undertaken; because it is already understood, the latter is also [not to be undertaken]. Now, regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*):

131.02 "It does not exist"—this too is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Here, what is being restricted? Is it that "it does not exist only in the counter-example," or "it certainly does not exist in the counter-example"? If it does not exist only in the counter-example, then...
131.04. "The cow [is non-eternal] because it possesses horns"—this is the reason (hetu) that has been obtained, for it does not exist in the counter-example (vipakṣa).

131.05. Now, if it is the case that it does not exist at all in the counter-example, then there is no further need to initiate the middle term; in that regard, the first term is for the purpose of pervasion (vyāpti), while the subsequent term is for the purpose of excluding its occurrence in even a single part of the counter-example. Furthermore, it is established in the similar example (sapakṣa).

131.07. If it is asked for what purpose this term is commenced—whether for the sake of possibility (*sambhava*) or for the sake of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of the first restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)—131.08. [If it is] for the sake of possibility, then since [possibility] is already obtained, it is redundant. Thus, when this definition is examined in terms of its co-occurrence (*saha-vṛtti*), there is either the introduction of an undesired reason or the abandonment of the intended reason. 131.09. [The intended meaning is as follows:]...

131.10–12: "The fault is that [the reason] is either swallowed up by the probandum (*grasta-hāni*) or that the reason is not distinguished from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). When the definition is examined based on the Sautrāntika position, since a counter-example is impossible, the reason is not distinguished from the counter-example. Thus, the meaning of "counter-example" must be stated; for we do not perceive the meaning of a counter-example when no counter-example exists.
131.13 Furthermore, the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is not possible when [the counter-example] is non-existent; thus, the scope of the ablative must be stated.

131.14 Since the sense of the locative (*adhikaraṇa-artha*) is not possible when the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is absent, one must state the sense of the locative (*saptamī-artha*) by saying "it does not exist in the counter-example" (*vipakṣe nāsti*). 131.15 Because, in the absence of a counter-example, [the probans] pervades both the subject (*pakṣa*) and its similar class (*tajjātīya*), such as "being produced" (*kṛtaka*).

131.16 The object [of inference], such as "you" (*tvam*) and so forth, must be considered a particular (*viśeṣa*). Because it is produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), it is then an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) non-universal (*asāmānya*).
131.17 [The opponent says: "It is a particular. To this, [the author replies: This definition is not a true definition because it is inconsistent with one's own established tenets (*svasiddhānta*).
131.18 That too was stated by the author of the *Hetuvārttika*: "When seven [possibilities] are possible, by the negation of six, there remains one."

131.19–20. To say that "the reason (hetu) has three characteristics by the exclusion of two terms" is also incorrect, because both [the reason] and the two-term definition possess the status of being a reason (*hetutva*); for in that case, it is said that a sevenfold combination is possible. 132.01. [The first type is: "It is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) only in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and it does not exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) only; it is established in the similar instance."

132.02 A property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) which does not exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), but is established as existing only in the similar instance (*samāna*); [it is] "not existing in the dissimilar instance" (132.03). "A property of the subject, established in the similar instance, and not existing in the dissimilar instance"—thus, when such a sevenfold possibility exists, having stated the six negations, this [author], by means of the inclusion of three terms, [establishes] the three characteristics.

132.05 He teaches [the word] "reason" (*hetu*); by that, he indicates the exclusion of one or two [of the three] characteristics. But that is not so, because the two [reasons] endowed with two characteristics are indeed reasons. For one who does not accept the position of permanence, [the reason] "because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is endowed with two characteristics;
and likewise, "because it follows immediately upon effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*)—these two possess the status of being reasons.

132.08 That which is this negative reason—"This living body is not soulless"—would not be a valid reason, because it would entail the consequence that it lacks breath and so forth, and so on; for it would involve two [contrary] propositions. 132.10 Therefore, this definition—that a reason is a property that excludes the counter-example—must be examined, whether it be accepted or not.
132.11 It establishes the reason, subverts what is desired, rejects what is swallowed up, and contradicts the treatise.
132.12 Thus: therein, that which exists in two ways among the similar class and is absent when that [class] is excluded—according to others, it exists in the similar class;
132.13 and is absent in two ways when that is excluded—meaning it does not exist in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*). And by this much, indeed—

132.14 A reason characterized by the three marks is not obtained according to the literal scriptural statement. If, first of all, this definition were to exist according to the literal scriptural statement, [namely] that it exists in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), by what means would this be obtained?
132.16 [One might ask: "But has it not been stated that both the valid reason and its fallacy are generally properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)?"

132.17 This has already been stated: it is not that by this [statement] it is obtained that "the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is the reason (*hetu*)," but rather that "that which is not the property of the subject is not a reason.

132.18 It is not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Furthermore, if it were to be obtained by implication (*arthataḥ*) that "the property of the subject is the reason and not a fallacious reason," 132.19—provided this were the meaning of the sentence—it would follow by implication that both the reason and the fallacious reason are properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
132.20 Thus, although the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is understood by implication as being true, it is not found to be necessarily restricted to the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
132.21 By the mere exclusion of what is not the property of the subject, only a possibility is obtained. And that is twofold:

132.22 the pervasive and the non-pervasive. Among these, the non-pervasive [reason] results in an undesirable [conclusion]: either the reason is obtained or the property of the subject is not obtained.
133.01 By stating "only" (*eva*), it follows that whatever is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is the reason (*hetu*); however, this [proposition] is not a property of the subject.

133.02 Because [the word] "only" (*eva*) functions as a partial occurrence (*ekadeśavṛtti*), it does not have the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); rather, the restriction serves another purpose. 133.03 You [opponents] imagine [this purpose]: for what purpose? It is for the sake of making known the distinction between the valid reason and the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). That [is the purpose].

133.04 How can an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) that serves another purpose exclude what is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*)? Or, if it is for the sake of excluding the non-pervasive, and for the sake of making known the rule regarding reasons (*hetu*) and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), even so, the statement "existent [is] in the similar class and in two ways" would be redundant. Why? Because of the emphasis having the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
133.07. The subject (*pakṣa*) is restricted and the property (*dharma*) is also restricted. Because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of that which is unrestricted, 133.08.

two groups of the property remain: the similar class (*sajātīya*) and its opposite (*tad-atyaya*). Among these, [the property] is absent in the opposite class due to over-extension (*atiprasakti*). 133.09.
Regarding the phrase "in its opposite" (*tad-atyaye*), it is present in the similar class (*sajātīye*); for what purpose? If it is for the sake of possibility (*sambhava*).
133.10 Therefore, since the possibility of both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) arises from the lack of restriction, what is the point of this [qualification]?

133.11 Regarding "in the similar class" (*sajātīye*) and "in two ways" (*dvedhā ca*), it should not be stated in any way. First of all, because it is already understood, the phrase "in the similar class" (*sajātīye*) need not be made; for by the word "existent" (*sat*), pervasion—

133.13 Because [the definition] is stated in a general way regarding both non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*), the statement "and in two ways" is a careless remark. Now, if it should be thought that the phrase "existing in what is similar" (*san sajātīye*) is undertaken for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), then the purpose of the restriction would be appropriate.
133.15 However, the undertaking [of the restriction] is not a proper restriction. How so? If, first of all, it is restricted in this manner: [text fragment]

133.16–17: "Only that which exists in the similar class," such as being produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) and so forth—this is the reason. Because [the reason] "being produced immediately after effort and so forth" is both existent and non-existent in two ways, that restriction is sublated. For it does not happen that one says, "Feed only the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya."

133.19 Now, if it is determined that [the term] "existent" (*san*) refers only to that which is of the same class (*sajātīya*), even so, both the preceding and the following [positions] are contradicted. 133.20 How? One [term] has an uncontradicted purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa-artha*), because one is being understood [as the subject]. Alternatively, 133.21 the phrase "and in two ways" (*dvidhā ca*) serves the purpose of restriction. In this case as well, what is being restricted? Is it "in the same class" (*sajātīye*)?

133.22 Thus, [the term] "in two ways" applies only to the similar class (*sajātīya*). If, first of all, it applies in two ways only to the similar class—134.01 [it follows that] it does not apply in another category (*pakṣa*), nor in its absence; thus it is said to be "in two ways. If this were so, then even regarding the similar class, 134.02 [the restriction] need not be made. For by the restrictive particle used in the sense of "attainment," the possibility [of its application] in other words belonging to the similar class has already been stated.

And because the phrase "in two ways" (*dvidhā ca*) is intended to exclude other possibilities (*anya-pada-dvi-dhā-nivṛtti-para*), its expression as "in two ways" implies possibility (*sambhava*). Thus, it is understood that [the property] exists in what is similar (*san sajātīye*). Therefore, one should by no means say "only in what is similar" (*sajātīye eva*). Since the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) provided by the very phrase "and in two ways" establishes pervasion of the subject (*pakṣa-vyāpti*), it follows that the property (*dharma*) belongs to the subject alone.

The restriction was stated for the sake of pervasion (*vyāpti*), so that there would be no contradiction with the restriction of the word "all" (*sarva*). Even if there were no such restriction, nevertheless the two middle terms should not be made [redundant]; this is the maxim of "the entry of a goitre and the exit of the pupil. Furthermore, [if it is argued] that it is only in two ways regarding the similar class (*sajātīya*)...

134.09 Even so, [properties] such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) are not valid reasons (*hetu*), for they do not exist in two ways within the similar class (*sajātīya*); and [thus] the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*) are absent.
134.10 For one who asserts a reason, it follows that the two terms and the two logical concomitances (*yukti*) accepted in one's own system are not reasons.
134.11 And it follows that the negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*) is not a reason. If you say, "It is simply not a reason," then why was it [even] formulated?

134.12 “The effort [to establish] its status as a reason (*hetu*) is not a solution. Furthermore, if the restrictive particles (*avadhāraṇa*) are not employed, then even so, the fallacies of being a property residing in only a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) and being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) remain attached. By this, the definition of a reason as “a property of the object of apprehension (*grāhyadharma*) which is pervaded by a part of that [object]” is refuted. Through this, [reasons] such as the non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) and so forth are excluded.

134.15 This too has already been answered. The statement "it is non-existent in its absence" is identical to the previous point because it is shown that [the reason] does not exist in the counter-example (vipakṣa). 134.16 Others maintain that the reason is the demonstration of a property that is invariably concomitant with such [a probandum]. By the phrase "it does not exist without such," they claim that two things are obtained: its non-existence in the counter-example and its non-existence when such [a probandum] is absent.

134.18–19. It is said that by the inclusion of "observation" (upadarśana), existence in the subject (pakṣa) is obtained; thus, for one who distinguishes the three characteristics, the subject is obtained as the self. As for the claim that non-existence in the counter-example (vipakṣa) and existence in such [a subject] are obtained through the apprehension of an inseparable connection (avinābhāva) of that kind—that is not logical, because without such [an inseparable connection], it is not possible.
134.21 Because it exists, its absence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is understood; however, its occurrence in such [a similar case] is precisely what remains to be established.
134.22 Why? For there is no such rule that whatever does not exist in the counter-example must necessarily exist in that which belongs to the same class.
135.01 And in this way, even "audibility" and so forth would become a valid reason (*hetu*); for audibility and so forth also do not exist without such [a similar case].
"It exists. Let it be that for the apprehension of such an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), [the reason] occurs in that and its like;
however, it has been stated that "it must also occur in the subject (*pakṣa*). But is this not already obtained from the inclusion of the term "demonstration" (*upadarśana*)?
It is not so obtained, because the inclusion of the term "demonstration" is for the purpose of expression; the inclusion of the term "demonstration" is an expression.
135.05 It is by means of this [reason] that the object is demonstrated; however, it does not possess this capacity with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*) and elsewhere simultaneously.

135.06 But where else could it be? Wherever its occurrence is possible. And where is its occurrence? In that which belongs to the same class (*tajjātīya*). Therefore, 135.07 this is what is meant: the expression of that which is inseparably connected (*avinābhāvin*) with things of that same class, only with respect to things of that same class.

135.08 [Objection: "The reason (*hetu*) is thus: your 'visibility' (*cākṣuṣatva*) becomes the reason. For visibility is not invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with impermanence; or, let it be so—yet even if such an invariably concomitant property is pointed out in the subject (*pakṣa*), by what means do you refute that which exists only in a portion of the subject (*pakṣa-ekadeśa-vṛtti*)? 135.10 [Response: Regarding this pointing out...

If it is argued that [the pervasion is obtained] by the inclusion of the "example" (*udāharaṇa*), we say no; for that [inclusion] is intended merely to make known the possibility [of the reason in the subject]. Now, if one should think that the pervasion is obtained through the inclusion of the "example," that is not correct, because the inclusion of the example is intended merely to make known the possibility.
By the inclusion of the example, only the possibility is made known—that [reason] exists in the subject (*pakṣa*).

Furthermore, it is not logical [to claim] that [the reason] is pervasive (*vyāpaka*). Now, if determinations were to be made here as well by some logical principle (*nyāya*), those would be capable of refuting non-pervasive reasons; thus, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before follows.
As for this example—namely, that "being produced immediately after effort" and so forth [is the reason] for impermanence, and smoke [is the reason] for fire—[it is likewise problematic].

135.17 Thus it has been stated that smoke, for its part, is not a prover of fire. Furthermore, [the property of] being produced immediately after an effort (prayatnānantarīyaka) is also [not a valid reason]. 135.18 Why is it not a reason? Because the property of being produced immediately after an effort does not reside in the subject (pakṣāvṛttitvāt).

For the property of being produced immediately after an effort is not a characteristic of sound (śabdadharma); indeed, there is no sound whatsoever that is produced immediately after an effort. 135.19 [Therefore, it is not a valid reason.]

Because sound has conjunction and disjunction as its source. Now, if effort is the cause of sound through a successive sequence—since all objects are indirectly causes of sound—then the qualification [“because it follows immediately after effort”] is inappropriate. Therefore, it should be stated that sound is impermanent because it arises from that [effort].
136.01 And as for this fact that sound follows immediately upon effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), which is stated by means of the term "existence" (*bhāva*) as the reason for its impermanence:

136.02 what exactly is it? Is it birth (*janman*) or perception (*upalabdhi*)? If it is first of all birth, 136.03 then that is not at all effective; thus, the mention of "following immediately upon effort" would be useless. For it does not happen [that something exists]...
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced by Devadatta. Therefore, it should be stated thus: "because it possesses birth.
If this [reason] "possessing birth" were to be deviant, then the mention of "being an immediate consequence of effort" would be meaningful.
Why? Because qualifiers are meaningful when [the reason] is deviant.
136.07 Now, if it is argued that by this statement of existence, "perception is preceded by effort," [the following is meant]:

136.08 Even so, since perception itself possesses efficacy, there is a qualification. For that which is being perceived 136.09 is not of two kinds—eternal or non-eternal, and either preceded by effort or otherwise. If you say this:
136.10–11. "The state of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*), which is perceived immediately after an effort, is eternal"—this [example] of yours is itself inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).

136.11–12. Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) "being produced immediately after an effort" is not pervasive (*avyāpaka*) with respect to the inference of the impermanence of sound, because the entire collection of sounds (*śabda-rāśi*) is made the subject (*pakṣa*). Alternatively, if one makes a particular sound the subject...

136.13 Regarding that [definition], it is stated that even in the first case, the property of "being immediately following effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva) is possible, but not in the second and subsequent cases. Thus, the fault of being non-pervasive (avyāpakatva) remains unremoved. Furthermore, if one were to say, "whatever is immediately following effort is impermanent," even so, another reason (hetu) must be stated; for the reason has been employed as a qualification of the subject (pakṣaviśeṣaṇatvena).

136.16–18. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that for that which does not follow immediately upon human effort (aprayatnānantarīyaka), there are three possible courses: something is eternal, such as space (ākāśa) and so forth;
something is non-eternal, such as lightning and so forth; or something is like a sky-flower (ākāśakusuma).
This is indeed the mark of a great logician and a great debater, insofar as you claim that what is non-existent (asat) does not follow immediately upon human effort.

136.19 And "something" (*kiṃcit*) is a term for variety (*citram*). However, something is eternal, but it is not the case that [eternality] is not immediately following effort (*aprayatnānantarīyakatva*). For it cannot be said that space (*ākāśa*) is not immediately following effort, because [the property of] being not immediately following effort is qualified by birth (*janma*), and there is no birth of space.
Therefore, space is not that which follows immediately upon effort. By this, non-existence (*abhāva*) is also explained.

It is exactly the same in the case of non-existence as well. Thus, these [other cases] do not constitute the characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*); this alone is the traditional definition of a reason, namely, the principle of logic (*nyāya*).
137.03 [1-1-36] "An example (udāharaṇa) is an instance (dṛṣṭānta) which, by virtue of its similarity to the probandum (sādhya), possesses that property. 137.04 This is the aphorism (sūtra).
137.05 The meaning of this is the definition of the example: "similarity to the probandum" (sādhya-sādharmya) means the state of having a common property with the probandum.

137.06 Here too, there is similarity only with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), and not similarity even with that which is not to be proven; nor is there dissimilarity only with that which is to be proven. 137.07 Why? Because [the probans] comes to possess those properties through its similarity to that which is to be proven. 137.08 From what [reason] does it not come to possess those properties from some similarity to that which is to be proven? It is not the case that it does not so come to pass, just as follows:
137.09. Formlessness and so forth are not properties of action; therefore, by virtue of similarity with the probandum (*sādhya*), that in which those properties exist is [the subject].

137.10. That which possesses those properties is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) because, through its similarity with the probandum, it possesses those properties. 137.11. When joined with this qualification, it becomes an illustration (*udāharaṇa*); by means of this, the two properties are illustrated.

137.12 “The relationship between the probandum and the probans” is the example (*udāharaṇa*). [Objection: But surely, because of the inclusion of the *kāraka* "instrument" (*karaṇa*), it is a verbal expression (*vacana*).
137.13 The example (*udāharaṇa*) and the instance (*d�ṛṣṭānta*) are two distinct meanings, and their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not tenable.
137.14 For indeed, the designation "possessing horns and so forth" is coreferential with "cow"; this is not the case here.

The fault [of this view] is that because the example is presented as a qualification of the statement, the example is not an independent illustration (*udāharaṇa*). Rather, it is that which is being expressed as possessing the property of that [subject] by virtue of its similarity to the probandum (*sādhya*). Regarding the term "possessing the property of that" (*tad-dharma-bhāvin*): "that property" (*tad-dharma*) means the property of that; "that" refers to the probandum (*sādhya*). And what is the probandum?

137.18 Dharma is twofold: the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*). At one time the property functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and at another time the possessor of the property [functions as such]. 137.19 Regarding the phrase "as a qualifier," it is appropriate to mention the "possessor of the property" (*dharmin*); for there is no separate mention of the property (*dharma*). 137.20 This is because properties such as "having the nature of arising" belong to the possessor of the property (*dharmin*), and not to the property itself when that property is the probandum (*sādhya*).
137.21 “Because of similarity with the example” is a contradiction; for there is no similarity whatsoever of a property (*dharma*) with an example.

137.22 Rather, it is the similarity with the probandum (*sādhya*) that constitutes the similarity of the example, which is itself the subject (*dharmin*), and the application (*upasaṃhāra*) is to the subject.
138.01 Therefore, since the probandum resides in the subject alone, [the similarity] belongs to that subject which is the probandum.
138.02 That property which is to be proven is that which exists and is found in the illustrative example; that is the *dṛṣṭānta*.

138.03 The *udāharaṇa* (exemplification) is: "Substances such as a cooking pot possess the property of being produced and are seen to be impermanent. 138.04 [And thus, whatever possesses the property of being produced is impermanent.]
138.05 [1-1-37] Or, by the reversal of that, it is the opposite.
138.06 Or, by the reversal of that, it is the opposite: an example characterized by dissimilarity to the probandum (*sādhya*) is one that does not possess the property of that [probandum].
138.07 This is called an "illustration" (*udāharaṇa*). An illustration is to be understood as occurring in the case of the *avīta* reason; however, others [hold a different view].

138.08 They recite the sūtra: "By virtue of similarity with the probandum (sādhya), the example possesses that property. Their intention, however, is this: let there not be identity between the example (dṛṣṭānta) and the illustration (udāharaṇa). What, then, is "possessing that property"? It is the connection with the probandum and the probans; and when there is such a connection with the probandum and the probans, it possesses that property.
Therefore, by means of the expression "existence" (bhāva), the connection with both the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana) is stated.

Regarding this, others criticize the sūtra; however, for us, this is not the reading of the sūtra, and therefore this fault does not apply. Even under that reading, it is said that the inclusion of the term "future" (bhāvin) is purposeless. Why?

138.14 Because all the members [of the syllogism] possess the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*). For it is said that all the members possess the property to be proven; they "bring it about" (*bhāvayanti*) or "make it understood" (*gamayanti*). This, however, is not the meaning of the Sūtra. 138.16 Others, however, explain the term *tad-dharma-bhāvin* differently as *tad-dharma-*.

138.17 Or, [the term] "one who possesses becoming" (*bhāvin*) may be according to the logic of "one who eats hot food" (*uṣṇa-bhojin*), or it may be according to the logic of "one who carries a staff" (*daṇḍin*).

138.18 If, first of all, it is according to the logic of "one who eats hot food"—that is, one whose habit is to eat hot food, thus "one who eats hot food"—or one whose habit is to cultivate that quality, thus "one who cultivates that quality" (*tad-dharma-bhāvin*); here too, "to cultivate" means "to bring about."
138.20–138.21: As for what was said, "this is not the meaning of the Sūtra," this is of no consequence.

However, the logical principle (*nyāya*) is as follows: one who possesses a staff is a "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*). One who possesses the state of having that quality is "one who will possess that quality" (*tad-dharma-bhāvin*). In this context, the inclusion of the term "will possess" (*bhāvin*) is redundant; how then can it be called "one who will possess that quality"?

139.02 Thus, that which is both a property (*dharma*) and an entity (*bhāva*) is a "property-entity" (*tad-dharma-bhāva*). That which possesses this is "one who has the nature of possessing that property" (*tad-dharma-bhāvī*). This being the case, the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—namely, "one who has the nature of possessing that property"—is untenable.
For it is not logical that something could be both a property and a non-entity (*abhāva*), such that there could be a relationship of qualifier and qualified.
[The opponent argues: "It would be established [as a valid example]. Therefore, it must indeed be stated that 'it possesses that property' (*taddharmī*). [The author replies: It need not be stated.

Because those properties exist in both ways—both as being affirmed and as being negated—the properties exist in both ways. In that regard, for a positive concomitant (*anvayin*), the inclusion of the example is that which possesses the property being affirmed.
139.08 Just as, for example, in a pot, the property of being subject to origination and impermanence are both existing properties (dharma).

139.09 Therefore, it is logical that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because that [property] is both a property and an entity (*bhāva*). Furthermore, as for this [term] "the possessor of the property" (*dharmin*), this too has not been fully understood; for in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is not...
139.11 [The opponent says: "The suffix -matup is obtained [in this sense]. Furthermore, we must certainly be instructed;

in that case, it should be stated as 'taddharmā' (possessing that property). And there are those who argue thus, for whom [the relation between] being produced and impermanence is [one of] non-existence. To refute that, this should be stated: "It is both that property and an existent entity" (*taddharmaś cāsau bhāvaś ca*).
139.14 When these three members have thus been established by their defining characteristics, there are three [objections] regarding them that are difficult to discern.

139.15 Thus, by this statement, one’s status as a great Naiyāyika is proclaimed. 139.16 Others say: "The example is established. But how is the meaning of this [to be understood], such that the probandum is to be proven?

139.17 This [reason] is likewise unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to impermanence; and just as it is distinguished by the fact that its cognition varies, so too that which is established is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) possessing both the probandum and the probans. In this regard, even those who have thundered forth [in protest], without abandoning their own tenets, are unable [to refute] the [logical connection] between being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*).

139.20–22. [The opponent argues that] the relationship between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) cannot be demonstrated because of the difference in time and because of the sublation of the entity. "Being produced" occurs at one time, and "impermanence" at another; and when the entity exists, its prior non-existence and its subsequent destruction do not exist. By this, it is shown that their demonstration of a relationship through an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is invalid.
It has been replied: "The reason is that which is followed by the probandum, and its non-existence where the probandum is absent."
140.02 [1-1-38] The application (*upanaya*) is the application of the probandum (*sādhya*) as "so" (*tathā*) or "not so" (*na tathā*), depending upon the example (*udāharaṇa*).
140.03 The application is the application of the probandum as "so" or "not so," depending upon the example.

And thus, regarding the statement "this [subject] is produced," what is the purpose of the reflection (*pratibimbana*) in the form "just as that"? When it has been established that the property residing in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is non-deviant, the application (*upanaya*) consists in the possibility of the same property being present in the subject (*sādhya*)— namely, "and thus this is produced"— or in the demonstration of its occurrence therein.

The meaning [of the word "existence"] is as follows: But surely, by the phrase "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*), existence is stated, because of the indication of the relationship between the probandum and the probans.

By the mere indication of the relationship between the probandum and the probans, it becomes: "Sound is produced; because of being produced, sound is impermanent. Furthermore, whether that quality of being produced exists or does not exist in sound is [determined] by the application (*upanaya*).

140.11 It is understood that "producedness exists in sound. When [the example] is given by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), it is "it is thus"; when by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), it is "it is not thus."

140.13 [1-1-39] The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the presentation of the reason (*hetu*). 140.14 "The restatement of the proposition" means: when the object of the proposition has been established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the conclusion serves to exclude] the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya-viparīta*). 140.15 [It is said: "The restatement of the proposition. This refers to the object that was the subject matter of the proposition; once it has been validated by every means of valid cognition, [the conclusion reiterates it].

140.16–140.18: "The restatement for the purpose of negating the [unwanted] consequence (prasaṅga-pratiṣedha) is the conclusion (nigamana). Regarding this meaning of the sūtra, having granted that there is no room for an opponent [to object], and desiring to dispel that fault, the statement is introduced:

"The application (upanaya) and the conclusion (nigamana) are not separate members [of the syllogism], because they do not differ in meaning from [the other members], and so forth. This is the statement.

140.19 Just as [the reason] is not connected with any object according to the scripture, so too the reason (*hetu*) and the application (*upanaya*) are not distinct from the thesis (*pakṣa*), because there is no difference in their meaning. 140.20 That [reason] is a "contrary reason" (*viparyaya-hetu*) because it occurs in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Regarding the lack of difference in meaning:
140.21 [it is argued that] because [identity] is not observed in the case of unity, and because it is observed in the case of plurality—just as in the case of many jars.

141.01. One [might argue] that there is the extraction of a single meaning and so forth, yet there is no oneness. Now, having made "having a single purpose" the subject (*pakṣa*), 141.02 one might say: "Oneness is the state of having a single purpose. Even so, there is no reason (*hetu*) for the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). 141.03 Because the reason and the application (*upanaya*) are already implied, the meaning of the proposition is simply "the state of having a single object"; for there is no distinction in the object.

141.04. That very same thing is the meaning of the reason (*hetu*), yet the meaning of the reason is one thing and the meaning of the application (*upanaya*) is another; thus, this reason is also unestablished (*asiddha*). 141.05. As for the claim that "the exclusion of others" consists in the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the relation, and the probandum (*sādhya*) as described by him, this has already been refuted by this very [argument]. 141.06.
Furthermore, when the conclusion is made with the words "just so" (*yathā tathā*), whether by the word "so" (*tathā*) all commonality or...

141.07. Is it the universal of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva-sāmānya*) that is denoted, or the particular instance of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva-viśeṣa*), or the universal of all things (*sarva-sāmānya*)? First of all, the universal of all things is not tenable as such, because it is impossible to designate it in that way. Nor is the particular instance of "being produced" tenable, otherwise there would be no remainder of "being produced" for the sound; and that universal of "being produced" has already been stated by the reason itself.
That too is incorrect. Since the application (upanaya) has the purpose of analogy, it is said that "the application has the purpose of analogy";
yet, it is nonsensical to claim that analogy does not function by relying at all upon the relationship between the probandum and the probans.
This is strange, for the generality of "being produced" (kṛtakatva-sāmānya) is indeed denoted in the proximity of the word [in the application].

141.13–141.15: "This quality of being produced (kṛtakatva) is indeed expressed even in the absence of the word [‘produced’]; yet, when it is qualified by the word, how can it be a universal? Therefore, the reason possesses both universality and particularity.

This has been refuted by the statement that the application (upanaya) is unnecessary because its purpose has already been served. Furthermore, as for what was said—that "as... so" constitutes a comparison (upamāna)—[that too is rejected].

141.16–17. Furthermore, by [the statement that] "the application (upanaya) is the comparison (upamāna), not the example (dṛṣṭānta)," the conclusion (nigamana) is also refuted. These two—the *vīta* and *avīta*—are independent arguments consisting of five members; moreover, one of them is characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*).

141.18 [1-1-40] *Tarka* (reasoning) is the process of deliberation (*ūha*) for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the true nature of an object whose true nature is not yet known, based on the logical consistency of possible causes.
141.19–20: *Tarka* is the deliberation for the purpose of knowing the truth regarding an object whose truth is unknown, by means of the justification of reasons.

141.21. The Sūtra [states]: "When the reality of an object is not known. Its meaning is as before: "in regard to an object whose true nature is unknown. 141.22. Just as that object exists, so is its state; this is its reality (*tattva*).
When this is not known, it is understood in a general sense. From what? 142.01. Because it is recognized in a general sense when its reality is not yet known.
142.02 Because he says "when its true nature (*tattva*) is not known," he thereby indicates that the universal (*sāmānya*) has been apprehended.
142.03 If, on the other hand, even the universal were not understood, he would not say "when its true nature is not known.
142.04 He would simply say "when it is not known" (*avijñāte*); thus, this compound "when its true nature is not known" (*avijñātatattve*) does not have [that] meaning.
142.05 Is it that the reality (*tattva*) is not known by [the person], or is it that the reality is not known [by him]? And what is the distinction here?

142.06 If the reality is not known by him, then this person whose reality is unknown is the determiner (*paricchedṛ*); in that case, when the reality is unknown, reasoning (*ūha*) regarding the object understood by that determiner results in being called "inquiry" (*tarka*). Alternatively, if the reality is not known...
"That whose reality is not known" means "in that [object] whose reality is not known";

this is correct by way of a genitive analysis (*ṣaṣṭhī-vigraha*). Since there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other], there is no comprehension of the meaning here; for what specific reason is there such a doubt as to whether this is a compound with a third-case analysis (*tṛtīyā-vigraha*) or a sixth-case analysis? It is logical [to accept the latter] because of the capacity of the word "meaning" (*artha*) to convey the sense.
142.11 Because [the compound] means "that whose reality (tattva) is unknown," it indicates that [the word *artha*] functions as an object (*karman*) because it is being sought.

142.12 This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Even without the inclusion of the word *artha*, it is understood in a general sense through the analysis (*vigraha*) using the instrumental case. 142.13 Even if the meaning is not explicitly stated—that "that whose reality is unknown" refers to comprehension (*avagati*)—this very meaning is indeed understood.
Even so, the state of doubt remains the same regarding the compound. Let there be no compound; let it be a sentence itself. [Objection:

"Its true nature is unknown"—by this very [phrase], the attainment of the intended meaning occurs. However, the reason for using a compound is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). Even when the meaning is not explicitly stated, it is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*); thus, it has been said here: "Its true nature is unknown."

142.17 There would be such doubt; furthermore, it would follow that there is no mention of the whole [collection]. And if the mention of "meaning" (artha) is prohibited on the basis of its capacity (sāmarthya), then it is appropriate [to say] that "ūha is reasoning" (tarka); for by implication (sāmarthyataḥ), the remainder is understood. Therefore, the mention of "meaning" is for the purpose of excluding the knower. Let it not be so.

142.20. Is not the designation of the whole [of the faculties] contradicted? No, because its purpose is to exclude [the notion that] they are attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*). Indeed, this deliberation (*ūha*) occurs in two ways:
regarding that which has its true nature known and that which has its true nature unknown. Among these, first, regarding that which has its true nature known:

deliberation, the desire to hear (*śuśrūṣā*), hearing (*śravaṇa*), retention (*dhāraṇā*), comprehension (*vijñāna*), deliberation (*ūha*), rejection (*apoha*), and adherence to the truth (*tattva-abhiniveśa*) are the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*).
143.01. Thus, when one discerns the determined reality, that is "discernment" (*vijñāta*); what is meant by "inference" (*ūha*)? 143.02.
That very object which was previously known by him is called "inference"; it is the determination of what was previously experienced. 143.03.
It is called "inference," but this is not "reasoning" (*tarka*). Furthermore, inference regarding an object whose reality is not yet known is "reasoning."

143.04. [The opponent says: "The mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣ�ṭhī-abhidhānam*) is because the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is impossible for an object whose true nature (*tattva*) is unknown. This must be stated. 143.05. An object whose true nature is unknown becomes the direct object (*karman*) when it is being cognized; and with respect to the direct object, the genitive case alone is more appropriate, as in "the cognition of a jar" (*ghaṭasya vijñānam*). 143.06. [The author replies: No, because of the transposition of case endings (*vibhakti-vyatyayāt*); this occurs precisely in place of the genitive.

The seventh case is to be understood as in other instances, where specific non-simultaneous conjunctions are the causes for the difference in action; why this transposition [of cases]? If by transposition some meaning is obtained, it is appropriate. As for the transposition: "in which there are specific non-simultaneous conjunctions" has the sense of the locus (adhikaraṇa).
Even those parts of an arrow, their specific conjunctions are also causes for [the production of] action distinct from [their own] substance.

Thus, we do not observe here a reversal of the effect; therefore, a reversal of the case-ending is improper. It is not improper; it is for the purpose of making known the particularity of that which has been understood in a general sense.

143.13–143.15: "Of that very [object] whose universal has been apprehended, its particulars must also be understood. And those particulars are either conjunct (*saṃyogin*) or inherent (*samavāyin*), by way of the logical possibility of their causes and the validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "Logical possibility" (*upapatti*) means occurrence; it is so called because a means of knowledge occurs with respect to this object.

143.16 This would be the meaning: the example is that this knower who knows the object to be known—one should know him in reality as "this"—is one who possesses the nature of arising or the nature of non-arising; thus, up to the point where the commentary states, "one [person] knows both. By means of this [knower] who possesses the nature of non-arising...

The deliberation that "it must be so" is *tarka* (reasoning). [Objection: Is this not indeed the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) itself? [Reply: It is said, "for the sake of the knowledge of reality"; however, this is not the knowledge of reality because it lacks final determination. For one does not determine it thus: "It is exactly so. Rather, [one thinks] that there must be a knower whose nature is non-arising.
144.01 He allows for the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But how does this [reasoning] serve the purpose of the knowledge of reality?
144.02 By means of the discernment of the objects of the means of valid cognition, he discerns the object of the means of valid cognition, thinking: "This meaning is logical.
144.03 The means of valid cognition, when operating, understand the object as it truly is, distinguished by reasoning (*tarka*).

144.04 Some maintain that *ūha* (presumptive reasoning) is not distinct from doubt (*saṃśaya*) and certainty (*nirṇaya*). This *ūha*, they say, is either doubt; if it is included therein, it should not be recited separately because it is already subsumed by that. Or, if it is certainty, it is likewise subsumed by that. Others, however, state that *tarka* (reasoning) is inference (*anumāna*); [it is] the logical reason (*hetu*).

"Reasoning (*tarka*), logic (*nyāya*), and inquiry (*anvīkṣā*) are called inference (*anumāna*)," so it is said. Others, however, describe reasoning itself as being dependent on logical justification (*yukti-apekṣa*), on the grounds that "inference is not distinct from deliberation (*ūha*), which consists of doubt and determination. This is not correct, because of a failure to understand the essential nature of cognition; for [reasoning] occurs generally with respect to an object whose true nature is not yet known.

144.10 You have raised a valid point; however, it is true that [doubt] occurs when the true nature of an object is not known, but you have not yet understood the actual nature of cognition (*pratyaya*).
144.11 You have failed to recognize that doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition whose essence consists in non-determination, characterized by the thought "What might this be?
144.12 A cognition whose essence consists in determination, characterized by the thought "This is exactly so," is certainty (*nirṇaya*). This [certainty], however, is distinct from doubt.

144.13 One who has fallen away from the occurrence of the cause, and has not yet reached a definitive conclusion because of the non-perception of a distinguishing feature—144.14 for a definitive conclusion arises from the perception of a distinguishing feature, and in this case there is no perception of a distinguishing feature. By this, the claim that "reasoning (tarka) is inference" is also refuted. What, then, is the essential nature of this [reasoning], given the phrase "because of the non-perception of a distinguishing feature"?

144.16–144.18: Even for those who state that "reasoning" (*tarka*) is "an inference that depends upon logic (*yukti*), characterized by the cognition [in the form] 'it must be so' regarding the essential nature of this [object]," they themselves must explain the distinction between reasoning and inference. Logic is the establishment through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Reasoning is merely that cognition which depends upon the establishment through valid means of knowledge.

144.19 It is merely a difference in designation. Now, if there is no establishment by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what is the reasoning (*yukti*)? [If you say] it is inference (*anumāna*), then it must be explained that it depends upon reasoning.
144.20 Thus, its capacity for dependence must be stated. Furthermore, in the apprehension of its own object, what does inference depend upon?
144.21 If it is said that reasoning depends upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even so, the purpose of grasping the object must be stated. How?

Inference is supported by perception and scripture. Now, regarding inference, its having the same object as perception and scripture—even in that case, reasoning (*tarka*) is connected with these three as objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus it would be. The two cognitions of determination (*avadhāraṇa*) have different causes, because they possess distinct characteristics, like [the cognitions of] perception...

145.03. Like inferential cognition (*anumāna-pratyaya*), inference (*anumāna*) is reasoning (*tarka*), because it depends upon the recollection of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*).
145.04. It is not like [ordinary] inference, because its own nature is not understood; nor does it depend upon the recollection of the relationship between the mark and the marked.
145.05. How is reasoning? Because there is no apprehension of the two; whereas where the two are apprehended—the locus (*dharmin*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*)—[it is inference].
Furthermore, inference operates where there is the apprehension of a mere property-bearer (*dharmin*) but not the apprehension of a mark (*liṅga*). [For example, one might think:
"There exists a specific kind of good action. Therefore, it is untenable that inference depends upon the recollection of the relationship between the mark and the bearer of the mark.
Moreover, inference operates upon the perception of a property residing in a property-bearer, whereas reasoning (*tarka*) does not. Reasoning—

145.09 Furthermore, it also proceeds by means of demonstrating a property residing in another, such as "this person must be so," or as in the case [of the inference]: "In this place horses are being driven; therefore, horse-driving is a property of the person. This is a property residing in another. 145.11 Since it is merely the exclusion of the possibility of it being a post (*sthāṇu*) through logical consistency, it is *ūha* (presumptive reasoning). This *tarka* (reasoning) serves to connect the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
145.12. That which is stated in debate is accompanied by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but this [statement] is not so, because it does not determine the means of valid cognition.

145.13 [1-1-41] *Nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is the determination of the truth through the examination of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), after having reflected and re-reflected.
145.14 Regarding this subject matter of *tarka* (reasoning), *nirṇaya* is the determination of the truth through the thesis and the counter-thesis, after having reflected and re-reflected.
145.15 Thus is the aphorism (*sūtra*). The connection and the meaning are as before. "Having reflected and re-reflected" means having performed repeated reflection (*vimarśa*).

145.16–18. From the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), and from both the thesis and the counter-thesis—by the word "thesis" is meant the proof (*sādhana*) whose object is the thesis;

by the word "counter-thesis" is meant the refutation (*upālambha*) of the proof whose object is the counter-thesis. Determination (*nirṇaya*) is that ascertainment of the matter which results from these two, namely, the proof and the refutation. But where does this [determination] occur?

145.19 Is the restriction (niyama) [that knowledge arises] from a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya), or rather from the proponent’s position and the opponent’s counter-position, or else through repeated deliberation (vimṛśya vimṛśya)?

145.20 When it is said that there is a restriction such that the definitive conclusion occurs only through repeated deliberation by means of the proponent’s position and the opponent’s counter-position, 145.21 this contradicts the statement that "knowledge is that which arises from the contact of the sense-faculty with its object. By this [same logic],...

146.01. It has already been replied: "Only after repeated deliberation. Now, [if it is argued that] determination (*nirṇaya*) arises from both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), then determination would necessarily depend upon both. 146.02–03. There is a restriction regarding the domain of reasoning (*tarka*); it does not apply elsewhere. Regarding this very domain of reasoning, after repeated deliberation, determination occurs precisely through the thesis and the counter-thesis.

146.04. "The determination occurs precisely through the thesis and the counter-thesis, after having deliberated again and again"—this is the general definition of determination (*nirṇaya*). Why is this restriction that it is the object of deliberation (*tarka*)? Because deliberation is mentioned immediately after [determination].
The restriction that it is the object of deliberation is because there is no determination otherwise; it is not [the case that] there is no determination at all.

146.07 Now, what is the definition of *nirṇaya* (ascertainment)? It is the determination (*avadhāraṇa*) of an object; thus, *nirṇaya* is the delimitation of an object. 146.08 This *nirṇaya*, occurring within the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is produced by the means of valid cognition either individually or collectively. 146.09 In the domain of reasoning (*tarka*), it is produced collectively; elsewhere, it is produced by one. In debate (*vāda*) and in treatises (*śāstra*), [it occurs] with or without deliberation (*vimarśa*); in debate, it pertains to the position (*pakṣa*).
146.10 There is no deliberation (*vimarśa*) regarding either the treatise (*śāstra*) or the debate (*vāda*), because both [the proponent and opponent] have already reached certainty.

146.11 Furthermore, because the categories accepted in the treatise are already certain. 146.12 It is incorrect to claim that the terms "proposition" (*pakṣa*) and "counter-proposition" (*pratipakṣa*) refer to proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upālambha*), for there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*); the terms "proposition" and "counter-proposition" do not denote proof and refutation.
"It is said [that they are] 'stated' (ucyete). What is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? Furthermore, why is it not according to the literal text?

Because the thesis (pakṣa) and the counter-thesis (pratipakṣa) are objects of action (karman), and [the means of cognition] do not define the object of action because that [object] is what is to be defined.
Therefore, by the words "thesis" and "counter-thesis," there is the inclusion of the proof (sādhana) and the refutation (upālambha), which are the two defining agents.

Since those two [inquiry and deliberation] are themselves without an object [of their own], it should not be said that they are not grasped from one [of the others]. Rather, it must be stated as follows: "Ascertainment (nirṇaya) is the determination of an object through repeated inquiry and deliberation, and through refutation and support. This being so, the object becomes qualified by its own [specific] nature. Furthermore, there is no distinction produced merely by brevity; therefore, [the definition] is not for the purpose of indicating a single subject matter.

146.19 The determination has as its object that which is the object of the proof and the refutation. For otherwise, if it were merely stated that "determination arises from proof and refutation," it would not be known where the determination occurs. By the terms *pakṣa* (proposition) and *pratipakṣa* (counter-proposition), there is the inclusion of the proof and the refutation, as well as their object. [The word] *artha* (object) is used for the purpose of...

146.22 Then it should not be stated [as a reason], because it is "being traversed" (*gamyamānatvāt*). Since one has reflected again and again upon the thesis (*pakṣa*) by means of both the position and its counter-position, when it is said that the determination [of the object] is reached, the word "object" (*artha*) need not be included [in the definition]. However, the inclusion of the word "object" is for the purpose of making known the ascertainment of one or the other through the power of the verbal testimony (*śruti-sāmarthyāt*), as it is "being traversed."

147.03 By what one does, one makes it known that there is a determination on one side or the other. To say that "the ascertainment of the matter is by means of the thesis (pakṣa) and the counter-thesis (pratipakṣa)" is incorrect. Why? Because it is understood from only one [of them]. This ascertainment is not by means of both the thesis and the counter-thesis together; rather, it is that which is established from one [side].

He says: "By both alone. How so? For when both have ceased, the deliberation (*vimarśa*) has indeed not ceased; [but] when both remain present, it has not ceased either. However, when one remains and the other ceases, then there is a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*). Therefore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), acting together, are the causes of definitive conclusion.
147.09 Thus. In this matter, when does the determination occur—is it in the first [statement], or 147.10 in the second, or in the third? It occurs everywhere because the object exists in that manner;
or rather, 147.11 it is appropriate that it occurs in the third. How so? First, one person establishes the thesis by means of the proof.

147.12 The second [type of respondent] either proceeds after seeing a proof (*sādhana*) or, having recognized a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), proceeds with the desire to manifest its defects (*doṣa*). Regarding that [first type], he states the proof once it has been set aside. Now, in the first case, if he thinks, "The proof is certain," he does not proceed; however, if it is a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*), [he proceeds].

Thus it is understood; for the purpose of demonstrating that [first position], one proceeds, and upon the cessation of that [proceeding], the proof of the second position also ceases. What is the reason? Because the proof of the first position is faultless.
And since there is no room for a second [position] when the proof of the first position is faultless, it ceases. It does not [cease] otherwise.

147.18–20. Regarding the second position, that in which one stands firm—that is the determination (*nirṇaya*). This determination is produced by combining the possibility and impossibility of the thesis and the counter-thesis. Some maintain that determination is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*) and not a separate category (*padārthāntara*). [The author replies: No.

147.21 Because inference depends upon the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and that which possesses the mark (liṅgin), and because it depends upon the recollection of that relationship between the mark and the possessor of the mark, there is an absence of that [recollection] at the moment of the final ascertainment (nirṇaya).

148.01 Since it is the result, inference is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), whereas the final ascertainment is the fruit of the means of valid cognition; the final ascertainment has its own object as its domain. 148.02 Inference, however, has both its own object and other objects as its domain; for example, the perception of smoke is an inference by way of the determination of smoke.
148.03 ...is also a determination (*nirṇaya*). And when one determines [the object] by means of smoke, then it is inferred:

"by this [means]"; thus, inference is the determination of fire, and its fruit is that very determination. And when, relying on the derivation of the action (*bhāva-sādhana*), it is stated that "inference is determination," then one must proceed with approval [of that definition]. And when...
If it is stated that "inference is determination" by relying on the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), then a refutation must be voiced:
because of the difference between cause and effect, inference is the cause and determination is the effect;
therefore, inference is not determination.
148.09 Thus ends the first daily lesson (*āhnika*) of the first chapter in the *Nyāyavārttika* by Uddyotakara. 148.10–11 Now begins the second daily lesson.
148.12 There are three types of discourse (*kathā*): debate (*vāda*), contentious discussion (*jalpa*), and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*). This [debate] is not...

148.13 What, then, is the restriction? It is the restriction of the subject matter of investigation (*vicāra-vastu-niyama*). Whatever object is investigated is investigated in three ways: 148.14 namely, as discussion (*vāda*), contentious debate (*jalpa*), and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*). Among these, discussion is with teachers and the like; contentious debate and destructive criticism are with those who desire victory. In this regard, according to the enumeration, the definition—

148.16. *Apadeśa* (the formal presentation) is stated to be the definition of debate (*vāda*); therein, there is the establishment [of one's own position] and the refutation [of the opponent's] by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*).
148.17. Thus is the aphorism (sūtra).

149.01. [1-2-1(42)] [Debate is] that which employs valid cognition and reasoning as its means of proof and refutation, is not contrary to established tenets (*siddhānta*), and possesses the five [members].
149.02 Debate (*vāda*) is the adoption of a thesis (*pakṣa*) and its counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), endowed with [proper] members [of proof].
149.03 In that regard, debate is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis. But what are these two, the thesis and the counter-thesis?

149.04 They are properties of a real entity (*vastu-dharma*) that reside in a single locus (*ekādhikaraṇa*), are contradictory (*viruddha*), exist at the same time (*eka-kāla*), and are not yet determined; such are the properties of a real entity.

149.05 Because a particular object is apprehended through the generality of the thing, yet not apprehended in its specific detail; 149.06 deliberation (*vicāra*) has the comprehension of that specific detail as its cause. Therefore, these two properties of the object are non-distinct and share a single substratum.
149.07 Two [properties] with different substrata do not induce deliberation, because both are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as for example:

149.08 “Intellect is impermanent; the self is permanent. Even though these two are not [inherently] contradictory, those which are contradictory cause an investigation to be undertaken, whereas those which are not contradictory do not. For example, as in the case of “a substance possesses action” and “it possesses qualities.
In that context, regarding the two [categories] called “time,” since there is no further investigation after the conclusion has been reached, these two are contradictory.

149.11 Thus, the two qualifying properties (*dharma*) are the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*); their "acceptance" (*parigraha*) is the restriction to such a state of being. 149.12 "This subject (*dharmin*) possesses such properties (*evam-dharman*), and not such-and-such other properties (*na evam-dharman*). This very acceptance of the thesis and counter-thesis is *vāda* (debate).

149.13 Since this discourse is common to all three paths for the sake of non-confusion, [the author] uses the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and "reasoning" (*tarka*) for the purpose of specification.

149.14. "Establishment and refutation" (*sādhana-upālambhaḥ*): in this [work], establishment and refutation are carried out by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and by reasoning (*tarka*).
149.15. The locative designation "in this" (*asmin*)—meaning "it occurs in this"—is for the purpose of indicating the subject matter (*viṣaya*).
149.16. In this investigation, how then can there be establishment and refutation by means of reasoning, given that it is not a valid instrument of cognition?

"Because it assists the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), reasoning (*tarka*) is not subsumed under the [standard] means of valid cognition, nor is it a separate means of valid cognition. This has been stated. How, then, can this [reasoning], being of the nature of non-valid cognition, serve as the instrument for establishing or refuting [an object]?
We do not say that reasoning is the instrument for establishing or refuting; rather, it functions by discerning the objects of the means of valid cognition.

149.20 Reasoning (tarka) assists the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); thus, the means of valid cognition, operating upon an object free from reasoning, 149.21 determine it. Since this [reasoning] is an assistant to the means of valid cognition, it is designated as "associated with the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇasahita) in debate. Why is this? Because within it there occurs both proof (sādhana) and refutation (upālambha).

150.02–150.04. Thus, *siddhi* (establishment) is the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the means of refutation (*upālambhana*). Now, that by which something is established is the means of proof (*sādhana*); that by which one refutes is the means of refutation (*upālambha*). If, first of all, the words "means of proof" and "means of refutation" are used in the sense of the accomplishment of an entity (*bhāva-sādhana*), then they are not logically consistent with the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and with reasoning (*tarka*), because the instruments of valid cognition and reasoning [are not themselves entities to be accomplished].

150.05 Because they do not cause understanding in others, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are instruments for establishing one's own realization; whereas the purpose here is the communication to others. Therefore, the establishment and apprehension [of an object] do not occur through the means of valid cognition and reasoning (*tarka*).
Furthermore, even if these two were understood as being established by their instruments (*karaṇa*), the phrase "endowed with five members" (*pañcāvayavopapanna*) need not be read separately.

150.08 What is the reason? [The phrase] "establishment and refutation by means of proof and reasoning" (pramāṇa-tarka-sādhana-upālambhaḥ) is explained by the word *sādhana* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

150.09 Since the meaning of the individual members [of the syllogism] has already been stated, the phrase "endowed with five members" (pañcāvayavopapanna) does not have that same meaning; rather, we shall explain its distinct meaning later. Furthermore, if these two words, *sādhana* and *upālambha*, are used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*), what is their object?

150.11 They are established by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) and by reasoning (*tarka*). [Objection: But was it not said that these are the "subject" and the "object"? [Response: It is true that the proof (*sādhana*) has the subject as its object, and the censure (*upālambha*) has the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) as its object; however, what was said was not correct. What is the loss of reasoning here? Because the censure does not have the counter-position as its object, there is no accomplishment through valid cognition and reasoning.

150.14–150.16: "Let there be non-establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*), but the censure (*upālambha*) is not the subject of the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*); we do not say that the censure has the counter-position as its object. Rather, the censure has as its object the means of proof (*sādhana*) belonging to the counter-position; that which is the proof for the counter-position—that is the object of the censure. How, then, is it being taught in the presence of the counter-position?

The term "objection" (upālambha) is connected by implication with the means of proof (sādhana) that is distinct from the counter-position (pratipakṣa). Furthermore, because of the lack of capacity, that which is fit for objection is indeed objected to; however, the counter-position is not fit for objection. How so? Because there is no difference between the nature of an object being objected to and an object not being objected to.
150.20 When an object that exists in such a state is being examined as existing in that very state, [certain] positions are obtained.
150a.01 Even when it is not being examined as existing in such a state, the proof remains the same;
for even the proof, 150a.02 as an instrument, never abandons its own essential nature (svarūpa). Therefore, regarding the proof—

"Furthermore, this objection is not tenable. Thus, the lack of an objection applies to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not to the object (*karman*), because of the capacity [of the instrument] within its own domain; every object is capable within its own domain, and the instrument is likewise so.
However, it has no capacity in another domain. And that which lacks capacity in another domain cannot [perform the action] by means of it.
Is it a deficiency in the action or in the instrument? To whom, then, does this censure belong, he who is defeated?

Who is it that is defeated? It is the person, not the action nor the instrument; for non-comprehension and misconception belong to the person, not to the action or the instrument. He is defeated because he employs an action and an instrument that are incapable of accomplishing the goal.

The cognizer also [is characterized] by the cognition of the meanings of the words as they have been stated. This very quality (*dharma*) of the person is manifested through the medium of speech; thus, by metaphorically attributing [the quality] to the speech, one is censured for the speech that expresses the quality of the person.
How, then, is this meaning obtained from the words of the Sūtra? It is obtained, he says. How?

Establishment by means of valid cognition and reasoning (*pramāṇa-tarka-sādhana*) refers to the establishment [of a thesis] by means of valid cognitions and by means of reasoning, as well as the refutation (*upālambha*) [of an opponent's position] by means of valid cognitions and reasoning.
The compound *pramāṇa-tarka-sādhana-upālambha* consists of both "establishment by means of valid cognition and reasoning" and "refutation by means of valid cognition and reasoning.
The word *sādhana* is elided because its meaning is already understood, just as in the case of the term *uṣṭramukhī* ("one whose face is like that of a camel"). Now, regarding *pramāṇa*—

Regarding the phrase "establishment and refutation by means of reasoning" (*tarka-sādhana-upālambha*), how is *vāda* distinguished from *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*? Is it not the case that this [phrase] is common to all three, since they all involve the adoption of a position and its counter-position?
It is not the same; for in *vāda*, there is reliance upon valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning as the instruments of establishment and refutation.

Because it is restricted [to the pursuit of truth], debate (*vāda*) consists solely of the establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*). When establishment and refutation are carried out by means of quibbles (*chala*) and so forth, they are merely contentious discourse (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*). For example, although "possessing horns" is common to both a cow and a gayal, when it is distinguished by such features as having a dewlap and so forth, it characterizes both the cow and the gayal as distinct.

"Likewise, it is the employment of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) for the purpose of establishing [one's own position] and refuting [the opponent's]. Because it is stated that 'disputation (*jalpa*) is the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the purpose of establishing and refuting,' there is a prohibition of points of defeat in formal debate (*vāda*) due to specific regulations; therefore, debate is characterized by the absence of such defeat. This is because it is defined as 'the employment of means of valid cognition and reasoning for the purpose of establishing and refuting.'"

There is no fault in [stating] that there are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) even in debate (*vāda*), because of the inclusion of "reproach" (*upālambha*). If it follows that all points of defeat apply [to debate] due to the inclusion of "reproach," this is merely a difference in terminology. If you think that points of defeat exist in debate because of the inclusion of "reproach," is it not merely a difference in terminology between "disputation" (*jalpa*) and "debate" (*vāda*)?
This is the distinction: since points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) exist both there [in the previous section] and here [in this one], the two subsequent terms are not intended for restriction.
For it is by the word "objection" (*upālambha*) that all points of defeat are encompassed.
Therefore, the subsequent terms are commenced for the sake of non-restriction: [a thesis] not contradictory to the established tenet (*siddhānta*), consisting of five...

"And endowed with the [proper] members" (*avayava-upapannaḥ*). By this phrase "contrary to the established tenet" (*siddhānta-viruddhaḥ*), it is indeed the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) that is obtained; it is not obtained from anything else. This very one is obtained through the expression "endowed with the five members. From the mention of "five," the deficient and the superfluous are obtained; from the mention of "members," those [two]—the deficient and the superfluous—are excluded.
151.05 “Appearances are obtained as non-existents. Even if one were to state again an object that has already been obtained, it would be like grinding what has already been ground.

151.06 Therefore, this is not the meaning. Now, if [the opponent asks], “What is the meaning of this phrase ‘not contradicting the established tenet’?”—it would be entirely purposeless. (Therefore, this is not the meaning. It is not purposeless, because by not contradicting the established tenet, one upholds the tenet.

151.08. "The upasiddhānta (the opponent's established conclusion) occurs when, having accepted [a premise], one proceeds with a discourse without restriction; this is what is excluded by this [rule]. 151.09. Therefore, it is not meaningless. Why, then, is this restriction made—that in formal debate (*vāda*), fallacious members (*avayavābhāsa*) and the *apasiddhānta* are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? 151.10. Because this restriction exists due to the instruction on debate given in relation to teachers and the like.
