151.11 One who desires to know reality (tattva-bubhutsu), or one who, together with teachers and others, desires the threefold fruit, engages in debate (vāda). 151.12 Therefore, for such a seeker of knowledge, the means of proof (sādhana) must be stated for as long as there is something yet to be known by him; because it is not subject to opposition, there is no debate with an opponent, but rather a disputational talk (jalpa) wherein all points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) are present. 151.13 [End of section].

It is logical that it is called "application" (*prayoga*), because it is defined as "the establishment [of one's own position] and the refutation [of the opponent's] by means of valid cognition and reasoning.

(151.14–15) If debate (*vāda*) consists of the establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition and reasoning, then there would follow the consequence of both [parties] being either established or unestablished.

(151.15–16) In the case where both the proponent and the opponent employ the expression of establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition and reasoning, they lack the authority [to do so]. (151.16)

151.17 Thus, there arises the contingency that both positions would be either established or unestablished. This is not a fault, because it is not so asserted; this is not being asserted [as follows]: 151.18 "The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) belong to both disputants," but rather, "the proof must be stated by both. This is what is being restricted, and not that the proof itself belongs to both. The same applies to the refutation (dūṣaṇa).
Others, however, describe the definition of debate (*vāda*) as "speech for the purpose of establishing one's own position and refuting that of another.

In this regard, the inclusion of "one's own position" and "another's position" as qualifiers of the subject is untenable, because of the impossibility of conceptual alternatives and the impossibility of forming a compound. Indeed, these two words, "own" (*sva*) and "other" (*para*), [function as] inclusive...
152.02 Or they may have the sense of exclusion, or the sense of that which is to be established and that which is to be refuted, establishing the positions of the proponent and the opponent;
152.03 or they may illuminate the thesis and the counter-thesis, intending the first and second positions;
152.04 or there may be the expression of multiple words by one person who intends multiple qualifiers. In that regard:

152.05 First of all, the sense of "avoiding possession" (*parigraha-parivarjana*) is untenable because the meaning of the particle *kim* is impossible [in that context]. The meaning of *kim* does not occur when there is possession. [For one asks: "To whom will this belong as property? And what is the purpose of property?
Thus, making something one's own is the meaning of possession; for whoever has the act of making something his own, that thing becomes his property.
That very point is now considered: what is that "own-making" (*svakaraṇa*)? It is the cause for the arising of the cognition "mine.

The presence and absence of the causal state have been indicated as the meanings of the terms "self" (*sva*) and "other" (*para*). For a person, there is no "own" (*sva*) in the sense of being his own; nor is there a "self" or "other" belonging to the author of the treatise for whose sake this [work] might exist. And as for that which...

152.11 That which belongs to oneself benefits that [self] for the sake of its own accomplishment, but it does not benefit the owner [in the same way]. 152.12 No benefit whatsoever is produced by the [opponent's] position; therefore, the terms "one's own" (*sva*) and "the other" (*para*) do not refer to the acts of grasping and abandoning. Rather, the terms "one's own" and "the other" have the sense of that which is to be established and that which is to be refuted.
152.14 Furthermore, it might be argued: "One's own position (*svapakṣa*) is to be established (*sādhanīya*), while the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*) is to be refuted.

152.15 Ah! What skill in understanding the meaning of the treatise! [For you say] that which is to be established (*sādhya*) would be "that which is to be established" (*sādhanīya*); one's own position is to be established. 152.16 From where does this follow? For the definition of a position (*pakṣa*) is: "A position is that which is intended to be established"; thus, it is "that which is to be established" (*sādhanīya*).
152.17 Even by means of the word, that very same thing is expressed; and this is stated for the purpose of delimitation: "one's own position" and "the position of another.

152.18 Thus, by means of the word "own," which functions through delimitation from the position of another, one is able to express an identical meaning. 152.19 Alternatively, the qualification is redundant, for even general terms function with reference to a specific instance.
152.20 Thus, it is not the case that these are general terms which apply to particulars;

rather, 152.21 even particular terms follow the distinctions of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. Furthermore, that which is to be established—152.22 the thesis (*pakṣa*), one's own position (*svapakṣa*), and the thesis to be refuted, the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*)—we do not understand this as something to be established.

153.01 Since sound is the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), let the thesis be that which is to be proven; however, the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) can never [be the thesis]. 153.02 For the refutation is not connected with the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*), because the opponent's position remains as it was. Now, what is the object of the refutation? If it is said to be the object of some establishment (*sthāpanā*), then how could a refutation [be related] to both one's own and the opponent's positions?
[The opponent says: "This is indeed irrelevant. What kind of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) is connected with the proof (*sthāpanā*), and what is this proof? [The proponent replies:

"Proof is that which consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*), is expressed as a statement that establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*), and is free from verbal defects. Refutation is the pointing out of the defects in that statement—whether it be deficient, redundant, or characterized by fallacious members (*avayavābhāsa*). This is the refutation.

It is connected with the *sthāpanā* (the proof) because it has that as its object. However, the remaining refutation is not connected with the *sthāpanā*, nor with one's own or the opponent's position; rather, it consists of the subsequent fault and the nature of the objection. It is true that there is no direct connection with the thesis (*pakṣa*), but it functions by way of the cessation of the *sthāpanā*.
153.10 Refutation does not negate the [proponent's] own position; rather, it is said that one refutes the opponent's position by means of the cessation of the establishment [of that position].
153.11 The employment of figurative language is inappropriate in a definition, because a definition has reality as its object.
153.12 A definition is that which excludes what is not the reality; there is no establishment [of a definition] through the employment of figurative language.

And if a refutation, proceeding through a series of steps (*pāramparyeṇa*), brings about the cessation of the opponent's position as it unfolds, then it would be useless to speak or act in such a way, [claiming] that "debate (*vāda*) consists of speech directed against the opponent's position. If this were asserted, what would happen? [The result would be that] the aphorism (*sūtra*) would become concise, yet both the proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) would remain [as they are].

153.16–17: [The opponent argues: "By way of a traditional succession (*pāramparyeṇa*), it would not establish the thesis for the opposing side. Now, so that there is no such succession in either case, 153.17–18: it must be stated according to its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) as follows: "Debate (*vāda*) is speech for the purpose of establishing or not establishing one's own position (*pakṣasthāpanā*).
153.18: For in this way, the definition is clear, and there is a connection with its respective object; thus, the establishment (*sthāpanā*) is also [included].

153.19. The objection that "the refutation is not connected with the prior [proposition]" does not result in the persistence of the same fault, because it is possible for [the refutation] to be connected with something. 153.20. Furthermore, even though the refutation is expressed in general terms as being connected with the proof (*sthāpanā*), by implication there is a restriction. 153.21. Therefore, this [objection] is untenable; for the objects to be proven and the objects to be refuted belong respectively to oneself and to others.

154.01. As for what was stated—that the two words [in the compound] refer to "one's own" and "another's," and that they signify the meanings of the prior and subsequent positions (pūrva-uttara-pakṣa)—154.02. this too is not tenable as "prior and subsequent positions," because one accepts a restriction regarding proof (sādhana) and refutation (dūṣaṇa).
154.03. Therefore, in this sūtra [which reads] "by means of proofs and refutations," there is a restriction regarding proof and refutation.

154.04 Stating one's own position (*svapakṣa*), establishing it, and refuting the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*): since this necessarily constitutes the scope of the reply (*uttara*), it follows that the proponent of the reply (*uttaravādin*) would be refuting his own very position.

154.06 And since the "own position" of the respondent is different from the "prior position" (*pūrvapakṣa*), by the words "own" (*sva*) and "other" (*para*), [the terms] refer to the prior and the subsequent positions respectively.

The designation "pakṣa" (position) does not refer to a mere word-meaning, nor is it a conventional term for "contemplation. By this, the meaning of "proposition and counter-proposition" and the meaning of "the first and second positions" are explained. This very same "pakṣa," being qualified by two attributes—by way of being that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) and that which is to be refuted (*dūṣya*)—is [designated as] one's own or another's...

154.10 It is correct that [the object] is denotable by a word; however, the dual number is not correct. We say that while the connection of a single [entity] with multiple qualifiers is not prohibited, the dual number does not occur. For when there is a relation with multiple qualifiers for a single [entity], neither the dual nor the plural number occurs; it is not as if [one says] "Devadatta" [in the plural].
154.13 Just as by means of the umbrella and the staff, speakers come to say, "The two who possess the umbrella and the staff have arrived.

154.14 Thus, because conceptual construction is untenable, the terms "self" (sva) and "other" (para) are untenable, and because a compound is impossible; [the phrase] "one's own position" (svapakṣa)—this being a compound word—in that regard, first of all, there is no comprehension of the essential nature of the qualifier and the qualified.
154.16. Regarding the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*): where a genitive case is compounded, there the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is [distinguished] from the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

154.17. It is apprehended separately, as in "the king’s man" (*rāja-puruṣaḥ*), because of their difference. And where there is a relationship between qualifier and qualified, 154.18. there a difference is observed, just as in the case of "the king’s man. Even when no difference exists, it is observed [as if there were one].

154.19 If it is argued that the genitive compound is observed even when there is no difference—as in "army-leader" (*senāpati*) or "ingredient of a drink" (*pānakāṅga*)—that is not so, because we do not accept it. For what person of sound mind would understand the referent of the word "drink" to be non-different from its ingredients, or the army to be non-different from its soldiers? And just as...

155.01 [The opponent argues: "An army (*senā*) and so forth are entities distinct from their constituent parts; thus it is said that this is a discourse on the quality and the possessor of the quality (*guṇa-guṇi-vāda*). Now, if you think:

'The meaning of the word is not the referent of the word *pakṣa*,' that is not so, because it has already been refuted. It has been stated how a word does not denote its own [phonetic] form; therefore, there can be no genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). By this same reasoning, there can be no descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*)."

It is refuted [as a karmadhāraya compound] because it would entail the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-svarūpa-asiddhi*)—since that which is "one's own" (*sva*) is not distinct from the "position" (*pakṣa*)—and because there is no difference [between the two]. By this, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is also refuted; furthermore, the means of proof (*sādhana*) would then result in having the prover itself as its object.

Therefore, it is not a *bahuvrīhi*. [Objection: But surely, the state of being provable (*sādhanīyatā*) can exist as the meaning of "one's own" (*svārtha*) by way of being a qualifier of the position (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇatvena*).

155.07. It is not possible [to say] that "the thesis (*pakṣa*) is to be proven" because it is a synonym (*paryāya*); for a synonym itself is not [the thesis]. 155.08. A *bahuvrīhi* compound in grammatical apposition with words that are synonyms is not possible;
for it does not occur that one says, "He cuts the tree with the tree," due to contradiction. Furthermore, if this word "thesis" (*pakṣa*) [is used] from its own perspective...

155.10 There is a contradiction in saying that "the statement of the opponent's position is the thesis" (*pratijñā*). What is the reason? Because the thesis has one's own position as its object. 155.11 Alternatively, if it is not distinct [from the opponent's position], then this does not follow: that "debate" (*vāda*) is speech for the sake of establishing or refuting one's own and the opponent's positions; nor is any other compound possible.
155.13 And this statement, "therefore, of one's own and the other's positions," is therefore without substance. Let that be for now.

155.14 [Let us consider] the meaning of the words *sva* (own) and *para* (other), the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between the two words *sva* and *para*, and then the compound (*samāsa*). 155.15 Why is it not formulated as: "Discussion (*vāda*) is speech for the sake of establishing one's own position and refuting the other's"? Why is it not thus?
When [the compound] is formed, that very same meaning is preserved and there is brevity. On this point, some offer a rebuttal:

"If indeed a compound were made, both the established and the unestablished would occur; this is not a flaw because the flaw remains as it was. This flaw is not avoided by forming the compound. How so?

155.19 [The phrase] "for the sake of the establishment of one's own position and the non-establishment of the other's position" means "for the sake of the establishment and non-establishment of both one's own and the other's positions. 155.20 [The opponent objects: "No, because it is not possible; for this compound is not semantically coherent [in the sense of] 'for the sake of the establishment of one's own position and the non-establishment [of the other]' (svapakṣasiddhyasiddhyartham).
155.21 [The author replies: "Why? Because it is contradictory; if one strives for the sake of establishment, then to say 'for the sake of non-establishment' is a contradiction."

155.22 If one strives for non-establishment [while claiming] it is for the sake of establishment, there is a contradiction; if, due to incapacity, there is no compound (samāsa), [then so be it]. 156.01 Even if there were a compound, however, because of incapacity, there would be no contingency of establishing or not establishing both positions. Others say: "There would be the contingency of using the singular or plural number. Indeed, if a compound were made, it would be a compound.

156.03 Because there is no manifestation of a distinction in the statement, therefore there is no compound based on a manifested distinction in the statement. How indeed [could it be]? 156.04 Debate (*vāda*) would be a statement for the sake of establishing one's own position and refuting that of another, not for the sake of multiple positions of oneself and others.

156.05 [Regarding the phrase] "of one's own and another's position," it is not so because of impossibility; there is no such thing as a statement for the sake of establishing only one [position] of oneself and another.
156.06–156.08: "Inference is the sole means of establishing the [two] sides"; even so, this [inference] does not exist [here], and therefore the suspicion is misplaced.

Others say that the rule for compound formation is non-mandatory (*anitya*). Others describe the non-mandatory nature of the rules for compound formation. They say this: "This rule does not necessarily require a compound in every instance; in some cases..."
156.09. Sometimes there is a compound and sometimes a sentence, as in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and *rājapuruṣaḥ*.
156.10. [This is] a compound. Why is it that when both [conditions] are present there is no compound? Because the rule for compounds is not mandatory (*anitya*). 156.11.
By saying this, it is implied that both conditions have been met; so, when both are present, why is there no compound?
156.12. Why is this [objection] not refuted? It is not refuted because it serves the purpose of brevity (lāghava).

156.13. Brevity exists in a compound; thus, in a compound such as *go*, there is brevity. Furthermore, words are employed for the sake of following the conventional usage (*anugati*). 156.14. If one were to employ a heavy expression, it would have to be justified; however, no acceptance of heaviness or lightness regarding phonemes (*varṇa*) is admitted.

156.15 If this is argued, it is not a valid rebuttal, because the objection has not been resolved. [Objection: "We do not admit the objection regarding the weight or lightness of a phoneme. [Response: No, for why would the objection not be resolved?
156.16–17 Furthermore, while it is accepted that the treatise is designated as a formal debate (*vāda*), the weight or lightness of a phoneme is not taken into account therein.

156.18 “Thus, it is not tenable [to say] ‘for the sake of proof or non-proof’—this too is not tenable. Why? Because of the impossibility of two ways (dvedhā). 156.19 Indeed, this term ‘non-proof’ (asiddhi), when being conceived, must be conceived in two ways: either with respect to manifestation (vyakti) or with respect to origination (utpatti). 156.20 That is not tenable, first of all, with respect to origination, because [it would apply to] the means of proof (sādhana), such as the thesis (pratijñā) and so forth.”

Because it would entail the abandonment of the means of proof (*sādhana-hāni-prasaṅga*); for a real entity (*vastu*) is not produced by the means of proof such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, but rather [it is already existent].

If the production of an effect were imagined, the purpose of the means of proof—which is to manifest that which already exists—would be lost. If you say, "It is manifestation," no; because manifestation requires a locus or substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). Or if you think it is "establishment" (*siddhi*)...

157.03. Manifestation is not establishment (*asiddhi*); this [definition] is logical, but the response is contradictory. Regarding "establishment" and "non-establishment" as the communication of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-pratyāyana*): as for these two, establishment and non-establishment characterized by the communication of the locus, when they reside in the locus, how do they belong to the "subject" (*pakṣa*) and the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*)? This is the meaning of the genitive case.
And this [subject] must be stated, yet it is difficult to state because the establishment or non-establishment of those two depends upon that subject;

therefore, since it is the object of that, it is the "pakṣa" (the thesis). This is not correct. Regarding these two—establishment and non-establishment—with respect to the object of the pakṣa: first, is it when the pakṣa is established, or when it is unestablished? If it is when it is established, then there is no locus for...

157.09. What is accomplishment (*siddhi*)? It is the means of cognition (*pratyāyana*). Why is that? Because accomplishment is that by which there is the cognition of that [object]. And why is that? 157.10. Because that object exists in such a way (*tathātva*), since that object exists as it is. How does it exist in such a way? 157.11. In accordance with how it is connected with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, non-discrepancy (*avisamvāditva*) with the means of valid cognition is that "existing in such a way."
157.12 Non-existence is existence. Now, if the subject (*pakṣa*) is not yet established, the communication of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) occurs through the employment of the means of proof (*sādhana*).
157.13 If there were communication of the locus prior [to the proof], the debate would be useless; for the establishment of the subject is the communication of the locus.
157.14 But how could it be non-establishment? Indeed, it is not by the refutation of the establishment of the opponent's position that [one's own] position is established.

If it should be thought that it has been stated [in verse 157.15] that "it is being performed" refers to the figurative application (*upacāra*) of the cessation of the proof-statement (*sthāpanā*), then this is the refutation: 157.16–17. When [the refutation] is employed, it directly negates the proof-statement; however, the negation of the opponent’s position is only figuratively attributed to the cessation of the proof-statement. This is not so, because there is no purpose [for such a figurative usage]. Indeed, without a purpose, [one does not resort to figurative speech]. 157.18. For, without a purpose, [figurative usage] is not accepted. Furthermore, there is no purpose for the negation of the proof-statement other than the negation of the opponent’s position. Therefore, it is not the case that the negation of the proof-statement is merely a figurative designation for the negation of the opponent’s position. 157.19. Moreover, the negation of the proof-statement is not established by the mere fact of its non-perception. Why? Because there is doubt regarding its non-existence. Just as, even when a proof-statement is not perceived, one cannot definitively conclude its non-existence due to the possibility of doubt, so too, even when the proof-statement is perceived, one cannot definitively conclude its existence due to the possibility of doubt. Therefore, since the proof-statement is not established through perception or non-perception, it follows that it is not established at all. Consequently, the negation of the proof-statement is not established. Thus, the statement "it is being performed" is not a figurative application of the cessation of the proof-statement. Nor is it a figurative application of the negation of the opponent’s position. Why? Because it is not established. Since the negation of the opponent’s position is not established, the statement "it is being performed" is not a figurative application of that either. Furthermore, the negation of the proof-statement is not established by the mere fact of the non-perception of the proof-statement. Why? Because there is doubt regarding its non-existence.
