157.18–19. A deviation from the primary meaning is indeed obtained; however, it is a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) due to the impossibility of [the literal] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of "the platforms cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*). 157.19–20. And this metaphorical usage has as its object words employed in common worldly usage according to worldly convention.
157.20. Furthermore, the meaning of a word is not such that this sentence is merely worldly speech intended for the purpose of establishing one's own position and refuting the opponent's position.

This is the [correct] position. Others, however, describe the non-establishment of the thesis (*pakṣāsiddhi*) as the failure to communicate the intended meaning of the proposition; but that [definition] does not apply to a case where the locus is different (*vyadhikaraṇaviṣaya*). How so? Because the contingency remains: "How is there non-establishment of the thesis? This contingency is like [the question] "How is there establishment? Therefore, establishment and non-establishment are indeed properties (*dharma*) of the thesis, since it is established that [the thesis is that which is to be proven].

158.03. And if the thesis (*pakṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), then in that case there is a contradiction regarding what resides in the observer. If establishment and non-establishment (158.04) are properties of the thesis residing in the observer, it becomes contradictory. Now, if [you say] "let there be no contradiction," and those two [properties] reside in the observer, even so, the manifestation and non-manifestation of the thesis are its establishment and non-establishment.

158.06 Thus it is contradictory. Now, if the establishment and non-establishment of the object (*padārtha*) occur in such and such a manner, then the establishment and non-establishment of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) through cognition would likewise be contradictory. What, then, are these two—manifestation (*vyakti*) and non-manifestation (*avyakti*)—which are properties of the thing (*vastudharma*) and which serve as the causes for designation and cognition, such that there are these two, designation and cognition?

158.09. "Manifest" and "unmanifest"—these are your [terms for] manifestation (*vyakti*) and non-manifestation (*avyakti*). There is an inconsistency regarding the word "object" (*artha*), because a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is untenable. Indeed, when the word "object" (*artha-śabda*) is employed, it functions in three ways: as a designation (*uddeśa*), a purpose (*prayojana*), or as the referent (*viṣaya*) of what is to be expressed. First, regarding the designation, the word "object" is used, for example, in the phrase "for the sake of a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇārtham*).
Regarding the word "bhakte" (in the sense of being used): thus, the fourfold statement is a summary. For what purpose is the word *artha* used in the context of the purpose (*prayojana*)?
[It is used] when that which is to be expressed (*abhidheya*) has arrived, just as one asks, "What is the meaning (*artha*) of the designation 'cow'?
That [usage] is not possible in the case of a mere enunciation (*uddeśa*), because it is specified by way of being either logical or illogical, according to our own position.

158.15–16. When the subject matter (*uddeśa*) is thus specified as "by way of being logical" and "by way of being illogical" regarding the opponent's position, this term "logical" (*yukta*) and "illogical" (*ayukta*) cannot possibly apply to fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) or fallacious proofs (*sādhanābhāsa*). 158.16–17.

For "being logical" (*yuktatā*) consists in the application of a proof (*sādhana-yoga*), whereas "being illogical" (*ayuktatā*) consists in the application of a refutation (*dūṣaṇa-yoga*). Alternatively, it refers to the actual state of the meaning of the words (*śabdārthasya tathātva*).

158.18 Regarding the state of being "proper" (*yukta*) or "improper" (*ayukta*): "properness" (*yuktatva*) is the state of being as it is (*tathābhāva*), while "improperness" (*ayuktatva*) is the state of not being as it is (*atathābhāva*). Nevertheless, because those two are taken as the objects (*karman*), there is a contradiction in whether the locus is communicated by way of "properness" or "improperness," for what is being communicated cannot itself be the act of communication (*pratyāyana*). Alternatively, the word "object" (*artha*) refers to the purpose (*prayojana*).

Even so, one who speaks of fallacious proofs and refutations would be a non-speaker. What is the reason? Because there is no purpose in the establishment or non-establishment of fallacious proofs and refutations;
for the establishment or non-establishment of fallacious proofs and refutations is not the [actual] purpose. And thus, the speaker of such would be a non-speaker, and being a non-speaker in that way—

159.02 It is a fault [to say] that it is "restrained. Now, if the word *artha* is used for the denoted object (*abhidheya*), then [the claim] that the nature of the denotation (*abhidhāna*) is not determined is also incorrect; for neither the author of the text (*grantha-kāra*) nor the commentator (*bhāṣya-kāra*) has specified that this kind of denotation is the expresser of both success (*siddhi*) and failure (*asiddhi*). Surely it has been specified by whom?

159.05 It is true that it has been stated that "establishment" (*siddhi*) and "non-establishment" (*asiddhi*) are what are expressed, and that these two constitute the denotation [of the term *vāda*]. However, 159.06 if these two—establishment and non-establishment—are the designations, then it follows that [the term] is a debate (*vāda*), and there is no other meaning for the word "meaning" (*artha*).

159.07 Therefore, even the word "meaning" (*artha*) is inappropriate. For one who asserts that "debate is speech for the purpose of establishment and non-establishment," [the term *artha* is redundant].

159.08–159.10: "Neither previously nor subsequently has the statement been examined as qualified by the refutation of the Naiyāyika's reason"—this is established by [the opponent's] own admission; furthermore, the sūtra is intended to qualify the entire statement. Thus, there is a contradiction. Therefore, when these words of the sūtra are thus analyzed, they do not constitute an independent [argument].

159.11–159.13: "They are contradictory" means that they contradict the world. Thus, first of all, the words of the Sūtra are incapable according to their own logic, and just as the words of the commentary (*vṛtti*) are incoherent, so it is said: "of one's own position" is improper because one's own meaning is not established, and one's own meaning has been refuted.

159.14–159.16: Furthermore, as for the phrase "of one's own position" (*svasya pakṣasya*), even though the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and locative (*saptamī*) cases are identical in form, the claim that it is intended to indicate the genitive case is also incorrect; for the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is impossible here. Indeed, apart from the position itself, there can be no probandum (*sādhya*) within the position; therefore, [the locative] is not applicable.

159.17–18. Since the seventh case-meaning does not apply [in this context], the qualification is purposeless; thus, there is an inconsistency regarding what is logical and what is illogical. 159.18–19. Because an alternative is untenable, [the alternatives] would have to be either the proof and refutation of what is logical and illogical, or the connection of the category (padārtha) with proof and refutation in such and such a manner. That is not the case, first of all.

159.20 Why are "proof" (*sādhana*) and "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*) mentioned separately from "the logical" (*yukta*) and "the illogical" (*ayukta*)? 159.21 Because they are stated separately as "those [are established] by means of proof and refutation," and because "proof" and "refutation" are expressed by the terms "the logical" and "the illogical.
159.22 Thus, the aphorism (*sūtra*) should be recited as: "The statement of proof and refutation is [established] by means of proof and refutation."

160.01 Because their purpose has already been fulfilled. Now, if you think that [the phrase] "by means of proofs and refutations" (*sādhana-dūṣaṇaiḥ*) is for the sake of qualifying those very two—what is correct and what is incorrect—[we reply: no, because it would entail the consequence of being stated first. If [you claim] the sūtra "by means of proofs and refutations" is for the sake of qualifying correctness and incorrectness, then the nominative case alone would be logical; thus, "proofs" (*sādhana*)...

160.04. Regarding the [objection that] these are "refutations" (*dūṣaṇāni*), it is not the case that in the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*) one says "the blue by means of lotuses. 160.05. If you say it is a "connection" (*yoga*), then if you think that connection with proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) constitutes "being connected" (*yuktatva*) and "not being connected" (*ayuktatva*), 160.06. if you maintain this, then because the reality has not been specified, such a connection with proof and refutation has indeed been specified.
160.07 Thus, because it is not specified, this [claim] that "there is a connection with a means of proof" is untenable. And when does this occur?
160.08 When that object has been determined, at that time there is no purpose for a means of proof whatsoever;
therefore, the communication of a subject by way of being tenable or untenable is a contradiction, and thus there is no connection, as it is not an object [of cognition].

160.10 Likewise, "suchness" (*tathātā*) and "non-suchness" (*atathātā*), as well as "fitness" (*yukta*) and "unfitness" (*ayukta*), [are not the means], because the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-artha*) is impossible in that regard.
160.11 Those two—characterized by suchness and non-suchness, namely fitness and unfitness—are the objects to be excluded (*vyavacchedye*), but they are not the exclusion itself (*vyavacchedasya*).
160.12 Therefore, since there is no sense of an instrument in the proof (*sādhane*), it is correct [to say] that [the instrument] belongs to fitness and unfitness.

To say "the communication of the subject matter" (*adhikaraṇa-pratyāyana*) is not appropriate as the connection of the treatise (*śāstra-sambandha*), because it would be irrelevant. By one who establishes the connection of the treatise, it was stated that "the undertaking of the treatise is for the purpose of removing doubt and error. This is said independently [of that previous statement]: "the communication of the subject matter is the establishment [of the goal]."
160.16. Nor do doubt or error exist among the members of the assembly (*prāśnika*), because they possess the capacity for discernment.

160.17. Therefore, it is not the case that the members of the assembly are those to be convinced. Furthermore, as for what was said—that by convincing the members of the assembly alone, the opponent will also be convinced—what is the reason? For it is said that the opponent... 160.18. [is already convinced].

160.19–21. "Because of attachment to one's own position (*pakṣa-rāga*), one does not understand even a true matter; one does not understand even a true matter"—this is called a contradiction. How then can it be said that "one has understood otherwise"? Or, if one is indeed understanding, yet does not grant the opponent their wish, even so, it is said that "one does not understand."
160.22 And as for the claim that what is called "contradiction" (*vyāhata*) consists in the communication [of the argument] to the judges (*prāśnika*), that too is not so.

161.01 Because of the difference in the instruments of cognition (*pratīti-karaṇa-bheda*), the instruments for the cognition of the judges are distinct from those for the cognition of the opponent (*prativādin*). 161.02 There is no rule that the action of an instrument whose object is one thing must belong to another.

And because of its absence: this rule that debate is solely for the purpose of convincing an audience does not hold, for debate is also observed between teachers and others even in the absence of an audience. However, when one who does not seek the truth, but rather desires gain, honor, or fame, initiates a debate, then there is a need for an audience.
161.06. It is true that there is a purpose, yet it is not a formal debate (*vāda*), because the threefold classification [of discourse] is not accepted.
161.07. This path of discussion is but one; its purposes are the realization of truth (*tattva-avabodha*) as well as gain and so forth.
161.08. It is not established by way of negation; for even if it is said that debate is not for those who desire praise, honor, or gain—
161.09 Because the threefold nature [of debate] is not accepted, it is not the case that the existence of categories depends upon acceptance;

rather, 161.10 there is acceptance when existence is already established. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate the distinction between *jalpa* (contentious debate) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) based on the difference in their definitions, just as there is a threefold path of discourse. Therefore, without knowing this distinction...

It is said [in response]: "Because the threefold [classification] is not accepted. Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the communication that has the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣasiddhi*) as its object:

the term "establishment of the thesis" is used figuratively (*upacarita*), just as the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) whose object is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is called "emptiness" itself. This figurative usage is not employed arbitrarily; rather, it is established through the possibility of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and by means of words as they are conventionally used in the world.

161.15. It has been stated that a designation (*ākhyāna*) is a figurative usage (*upacāra*), and that the employment of figurative terminology is not appropriate within a formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

161.16. Regarding the statement "the utterance for the sake of that [definition]," this too was indeed stated for the purpose of making known the fourfold types of statements: 161.17. namely, the proof (*sādhana*), the fallacy of proof (*sādhana-ābhāsa*), the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), and the fallacy of refutation (*dūṣaṇa-ābhāsa*). These will be connected and will be fully established. That, however, is incorrect; it is logical—
161.18 Because it has been qualified by the term "unreasonableness" (*ayuktatvena*), when it has been thus qualified, how can there be an inclusion of the fourfold statement?

161.19 Regarding the topic of the *adhikaraṇa* (the subject matter), one must state the meaning of *adhikaraṇa* as that which is taken up by both the proponent and the opponent; for in a formal debate (*vāda*), there is nothing whatsoever for the sake of the judges (*prāśnika*). 161.20 This is because [the purpose is] the communication [of the truth].

161.21. If it is argued that it is called the *adhikaraṇa* (locus) because it is the substratum (*ādhāra*), no; for the answer has already been stated: the communication pertains to the thesis (*pakṣa*), not to the audience (*prāśnika*). 161.22. If it is argued that [the name is justified] because it exists when that [audience] is present, no; for it is seen otherwise as well. 162.01. For debate is also observed with teachers and others; therefore, examination (*parīkṣā*) applies to that debate.
162.02. It must be stated: "What [is it], for whom, and where? Debate (*vāda*) is the application of proof and refutation, having the establishment [of a position] as its object.
162.03. Thus, its examination consists in the thorough knowledge of proof, refutation, and their fallacies; the qualification for it is for the sake of that [knowledge]. 162.04.
Regarding the locative case in the word "in that" (*tasmin*), there is no [need for it] since [the debate] occurs between the assembly of judges and the respondent.

162.05–162.07: Having raised the objection that there is a connection to the discussion of speech—whether pleasant or unpleasant—the counter-argument was stated. That [counter-argument] is irrelevant because it lacks a direct or indirect connection with either proof or non-proof, and because of the qualification of "proper" and "improper.
Furthermore, by the subsequent [statement], one has given one's own hand to the one who expresses disconnected categories in both the preceding and following parts.
"Because it is unrelated. If, however, the subsequent statement is indeed disconnected, then it should be stated as follows:

"It is not because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra"; for this very Sūtra, when examined together with the Vārttika, does not cohere with reason. Therefore, let it remain exactly according to the established rule.
162.11 [1-2-1(43)] Debate (*jalpa*) is an objection established by means of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), as previously described.
162.12–162.13 Debate is an objection established by means of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat, as previously described; it is the complete [form].

162.14. *Vāda-lakṣaṇam*: "Chalpa" (wrangling) is the refutation by means of proving [one's own position] through the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). As it has been said: 162.15–16. "It is not correct to say that [wrangling] is 'endowed with what has been stated,' because the restriction regarding the points of defeat in wrangling is not accepted. 162.16. If it were said thus, it would not be a refutation established by reasoning (*tarka-sādhana-upālambha*) that is consistent with one's own tenets (*siddhānta-aviruddha*) and possesses the five members [of a syllogism].

"Speech (*jalpa*) is the taking up of a position and its counter-position, characterized by the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) as means of censure.

This cannot be correct. [The definition] "not contradicting one's own tenets (*siddhānta*) and consisting of five members (*pañcāvayava*)"—because of the hearing of the word "censure" (*upālambha*) in those two phrases, there would be the consequence of including all points of defeat; therefore, [the restriction is] for the purpose of limitation.
162.20. These two terms are for the purpose of restriction [to mean]: "consistent with the established doctrine" (*siddhāntāviruddha*) and "endowed with the five members" (*pañcāvayavopapanna*).
162.21. Furthermore, there is nothing that must be restricted; therefore, these two terms are not to be extended [to other types of debate] for the sake of restriction.
163.01. Thus, it should not be said that [the definition] is "endowed as stated," for this fault does not apply because the extension [of the definition] occurs where it is possible.

163.02. That with which [the definition] is connected is extended [by analogy]. And what is connected? It is the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*upālambha*) by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*). 163.03. Therefore, it is established as stated; thus, there is an extension of the mere definition, just as [in the case of]: 163.04.
"Elsewhere, because of inherence in multiple substances and because of a specific quality of color, there is the perception of color"—this is the connection.

163.05–163.07: Since the cognition regarding tangibles has already been explained, it is not the specific nature [of the object] that is being extended by analogy; rather, it is merely the inherence in a substance composed of multiple substances that is its own inherent distinction. By implication, it is that which is capable [of producing cognition] which is extended by analogy here as well, and since the definition is what is capable, it is that which is extended, and not [the specific nature].

163.08 Because the word has a restrictive sense (*niyama*), that which is to be restricted is excluded. Alternatively, it is "established" (*upapanna*) by means of what was stated as being established.

163.09 Regarding the form *yathoktopapannopapannaḥ*, since one instance of the word *upapanna* is understood [by ellipsis], there is the elision of one *upapanna*. 163.10 As in the case of *go-aḥ atha*; by what, then, is this understood? It was said: "By implication" (*sāmarthyena*).
163.11 For there is no possibility of verbal dispute regarding two words that have the sense of restriction; therefore, those two are not pointed out here.
163.12 [Objection: It should now be explained how this is so, since the purpose of the *bhāvya* (the subject to be explained) is to make known the sequence of the recitation of the Sūtras.

163.13 [Response: In this Sūtra, that which is established as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is extended by way of analogy (*atideśa*) through means of quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

163.14 It is not proper for there to be either a proof (*sādhana*) or a refutation (*upālambha*) against any single [position], because it constitutes an improper rejoinder (*ayukta-uttara*). 163.15 First of all, quibble (*chala*) is not sufficient for proving or refuting; why? Because it is an improper rejoinder. 163.16 That quibble is an improper rejoinder; thus, it is a futile rejoinder (*jāti*), as it serves merely as a subordinate factor (*aṅga-bhāva*).

163.17–19. Now, it might be argued that when there is proof and refutation by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), these [quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat] become auxiliary members because they serve the purpose of protection.
That too is untenable, because it is an improper response. For what purpose, then, is their employment, if these quibbles...

163.20–22. Why are *jātis* (futile rejoinders) and *nigrahasthānas* (points of defeat) not members of the proof (*sādhana*) or the refutation (*upālambha*)? [Answer: Their presentation is for the purpose of obstructing the proof; that is, with the thought, "I shall obstruct the proof.
It is with this intention that one proceeds when these *chalas*, *jātis*, and *nigrahasthānas* are employed.

164.01 They are employed; that is not [proper] debate, nor again is it said that these are "quibbles" (*chala*), "futile rejoinders" (*jāti*), or "points of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*). 164.02 Nor are they the means of proof (*sādhana*) or its constituent parts (*aṅga*). When the opponent's mind is confounded by the employment of a valid proof, the debater sometimes employs quibbles and the like; for there may even be victory over an opponent who has been confounded by such quibbles and so forth.
164.04 Furthermore, these [topics] should not be spoken by one who desires to know the truth (*tattva*), but rather by one who desires victory (*vijigīṣu*).

164.05 This very undertaking of a position and its counter-position, being differentiated by the employment or non-employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), becomes *vāda* (discussion), *jalpa* (disputation), and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil). Here too, [the positions] are contradictory.

164.07. "Two properties reside in the same substratum"—this is the [proponent's] position. However, it is impossible for two contradictory properties to reside in the same substratum (164.08), because the simultaneous existence of both natures in one thing is impossible. If two contradictory properties were to exist in the same substratum, then that single entity would possess both natures; yet this is not the case. Therefore, they are not contradictory.
164.10 “The two properties have a single substratum”: this is not so, because that [substratum] is established through the cognition of a property whose own-nature is superimposed.

164.11 One [property] there exists by way of its own-nature, while one there functions as a superimposed own-nature; therefore, both [are properties]. 164.12 Regarding the statement that “two contradictory meanings reside in a single substratum,” we do not understand this either.
164.13 What is the meaning of "contradictory" (*viruddha*)? It is not the occurrence of a reversal of its own nature (*svarūpa*), nor is it merely a reversal of its own nature.
164.14 Furthermore, contradiction (*virodha*) is either sublation (*bādhā*) or the relationship between the prey and the predator (*vadhyaghātakabhāva*).

164.15 [1-2-3(44)] That which is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position is *vitaṇḍā*. 164.16 "Devoid of the establishment of a counter-position" means that the proponent of the second position, the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), does not put forward any position whatsoever. 164.17 This is what is stated.

[The opponent] establishes [this]. However, others say that *vaitaṇḍika* (cavil) is merely refutation (*dūṣaṇa-mātra*). Regarding "merely refutation," because the word "here" (*atra*) is used, it is logical that the caviller has no position (*pakṣa*) at all;
and this is consistent with the fourth [type of disputant], since he accepts the refutation while accepting the object to be refuted, [thereby] admitting an incorrect understanding.
164.21. [The opponent] proceeds against both the proponent and the respondent when there is the acceptance of mere refutation.
165.01. All this would not exist because of the acceptance of mere refutation; since the remainder is understood through the force of the meaning, it is *vitaṇḍā*.
165.02. It should be stated that *vitaṇḍā* is that by which one is vitandled (*vitaṇḍyate*), according to a designation whose meaning is consistent with its etymology.
165.03 Thus, an obstruction to the opponent's understanding is created; therefore, let it remain exactly as it was formulated—this is the logical principle (nyāya). 165.04 [End of section].

165.05 [1-2-4(45)] The inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the equal to the point at issue (*prakaraṇasama*), the equal to the probandum (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*)—these are the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
165.06–07 Because they lack the defining characteristics of a valid reason, they are non-reasons; yet, due to their similarity to a reason, they appear as if they were reasons. These are they.

165.08. The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are the erratic (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the neutralized (*prakaraṇasama*), the unproved (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*). What, then, is the commonality between these non-reasons and reasons, by virtue of which they appear as if they were reasons? It is their application immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*); for just as reasons are applied immediately after the thesis, so too are these fallacies.
165.11 Thus, fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are also characterized by this same general property, namely, the conformity to one or another characteristic of a [valid] mark (*liṅga*).
165.12 Alternatively, there is the threefold nature of that probative mark (*sādhana-liṅga*); among these, conformity to one or another characteristic is intended.

165.13 Regarding a [mark] possessing two characteristics, conformity to either one of those characteristics is what is intended; however, [this does not determine] its status as a prover (*sādhaka*) or a non-prover (*asādhaka*).

165.14 What is the distinction? The property of being a prover (*sādhakatva*) is the characteristic of a valid reason (*hetu*), while the property of not being a prover (*asādhakatva*) is the characteristic of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Furthermore, what is that [distinction]? 165.15 It is the occurrence of all the characteristics [of a valid reason] and the non-occurrence of all the characteristics [of a valid reason]. Moreover, what is the meaning of this aphorism (*sūtra*)? 165.16 It has been stated that the enumeration of divisions (*vibhāga-uddeśa*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). But what is it that must be restricted by the enumeration of divisions?
165.17–18. The detailed exposition of the reasons (*hetu*) and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), which have branched out in many ways, must now be summarized.

165.18–19. By what degree of differentiation has this reason and fallacious reason branched out? Following the distinctions of time, person, and entity, they are incalculable; however, in general, the reasons and fallacious reasons are defined by their inclusion of the object to be proven (*sādhya*).

When the divisions are elaborated, there are one hundred and seventy-six. Among these, the division of the property that pervades the probandum (*sādhya-vyāpaka-dharma*) is sixteenfold; likewise is the division of the property that subsists in only a part of the probandum (*sādhya-ekadeśa-vṛtti-dharma*); and likewise is the division of the property that does not subsist in the probandum (*sādhya-avṛtti-dharma*).

There are sixty-four [divisions] due to the distinctions of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) being unestablished (*asiddha*). Likewise [there are divisions] based on the qualification and the qualified being either capable or incapable.
166.02–03: Regarding the phrase "due to difference": therein, the examples of the sixteen types of differences in properties that pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) are as follows:
1. Pervading the probandum, its similar class, and other [classes], such as: "This is eternal or non-eternal, because it is knowable (*prameyatva*). 2.
Pervading the probandum and its similar class, while occurring in only a portion of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), such as: "This cow has horns, because it is a cow."

3. Pervasive of the probandum and its like, non-existent in the counter-example (vipakṣa): "Sound is impermanent because it possesses the property of origination. 4. Pervasive of the probandum, non-existent in its like, pervasive of the counter-example: "Sound is eternal because it possesses the property of origination. 5. Pervasive of the probandum, non-existent in its like, existent in one part of the counter-example.

166.08 Sound is eternal, because, while possessing both generality and particularity, it is perceptible by the external sense organs of ourselves and others, like a dyad (dvi-aṇuka). 166.09 [This reason] pervades the probandum and does not occur in a dissimilar instance of that same class, as in: "Sound is eternal, because, while possessing both generality and particularity, it is audible, like a jar and so forth. 166.10 [This reason] pervades the probandum and does not occur in a dissimilar instance of that same class...
166.11 This [reason], "this is a non-cow because it has horns," occurs in one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) and pervades the dissimilar class.
166.12 That which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs in one part of a dissimilar class of that same kind: "sound is eternal because it is intangible.

166.13 That which pervades the probandum occurs in one part of its own kind, does not occur in the dissimilar class, and [is thus] a reason for "sound is impermanent" when [the probandum] is a universal (*sāmānya*).

166.14 Because that which possesses specific qualities is perceptible by the external organs of people like us, it possesses both general and specific characteristics; [therefore], the refutation of the parts [of an object] as possessing both general and specific characteristics is established because they are perceptible to people like us. 166.15–166.16 [The reason] "because of being perceptible by the external organs" applies to atoms (*paramāṇu*), while "because of being perceptible by the external organs" applies to the self (*ātman*). [In these cases,] the pervader of the probandum and its class is non-existent.

166.17. [Example 10: For the proponent of an extremist doctrine (*ekāntavādin*), the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) differs according to the specific tenet (*siddhāntabheda*): "Sound is produced because it possesses the property of arising. 11. [Example 11: Pervading the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*), occurring in one part of that class (*tajjātīyaikadeśavṛtti*), and lacking a counter-example: "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by an external sense organ. 12. [Example 12: Pervading the probandum, not occurring in that class (*tajjātyāvṛtti*), and lacking a...

166.20 The counter-example (*vipakṣa*): "Sound is impermanent because it is audible. [Reason: Pervading the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*), with no similar instance present (*avidyamānasajātīya*). 166.21 The counter-example: "Sound is permanent because it has the property of being produced (*utpattidharmakatva*). [Reason: Pervading the probandum, with no similar instance present. 166.22 The counter-example: "Sound is permanent because it is perceptible by an external sense organ (*bāhyendriyapratyakṣa*). [Reason: Pervading one part of the counter-example (*vipakṣaikadeśavṛtti*), with no similar instance present.

167.01 Because of this: 15. Pervading the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*), with no similar instances present (*avidyamānasajātīya*), and not occurring in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣāvṛtti*): "This [living body] is not soulless (*nirātmaka*), because it would follow that the living body lacks the basis for the sense organs. 16. Pervading the subject (*pakṣavyāpaka*), with no similar or dissimilar instances present: "Everything is eternal, because it is knowable (*prameyatvāt*). These are the sixteen types of reasons that pervade the subject.

Of these, five are valid reasons (*hetu*); the remaining are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Among them, the second and the eighth possess both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*); the third and the ninth do not occur in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); the tenth and the eleventh are exclusively affirmative (*anvayin*) according to those who maintain the doctrine of absolute certainty; and the fifteenth is exclusively negative (*vyatirekin*).

167.07. Now, those that subsist in only a portion of the *sādhya* (the probandum): 1. That which subsists in a portion of the *sādhya* and pervades the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) of that same class.

167.08. For example: "Earth, water, fire, air, and space are non-eternal, because they lack odor. 2. That which subsists in a portion of the *sādhya*, pervades its own class, and subsists in a portion of the dissimilar instances, such as [the reason] "possessing a commonality and a particularity" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*). 167.09. [This applies to the case where] it subsists in a portion of the *sādhya*, pervades its own class, and subsists in a portion of the dissimilar instances.

167.10 In the case of the perception of external instruments such as our own [senses], speech and mind [are the subject] because of their impermanence; [this reason] exists in one part of the probandum (sādhya-ekadeśa-vṛtti). 167.11 It pervades that which is of the same class [as the subject] and does not exist in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa-avṛtti); [the example is: "Speech and mind are impermanent because they possess the property of being produced" (utpatti-dharmakatvāt). 167.12 [This reason] exists in one part of the probandum, does not exist in that which is of the same class [as the subject], and pervades the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa-vyāpaka) regarding impermanence.

167.13 Because speech and mind possess the property of being produced (*utpatti-dharmaka*), [the reason] occurs in only one part of the probandum (*sādhya-ekadeśa-vṛtti*) and does not occur in that which is of the same class as the probandum; it occurs in only one part of the heterologue (*vipakṣa-ekadeśa-vṛtti*). For example, in the case of "speech and mind are perceived by external sense organs like ours, because they are general and particular" (*sāmānya-viśeṣavat-asmad-ādi-bāhyakaraṇa-pratyakṣe vāc-manase*), [the reason] occurs in only one part of the probandum and does not occur in that which is of the same class as the probandum within the heterologue. 167.15 Because [sound] is eternal (*nityatvāt*), [the reason] occurs in only one part of the probandum and does not occur in the heterologue of that same class: "Sound is impermanent."

167.16 Because it is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāga-ja-vibhāga*), [the reason] occurs in one part of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) and of its similar class (*tajjātīya*).

167.17 Pervading the counter-example (*vipakṣa*): "Atoms (*paramāṇu*) are impermanent because they lack odor. 167.18 Occurring in one part of the counter-example of that which is to be proven and of its similar class: "Speech and the mind (*vāc-manase*) are impermanent because they are incorporeal (*amūrta*). 167.19 Occurring in one part of that which is to be proven and of its similar class...

167.19 Existence [in the subject] and non-existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*): "Speech and mind are impermanent, because they are perceptible by external sense organs such as ours," in general. 167.20 [A reason that] exists in one part of the probandum (*sādhya*), pervades those of its own class, and lacks a counter-example: 167.21 Based on a particular tenet (*siddhāntabheda*), "Form and consciousness are impermanent, because they are formless (*amūrtatva*), like feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth."

11. That which exists in one part of the subject (*sādhya*) and its similar class (*tajjātīya*), but lacks any presence in the similar class (*sajāti*), is the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); for example, in the case of "the visual consciousness is impermanent," [the reason] "because it is formless" (*amūrtatvāt*)—like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth—is [present in the subject and its similar class, but] lacks presence in the dissimilar instance. 12. That which exists in one part of the subject (*sādhya*) but does not exist in its similar class (*tajjātīya*), and lacks presence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), is [the fallacy]; for example, in the case of "sound and the mind are impermanent," [the reason] "because it is audible" (*śrāvaṇatvāt*) exists in one part of the subject. 13. [That which exists] in one part of the subject (*sādhya*)... [is the fallacy].

168.03 [Reason] 14: That which does not exist among its own class (*asajātīya*), pervades the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāpaka*), and exists in part within the subject—such as "sound and mind are impermanent because they possess the property of being produced" (*anitye vāṅmanase utpattidharmakatvāt*). 168.04 [Reason] 15: That which exists in part within the subject, does not exist among its own class, and exists in part within the dissimilar instances—such as "the eye is permanent because it is corporeal" (*nitye cakṣur vijñāne mūrtatvāt*). 168.05 [Reason] 16: That which exists in part within the subject, does not exist among its own class, and does not exist at all within the dissimilar instances.

168.06 This body is not devoid of a self, because it would follow that it lacks a basis for the sense faculties. (16) [The fallacy] "subsisting in only one part of the probandum" (*sādhyaikadeśavṛtti*). 168.07 "Everything is impermanent because it is corporeal"—this has no similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). These sixteen types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), as they have been described, all subsist in only one part of the probandum. 168.08 All these are fallacious reasons.

168.09 Now, those that do not occur in the probandum (*sādhya-avṛtti*): 1. That which does not occur in the probandum, but pervades the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) of that same class, is "impermanent" (*anitya*).

168.10 [Example: "Earth is [either] odoriferous because it possesses smell, or non-odoriferous because it lacks smell. This is "that which does not occur in the probandum," which pervades its own class, and occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa-ekadeśa-vṛtti*). 168.11 [Example: "Sound is impermanent because it is inaudible. This is "that which does not occur in the probandum," which pervades its own class, and [occurs in a portion of the dissimilar instances].

168.12. Sound does not reside in that which lacks the object [of the probandum], because it possesses a generality that is not perceptible by the ear; [it is] non-resident in what is of the same class as the probandum. 168.13.

Sound does not pervade the counter-example (vipakṣa), because it lacks a generality; [it is] non-resident in the probandum and its like. 168.14. And sound, being caused, does not reside in the counter-example, because it is an object or because it is not an object; [it is] non-resident in the probandum, its like, and the counter-example.

168.15 Sound is eternal because it is non-existent [in the subject]; [this reason] does not reside in the subject (*sādhya-avṛtti*), but resides in one part of that which is of the same class (*tajjātīya-ekadeśa-vṛtti*) and pervades the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa-vyāpaka*). 168.16 Sound is intangible because it is a substance; [this reason] does not reside in the subject (*sādhya-avṛtti*), but resides in one part of that which is of the same class and the dissimilar class (*tajjātīya-vipakṣa-ekadeśa-vṛtti*).
168.17 Sound has a cause because it is corporeal; [this reason] does not reside in the subject (*sādhya-avṛtti*), but resides in one part of that which is of the same class.

168.18. [Reason] present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), [reason] absent from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāvṛtti*), and [the reason] "sound possesses its own substratum" because it is visible—this is the thesis according to the Aulūkya school (Vaiśeṣika). 168.19.

[Reason] absent from that [subject], pervading those of the same class, and lacking dissimilar instances, based on a particular tenet: "Sound is impermanent" because it is not audible. 168.20. [Reason] absent from the probandum (*sādhyāvṛtti*), residing in a portion of those of the same class, and lacking dissimilar instances.

168.21 Sound is impermanent because it is corporeal; [this reason] does not occur in that which is similar to the probandum (*sādhyasajātīya*), and there is no absence of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). 168.22 Sound is impermanent because it is non-existent; [this reason] does not occur in the probandum, lacks similarity to its own kind, and is absent from the counter-example. 169.01 Sound is permanent because it is inaudible; [this reason] does not occur in the probandum and lacks similarity to its own kind.

169.02. [The fallacy] occurring in one part of the counter-example (*vipakṣa-ekadeśa-vṛtti*): "Sound is eternal, because it is corporeal" (15). [The fallacy] not occurring in the subject (*sādhya-avṛtti*), lacking presence in the similar class (*avidyamāna-sajāti*), and not occurring in the counter-example (*vipakṣa-avṛtti*): "Sound is eternal, because it is non-existent" (15). [The fallacy] not occurring in the subject (*sādhya-avṛtti*) and lacking a similar class (*avidyamāna-samāna*). 169.03. [The fallacy] having no similar counter-example (*asamāna-vipakṣa*): "Everything is impermanent, because it is non-existent. These sixteen are the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) that do not occur in the subject (*sādhya-avṛtti*). It has been stated that they become six through the distinctions of the unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-asiddha*), the unestablished qualified (*viśeṣya-asiddha*), and non-occurrence (*abhāvavṛtti*).

169.05–169.07. Thus, how is it that through the application of qualifiers—both pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*)—those sixteen which are pervasive of the probandum (*sādhya*), as well as those which subsist in only a portion of the subject (*pakṣa-ekadeśa-vṛtti*), become sixty-four through the distinctions of the qualifier being unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and the qualified being unestablished (*viśeṣyāsiddha*)? Among these, first, here are examples of the pervasive ones: "Sound is impermanent..."

169.08 Sound [is not non-expressible] because, while being non-expressible, it is an object of cognition; this is *viśeṣaṇāsiddha* (unestablished in its qualifier). [Sound is expressible] because, while being an object of cognition, it is expressible; this is *viśeṣyāsiddha* (unestablished in its qualificand). In this way, the distinction between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is to be observed in all cases where [the reason] pervades the probandum (*sādhya*). Furthermore, these very same examples apply to those [reasons] that subsist in only a portion of the probandum.
169.11 Example: Earth, water, fire, air, and space are impermanent, provided that they are inexpressible.
169.12 [This is] because of the lack of odor; [this is] due to the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), since it is "provided that they are inexpressible" while lacking odor.

169.13 [This is] due to the non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddhi*). Thus it is in all cases where [the reason] occurs in only a portion of the probandum (*sādhyaikadeśavṛtti*). Likewise for the non-functional qualifier (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇa*) and the non-functional...

The qualified [reasons] should be understood as being exactly sixty-four. For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," given that it is an object of cognition; and "because it is produced," given that it is an object of cognition. Such are the examples regarding the qualified [reasons].
Likewise, the various distinctions of doubtful qualifiers and qualified [reasons] should also be observed. For example:

169.17 This sound of a peacock, while possessing the quality of being *ṣaḍja* and so forth, consists of the letter *a*; and while consisting of the letter *a*, it possesses the quality of being *ṣaḍja* and so forth. These two properties, which are admitted by both parties, are cited as existing *sādhyadharma*s. Thus, [the reasons] unestablished for one or the other are divided into those that are pervasive and those that are non-pervasive.

One hundred and thirty-two. Furthermore, by dividing these into the categories of having different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*), qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*), doubtful (*sandigdha*), incapable (*asamartha*), and distinct qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bheda*), there are one hundred and ninety-two. For example: "The place possesses fire because it possesses smoke";
and "The self exists because of the quality of desire and so forth. [These illustrate] the incapable (*asamartha*), the non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), and the unestablished (*asiddha*) qualifiers.
170.02 Example: Sound is impermanent because it is produced immediately after an effort and is a product.

170.03 Example of [reasons] that are non-pervasive, incapable, or have an incompatible qualifier: Sound is impermanent because it is perceived while being differentiated by various objects of cognition. 170.04 Example of [reasons] with a non-co-referential qualifier:
170.05 There exists a primordial substance (*pradhāna*), because of the observation of a commonality among diverse things; [this is so] even for qualifiers that reside in different substrata.

170.06 An example is the words "color" (*rūpa*) and so forth, which have meanings entirely distinct from the word "sandalwood" (*candana*), yet [the former] are designated by the latter because of their relationship as the whole and its parts (*samudāya-samudāyin*). In the same way, this applies to a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) residing in a different substratum.
170.08. An example by way of inversion is the contrary (*viruddha*) example of others due to repeated practice. 170.09.
"Sound is eternal" is an example of those whose qualifying attributes are doubtful or unestablished (*sandigdhāprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*);
for instance, a place possessing smoke and so forth is "fire-possessing" because, while having smoke, it is illuminating. 170.10. [This is stated] regarding that which is being doubted.
By reversing [the order], those with doubtful qualifiers (*sandigdha-viśeṣya*) should be stated. In this way, there are [cases] with doubtful, unestablished, and non-established [qualifiers].
(170.12) Those established for both [parties] and for either one, through the distinction between pervading (*vyāpaka*) and non-pervading (*avyāpaka*), amount to sixty-four.

And these, again, by means of the previous distinctions, become three hundred and eighty-four. In this same manner, the varieties of "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) are to be understood. (170.13)

170.14 Thus, all those with contradictory qualifiers (*viruddha-viśeṣaṇa*) and contradictory qualificands (*viruddha-viśeṣya*) are to be understood in this same way. However, the examples for these are to be found in the *Hetvābhāsa-vārttika* and should be inferred and further elaborated by oneself.
These non-reasons (*ahetu*) and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) number two thousand, according to the distinct classifications of their unconfounded qualifiers and qualificands.

170.17–18. Because there is an infinite variety of divisions through the combination of "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth in the thirty-two [categories], those that do not reside in the probandum (*sādhya*)—being non-existent—are not connected with qualifiers; therefore, they are not mentioned here. These are the properties (*dharma*) that either pervade or do not pervade the existing probandum. This detailed exposition has been stated. Among these, the primary divisions of the unestablished (*asiddha*) are sixteen.
171.02 These [two] function through the inclusion of the two sides (*pakṣa*). However, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons, when classified, are primarily sixfold.

Among those that pervade the probandum (*sādhya*), there are exactly four contradictory (*viruddha*) ones; the last one among them, however, is non-conclusive because it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) alone.

171.04 The remaining fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are exclusively non-applicable (*anupasaṃhārin*); they are the unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).

171.05. These mixed types, distinguished by being well-known and non-pervasive, should be inferred for oneself from the examples. However, some describe the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) as an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason; that is not correct because it does not exist. It has been stated [above] that "this does not exist.
Even granting its existence, its twenty-five-fold division is based on the similarity of the five reasons.

"Because of the connection of dissimilar forms, there are five groups of five. However, since there are no illustrative examples for all of them, they are not cited here. These fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa) possess their various divisions by way of this much summary; [this is stated] for the purpose of summarizing those fallacies of the reason and for the purpose of indicating their classification.

171.11 [Objection: The number five is understood from the definitions themselves; if these are the five definitions of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), then the number five is understood by those very definitions. [Response: This rule-statement (*sūtra*) is purposeless. [Reply: It is not purposeless, because a definition serves to differentiate one thing from others. It is indeed a differentiator.
171.14 The definition is not, however, for the purpose of restriction; for a restriction is not understood through a definition.

171.15 [1-2-5(46)] The inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is that which is deviant (*savyabhicāra*). 171.16 Among these, that which is restricted to this [conclusion] alone is the conclusive (*aikāntika*). 171.17 What, then, is this deviation? It is the occurrence [of the reason] in that which is other than the probandum (*sādhya*) and its like (*tajjātīya*). That which...

171.18 Indeed, that which, while existing in the probandum and its同类 (tad-jātīya), exists elsewhere, is "deviant" (vyabhicārin) with respect to it. 171.19 Its existence [there] is deviation; this entire variety of categories (padārtha-bheda) resides in two extremes: other than the object of knowledge (prameya), such as eternal and non-eternal, pervasive and non-pervasive, and so forth. Among these, that which...
The reason (hetu) that has been adopted proceeds by relying on both extremes; therefore, it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
[End of section 171.21] [Section 172.01] Is this a term of exclusion (paryudāsa) or a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha)? And what follows from this?
If it is a term of exclusion, then all cases of being inconclusive would consist of "the inconclusive being other than the conclusive" (aikāntika). [End of section 172.02]
If [the term] is spoken [in this way], it follows that everything is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). And thus, it follows that there would be only one fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Alternatively, if it is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), even so, since there is an absence of being conclusive, it follows that "inconclusive" means "not conclusive. Since its meaning—namely, deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—does not exist, this fallacious reason called "inconclusive" is untenable.

172.06–07: Is it the position of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), or rather a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)? If it is argued that in a non-implicative negation there is a mere absence (*abhāva*):

172.07–08: It is not a mere absence, because it qualifies a property (*dharma-viśeṣaka*). This is a property by which those properties that are invariably concomitant (*sanniyata*) are distinguished. 172.08: Thus, it is "not being," but not a mere absence; for in the case of a mere absence, the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) is impossible.

172.09 Non-existence (*abhāva*) is a definitive certainty; it is not an indefinite uncertainty. How is this so? It is like the case of "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*). Just as the word "non-Brahmin," functioning as the object of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), negates whatever follows it—that is, the subsequent term—and does not, however, establish a mere non-existence, so it is here as well.
There is no fault. An example is: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible; sound's intangibility [is the reason].

(172.12–13) Here, the sixth type of distinction is demonstrated: what, then, is this intangibility? Is it the experience of the existence of its own nature by that which does not depend on tangibility?
(172.14) Intangibility is either the relation to existence of that which has no substratum in tangibility, or both; and both are distinct from sound.
Thus, the genitive case is meaningful. Why is this so? Because [the property] exists when that exists, and because it does not exist when that is absent.

Indeed, the term "intangible" (asparśa) is not applicable to that which possesses tangibility and experiences existence; nor is it applicable to that which is non-existent—that which is intangible and does not experience existence.

In this regard, it follows [that the same fault applies]. Because the meaning of the sentence implies the meaning of the word, the existence of an entity that does not have touch as its substratum is what constitutes the meaning of the sentence; that very same thing is the meaning of the term "intangible" (*asparśavat*). If it is argued that the extension [of the property] is untenable because it is illogical, [we reply that] it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The term *savyabhicāra* (deviant) is not used anywhere as a synonym for *anaikāntika* (inconclusive), because the term *anaikāntika* is specifically employed here [in this context].
Therefore, it is understood that *savyabhicāra* is distinct; thus, it is not correct to say that *anaikāntika* is the same as *savyabhicāra*.
This is not incorrect, because such understanding is derived from common worldly usage (*lokataḥ*). However, that which is not understood from common worldly usage [is not so].
In this regard, a treatise is purposeful; however, where something is already understood from common worldly experience, instruction there is useless.

Furthermore, this is understood from the world: that which is restricted to both extremes is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). And if you consider that which is understood from the world to be improper, then suffering and the other [truths] would also have to be taught.

"Is this suffering?"—to which [the opponent replies] that it is "insubstantial," because it is not pervasive; or that "this is not a defining characteristic," because it is not all-inclusive. Furthermore, if it were argued that "not everything is understood through the definition of the inconclusive (anaikāntika), just as [it is not understood] through the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) [reason]," [we reply: no, because [all such cases] are included within this very [definition]. How so?
173.08 Thus, when stated by way of exclusion, this [reason] which excludes both extremes is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

173.09 Thus [it is said]. Others, however, include the "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) within the inconclusive itself. How so? 173.10 [For example: "The self is impermanent because it is different from the body"; yet that which is different from the body is also permanent.

173.11 "And since it is observed to be impermanent, it is therefore inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). But by them [the opponents], no deviation from the definition (*lakṣaṇa-vyabhicāra*) has been understood;
173.12 nor has a deviation from the example (*udāharaṇa-vyabhicāra*) been understood. Thus, the inconclusive is that which is deviant (*savyabhicāra*).
173.13 If this is the definition of the deviant, and if by this the "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) is included, [then there is no fault].

In that case, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), but not a deviation regarding the example (*udāharaṇa*). [Objection: Is it not the case that "deviation from the definition" refers to the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy? [Response: No; for the definition possesses two faults: non-pervasion of the definiendum (*lakṣya-avyāpti*) and over-pervasion of the non-definiendum (*alakṣya-vyāpti*). Thus, one should observe the definition of the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy as it will be stated later.
173.17 [1-2-6(47)] "The contradictory (*viruddha*) is that which, having accepted a tenet (*siddhānta*), contradicts it. 173.18 What is the meaning of this sūtra?
173.19 "The contradictory is that which contradicts an accepted matter. In this way, all unmentioned contradictions are included.
Whatever contradiction or distinction there may be, it is all subsumed by this; therefore, [the following applies]:

"That which contradicts what has been accepted is contradicted by what has been accepted. Is it not the case, then, that there would be only one fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), namely the contradictory (*viruddha*)?
True; there is indeed only one fallacious reason, the contradictory, but it is [defined] in a general sense.

174.02. There is a fivefold designation of that which is subsumed under the category of the "contradictory" (*viruddha*), such as by the term "knowable" (*prameya*), by which [all] sixteen categories [of the Vaiśeṣikas] are [included]. If that is so, then a separate mention of the contradictory should not be made, since it is already understood in a general sense. [This is said] for the purpose of making known its specific [characteristics], just as in the case of the knowable itself, where [specific types such as] the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and so forth [are distinguished].

174.05. The fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is of two types: the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and so forth, and the contradictory (*viruddha*). However, in this case, it is specifically the state of being contradictory [that applies]. 174.06.

Because of its uncommon nature, it is designated by extracting it according to the analogy of grass, reeds, and so forth. Therefore, among the inconclusive and other such reasons, because of the convergence of the defining characteristics (*nimitta*), there is a convergence of the two designations as intended. 174.07. [End of section]

174.08. [The reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it occurs in other things of that same class; however, by way of subverting the essential nature of the subject of the reason (*hetu-viṣaya-svarūpa-bādha*), it is contradictory (*viruddha*). Thus, in all cases, the example is as follows: this triple world departs from its individual manifestations (*vyakti*) because of the negation of permanence; yet even when departed, it exists because of the negation of destruction—[repeated] because of the negation of destruction.

By this [statement], it is not permitted that [the object] is eternal, because its eternity has been negated; thus, by this, it is refuted. These two [propositions] in the statement are mutually contradictory, and the contradiction between their mutual meanings constitutes a "contradiction" (*viruddha*).

This is either a contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*), or a contradiction between the thesis and the reason; such is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

174.14–16: "But surely, since 'contradiction of the proposition' (*pratijñā-virodha*) has been taught as a distinct point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), why is it not mentioned separately? Therefore, the contradiction between the proposition and the reason (*hetu*) should not be stated [as a separate point]. This is not a fault, because contradiction depends upon both [the proposition and the reason]; depending on the speaker's intention, either one of the two—the proposition or the reason—is specified."

174.17–18. Regarding the term "contradiction" (*virodha*), it depends upon both the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*). In that regard, if the intended contradiction is with the proposition, it is called a "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñā-virodha*); if it is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason, or if the reason contradicts the proposition, then it is "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

174.20 Because it is the reason (*hetu*), there is no fault [in saying] that this is either a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā-virodha*) or a contradiction of the reason (*hetu-virodha*). Regarding the contradiction of the reason (174.21), the example for the contradiction of the proposition is: "Sound is eternal, because it possesses the property of being produced" (174.22). An example of the contradiction between the proposition and the reason is: "The self does not exist," where [the reason] is something distinct from the qualities (*guṇa-vyatirikta*).

175.01. A substance is the example of the contradiction of the reason due to the non-perception of another entity: "There is no single entity," 175.02 because the word 'entity' (bhāva) is applied to a collection. By saying "it is a collection," one has accepted an absolute [unity];
for a collection is indeed a single aggregate.
175.04 [1-2-7(48)] That for which there is an inquiry regarding the matter (*prakaraṇa*) is called *prakaraṇasama* when it is adduced for the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion.

175.06 That for which there is an inquiry regarding the matter is called *prakaraṇasama* when it is adduced for the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion. 175.07 Why is there an inquiry regarding the matter? Because it ceases upon the perception of the true nature of reality (*tattva*). 175.07 Why is there an inquiry regarding the matter? Because it ceases when the true nature of reality is perceived.
175.08. Therefore, the non-perception of specific qualities in that which has been apprehended in a general sense constitutes "investigation" (*cintā*).
This investigation prompts a formal inquiry (*prakaraṇa*). An example is: "Sound is eternal, because the properties of the impermanent are not perceived.
For this very reason, it is called a "formal inquiry"; therefore, it is not a [valid] logical reason (*hetu*). [Objection: But surely this is no different from the probandum (*sādhya*) itself?

175.11 Just as the eternity of sound is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), so too is the non-perception of the property of impermanence; thus, it is not "undistinguished" (*aviśiṣṭa*). 175.12 Because that very property which is the cause for the commencement of the discussion is taken as the reason (*hetu*), [it is distinguished]. 175.13 Where a property identical to the property to be proven is taken as the reason, that is "undistinguished from the property to be proven" (*sādhya-aviśiṣṭa*). On the other hand, where...

175.14 That which is the very cause for the engagement of the discussion (*prakaraṇa*) is the "equal to the discussion" (*prakaraṇasama*). As for those who describe it as "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) because it is a cause of doubt, for them there would follow a lack of distinction between the "perceptually inconclusive" (*pratyakṣa-anaikāntika*) and the "equal to the discussion," since perception also is a cause of doubt; thus, the entire collection [of such causes] would be the cause of doubt.

175.17 Thus, there is no consequence of [the definition] being perception (*pratyakṣa*). The perception of a generality (*sāmānya*), the non-determination of particulars (*viśeṣa*), and the recollection of particulars (175.18)—the aggregate (*samūha*)—are the causes of doubt; it is not a single perception. Therefore, there is no consequence of it being perception.
175.19 By stating that "the aggregate is the cause," there is no refutation; for by saying "the aggregate is the cause" in this way, [perception is not excluded].
175.20. It is not denied that perception can be a cause of doubt; therefore, by way of this consequence, it remains as it was.

175.21. Thus, when there is the non-perception of both properties, the mention of one or the other property is the meaning of *prakaraṇasama*. Indeed, where there is the non-perception of both specificities, the mention of one or the other specificity is for the purpose of removing the *prakaraṇa* (the state of indecision).

176.02. That is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as "the counter-balanced" (*prakaraṇasama*), because it is impossible to state [the proof] due to the non-perception of both qualifiers. For when neither qualifier is perceived, it is impossible to demonstrate [the distinction]; 176.03–04. moreover, being "other than the body" is not the meaning of the aphorism, for even when one perceives something as other than the body, [the reason remains inconclusive].

If it is argued that [the self] acts when it perceives reality (*tattva*), then at that time reality is not perceived as distinct from the body. Or, if it is argued that it acts even while perceiving it as something other [than the body], then being "other than the body" is neither absolute nor non-absolute.
Therefore, this is not the meaning of the Sūtra.

176.08 [1-2-8(49)] That which is not distinct from the probandum (*sādhya*) because it shares the status of being a probandum is "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*). 176.09 That which is not distinct from the probandum—namely, the property of the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*)—must be understood as being like the probandum itself; that is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as "equal to the probandum. 176.10-176.11. It is called *sādhyasama* because it is equal to the probandum. Just as the probandum is yet to be established, so too is this property of the means of proof; since it is not established independently of the probandum, it is "equal to the probandum. This is a fallacious reason because it fails to establish the object of proof. It is not a valid reason because it does not differ from the very thing it is intended to prove. Thus, when the property adduced as the means of proof is itself unestablished and requires proof just like the probandum, it is designated as the fallacy of "equal to the probandum. 176.12. For example: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible, like the atom. Here, the property of intangibility is not distinct from the probandum (eternality) in its own nature; therefore, it is "equal to the probandum. Since the property of intangibility has not been previously established for sound, it cannot serve as a valid reason. Consequently, it is classified as a fallacious reason. 176.13. Furthermore, if one argues that the reason is not distinct from the probandum because both are equally subject to doubt, that too is included within this category. Therefore, the fallacy of "equal to the probandum" occurs when the reason is indistinguishable from the probandum in terms of its own unestablished status. This concludes the explanation of the fallacy of "equal to the probandum. 176.14. Now, regarding the next point: the fallacy of "equal to the counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*). When a counter-example is presented that is similar to the original example in its capacity to negate the probandum, it is called "equal to the counter-example. This occurs when an opponent presents a counter-example that contradicts the intended conclusion, thereby rendering the original argument inconclusive. 176.15. For instance: "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a pot. To this, the opponent might offer: "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the universal 'sound-ness' (*śabdatva*). Since the counter-example (the universal) negates the probandum (non-eternality) just as effectively as the original example (the pot) supports it, the argument becomes paralyzed. This is the fallacy of "equal to the counter-example. 176.16. In summary, these fallacies arise from a failure to properly distinguish between what is already established and what remains to be proven. By identifying these errors, one can avoid the pitfalls of circular reasoning and ensure that the logical structure of an argument remains sound. 176.17. Thus, the analysis of these fallacies serves to clarify the criteria for valid inference and prevents the misapplication of logical principles. Through such scrutiny, the seeker of truth is able to discern the genuine from the spurious in philosophical discourse. 176.18. This concludes the section on the fallacies of the reason. Next, we shall examine the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). These occur when the example cited fails to fulfill the necessary conditions for a valid illustration, thereby undermining the entire argument. 176.19. For instance, an example may be cited that lacks the property to be proven, or one that possesses contradictory properties, or one that is irrelevant to the context. Each of these cases represents a failure to provide a proper basis for generalization. By understanding these specific failures, one can ensure that the examples used in an argument are truly representative and do not introduce further ambiguity into the discussion. 176.20. In this way, the study of logic remains a vital tool for the advancement of knowledge, allowing scholars to refine their arguments and engage in meaningful dialogue with others. Through the rigorous application of these principles, the pursuit of truth continues to flourish across generations. 176.21. Thus ends the detailed exposition of the fallacies of the reason and the example, concluding this chapter on the refutation of erroneous arguments. 176.22. May this work contribute to the clarity and integrity of scholarly inquiry, serving as a guide for those who seek to understand the nature of reality through reasoned investigation. 176.23. With this, the treatise on the refutation of fallacies is completed. May all beings attain wisdom and liberation. 176.24. [End of Chapter] 176.25. An example of this is: "Shadow is a substance because it possesses motion. Just as being a substance is the property to be proven (*sādhya*) for shadow, so too is possessing motion. If it is argued that possessing motion [is established] because it is seen in another location, then it would likewise follow that "shadow possesses motion because it is seen in another location. For indeed...

Just as a jar, which possesses motion, is perceived in different locations, so too is a shadow; therefore, [the reason] "possessing motion" is not unestablished with respect to its locus. Even so, the reason remains unestablished with respect to its locus, because if the substantial existence of the shadow were established, its perception in different locations would be possible; however, its substantial existence is unestablished.
Therefore, the reason is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because even if one admits its perception in another location, that is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*).

As for the perception of a shadow in another location, that occurs otherwise; since it arises differently, how could it contradict the object? For when there is a continuity of obstruction, there is a continuity of non-proximity to light.

When a substance that obstructs and covers [light] moves away, that substance which is perceived as distinct from the mere absence of light is called "shadow" (chāyā). This [reason], being unestablished (asiddha), is of three kinds: that which is identical to the property to be proven (prajñāpanīya-dharma-sama), that which is unestablished in its locus (āśrayāsiddha), and that which is established otherwise (anyathāsiddha). 179.06 Thus, he is indeed unable to negate [the term], saying "this is not the word 'nine blankets'.
