"Because of the determination of a property (*dharma-adhyavasāya*)" has been explained. There is no doubt regarding what is already apprehended or what is not yet apprehended.

(184.18) Doubt is not tenable with respect to an object already apprehended, because it has been determined; nor is it [tenable] with respect to what is not yet apprehended, because it has not been seen. It is not from the determination of a common property (*samāna-dharma*) that doubt arises, for even when such a property exists, [doubt] may be absent, and even when it exists, [certainty] may be present. (184.19)
Doubt arises precisely from the lack of determination regarding the property (*dharma*), because it occurs even otherwise; indeed, doubt is observed to exist in other circumstances as well.
For example, doubt arises when there is a conjunction of two contradictory properties that do not deviate [from their respective loci] and when the true nature [of the object] is not perceived.

Furthermore, as in the case of the "equal-to-the-point-at-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy, this property does not reside in only one [of the two alternatives], because it exists in both. It is not the case that this property resides in only one of the similar [alternatives].
And it must be that which exists in a single mode of occurrence to be considered common.
185.04 [2-1-2] And because of the determination of conflicting views; 185.05 [2-1-3] and because there is agreement even regarding what is conflicted.
By this, the argument "because of the determination of non-conflicting views" is refuted; for [the reason applies] to that which is conflicted.

Doubt arises from the lack of a settled determination (*avyavasthā*) following conflicting assertions (*vipratipatti*), not from mere conflict alone or from mere lack of settlement alone. Furthermore, since there is no conflict where there is agreement, this is the meaning of the Sūtra.
185.09 [2-1-4] Furthermore, because non-determination (avyavasthā) is established within that which has determination as its nature, [non-determination does not exist].
185.10 Or, because determination is established within that which has non-determination as its nature, non-determination is not perceived.
185.11 Such is the meaning of the aphorism.
185.12 [2-1-5] Likewise, there is perpetual doubt because of the occurrence of the persistence of those properties.

185.13 Likewise, there is perpetual doubt because of the occurrence of the persistence of those properties, due to the persistence of common properties and so forth. 185.14 "Doubt is eternal" is the meaning of the sūtra.
The answer to this is as follows:

[2-1-6] Precisely because of the aforementioned determination, when there is dependence upon its specific qualities, doubt arises; it is not the case that there is no doubt, nor is there perpetual doubt.

185.18–19. Because doubt arises precisely from the aforementioned determination when there is a dependence upon its specific qualities, it is neither the absence of doubt nor absolute doubt; this is not due to a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra—such is the meaning of the Sūtra. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no doubt when the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) are apprehended, that is not so, because [the objection] is based on a lack of understanding; we do not say that the *dharmin* which is perceived [is such].

186.01. [The opponent says: "Its property is apprehension. However, those two—the post and the person—were previously apprehended by me; this common property is now apprehended in both of them. By this, [the objection] is refuted on the grounds that it occurs in only one instance. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no doubt regarding something else because of the determination of a different object—[that too is refuted].

Because it is not accepted [as such]. Others [argue] that I do not employ the mere existence of a distinct entity (*arthāntara-bhāva-mātra*) as the cause of doubt; rather, it is a specific kind of distinct entity. What, then, is this specific [entity]? It is the relation between the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*).
They consider the resolution to be: "When the locus has been perceived, there is doubt regarding the property," but they do not [accept the following]:...
186.07 We observe that there is a relationship of property and property-possessor (*dharma-dharmin*) between color and touch. And for what reason is that?

186.08 Because the state of being distinct entities (*arthāntara-bhāva*) is not excluded; just as there is a state of being distinct entities between color and touch, so it is between property and property-possessor. Thus, it is not logical that there should be doubt regarding one distinct entity upon seeing another distinct entity, even in this case.

"That very [objection] is not [valid], because it is not admitted. We do not say that there is doubt regarding a different subject (*dharmin*) based on the perception of a different object; rather, doubt arises regarding the subject itself when one perceives a subject characterized by common properties and so forth, even though it lacks specific distinguishing features. Even if this is so, [the objection] "because of the absence of similarity" refers to the specific...

186.13–186.15: "Non-determination of both [alternatives] due to similarity" means that just as a specific distinction is not determined by the observation of common properties, so too it is with doubt. Since the cause exists, the effect exists;
this is not a description of similarity, but rather a description of the properties of cause and effect, and thus...

186.16 This [reasoning] applies even to other effects; for no effect whatsoever can come into existence without the presence of its cause. By this, the refutation based on the "determination of multiple properties" (*aneka-dharma-adhyavasāya*) is answered.
186.18 Whatever is the rebuttal regarding the determination of common properties (*samāna-dharma-adhyavasāya*), that same rebuttal applies to the determination of multiple properties.

Regarding the word "api": as for the claim that [doubt does not arise] because there is an absence of both what has been apprehended and what has not been apprehended, we do not say that it is due to a lack of full comprehension (*aparijñāna*). Rather, doubt arises when one thing has been apprehended while another remains in question. Furthermore, doubt is a cognition characterized by the non-determination of specific qualities with respect to a subject (*dharmī*) that has been apprehended in a general sense.

186.22 Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, as for the statement "because it does not exist even when [the other property] exists," this is not due to a failure to understand the meaning of "common" (*samāna*).

187.01 For "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is not the common property; otherwise, there would be the designation of a common property [where none exists]. 187.02 "Common property" refers to that which, while being common, subsists in something else of the same class as that which is intended to be expressed. It is not [merely] that which is common.

Furthermore, regarding this very fact of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), it is not the case that [doubt] arises solely from the determination of a common property (*samāna-dharma*), because it is observed otherwise as well. This is not so, because [such a claim] has been refuted and because there is no definitive determination (*anavadhāraṇa*). It has been refuted that doubt arises from the determination of a property that is non-deviant with respect to a contradictory [reason] (*viruddha-avyabhicāri-dharma*); for by means of that very lack of definitive determination, the true nature [of the object]— 187.03 Again, the state of being produced is thus; furthermore, this [doubt] does not arise solely from the determination of a common property, because it is observed otherwise as well. 187.04–187.05 That is not so, because of its refutation and because of the absence of definitive determination. It has been refuted that doubt arises from the determination of a non-deviant contradictory property; for by means of that very absence of definitive determination, the reality—

This has been refuted by the argument of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Furthermore, it is not determined that [doubt arises] solely from the perception of common characteristics (*sāmāna-dharma*); rather, doubt may arise from other factors as well. It was stated that doubt arises from the apprehension of multiple properties (*aneka-dharma*), and this has already been answered by the point that it arises precisely from the apprehension of instability (*avyavasthā*). We do not say that doubt arises from conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*) alone.

187.09. [Objection: Doubt arises from mere non-determination (*avyavasthā-mātra*). [Response: Doubt does not arise from non-determination alone, because the non-determination of perception (*upalabdhi*) and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) functions as a qualifier for the preceding term. Since perception and non-perception are qualifiers of the preceding term and are not independent causes of doubt, this has already been stated in the Sūtra itself.

Furthermore, regarding this [distinction] between "misapprehension" (*vipratipatti*) and "correct apprehension" (*sampratipatti*), there is no change in the object (*artha*) due to a change in its designation (*saṃjñā*). This is because when the conditions (*nimitta*) for the referent of the term "misapprehension" are encountered, it becomes "correct apprehension.
Thus, although a name has been assigned, misapprehension does not thereby cease to exist; misapprehension is indeed present.

Because it is of such a nature, it is a cause for doubt. Furthermore, as for the claim that "there is no lack of determination (avyavasthā) because there is determination within the undetermined self, and because the lack of determination itself is undetermined," that too is not [a valid objection] due to contradiction (*vyāghāta*). There is no contradiction in the fact that there is determination within the undetermined self; nor is there a [lack of] cause.
187.18–19. By means of an internal combination, the application of another name for an object contradicts the actual state of that object as it truly is.

187.19–20. For an object remains exactly as it is whether another name is applied to it or not. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is "extreme doubt regarding its being so" because of the occurrence of its constant possession of those properties, that too is due to a failure to fully understand the meaning of the Sūtra.

Thus it has been said. This doubt does not arise from the common properties (*samāna-dharma*) alone; rather, it arises from the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding that object, provided there is an absence of certainty as to its perception or non-perception, and accompanied by the recollection of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-smṛti*).
And this being the case, there is neither a total absence of doubt nor an absolute state of doubt, because of the determination of one or the other property.

188.02 Thus, it is not correct [to say] that doubt does not arise from this; for when there is a determination of one of two properties, there is no doubt, because the determination of one property is the cause of certainty (nirṇaya). 188.03–188.04 Thus.
188.05 [2-1-7] Where there is doubt, there is this sequence of successive rejoinders.
188.06 Where there is doubt, there is this sequence of successive rejoinders. What is the meaning of this sūtra? It is not that one should personally suppress the doubt;

rather, when the opponent has suppressed the doubt, then one should state the rejoinder in this manner. 188.07 It is not that the doubt is to be suppressed by oneself, but rather, when the doubt has been refuted by the other, then the rejoinder should be stated in this way.
He will train his disciple.
188.09 Now, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which have reached their proper occasion, are being examined.
What, then, is to be examined among them? First, regarding their existence: is it the case that the means of valid cognition exist or do they not?
There is doubt because of the commonality between existence and non-existence, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and because no specific distinction [between them] is perceived.
Having set aside doubt, he objects by adopting the opposing position:
[2-1-8] "And there is no validity for perception and the other means of knowledge, because they are not established in the three times. The meaning of this is that in all three [times],...
188.15. At the wrong times, authoritative means of knowledge do not establish the object.
188.16 [2-1-9] For, regarding the prior establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perception does not arise from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects.

188.17–188.18 "For, regarding the prior establishment of the means of valid cognition" is the sūtra; it is not [the case that perception arises] from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects.
If the prior cognition [is not the cause], there is the fault of contradiction with the meaning of the Sūtra, which states that "perceptual knowledge arises.
Since the contact between the sense organ and the object is not its cause, that which was stated— that [knowledge] has arisen from the contact between the sense organ and the object— is contradicted.
189.01 [2-1-10] If establishment occurs subsequently, there is no establishment of the object of cognition (*prameya*) from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
189.02 "If establishment occurs subsequently" is the aphorism. It means that the designation of an "object of cognition" is not caused by the means of valid cognition.
189.03 This is a contradiction; for without the means of valid cognition, the object of cognition does not attain its own nature, nor do the means of valid cognition...
The establishment of the object of cognition is dependent [upon the means of cognition].
189.05 [2-1-11] If [cognitions] were established simultaneously, there would be an absence of sequential occurrence because each cognition is restricted to its respective object.
189.06 Of cognitions.
189.07 [2-1-12] Since [the three times] are not established, the refutation is untenable.

"Simultaneous establishment" is the sūtra. [The opponent argues: "If there were simultaneous existence when there is a conjunction of the sense organs, their objects, and the cognitions, then the observed sequential operation would not exist; thus there is a contradiction.
Furthermore, the fault that "cognitions do not arise simultaneously" would be contradicted. To this, the following resolution is offered:

189.11 Because there is no fixed rule regarding the prior existence, instability, or simultaneity of the cause of apprehension and the object that is the content of apprehension (upalabdhi-viṣaya), 189.12 this constitutes the demonstration of the unestablished nature (asiddhatā) of the statement, as well as the [proposition] that perception and the other means of knowledge lack validity (aprāmāṇya).

189.13 There is a contradiction between the two terms of the thesis (pratijñā-pada); for the meaning of the claim "perception and the others do not establish an object" is as follows: [it implies they are non-existent].
189.14 And how is this [statement] contradicted? [It is because] perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish an object.

189.15 Just as there is a contradiction in saying "this thing is not perceived" while simultaneously saying "this is not perceived," so too is there a contradiction in saying "perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish an object. Or else, how could it be otherwise that perception and the others [do establish objects]?

189.17 Words such as "perception" (pratyakṣa) do not achieve their purpose without something that establishes an object; therefore, by negating dharma [as the object], 189.18 the acceptance of perception and so forth [is undermined]. By one who says thus, "there is no validity for perception and so forth," 189.19 it is not that perception and so forth are negated, but rather that being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) is the dharma [in question]. Now, if...
Because an entity (bhāva) lacks independence, those [means of knowledge] such as perception and the rest are also negated;

thus, this expression "entity" refers to that which is not independent, and by the negation of the entity, there is a negation of those things possessing it— yet even in this way, the contradiction is not removed, for there is the non-existence of perception and the rest.
190.01. Since the means of cognition such as perception do not exist, by what means do you establish their non-existence?
190.02. In the absence of perception and the other means, there is no other basis for establishing [anything], because of the negation of specific [objects].
190.03. By saying that there is no authorization of other means of cognition and that perception and the others are invalid, [you imply] perception and the others—

190.04 Either a distinct means of valid cognition (*vyatireki-pramāṇa*) would have to be admitted, or the qualification [“not being a means of valid cognition”] regarding perception and the others would be redundant. 190.05 [The opponent asks: “What is the point of this qualification if it is not admitted that there is a distinct means of valid cognition? [The response is: It is to show that perception and the others are not means of valid cognition; they are indeed not means of valid cognition.

To say that "they exist" is likewise contradictory, for you are asserting that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not exist at all. Furthermore, as for that other means of valid cognition which is admitted, since it too is unestablished with respect to the three times, this reason is ineffective; for it does not establish [the point] in any of the three times.

"How can that [scripture] possess validity?"—thus the contradiction remains unresolved. Alternatively, if this is merely a negation of *dharma*, even so, since perception and the other means of knowledge—which are distinct from validity—are admitted, then by the logic of the "negation of the king's men," what is their intrinsic nature? Thus, the persistence of the inquiry leads to a contradiction.

190.13 If no distinct entity [other than the means of knowledge] is admitted, the meaning of the genitive case and of the suffix -taddhita must be stated. If there is no validity (prāmāṇya) of perception and the others that is separate from perception and the others, then what is the meaning of the genitive?
190.14–15 Therefore, a property (dharma)—whether being enjoined or being negated—must necessarily be admitted; upon its admission, [the following applies].

Furthermore, the individual nature of perception and the other means of knowledge must be stated; thus, the contradiction remains unresolved. By this, the meaning of "devoid of that" (*tad-hita*) has been explained. Moreover, this reason—"because it is not established in the three times"—is also misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*);
for "temporality" (*traikālya*) is the existence of the three times, since its object is the three times, and [the reason] is the non-establishment of that.

190.19–21. [Objection: This point—that the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is such that they do not establish an object in any of the three times—is likewise not the meaning of the reason (*hetu*), because it is already implied by the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*). That very meaning of the thesis—namely, that the means of valid cognition do not establish an object—is itself the meaning of the reason in all three times.

191.01 [The opponent says: "They do not establish an object. Furthermore, regarding this statement that "an object being cognized by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the object of cognition (prameya)," 191.02 [we reply: there is no refutation of the designation "means of valid cognition" and "object of cognition" because this designation is applicable across the three times. 191.03 And the cause for this designation is that which is connected to the three times: it will be cognized, it is being cognized, and it has been cognized.

191.04. That by which something has been measured, will be measured, or is being measured is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that which has been measured, will be measured, or is being measured is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
This being so, it is established that this object will be cognized through these causes—that is, its apprehension will occur—and thus it is the *prameya*.
If this were not admitted, worldly discourse regarding objects would be impossible; therefore, there is a contradiction.

This is a fault. However, for one who does not accept the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) across the three times, such conventional usages as "bring the cook" and so forth would be contradicted. Thus, the statement beginning with "the invalidity of perception and the other [means of knowledge] because they are not established in the three times" is a negation of the means of knowledge. Now, by this [negation], perception—
191.10 What is being done regarding these [means of valid cognition]? Is their existence being negated, or is their non-existence being made known?

191.11 And what follows from this? If, first of all, their existence is being negated, that is not tenable, because it involves a contradiction and because the meaning of the negation is not understood. By one who says "their existence is being negated," the means of valid cognition [are themselves negated].

191.13 They do not become [objects] that have been approached, for there is no activity or cessation with respect to what is non-existent. Nor does this negation possess the power to alter an existing entity, because it is merely indicative (jñāpaka).
191.15 This negation is an indicator of the absence of possibility; it does not bring about the cessation of possibility itself.
191.16. Now, if it is intended to make known non-existence (*asambhava*), then the negation would necessarily fall under the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

191.17. [The opponent objects: "Because of the impossibility [of negation] in the three times, negation is untenable. 191.18. This negation, too, is not tenable in any of the three times; this is the meaning of the Sūtra. [The opponent concludes: "This is a contradiction; therefore, the means of valid cognition do not establish an object."

191.19–21: By stating, "They establish [their position] because they admit the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the negation," [the opponent] asserts that the negation is unestablished due to its non-existence in the three times (*traikālyāsiddhi*). Consequently, it follows that perception and the other means of knowledge are invalid because they are unestablished in the three times. This is not a fault, for there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavyāghāta*).
191.22–192.02: "Because of the instruction and the teaching, there is a contradiction with one's own words: 'How is it that what I teach is not accepted?

[Thus: Indeed, by saying that 'that which is not effective in all three times is not a means of proof,' one accepts through one's own speech the very non-effectiveness of the negation. For example, someone..."

192.03 Just as one who wishes to burn another with the flame of his own finger might or might not burn the other, yet he certainly experiences the burning of his own finger; so too, regarding this negation that perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish [their objects], is this a negation of the capacity of perception and the others, or is it a negation of their existence? If—

192.06 [Objection: It is the negation of capacity that is intended, not the negation of perception and the other means of knowledge. Since their capacity has been negated, it follows—as before—that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of perception and the others must be stated. 192.07–08 [Response: Or is it the negation of existence? In that case as well, how are they non-existent? Is it in a general sense or in a specific sense?

192.09 Thus, if the mention of perception and so forth were intended in a general sense, it would be entirely useless to say that "the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) do not exist. Nor is there any logical principle for the negation of the subjects (dharmins). Furthermore, if it is a negation of specific [means], even then there is the admission of other means of valid cognition; for one does not [negate] what has not been admitted.
192.12 A negation of a particular presupposes the existence of a general category. [Regarding] perception and the other means of knowledge:

192.13 "The lack of authority of perception and the others is due to their non-establishment in the three times; the authority of perception and the others is due to their establishment in the three times"—192.14 these two statements must have either the same meaning or different meanings. If they have the same meaning, then regarding perception...
192.15–16. It must be stated exactly thus: "The validity of these [means of knowledge] is established by the proof of the three times," for these [terms] have an identical meaning.

192.16–17. And how is there comprehension of this sentence? If it is from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the contradiction remains unresolved. 192.17. If it is from something else, then that is merely a difference in terminology; if they have different meanings, then by what [means] is that [sentence] [established]?

192.18–192.20: Since the meanings of these two statements—"the establishment of the three times has been understood" and "perception and so forth do not exist"—are distinct, the word "perception and so forth" (pratyakṣādi) is not non-co-referential with "do not exist. Furthermore, this [word] which is not non-co-referential with "do not exist" is not capable of expressing the non-existence of perception and so forth. Indeed, this [word], being non-co-referential with "do not exist," [is not capable of such expression].

192.21 The word "jar" and so forth does not establish the absence of the jar; rather, it [negates] the conjunction of the house and the jar, or a particular time, or the capacity of the jar. Likewise, by this [word] "non-existent" (nāsti), which has the same locus as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is no negation of the means of valid cognition themselves.
It is possible to establish this; moreover, by this [argument], there would be a negation of those [means of knowledge] accepted in other systems.
Whether it be a negation of their capacity or a negation of them at a specific time, in every case, the means of knowledge are accepted, and they are negated by this very negation.
To say that they are being negated is a contradiction. Furthermore, if the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is being demonstrated, how can it be demonstrated?

To whom is it demonstrated, and who is the demonstrator? If you argue that one who has not yet understood is the person to be demonstrated, then by what means has the demonstrator himself understood it? If it is by a *pramāṇa*, there is a contradiction.

193.08–193.10: Because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted, there can be no example for the proponent and the respondent in any other way. Furthermore, if one accepts a distinction between the object to be communicated and the communicator, there is a contradiction;

for if you perceive the object to be communicated and the communicator as distinct, there is a contradiction because you must accept a means of valid cognition that establishes that distinction. Alternatively, if [you do not accept such a distinction]...

193.11–12: "You do not establish [anything]; what is being established?"—thus, the contradiction remains unresolved. Regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): 193.12–13: One who asserts that they do not exist must be questioned: "In what way do they not exist? If he says there is a means of valid cognition, it is a contradiction. If he does not say so, his point is not established. Thus it is.
To the extent that this statement is investigated, to that same extent it dissolves away.

193.15 [2-1-13] Furthermore, because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are negated, the negation itself is untenable. 193.16 Regarding the reason "because it is not established in the three times" (traikālyāsiddheḥ), one must either provide an example for this reason or not. Furthermore, because the invalidity of perception and the other means of knowledge is admitted, even that which is adduced does not establish the object;

193.21 Thus, this very reason is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the established tenet (*siddhānta*). 194.01 Having accepted that [tenet], it is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it opposes it; for its meaning of the statement (*vākya-artha*) is the tenet, and that meaning of the statement is: "The means of valid cognition do not establish an object. 194.03–194.05: "The means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, lack authority for establishing an object because they are not established across the three times"—this [is your claim]. These two modes of verbal activity of yours are not possible, because they are refuted by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

194.21–195.02: Since there is no fixed rule regarding the prior, posterior, or simultaneous occurrence of the causes of apprehension and the object that is apprehended, as observed in various instances, the statement of their distinction was made accordingly. Therefore, this Sūtra was formulated for the purpose of making known the origin [of that distinction]. Why, then, was this Sūtra not stated in that very same context?

195.03–04. Since there is no distinction between what is stated there and what is stated here—meaning that there is no difference whatsoever in every respect—it follows that this matter must be elucidated. He provides one example of the [first] method from the word "from sound" (śabdāt);
as for the remaining two methods, their examples should be understood as previously described, such as "like the accomplishment of a musical instrument" (ātodya-siddhi-vat).
195.06 Just as a musical instrument established beforehand is inferred by means of the sound established afterward—
such as "the lute is being played" or "the flute is being filled"— that which is the unique property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) of the sounds of the lute and the flute,
namely their having the lute and so forth as their cause, one who perceives that [property] [perceives] the sound of the lute or the sound of the flute.
195.09 Thus it is established that the musical instrument is already established, while the sound is established subsequently. Regarding their coexistence:
195.10 An example is when, upon seeing smoke, one perceives fire as qualified by the smoke; [here] the smoke is already established.

195.11 The sun, which is the cause of perception, is the illuminator of things established subsequently. This is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*).
195.12 And thus this designation arises through a mutual correspondence (*samāveśa*), by virtue of the cause for the designation.
195.13 Correspondence is a restriction (*niyama*) by virtue of the cause for the designation, because it is dependent upon that cause for the designation.

195.14 Thus, the cause for the designations "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and "object of valid cognition" (*prameya*) consists in being the cause of apprehension and being the objective domain of apprehension, respectively.

But when a single [entity] is connected with multiple causes (*nimitta*), how then [is it designated]? Since the designation (*samākhyā*) is dependent upon the cause, that entity—while being connected with multiple causes—is expressible by multiple words; and for the purpose of making this meaning known, there is the Sūtra.
195.18 [2-1-16] And cognizability is like the validity of a scale.

195.19 "And cognizability is like the validity of a scale" means: what is being stated? Just as a weighing substance, which is the means for the full cognition of weight, is the cause for determining the exact measure of the weight of a composite whole—

196.01 Because it is [the means] of cognition, it is a *pramāṇa*; and when its extent is delimited by gold and so forth, it is designated as "this balance. Thus, while established as the object of delimitation (*pariccheda-viṣaya*), it is the *prameya*. This very same example should be understood as the meaning of the system (*tantra-artha*) without exception, just as the designations *pramāṇa* and *prameya* apply, so too do the [designations of] the factors of action (*kāraka*).
196.04 All words function according to the rule of the convergence of causes (*nimitta*), and thus it is said in common usage:
196.05 Example: "The tree stands" (*vṛkṣaḥ tiṣṭhati*). Here, a single entity is denoted by multiple agent-words (*kāraka-śabda*).
Because of its independence (*svātantrya*) in its own state of being, the tree is the agent (*kartṛ*). But what, then, is the tree's independence in its own state of being?
196.07–09. For a tree, while standing, does not employ another causal factor for its own persistence;

thus, when this word "standing" (sthiti) expresses the negation of motion, it is so. But even when it is a denoter of existence, since it stands as the cause for manifesting [the object], it manifests that which exists.

196.10 Thus it is said that [the word] denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). But when it expresses a connection with a house and so forth—as in the case of the word "exists" (asti)—196.11 as in the specific instance, "Devadatta is in the house," it is understood that he exists. 196.12 At that time, it does not express existence (*sattā*), nor does it negate motion; rather, even then, it expresses the connection with the house.
The action of experiencing the connection with Devadatta’s house; even in that case, he does not employ other factors of action (kārakas).

Thus, he is independent. But when this word *sthiti* (abiding) is used without its [verbal] form being broken, as in "the tree stands" (*tiṣṭhati vṛkṣaḥ*), since it is not broken, even then, in regard to its own abiding, he does not employ other factors of action.
196.16 He becomes independent; or he employs a part of the aggregate for its own maintenance, as in "the tree stands by its roots.
196.17 Thus, [one says] "the palace is supported by pillars"; or else, maintenance is the state of having a single object for preceding and succeeding cognitions.
196.18 That entity which, having been previously established, is again perceived when other causes are present—whatever...
196.19 Its state of having multiple objects at non-simultaneous times is its stability (*sthiti*);
in that state, 196.20 that which is the auxiliary means—the eye and so forth—is the instrument (*karaṇa*), like the cognition of a whirling firebrand or a lamp.

197.01 If it is argued that this is a false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*), we say no, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). Now, you might think that no single entity exists [simultaneously] at multiple non-simultaneous times.
If it is not an object of cognition, how then does the cognition "this very same tree stands" arise?

For such a cognition never occurs based on the initial perception alone, [thinking] "this very same tree stands. Even when there is difference [between moments], the cognition of stability is observed, as in the case of a wheel that stands while spinning.

197.05 Thus, while it is said that "the lamp remains burning," in the case of unstable and diverse phenomena such as the whirling of a wheel or a lamp, those cognitions which arise based on their existence— namely, the false cognitions that perceive "that" in what is "not that"— 197.06 just as these are false cognitions, so too are they [false] regarding the stability of trees and other things; therefore, this is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
197.08–09: Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever that you have put forward to establish the multiplicity of trees and so forth, [your position fails]. 197.09–10:

It is stated that false cognitions arise in accordance with correct cognitions; therefore, it must be explained where these correct cognitions themselves exist. Furthermore, for you, what is the purpose in their persisting over a period of time?

197.11 The means of valid cognition has been stated. [The existence of] the causes of the cognitions of color, taste, and touch is established by the synthesis of single and multiple cognitions. 197.12 Alternatively, it is the experience of the cause at the time of the effect, by virtue of being the substratum of the effect.
197.13 Thus, if something is its substratum, it experiences the time of that thing's existence, just as...
A pot of milk is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the effect within its cause; therefore, by that [locus] as well, the time of the effect must be experienced.

If it is argued that [the effect] is indeed without a locus—namely, if you think that the effect arises without depending on a cause—then where and what could possibly exist? For in that case, there is an absence of any illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
197.17 Someone might say: "There is an example admitted by both parties that the effect exists without a substratum.

197.18 [To this we reply: "In the case of 'having a substratum' (*ādhāravat*), there is likewise no example"—this is the same [objection]. "It is the same" is not a valid answer. 197.19 [We reply: By your own admission, you have already conceded that there is no example for our position; however—
[The opponent says: "In your position as well, it does not exist. [The proponent replies: "If you say there is a contradiction, then suppose you think:
'I do not admit the absence of an example; rather, a contradiction is being pointed out in your position. How so?
One who says, 'That which is a logically possible example makes the thesis invalid,' thereby contradicts his own established tenet."
198.03 That [objection] does not invalidate [our position], because it arises from a lack of full understanding. You have neither understood our position nor your own.

198.04 First, in our position, it is well-established that an effect possesses a substratum (*ādhāra*). In your position as well, 198.05 form and the other [sensory objects] are effects and possess substrata; thus, there is a contradiction with your own tenets regarding the aggregate of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*).

198.06 If you consider "substance" (*dravya*) to be independent of [qualities] such as form (*rūpa*), what is the meaning of this term when it is devoid of them? 198.07 As for the statement that "form and the others are derived from the elements" (*bhautika*), [it is like saying] a jewel is the support of its radiance because it conforms to the movement, stability, and transformation of that [jewel]; or a bowl is the support of jujube fruits because they fall into it by its power; or [the support] of oil [is the vessel].
198.09. [The argument that] "sesame is the substratum (āśraya) because, by its power, there is no flowing or shaking," and so forth, is refuted; for they are not dependent (anāśrita). 198.10.

If form and the other [aggregates] were independent (svatantra), they would be separable from one another—just like sesame, mung beans, black gram, and so on—based on a single underlying entity. 198.11. But they are not separable; therefore, they are dependent (paratantra). Thus, this is established.

198.12–13. Or, stability (*sthiti*) is the state of having a single object for preceding and succeeding cognitions together with memory; this is to be attained through perception. Because it is desired [as such], the tree is the object (*karman*); the suffix *ka* [in the word *karmaṇi*] has the sense of a factor (*kāraka*), namely, the state of being the object of an action (*kriyā-viṣayatva*).
198.14. That which indeed remains as the state of being the object of an action—this is the object (*karman*) by this definition of the object.

Likewise, that which is employed even if it is not desired is included under the term "immediate realization" (*ānantarya-pratipatti*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*). The sense of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) is as follows: in the expression "one makes the moon known by means of a tree," having grasped the tree, one immediately realizes the moon; thus, the tree is denoted by the word "instrument" (*karaṇa-kāraka*), because it is that which is intended to be reached through the action.
198.18. That object which is intended to be reached by means of the action is designated as the recipient (*sampradāna*).
198.19. In the expression "he pours water for the tree," the water being poured is the object (*karman*); by means of that object, the water, 198.20.
he reaches the tree; thus, the tree becomes the recipient. [That which] departs or remains...

199.01 That is the *apādāna*, as in "he falls from the tree"; the tree is designated by the term *apādāna*. That which falls is what departs; while that [tree] departs, the tree remains. It is the cause of stability (*ghṛti-hetu*).
199.03 The *adhikaraṇa* is that in which something is contained; that which is the cause of the stability of the thing contained is the *adhikaraṇa*.
199.04 "The birds are in the tree"—the connection with the tree is the cause for the obstruction of the birds' weight;

thus, 199.05 the tree is denoted by a word expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This being the case, it is not merely a substance (*dravya*) that is a factor of action (*kāraka*), nor is it merely an action (*kriyā*). What is meant? This term "factor of action" does not apply to action alone.

199.07 It is not in the substance alone; for one who perceives a pure substance does not employ a term for an agent (kāraka). Nor [does one employ it] for the action alone. However, when the action is perceived as related to a substance, then 199.08–09 one designates it with a general term for an agent, namely "the agent" (kāraka). And this is the generality of agents.
199.10 When the specific distinction is not intended to be expressed, and only the state of being the cause of an action (*kriyā-nimittatva*) is intended,
the term "kāraka" (factor of action) is employed. 199.11 But when the specific distinction is intended to be expressed,
then [it is designated] by means of its unique characteristic of a *kāraka*, such as independence (*svātantrya*) and so forth, which distinguishes it from others.
An entity being distinguished by its specific qualities is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), or the instrument (*karaṇa*) for everyone.

Furthermore, the designation of an *kāraka* as an "agent" is based on its own action; however, the employment of the term *kāraka* depends upon the primary action. And thus, according to the treatise, of what [action] is one an agent, a producer, or a bringer-about?
199.16 Because of [the distinction between] the action [itself] and [its auxiliaries], there is such a designation; therefore, this was not stated with reference to its own action alone.

199.17 Rather, it refers to the principal action; within that very principal action, some [auxiliaries] are remote helpers, while others are proximate helpers. 199.18 Thus, some assist in one way or another—[that is the meaning].

199.19 And terms such as "agent" (*kartṛ*) and so forth are dependent [on action]. This has been stated previously. If the application of the term "factor of action" (*kāraka*) were based solely on the connection with an action, then the word "cook" (*pācaka*) would apply only when one is currently cooking; consequently, one could not say "the cook cooked" (*apākṣīt pācakaḥ*) or "the cook will cook" (*pakṣyati pācakaḥ*), because the [agent's] capacity (*śakti*) persists throughout the three times.

200.01. Power (*śakti*) persists throughout all three times (*kāla*), and it is with reference to power that there is the designation of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) for the past and the future, as in "he cooks," "he cooked," and "he will cook. 200.02. Since power exists in all three times, the manifestation [of action] across the three times is not illogical. Just as a substance (*dravya*) is connected to the three times, so too is power; therefore, just as...

200.04. Just as the three times are not manifested in a substance (*dravya*), so too they are not manifested in a capacity (*śakti*). Consequently, one would have to say "he cooks even though he does not cook" (200.05). One would likewise not be able to say "he will cook, the cooker" or "he cooked, the cooker. This is not a fault, because the connection with action is the cause for the manifestation of the capacity; by this word "action" (*kriyā*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu-artha*) is expressed.

200.07 That which is his primary instrument is the agent (*kartṛ*). When this agent is connected with an action, he then manifests a capacity (*śakti*). But what is this capacity? It is a property of the agent distinct from both the action and the agent itself. 200.08–09 This efficacy (*sāmarthya*) and the thorough knowledge of the means are established through their connection with the action; when there is the knowledge of the means—

200.10 At that time, when there is a connection between capacity and action, the word for an agent (*kāraka*) functions in its primary sense, as in "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "a cook" (*pācaka*). However, when the word "cook" is applied based solely on the capacity for knowing the means— even in the absence of a connection to the actual action— due to the deficiency of one or another [factor], then it functions metaphorically (*upacārataḥ*), as in "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*).

200.13 “The cooker will cook; he is a cooker. And this word *kāraka* (agent) [is used] in the sense of "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) and "object of knowledge" (*prameya*). 200.14 Why? Because of its connection with a specific action (*kriyā-viśeṣa-yoga*). Just as these words such as "cooker" (*pācaka*) function when there is a connection with a specific action, so too do the words "means of knowledge" and "object of knowledge. Now, sir, regarding the agent... 200.15... [it functions] because of the connection with a specific action, just as these words such as "cooker" function when there is a connection with a specific action. Thus it is with the words "means of knowledge" and "object of knowledge" as well. Now, O venerable one, the agent—

200.16 Because words converge upon their respective causes, there is a restriction [regarding their application]. Direct perception and the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are being experienced;

200.17 since the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the domain of apprehension, this is considered therein: Are these [means], such as direct perception, established through another means of valid cognition distinct from direct perception and the rest in their own apprehension? 200.18 [Is there another means of valid cognition for the establishment of] direct perception and so forth?

200.19 If the means of proof (*sādhana*) were itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that another means of valid cognition is required to establish it; yet [the proponents] do not employ such a one.
200.20 Therefore, the apprehension of the means of valid cognition occurs entirely without a means of proof.

201.01 [2-1-17] If the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were itself through a means of valid cognition, there would be the consequence that the means of valid cognition require another means of valid cognition for their establishment. 201.02 What follows from this? 201.03 From the establishment of the means of valid cognition being through a means of valid cognition, there arises the consequence that the means of valid cognition must be established by yet another means of valid cognition.

If the establishment of the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) requires another means of valid cognition as its proof, then because perception and the other [means] are themselves what are to be established, that which is to be established cannot be the means of proof. Furthermore, if there were another means of valid cognition,
then the apprehension of the means of valid cognition would be without any proof whatsoever.
201.07 [2-1-18] Or, through their cessation, there is the establishment of the objects of knowledge (prameya), just as there is the establishment of other means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

201.08 Or, through their cessation, there is the establishment of the objects of knowledge, just as there is the establishment of other means of knowledge; just as the means of knowledge cease when they have apprehended themselves, so too do they cease upon the establishment of the objects of knowledge.
201.09 Just as the means of knowledge cease once they have been perceived by themselves, so it is also with the establishment of the objects of knowledge.
The reply to this is:
[2-1-19] "Not so, because its establishment is like the light of a lamp.
Regarding the phrase "not so, because its establishment is like the light of a lamp": the light of a lamp [is established] by means of a jar...

201.13 Because it is a constituent factor for establishing the initial apprehension, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and that [means of valid cognition] is apprehended precisely through perception and the other [means of valid cognition].
201.14 This [person] does not employ a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and the others for the apprehension of the self; rather, [the self] is apprehended by those very [means].
201.15 Likewise, the means of valid cognition themselves are also apprehended precisely through perception and the others—this is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

"This is merely a [statement]; what is the reasoning here? This reasoning is stated: Perception and the other [means of knowledge] do not require another means of knowledge for their own apprehension, because they are instruments for determining [their objects], like a lamp.
Just as a lamp, being an instrument for determining [objects], does not require another means of knowledge for its own apprehension.
Thus, in that manner, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are such that they do not require other means of valid cognition;

this is established. Furthermore, because it possesses both general and particular characteristics (*sāmānya-viśeṣavattvāt*), whatever possesses general and particular characteristics does not, in its own apprehension, require a means of valid cognition distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest—just as a lamp [is not required to illuminate itself]—this is what is to be understood.

Because it is cognizable, that which is to be known does not require another means of valid cognition distinct from perception and the rest, just as a lamp [does not require another lamp]. Because they are dependent or because they are instruments, and so forth— just like a lamp— the sense organs and other such factors, being components of perception,
do not require another means of valid cognition distinct from perception and the rest.
[The opponent says: "It is the same [in both cases]. If you argue that it cannot be apprehended by itself, then you must consider this:

if perception and the other means of knowledge were apprehended by perception and the others themselves, it would follow that the very same thing is apprehended by itself; but this is not the case. [The author replies:
This is not a fault, because the probandum cannot be the probans. For there is a distinction between objects based on their common characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-sāmānya*).

202.08. Many objects are subsumed under the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, there is no fault in the fact that by means of one [cognition], another is apprehended.

202.09. Just as when water has been drawn out, one who has taken the water that was drawn out also perceives that which remains in the reservoir as "it is real" (*bhūtam*), yet it is not said that the latter is apprehended by the former.
202.11 However, it is not the case that one such entity grasps another such entity, nor is this an absolute rule that it is never by means of that very same thing that there is a grasping of it.
202.12 It occurs; for instance, it sometimes happens—as in the case of the self—that the knower becomes the known.
202.13 When one knows the self. If you argue that there is a distinction of causal conditions (*nimitta*) here, and you think that when...

202.14 This self is the knower; when that which is to be known is other than it, then [the relationship] is the same as [the case where] there is another cause. 202.15 Just as the knower, depending on a connection with pleasure and so forth, apprehends the self—which is qualified by those—as "I am happy" or "I am suffering," so too does the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), while abiding as the object of a means of valid cognition...

202.17 Regarding "the object of cognition" (*prameya*): it is because it is impossible for there to be anything that is not within the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge. If some object were indeed within the scope of perception and the others, we might then establish a means of knowledge distinct from perception and the rest.
But such an object cannot be established by anyone; for all this—both the existent and the non-existent—is [known through] perception.

The object belongs to perception and the other means of knowledge themselves; therefore, it is apprehended by perception and the rest alone. Others, however, without employing a specific reason, resort to a mere example using the analogy of the light of a lamp:
"Just as, it is said, the light of a lamp is perceived without the light of another lamp, so too [is the case here]."
It is said to those who maintain that even the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) will be apprehended without another means of valid cognition: 203.01. [This is stated] regarding them.
203.02 [2-1-20(*)] Because cessation is observed in some cases and non-cessation is observed in others, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). For example, as with a lamp:

what is the cause for a restriction here? Furthermore, when illuminating the form of a pot or similar object, why does the light of the lamp not cease? In this same way, why would the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) not [cease]? And this is the analogy of the lamp-light.

203.06–203.08: "Let it be so in the case of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), but not in the case of the object of cognition (*prameya*). Even here, the reason for this restriction must be stated. "Let the lamp and its illumination serve as the example, but not the pot and such things.
In this case too, the reason for the restriction must be stated. Thus, since [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in both ways, one must state a specific reason (*viśeṣa-hetu*).

203.09. An objection is raised that an example is not applicable when a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) is accepted, because [the opponent] grants the application [of the reason] to one side. 203.10. There is no refutation here; for if this example of the light of a lamp is indeed grasped by a specific reason such as "being luminous" (203.11), then, being granted in one case, it cannot be [refuted].

203.12–13. [The opponent argues: "To refute [this], [you claim] it is 'inconclusive' (anekānta)"; this fault does not apply, because perception and the other means of knowledge are themselves perceived by perception and the others.

203.13–14. [The proponent replies: If it is argued that there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) if perception and the others were perceived by perception and the others—namely, if those [means] were perceived by yet others, and those [others] by yet others—then, in the case of such an infinite regress, the first...

There would be no apprehension of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If, on the other hand, there were a fixed determination, then the initial apprehension of the means of valid cognition would result in being invalid. This fault does not apply, because of the perception of the object of consciousness, its cause, and [the means of] apprehension; for one who perceives the object of consciousness and the cause of consciousness, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of consciousness is established.

The object is the thing to be known; the means of knowledge is the cause of cognition. Through the apprehension of both the means of knowledge and the object to be known, all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*)—which has as its purposes virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, and which has as its purpose the avoidance of their opposites—is established. Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever that must be accomplished by an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), such that one would be driven to it.
One would incur an infinite regress. Therefore, the apprehension of perception and the other means of knowledge by means of perception and the others does not result in an infinite regress.

204.03 Thus, it has been established in general that these means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exist as the instruments for establishing the objects of cognition (*prameya*). Now, therefore, follows the examination of the specific characteristics of those [means] already established in general. Among them, perception (*pratyakṣa*) was mentioned first; that shall now be examined.
204.06 [2-1-21(20)] The definition of perception is untenable because it is incomplete.

204.07 The definition of perception is untenable because it is stated incompletely. This definition of perception which is stated—204.08 namely, "that which arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object"—is incomplete. Why? Because there are others...

204.09 Furthermore, there are causes for perception that have not been mentioned, such as the conjunction of the self and the mind (ātma-manas-saṃyoga), and so forth. 204.10 Now, if it is argued that "that which is produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object" is the definition [of perception], 204.11 this too cannot be the definition; why? Because it merely indicates the cause of production (*utpatti-kāraṇa*), namely, the contact of the sense organ with its object.
204.12 "It has arisen"—this is stated as a reason (*kāraṇa*), yet the designation of a reason is not [the definition] of a real entity (*vastu*).
204.13 Nor is it its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); for the sequential production from a lump of clay and so forth is not the characteristic of an effect such as a jar.
204.14 There is no fault in either case: if it is a reason, there is still no fault; and if it is a characteristic, there is likewise no fault.

204.15 There is no fault. How so? First, regarding the position that it is a cause (*kāraṇapakṣa*), it has been stated: "This sūtra is not for the purpose of defining [the cause] alone. 204.16 Rather, it is stated [to define] that which is the unique [cause] of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consisting in perception (*pratyakṣa*), namely that which excludes [other means such as] inference (*anumāna*) and so forth. 204.17 Thus, there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*) and so on, nor to the sense-faculty and the mind (*indriya-manas*).
204.18: In that case, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) must also be added [to the definition], if the contact between the sense-organ and its object is mentioned because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
204.19: But it has been stated here that for this very reason, the contact between the sense-organ and the mind (*indriya-manas-sannikarṣa*) need not be added either;
rather, everything that is unique must be stated. However, it is further qualified by the mention of "elsewhere" (*anyatra*).

205.01. Even in the case where this is taken as a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no fault, because the contact between the sense faculty and the object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) is unique (*asādhāraṇatva*).
205.02. Contact between the sense faculty and the object is the cause (*kāraṇa*) for the production of perception, because it distinguishes [perception] from both similar and dissimilar classes.
205.03. And because it is a differentiator, it is also a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, the expression is used according to its actual meaning; [it refers to] the self—

205.04. How is it that [cognition arises] from the conjunction of the mind (*manas*) and the conjunction of the sense organ with the mind? This is because the arising of cognition is observed [to depend on these]. 205.05. Since a quality produced by conjunction does not arise in a substance that is not conjoined, [the sense organ] would function independently of the conjunction with the mind.
205.06. Furthermore, if the sense organ were to operate [independently], there would be the simultaneous perception of multiple objects; however, this does not occur. Therefore...
205.07. "Contact with the mind (*manas-sannikarṣa*) is also a cause. This is the aphorism (*sūtra*) together with its stated commentary (*bhāṣya*).
205.08 [2-1-22(21)] There is no production of perception in the absence of contact between the self and the mind.

205.09 "There is no production of perception in the absence of contact between the self and the mind"—that is to say, in the absence of contact between the self and the mind, cognition does not arise, just as it does not arise in the absence of contact between the sense organ and its object. It is not so.

205.11 Because the answer has already been stated, this [objection] has already been answered; therefore, this sūtra is not intended to define the cause, but rather 205.12 it is a statement of a specific cause. And those who describe the nature of a cause on the grounds that [the effect] exists when [the cause] exists—[they argue] that indeed, when there is contact between the sense organ and the object, cognition arises, and when it is absent, it does not arise.
Therefore, the contact between the sense faculty and its object is the cause.
205.15 [2-1-23(22)] This same consequence applies to direction, location, time, and space as well.

205.16 There is this same consequence regarding direction, location, time, and space: 205.17 since knowledge occurs even when these exist—because it exists when they are present—it follows that these too must be causes.

205.18 But by what reasoning is it established that space and so forth are not causes, since their causal efficacy is not perceived? For no efficacy of space and so forth is perceived in the production of cognition; therefore, they are not causes, [but rather] due to mere proximity.
If you think: "Space and so forth are the cause of the production of cognition merely through their proximity," [then...]
That is incorrect, because proximity is unavoidable; for [space] and so forth are eternal and all-pervading.

Because they are eternal and all-pervading, their proximity cannot be avoided. In that case, a reason must be stated for their being a cause; for mere proximity is not the cause for being a cause. How so?

206.04 [The opponent argues: "The perception of color (rūpa) is like the existence of the tactile quality of fire (tejas). Just as in the perception of color, a specific quality of fire is the cause, and not the tactile quality of fire itself—since its efficacy is not observed merely through its presence—the efficacy of color, however, is observed because the perception follows the presence and absence of that [color]; for wherever color exists, [perception occurs].

In that case, where there is no perception, nothing is perceived there; therefore, form alone is the cause of perception, not touch. For example, lunar form illuminates without the heat of the touch of fire, and [the light] illuminates what is situated in a room or similar place without the heat of touch, but with form.

206.10 And thus, while cognition arises from the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the object, it does not arise from [factors such as] direction and so forth. 206.11 This is because [the self, etc. are merely present, whereas the capacity of the others is not observed. If this is so, then 206.12 the conjunction of the self and the mind must be added [to the list of causes]. It need not be added, because it is already understood. By what is it understood?
206.13 [2-1-24(23)] Because the self has cognition as its mark, there is no non-inclusion.
206.14 Because the self has cognition as its mark, there is no non-inclusion. It has been stated that cognition is the mark of the self.

206.15 Therefore, even though the conjunction of the self and the mind has not been explicitly mentioned, it is to be inferred. How, moreover, is cognition the mark of the self? [Because it is] its quality...

[Objection: Because [it is] so, there is the establishment of its being a quality (*guṇabhāva*). [Response: If you think that the very state of being a quality of cognition is unestablished, how then will its being a quality of the self (*ātmaguṇatva*) be established? [Objection: It is because of its inherence (*samavāya*) in the self, just like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. [Response: For neither a substance (*dravya*) nor an action (*karman*) inheres in the self; therefore, it is not a substance, nor...
206.19–206.21: Knowledge inheres in the self, like pleasure and so forth; therefore, it is not a quality of the earth and so on, because it is an object of self-cognition.

Whatever is perceptible and self-cognized is not a quality of the earth and so on, just as pleasure and so forth [are not]. And whatever is perceptible and cognized by both self and other is a quality of the earth and so on.

206.22 Just as form and so forth are not [perceived in this way], knowledge is not [so perceived]; therefore, it is a quality of the self (*ātma-guṇa*). And what was said here? What was said? 207.01 It was not stated that every single cause of perception must be mentioned. Now, why is the contact between the sense organ and the mind (*indriya-manaḥ-sannikarṣa*) not mentioned? 207.02 [Why is it not stated?]

207.03 [2-1-25(24)] And because it has the non-simultaneity of cognitions as its mark, [the existence of] the mind [is established]. 207.04 And because it has the non-simultaneity of cognitions as its mark, there is no [simultaneous] production of cognitions due to the mind.
207.05 It has been stated that this is the "mark" (liṅga). By that, the mind is also included; thus, there is no contradiction with the sūtra concerning simultaneous production.

207.06–207.08. Regarding this statement that "the non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark (liṅga) of the mind," because it serves another purpose, it is incorrect [to claim] that "the mind is the cause of cognition. The sūtra has another purpose;
it does not, however, by that [statement], declare or indicate that the mind is the cause of cognition. For cognition is not independent of something else.

207.09–207.11: Even though the capacity of the mind to illuminate that object is not explicitly stated in that sūtra as being the cause of cognition, nevertheless, by the force of logical reasoning, it is understood that the mind is the cause of cognition. For cognition is not independent, nor are the eyes and other sense organs independent.

207.12 Thus [it is asked]: Why is the contact between the sense organ and the object (indriya-artha-sannikarṣa) mentioned, and why is the contact between the self and the mind (ātma-manas-sannikarṣa) or the contact between the sense organ and the mind (indriya-manas-sannikarṣa) not mentioned? 207.13 [Answer: Because...
207.14 [2-1-26(*)] And because the contact between the sense organ and the object is the specific cause of perception, it is mentioned by its own name.
207.15 / Contact between the sense organ and the object is the cause of perception alone, whereas contact between the self and the mind [is the cause] of perception and other [cognitions].
207.16 Because it is common to perception and other [cognitions], [the contact between] the sense organ and the mind—

207.17. The conjunction [of the self and the mind] must be mentioned if it is not stated because it is common [to all cognitions]. 207.18–19. The conjunction of the sense organ and the mind must be mentioned because it is uncommon, just like the conjunction of the sense organ and its object.
207.19. It has been said that this [mention] is not for the purpose of defining the cause; for it is not the case that everything which is uncommon [must be mentioned].
That must indeed be stated; however, it is not to be stated as something common—this is the meaning of the Sūtra.

208.01 [2-1-27] And because for those who are asleep or whose minds are preoccupied, [perception occurs] due to the contact between the sense-faculties and their objects; this sūtra is intended to emphasize the primacy of the contact between the sense-faculty and the object. The rest is explained in the Bhāṣya.
208.03 [2-1-28(25)] And by means of these, there is the designation of specific cognitions;

furthermore, there is another reason for their primacy. And by means of these, there is the designation of specific cognitions: because this perceptual cognition, when arising, is designated by its object or by its cause, and that which is unique [to it].
208.06. By that [designation], a designation is seen, as for example: "a rice sprout."
208.07 [2-1-29(26)] It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory (vyāhata).
208.08 Because it is contradictory, it is not a valid reason. By the phrase "because it is contradictory," he refutes the three sūtras.
208.09 Because the contact between the sense organ and the object is the cause of perception, and because for those who are asleep or whose minds are distracted...
208.10 Because the contact between the sense-faculties and their objects is the cause [of cognition], and it is by means of these that specific cognitions are designated;

208.11 thus, this set of three sūtras indeed refutes the view that the contact between the self and the mind is the cause of cognition—this is a contradiction. Since the self is known through the mark of cognition, there can be neither non-apprehension nor non-restriction [of its existence].

208.13 And because their non-simultaneity is the mark [of the existence of the mind], it is not [due to] the mind. 208.14 If there were no dependence on the conjunction with the mind, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the simultaneous arising of cognitions; thus, there is a contradiction with what is observed. 208.15 Now, lest there be such a contradiction, [one might argue that] cognition arises from the contact between the self and the mind. Why is this merely a statement of the position? From the self— [text continues].
208.16. Here, the conjunction with the mind (*manas-saṃyoga*) is not being stated. What has been said? It was said that this [sūtra] is not for the purpose of determining the cause.

208.17. Rather, even the sūtra is a statement regarding a specific cause. Furthermore, this set of three sūtras beginning with "And because the sense-faculties and the objects are the causes of perception, [the cause is] the contact" (NS 3.1.29–31) is also [of this nature].
209.01 [2-1-30(27)] Not so, because of the predominance of the specific object.

209.02 Not so, because of the predominance of the specific object. By this set of three sūtras, the causal status of the contact between the self and the mind is not denied; rather, it is the predominance of the contact between the sense organ and the object that is [affirmed].
209.04 It is established; and by establishing its predominance, while it is being established, the conjunction of the self and the mind is not negated.
209.05 There is the statement regarding the cause of action in the mind for those whose minds are asleep or distracted, [concerning] the sense organs and their objects.
209.06 By the statement regarding the causality of contact and so forth, it has been stated that the conjunction with the mind is also a cause.

In this regard, it must be stated that mental activity (*manasikāra*) is the cause [of cognition]. Now, since the experience of pleasure and pain has the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as its cause, the unseen force is the cause; just as there exists within the self another quality produced by desire, characterized by effort (*prayatna*), which is the cause of action, so too does a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—designated as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—exist within the self.

209.10 Driven by that [dharma and adharma], the mind is either conjoined or disjoined; for if the mind were not being impelled by that, 209.11 then, due to the absence of any other cause for action, its capacity for all objects would cease. For, in the beginning, apart from dharma and adharma, no other cause for action is possible in the mind.
209.13 Thus, for this reason, it is the unseen cause (adṛṣṭa).
209.14 Thus, the definition of perception has first been established; hereafter, now, while demonstrating that perception is included within inference, he says this: 209.15 [He says: "..."
209.16 [2-1-31(28)] Perception is inference because it is an apprehension resulting from the grasping of a single part.

209.17 Perception is inference because it is an apprehension resulting from the grasping of a single part. That knowledge which arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object, such as "this is a tree"—this, they say, is perception; that is indeed inference.

209.19 Why is it so? Because the perception of a tree occurs through the apprehension of a single part; having apprehended this one part, one perceives the tree. 210.01 And yet, that single part is not the tree itself. In that case, just as the cognition of another [thing] arises from the sight of something else, so too the cognition of the tree from the apprehension of a single part is inference (*anumāna*). Just as [one infers fire] from smoke...

210.03 Just as there is the apprehension of fire upon perceiving [its] smoke, so too there is the apprehension of a tree upon perceiving a part; thus, there is no impossibility of conceptual construction (vikalpa). 210.04 It is argued that by grasping a single part, one apprehends a distinct entity (arthāntara). What is this distinct entity which is apprehended through the grasping of a single part? First, regarding the position that [the object] is a collection of parts (avayavasamūhapakṣa):

210.06 If it is argued that the other parts [of a tree] are distinct substances and these [parts together] constitute the whole (*avayavin*), [we reply: no, if—210.07 first of all—it is said with reference to a tree as merely a collection of parts, then according to this position, the tree would be that which consists of those parts being perceived while other parts not being perceived are excluded. Or else, 210.08 [if the tree were something more], it would be distinct from the perceived parts.

Even if the position that a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) arises is adopted, [the tree] would still be [perceived as] separated by the intervening parts located in the nearer portion; and yet, that tree is [designated as] a distinct object. Now, in this case, upon the perception of one part, does one apprehend the other parts or a distinct substance? This is the case under the theory of the aggregate of parts (*avayavasamūhapakṣa*).

210.12 To that extent, there is an absence of the cognition of "tree" regarding the rear portion, because that rear portion is not a tree, just like the front portion. Just as this front portion is not a tree, so too the middle and rear portions are not a tree. Thus, this cognition of "tree" arising with respect to a collection of parts that is not a tree is without an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*), [whether it be] the front portion or the rear portion.
210.15 Furthermore, this so-called "middle part" does not exist. How so? The term "part" (*bhāga*) is a name for a constituent member (*avayava*).

For one who does not admit a distinct entity as a whole (*avayavin*), the statement "it is a part" is devoid of meaning. 210.16–17 Moreover, a "part" is either a posterior portion (*para-bhāga*) or an anterior portion (*arvāg-bhāga*); and these [distinctions] do not hold when the whole is rejected.
210.18 “Connected” (yukta). Now, if it is said that a "part" (ekadeśa) is a "portion" (bhāga), what is this "part"?
210.19 For the part is the substratum of the whole; and by one who denies the whole, the part is also denied.
210.20 Now, [regarding] the elements (bhūta) which are excluded from being effect and cause—by means of their mutual proximity and support, there is a "part"...
210.21. "Abiding" (*avasthāna*) is the meaning of "part" (*avayava*). Oh, what skill in the meaning of words! [Yet] they are neither effect nor cause. 210.22.
They exist by way of being grasped through mutual proximity; yet they do not perform mutual assistance. 211.01.
And it is strange that they are called "parts. Others, however, [perceive the whole] by seeing the near portion... the far [portion].
211.02 Having performed an inference based on a part, they determine the cognition of "tree" regarding what is not a tree, which arises from the synthesis [of parts].

211.03 In this position, how could there be an absence of the cognition of "tree," given that both the near part and the far part are non-trees? Nor can a cognition of "tree" arise from a synthesis of what is not a tree. No.

211.05 And in this view, there is an inference: having perceived the near part, one infers the far part. Thus, it is not the case that the object of inference is unknown. How could it be unknown? If it is inferred in this way: "This is a tree because it possesses a near part," then which is that tree whose near part [is perceived]? 211.06–211.07 [If the tree itself is not yet known,] how can it be the subject of inference? If it is argued that this tree is inferred because it possesses a near part, then what is that tree? Whose near part [is being referred to]?

211.08. For one who does not accept a whole (*avayavin*) as an object distinct [from its parts], the property of being a "devotee" (*bhāgavat-tva*) is a mere posterior part, which is perceptible. 211.09. Nor does inference proceed when the locus (*dharmin*) is unperceived; nor does he ever perceive a locus, because it is accepted as non-existent, and inference does not function upon another inference in this manner. 211.10.
