Nor does he ever perceive a locus, because it is accepted as non-existent, and inference does not function upon another inference in this manner. 211.10. Nor does he ever perceive a locus, because it is accepted as non-existent, and inference does not function
211.11 Because there is no such synthesis [of past and present], for in inference there is no synthesis of this kind.
211.12 This inferrer does not, having previously perceived fire and having apprehended smoke as its qualifier, synthesize them.
211.13 [He does not think] "This is smoke and this is fire," nor is it inferred that "fire is here" by means of such a synthesis.

"It must be so. For what reason? Because it would be futile. In this state, inference is useless, because the fire, which serves as the qualifier, is already perceived; therefore, there is no synthesis in the case of inference.
Furthermore, even if there were synthesis, it would not be a synthesis with respect to the whole, nor with respect to the tree, for this [fire] is not a single part.
211.17 From the perception [of one part], one understands the aggregate, but not the tree; rather, one understands only the remaining members of the aggregate.

211.18 For what reason? Because an aggregate is not admitted apart from its constituent members. 211.19 Indeed, you do not admit an aggregate distinct from its members, for that which is non-existent—
The whole (samudāya) can be inferred. Furthermore, having perceived this near portion, what else does he infer?
It is not logical to infer that "this near portion possesses a far portion," because it is impossible for the near portion to possess a far portion;
for the near portion is not [itself] a portion.

212.02 Because the state of possessing parts (*bhāgavat-tva*) is impossible, for there is no further part (*apara-bhāga*) of a part. Now, 212.03 if you maintain that a part possesses a part, that part does not possess [another] part; rather, it is the possessor of parts (*bhāgin*) itself.
212.04 Furthermore, it is incorrect to say that inference has the possessor of parts as its object, because both are perceptible. For in this case, both are indeed perceived.

212.05–212.07. Perception pertains to the proximate part (*arvāgbhāga*), and here the possessor of that part (*bhāgin*) is inferred by virtue of its being like the proximate part; thus, the inference of the remote part (*parabhāga*) is logical in our position, but in your position it is not logical because one perceives only a portion. Furthermore, that perception of the proximate part does not possess the assistance of the recollection of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*).

212.08 Furthermore, because the near and far parts of two connected objects are not seen, this observer [does not perceive them]. 212.09 He does not see the connection between the near and far parts; nor are the near and far parts themselves connected.
212.10 Moreover, there is no recollection without prior experience, and there is no perception of a logical mark (*liṅga*) without recollection—only the [mark] itself.

212.11 How, then, does he [the opponent] infer this? [He argues: "This [atom] does not perceive its near-side part and far-side part as being connected, because it is eternally separated from the far-side part by the near-side part; thus, it eternally perceives only the near-side part alone, and never at all the far-side part, because it is obstructed by the near-side part. This is true.
212.14 There is no perception of both [parts], and although both are indeed connected, inference is impossible.
212.15 Because both are not seen, and because the relationship of property and property-possessor (dharma-dharmin) is untenable between the near side and the far side, there is no inference.
212.16 For where inference occurs, it is when the property of the property-possessor is established, and [it functions] with respect to another property.

212.17 Furthermore, inference [is not possible here], because the further part is not a property of the nearer part, nor is the nearer part a property of the further part; therefore, there is no inference. And as for this statement—that the cognition of a tree arises from a unifying cognition—that is incorrect, because since the tree is not established, there can be no unification.
For what is called "recognition" (pratisandhāna) is a cognition that, colored by a previous cognition, occurs with respect to another aggregate [of parts].
For example, [the thought] "I have perceived color and taste"—
in your position, however, having grasped the near part and inferred the far part, such a recognition-cognition as "the near part and the far part" would be appropriate only to this extent.

But from what source does the cognition of a "tree" arise? It cannot be that the near portion is the tree and the far portion is not; for the cognition of a "tree" with respect to the near and far portions—which are themselves not the tree—is a cognition of "that" in what is "not-that. It cannot be established through inference, because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) functions by determining an object exactly as it is.

213.05 Furthermore, this cognition that [perceives] something as "that" when it is not that occurs by way of conforming to a primary [referent]; thus, the cognition of a tree [requires] a primary [referent].

213.06 That primary referent must be stated, for there is no cognition that [perceives] something as "that" when it is not that—whether it be one who has not grasped a universal or one who has not superposed a property contrary to it—and yet no such primary referent exists for a tree.

Because [the whole] is not admitted [as a separate entity], the cognition of a "tree" does not arise from the synthesis of inferences. By this, the cognitions of the near part and the far part are also refuted. For one who does not admit [the existence of] a final whole, there is no such thing as a "near part" or a "far part. Why? Because there is no perception of a large substance [without such parts].

213.11 For that which possesses characteristics and has its further part obstructed, this is the name "near part" (*arvāg-bhāga*); likewise, for such a thing that is obstructed, there is the "further part" (*para-bhāga*). 213.12 Furthermore, you do not admit any substance that exists as a whole (*avayavin*) which could be denoted by the terms "near part" and "further part. [This applies] to atoms (*paramāṇu*).

If you think that cognitions of trees and so forth arise with respect to those [atoms] arranged in such a way—namely, when they are situated in a particular configuration through their mutual proximity and aggregation—we reply:

we do not admit the existence of any composite substances whatsoever; rather, it is only with respect to those very atoms, when they are established in a specific configuration through their mutual proximity and aggregation, that those words [are applied].

The designations "this side," "that side," and "tree" do not function as distinct referents for the word "thus" (*tathā*), because they do not denote anything other than that [arrangement]. Thus, when things are so arranged, the application of such designations proceeds based on prior convention.
Furthermore, there is no basis for the application of terms such as "prior" or "posterior" in the case of atoms, as there is in the case of what is conventionally established.

213.20 "In a cow, there are sheep of that same form"—thus, first of all, it has been stated that the cognition of a "tree" is absent in the view that [the object] is a collection of parts (avayava-samūha).

213.21 However, in the view that a distinct substance (dravya-antara) arises [as a whole], the whole (avayavin) is not to be inferred, because it is perceptible, just like the near part [of the tree].
214.01 Just as one perceives this near part, which is connected with the sense organ, through direct perception (pratyakṣa), so too [is the whole perceived].

214.02. Even in the case of a tree, the tree is not to be inferred. Now, if one maintains that even a tree connected with the senses is indeed to be inferred, then, like the tree, its near portion would also have to be inferred; and thus it becomes contradicted [to say] that "having grasped the near portion, he perceives the tree," for [under such a view] everything would be nothing but inference.

In that position, there is an absence of inference because the subject (*dharmin*) has not been apprehended through perception; for inference operates only upon a subject that has not been apprehended through perception. As for what was said regarding inference concerning objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), that does not exist, for an object beyond the senses cannot be inferred. Why? Because the subject has not been apprehended.

...because of this, it has been said. But what is the distinction between inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) and inference preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa-pūrvaka*)? If all inference is indeed preceded by perception, then this is the distinction: that which is preceded by perception proceeds upon the establishment of the three factors (*trika*), namely, where there is the apprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), and the subject (*dharmin*).

214.11 Having first apprehended the substratum (dharmin), one then infers another property (dharma) through the perception of the property and the substratum; that is "inference based on what was previously perceived" (pratyakṣapūrvaka). On the other hand, when, having perceived the probans-property (sādhanadharma) and the substratum, one infers another property that is absolutely beyond the senses (atyantaparokṣa), that is "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). But in your position, this is not so.

The cognition of a tree arises from inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa-anumāna*), not from perception preceded by [the perception of] a subject (*dharmin*), because such a subject is not admitted and because perception has been refuted. Furthermore, this reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the apprehension of a tree occurs through the grasping of only one part [of it].
How so?

214.17 [2-1-32(29)] "Not by means of perception, because even that much is apprehended. 214.18–19: By one who says, "Perception is inference," in this way, perception is denied; and because of the denial of perception, that which is the perception of a single part [is also denied].

That [position] is contradicted. How so? That which you rely upon as the apprehension of a single part—that much alone establishes the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is it asserted in this way:
that everything is the object of perception; rather, only that which is perceived through the contact of the sense organ with its object [is so].
215.01. To that extent, it is the object of perception; otherwise, perception is not inference. 215.02.

Because it lacks a mode [of operation], whereas inference possesses a mode, perception is said by those explaining the Sūtra to be without a mode—[in contrast to] inference. 215.03. And because its object pertains to the three times, inference is not perception, for [perception] does not pertain to the three times.

Inference has an object [that is not directly perceived], whereas perception does not; furthermore, because it depends on the assistance of the recollection of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), inference is not perception. There is an assistance from the recollection of the relationship between the mark and the bearer of the mark in the cognition that reflects upon the mark (liṅga-parāmarśa-jñāna), but there is no such thing for perception; therefore, perception is not inference. For this reason as well:
There is no consequence of perception being [classified as] inference, because [inference] is preceded by that; inference is preceded by perception, but perception is not preceded by inference.

And this is the distinction between the two: [inference arises] from the connection with the sense faculty. That cognition which does not arise from the connection of the sense faculty with the object to be inferred is called inference.
This very distinction, established by the means of valid cognition, is being rejected by one who attributes identity to perception and inference.
Thus [it is said].
215.12 [2-1-30] Nor is there perception of a single part [of the whole] because of the existence of the whole (avayavin).

215.13 Nor is there perception of a single part because of the existence of the whole; as for what you state: 215.14 "This tree is recognized through the apprehension of a single part," that is untenable, because the single part—

215.15 And perception [of the whole] is the perception of the composite (avayavin) associated with that [part]; for when one part is in contact with the sense organ, 215.16 the composite associated with it is not in contact.
Therefore, just as the part is perceived due to contact, so too the composite would have to be perceived due to contact. Why [is this not so]? Because of the composite—
215.18 Because it exists, this whole (*avayavin*) indeed exists as distinct from its parts; for that which occupies the place of the parts [is perceived].
215.19 Since it has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), its non-perception when only one part is perceived is untenable. For what reason?
215.20 Because the causes for the perception of largeness, multiple substances, color, and so forth, are present in the whole just as they are in the parts.

216.01 Therefore, it is illogical to say that while the parts exist, only a portion is perceived and not the possessor of the parts (*avayavin*). It is not [the case that] the perception of the whole is logical; why? Because an alternative is untenable. For this [whole], existing in its parts, must reside either in a single part in its entirety or by way of a portion. If it resides in a single part in its entirety...

The remaining parts would be rendered useless, for nothing at all is produced for the whole by those remaining parts. Furthermore, this whole, being composed of a single substance, would not be perceived; what is the reason? Because the state of possessing magnitude and multiple substances is the cause of perception. Moreover, its destruction would not follow from the [destruction of its] causes.

216.07 Because division of substance is impossible—for indeed, division is not possible for that which is one—and because magnitude is not logical for that which is being produced by a single [cause], since multiplicity of causes, magnitude, and accumulation are impossible; therefore, it does not exist in its entirety within a single [substance]. Nor does it exist in part, for there is no [part] distinct from its causes.
216.10 Other parts [of the whole] are possible; thus, when this one part is perceived, the whole possessing parts (avayavin) is being perceived.

216.11 It is not perceived in its entirety; this perception of a single part remains unceased. Now, 216.12 how could the whole possessing parts be perceived while it is being perceived, if it were entirely [present] within the parts being grasped?
216.13 It might be [conceived as] complete, yet it is not perceived as complete while its parts are being grasped, because of the consequence that the remaining parts would be redundant;

this has already been stated. Furthermore, there is no perception of all the parts simultaneously, because the middle and far parts are obstructed by the near part; therefore, there can be no alternative mode of perceiving the whole (*avayavin*).
Furthermore, the dilemma regarding the mode of subsistence does not arise, because the terms "whole" and "part" are inapplicable to a single entity.

It is not a valid question to ask whether the whole subsists by means of a part or by means of the whole itself; for the whole is neither a part nor the whole. Indeed, "the whole" refers to that which is one and without remainder.
216.19 “Designation” and “part” are designations for something [only] when there is multiplicity.

216.20 These two terms, “whole” and “part,” are untenable with respect to a single [entity]. How then [can they apply]? [They apply] to the parts as the whole [applies] to its members. 216.21 [This occurs] through the relationship of locus and located: the whole is the located, and the parts are the loci.

217.01 Thus [it is asked]: what is this logical consistency (*yukti*) of speech, that it does not function by way of a single part, nor does it function as a whole, and yet it functions? 217.02 That which is as it is, is designated as being as it is—this alone is the logical consistency of speech. The terms "whole" (*kṛtsna*) and "part" (*ekadeśa*) do not apply to the possessor of parts (*avayavin*), because the whole is a unity.

Thus it has been said. Therefore, [the statement that] "the whole exists in its parts" is merely a description of the relationship between the locus (āśraya) and the located (āśrita), and of their respective properties (dharma).
What, then, is this "subsistence" (vṛtti), characterized as the state of being a locus and a located for a single entity in multiple locations?
Furthermore, one who asserts that a single thing subsists in many places should not be questioned [on this point].

217.07 Why? Because of contradiction in both ways. One who asserts that "one [entity] exists in many places" must be questioned: does it exist in one part or by its entire self? Why? Because of contradiction in both cases. If that which exists in many places exists in each individual part by its entire self, then it is not one.

217.10 It follows that "the manifold exists in many places" means "the manifold exists in many places. And thus, in response to this inquiry, there is a contradiction regarding the locus (adhikaraṇa). 217.11 Now, if one asks how a single entity existing in many places does so—does it exist in each part by way of a single portion?
217.12 Even so, it follows that "the single does not exist in many places," and thus [the claim] that "the manifold exists in many places" is established.

217.13–14: And those parts which, being present there, each reside in the individual components—these are the "possessors of parts" (*avayavin*). This follows [from your position]: on one view, a single thing does not reside in many; rather, it is the many that reside in the many. 217.15: Or, if the meaning is that it resides in each [component] by way of complete presence (*parisamāpti*), then it does not reside in [the whole] as a single entity.

Nevertheless, the inquiry regarding the locus is resolved. Just as this object exists in many places simultaneously, so too does that very same object exist by way of being fully present in each individual [locus]; thus, in every respect, the inquiry regarding the locus is resolved, because such an inquiry sublates the [notion of a single] locus. This...

Indeed, when an inquiry is conducted, it subverts the subject under discussion; therefore, by virtue of being a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the nature of *dharma*, it does not exist [as a real entity]. This conceptual construction has no substratum anywhere; thus, it should not be subjected to further inquiry.
The same applies to all [qualities] that reside in multiple substances, such as number, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, generality (*sāmānya*), and so forth.

The fault of the contradiction regarding the locus of the inquiry must be stated: [if it is argued] that there is a distinction [of the whole] due to the distinction between its being perceived and not being perceived, as in the case of the parts (218.03);

if this is said, then just as there is a distinction between parts that are being perceived and those that are not being perceived (218.04), so too a distinction would necessarily follow for the whole which rests upon parts that are both perceived and unperceived; and from that...

218.05 There is no single composite whole, nor is there a distinction [between parts], because even when one [part] is seen, [the whole] is perceived; and even when one [part] is being grasped, 218.06 both perception and non-perception are observed, as in the case of Devadatta and others. Just as Devadatta and others 218.07 are perceived together with some things and not perceived together with others, yet he does not become distinct [or divided] by that much.

218.08. Likewise, there is no fault regarding the whole (*avayavin*) either, because it has been apprehended. Furthermore, as for what you have stated—that its apprehension occurs through the apprehension of one part, while its non-apprehension occurs through the non-apprehension of one part—this conceptual distinction is groundless, because the whole has indeed been apprehended. The whole is apprehended as co-present with those parts.
218.11 What is it that has not been perceived of this [whole], by virtue of which there could be a basis for the conceptual construction of its being perceived or not being perceived?
218.12 If it is argued that the middle part and the far part have not been perceived, we say no; for those two are not other than the whole (avayavin). 218.13 [Objection:
The whole is one thing, while the middle part and the far part are two other things. [Reply: Because they are other than the whole, [they would be distinct from] the whole.
The middle part and the far part are not perceived. What is the reason?

Because of the absence of a cause for perception. Just as there is a contact of the sense organ with the whole (avayavin) together with its near part, which serves as the basis for perception, such is not the case with the middle part and the far part; therefore, [they are not perceived] by means of the near part.

It is perceived together [with the whole], but not with the middle part or the far part; however, in the view that it is a collection of parts, there is in every way an absence of the cognition "tree. For how could a tree be either a collection of roots, trunk, branches, and foliage, or the attainment of those constituent members? In both cases, there is an absence of the cognition "tree."

218.20 Because there is an intervention by other parts [between the sense organ and the object], there is no perception of the whole; and perception through contact is also untenable. 219.01 This is because those things that possess contact are not perceived. For when that which possesses contact is not perceived, there can be no perception of the contact itself, such as in the cognition: "This is conjoined with that. This [cognition] occurs in association with the perception of a single part, as in the case of a tree—
Cognition is possible on the view that a distinct substance arises, but not in the case of a mere collection.
219.04 [2-1-33(32)] Because it is yet to be proven, there is doubt regarding the whole (avayavin).
219.05 Because it is yet to be proven, there is doubt regarding the whole: "Is a distinct substance produced from its causes?
219.06 This is what remains to be proven. But what is it that must be proven here? Is it non-distinctness, or rather, the existence of the whole?

219.07 If there is no mark (*liṅga*) for the whole (*avayavin*) because of disagreement regarding the subject (*dharmī*), then one who disagrees regarding the subject cannot obtain consent from anyone. Furthermore, there is no seed for disagreement regarding the subject, because of the absence of similarity; for without similarity, there can be no disagreement.
The seed exists. For what reason? Because "misapprehension" (*vipratipatti*) is a contrary apprehension.

And the cause of that [misapprehension] is the superimposition of a contrary property upon an object whose specific difference has not been understood, based on the perception of a common property. Furthermore, for one who does not accept the existence of a whole (*avayavin*), there can be no similarity anywhere in relation to a whole.

219.13 Nor is there the superimposition of properties contrary to that; therefore, there is no misconception. Now, if [the property] is non-distinct (*avyatireka*), 219.14 then that which is to be proven must be established; in that case, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) demonstrating this non-distinction must be stated. For there is no cognition whatsoever that is devoid of a means of valid cognition. This means of valid cognition is the fact that [the word] does not possess other objects as its constituent parts. 219.15–16 [The opponent says: It is not so. Why? Because it is not observed. 219.16 A separate entity (*arthāntara*) cannot be a constituent part (*avayava*), just as a cow is not a constituent part of a horse; and [yet] threads are the constituent parts of the cloth. Therefore, this [cloth] is not a separate entity from them. This much, for now, is a statement according to the literal text, yet it is devoid of a reason (*hetu-hīna*), for there is no reason provided here. But surely [it is supplied] by the application (*upanaya*)?

219.19 When a cause is being manifested, it possesses the state of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*); the threads are not something other than the cloth, because they are its constituent parts. 219.20 [Objection: No, because that would involve a contradiction. If they were something other than the cloth, the state of being a constituent part of the threads would not be established.
220.01 Why? Because it depends upon the whole (*avayavin*). A constituent part depends upon a whole, and there is no whole...

220.02 There is some basis for rejecting [the objection], because it is observed that [the term "parts"] applies to other things as well; otherwise, it would be contradictory. 220.03 It might be argued: "A part is observed to exist when there is a distinct object (arthāntara), but not when there is no distinct object," as in the case of threads [relative to a cloth].

220.04 If it is argued that there is no such over-extension because of the use of the genitive case and the qualifying term—as in "the parts of a cloth" [rather than "the cloth's parts"]—[we reply: the threads are indeed distinct objects from the jar. If you say this is due to the specific use of the genitive and the qualifier, [then consider] the parts of a cloth.

When this has been said, what is the consequence regarding jars and the like? Is it not the case that it was already stated here: "Because of contradiction"? No; for if there were no distinct entity [the whole], there would be no constituent part (*avayava*), nor would there be the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), nor would the thread be a constituent part of the thread.

Nor is the meaning of the genitive such that "the thread is a constituent part of the thread"; rather, the threads possess the status of being constituent parts by virtue of their production [of the whole].

220.08. [The argument] "neither positive concomitance nor negative concomitance" is not a valid reason because it is over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*); it is not something other than the cloth. 220.09. Furthermore, by taking the threads as the subject (*pakṣa*) and stating "because they are its parts," one asserts that the threads possess parts.
But this is contradictory, for it is not the case that "the threads are the parts of the threads."

220.11 Now, if the cloth (*paṭa*) is made the subject (*pakṣa*), even so, the reason (*hetu*) is misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*), because "being a part" (*avayavatva*) is a property of the threads. 220.12 Being a part is a property of the threads; it is not a property of the cloth. This is because the word "part" (*avayava*) 220.13 denotes a specific cause. There is a contradiction if there is no whole (*avayavin*). If [one accepts] a whole...

220.14 You do not admit another entity; for whose sake would the threads be the cause? Indeed, they are not the cause [of anything else]. 220.15 [If you say] "it produces itself," we have nothing at all that is to be produced by you. Those very threads—220.16 when situated in a particular configuration, receive the designation "cloth"; [otherwise], the threads do not receive the designation "cloth."
It has been stated that [these things] are denoted by the word "cloth" (*paṭa*); however, this is contradictory because a primary [referent] is impossible.

For there is no commonality whatsoever between threads that are not yet cloth and the cloth itself. And it has been stated that in the absence of such a commonality, there can be no seed for a false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*). Furthermore, as for what is said regarding the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*)—

220.20 Is this "abiding" (avasthāna) a distinct entity (artha-antara) or not? If it is a distinct entity, it must be stated what that is; if it is not so stated, then this statement—"abiding is a particular configuration" (saṃsthāna-viśeṣa)—is empty.
For us, however, a particular configuration is conjunction (saṃyoga), and that is a distinct entity.

221.02. No, because it is not accepted; for I do not establish conjunction as a distinct entity (arthāntara) on the grounds that it is the non-conjunction of other things. 221.03. One thing cannot be the conjunction of another, just as there is no conjunction between a cow and a horse. [Objection: Let there be conjunction between two fingers; therefore, it is not a distinct entity. [Reply: This has already been answered, for this has already been answered—what is there to say?

221.05 Thus, the conjunction [of the reason] with both the relevant meaning (arthāntara) and the irrelevant meaning (anarthāntara) is uncommon (asādhāraṇa), and it is also a part of the proposition (pratijñaikadeśa).

221.06 [Objection: Conjunction is not a different entity (arthāntara) because it possesses the nature of conjunction; and conjunction is a different entity because of its status as a qualifier (viśeṣaṇabhāva). 221.07 When it is said, "Bring the two substances that are conjoined," those two substances which one perceives as being in conjunction are distinguished from all others.

221.08. One brings [the substance] when it is conjoined, not because of the qualifier, since that would be established otherwise. As for what you have stated (221.09)—that "one brings the substance when conjoined"—because of its status as a qualifier, conjunction is a distinct entity (arthāntara). (221.10) That is possible otherwise; how [then] could there be proximity ending in resistance?

221.11 The conventional usage of "conjunction" (saṃyoga) occurs as long as substances approach until they become obstructed. 221.12 Regarding that obstruction, the conventional usage of "conjunction" is not a separate entity; thus, it is not accepted that there is a conjunction [as a distinct] entity. 221.13 Therefore, proximity and obstruction must be explained through the conjunction with what is already conjoined (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*), which consists in the minimal distance [between them].

221.14 Proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is the conjunction of substances possessing form and touch; resistance (*pratighāta*) is that which does not undergo conjunction. 221.15 Therefore, the meaning of proximity and resistance must be stated. And if conjunction were not a distinct entity, then fields, water, seeds, fire, fuel, and so forth would be situated everywhere.

221.17 In every case, those very same [causes] would perform the effects such as the sprout and its maturation; therefore, that which is required by them—221.18—that object is something else, and "conjunction" (saṃyoga) is merely a designation for it. The field, water, seed, fire, and fuel are always dependent upon one another for the production of effects such as the sprout and its maturation. 221.19 [They are not independent.]

221.20 Because of the absence of an [independent] commencement, like a staff and so forth; just as a plurality of causes such as a staff and so forth, depending on auxiliary conditions such as conjunction, 221.21 never produces an effect such as a jar or a cloth, so too is the seed and so forth.
221.22 Therefore, that too is dependent. As for what is said here by the opponent—that the production of an effect occurs without...

222.01. Therefore, it is "like sound, a magnet, and action. The meaning of this is as follows: just as sound, in initiating another sound, initiates it without conjunction; just as a magnet attracts iron without conjunction;
and just as action produces conjunction and disjunction without [conjunction].

222.04 [Objection: "In that way, through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or otherwise, the production of an effect will occur even without conjunction. 222.05 [Reply: No, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason (*hetu*). We do not say that there is a conjunction for the production of an effect; rather, we say that the field, water, seed, fire, and fuel are dependent [on one another]. And if some cause were independent, [it would produce its effect alone].

222.07 It would have to be productive at all times; thus the reason would be inconclusive. However, that cannot be established by anyone. When one sound initiates another sound, it does so in dependence upon proximity to a location in space delimited by its own cause, because sound is not all-pervasive. [This is] like a magnet.

222.10 Furthermore, even iron attracts [only] by depending on proximity to its own substrate; if it were independent [of such dependence], 222.11 it would attract [everything], and this iron would not remain stationary anywhere. Therefore, it is not independent. Action (*karman*) also, 222.12 through proximity to its own substrate, produces conjunction while depending on orientation (*abhimukhya*); action does not produce [conjunction] independently.

222.13 Regarding "in reverse order": if one were to produce a conjunction independently, then an action produced in Devadatta—who has no connection with Pāṇḍya or Mathurā—would produce a conjunction in Yajñadatta—who has no connection with Takṣaśilā. 222.14–15 But this is not the case; nor is it asserted that conjunction is the cause of everything, but rather...

If it is argued that [the definition] "it initiates [action] while depending [on something else]" contradicts the Sūtra— should you think that if it performs action while depending [on something], then the Sūtra of the Great Sage would be contradicted, namely: "Action is a single substance, devoid of qualities,
and the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction"— there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.

222.19 Because of a failure to understand the meaning, you have not grasped the meaning of the Sūtra; this is not the meaning of the Sūtra that action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction [and thus] does not depend on the substratum and so forth. Rather, 222.20 the meaning of the Sūtra is that it does not depend on any other subsequent cause that arises later, just as a substance, once produced, [does not depend on further causes for its existence].

Just as [an action] initiates later by depending on a final conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or just as a conjunction [depends on its causes], so too, when qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) are about to be produced, they depend on instrumental causes (*nimitta*) known as latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), effort (*prayatna*), and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Or, just as color and other qualities existing in their causes [depend on them] when the color and other qualities of the effect are about to be produced, [they depend on] the production of the substance (*dravya*).
223.04 They depend [on other factors] because they serve as the substratum (*ādhāra*) for that which is to be produced; that is, the substance (*dravya*) which is to be produced is their substratum.

223.05 But action (*karman*) does not depend on a subsequent cause; thus, the independence of action is stated in the treatise (*śāstra*). 223.06 It is not, however, the case that it does not depend even on its substratum and so forth. In the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there is dependence.

223.07 If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence [of the action being eternal], [we reply: if the meaning of "independence" is that the action does not depend on any other subsequent cause (nimitta), 223.08 then even so, the action would still be dependent when producing conjunction (saṃyoga).
223.09 This is because it depends upon disjunction (vibhāga); for indeed, an action does not produce conjunction without disjunction.

Therefore, it follows that action depends upon disjunction; and consequently, the same fault of contradicting the Sūtra remains. [Objection: This is not so, because of doubt. Is conjunction produced by an action that depends upon disjunction, or is the obstructer removed by disjunction? Thus there is doubt. We, however, say: disjunction...

223.13 Once produced, it effects the cessation of the prior conjunction. When the conjunction has ceased, because the obstacle to action has been removed, it produces [a new] conjunction. Just as gravity is a cause of action independent [of other factors], so it is taught in the treatise. And yet, when the conjunction between the stalk and the fruit has ceased due to their disjunction, [gravity acts].
223.16 Weight, having acquired its activity, performs the action of falling; likewise, karma [performs its action], so there is no fault.

223.17 Or, for example, conjunction, after the destruction of the conjunction with the substance that is the common effect, is the cause—without requiring anything else—in the commencement of another substance; thus, it does not commence a substance while depending on disjunction.

223.19 Likewise, action, when initiating conjunction, does not depend upon disjunction. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra. As for what was said—that action produces conjunction even without [a prior] conjunction—that too is not a contradiction, because it is not the case that conjunction exists [prior to the action] and yet action produces conjunction.
224.01 This is contradictory; for if there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*), this sentence does not remain meaningful [in its intended sense].
224.02 Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, by this [statement], motion, disjunction, and conjunction are negated.
Furthermore, it is contradictory to say that "action produces conjunction. Now, if you think [this is said] with reference to the views of others...

224.04 It has been stated that there is a refutation of conjunction, disjunction, and action; it was not by us that conjunction, disjunction, and actions were accepted. Even so, the contradiction remains: those conjunctions, disjunctions, and actions which are accepted in the doctrine of others—those [are what you have refuted].

224.07 How do you establish [these]? If by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can they be accepted by another? Or if without valid cognition, how do you establish them? For it is not logical that there be any establishment whatsoever without valid cognition. If you do not establish them in this way, then this [position] of the opponent’s side is contradicted.
224.10 Conjunction, disjunction, and motion are well-known [categories]. Now, you might think:

"Those conjunctions, disjunctions, and motions that are accepted by you do not exist; however, there is no negation of conjunctions, disjunctions, and motions themselves. How, then, is there the conventional usage of 'motion' when a rarefied substance arises in another location?"
224.13 That continuum which arises in different locations is designated as "motion" (gati).
224.14 When there is uninterrupted arising, it is designated as "conjunction" (saṃyoga); that is, when two things arise without an interval between them.
224.15 That uninterrupted arising is conjunction; from the reverse of conjunction comes disjunction (vibhāga). In this regard:

224.16 Thus it has been said by those who maintain that [the object] resides in the tree: "No, because there is a lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For there is no valid cognition for momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Furthermore, the cause for the cognitions of "with an interval" and "without an interval" must be stated. If you do not accept conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) as the alternative causes, then [you must explain] the cognition of "with an interval" and [the cognition of] "without an interval."

224.19 Thus, the cause for the distinction between cognitions must be stated; for no distinction among cognitions is observed without a distinction in their objective causes, as is the case with [the distinctions between] color-form and so forth. And this cognition that "it moves" regarding what is stationary, or "it is conjoined" regarding what is unconjoined, or "it is divided" regarding what is undivided—none of these would exist without a universal substrate (sārva-pradhāna).
224.22 None of these false cognitions occur without following the primary [object];
225.01 therefore, the primary must be stated, for a figurative [cognition] is not observed to exist without a primary, as in the case of a post and a person.
225.02 Just as when a post exists, there is the cognition "person" regarding the post, or when a person exists, [there is the cognition "post"] regarding the post.

225.03 [The opponent says: "It is the cognition of a person (*puruṣa-buddhi*). Furthermore, if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) were not a distinct entity (*artha-antara*), then for this cognition "the one with earrings" (*kuṇḍalin*), some cause—whether being affirmed or negated—would necessarily have to be accepted as a distinct cause. It could not have the earring as its cause, nor could it have Devadatta as its cause.

225.06 You do not establish another basis (nimitta), and without another basis, [the cognition] cannot arise in any way from Devadatta and the earring, which are established as distinct entities. 225.07 Therefore, one must necessarily admit another basis that is being affirmed or negated. 225.08 Consequently, the cognition "one who possesses earrings" (kuṇḍalin) must occur based on Devadatta and the earring as they are established in their respective states.
225.08 Therefore, another basis that is being affirmed or negated must necessarily be accepted.

225.09 If that which is being negated here is negated elsewhere, then the object (*viṣaya*) of what is being negated must be stated; therefore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) cannot be negated in any way. Furthermore, because it is the cause of the cognition "it is here," this cognition "it is here" does not occur without a relation (*sambandha*).

It occurs just as in the case of "jujube fruits in this bowl. This [cognition] is not caused by the jujube fruits alone, nor is it caused by the bowl alone; that which is its cause is conjunction (*saṃyoga*). If the cognition "here" were due to conjunction, then there would be no restriction [of its occurrence], provided that the cognition "here" arises from conjunction when [the objects] are absent.

In this case, the cognition "here" would not arise [from conjunction alone], just as when people see from afar that there are *tilaka* trees here in the forest and *kiṃśuka* trees here in the forest; for what causes the cognition "here" for those who do not perceive the intervening space? Indeed, conjunction is not the cause of the cognition "here," because both [the object and the intervening space] are the causes of the cognition "here."

225.18 There is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and non-perception of distinction (*vibhāgādarśana*). Among these, one is primary (*mukhyā*) and one is secondary (*bhāktī*). That which [arises] from conjunction is the cognition of reality (*tattva-buddhi*); that which arises from non-perception of distinction is the secondary one.
And this secondary [cognition] arises from the perception of a commonality with the primary; it does not negate the primary.
225.21 For a figurative cognition cannot arise through the total rejection of a primary [referent].
It is not tenable that all [cognitions] will be merely figurative, because it has been stated that they depend upon a primary referent. Furthermore, as for this which is said:
"A cognition of 'here' is observed even without conjunction, as in the case of 'there are tilaka trees here in the forest.'"
"There are *kiṃśuka* trees here in the forest. In this regard, it must be considered: is there no relationship (*sambandha*), or is there no conjunction (*saṃyoga*)?
We, however, say that there is no conjunction, but there is a relationship;
for the forest is indeed related to the *tilaka* trees and so forth. But what, then, is this thing called a "forest"?
226.05 This is not difficult to explain. It has already been stated that the number "plurality" (bahutva) possesses qualifiers, and this applies even when [the objects] are situated vertically.
226.06 When there is a cognition of conjunction (*saṃyukta-buddhi*) regarding two substances, why does the cognition of "here" (*iha-buddhi*) not arise with respect to those very same two substances?
226.07 Since it does not arise when that conjunction exists, what is the basis for this restriction? It is not due to a lack of understanding.

226.08 We say that the cognition "it is here" does not occur without a relation and without a cause; it is not, however, the case that the cognition "it is here" occurs only when there is conjunction. Nor is the cognition "it is here" produced by a conjunction that does not depend upon a subsequent substratum; therefore, it is not preceded by that [conjunction]. Furthermore, regarding this [objection] that [the cognition occurs] when no relation exists...

226.11 The cognition "there is an inherence of this substance here" would not occur; for example, as in the case of the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads. 226.12 Inherence is the cause of that cognition, but there is no inherence of inherence. 226.13 [Otherwise] the cognition "inherence is here" would not exist. To this it was said: what was said? It was said, "false"—
226.14 This is merely a cognition; furthermore, what commonality could there be between inherence and the substances that possess inherence?

226.15 That upon which that false cognition proceeds—namely, the non-perception of difference—is present in those things that possess inherence and in inherence itself; thus, a false cognition is appropriate.
226.16 Their difference is not perceived, and this [non-perception] exists in inherence as well; therefore, a false cognition is justified.

226.17 And because of the difference in the properties of sentences, there is no fixed rule. It is not the case that whatever property exists in one sentence exists also in another sentence. For example, in the three-word phrase "the king’s man goes," all three words possess their respective meanings. [Likewise,] "the state of water exists" [is a separate sentence].

226.20 It is not the case that, merely because of the commonality of the sentence, even in a single sentence all three words must necessarily possess distinct meanings. 227.01 What, then, is the meaning of this sentence? "The state of water comes into being" (udakasya bhāvo bhavati).
227.02 To the extent that it is said "water comes into being," to that same extent it is said "the state of water [comes into being]."
"It exists. In this way, other sentences such as "the existence of jujube fruits in a bowl" (227.04) are also [to be understood].
Just as when the state of being contained (*vṛtti*) is demonstrated, there arises a cognition regarding the jujube fruits which possess that state;
this is what is meant by the statement "the jujube fruits exist in the bowl. Likewise, here too, it is the inherence (*samavāya*) of one substance in another substance.

By saying this, it is stated that "substance exists in this substance. Therefore, without having understood the meaning of the sentence, the distinction is stated: "the inherence of this substance here [occurs] even in the absence of a cause.
Thus, it is established that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a distinct category (*artha-antara*). And in the case of its logical establishment, it is not a mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*).

227.09. "Specifically, those threads, being situated [as they are], become the cause for the cognition of a cloth. Others, however, explain this statement—"because it is not a part of another object"—as referring to the relationship between parts and the whole (*avayava-avayavi-bhāvāt*).
But how can this be obtained from them? For this meaning does not follow from the phrase "because it is not a part of another object."

227.12 Regarding this statement, it is heard [in the text] that "it is obtained by means of the application (upanaya)"; he says: because this application—227.13 "the parts are the threads, the whole is the cloth"—is made on the grounds of the relationship between part and whole (avayava-avayavitva), 227.14 the reason (hetu) is thereby obtained. True, it is obtained; however, it becomes contradictory (viruddha), for the threads are not parts of themselves.
And [it follows that] neither the whole nor the cloth is a part of itself, nor is it the whole. What is the reason?

Because the words "part" (*avayava*) and "whole" (*avayavin*) are relative terms; these two are relative terms, namely "part" and "whole. Furthermore, the application of relative terms does not occur through the rejection of either one of the two.

Therefore, this too is not the meaning of the Sūtra. Furthermore, the conventional usage of "part" (*pradeśa*) and "possessor of parts" (*pradeśin*) is observed even when there is no difference in substance, as in the expression "a part of space. This has already been answered; it has been stated that the meaning of "part" (*avayava*) is one thing and the meaning of "part" (*pradeśa*) is another. What is the meaning of "part"? It is a designation for a specific cause.
227.21. "Part" (*avayava*) is a designation for a substratum (*ādhāra*); it is not [the case that] a location (*pradeśa*) is pointed out in this [space], 228.01.
nor is space pointed out anywhere, and there is no cause whatsoever for space; therefore, 228.02.
the sense of "cause" is not the sense of "substratum. Thus, this term "location" (*pradeśa*) applied to space [refers to] a substance possessing locations...

228.03 It is to be understood through its generality (*sāmānya*). But what, then, is the generality of conjunction with a substance that possesses spatial parts? It is its non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*).

We shall explain this point further below. If it is argued [that the reason] is "because it consists of those parts" (228.05), then you might think that this is another reason which does not prove that the whole is not a distinct entity from its parts.

What is the meaning of "having those regions as its essence" (*tad-pradeśātmakatva*)? It means that the threads are not something other than the cloth, because they are the objects designated as its regions.

Those things which are designated as the regions of something constitute its essence, just as the regions of space [are its essence]. And since the threads are designated as the regions of the cloth, therefore [they are not different from it].
"The threads are of the nature of the cloth"—this statement, taken according to its literal sense, is as before devoid of a logical reason (hetu).

Since neither a distinct entity nor a non-distinct entity is observed to possess the nature of being that specific location (tad-pradeśa), the term "location" (pradeśa) is inconclusive (asādhāraṇa). Furthermore, because it is a synonym for "cause," the designation of being that specific location is contradictory (viruddha) with respect to the threads.
[The reason] is unestablished due to a lack of connection. Furthermore, this example—that "it is a portion of space"—is also unestablished.
How so? When one says "a portion of space," it refers to the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) of conjunction;
however, space itself is not merely the non-pervasive occurrence of conjunction. Therefore, the example is unestablished [as being distinct] from other substances.
228.15 Because no other substance is produced, the whole is not something other than its parts; indeed, it is not [produced] from other substances.

228.16 A distinct substance being produced is never observed, and a person is certainly not produced from cows, elephants, and horses, whereas a cloth is produced from threads; therefore, since that [cloth] is not a different entity from them, this [argument] also suffers from the same deficiency of reason as the previous one.

When manifested by the application [of the reason], the cause is "origination from them. This too is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) with respect to the exclusion of both the distinct entity and the non-distinct entity; for, while origination from a distinct entity such as yarns (*turī*) is observed in the case of a distinct entity such as a cloth, it is contradictory when the cloth is made the subject (*pakṣa*), because it would imply an unrelated object: "the cloth does not originate from the cloth."

228.21 Therefore, by that word "from" (*ataḥ*), the threads are connected [to the cloth], such that "the cloth arises from the threads. Even so, 229.01 it is contradictory [to say] that the thread does not arise from the threads, nor is the whole (*avayavin*) other than the parts (*avayava*).
229.02 Because there is no difference between the whole and its parts—since those which are wholes do not exist as entities distinct from their parts, those [parts] are the whole.
229.03 Just as the wheels and so forth are intermediate parts of a chariot, they [the threads] would be intermediate parts of another whole distinct from the cloth.
229.04 If the threads were also distinct entities from the cloth, then they too, being separate from the cloth, would be intermediate parts of yet another whole;
however, they are not intermediate parts of another whole separate from it. Therefore, it is not [the case].

229.06. If [the reason] means "something else," then in that mere statement there is the fault of the reason being deficient and the fault of it being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). 229.07. As for the reason: because there is no other constituent part apart from those [threads], the statement "the threads are not the constituents of the threads" is contradictory (*viruddha*).

229.08. Furthermore, because a distinct entity (*artha-antara*) has been rejected, the claim that "the constituent part is the possessor of parts" would not be possible. As for this which is also said: "those which..."

229.09. Parts are distinct entities from the whole; apart from that [whole], they would be parts belonging to something else. 229.10. For example, like wheels and so forth. This is not so, because both positions lead to contradiction. By stating that "wheels and so forth are parts," one accepts them as being distinct entities. Or, if this is not accepted, what is the meaning of this statement?

229.12 “The wheel and so forth are the parts of the chariot. Those things which are accepted as being the parts of the chariot, such as the wheel and so forth, 229.13—since they are the negation of being separate entities, they are neither the parts of the chariot nor the parts of anything else; thus, the domain of the terms ‘part’ and ‘whole’ is cut off. 229.14 Therefore, this [argument] is not a valid reason, for there is no whole other than the parts.

229.15–17. Because it is delimited by the location of the production of another substance, that which is admitted by both parties as being a distinct entity is seen to arise in a different location, such as a cow [arising] from a horse; however, a cloth does not arise in a location distinct from its threads. Therefore, it is not a distinct entity from them. In this case as well—
229.18 The deficiency of the reason (*hetu-nyūna-tā*) and its lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇa-tā*) are as stated before; thus, "because it arises in that location" is not a valid reason.
229.19 [The argument] "the thread arises in the location of the thread" is contradictory, or else it is a denial of arising because it entails the negation of the cloth.
229.20 If the cloth does not arise from the threads, what is the meaning of the word "arising"? It is none.
229.21 "The thread arises, not the cloth"—this is because of the exclusion of the locus of arising; such is the meaning of the word 'arising' (utpatti).

230.01 It must be stated [thus]. And when that [arising] is examined, it expresses a birth (*janman*) that is unprecedented (*apūrva*), through the distinction of properties such as manifestation (*vyakti*) and so forth;

thus, it is contradictory. There is no whole (*avayavin*) other than the parts (*avayava*), nor is there another whole distinct from its own constituent parts, nor is there any object distinct from those parts.

230.03 Because of its existence. Here, that which is the whole (*avayavin*) of various parts (*avayava*) must be a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) from those other parts; for example, a jar (*ghaṭa*) is a distinct entity from its constituent parts such as the wheel and so forth.
It is called a "jar" because it exists as the whole of the various parts distinct from the wheel and other components, and not otherwise.

230.06 [Objection: A cloth is the whole (avayavin) consisting of parts other than the threads.
