Furthermore, regarding the claim that "it is not conjoined with its own cause," this must be considered: is it not conjoined with its own cause because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*), or is it because it is not a [separate] entity?
235.06 “Because it is not a separate entity. But we say: because it is a quality (*guṇa*), it is not a separate entity; and a quality is [as follows]:

235.07 the coiling of a snake is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and that has been established as being a separate entity (*arthāntara*). Furthermore, if it were a separate entity, it would be contradicted by observation. In your view, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are mutually... [incomplete]
235.09. They are distinct entities, and there is neither conjunction nor non-attainment between them; thus, there is no conjunction nor non-attainment between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*. 235.10.

[The claim that] there is neither conjunction nor non-attainment for both because they are all-pervading (*vyāpaka*) is contradictory. There is no whole (*avayavin*) other than its parts, because no effect of a different weight is perceived. As for the statement "because no effect of a different weight is perceived," this is not established in any way whatsoever.

235.12 Where is the whole not connected with its parts? And where is there no perception of the effect of a different weight? 235.13 Because the effect of a different weight is not perceived, there would be neither the effect of a different weight, nor weight, nor a difference in weight;
nor is there a whole, because water is excluded from the water-pot, or because the potsherds are excluded.
235.15 It is logical. However, some [hold that] by the statement "because another effect of gravity is not perceived," he prohibits the initiation of another quality (guṇa).
235.16 This is because the prohibition of the initiation of another gravity is intended merely as an illustration. How so?
235.17 Because it would follow that the effect would possess a form and other qualities preceded by the form and other qualities of its cause, just like another gravity. If...

Even if the color and other qualities residing in the cause were to initiate the color and other qualities of the effect, then the heavinesses residing in the cause would also initiate another heaviness in the effect; and consequently, like that other heaviness, the effect would be perceived [as possessing weight], yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, the effect does not possess color and other qualities preceded by the color and other qualities of the cause.
235.21 “It is an effect. This property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been established; however, because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*), it proves nothing.

235.22 How so? Having accepted that [the world] is an effect, the nature of form and so forth are denied as being effects; yet, by virtue of having accepted it as an effect, 236.01 what was to be denied becomes admitted, namely, that the nature of the cause and so forth is the nature of the effect.
236.02 For one who says that [things] do not begin because they lack a cause, the effect would be devoid of qualities; however, this is not seen to be devoid of qualities.

236.03 Therefore, due to this contradiction, this is not a valid reason (*ahetu*). Furthermore, if the effect does not exist at all, then the statement "the effect possesses color and so forth preceded by the color and so forth of the cause" is meaningless; for when there is no water-jar (*kamaṇḍalu*), it is not the case that there is no water.
236.05. It was rightly said that [the example] is a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). By this, the apprehension of color and so forth in the effect has been refuted.
236.06. As for this reason—that it would entail the consequence of possessing another gravity (*gurutva*)—this too is not anything at all, because it is accepted [by us].
Indeed, the very acceptance [of the consequence] is pointed out as a fault. If, then, there were another gravity...

And because it is an effect-substance like other forms and so forth, an effect of another gravity would be perceived, just as there is an effect of another form and so forth; yet no such effect is perceived. For we do not observe a difference in effect between two things when they are connected on a scale, even though two separate lumps have been placed there, in the same way that we observe a difference in effect when they are separated. Therefore, [the gravity] remains the same whether they are joined or separated.

236.11 Nor is there the production of a separate substance. However, some, having proposed the thesis that "the scale possesses an effect-substance [due to weight]," state the reason "because there is no specific sinking. This [reason] is misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*), because the absence of specific sinking is not a property of the scale. It is not [a valid reason].

236.14 Indeed, we consider it logical that the property of a scale (*tulā-dharma*) is the absence of a specific downward bending (*avanamana-viśeṣa-abhāva*). Because it does not serve as the substratum for a specific downward bending, a scale does not possess an effect-substance (*kārya-dravya*), unlike other heavy objects.
236.15–16 First of all, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the state of not being the substratum for a specific downward bending does not reside in a non-scale.

Likewise, this non-perception [of weight] is also an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), because it is observed that when substances possessing weight are in conjunction, there is no production of a specific degree of downward bending (*avanamana-viśeṣa*). For example, when a substance possessing weight is being weighed, even though particles of dust (*truṭi*) possessing weight have fallen into it, if they possess great weight [the scale does not bend further].
And when it is being opened, it does not produce a specific degree of downward bending for those things endowed with only a certain weight.

If it is argued that there would be the consequence of [the result] being equal, less, or more—namely, if the weight of the effect were equal to the weights of the causes, then as long as it is unconnected by two *vipalas*, it would be so; but when it is connected, it would be twice that amount. Or else...

237.02 If the heaviness of the effect were greater than the heaviness of the cause, then it would follow that [the weight] is excessive. Alternatively, if the heaviness of the effect were less than the heaviness of the cause, then a difference [in weight] would be perceived; however, this is not the case. Therefore, there is no heaviness of the effect, because the exact measure of the heaviness of the effect and the cause has not been determined—if indeed this were determined.

It might be said that "this much is the heaviness of the cause" and "this much is the heaviness of the effect. This is indeed fit to be stated; however, the consequence is that the effect would be equal to, greater than, or less than [the cause]. But that has not been determined—namely, that "this much is the heaviness in the cause" and "this much is the heaviness in the effect"—if the heaviness of the cause and the effect has not been ascertained.
237.08 This cognition— “two palas,” “five palas”— which arises when a substance is being weighed by a scale,

[237.09] neither obtains nor does not obtain [its object], because it determines the weight of a collection of substances. As for this which you consider to be "two palas" or "five palas," here the weights of the cause and the effect are not being determined.

237.11 However, from the final [atom] down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), a collection of substances (*dravya-samāhāra*) is measured; in that regard, it is not appropriate for a human being to say, "the weight of the cause is this much" or "the weight of the effect is this much. 237.12 Nor is the collection the cause; rather, the final substance, in which no further effect has been initiated, is the cause.
However, regarding those who maintain that [certain things] begin by initiating [others], this is said:

"The subsequent effect-substance does not exist in the same location as its cause, because it is corporeal, like a jar and so forth. As for the remaining investigation into the nature of origination (*ārambhaka*), it is not refuted here because it is irrelevant to the present topic. Therefore, [the opponent's position] is without inferential support.

237.17 If the heaviness of the effect were like [the heaviness] of another substance, then when there is an accumulation of substance, no difference in the effect would be perceived. 237.18 How is this to be understood? Who says that the heaviness of the effect is not perceived?
237.19 If it is perceived, what is that falling? For there is no falling of the effect without the heaviness of the effect.

237.20 There is another cause; therefore, the effect [is not heavy], just as in the case of other weights. By this, it is refuted that there is no heaviness of the effect because no difference [in weight] is perceived during the depression of the scale. Now, if you think that the effect is caused to fall by the very weights of its causes and that there is no heaviness of the effect itself, then the falling of the effect must have another cause.
238.03 Therefore, it is not established that the effect [is weight] like another weight. Because of the lack of conjunction between cause and effect:

238.04 where weight is the cause of falling in a different substrate, there conjunction serves as the auxiliary factor, 238.05 as in the case of the conjunction with a substance possessing weight, such as the scale-pan; but this is not the case for the effect—
238.06. Because the two causes are inseparable (*ayuta-siddha*), their conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is impossible; for conjunction is the existence of that which is unconnected. 238.07.
Furthermore, an effect does not exist unconnected to its cause; rather, it is born and becomes connected at one and the same time. 238.08.
Therefore, the cause and the effect are not conjoined, and thus gravity cannot cause [the effect] to fall by means of inherence (*samavāya*).

238.09. If [you argue that it does not fall] because [the cause] is not mentioned and because of contradiction; or if you think: "It is true that there is no conjunction between cause and effect, but there is inherence (*samavāya*), and inherence, depending upon gravity, will cause the effect to fall"—this is not established, for the gravity of the effect is not mentioned, nor is there inherence.
238.12 It has been mentioned by the author of the Sūtras in some places as being a cause of action, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for instance, [it is stated]:
"And from impulsion, impact, and conjunction-with-the-conjoined, there is motion in the earth. 238.13 This is not merely because it has not been mentioned;
238.14 furthermore, it is due to contradiction: if inherence (*samavāya*) were the cause of action, then even the form and other qualities of the cause would [be so].

If it is argued that [the qualities] such as color (rūpa) and so forth should fall because they are inherent in the same object as the effect, then let them fall; what is the harm to us? If this is said, we reply: no, because it would follow that gravity (gurutva) also falls. Just as color and so forth follow the effect-substance, so too would gravity follow it. And if gravity were to follow, one must explain from where it falls; but it does not.

238.18 There exists another heaviness (*gurutva*) which is the cause of the falling of [the first] heaviness; therefore, it is not the case that heaviness falls, nor do color-form (*rūpa*) and the other qualities fall. 238.19 If color-form and the others did not fall, they would remain while the substance (*dravya*) falls; thus, color-form and the others would be non-substantial (*adravya*), and a substance devoid of color-form would be perceived. Alternatively, if they fall as the substance falls—

238.21 Those possessing activity attain form and so forth; yet, if they neither remain nor fall, this is a contradiction of reason (yukti-virodha) that you must necessarily accept. 238.22 "They move, they fall, or they remain"—if you say this, the opponent replies: "I know the distinction between what is logical and what is illogical. [The opponent says: "It is logical. 239.01 "I know the various causes for these," says the other. It is logical.
239.02. It is argued that what is measured is untenable, and what is unmeasured is likewise untenable. Then this [notion] that "it falls," "they fall," or "they stand" is also untenable;
for it has been stated that this would entail a second gravity in gravity, and because no substance devoid of color-form (*rūpa*) and the like is ever perceived.
Furthermore, because color-form and the like are never perceived as being without substance (*adravya*). And as for that which falls or moves...

239.05 Or, one abandons what has been attained and attains what has not been attained; however, it is not the case that form and so forth abandon what has been attained. 239.06 Nor is it logical to say that form and so forth attain what has not been attained, or that they do not attain what has not been attained. 239.07 When there is attainment between two substances, form is also attained; since there is no doubt [regarding this], what is this?
239.08 It is doubted whether [the non-perception] has acquisition as its condition and acquisition as its cause, or rather non-acquisition as its cause and non-perception as its cause.

239.09 We, however, say that it has non-acquisition as its cause and non-perception as its cause. For one does not perceive the non-acquisition of two substances when those two forms have already been acquired; and if you think the same applies to substances as well—then consider this: 239.10 [If you think] even so for substances... if you should think thus.

"Just as for two visible forms, the condition of non-perception is caused by non-attainment (*aprāpti*), so too for two substances, [non-perception] will be caused by non-attainment and not by attainment (*prāpti*). This is not a fault, because the duality of conditions has multiple causes; indeed, a duality of conditions is never observed to have a single cause.
For example, although there is no actual anger or fear in images depicted in a painting, cognitions of someone being angry or afraid still arise;

yet, for that reason alone, cognitions of someone being angry or afraid ought not to manifest even when there is an absence of anger or fear in real persons. In this way, this condition of attainment (*prāpti-pratyaya*) is in some cases caused by conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

In some cases, it is observed that [gravity] does not reach [the ground]; therefore, it is established that gravity does not fall, nor do form and the other [sensory objects] fall. Others, however, maintain that the gravity of the cause is obstructed by the gravity of the effect;
for they say that the gravities of the causes are indeed obstructed by the gravities of the effects, and thus there is no downward motion.

239.20 There is no distinction [between them], yet we see that this is not tenable. Why? Because of the observation of their falling (pāta-darśanāt). If the cause were to remain stationary while the effect falls, then we might accept it;
however, the weight of the cause is not obstructed by the weight of the effect, and this is not the case. Therefore—

240.03 That is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that [the cause] lacks a substratum. Furthermore, if the heaviness of the cause were obstructed by the heaviness of the effect, then when the effect falls, the cause would not fall;
thus, the effect would be without a substratum. By this same reasoning, the destruction of the heaviness of the cause by the heaviness of the effect is also refuted.

[The reason] has been explained. Furthermore, there would be no falling of separated [causes]; this is the additional [point]. If the heaviness of the cause were destroyed by the heaviness of the effect, then because of the destruction of the causal substance, there would be no falling of the separated causes, and indeed there would be no heaviness at all, if the effect—

240.09 Even if heaviness were destroyed due to the heaviness of its cause, nevertheless, there would be no heaviness anywhere at all. For there is no past effect belonging to any atom; therefore, atoms would be weightless.
And since heaviness is absent in the atoms, from what could the heaviness of the effect arise? Therefore, [your objection] is not a valid refutation.
240.12 This [argument] holds that the heavinesses of the causes are subject to destruction and obstruction by the heavinesses of the effects.
240.13 Therefore, the previous refutation remains valid because it is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since there is no ascertainment of the heaviness of cause and effect.
240.14 And thus, this is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the non-existence and non-distinctness of the whole (*avayavin*).

240.15 Because it is something to be proved (*sādhya*), there is doubt regarding the whole (*avayavin*); this is incorrect. And because it is something to be proved, it is not logical to say there is doubt regarding the whole.

240.16 It is not reasonable to claim there is doubt because of its being a *sādhya*, for it has never been stated anywhere that being a *sādhya* is a cause for doubt. Therefore, doubt does not arise from the fact of being a *sādhya*. Who [would say such a thing]?
240.18 He says this: "Because it is yet to be proven (sādhya), there is doubt; moreover, because it is yet to be proven, there is disagreement (vipratipatti). From disagreement [arises] doubt.

240.19 Regarding the statement "because it is yet to be proven": having superimposed the state of being yet to be proven upon the disagreement, which is the effect of that state of being yet to be proven, 240.20 it was stated: "Because it is yet to be proven, there is doubt regarding the whole (avayavin)."

241.01 [2-1-34(32)] "The non-apprehension of the whole [would follow] because the composite object is unestablished. (NS 2.1.34) "The non-apprehension of the whole" is a sūtra intended to dispel doubt.
Regarding "because the composite object is unestablished": it would follow that there is no apprehension of any objects whatsoever, if the composite object were not established.

241.04 There is no intermediate entity distinct from the parts. How so? First of all, it has been stated that atoms do not become objects of perception because they are beyond the senses (atīndriya). Furthermore, you do not admit the existence of composite substances (avayavi-dravya). And if such a substance is not accepted, then this cognition of a substance as "a jar" and this cognition of its qualities—how could they arise?

241.07 “Dark” is a cognition of action; “moves” is a cognition of generality (*sāmānya*); “exists” is a cognition of particularity (*viśeṣa*); 241.08 “pot” is a cognition of inherence (*samavāya*); and “color and so forth are here in the jar” [is a cognition of relation].
241.09 Likewise, there are other cognitions as well: “one,” “large,” “conjoined,” “separated,” “distinct,” “remote,” and “proximate.”
241.10 And thus [the parts] would not exist; yet there is the apprehension of everything—the manifold of substances, qualities, actions, and so forth.
241.11 Because we perceive the apprehension of everything, we see that there exists a whole (avayavin) distinct from its parts.
241.12 Alternatively, "non-apprehension of everything" means non-apprehension by all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); how could this be [the case] for perception?

Because it has as its object something present and large; for that which is both present and large is the object of external sensory perception, such as a jar (ghaṭa). Furthermore, if composite wholes (avayavin) are denied, there would be no object of external sensory perception, because such a thing [the whole] would not exist.
Consequently, inference and the other means of knowledge would also be non-existent. Yet this cessation of all means of valid cognition occurs while objects are nonetheless perceived.

241.16 Because it is apprehended by all the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and the rest, we see that the whole (avayavin) exists. This [sūtra] is intended to demonstrate the contradiction that arises if one does not accept the existence of the whole; this contradiction, in all its forms, is 241.17–18 the annihilation of the cognitions observed in the world.
241.19 [2-1-35(33)] And because of the possibility of supporting and attracting.
241.20 And because of the possibility of supporting and attracting; the meaning is that the "whole" (*avayavin*) is a distinct entity. What is this?
242.01 Supporting (*dhāraṇa*) means that when there is a concomitance with the grasping of one part, there is the reaching of another location by the whole.

242.02. Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the prevention [of movement]. When one perceives a single part of a whole (*avayavin*), one perceives the whole together with that perception of the single part; the prevention of that whole from reaching another location by means of that perception is retention. Attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) is the perception of a single part—

242.05. Given their coexistence, how is it that the whole (*avayavin*) reaches another location as before? This is known from common experience (*lokataḥ*). 242.06. Indeed, people in the world employ [the terms] "holding" and "pulling" in this manner. How do these two—holding and pulling—establish the whole? Because they are not observed in either that which is partless (*niravayava*) or in a mere part (*avayava*). It is not so.
242.08 For it is observed that holding and pulling occur both in the case of a partless [whole] and in the case of a part; and it is observed that holding and pulling occur [in the latter].

242.09 Therefore, these two are properties of the whole (*avayavin*). As for what was said here—that holding and pulling are caused by cohesion (*saṃgraha*) and not caused by the whole—[that is incorrect], because they are absent in cases such as a heap of dust, whereas they are present in grass, stones, wood, and so forth, when bound together with lac (*jatu*).
"And because [holding and pulling] are observed in things that are held together"—this is not so, because it is not determinative. We do not say that [these properties] exist in every case;

rather, holding and pulling occur in the case of a composite whole (*avayavin*), but they do not occur elsewhere. Nor is there a contradiction, because these are observed only in composites, such as grass, stones, and wood when they are held together by lac.

242.14 They are attracted and they are held; thus these [properties] belong only to the whole (*avayavin*). And if attraction and holding were to occur in both the partless [atom] and the part [the whole], there would be a contradiction. As for this which is said—that they are produced by cohesion (*saṃgraha*)—it is not so, because there is no specific cause [to distinguish them]. Holding and attraction are produced by cohesion.

242.17 “It is not due to the action of a composite whole (avayavin),” [you say]. Furthermore, you do not state a specific reason (viśeṣa-hetu). 242.18 And it must be explained why there is no cohesion (saṃgraha) in things such as a heap of dust. Whatever is your reason for the absence of cohesion here, that very same reason applies to the holding and pulling of an existing composite whole. 242.19–20. Thus, since the reason is the same, the absence of cohesion in a heap of dust and the like does not prove the non-existence of the composite whole. Therefore, this [argument] is not a valid refutation of the composite whole. 242.20–21. Moreover, if the composite whole did not exist, then the atoms would be separated from one another; consequently, they would not be perceived by the senses, because they would lack the quality of being an object of sensory perception (bāhyatva). 242.21–22. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then when a cloth is burned, only its constituent parts—the threads—would remain. But this is not observed. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.22–23. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then since atoms are supersensible (atīndriya), the objects of the senses would be unperceivable. But they are indeed perceived. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.23–24. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then since atoms are partless, there could be no distinction between the front and back of an object, nor could there be any increase or decrease in size. But these distinctions are observed. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.24–25. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then since atoms are eternal, all objects would be eternal. But they are seen to be non-eternal. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.25–26. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then since atoms are minute, large objects such as mountains and the earth would not be perceivable. But they are indeed perceivable. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.26–27. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then since atoms are partless, there could be no conjunction (saṃyoga) or disjunction (vibhāga) among them. But these are observed. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.27–28. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then since atoms are supersensible, the objects of the senses would be unperceivable. But they are indeed perceived. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.28–29. Furthermore, if the composite whole did not exist, then since atoms are partless, there could be no distinction between the front and back of an object, nor could there be any increase or decrease in size. But these distinctions are observed. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 242.29–243.01. But these are observed. Therefore, the composite whole exists. 243.03–04. "Non-existence"—what, then, is this that has been stated? It is that specific relation belonging to what is perceived in one part [of a whole] and which is concomitant with it. Furthermore, that [relation] does not exist in things such as a heap of dust;
therefore, there is no holding or pulling in those cases. Thus, this is a reason characterized by negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*). Now, at this point—

243.02 Intending to present the application of a positive (anvayin) reason, he says this: "Now, one who rejects the whole (avayavin), fearing lest there be a loss of perception, asserts that a collection of atoms is the object of vision. What is he to be questioned about? He is to be questioned regarding the object of the cognition of unity: "This cognition, 'this is one'..."

243.05–243.07: Is this [cognition] "this is a substance" one that has multiple objects or one that has a single object? If it has multiple objects, it is untenable because such a cognition is not observed in regard to many things; nor is it logical for there to be a single cognition "this is one" with respect to many things. If, on the other hand, it has a single object, then that which is the object of this unitary cognition is the whole (*avayavin*).
243.08 Cognitions of one and many have distinct objects because they possess specific characteristics, like cognitions of objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
243.09 Alternatively, cognitions of one and many have distinct objects because their objects are either aggregated or non-aggregated,
just as [one says] "this" and "this and this."
243.11 [2-1-36(34)] If it is argued that the perception is like that of an army or a forest, we say no, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.

243.12 If it is argued that the perception is like that of an army or a forest—if you think that even in the absence of a distinct object, and in the absence of a distinction between one and many, a specific cognition is observed; for the cognition of an "army" is one thing, and the cognitions of individual "elephants" are another.

243.14–15: [The opponent argues: "There are cognitions of individual *khadira* trees and so forth, and there is also a cognition of a 'forest' which is distinct from them; therefore, the army and the forest are not non-different entities. 243.15–16: To that extent, this sūtra is irrelevant to the side of the proof (*sādhana-pakṣa*), because it serves merely as an example and is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, it is not a valid reason. 243.16: Furthermore, this sūtra is disconnected [from the argument], as its purpose is merely illustrative. It is inconclusive.

243.17 However, in the case where [the forest] is considered an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is not unestablished; for by what means could there be no difference in meaning between an army and a forest? 243.18 It is accepted that armies and forests are indeed distinct entities, as has already been stated. Furthermore, because a cognition of non-difference can have multiple causes, it is not logical [to claim it proves identity]; this cognition of non-difference exists precisely as one directed toward a non-distinct [whole].
244.01 And since, when a difference is perceived, no difference is seen [in the underlying unity], there is first the cognition of identity in that which is non-different.
244.02 That which is established as one through the consensus of both parties—that being "one," the cognition of it as "many" would not exist.
244.03 For the synthesis of "one" is unimpeded; thus, even when the "many" is perceived, there is no perception of difference.

244.04–06. Due to the non-perception [of difference], there arises the cognition of non-difference; this is because of the cause of being at a distance from the perception of difference, as in the case of an army, a forest, and so forth.

Those parts of the army or the forest, such as elephants and the like, which are perceived individually as distinct, do not manifest their difference due to the cause of being at a distance; and when difference is not perceived...

244.07 A non-differentiated cognition regarding differentiated objects is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for anyone; why? 244.08 Because atoms (*aṇu*) are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

It has been established that atoms are beyond the reach of the senses. Furthermore, any object that is perceptible by the senses possesses a perceived distinctness; when its distinctness is not grasped from a distance, it becomes the cause for the cognition of non-difference. This is just as, among things of a perceived genus, the genus is not grasped from a distance.

Furthermore, for those things whose movement is being perceived, there is no perception of that movement from a distance. This is because the non-perception of a thing currently being perceived must have another cause; and this non-perception of a perceptible object is seen to have another cause, as in the case of the individual components of an army or a forest, whereas atoms [are not so perceived].
They are not perceived because they are beyond the senses; therefore, their non-perception is not due to any other cause.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction for one who holds that atoms—which do not possess produced particularities (*viśeṣa*)—are not the causes of distinct cognitions, yet [asserts] that atoms become the causes of cognitions such as "jar" and so forth. He should be asked: do the atoms produce [particularities]?
Do the *viśeṣas* (particularities) produce a distinction in cognition, or do they not produce a particularity? What follows from this?

If they have produced a particularity, then it follows that whatever that particularity is, it is the whole (*avayavin*). On the other hand, if they have not produced a particularity, then those very [atoms] would be both beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and perceptible by the senses (*aindriyaka*), which is a great contradiction. This is the *viśeṣa*.

245.01. When there is mutual proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of atoms, they will be perceived as having conjunction as their accessory (*saṃyoga-upakaraṇa*). 245.02. However, because atoms are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), conjunction cannot be perceptible. For [perception occurs] when one thinks, "This is conjoined with that. Therefore, conjunction is not a distinct entity (*viśeṣa*).
245.04 And this cognition of unity with respect to what is manifold is a false cognition, and it has a false cognition as its cause.
245.05 [The cause is] the perception of a commonality and the non-perception of particulars; however, because atoms are beyond the senses, there is no perception of a commonality among them.
In the absence of that, how could there be a non-perception of particulars? If there were a perception of a commonality, [there would be a perception of particulars].

245.07 Or, when there is no perception [of the object], there can be no superimposition of qualities contrary to it. Nor is it logical for a conceptual cognition (*naimittaka-mithyā-pratyaya*) to arise in the absence of a cause (*nimitta*). By this, metaphorical (*bhākta*) and analogical (*aupamika*) cognitions are also explained. "Metaphorical" (*bhakti*) refers to [the attribution of] a quality to that which does not possess it.
245.10 There is a similarity with those things that come into being; it is called "participation" (*bhakti*) because it is shared by both, as in the case of the Vāhīka.

245.11 Taking up a faint internal cognition, one says "the Vāhīka is an ox," but this is not so because atoms are beyond the senses. 245.12 Furthermore, even the cognition based on analogy (*upamāna*) is not tenable, for [the Vāhīka] does not possess the nature of that [ox], whereas those [oxen] do.

245.13 Because of a lack of commonality (*asāmānya*), for that which is not such [as the object] but possesses a commonality with things that are to become so, the cognition of analogy (*upamāna-pratyaya*) is appropriate there; as in "the boy is a lion," where he is like a lion. 245.15 But what is it that is being compared here? It is valor (*saurya*), and not the atoms (*paramāṇu*), because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*); [otherwise, the comparison would be] false.

"There is a cause for these cognitions"—this is false, because these are also erroneous cognitions due to the absence of a primal substance (*pradhāna*). If it is argued that the cognition of non-difference regarding the objects of other sense faculties is the primal substance, then you must consider this:
if you think that the cognitions of "one" and so forth regarding the objects of the ear and other senses constitute the primal substance, then in its absence [those cognitions would not exist].

245.19 However, because there is no specific reason [to distinguish them], the examples remain unsettled as being "false cognitions. This being the case, 245.20 the employment of an example does not establish itself; for there is the cognition "that" with respect to what is not that, and the cognition "that" with respect to what is not that. And yet, this cognition "that" exists with respect to atoms when they are accumulated. And that...

246.02–246.04. Is it that one doubts whether "that" exists in what is not "that," or rather that it does not? Regarding sounds and so forth, there is a single cognition; regarding jars and so forth, there is a single cognition [of their parts]. One who asserts that the single cognition [of sounds] is a primary [cognition] while the single cognition [of jars] is a false cognition must nonetheless accept jars and the like; for if jars and the like were not accepted, there would be no basis for the single cognition that serves as the seed for the universal of sound and so forth.
246.06–246.07: [The opponent claims: "Because of their similarity with aggregated atoms (*paramāṇu*), sound is the cause for the arising of a single cognition.

To this, it was said: "No, because atoms are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, those things such as sound which you accept as the causes for the primary cognition are themselves indeed aggregated.

246.09 Because they are aggregates (*sañcita*), this single cognition (*eka-pratyaya*) is not tenable even with respect to them; and as for the single cognition regarding sound and so forth [246.10], it is metaphorical (*bhākta*), caused by the exclusion of a collection (*samuccaya-nivṛtti-nimitta*), because of their oneness (*ekatva*) as a substance-universal (*dravya-sāmānya*). Those substances which possess oneness—[246.11] the exclusion of a collection is a property (*dharma*) of those substances—and such a collection exists in the case of sound and so forth.

246.12 Because of that [exclusion], due to the commonality of a substance possessing unity, the cognition of "one" regarding sound and so forth is figurative (*bhākta*). 246.13 If it is argued that in all cases this is caused solely by the exclusion of a collection (*samuccaya*), [we reply: no; for in the case of "two," there would be doubt regarding the cognitions of one or many.
246.14 It would not be so; if this cognition of "one" everywhere were to arise solely from the cause of the exclusion of a collection.

Regarding the statement "not two," there might be a doubt as to whether it means "one" or "many," because the negation of "two" is common to both. However, when such a doubt exists, the term "one" is used for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*); that which is the object of restriction is "oneness. Just as the cognitions of "three" and so forth have "threeness" and so forth as their objects, so too do the cognitions of "two" and so forth [have duality and so forth as their objects].

246.18 The [cognitions] regarding sound and so forth should be seen as having "conjunction" (samuccaya) as their cause; why? Because of the commonality with substances possessing duality and so forth.
246.19 The conjunction of sound and so forth with a substance possessing duality and so forth is the same; because there is conjunction everywhere.

246.20 If it is argued that this is indeed so, [we reply: no, for in the case of the cognition of "one," if there were a movement toward a universal (sāmānya), there would be no doubt regarding the understanding of that universal.
246.21 Because they are based on a collection (*samuccaya*), there are notions such as "two" and so forth, but not for a single [unit]. [This is] in response to the negation [of the notion of one].

247.01 Regarding "two," "three," and so on, if there were a general cognition (*sāmānyamati*) regarding the general [category], there would be no doubt. Therefore, since your determination [is as follows]: 247.02 "Duality and so forth"—for one who does not admit unity and duality and so forth, [the notion of two] does not exist.

247.03 [Objection: It is not the cessation of a collection, for there is no collection for one who does not admit unity. Of what [duality] is there a negation for one who does not admit duality? Furthermore, for one who does not admit that unity, duality, and so forth are distinct entities, there would be no cognition of "one hundred is one" or "two is one," because of the non-apprehension of difference.
247.06 There is a single cognition regarding sound and the other [sensory objects], because no difference is perceived among sound and the rest as they are being apprehended.
247.07 Therefore, there is a cognition of non-difference regarding them; however, this is not the cause for the apprehension of non-difference in atoms.
247.08 It has been stated that this is because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses, and because the inquiry into the single cognition was intended merely as an illustration.

247.09 One who maintains that the cognition of a whole (*avayavin*) is not a distinct object (*artha-antara*) from its parts should be questioned regarding the cognition of multiple [parts] just as he is regarding the cognition of one.

For him, just as the cognition of one is untenable, so too do the cognitions of many fail to obtain. And just as with the cognitions of one and many, he should be questioned regarding the cognitions of jars and other such things.
247.12 Thus [it is said]. In this manner, one may also interrogate regarding the notions of dimension, conjunction, motion, and specific universals.

247.13 And in their case, there is the following consequence: if you do not admit the composite whole (*avayavin*) as a distinct entity, then the notions "large," 247.14 "conjoined," or "the horse moves" would not be possible; for these do not apply to supersensible things.

247.15 These notions are applicable to atoms. 247.16 Is it that these notions—such as "one" and so forth—apply to a mere collection of atoms, or do they apply to something that exists as a distinct entity? When such a doubt arises, 247.17 a specific reason must be stated. This specific reason is: because [the notion of "one"] is in grammatical apposition with the notion of "large."

247.18–247.20: That which is indeed observed as a single cognition that has a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with "the great" (*mahat*) is endowed with that property (*tad-dharma-yukta*). For example, in the case of "the blue lotus," the cognition of the blue lotus proceeds as being connected to both properties; and there exists a single cognition that has a common substratum with "the great."
247.21 Therefore, the cognition of "large" arises from a single [object]. If it is argued that this is merely the perception of a pre-eminent collection of atoms (aṇu-samūha), [we reply:

248.01 Now, if you think that we do not admit a composite whole (avayavin) as a distinct entity, but rather that the cognition of "large" occurs for one who perceives a pre-eminence in a particular collection of atoms compared to another collection of atoms—this [is our position]. 248.02 [That is to say,] this very [cognition of "large"]...

248.03. Therefore, the notion that "this is that" where it is not [that] leads to the same consequence as before. Furthermore, regarding those atoms which are not large, and in the aggregates of atoms which are not large, this notion of "large" is a false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*) in the sense that "this is that" where it is not [that].
248.04–05. And since a false cognition does not occur without a primary cause (*pradhāna*), the same consequence follows as before. [The opponent argues: "An atom..."
248.06 If it is argued that the Pradhāna is established because of the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) that "the sound is great," and if you think:
248.07 "The notions of 'great' and 'minute' observed with respect to sound—such as 'the sound is great' or 'the sound is minute'—are the Pradhāna elsewhere [than sound]," [we reply:

no, because the notions of "great" and "minute" do not consist in the apprehension of intensity (*manda-tīvratā*), since there is no determination of magnitude (*iyattā*) in the case of sound. 248.08 [Therefore,] it is not [the Pradhāna].

248.09. [Objection: Greatness (mahattva) is not [the cause of the cognition], because [sound] is a quality (guṇatvāt); in that case, the cognition of "small" or "great" would not apply to sound. [Reply: It does not fail to apply. Why? Because it has another cause. What is that cause? It is dullness (mandatā) and intensity (tīvratā). Why?
Because there is no determination of its magnitude (iyattā-anavadhāraṇāt). For one does not determine [it] by thinking, "This sound is great."

One determines [the size] as "this much. Just as when one determines the sizes of a *kuvala*, an *āmalaka*, and a *vilva* fruit—one perceives the *āmalaka* as larger than the *kuvala*, and the *vilva* as larger than the *āmalaka*—one delimits them by their specific measure, thinking, "This has such a magnitude. However, that [measure] does not exist in the case of words; even in the case of words, it is not so.

Having perceived a sound previously determined, one determines from that sound whether it is "large" or "small. This determination is not being denied; rather, this is what is being considered: regarding this cognition of smallness or largeness in sound, does it arise from a connection with [actual] dimension (*parimāṇa*), or from some other cause? It is from some other cause.

This is logical, because no connection of one quality with another quality is perceived. Indeed, no connection of one quality with another quality is observed, such that a connection with dimension (*parimāṇa*) could also be inferred from the cognition of "large" (*mahat*).
If it is argued that sound possesses qualities just like a substance, we say no; for this cognition of "large" occurs only in respect to substances.
[Sound] exists because it is conjoined with the dimension of magnitude (*mahat-parimāṇa*). Furthermore, this cognition of "large" occurs even with respect to sound.
Therefore, because it is the object of the cognition of "large," sound is conjoined with the dimension of magnitude. [This is not so], because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For even when something is the object of the cognition of "large," its conjunction with the dimension of magnitude is not observed [in all such cases].
249.03 "Just as [one says] 'it has large dimension' (*mahat-parimāṇa*). Well then, how is there the cognition of "large" (*mahat*) with respect to a substance?

If you do not admit that it possesses large dimension even while being the object of the cognition of "large," 249.04–249.05 then how can it be said that "the substance is conjoined with large dimension"? It is not so, because it is the object of the cognition of "large."

A substance is that which is endowed with the dimension of greatness (*mahat-parimāṇa*). However, when there is a conjunction with the dimension of greatness, the cognition "it is great" arises with respect to the substance. Furthermore, the conjunction of the dimension of greatness in a substance occurs because specific cognitions are not accidental; for if specific cognitions were not accidental, [the dimension of greatness would follow].

249.09. The application of measurement applies to substance as it does to sound; there is a cognition of "greatness" regarding sound, and for that reason also, [it is not] 249.10. without cause. And who says that this [cognition] regarding sound is without cause?
What is its cause? 249.11. It has dullness and intensity as its cause; dullness and intensity are properties of sound, therefore [the cognition arises].

249.12. "The cognition of smallness and greatness occurs with respect to sound. But what is this dullness and intensity? 249.13. Dullness is the state of being an object of a general cognition due to the generality of a small substance; and intensity is the state of being an object of a general cognition due to the generality of a large substance, which is [also termed] sharpness. Regarding the term "conjoined," there is duality—

249.15 The apprehension of the whole (*avayavin*) is established by its having a common substratum (*samānāśraya*) with its acquisition (*prāpti*). How so? Because [the notions] of conjunction (*saṃyukta*) and magnitude (*mahat*) have a single object, due to their being synthesized (*pratisandhāna*), like the cognition of a blue lotus and so forth. And just as the two cognitions—“it is blue” and “it is a lotus”—which are being synthesized have a single object, so too [is the case here].

Furthermore, there is a synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) such as "the two are conjoined" and "they are large"; from that synthesis, it follows that they have a single object. By this, the cognitions "one [tree] moves," "the large [forest moves]," and "the *khadira* tree [moves]" are explained. If you argue that [the cognition of movement] depends on two aggregates (*samudāya*), then you must consider that it relies upon two aggregates.

If it is argued that the notions of "conjoined" and "large" arise [from atoms], and likewise that the notions of "one," "many," and "large" also depend upon a single collection (*samudāya*), this is not so, because the conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are untenable. Are the notions of being conjoined, large, and so forth dependent upon a collection? What is this "collection"? Is it the many constituent members themselves, or is it the attainment (*prāpti*) of the many?

250.03 If it is argued that the "collection" (*samudāya*) is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of many [parts], then there would be the cognition: "the two acquisitions have been acquired. 250.04 For what reason? Because the collection is accepted as being the acquisition itself. [If so,] there would not be the cognition: "these two things are conjoined," because the collection, in its acquisition of another collection, becomes a single entity; thus, [there is no separate] acquisition.

The cognition [of "two"] would not occur because the aggregate is a single entity. Alternatively, if the aggregate were the multiple constituent parts, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) based on duality; that is, the coreferential cognition "these two things are conjoined" would not occur. Therefore, [the number] "two" resides in a substance (*dravya*) which serves as the substratum for duality and is large in magnitude.

250.09 [The opponent says: "It is the locus of conjunction. If it is argued that "conjunction exists," it has already been stated here how conjunction is not a distinct entity (arthāntara). 250.10 Furthermore, this proponent of the collection of parts (avayavasamudāyavādin) must be questioned: regarding this cognition [arising] from a cow, a horse, or a person, which is caused by a universal (jāti), where does that [universal] reside? For the universal does not exist at all; how then [could it exist]?
250.12 [The opponent argues: "There will be a cognition based on a universal (jāti). [The response: The persistence of the cognition [is] due to a specific universal (jāti-viśeṣa).

250.13 The non-rejection of the gender-mark (liṅga) is not the cause for the persistence of the cognition in the absence of a specific universal. 250.14 There exists [such a cognition], and a cognition cannot possibly remain without a cause; and yet this [cognition] does exist.

There is a recurring cognition, "these are earrings," and there is also an exclusionary cognition, "these are not earrings. Therefore, a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) cannot be designated by such a cognition because it would have a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Furthermore, since [the universal] is not manifested [therein], the mention of a substratum is [unjustified]; nor is this specific universal one that has a different substratum.

The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) must necessarily be stated [in the sense that] "it is manifested"; the locus is the state of being situated (*anu-samavasthāna*). Now, if you think that atoms themselves, existing in such-and-such a state of arrangement, manifest this or that genus, and therefore a composite whole (*avayavin*) is not established—regarding that point:

251.01 It has been stated that inherence (*samavasthāna*) is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is a distinct entity (*artha-antara*). And as for this inherence, which you believe manifests a particularity of the genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*): does it manifest it by reaching [the object] with the eye, or without reaching it?
251.02–03 If you say it manifests it by reaching it, then because the middle part and the far part are not reached, there would be no manifestation of them.

251.04 If it is argued that when [the parts] have reached their state of conjunction, the specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*) is manifested, [but] because the middle and the other parts are obstructed by the near part, there is no manifestation due to non-reach (*aprāpti*), and manifestation occurs only as far as there is reach—[we reply: no, because that much [reach] does not constitute the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). Or, if you think that as far as [the object] is reached by the eye...

251.07 When the inherence (samavasthāna) is attained, the manifestation of the universal (jāti-vyakti) occurs to that same extent; thus, the substratum (adhikaraṇa) of the universal is attained. This being so, this aggregate which is perceived as "this is a tree" undergoes differentiation.
What is the reason? [Because] the differentiation of that tree is attained.

To whatever extent a birth is manifested, it follows that each of those is a tree; consequently, a single tree would be perceived as many, and thus there would be no single cognition [of "tree"]. Furthermore, since the proximal part is not a tree, "treeness" would not exist anywhere. Therefore, one must state that the object of the cognition of "tree" is the aggregate.
Because it is the cause for the manifestation of a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*), the whole (*avayavin*) is a distinct entity (*artha-antara*).
Thus: that which has aggregated atoms as its locus is "that which has aggregated atoms as its locus" (*samudita-aṇu-sthāna*);
and being both "having aggregated atoms as its locus" and a "distinct entity," it possesses the quality of being the cause for the manifestation of a specific universal.

251.16–251.18: It is not established that atoms [exist] as such, for one who does not accept a composite whole (*avayavin*) as a distinct entity must state the meaning of the word "atom" (*paramāṇu*). This is because the word "atom" denotes the ultimate limit of minuteness. Indeed, if neither the large nor the minute exists, it is not logical to apply the qualification "atom."

251.19 When there is a connection with the excellence of dimension (*parimāṇa-prakarṣa*), the qualification "atom" (*paramāṇu*) is meaningful; in its absence, it is meaningless. 251.20 Thus, this connection with the excellence of dimension is established only when a whole (*avayavin*) exists.
252.01 According to the view of some, an atom is the most subtle aggregate (*saṃghāta*) of the qualities of existence (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), and darkness (*tamas*).
We see that this is not tenable because it involves a contradiction; for the claim that "it is the most inferior [of all] and yet a composite" is contradictory.
Indeed, a composite cannot exist without that which is being composed, just as threads are not something other than the cloth [they compose].
This is because they are its cause, like the shuttle and other such tools; for it is observed that the shuttle and so forth are causes of the cloth that are distinct entities.
And thus, the threads are a different entity from that [cloth], because of a difference in capacity, like poison and an antidote;

because they are the objects of distinct cognitions, like color and touch; the colors and touches of the threads and the cloth have different causes because they possess specific qualities, like color and touch; some, however, formulate the reason as "because of having different forms" with respect to the atom.
[They] object: "Even in a single atom, a difference in form is observed, such as red or black," and so forth.

To this, one should respond as follows: This [objection] is not valid because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason (*hetu*). We do not say that the whole (*avayavin*) is different from its parts (*avayava*) because their forms are distinct; rather, we mean that the forms of the threads and the cloth have different causes.
Having thus formulated the position, we state the reason: "because it possesses specific qualities. And so, this is not a refutation.
However, since this discussion would expand into a vast array of texts, we desist; perception has been examined through its successive stages.
252.14 Now, inference (*anumāna*), which has reached its proper occasion, is examined. What is this inference?

252.15 It was stated that "inference is preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam*). Here, the examples [of the types] beginning with *pūrvavat* are: the swelling of a river, the movement of ant eggs, and the cry of a peacock. [These are] examples of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
The Sūtra on the Door.
252.18 [2-1-37(35)] Because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to obstruction, impairment, and similarity, inference (*anumāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). 252.19–20.
"Because of deviation due to obstruction, impairment, and similarity, inference is not a valid means of knowledge"—this is the point therein.

252.21 Obstruction (*rodha*) is the cause of the prevention of fluidity; injury (*upaghāta*) is the affliction caused by ants' nests. 253.01 Similarity (*sādṛśya*) [is not a valid ground for inference] because of the deviation found in the case of the sound of a peacock and the sound of a man, which share the same status as producers of a similar cognition. 253.02 "Inference is not a means of valid knowledge" (*anumānam apramāṇam*). The rest is in the *Bhāṣya*. As for the claim that inference is not a means of valid knowledge...

253.03 What has been stated is incorrect, because there is a contradiction between the two terms of the proposition (*pratijñā*). 253.04 "Inference" (*anumāna*) is the name for that which establishes supersensuous objects (*atīndriya-artha*). 253.05 "Invalidity" (*apramāṇa*) is its negation. This is a contradiction between the two terms of the proposition; it is the non-perception of identity between that which is admitted and that which is negated. 253.06 [This constitutes] the proposition.

253.06. Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the two reasons, because [the inference] "inference is not a valid means of knowledge" contradicts [its own] proposition (pratijñā), is undermined (upaghāta), and resembles [a fallacious reason].
253.07. "Because it is deviant" is the reason; that which is deviant is not a valid means of knowledge.
253.08. Just as, for instance, the possession of horns is [used] to establish the existence of a cow—this very reason contradicts the proposition, [and thus] the proposition...

253.09 And [the phrase] "and the reason" (*hetu*). Furthermore, regarding this statement that "inference is not a means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*), does it mean that inference in its entirety is not a means of valid cognition, or only a specific type of inference? What follows from this? If the position is that inference in its entirety is not a means of valid cognition, then because the reason (*hetu*) exists only in one part [of the subject], it lacks pervasiveness (*avyāpakatva*). [If the reason were] complete...

253.12 Inference is what is under consideration; there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in every inference. For it is not possible for that which establishes the invalidity of deviation itself to be non-deviant. Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whatsoever for [establishing] non-deviation in the face of deviation; thus, because it is not pervasive, it is not a valid reason. Now, as for that which is deviant...

253.15 You say that this is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it is a qualification of the thesis; therefore, another reason (*hetu*) must be formulated. 253.16 Furthermore, this is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*): that which is erring (*vyabhicārin*) is not a valid means of knowledge. As for those examples which are stated by you to be erring, there is indeed error even in them.
253.18. This sūtra serves as a means for pointing out the fallacy of the unestablished (asiddha) by asserting that [the reason] does not exist.

253.19 [2-1-38(36)] It is not [the case that the inference is invalid] because of partiality, fear, or similarity, since there is a difference in meaning. 253.20 Regarding the statement that "there is a flood in the river even from an obstruction," one does not [infer] a connection with a region where it has rained above merely by means of the river's flood. 253.21 [This is because] the flood could also arise from an obstruction.

A river is established [as being full] either by a specific flood or because of its non-deviation from that; however, it is unestablished due to damage [to the bank]. Furthermore, there is deviation in the mere movement of ants' eggs, but not in a specific movement.
What, then, is this specific [movement]? It is the movement of many undisturbed ants across many locations.

254.04. That upward movement caused by a large number of ants forming a swarm is invariably concomitant with future rain. 254.05. Nor is there any deviation regarding sound, because it is not mere sound that constitutes the inference; [as in the case of] a peacock— 254.06.
for it is not the presence of a peacock that is being proved here, but rather [the presence of] a bird based on the specific quality residing in the sound.
The word "anuṣaṅga" and so forth is inferred as being qualified by a peacock; thus, there is indeed deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [Objection:
It is unestablished (*asiddha*) as a reason because it does not exist. [Response: It has been stated that inference has the three times as its object because it grasps the three times.
Regarding this, some say that time itself does not exist; but that is not so, because there is no lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
254.10 For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the non-existence of time. [Objection: But surely non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) establishes the non-existence of time.
[Response: It does not establish it, because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This non-apprehension has three possible causes;
therefore, by means of non-apprehension, one might infer a deficiency in the causal conditions (*kāraṇa-vaikalya*), but not that the object itself is simply non-existent. This is precisely the point.

254.13 Why? Now, if this is the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*)—that there is "non-apprehension" because of the non-existence of that which is being apprehended—then likewise, 254.14 the reason (*hetu*) does not exist, because it is already implied by the meaning of the proposition; for the reason is implied by the meaning of the proposition.
254.15 [Objection: No. Furthermore, a property (*dharma*) cannot exist when its substratum (*dharmin*) is absent, due to the lack of a locus. Or, if...

Furthermore, even the property (*dharma*) does not serve as a means of proof, for we do not observe that which is non-existent serving as a means of proof regarding priority and posteriority (*parāpara*). Moreover, since the cognitions of priority, posteriority, and so forth possess a cause, the negation of time is not logical;
and he who does not accept time must state the cause for those cognitions of priority, posteriority, and so forth. [He cannot say: "It is not."
254.19 For, even when the cause (*nimitta*) does not exist, we observe conditions (*pratyaya*) that possess specific temporal characteristics and are themselves caused by that [cause].

254.20 [This is] like the conditions for form (*rūpa*) and so forth. If it is argued that because time is a single unity, a distinction between conditions is untenable—[that is,] if you think that since time is one, a distinction between conditions such as "prior" (*para*) and "posterior" (*apara*) is not logical, as it would not be distinct [from them]...

255.02 [The opponent argues: "A cause produces distinct effects; therefore, it is not dependent [on other factors]. 255.03 [The response: "It is like the distinction in cognitions regarding a father and so forth. Just as, with respect to a single person who remains undivided yet conforms to various distinctions of relationship, there arise cognitions such as "he is a father," "he is a son," and "he is a brother"—in that same way, time is one, yet [it appears as such] through the specific distinctions of cause and effect.
255.05 "Time is the cause of relative notions such as 'prior' and 'posterior. Thus has time been established.
255.06 The following sutra is intended to refute that established [existence of] present time.
255.07 [2-1-39(37)] There is no present [time] for that which is falling, because of the occurrence of the times of having fallen and about to fall.

255.08 There is no present [time] for that which is falling, because of the occurrence of the times of having fallen and about to fall. For a fruit that has detached from its stalk and is approaching the ground—that which is above the fruit, taking it as the limit, up to the stalk—[is the time of having fallen].
255.09 For a fruit that has detached from its stalk and is approaching the ground—that which is above the fruit, taking it as the limit, up to the stalk—[is the time of having fallen].
255.10 Thus, he has fallen from the path, having made that which is below it—the limit defined as "the earth"—his destination.
255.11 He must have fallen from a path; there is no third path now existing where he could fall.
255.12 And apart from a path, there is no cause for the manifestation of time; therefore, present time exists.
255.13 By saying "it does not exist," one contradicts both the present time and the two times [past and future] that have been accepted.
255.14 This sūtra is for the purpose of making this point clear.
255.15 [2-1-40(38)] There is also the non-existence of those two, because they are dependent upon the present.

255.16 There is also the non-existence of those two, because they are dependent upon the present; the other two times are dependent upon the present. 255.17 For one for whom the present does not exist, if the present is not accepted, then [the existence] of those two times which were accepted [is untenable].

"The non-existence of the two times [past and future]. Nor is this time manifested by the path; rather, it is manifested by action (*kriyā*). When one perceives the connection between a substance and an action—such as "it falls"—this time, characterized by that connection, is called "present. It is "past" when the connection with the action has passed away. But when...
255.21 When the causal factors for an action are present before one and their power is unimpeded, then that action will come to be.
256.01 "Action" refers to the future time. And if this [agent] does not perceive the present action, why does he perceive the past and the future? It is not time [that perceives].

256.03 The past [cause] does not have a past fruit, because time is always present and the fruit likewise exists in the present. 256.04 [The expressions] "has fallen," "is falling," and "will fall" function as adverbs qualifying the action; since they are objects of the verbal suffixes (*pratyaya*), they relate to the action (not the fruit).
256.05 Thus, the possibility [of temporal designation] resides in the action and not in the fruit; it is the action that serves as the cause for manifesting time, not the path to be traversed.

256.06–256.08: Because of its remaining in that same state, that destination which is to be traversed remains exactly as it was when action had not yet arisen; likewise, the result remains exactly as it was when action had already arisen. Since there is no difference [between the two states], the temporal path (adhvan) cannot be the cause for the manifestation of time.
Now, you might think: even if the present time is not admitted, the past and the future exist in mutual dependence upon one another.
256.09 This sūtra is intended for the purpose of refuting that [position].

256.10 [2-1-41(39)] There is no establishment of the past and the future through mutual dependence. 256.11 "There is no establishment of the past and the future through mutual dependence" means that the past and the future are not established as mutually dependent. How so? In the absence of the present, what is the past, and how [is it established]?

"Or" (*vā*)—what is it that is future? And "how"? It cannot be said; this is undeclared (*avyākaraṇīya*). [The term] "present" (*vartamāna*) is used because there is an elision (*lopa*). Furthermore, because of the specific prohibition: since this prohibition—"for one who is falling, the time of having fallen and the time yet to fall are possible"—is accepted as referring to the present, and not to the present...

If time is not admitted, there is no meaning for the word "of one falling," and if the meaning of this word is not admitted, it is not proper to say "of one falling. This is a contradiction: [the object] exists and yet does not exist; and while there is the usage "of one falling," nothing is established through mutual dependence.

256.19 Because, in the absence of one, there is the absence of the other, and thus the absence of both. If establishment were through mutual dependence, 256.20 then as long as the one does not exist, the other does not exist; thus, there would be the non-existence of both. Furthermore, the present time is manifested by the existence of an object, as in [the expressions] "the quality exists" and "the action exists," for whom this [time] belongs.
256.22 There is none for him.
257.01 [2-1-42(40)] If the present does not exist, there would be no apprehension of anything at all, because direct perception (pratyakṣa) would be impossible.
257.02 If the present does not exist, there would be no apprehension of anything at all, because direct perception would be impossible. How is it that the meaning of the Sūtra is not contradicted?
257.03 Furthermore, why is direct perception impossible if the present does not exist? Because this direct perception has the present as its basis.

"Because it is an effect, like milk. Whatever is an effect is observed to have a present substratum, as is the case with milk. And since perception is an effect, it must therefore have a present substratum. [However,] because the present time is not admitted, perception would result in being without a substratum; and since there is no effect that is without a substratum, [the status of] perception— 257.04 ...because it is an effect, like milk. Whatever is an effect is observed to have a present substratum, just as milk is. 257.05 Perception is an effect, and therefore it has a present substratum. 257.06 Since the present time is not accepted, perception results in being without a substratum. And since there is no effect that is without a substratum, perception—

257.07 There would be the impossibility [of perception] because of the impossibility of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and from the impossibility of direct perception, there would be the abolition of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And when all means of valid cognition are abolished, 257.08 there would be no apprehension of anything. Yet there is the apprehension of everything; we observe this from the apprehension of everything.
257.09 There exists the present cause of direct perception, the object of direct perception, and direct perception itself; such is this [case].
The present time, being thus established, is divided into two kinds:

in some cases it is manifested by mere action (*kriyāmātra*), and in other cases it is manifested by a continuum of action (*kriyāsantāna*). That which is manifested by mere action exists as "substance" (*dravya*), while that which is manifested by a continuum of action is, for example, "he cooks" or "he cuts"; such is the continuum of action.

Furthermore, [action] is twofold: that which has a single form of activity and that which has various forms of activity. That which has a single form of activity is, for example, "he cuts. For in that case, the action of repeatedly raising and lowering [the axe] until it falls has a single form.
And that which has various forms of activity is, for example, "he cooks. For in that case, there are many actions and many [phases].

257.16 The constituent forms (*ākāra*) are as follows: the bringing of fuel, the kindling of the fire, placing the pot upon it, pouring in the water, 257.17 cooking the rice, stirring with a ladle, skimming off the scum from below, and removing [the pot] from the heat. Such a continuum of actions (257.18) is designated by the single word "cooks" (*pacati*); for here, there is an uninterrupted continuity of the series of actions.
257.19 When there is the intention to express that there is no beginning of diversity and no cessation, it is [the state of] the non-beginning of the continuum (santāna).

257.20 When there is the intention to express cessation, one says "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*) or "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*). And as for this which is being cut or being cooked, 257.21 that is "being done" (*kriyamāṇa*); while that is not being done, [it is not so].
258.01 [2-1-43(41)] But because of the possibility of both "having been done" and "to be done," there is apprehension in both ways.
258.02 But because of the possibility of both "having been done" and "to be done," there is apprehension in both ways. Of what present thing? How?
258.03 In both ways: as something isolated and disconnected from the past and future, and as something conjoined with those two.
258.04 Thus [it is asked]: "But how can there be a substance for one who is liberated? For in this case, that which is solitary and pure is designated as "present," as in "he cooks" or "he cuts.
How is it here that some actions are past, some are future, and one is present? And another [says]:

258.07 In the world, when there is a desire to express an object starting from its proximity, there is a single mode of usage for that which is present. Sometimes one uses the present tense for the past; being already arrived, one says, "I am coming here. Sometimes one uses it for the future; being already standing still, one says, "I am going here."
"I am going. In this way, it should be inferred in other applications as well.

258.11 Now, analogy (*upamāna*), which has reached its proper occasion, is examined. What, then, is analogy? It was stated that it is "the means of establishing the probandum through similarity to what is well-known"; this is the objection to that [definition].
258.13 [2-1-44(42)] Because of similarity that is absolute, partial, or occasional, analogy is not established.
258.14 [2-1-45(43)] Since analogy is established through well-known similarity, the aforementioned defects do not apply.
258.15 "Because of similarity that is absolute, partial, or occasional, analogy is not established"—this is not because of absolute similarity.

258.16 An analogy occurs when it is said, "As is a cow, so is a cow," because of their abundant common characteristics. 258.17 But an analogy is not established by [mere] similarity; for it is not the case that "As is a cow, so is a buffalo.
258.18 Nor does it occur through partial similarity, as in "As is Mount Meru, so is a mustard seed. No.
258.19 And since there is no other means of knowledge [than these], analogy is not established.

[Objection: Because of the prohibition of analogy based on absolute or partial similarity, there is no prohibition of analogy [in general]. [Response: That analogy which is based on absolute, majority, or partial similarity is what is prohibited by that sūtra; it is not a prohibition of analogy as such.

This being the case, if it is not so, the nature of that analogy must be stated otherwise. Or, if you think that there is no such thing as the nature of an analogy, then how can this statement—"Analogy is not established because of similarity in its entirety, for the most part, or in a single respect"—be maintained? For one who does not accept analogy must speak in this manner [regarding its nature].

259.05. "Analogy is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it does not bring about the comprehension of an object. [Response: This is not a refutation, because analogy has as its cause both well-known similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). This refutation which you have made—that analogy is not established due to extreme similarity and so forth—is untenable, because that is not what we accept. Who...?

259.08. Indeed, he said this: "Comparison is not [based] on absolute similarity and so forth; rather, comparison is based on well-known similarity. 259.09. Relying upon the relationship between the probandum and the probans, there is thus no refutation because of its non-existence in every respect.
259.10. Furthermore, comparison is established even through absolute similarity; by that very action, that action is compared.
259.11 As in the case of "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa" or "like that between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. Furthermore, there is also comparison by way of greater similarity (bhūyas-sādharmya).
259.12 When there is a desire to know the strength of a cow, then there is comparison by way of greater similarity:
259.13 "As is a buffalo, so is a cow. There is also [comparison] by way of partial similarity (ekadeśa-sādharmya) when...

It serves as the cause for the desire to know existence-in-general (*sanmātra*), just as one might wonder what the nature of the existence of Mount Meru is, [thinking] "as it is with a mustard seed, so it is with Meru"; therefore, this is not a negation. Let it then be an analogy (*upamāna*);
[but it is actually] inference (*anumāna*).
259.17 [2-1-46(44)] The establishment of the imperceptible by means of the perceptible.
259.18 [2-1-47(45)] We do not see the purpose of comparison as a means of valid cognition when the gavaya is imperceptible.

259.20 [2-1-48(46)] Because of the conclusion with the word "thus" (*tathā*), there is no lack of distinction in the establishment of analogy (*upamāna*). Just as by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) the nature of fire—which is not perceived—is inferred from the perceived property of smoke, such as its upward movement; so too, by means of the perceived cow, the unperceived gavaya [is known].

260.03. [The claim that] "comprehension" [is the result] because it establishes an object not perceived by the senses means that analogy is inference; this is not so, because of a lack of understanding. 260.04. You have not correctly understood the definition of analogy.

260.05 And we do not see the purpose of analogy when the gavaya is not perceived. Now, [if it is] when the gavaya is perceived— 260.06 what is the purpose of analogy? That comprehension of the relationship between a name and the named object is the purpose of analogy.
260.07 Thus, analogy is neither scripture nor perception; for this gavaya is known neither from scripture nor from perception.
260.08 Thus he understands. Furthermore, because it serves the purpose of another, comparison (*upamāna*) exists for the sake of another;
for it is not the case that the mere cognition of similarity—such as "as is a cow, so is a gavaya"—is comparison without [the aid of] scripture (*āgama*).
260.09–260.10 For scripture alone cannot constitute comparison without the cognition of similarity. Nor...

And thus is inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, just as the consideration of the mark (*liṅga-parāmarśa*) is inference when it is assisted by the recollection of the relationship between the mark and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgi*), and that [consideration] is a form of perception (*pratyakṣa*); likewise, analogy (*upamāna*) is the perception of similarity (*sārūpya-pratyakṣa*) which depends upon the recollection of the relationship [between the object and its name] produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by authoritative testimony (*āgama*).
Furthermore, because there is a difference in the mode of apprehension, inference is not like this: "As is smoke, so is fire.
