There is [a case] in analogy, such as: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya. Where there is a difference in the mode of apprehension, that is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as analogy does not arise from perception, because it is not previously established by inference.
260.17 This was answered by him [with the following].

260.18 Now, it is the turn of *śabda* (verbal testimony) to be examined. What, then, is this *śabda*? It has been stated that *śabda* is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta-upadeśa*). An objection to this is raised: verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because even though it exists, it is not established [as such]. For even when this *śabda* exists, if it is not heard, it is not a cause for comprehension; nor is it a cause for comprehension [if it is not understood].

And [it is argued that] the reason is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, because there is no object, there is no object for verbal cognition (*śabda*) distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Nor is it a means of valid cognition because it lacks an object; furthermore, it is not a means of valid cognition because its nature is non-cognitive (*avijñānātmakatva*). Whatever is a means of valid cognition has the nature of cognition, just as perception does.
And that which is non-conscious in nature is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like a jar and so forth, because it is perceptible by external sense organs.

Like a jar and so forth, it is not a means of valid cognition because it does not inhere in the self (*ātman*). It is not a means of valid cognition like a jar and so forth because it is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), like number (*saṃkhyā*); for even though [it exists], it is not a means of valid cognition.
[The opponent claims: "It is non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). [We reply: That is not so, because it is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For that which is sometimes perceived does not become a non-means of valid cognition simply because it is not perceived [at other times]; thus, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, that by which something is measured is called a means of valid cognition; and when is it measured? It is when it is perceived. When...
261.08. Furthermore, as for the claim that "this [object] does not exist because of the absence of an object," who says this? [Who says it is] distinct from perception and inference? 261.09.
The reason—that "the object does not exist"—is unestablished; for it has already been stated how there is a distinction [of the object] from perception and the other [means of knowledge].
261.10. As for the further argument: "because it is not of the nature of cognition, because it is perceived by external organs, and because it does not inhere in the self..."
And as for that [argument], it is not [conclusive] because of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntāt*), like a lamp.
It has been stated that "the lamp [is valid] because it is a factor of perception (*pratyakṣa-aṅga-tvāt*). Therefore, due to its inconclusiveness, it is not a valid reason (*ahetu*).
Furthermore, this [other argument], "because it is a quality of space (*ākāśa-guṇa-tvāt*)," is likewise inconclusive; just as in the case of space, whatever...

261.14 That [dimension] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the agent of the cognition of "greatness"; therefore, [it is not a means of valid cognition] because it is a quality of space (*ākāśa*).
261.15 Thus, this is not a valid reason. Verbal testimony (*śabda*) is inference (*anumāna*) because it depends upon memory;
for whatever depends upon memory is inference, and verbal testimony depends upon memory in the communication of meaning. Therefore, [verbal testimony is] inference with respect to the three times.
261.17 Furthermore, because it has an object, inference has the three times as its object, and so too does verbal testimony; therefore, [verbal testimony] is inference.
261.18 Because positive and negative concomitance are established, that which possesses positive and negative concomitance is inference;
261.19 just as the perception of a particular smoke leads to the cognition of fire, so too does verbal testimony through positive and negative concomitance.
261.20 It establishes the object in this very way; therefore, it is inference.
262.01 [2-1-49(47)] Verbal testimony is inference because the object [known through it] is something to be inferred from its non-perception.
262.02 And this verbal testimony is an inference because its object is one that is not perceived by direct perception; such is the meaning of the sūtra.
262.04 [2-1-50(48)] Because apprehension functions in two ways.

262.05 For this reason as well, there is inference from apprehension because it functions in two ways: when there is the state of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not being another means of valid cognition, a distinction in the cause of apprehension is observed, as in the case of perception and inference. Otherwise, in perception...
262.07. Perception occurs otherwise in inference, but not so in the case of verbal testimony; therefore, it is not a separate means of valid cognition.

262.08 [2-1-51(49)] And because of connection (sambandhāt). 262.09 And because of connection; the meaning of the sūtra is "because it conveys a connected object. Inference is that which conveys a connected object, and so too is verbal testimony (śabda). As for that which depends upon memory—

Because it is [based on] inference, [the claim that] verbal testimony is [independent] is not tenable due to the lack of exclusivity (*anaikāntya*). For even in inference, there exists a dependence upon memory—as in the case of doubt, as in the case of reasoning (*tarka*), and as in the case of comparison (*upamāna*).

By this, the [alleged] capacity to have all three times (*trikāla*) as its object is refuted. As for the further argument that [verbal testimony is independent] because of the establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): [this too is refuted].
The establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exists even in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*). For example: where there is a jar, there is the cognition of the jar;

where it is not present, there is the absence of that [cognition]. As for this [objection] that [inference] has as its object an entity that is not being perceived—that is true; inference indeed has as its object an entity that is not being perceived, yet it is not [unreliable].
Furthermore, worldly perception or inference does not depend upon heaven, unseen merit (*apūrva*), deities, and so forth;
rather, it is through the power of the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) that there arises a conviction regarding an object from a word (*śabda*).
262.19 [2-1-52(50)] Through the power of the instruction of a reliable person (āpta), there arises a correct cognition of the object from the word.
262.20 For one does not comprehend heaven and so forth from the mere word;
rather, having established its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by virtue of being uttered by a specific person, one [comprehends] heaven and so forth from such a word.

One understands [the object] in this way, but it is not so in the case of inference; therefore, verbal testimony is not inference. Thus, the cognition characterized in this manner arises from words and not from inference. By this, the fact that [verbal testimony and inference] do not function in the same way has been explained. As for the further point regarding "because of the relation": there exists a relation between the word and its meaning.

263.05 There is a relationship that is both permitted and prohibited. The relationship characterized by the signifier-signified (vācya-vācaka) relation is permitted: "this is the meaning of this word; it is the signified. However, that which is accepted by some as an inherent (svābhāvika) relationship between word and meaning is prohibited.
263.08 How can there be an inherent relationship between word and meaning?

263.09 [2-1-51] Non-apprehension by means of a valid cognition (pramāṇa). 263.10 Non-apprehension by means of a valid cognition: therein, first of all, there is no apprehension of the object of a word by means of direct perception (pratyakṣa), because its object is beyond the reach of the senses (atīndriya-viṣayatvāt). Since the object of a word is indeed beyond the senses, therefore it is not [apprehended].

[Objection: It is apprehended through direct perception. [Response: If it is argued that it will be apprehended through inference, that is not so, because inference is untenable in this case. Does the word reach the location of the object, or does the object reach the location of the word, or do both? First of all, the object does not reach the location of the word.
263.15 [2-1-53(52)] There is no connection [between sound and its cause] because of filling, burning, splitting, and non-perception.
263.16 Because of filling, burning, splitting, and non-perception; this [sound] is to be articulated by means of a specific location, place, and organ situated in one part [of the body].

263.17 Regarding the word "sound": if it were [identical with its cause], then upon the utterance of the words "food," "fire," or "sword," the acts of filling, burning, and splitting would be perceived.
263.18 A material object, such as a sweetmeat or the like, would be perceived as it approached, just like a cow or similar entities.

Consequently, 263.19 worldly linguistic practice (*loka-vyavahāra*) would be cut off. Alternatively, if the word were to reach the vicinity of the object, that too would be untenable because of a contradiction: [the claim] that "the word is eternal" and yet "it comes by way of a continuous series" (*santāna-vṛtti*).
264.02 This is contradictory. Now, if it does not move, then it must exist at the very location of the object and thus be eternal.

264.03 If this is claimed, the contradiction is not removed; furthermore, because of the impossibility of the effort involved in the place and the articulatory organs (*sthāna-karaṇa-prayatna*), it cannot exist at the location of the object.
264.04 If it does not move and does not exist there, then how can it be manifested as a single, pervasive entity?

264.05 If [you argue that they are not perceived], it would follow that all objects would be perceived. If you think that all sounds indeed exist pervasively, yet are manifested when the causes such as the place of articulation (*sthāna*) and the effort (*karaṇa*) are present, then it follows that there would be the perception of all objects; for that which is the manifestor of one sound would also be the manifestor of other sounds.

264.08 And since the sound is manifested as it remains pervading [space], when it stands pervading its own object, then wherever cows may be situated, the manifestation of the word "cow" would result in the communication of the object possessing the hump and other such features. 264.09 Just as a universal (sāmānya), remaining pervasive within its own domain, is perceived everywhere, so too [would the word be].

264.11 There will be a rule that sound also exists pervading its own object. 264.12 It is not right for it to be so; for while the perception of the substratum is the cause for the manifestation of a universal, 264.13 there is no such perception of a substratum for sound, nor does it function within its denotable object; therefore, the example is dissimilar.

And if a word were to function by means of its denoted object (*vācyārthavṛtti*), then even one who has not made a convention would understand [the meaning] upon perceiving the denoted object, just as one understands a universal (*sāmānya*) even without having made a convention. Therefore, it is not understood even through inference. For this reason as well, there is no connection with anything other than its own substrate (*svālaya*).
264.17 Because sound is a quality (*guṇatvāt*), it does not have inherence (*samavāya*) with anything else, such as a cow or the like, in relation to sound.

264.18 This is because sound resides in space (*ākāśavṛttitvāt*). Nor is there inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) between sound and its object, because those two do not originate from a single [cause]. 264.19 One might think it will be understood through analogy (*upamānāt*), but that is not so, for there is no analogy either.
264.20 This is not the subject [of this discussion]. Since it will be understood from scripture (*āgama*), that very point is what is being investigated here:

264.21 Are the word and its object connected, or are they unconnected? As for this which you state—namely, that "verbal testimony (*śabda*) is inference because it depends on memory and so forth, and because it shares the characteristics of inference"—for that very reason, it is not inference.

265.02 For there is no similarity of a thing with itself. Now, [if it is argued] that because of the similarity with memory and so forth, 265.03 verbal testimony (*śabda*) and inference (*anumāna*) are one and the same, then in that case, it follows that there is only one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For indeed, the commonality (*sādharmya*) of all means of valid cognition is the quality of determining an object (*artha-paricchedakatva*). Let there be one means of valid cognition; what is the harm to us?
"It is sublated. How is it not sublated? That which is desired is being negated. What is desired?

That perception and inference are distinct. Now, if non-difference is asserted by relying upon the universal (*sāmānya*), then one should remain indifferent; for while there is non-difference by relying upon the universal, there is difference by relying upon the particular (*viśeṣa*).

Thus, nothing is contradicted. Furthermore, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not inference (*anumāna*), because it causes the cognition of both its own nature and that of others. Whatever causes the cognition of both its own nature and that of others is not inference, just as a lamp; for a lamp is a means of perception (*upalabdhi-sādhana*) not only for the person by whom it is produced, but also for another.
The word "api" (also/even) implies that it is likewise; therefore, it is not inference.
265.12 [2-1-54(53)] Because of the established relationship between word and object, there is no refutation.

265.13 Because of the established relationship between word and object, there is no refutation. If word and object were unrelated, there would be no established cognition of word and object. A word, being related, conveys its object.

Because it is the cause for the restriction of cognition, like a lamp. That which is the cause for the restriction of cognition is seen to be connected and to convey its object, just as a lamp is. And sound possesses this same property;
therefore, sound also is connected and conveys its object. Alternatively, "cognition" itself may be made the subject of the proposition.
Because of the rule that the cognition of an object arises from the word and its referent being connected, it is like the cognition "the one who wears earrings" (kuṇḍalī).

265.20 [2-1-55(54)] Because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is conventional (sāmayika). 265.21 It is not established by a [permanent] relation between word and meaning; rather, the determination of word and meaning is brought about by convention (samaya). But what is this convention? It is the designation (abhidhāna)—

266.02–266.04: Someone might say, "The determination of the relationship between word and meaning occurs through a convention (*samaya*) that prescribes the restriction of what is to be expressed. If we have stated that such a connection is thus authorized, this very establishment of the relationship between word and meaning can also occur otherwise; therefore, [the opponent's argument] is not a valid reason. Furthermore, this connection is characterized by the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*).

Even for one who maintains that the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*svābhāvika*), this must be admitted. For one who maintains an innate relationship, there can be no cognition of a specific [meaning] from the apprehension of a word if the relationship between that word and its meaning has not been previously established. Furthermore, from what source is that convention (*samaya*) to be understood? It is understood from the knowledge of the words and from common worldly usage; thus, this is the treatise (*śāstra*).
266.08 It was established for the sake of preventing the loss of words. Furthermore, the convention [of language] must be understood from the world, such as from one's mother and others.

266.09 Having observed those various words being employed for those various meanings, he too, having been trained in exactly that same way, employs those very words for those very meanings; he does not, however, treat them like a script.
"Someone is teaching," he said.

266.12 [2-1-56(55)] And because there is no restriction regarding specific universals (jāti-viśeṣa), 266.13 and because there is no restriction regarding specific universals, the relation between word and meaning is not intrinsic (svābhāvika).
266.14 If the relation between word and meaning were intrinsic, it would not [vary] with respect to specific universals.
266.15 There would have been a fixed relationship between word and object; however, there is indeed usage according to one's will regarding specific universals (jāti-viśeṣa).
266.16 Usage according to one's will is observed, but not among those things connected by an inherent (svābhāvika) relation regarding specific universals.
266.17 Deviation is observed; for a lamp does not illuminate for us in one way and in another.
Regarding the phrase "distinction of birth" (*jāti-viśeṣa*): furthermore, by the term "distinction of birth," "place" (*deśa*) is designated.
266.19 [2-1-57(56)] Its lack of authority [is established] due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology.
266.20 "Its lack of authority is due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology" is the sūtra. The word "its" (tat) refers to the subject under discussion.
267.01 Because it is expressed by the term "word" (śabda), it is a qualification of the specific word; for although it is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), [it is specified here].

267.02–03. One expresses that word again by means of another word; this reflection concerns a specific word, intending to make it known. It does not concern the mere word itself; otherwise, it should have been stated thus: "Verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because of the defects of falsehood (*anṛta*), contradiction (*vyāghāta*), and tautology (*punarukta*). Non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is the failure to communicate the object, while falsehood (*anṛtatva*) is [the communication of] something otherwise [than it is].

267.05. Contradiction (*vyāghāta*) is the non-coexistence of two words or two sentences regarding their meaning; repetition (*punarukta*) is the stating again of what has already been stated. Examples are found in the *Bhāṣya*. Among these, the reason for falsehood is the non-perception of a result (*phalādarśana*). "One should offer the *agni-hotra*" is an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*); its contradiction is as follows: [the result is not seen].

267.08–267.10: Due to the impossibility of a [viable] result, there is a prohibition against the *uditānudita* (post-sunrise/pre-sunset), the *samaya* (twilight), and the *adhyuṣita* (at dawn) times; nor is there any other time in which the *agnihotra* offering could take place. Furthermore, among the statements regarding the *uditānudita*, the *samaya*, and the *adhyuṣita*, there is a mutual contradiction between the first and the last; if all three were stated together, it would be a tautology.

267.11 An illustration is given in the Bhāṣya: having presented these sentences as examples, [it is argued that] because they have a single author, the remaining sentences lack authority. Or else, there is a denial of the authority of sentences such as those concerning the *agnihotra*, on the grounds that they are Vedic; furthermore, regarding their being redundant like other sentences, the latter [argument] follows from the former.
Or rather, it is not a sentence, because it is produced by a single [person].

267.15 [2-1-58(57)] Not so, because of defects in the object, the agent, or the instruments. 267.16 Not so, because of defects in the object, the agent, or the instruments. As for the claim that the Vedic statements are not authoritative because they are false and because no results are observed—that must be examined here: is it the non-observation of results that renders the Veda...
"Is it because the statements lack authority, or because of a deficiency in the ritual action, the agent, or the instruments? To this we reply:

"It is not because of a deficiency in the ritual action, the agent, or the instruments; rather, the incompleteness of the causal factors is inferred from the non-perception of the result. Or, there is a contradiction because the sacrifice is established as having the instrument as its means; yet this sacrifice was not performed by me directly.

268.01 It is accepted that [the sacrifice] is for the sake of obtaining a son; however, it is the parents who, when engaged in the sacrifice, procreate a son. 268.02 In this regard, it is not known whether the birth of a son fails due to a deficiency in the parents, or rather due to a deficiency in the sacrifice. Furthermore, the mantras are employed as the means for accomplishing the sacrifice.

268.04. They are auxiliary elements of the *iṣṭi*; even there, it is not known whether the *iṣṭi* fails due to a deficiency in the mantras, or 268.05. whether it is because of a deficiency in the cause, such as the sacrificial grass, fuel, and so forth.
268.06. Just as when mantras are employed in a state of deficiency or excess, the *iṣṭi* is not accomplished, so too [is it in the other case].

268.07–268.09: Also because of the deficiency in the means, such as the *darbha* grass, the fuel, and so forth. It is not only due to a deficiency in the means that the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) fails to be accomplished;

likewise, it is due to the lack of excellence in the performer of the sacrifice and the ritual action itself. Having set aside the idea that the mere performance of the sacrifice is the sole cause for the perfection of the sacrifice, it has been stated [that other factors are required]. In that regard, regarding the son—

268.10 It is not reasonable for one who possesses human attributes to say, "Because birth is not seen, [the mantras] are ineffective," on the grounds that there is no production of a son. If it is argued that there is doubt because [the result] is observed in both ways, we say no, because that would entail the abandonment of what has been accepted. Now, if you think that the birth of a son has three causes and that [in some cases] there is a deficiency of one of those causes...

268.13–15. It is understood that the non-existence of a son is due to a deficiency in the causal factors. In this regard, just as the non-production of a son occurs due to a defect in the parents, so too it is doubted whether [the Veda] fails to produce results because the mantras lack authority.
This does not constitute an abandonment of a previously accepted position; for you previously asserted that the Veda lacks authority, yet now you state otherwise.
268.16 By saying that "the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is doubtful," you abandon your previous position.

268.17 If you say it is "equal" [to our case], then do you think this is equally so for you as well—that there is doubt whether the non-birth of a son is due to a defect in the father or due to the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedic sentences? No, because there is no proof [for such a claim].

268.19 It is not by me that this is being established—namely, whether the Vedic statements are authoritative or not—but rather it is being established by you. In that case, because of the deficiency of one of the factors of your proof, I point out that the reason is doubtful, as in the case of "the birth of a son does not occur," since [your reason] lacks its necessary concomitants; thus, the instruction regarding wood is not [valid].

269.02 "Like churning": this sacrifice is not taught as the direct cause of the birth of a son; rather, it is taught that "one who desires a son should perform the sacrifice. Just as there is the instruction that "one who desires fire should churn wood," in that case, it is not because of a deficiency in the agent or the action that fire fails to arise; such is the nature of the instruction.
269.05. Likewise here as well, [the objection] is futile; thus there is no fault. Furthermore, because the attainment of the fruit is observed when there is a totality [of causes].

Where all the causes are present, the production of the fruit is seen; thus there is no fault. And as for this statement that "it lacks authority due to the faults of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology," that too applies to the Veda...
269.08 Because it is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), [the reason] is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Now, as for those statements that possess such characteristics, they are made the subject;

since the properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) are employed therein as qualifiers, a reason must be stated to establish their lack of authority. If it is argued that "lack of authority arises from being false," then what is this falsity?

If [the opponent argues that] "nāma" (by name) refers to the designation of an object that is not as it actually is, yet this is not the very meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) that "it is invalid" (*apramāṇam*), [we reply: it is improper to say either that its falsity (*anṛtatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) or that there is the fault of contradiction (*vyāghāta*). 269.13–269.14.

269.14 [2-1-59(58)] Because a fault is stated regarding the difference in time after having accepted [the rule], there is no contradiction. 269.15 This very laying of the fire (agny-ādhāna) is the undertaking of a restriction: "One should offer when the sun has risen; one should offer before the sun has risen; one should offer when the twilight has passed. 269.16 [This is the meaning.]

269.17 Thus. When this [person], having accepted a time limit, lets it pass, then, because of that lapse of the accepted time, 269.18 he is censured by words of reproach; there is a contradiction (*vyāghāta*) because neither of the two [propositions] has been stated as a negation. This is not otherwise.
269.19 If, on the other hand, this were a statement of the negation of both, then this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*), namely the contradiction, would occur.
269.20 Furthermore, these are not prohibitive statements such as "the offering should be made when the sun has risen" and so forth;

269.21 therefore, this [objection] does not apply. However, if these sentences were indeed prohibitions of the injunction for the fire-oblation (homa), 270.01 then the mention of "at sunrise" and so on would be entirely purposeless, and it should have been stated simply as "the Agnihotra."
270.02–04. "One should offer oblations"—this statement is not to be performed. And thus, the coherence of the meaning is as explained above:
in this way, the preceding and following statements become consistent, because, having referred back (*anūdya*) to the offering, it prescribes a specific time.
Thus, this is not a contradiction as we have previously asserted; such is the rule.
270.05 A reason must be stated; this very statement beginning with "udita" (uttered) is the reason for the restriction. How so?

This [following] statement must be considered either as being constructed at will, or as a restatement of what has already been expressed. A restatement of what has been expressed is the logical rule (*nyāya*), because in that case there is no contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is not [the case otherwise].

270.08. [Objection: "This is a contradiction. [Response: Furthermore, this is not the fault of tautology (punarukta), because it is established as a restatement (anuvāda). 270.09–10. [2-1-60(59)] Because of the establishment of the restatement; [2-1-61(60)] and because the meaning is grasped through the analysis of the sentence.

270.11 [This is] because of the validity of the restatement (*anuvāda*). "Tautology" (*punarukta*) is the repetition of that very same meaning when no distinction has been made by means of a qualifying factor (*aṅga*). 270.12–13: On the other hand, "restatement" (*anuvāda*) is the repetition of something that exists when a distinction has been made by means of a qualifying factor, due to the commonality of the hearing (*śruti*). This being so, there is no fault as previously stated. An example is given in the *Bhāṣya*: "son..."

270.14 The sentences concerning desire-sacrifices (*kāmeṣṭi*) are authoritative because they are part of the Veda, just like the sentence: "The earth is the place for sowing; sowing is great. And for this reason as well: 270.15 Because of the fixed rule regarding words and so forth, just like the sentence: "Twelve months make a year. And for this reason as well:
270.16 Because a specific agent is mentioned, just like the sentence: "Fire is the remedy for cold."

Alternatively, taking all Vedic sentences as the subject, it is stated: "Vedic sentences are authoritative because they possess a division of meaning, like the sentences of Manu and others. Just as the sentences of Manu and others possess a division of meaning—and being possessed of a division of meaning, they are authoritative—so too [are the Vedic sentences]."
The Vedic sentences possess a division of meaning; therefore, they are a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). And this division is threefold.
270.21 It exists.
271.01 [2-1-62(61)] Because of the application of words as injunctions, explanatory passages, and restatements.

271.02 Because of the application of words as injunctions, explanatory passages, and restatements, the Brāhmaṇa texts are indeed threefold: 271.03 they consist of injunctive statements, restatements, and explanatory passages.
And.
271.05 [2-1-63(62)] *Vidhi* (injunction) is that which prescribes (*vidhāyaka*).

271.06 In this context, *vidhi* is the prescriber; that sentence which is prescriptive and indicative is *vidhi*. 271.07 Furthermore, *vidhi* is either a mandate (*niyoga*) or a permission (*anujñā*); it is that sentence which enjoins, saying, "One should do this."
271.08. *Niyoga* (injunction). But *anujñā* (permission) is that which permits what is to be done; it is the sentence of permission.
271.09. For example, this very *agni-hotra* sentence permits the fact of being preceded by the attainment of the means [of accomplishment].
271.10 [2-1-64(63)] Praise, censure, the deeds of others, and ancient accounts—these are *arthavāda*.
271.11 Praise, censure, the deeds of others, and ancient accounts—these are *arthavāda*. Examples of these are given in the Bhāṣya.
271.12 [Examples] are in the Bhāṣya.
271.13 [2-1-65(64)] Anuvāda is the restatement of that which has been enjoined by an injunction (vidhi).
271.14 Is anuvāda the restatement of what is enjoined by an injunction? It is the statement of the meaning of an injunction; likewise, it is anuvāda.

271.15 Furthermore, the restatement of what is enjoined by an injunction is twofold: the former is a restatement of the word (śabdānuvāda), and the latter is a restatement of the meaning (arthānuvāda), as for example:

271.16 Repetition is of two kinds: repetition of words and repetition of meaning. Repetition of words is, for example, [saying] "impermanent" or "permanent. Repetition of meaning is, for example, [saying] "impermanent" and "subject to cessation."
271.18 [2-1-66(65)] There is no distinction between restatement (anuvāda) and tautology (punarukta), because both involve the repetition of words.
271.19 There is no distinction between restatement and tautology, since both result in the repetition of words. What is the meaning of this sūtra?
272.01 The meaning is: the repetition of words whose meaning is already understood is common to both restatement and tautology; for even tautology...

A word whose meaning is already understood is being repeated; this is also the case in a restatement (anuvāda). Therefore, because of the repetition of words whose meanings are already understood, both [the original statement and the restatement] are incorrect.
272.04 [2-1-67(66)] "As in the case of the instruction to go more quickly, there is no lack of distinction due to repetition.

272.05 Regarding the statement, "As in the case of the instruction to go more quickly, there is no lack of distinction due to repetition": just as one says, "Go quickly," 272.06 or "Go more quickly," the excellence of the action is understood through the suffix *tarap* expressing haste; so too [is it here].
272.07 Even by means of repetition characterized as a restatement (*anuvāda*), an excellence of action (*kriyātiśaya*) is expressed. Its formal application (*prayoga*) is as follows:

272.08 The repetition characterized as a restatement is purposeful, because it is the cause of a specific cognition (*pratyayaviśeṣa*), just like the instruction for moving more quickly [from the word "quick" to the word "more quick"]. Now, when the word "more quick" (*śīghratara*) is employed from the word "quick" (*śīghra*), it is a specific cognition—

Because it serves as a cause for a specific distinction (*viśeṣa-hetu*), it does not incur the fault of redundancy (*punarukta-doṣa*). Likewise, repetition characterized as a restatement (*anuvāda-lakṣaṇa*) will not suffer from the fault of redundancy because it serves as a cause for a specific modification of cognition (*pratyaya-viśeṣa-hetu*). What, then, is this specific distinction? It must be stated; therefore, it is said: when the word "cook" (*pacatu*) is employed for the first time, the act of cooking (*pāka*) is to be brought about.

272.14 Thus, from the second word *pacatu*, there arises for the agent the cognition of being the one who cooks; furthermore, there arises the cognition of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), namely, "I alone must cook," or the cognition of continuity (*sātatya*), namely, "I must cook constantly. 272.15 Or, there arises the cognition of entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇa*), namely, "I must cook quickly."

272.18 However, since no distinction whatsoever is perceived in the case of a tautology (punarukta), there is a great difference between a tautology and a restatement (anuvāda). Thus, other applications of restatement within a sentence should also be understood. 272.20 Is it then established that the authority of Vedic sentences is proven solely by the removal of [the faults of] negation and [fallacious] reasons? Or not?
The cause [is this]: since there is no establishment [of an object] without a means of proof (*sādhana*), from what then [does it arise]? From valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What is that valid cognition? It is the state of possessing a distinct differentiation of objects.
273.01 [2-1-68(67)] And its authority [is established] because of the authority of the *mantras* and *Āyurveda*. 273.02 [It is established] from the authority of the trustworthy person (*āpta*).
273.03 And its authority is like the authority of the *mantras* and *Āyurveda*, due to the authority of the trustworthy person; the word "and" (*ca*) [indicates this].

This is for the purpose of drawing out the previous reason: just as the sentences of the *Mantra* and *Āyurveda* are authoritative because they were uttered by a specific person, so too are the sentences of the Veda; thus, "being uttered by a specific person" is the reason. What is the authority of the *Āyurveda*? It is that which is taught by the *Āyurveda*: "Having performed this, the desired [result] is attained."

273.07 By performing this, one attains [the goal] and abandons the undesirable; such is the nature of that which is being practiced. 273.08 This non-erroneousness is its validity. What constitutes this? It is constituted by the validity of the authoritative person (*āpta*). Furthermore, what is the authority of authoritative persons? It is their state of having directly realized the Dharma—that which they teach regarding the categories of reality.

He is directly perceived by them; thus there is compassion for living beings (*bhūtadayā*) toward him to whom they teach. There is also sympathy (*praty-anukampā*) for him, or he has the desire to explain [the truth] for the sake of their correct understanding.
An authoritative teacher (*āpta*) is one distinguished by these three qualifications; the instruction given by such a person is [authoritative].
273.13 That which is performed is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and by way of the non-contradiction of observed statements, it is possible to infer the remainder [of unobserved matters].
273.14 For example, regarding a matter already perceived, such as "one desiring a village should sacrifice," and so forth; by that, the inference of the remainder is a means of valid cognition.
273.15 Thus, even a worldly statement is characterized by these same three types of qualifications.

The application of this [inference] is: "The Vedic sentences are authoritative, because they were uttered by a distinguished speaker, like the sentences of the Mantras and Āyurveda; or else, because they have a single author, like the sentences of the Mantras and Āyurveda. Taking the sentences of the Mantras and Āyurveda as the subject (*pakṣa*), there is a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) based on their being exponents of supramundane objects.

A reason must be stated. If it is argued that "the quality of being composed by a person (*pauruṣeyatva*) is unestablished because [the Vedas] are eternal," and if you think: "The Vedic sentences are eternal; and because they are eternal, they possess authority; therefore, the quality of being composed by a person is unestablished"—[we reply: No, it is not unestablished. If their eternity were established, this would be correct; but that is not established. Therefore, it is not [unestablished].

274.04 This is logical. [Objection: If they are not eternal, how can they be means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that a means of valid cognition is that which establishes the object of cognition (*prameya*)? 274.05 [Reply: It is not because of eternality that it is a means of valid cognition; for some say that there is no eternal means of valid cognition whatsoever. 274.06 [They argue: Precisely because they are means of valid cognition, they are non-eternal. However, we see that this is not correct, for even that which is eternal...
274.07 Just as the mind and the self [are called] "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) because the word *pramāṇa* denotes a collection (*samudāya*).

274.08 Indeed, this word *pramāṇa* applies to a collection; therein, there are many things, both eternal and non-eternal. 274.09 Because the members of the collection are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the means of valid cognition, they are called "means of valid cognition," just as a lamp [is called so]; and thus it is.

[The opponent claims: "There is also a permanent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth are presented as the probans for the permanence of other things, then, because atoms and the like are themselves permanent and possess the status of a means of valid cognition, [the reason] becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since they are permanent despite being a means of valid cognition. Therefore, this is not a valid reply. Consequently, it is logical that [the subject] possesses the differentiation of its object.

[The argument is: Because [the Vedic sentences] possess a connection [to their meanings], they are non-eternal, like worldly sentences. Just as worldly sentences possess a division according to their objects, so too do Vedic sentences; therefore, they are not eternal. [Objection:
Even worldly sentences are eternal. [Response: Now, you might think that even these worldly sentences—
If those [words] were also eternal because they possess the differentiation of meaning (*artha-vibhāga*), then there would be no differentiation of meaning;
for this differentiation of meaning that exists in worldly sentences would not exist [in eternal words]. But it is observed that those [worldly sentences] are non-eternal.
If this is argued, then a specific reason must be stated; for while the possession of the differentiation of meaning is equal, and the [nature of] meaning is equal—

If [it is argued that] there is a distinction such that worldly [words] are non-eternal while Vedic [words] are eternal when both function as communicators (*pratipādaka*), then a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) must be stated. For you as well, since both are equally non-eternal, a specific reason must be stated. It has been stated that the reason is "possessing a division of meaning" (*arthavibhāgavattva*). Furthermore, because they possess phonemes (*varṇavattvāt*), worldly sentences possessing phonemes are non-eternal.

And thus, the Vedic sentences are likewise non-eternal; for that reason, they too [are non-eternal], because, while possessing both generality and particularity, they are perceptible by the sense of hearing, like worldly sentences. Furthermore, because they consist of words, they are like worldly [sentences]. If it is argued that "because the act of seeing is for the sake of another," you might think that the act of seeing—

The word "seeing" (darśana) is for the sake of another; the purpose of utterance is to communicate to another, for no one utters a word for their own comprehension. And if this [word] were eternal, it would be logical that the cognition of the meaning arises from the word. But if it is non-eternal—having arisen and then perishing—then it has ceased for the listener.
[The opponent claims: "The object of hearing is always something unprecedented (*apūrva*). [We reply: It is not logical that there should be comprehension from hearing something unprecedented.

For indeed, a resident of Nārikela Island does not achieve comprehension of an object possessing a hump and so forth merely from hearing the word "cow" (*go*), which is unfamiliar to him. And thus, for one who maintains that words are non-eternal, all words would be like that; therefore—

275.09. It might be argued that for this [word] as well, a restriction of cognition is not established from the word itself. This is not so, because of the lack of exclusivity (*anaikāntāt*). For in the case of lamps and the like, which perish in an instant, the communication of something previously unknown is observed. This is not due to a difference in nature from the example;
for a lamp, though unspoken, brings about the comprehension of the object to be illuminated through its connection with that object to be illuminated.
[The opponent asks: "Does it not produce [the cognition] unless it is expressed? [The author replies: Who says such a thing?
[For us,] the word expresses [the object] because no [other] relation is observed; thus, the expression [of the relation] is untenable. This has already been stated:
that there is no relation between word and object characterized by contact (*prāpti*), but rather one characterized by the signifier-signified (*vācya-vācaka*) relationship.

That relationship is human-made and it is produced; and because the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless, this is understood from common worldly experience. However, those who describe the cycle of existence as having a beginning are to be rebuked in this way.
Now, as for this assertion that "the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal," how does that relate to the tradition (*sampradāya*)?

275.18 Because there is no interruption, those very Vedic sentences continue through the traditions and practices during the fourfold aims (*caturvarga*) of each Manvantara. 275.19 Due to this lack of interruption, worldly words are not employed [in their place]; therefore, the Vedas are eternal (*nitya*). Just as mountains and rivers are eternal, so too are Manu and the others.
This is the same regarding [the eternality of] sentences. Why? Because there is no interruption in the tradition (*sampradāya*), there is no eternality.

Furthermore, because of this very lack of eternality, the proofs for non-eternality that have been stated are not refuted; those proofs for non-eternality which were set forth by me are not invalidated, and since they are not invalidated, [the sentences are] non-eternal.
When there is an uninterrupted tradition, there is eternal conventional usage.
Thus ends the first daily lesson (*āhnika*) of the second chapter in the *Nyāyavārttika* by Uddyotakara. Now begins the second daily lesson.

277.06. *Vaktṛka* refers to a tradition of oral report; the elders say, "They tell [this]. By implication, this is an *arthāpatti*. 277.07. *Arthāpatti* means an implication, an attainment, or a consequence—that which follows from a statement when something else is being enjoined. 277.08. When another meaning is necessarily implied by implication (*arthāt*), that is an *arthāpatti*; for example: "When there are no clouds, there is no rain."

277.09 Thus, what is established here by implication? It is that [the effect] exists when the [causes] are present. "Possibility" (sambhava) is the cognition of the existence of another thing through the apprehension of a thing that exists in an inseparable relation (avinābhāvin). For example, from the apprehension of a *droṇa* measure, there is the existence of an *āḍhaka*. "Non-existence" (abhāva) is the apprehension of the opposite through the apprehension of its contrary.
Just as when there is a conjunction of wind and clouds that acts as a support, the falling of water is prevented because its heaviness is obstructed;
by that non-falling of the water, one infers the opposing conjunction of wind and clouds.

These [means of knowledge], such as tradition (*aitihya*) and the rest, being of this nature, are included within these very [categories] because there is no difference in their defining characteristics.

They are not mentioned separately because there is no object [for them]. Furthermore, since objects do not exist apart from the means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), objects for *aitihya* and the like are impossible; therefore, they are not separate means of valid cognition.
If you think they are distinguished by a difference in their purpose, then in that case, the number [of means of valid cognition] would be reduced to eight. Moreover—

The accepted eightfold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not hold, because one accepts a distinction in the means of valid cognition based on a distinction in their purposes. [Objection: A distinction in purpose is observed even when there is a single instrument; thus, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anekānta*). Or [alternatively]: [there is no multiplicity of means of valid cognition].

277.21 Now, if you consider there to be a distinction [of sense-faculties] due to a difference in their functions, it follows that a single sense-faculty would become multiple. 278.03 [2-2-2] Because tradition (*aitihya*) is not distinct from verbal testimony (*śabda*), and because presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), possibility (*sambhava*),

and non-existence (*abhāva*) are not distinct from inference (*anumāna*), there is no refutation. 278.04–05 Because tradition is not distinct from verbal testimony, and because presumptive testimony, possibility, and non-existence are not distinct from inference...

278.06 And because it exists, there is no negation [of *aitihya* as a means of knowledge]. Since it possesses the same defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), *aitihya* is included within *śabda*. 278.07 The definition of *śabda* does not exclude *aitihya*; this distinction is subsumed under the general category. 278.08 Within inference (*anumāna*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), probability (*sambhava*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) are included, because they possess the same defining characteristic. How is *arthāpatti* [included]?

It is subsumed under inference (*anumāna*), because the negation of one of two [alternatives] has as its object the affirmation of the second. Wherever, between two things, the negation of one thing occurs, there the affirmation of the second is observed; for example, from the statement "he does not eat by day," it follows that he eats at night.
Thus it is understood. However, some say that this is not a case of *arthāpatti* (presumption) regarding the statement "he does not eat during the day.

Rather, there are two restrictions here: "he eats only during the day" and "he does not eat at all during the day. Since both [possibilities] would apply, one need not state "he eats at night. But this is not correct, because it is impossible.

The meaning "he certainly does not eat during the day" is refuted by impossibility; for there is no one who "certainly eats during the day," since even while eating he does not "certainly eat"—how much less so when not eating? Therefore, because the meaning is refuted by impossibility, this [statement] serves as a negation of time: "not during the day."

"He eats. Otherwise, it would be meaningless, because the exclusion of other actions is impossible [as a primary meaning], and since the negation of time has been rejected and is not accepted, let the sentence be meaningless—let it be meaningless! What is harmed for us? That which was accepted is what is being set aside; and what was accepted? Another action.

Where there is a negation, it is a negation of time; and this is not without purpose, because when one of two [alternatives] is negated, the second is thereby admitted. What, then, is presumption (*arthāpatti*)? It is simply inference (*anumāna*). Which [inference]?
That which is "observed in general" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*). By this, possibility (*sambhava*) and impossibility (*abhāva*) are explained. Possibility is inference.

279.07 [2-2-3] Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*).

279.08 Likewise, in this case, this presumption is not a valid means of knowledge because it is inconclusive. That presumption which you seek to establish as a valid means of knowledge is not a valid means of knowledge; thus, the object [of knowledge] is never [established by it].

279.10 It is a prover [of the contrary]: for instance, it follows by implication that "when clouds are absent, rain does not occur. 279.11 Since [rain] occurs when [clouds] are present, yet at times it does not occur even when they are present, this is an inconclusive presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

279.12 If one takes "presumptive testimony in general" as the subject (*pakṣa*), then its inconclusiveness is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), provided that "presumptive testimony in general" is indeed the subject.

279.13 Therefore, it is impossible for [the reason] to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). If that which is inconclusive is then made into a thesis (*pakṣa*), then we too say: "It is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). 279.15 Thus, there is no reason (*hetu*), because a reason is a qualification of the proposition (*pratijñā-viśeṣa*); that which is inconclusive—[that is the reason].
The proposition is "it is not a means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*); the reason is "because it does not exist"; and the point to be proven is "and this object is not established.

Because of the absence of a reason, there is a contradiction with what has been accepted. By one who says that an inconclusive presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) is not a means of valid cognition, it is accepted that a conclusive one is a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, this statement is pointless: that an inconclusive presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even that presumptive testimony which you consider [to exist] is not inconclusive.

279.21 [2-2-4] Because there is the conceit of "presumption" (*arthāpatti*) regarding what is not a presumption (*anarthāpatti*). 280.01 Because it is designated as a "presumption" when it is not a presumption, this is not a [valid] presumption; it is inconclusive (*anaikāntikī*).
280.02 And since rain occurs when clouds exist, how is this [example of] presumption not inconclusive?

"It exists when [the causes] exist" means rather that it exists when they exist. As for the fact that rain does not occur even when clouds are present, this is a case of the obstruction of the cause; it is not the object of inference by implication (*arthāpatti*).
Rather, its object of inference is that "when the cause exists, the effect occurs. How could this [reasoning] be inconclusive?
280.06 If an effect were to arise even in the absence of a cause, that has never been observed; therefore, [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntikatva). 280.07.
280.08 [2-2-5] Furthermore, the invalidity of the negation is due to its being inconclusive (anaikāntikatva).

280.09 Furthermore, the invalidity of the negation is due to its being inconclusive. This negation which is being made by you—namely, that "presumption (arthāpatti) is not a means of valid cognition because it is inconclusive"—this too is inconclusive.
280.11 Because existence (*sattā*) is not negated, there is no negation by this [reasoning], nor is existence negated through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). How so?
280.12 There is no negation of existence because it is the specific [form] of the presumptive implication that is negated, not the presumptive implication itself.
280.13 Therefore, since existence is not negated, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Now, if you think that there is no negation...

For that which is known as "inconclusive" is that which functions both within its own object and elsewhere among things of a different class. And there is no such thing as an inconclusive means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the negation is not inconclusive.
280.18 [2-2-6] Or, if that [perception] were valid, there would be no invalidity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

281.01: It is not so; for it is never observed that an effect arises when its cause is absent. This is the meaning of the following sūtra: 281.02:
That which was stated by you—that [a reason] functioning outside its own domain is inconclusive—is intended to demonstrate a contradiction (*vyāghāta*).
281.03 Furthermore, it is contradictory to say that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntikī*). Or else, [if you mean] ignorance;
for even when one speaks of the conventional usage of "inconclusiveness" without having understood it, it is said: "Presumptive testimony is not a valid means of knowledge because it is inconclusive.
281.05 Thus, in such a case, one should remain indifferent; one should not pay attention to the words of a madman.

281.06 Non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it lacks an object (*viṣaya*). That which has no object is not a means of valid cognition, just as the word "cow" is not a means of valid cognition when used to denote a horse; and so too is non-existence. Therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition. And who says that non-existence is a means of valid cognition? Rather, the cognition whose object is non-existence is the means of valid cognition; by that [cognition], [non-existence] is cognized.

281.09 Thus [it is asked]: "What, then, is its object? It has been stated that it is non-existence (*abhāva*). Regarding that, for the sake of illustrating the manifoldly differentiated proliferation (*prapañca*), there is the aphorism (sūtra). 281.10 [Sūtra: "Non-perception is the non-perception of that which is perceptible. 281.11 [Commentary: Here, "perceptible" means that which is capable of being perceived by the senses when all other conditions for perception are present. "Non-perception" is the absence of that perception. This is the definition of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). 281.12 And this non-apprehension is of two kinds: the apprehension of something else and the apprehension of its own nature. Of these, the apprehension of something else is, for example, the cognition of a pillar in the place where a person might be expected. The apprehension of its own nature is, for example, the cognition of the bare ground itself. 281.13 Furthermore, this non-apprehension is of three types: that which is based on the nature of the thing itself, that which is based on the nature of the cause, and that which is based on the nature of the effect. Among these, the non-apprehension based on the nature of the thing itself is, for example, the non-perception of a jar on a spot of ground that is visible and well-lit. 281.14 The non-apprehension based on the nature of the cause is, for example, the non-perception of smoke in a place where fire is absent. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the effect is, for example, the non-perception of fire in a place where smoke is absent. 281.15 Moreover, this non-apprehension is further divided into four types: that which is characterized by the presence of the object, that which is characterized by the absence of the object, that which is characterized by both, and that which is characterized by neither. Among these, the non-apprehension characterized by the presence of the object is, for example, the non-perception of a jar on a spot of ground that is visible and well-lit. 281.16 The non-apprehension characterized by the absence of the object is, for example, the non-perception of a jar in total darkness. The non-apprehension characterized by both is, for example, the non-perception of a jar in a place where there is no light and no observer. The non-apprehension characterized by neither is, for example, the non-perception of a jar in a place where there is light but no observer. 281.17 Furthermore, this non-apprehension is of five types: that which is based on the nature of the thing itself, that which is based on the nature of the cause, that which is based on the nature of the effect, that which is based on the nature of the genus (*jāti*), and that which is based on the nature of the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*). The non-apprehension based on the nature of the relation is, for example, the non-perception of a potter in a place where a jar is absent. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the counter-correlative is, for example, the non-perception of a jar in a place where its counter-correlative, the non-jar, is present. 281.23 Furthermore, this non-apprehension is of eight types: that which is based on the nature of the thing itself, that which is based on the nature of the cause, that which is based on the nature of the effect, that which is based on the nature of the genus, that which is based on the nature of the specific characteristic, that which is based on the nature of the relation, that which is based on the nature of the counter-correlative, and that which is based on the nature of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Among these, the non-apprehension based on the nature of the thing itself is, for example, the non-perception of a jar on a spot of ground that is visible and well-lit. 281.24 The non-apprehension based on the nature of the cause is, for example, the non-perception of smoke in a place where fire is absent. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the effect is, for example, the non-perception of fire in a place where smoke is absent. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the genus is, for example, the non-perception of a cow in a place where the genus "cowness" is absent. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the specific characteristic is, for example, the non-perception of a white cow in a place where a black cow is absent. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the relation is, for example, the non-perception of a potter in a place where a jar is absent. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the counter-correlative is, for example, the non-perception of a jar in a place where its counter-correlative, the non-jar, is present. The non-apprehension based on the nature of the pervader is, for example, the non-perception of a tree in a place where a śimśapā tree is absent. 281.25 Furthermore, this non-apprehension is of nine types: that which is based on the nature of the thing itself, that which is based on the nature of the cause, that which is based on the nature of the effect, that which is based on the nature of the genus, that which is based on the nature of the specific characteristic

281.11 [2-2-8] Because that which is characterized is characterized by the absence of characteristics, those things not characterized are established as such through the establishment of their objects of cognition. 281.12–13: Because those things not characterized are characterized by the absence of characteristics within those things that are characterized, they are established as such through the establishment of their objects of cognition. Those things not characterized...

When commanded, "Bring the garments," [the agent] perceives those garments among the two sets present which do not bear the [expected] marks; he understands them precisely by the absence of those marks. Because the command and the comprehension share a single object, having understood [them], he brings them; and that cause of comprehension is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is established that non-existence is an object of cognition.

281.18 [2-2-9] If it is argued that there is no absence when the object is non-existent, we say no, because the definition of another [state] is established. 281.19 If it is argued that there is no absence when the object is non-existent—suppose you think that where something exists, there is its absence; yet marks do not exist on unmarked garments. Therefore, that is not so.

281.21. It is not because of a lack of thorough knowledge that [things] do not exist; nor have you understood our intention, for we do not say that what exists in a certain place does not exist there. Rather, perceiving garments marked with specific characteristics, one recognizes others as being distinguished by the absence of those characteristics. Otherwise—
This object is apprehension; therefore, the sūtra on the object has been stated, because no other definition is possible.
282.04 [2-2-10] Because that is established, it is not a reason regarding those things that have not been characterized.

282.05 Because that is established, it is not a reason regarding those things that have not been characterized. As for those characteristics which exist in the cloth that has been characterized, 282.06 the claim that "these do not exist in anything at all" is contradicted by the fact that those which do exist are absent [in other things].
On this point it has been said: "Not due to lack of full comprehension. And this sutra is for the purpose of making this meaning known.

282.08 [2-2-11] It is not because of the establishment of dependence on characteristics existing in their own state. 282.09 We do not say that non-existence occurs only in those things which exist; rather, it is in relation to certain established characteristics that [non-existence is predicated] of those [things].
Those [characteristics] do not exist; one should understand them as being devoid of characteristics.
282.12 [2-2-12] And because non-existence prior to origination is established;

282.13 [(2-2-13)] and because there is disagreement when the cause of deliberation is questioned, there is doubt. 282.14 Regarding "and because non-existence prior to origination is established": indeed, there are two kinds of non-existence prior to origination.

282.15 Non-perceptibility [is the state] after destruction, and non-existence [is the state] prior to destruction. In this regard, that which is this non-existence [of characteristics] in those who have not been characterized is untenable, but the other is not.

Since the object does not exist, there is no non-existence; because its establishment [depends on the object], it is not a reason for those who have not been characterized. Thus, both of these are sūtras concerning quibble (*chala*).

282.18–19: Whether the answer given was understood or not, whether it was irrelevant or not understood, for that reason it is not to be employed; this is called "quibble" (*chala*). By one who states the qualification "verbal testimony (*śabda*) is authoritative because it is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*)," it is made known that verbal testimony is of various kinds. How could a qualification be meaningful when there is no distinction?

And it is not logical for a qualification to be purposeless; therefore, the word "distinct" (*nānābhūta*) is appropriate as a qualification by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). Regarding that [word], there is an investigation as to whether it is permanent or impermanent;
such investigation is examination (*parīkṣā*).

283.04 And when there is an inquiry into the cause of deliberation (*vimarśa*), doubt arises from conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*). Regarding the term "conflicting opinion" (283.05), the meaning has already been stated. In this regard, some maintain that sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa-guṇa*) and possesses the property of being manifested, like magnitude (*mahattva*).
Some, however, say: "Sound is eternal (*nitya*)," because it is a quality of space, which is a single substance that does not perish and serves as its substratum.

283.07 That which is a single substance possessing an imperishable substratum and is a quality of space is observed to be eternal, such as the magnitude of space (ākāśa-mahattva); likewise, sound [is so]. Therefore, it is eternal. Being thus eternal, its nature is that of being manifested; conjunctions, disjunctions, and sounds are its manifestors. [Sound] co-exists with odor and the other qualities.

Others maintain that sound is inherent in substances, existing like odor and so forth, and is characterized by manifestation. Others, however, say that sound, being inherent together with odor and the rest, is manifested just like odor and the rest;
its manifestors are the impacts of specific elemental transformations. Thus, sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*).

283.13 Others say that [sound] has the nature of arising and ceasing. Still others describe it thus: "Sound is impermanent, a quality of space (ākāśa-guṇa), and characterized by arising and ceasing; sound is born from the agitation of the primary elements (mahābhūta).
283.14–15 Others say that [sound] is not dependent [on a substratum] and has the nature of arising and ceasing. Therefore, there is doubt in this matter.
283.16 “Reality” (tattvam): “It is impermanent”—this is reality. What is this so-called impermanence?

283.17 It is that from which the notion “it is impermanent” arises. Furthermore, some say it is prior non-existence and non-existence after destruction. 283.18 First, some describe it thus: that which possesses prior non-existence and non-existence after destruction is impermanent. This is not because of a [logical] connection.

283.19 For an entity is not connected with prior non-existence and non-existence through destruction. Furthermore, it would follow [absurdly] that these two are unarisen. And if you consider prior non-existence and non-existence through destruction to be impermanence, 283.20–21 then prior non-existence exists while the thing has not yet arisen, and non-existence through destruction exists after the thing [has ceased].
283.22 Thus, if prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) did not exist, the cognition of impermanence would arise without a cause.

Regarding the statement "the existence of the impermanent is impermanence" (284.01): because prior and posterior non-existences are themselves absences (*abhāva*), they cannot be designated by the word "existence" (*bhāva*).
284.02 That which is called "impermanent" is that for which there is no absolute existence; of that impermanent thing, [that which...]

That existence is impermanence; moreover, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) are negations of existence, and as such, they are not [themselves] existences.
(284.04) It is not appropriate to express them by means of a term denoting existence; therefore, prior and posterior non-existence are not impermanence.

(284.05) Furthermore, there is no sense in which it could be expressed as a genitive relation, because in the rule "the suffixes *tva* and *tal* denote the state (*bhāva*) of that," the word "of that" (*tasya*) indicates the substratum (*dharmin*), while [the suffixes] denote the state (*bhāva*).

284.06 Thus, the property belongs to the substratum; yet non-existence is not a property, nor is it denotable by that word at the time of the property. 284.07 [Objection: The substratum exists, and there can be no genitive relation for that which does not exist. [Reply: Now, if you think that what comes into being did not exist previously and will not exist afterwards, even so, it is not [the case].

Something has been refuted; we too say that what did not exist previously does not exist subsequently. However, as before, the meaning of the genitive case is not present in such expressions as "the prior non-existence of the jar" (*ghaṭasya prāg-abhāvaḥ*) or "the posterior non-existence of the jar" (*ghaṭasya pradhvaṃsābhāvaḥ*). How so? Because here no relationship denoted by the genitive case is expressed.

The meaning is that this entity did not exist previously and was born afterwards; and after its destruction, it will no longer exist—this is called "impermanent" (*anitya*), and its state is "impermanence" (*anityatā*). Furthermore, because [these two] are impossible in the present, if impermanence were defined as prior non-existence and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), [it would be untenable].

284.15–16: If you think that because there is neither prior non-existence nor non-existence through destruction while an entity is present, it is impermanent, then such an expression would not be possible. If you say, "It is like the word 'cook' and so forth," and you further think that just as these words such as "cook" have the three times as their object, so too this word "impermanent" has the three times [as its object]— [The opponent continues: Just as those words such as "cook" refer to objects across the three times, so too this word "impermanent" refers to the three times. Therefore, even though the entity exists in the present, the designation "impermanent" is applied by way of its connection with prior non-existence and non-existence through destruction; thus, there is no fault. But how is it that the word "cook" and so forth have the three times as their object? It is because they denote a person who possesses the capacity for cooking and so forth at all three times. For example, one says, "Devadatta was a cook," "Devadatta is a cook," and "Devadatta will be a cook. Since the word "impermanent" likewise denotes a thing possessing the capacity for impermanence, it follows that it too has the three times as its object. Therefore, the word "impermanent" applies to a thing existing in the present by virtue of its connection with prior non-existence and non-existence through destruction. Consequently, the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this we reply: if the word "impermanent" were to denote a thing possessing the capacity for impermanence, then just as the word "cook" and so forth denote a person possessing the capacity for cooking and so forth, it would follow that the word "impermanent" would also denote a thing possessing the capacity for permanence. Why? Because the capacity for impermanence and the capacity for permanence are mutually exclusive. If one accepts that the word "impermanent" denotes a thing possessing the capacity for impermanence, then one must also accept that the word "permanent" denotes a thing possessing the capacity for permanence. And since the capacity for impermanence and the capacity for permanence are mutually exclusive, it follows that the word "impermanent" cannot denote a thing possessing the capacity for permanence. Therefore, the word "impermanent" does not denote a thing possessing the capacity for impermanence. Consequently, the word "impermanent" does not have the three times as its object, and thus the aforementioned fault remains unavoidable.
