"It will be the object. It is not gross, because it has the three times as its object; the application [of the term] "gross" [is thus inappropriate].
It is observed that the word "cook" has the three times as its object: "he was a cook," "he will be a cook," and "he is a cook.
If you think that the cognition [itself] has the three times as its object, then consider this: the cognition...

284.21–22. Furthermore, [the opponent claims] that it has the three times as its object; but that is not so, because it is not observed. For indeed, when the impermanent does not exist, there can be no "impermanence.
284.22. Thus we see the formal argument (*prayoga*). Therefore, it is illogical for cognition (*pratyaya*) to have the three times as its object. 285.01.

Consequently, neither prior non-existence (*prāk-abhāva*) nor non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsa-abhāva*) constitutes impermanence; others hold that the state of being a cause of destruction (*vināśa-hetu-bhāva*) is what constitutes it.

285.02 Others, however, say that the existence of a cause of destruction is impermanence (*anityatā*). But this is not logical, because [the cognition of impermanence] is observed even when the cause of destruction is absent. 285.03 For prior to the existence of the cause of destruction, the notion of impermanence is seen. 285.04 If impermanence were the existence of a cause of destruction, it would have to exist while jars and other such things are still present, before the separation of their shards has occurred.

285.05 It would not occur in the case of jars and the like; for indeed, when there is no fever, the cognition of one being "feverish" is never observed. 285.06 Furthermore, because there exists a cause of destruction, it is logical that the cognition [of the object] is "not impermanent," just as the cognition of a horse does not arise from the nature of a cow. Now, if you think that for which there is a cause of destruction...

285.08 "There exists that which possesses destruction; whatever possesses destruction is impermanent. We do not understand this either. [To say] "that which possesses destruction" means "that for which there is a cause of destruction";
rather, it is proper to say "that which possesses a cause of destruction" means "that for which there is a cause of destruction. And it is not [the case] because of connection with something else.
285.11 A cognition based on another cause is not logical; for it does not follow that one is "possessed of earrings" simply because of a connection with a staff.

285.12 If it is argued that this has been stated because we observe the usage "the body is subject to destruction," then you might think: 285.13 The usage "the body is subject to destruction" is observed, and such usage does not occur in the absence of a relationship [between the terms].

It must be so; for the possessive suffix *matup* is not observed when the possessor is non-existent. This *matup* is never seen where the possessor is absent—for instance, one does not say "one possessing earrings" (*kuṇḍalin*) with respect to non-existent earrings—nor is there a relationship with non-existent destruction. Therefore, the formulation "the body possesses that destruction" is incorrect. If it is argued that such usage is indeed observed:
285.17 Now, if you think that this application [of the argument] has been observed—namely, "this body is perishable" and "your objects of sense are unstable"—[we reply:

285.18 It is not so, because it is a figurative usage (*upacāra*). By means of this figurative usage, there will be an application [of the term] "perishable" to that which possesses destruction as its necessary condition. 285.19 "The objects are unstable" refers precisely to impermanence (*anityatā*); therefore, it is not a cause of destruction.
285.20 Existence is impermanence. Impermanence is the absolute disappearance of that which has reached the conditions for perception;
285.21 so say others. Others, however, describe the meaning of the term "impermanence" differently:
that a thing which has reached the conditions for perception is no longer perceived at all in its very own nature because it has disappeared—that is impermanent.
Thus it is said. But this is an empty designation; that which has reached the condition of being perceptible is utterly vanished.

One who says "it is not perceived" contradicts the established tenet (*siddhānta*). For there is no such tenet as "whatever thing has arisen is not perceived. Furthermore, regarding a thing that has not yet acquired its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*):
It has been described in many ways that disappearance (tirobhāva) is not logical; therefore, this impermanence (anityatā) is not tenable.

Furthermore, for those who describe it thus: "that very entity, having not existed and then coming into being, or having existed and then ceasing to be, is called 'impermanent'"; and for them, that state is designated as "impermanence" by means of an abstract suffix (bhāva-pratyaya). This—

But that is not tenable, because an abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) is not observed in its own sense; for no abstract suffix is ever seen to be used in its own sense. If it is argued that it is like the word "vinaya" and others—on the grounds that [the suffix] *ṭhak* is seen after words such as "vinaya" in its own sense, as in "vainayika," which means simply "discipline"—we say no, because that is not accepted. For is it not the case that the suffix *ṭhak* is indeed seen after "vinaya" and so forth in its own sense? [The answer is: "Discipline itself is 'vainayika'."
286.10 Thus, [this is] not [the case] because it is not accepted. This is not a cognition (*pratyaya*) with respect to its own object, but rather it is a connection through discipline (*vinaya*);

286.11 it is called "disciplined" (*vainayika*). It should be understood in this way in all cases. Even for those whose distinctions are not perceived, a distinction is to be inferred through inference (*anumāna*). And as for those cognitions whose distinctions you do not perceive—

286.13. Even regarding those [qualities], one considers them to be for their own sake through inference; is the distinction to be inferred? What is the inference? 286.14. If the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has the distinction as its object, then every genitive is seen to have the distinction as its object, just as the genitive is used when there is no difference in meaning.

286.15. It has been stated that this is not the case in the doctrine of the relationship between quality and the possessor of quality (*guṇa-guṇi-bhāva*). Therefore, what is this [term] "impermanence" (*anityatā*) now?

Sound is indeed inexpressible; it is not inexpressible because there is no distinction between its dependence on and independence from a limit (*avadhi*). 286.17–18: That existence of a thing which is delimited by both ends is impermanence (*anityatā*);
whereas that existence of a thing which is not delimited by either end is permanence (*nityatā*), as for example, inherence (*samavāya*), which, though being one, [is permanent].
286.19 When distinguished by its effect, it is designated as the cause; when distinguished by its cause, [it is designated as] the effect.
286.20 And how is it that this cognition—namely, "effect" and "cause"—is not without a cause?
286.21 Because it occurs at certain times, it does not have a non-entity as its cause; for a cognition of a non-entity would be distinct [from the object]. Nor is it without a cause.

286.22 And because it is distinct from existence (*sattā*), it would follow that this [object] is "existent" by virtue of existence; however, this is distinct from the cognition of existence (*sattā-pratyaya*).
287.01 It is distinct from that; therefore, it does not arise from existence, because here it is caused by a qualifier and has a relation as its cause.
287.02 Here, in the case of "the cloth is in these threads," a cognition arises characterized by a substratum (*ādhāra*); and this does not occur when [the object] is non-existent.
287.03 Since it is possible for there to be the notion "here" (ihapratyaya) with respect to a relation, that which is this notion "here" is inherence (samavāya).

287.04 When there is inherence in an effect, [that substratum] is designated as the cause; because of its connection with a particular quality, a word is applied to a certain object. 287.05 In expressing that [inherence], the suffixes -tva and -tal are used; since inherence in the effect exists, this [notion of "being here"] occurs.

287.06. Causality is inherence in the effect; by this, being-an-effect is explained. The cause is inherence as qualified by the causal factor; being-an-effect is like inherence. Just as inherence is so, even existence (sattā), though being one, is called "non-eternal" because it relates to entities delimited by both ends [beginning and end].
287.09. From the opposite [of this], there is permanence. Due to its connection with this impermanence, sound is impermanent.
287.10 [2-2-13(14)] Because it has a beginning, because it is perceptible by the senses, like that which is produced, and because of its metaphorical designation.

287.11 "Because it has a beginning"—beginning means origin or cause; because it possesses a cause, it is non-eternal. 287.12 This is the meaning of the aphorism. Furthermore, what is this so-called "possession of a cause"? It refers to the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

287.13 The conformity to difference and the property of having the nature of arising do not exist in those things manifested by it. For nothing whatsoever is observed to conform to the difference in its efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) while being manifested. If it is argued that there is doubt because perception occurs immediately after conjunction and disjunction—should you think that [manifestation] follows conjunction and disjunction—then...
Immediately after [the conjunction and disjunction], the sound is perceived; and that perception immediately following them is consistent even with something being manifested (*vyajyamāna*).
Therefore, there is doubt: is this [sound] manifested by the conjunction and disjunction, or is it produced?
It is not manifested, because it is perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*). What is this "perceptibility by the senses"? It is proximity to the sense organ.

287.19–20: "It is perceptible by the senses"—what follows from that? If "perceptible by the senses" means that which is grasped through proximity to the sense organ, then it is not manifested. For it is not logical for that which is being manifested to have proximity with the sense organ.
How so? 287.21: Thus, the auditory organ does not first go to the location of the sound, because it is formless; and whatever is formless is devoid of action.

288.01 Just as form and so forth are non-material, and space is likewise, therefore it is devoid of action. If it is argued that [space] possesses action because of the inherence of the quality that is the cause of action— should you think that wherever the quality which is the cause of action exists, that thing is seen to possess action, as in the case of a clod of earth, and space is likewise— therefore...

288.04 This [quality] is also possessed of action; [this is not so], because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, quality (*guṇa*) is the cause of action. 288.05 [Objection: "The self is not possessed of action," [but this is] inconclusive, because even that which exists does not possess action.

288.06 [Response: It is not a reason [for non-action], because of the obstruction by great dimension (*mahat-parimāṇa*); for although impact (*abhighāta*) exists in space (*ākāśa*), it does not [produce action].

288.07 The cause for the absence of action is the obstruction by a large dimension (*mahat-parimāṇa*). Because of the largeness that exists in space, the impact residing therein—which is inherent in the same substrate (*ekārthasamaveta*)—is obstructed. This is just as, for example, the heaviness of a clod of earth is dependent [on other factors] because its conjunction is obstructed by a conjunction residing in the same substrate.

If you say this results in an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*): suppose you think that if gravity, being obstructed by conjunction, does not initiate action, then it initiates action upon the removal of that obstruction. But in that case, it follows that gravity is a cause of action that is dependent [on other factors]. And if that were so, there would be a contradiction with the treatise (*śāstra*), which states that [gravity] is independent (*nirapekṣa*).
288.13 "Heaviness is the cause of action"—this is indeed the teaching. It is not [the case] that it is independent, because otherwise there would be a different interpretation.
288.14 This is not the meaning of "independent" in the sense that heaviness does not depend on anything at all;
rather, 288.15 it means that it does not depend on any other subsequent cause. Thus, heaviness is the cause of action when it is independent.

288.16 There is no contradiction; for thus says the treatise: "In the absence of conjunction, falling occurs due to gravity" (288.17). Furthermore, because of the absence of an object [to obstruct it], the mere conjunction of the qualities that cause action is the reason for possessing action; however, when there is a conjunction of the qualities that cause action, if [the substance] is corporeal...

288.19 When the object of action is a material form (*mūrti*) and the cause of action is an unobstructed quality (*guṇa*), then 288.20 action arises. Therefore, because it lacks action, space does not move; sound also [does not move], 288.21 precisely because it is devoid of action. Furthermore, there is no perception of that which has not been reached, [otherwise] there would be the perception of all sounds.

By way of reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), the existence of a continuum (*santāna*) is established through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). In this regard, the first sound is caused by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*); from that [first sound], subsequent sounds arise in all directions according to the analogy of a cluster of *kadamba* flowers.
From each of those, a single sound arises individually according to the analogy of decreasing intensity—such as "weaker" or "weakest"—without obstruction of its substratum.
289.03 Being followed [in succession], it then appears; because of the extreme slowness of the final [sound], there is the production of another sound.

289.04 The obstruction of its capacity occurs due to some kind of impediment. Therefore, regarding the cessation of the series of sounds (śabda-santāna), that [sound] which reaches the region of space within the ear-cavity is perceived.
289.06 It is not the other; therefore, it is perceptible by the senses, and since that is not possible otherwise, it follows that it is impermanent.

289.07 If you say it is one and the same, no, because it would follow that it is perceived by everyone simultaneously. Or, if you think: "I do not admit there are intervals within the sound, but rather this single sound remains pervading space."

289.09. Being manifested by conjunction and disjunction, it is perceived, just as a jar or similar object situated in a room [is perceived] through the conjunction with a lamp. And that is not so, because it would follow that it would be perceived by everyone;
for if a single sound were situated pervasively and, being manifested by conjunction, produced a cognition of the object for those possessing the auditory organ—[then this consequence would follow].

289.12–14. If you think that sound is manifested by anything whatsoever situated anywhere, then it would be perceived by all those possessing the sense of hearing; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, this notion—that there is manifestation in a particular location—is a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). If you argue that there is manifestation [only] in one part, we say no, because neither identity (*tādātmya*) nor non-identity (*atādātmya*) is possible [between the whole and its parts]. Now, if you think...
"It is true that [the word] remains established as something extended, yet one part of that which is so established is manifested by a cause.

This is not so, because neither identity nor non-identity with it is possible. Regarding those parts of the word that you consider—whether they are identical to the nature of the word or not? And what follows from this? If they are identical to the nature of the word...

289.18. Therefore, [if it is argued] that there are many sounds, this is a contradiction; for if they are not of the nature of sound, then [the claim] does not hold. 289.19. It follows that the cognition of an object arises from sound; and their intrinsic nature must be explained. 289.20. This is because sound functions in space (ākāśa) and because it does not denote a single part [of the whole]. "A single part" refers to a compound.

289.21 This is a single word and it is also a location (*deśa*). In this context, the word "location" has the sense of a substratum (*ādhāra*) or the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*). First of all, the sense of a substratum is not tenable, because sound resides in space (*ākāśa*); sound resides in space because it is a quality of that [space]. Therefore, there is no substratum distinct from space.

290.03 Furthermore, there is no sense of "cause" [here], because you yourself accept that sound is unproduced (*akṛtaka*) when you assert, "Sound is unproduced. Therefore, you ought not to say that a "part" (*ekadeśa*) is the cause, nor is another [meaning] possible. 290.04–05 Thus, the statement that a "part" of the sound is manifested is empty; for a "part" of the sound does not exist.
Furthermore, there would be no cognition of meaning through manifestation, because all phonemes (varṇa) are pervasive, just like [the universal] "phoneme-ness" itself.

On this view, there is no manifestation of a portion of a phoneme, nor is it possible to define a portion of a phoneme; and even from such a defined portion, the cognition of meaning does not arise from the phonemes.
Because it is not admitted that meaning is conveyed [by them]. Even the phonemes (*varṇa*), taken individually, do not convey meaning;

how much less so their parts? By this, the argument for plurality is refuted. Just as there is a fault in the manifestation of a single [phoneme], so too there is a fault in the pervasiveness of multiple sounds, namely, the resulting cacophony (*kolāhala*).
It would be so, if it were admitted that multiple sounds exist simultaneously in space;
for if one accepts that when a single sound-manifesting cause is employed, there is the manifestation of all sounds occupying the same location,
then there would be a cacophony (*kolāhala*), just as there is the excessive clamor produced by the performance of wrestlers and actors in an assembly.
When [the organs] are turned toward them and [the sounds] resound, it follows that there is no rule stating that [a single sound] is not manifold and all-pervading.
And if multiple sounds were to exist simultaneously in space, then whatever manifestor is employed would manifest all [sounds] occupying the same location. This being so, when—

At that time, while lutes are being played, even the braying of a donkey is heard; for there is no observed restriction among manifestors regarding objects to be grasped by the same sense organ that occupy the same location. If it is argued that its manifestation occurs because of this [manifestor], that is not so, because it has never been observed. Furthermore, suppose you think that when multiple sounds are brought together...

290.21–291.02: [The opponent argues: "When the manifesters differ, the individual manifestations—which conform to the differences among the manifesters—arise for each respective sound; therefore, [the word is not eternal]. This is not so, because it is not observed. For no restriction regarding the manifesters is observed in the case of things that occupy the same location and are perceptible by a single sense organ. Indeed, a lamp does not [manifest] only that which is perceptible by a single sense organ.

If it is argued that [the cognition] does not manifest multiple objects encountered simultaneously because it would be like a universal (*sāmānya*), we say no, because that is not accepted. Now, if you think that when there is a conjunction of multiple objects,
universals are connected with all individual instances (*vyakti*), and that upon this multiple connection, the universal—

291.06 [The opponent claims: "A certain universal (*sāmānya*) is manifested by a certain object. [The author replies: Even when there is a conjunction of many objects, it is not the case that one manifestor manifests one particular sound; for that is not accepted. Furthermore, it is not accepted that a universal is connected with many objects of different classes (*bhinna-jātīya*), but rather—

291.09. The universal "cowness" (gotva) pervades all its own objects; it exists only in cows and not in horses and the like. "Horseness" (aśvatva) exists only in horses and not in cows and the like. Therefore, this example is unequal. Furthermore, [you argue that] sound is not manifested because it is not perceived when the manifesting agent is absent.
291.10–11. If you think that sound is perceived only when it is manifested by conjunction and disjunction, [then...]

291.12 That [wind] too would not be perceived in the absence of conjunction, yet it is perceived when there is the conjunction of the axe and the wood during the cutting of wood. 291.13 If it is argued that "the wind arises from impact," it has already been stated here: suppose you think that wind is produced from the impact of the axe and the wood; that wind proceeds by way of a continuous series (*santāna*), and that series—

Functioning by means of its activity, it reaches the space within the ear-cavity; upon reaching that, the sound situated therein is perceived. It has been stated here that just as one sound exists in the space beyond the ear-cavity, so too do all sounds exist; thus, whatever manifestor is employed [is effective].

If anything could be the manifestor of any sound whatsoever, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving all sounds; yet such a restriction would not exist. Furthermore, even when the cause [of manifestation] is present, it is not manifested everywhere.
Indeed, that which is manifested is never seen to be manifested everywhere when its cause is present, just as...

291.21 Those seeking a jar, having entered a room or similar space that is devoid of jars and other objects while carrying a lamp, do not perceive jars and the like; thus, they do not apprehend jars and such through manifestation (*abhivyakti*).

Furthermore, we do not observe that [manifestation occurs] from sound anywhere, even when there is the conjunction of the impact of the palate and other [articulatory organs]. Therefore, it is not [the case that sound manifests them].
"It is manifested. If it is argued that [the universal] exists everywhere, we say no, because the answer has already been stated. Now, if you think:

"The criticism applies to one for whom words function only in a single location; but for us, all [words] are pervasive. Therefore, this fault does not apply," we reply: no, because the answer has already been stated. This statement has already been answered.

Furthermore, because one applies a further effort for concentration [on the sound], it is therefore not manifested. Also, since the sound located in a distant place is not perceived at the same location as the *nāda*, the *nāda* is not the manifestor.
It has already been refuted that these conjunctions and disjunctions of air are the manifestors.

292.08 And because of metaphorical designation like that of "produced" (*kṛtaka*): just as "intense" or "weak" is metaphorically designated as "produced," so too is "intense pleasure" or "weak [pleasure]" metaphorically designated as "pleasure. 292.09 Furthermore, "intense sound" or "weak sound" is metaphorically designated [in this way]. And here the formal argument (*prayoga*) is: sound is impermanent, because it has intense or weak objects, like pleasure or pain; thus it is "produced."

292.11 By this sūtra, "as in the case of [the term] 'produced' (kṛtaka-vat) through metaphorical application" (upacārāt), there is a collection of all properties that serve as means of proving impermanence. 292.12 This is because the inclusion of the phrase "as in the case of produced" is for the purpose of providing an illustration (udāharaṇa-artha). Just as, for example, in the case of sound—which possesses both generality and particularity, is perceptible by external sense organs such as those of ourselves and others, and is not perceived despite the absence of any cause for its non-perception—it is [inferred] as a quality. 292.13 [Thus, it is established as impermanent.]

[The opponent argues: "Because it is external to our senses like [other objects] such as ourselves," and so forth. If you say that because the word *tīvra* (intense) has as its object an intense thing (*artha*), it does not have sound (*śabda*) and the like as its object—then you must consider this:
by the word *tīvra*, an intense thing is denoted, not sound; nor can a word whose object is one thing be a communicator of a different thing.

292.17 Thus, because the word "intense" (*tīvra*), which stands in grammatical apposition with the word "sound" (*śabda*), is denotative [of the same object]. 292.18 It is true that this word "intense," when uttered in isolation, indicates a common property among substance, quality, and action; however, when the word "sound" is uttered alongside it, the word "sound" likewise denotes a sound that possesses manifold properties.

Furthermore, when these two terms "intense" (*tīvra*) and "sound" (*śabda*) are expressed as having entered into a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), then by the word "intense," other properties (*dharma-antara*) are excluded, and by the word "sound," other substrata (*dharmi-antara*) are excluded. Because both words are employed, the [specific] sound is understood; therefore, it is logical that [the object] is the domain of the word "intense."

293.02 “Sound is impermanent. [Objection: Because the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is of such a nature, the perception [of sound] possesses intensity or dullness, just as is the case with color-form (*rūpa*). [Reply: No, because suppression (*abhibhava*) is logically possible. The rest is in the *Bhāṣya*. [Objection: Perception conforms to the differences in its causes (*nimitta*). [Reply: No, because a difference in perception is not observed in a single [object]. Now, you might think:

The sound does not differ; however, while the sound remains undifferentiated, its apprehension conforms to a difference in the causes [of that apprehension]. And as for the claim that "there is suppression because of apprehension," this is not so, because a difference in apprehension is never observed in a single [object], provided the sound is undifferentiated.
If the sound were undifferentiated, a difference in apprehension would not occur; for we do not observe a difference in apprehension regarding an object that is itself undifferentiated.

293.08 Now, if you think that the apprehensions differ even when the object is not different, then there would always be a difference in apprehension; consequently, the notions of "different" and "not different" would not occur [as distinct].
Furthermore, the suppression of one apprehension by another is untenable, because two apprehensions cannot exist simultaneously. For indeed—
293.11–13: If [the two cognitions] were simultaneous, there would be no single apprehension that could suppress the self [of the sound];
nor is this suppression possible. Therefore, the sound is distinct [from the cognition].

Furthermore, since suppression is untenable, and because manifestation occurs at a location identical to that of the manifestor due to the absence of reaching [the object], it is manifested in a place co-extensive with the manifestor.
293.14 Thus, in this position, suppression is not possible; why? Because [the sound] occupies the same location as the manifestor (vyañjaka).
293.15 For a sound that has not reached the same location as the manifestor cannot be suppressed, because it has not been reached.
293.16 Indeed, that which has not been reached does not become a suppressor. If, on the other hand, something could be a suppressor even without being reached—
293.17 You might think that there would be the consequence of never hearing the sounds of a lute; for if [sounds] such as those of a conch or a donkey do not reach [the ear], they would be [unheard].

293.18 [If you say they are] "overpowered," then the sounds of the lute and so forth would never be heard at all. 293.19 If you argue that [they exist] everywhere, no, because the previous fault persists. Or if you think that which is manifested occupies the same location as its manifestor—
293.20 He accepts [the existence of] sound; this is his fault. For us, however, all sounds occupy the same location.

293.21 Therefore, [he argues] there is no fault here. [We reply: No, because the previous fault has not been avoided. Even if sounds occupy the same location, 293.22 there is no restriction regarding the manifestors; whatever manifestor is employed, it does not manifest everything.
294.01. [The claim] that sound has manifestation as its cause does not avoid the previously mentioned fault. Furthermore, 294.02.
regarding the co-location [of sounds], there would be the suppression of the sounds of the lute and the flute by the sound of the conch;
294.03. thus, it would follow that the sounds of the lute and so forth could not be heard. Therefore, the sounds themselves are distinct, and of these...
294.04 When distinct [sounds] occupy the same location, those that inhere simultaneously in the space within the ear-cavity—among them, the sound that is more intense is the subduer of the other.
294.05–06 And what is called "subduing" (abhibhava) is simply the non-perception of the weaker [sound] due to the perception of the stronger one. And if...
294.07. Sound, as a process within a continuum, reaches the region of space enclosed by the ear-cavity and is then perceived.

294.08. However, the cognition of direction and location—such as "the sound is from the east" or "the sound is from the north"—would not occur; for such a cognition of direction and location is never observed when objects are in close proximity, as is the case with odors and the like. Nor [is it due to] the material cause (*upādāna*).
294.10 Because the designation of direction and place is based on a cause (nimitta), this designation of direction and place that occurs with respect to sounds is not [inherently so].

294.11 This designation of direction and place would be identical to that which arises from causes distinct from "prior," "posterior," and so forth, due to the perception of a single location; therefore, it is not caused by sound.
294.13 Then, from what does this [perception] arise? It must be stated that it is due to a difference in causes (nimitta).
294.14 Those causes of sound, which consist of conjunctions (saṃyoga) and provide assistance, possess direction and location;
294.15 because of the difference among those causes, there are cognitions of direction and location. This applies to those sounds whose causes are being perceived.

294.16 Among these, this [notion] is appropriate for those for whom no signs (nimitta) are perceived; however, regarding those [objects] where there is a cognition of direction and place, 294.17 it is neither appropriate nor inappropriate.
This is because, at the outset, the stream of sound (śabda-santāna) is directed toward a distinction of signs (nimitta-bheda).
294.18 As for that stream of sound which arises from a particular sign, it [arises] from all sides.

294.19–21. There, one sound follows after another; that initial sound which is connected with the portion of the space of the ether facing the ear-cavity is the cause for the designation of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, regarding the sound.
However, when there is no discernment of the initial sound, the opposite occurs.

294.22 Thus some say that there are no notions of direction or location with respect to sounds. 295.01 Why? Because when the object of the visual faculty is established, there is a determination of direction and location; for instance, among those born blind, 295.02 there are no notions such as "prior" or "posterior" regarding sound. Others, however, [use] the designation of direction and location...
295.03. They assert that the eye and the ear function without reaching [their objects]. To them, the answer has been stated by those explaining the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra* at 295.04.

295.05 [2-2-14(15)] It is not so, because the absence of a jar is a generality (sāmānya) and is eternal; for even in the case of eternal things, there is a figurative designation (upacāra) as if they were non-eternal.

295.06 And 295.07: "It is not so, because the absence of a jar is a generality and is eternal; for even in the case of eternal things, there is a figurative designation as if they were non-eternal"—this is the [meaning of the] Sūtra.
The purpose [of this section] is to demonstrate that the previous reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The remainder is in the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

[2-2-15(16)] There is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) because of the distinction between the difference of reality (*tattva*) and figurative application (*bhākta*). Regarding the term "permanence" (*nityatva*) here—
295.11 What, then, is reality? It is the contact with the existence of a thing that is not delimited by either extreme [of past or future].

295.12 Through its opposite, there is impermanence; and this does not exist in the case of non-existence (abhāva). However, that [term "permanent"] is used figuratively, as in "the absence of a jar is permanent," as if it were permanent, yet it is not actually permanent because the two times [past and future] are not experienced.

Destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) does not exist prior [to the destruction], nor does it exist at the time of the jar; prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) does not exist at the time of the jar, nor at the time of its destruction. How then is it said to be "eternal-like" (*nitya iva*)? By what figurative application (*bhakti*)? This figurative application is that prior non-existence is the absence of a cause, while destructive non-existence is the absence of destruction.
295.17 Both non-existence and existence have eternal objects; because of this commonality, it is "eternal-like," yet not [absolutely] eternal.
295.18 Furthermore, that which is graspable through the proximity of the sense faculties is "sensory" (*aindriyaka*).

295.19 [2-2-16(15)] Because of the qualification by inference based on the continuum (santāna), there is no deviation. We do not [establish] impermanence because of its being perceptible by the senses; rather, by this [inference], we refute the manifestation (abhivyakti) of sound.
For it has been stated previously that it is not logical for that which is being manifested to possess the quality of being perceptible by the senses.
296.04 [2-2-17(18)] Because the term "portion" (*pradeśa*) is used to denote the causal substance (*kāraṇa-dravya*), there is no deviation [of the reason] even in the case of eternal things.
296.05 Thus, because the causal substance is denoted by the word "portion," there is no deviation even in the case of eternal things; for indeed—

296.07. For eternal substances, the term "part" (*pradeśa*) denotes a cause. [Thus one speaks of] "a part of space" (296.08). [One also speaks of] "a part of the self. In these cases, the causal substance of space and the self is not being denoted;
for example, why is it not so denoted in the case of a produced thing? Because it does not exist. Indeed, those [causes] do not exist.
296.10 “The regions of space and so forth do not exist. Why? Because they are not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

296.11 If the regions of space and so forth were to exist, they would be perceived through a means of valid cognition; how then can it be said that they are not perceived through a means of valid cognition? This is because no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is tenable. By the word “region” (*pradeśa*), is the cause (*kāraṇa*) being denoted? 296.12 [Or rather,] by the word “region,” is the effect being denoted? [In either case, no such entity is established.]

296.13 Or, [space] is not a cause because it is unproduced; since space is unproduced, it is therefore not [a cause]. 296.14 The meaning of "cause" is not expressed by the word "location," nor is it a support, because it is unsupported; space is unsupported.
296.15 Thus, the sense of it being a support cannot be asserted. If it is argued that this contradicts common worldly usage, we say no, for it is otherwise.
296.16 Because that is untenable: if you maintain that space is partless (*niḥpradeśa*), does it not contradict common worldly experience?

296.17 [For instance, one says] "the sun is covered by its eastern part"; this would not be possible otherwise. 296.18 Regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*), if it is described as having a non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*) by means of the term "part" (*pradeśa*), there is no contradiction with common worldly experience; for since...

The non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpya-vṛttitva*) of conjunction is expressed by the term "region" (*pradeśa*). And this [conjunction] is common to space and to a substance that possesses regions. Indeed, the conjunction that exists between two limited objects such as *āmalaka* fruits does not pervade them both, just as they themselves possess regions.

297.03 Even the conjunction with space does not pervade space; because it shares the common property of being a substance possessing parts, like that which has parts, 297.04 the cognition "space" is a figurative (bhākta) one. What, then, is this figurativeness? It is the state of being as if it were so for that which is not so. Figurativeness (bhakti) is so called because it partakes (bhajyate) in a commonality with those things that possess such a nature in both respects. For this reason...

297.06 Because of its similarity [to space], the word "region" (pradeśa) functions as a superimposition upon space. Since space shares a commonality with substances that possess regions—namely, that conjunction has a pervasive occurrence (vyāpya-vṛttitva)—the word "region" is therefore applied to space as well. If it is asked, "Is this not so in reality? Why? [the answer is: No, because it is not established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

297.09 Because of non-apprehension. Now, if you think that spatial divisions (*ākāśa-pradeśa*) are metaphorically designated in space because they share the commonality of being substances with parts, but do not exist in reality—[we reply] that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this, and thus there is no [proof of] a spatial division through a means of valid cognition; for there is no perception or other [means of valid cognition] that establishes spatial divisions of space and so forth.

297.12 [The opponent claims] that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible; however, this is because [space] is not designated by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*). If there were spatial divisions (*pradeśa*) of space, they would have to be designated by way of their own nature, just as the threads are the spatial divisions of a cloth.
But when it is asked, "What are the spatial divisions of space?", they cannot be designated by way of their own nature. 297.13–14 [Therefore, such divisions do not exist.]

297.15 And the impossibility of the word *kim* (what) is as before. Furthermore, regarding those intermediate spaces of ether (*ākāśa*) that one considers—do they consist of ether or not? What follows from this? If they consist of ether, it follows that ether is manifold. 297.17 If, on the other hand, they do not, then their intrinsic nature must be stated; and how could they be the "spaces" (*pradeśa*) of that [ether]?
Thus it should be said: "Being non-spatial in nature, they are regions of space.

For what purpose is this stated? For example, when it is said that "threads are the regions of a cloth," the sense of being a cause is understood, as well as the sense of being a support; however, this [duality] does not exist in the case of the regions of space. Regarding "region"—

297.21 If it is argued that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is without a substratum because [space] is non-existent, we say no; it is not without a substratum because it resides in space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, 298.01 if you think:
"If there are no spatial points of space, then conjunction, which has those spatial points as its locus, would be without a substratum," [we reply:
it is not without a substratum because it resides in space. For it is by you yourself that space is spoken of [as existing].

298.03–04. If it is argued that because there is a substratum (*āśraya*), there is no lack of support, and therefore [all things] occupy the same location (*samāna-deśa*), we say no, because this is not a valid refutation (*abādhanāt*).

298.04–05. Now, if you think that those conjunctions of corporeal substances which exist in a location of space would all necessarily occupy the same location due to the absence of distinct spatial parts (*pradeśa*), then even if they do occupy the same location in this way, it does not follow [that they are identical].

298.06–07: "Something is obstructed"—thus, because it shares the common property of being a substance with spatial divisions (*pradeśavat-dravya-sāmānya*), the notion that "this is a space-division" (*ākāśa-pradeśa*) is a figurative cognition (*bhāktaḥ pratyayaḥ*). [Objection: Since [space] lacks spatial divisions, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving all sounds everywhere at all times.
298.07–08: [Reply: No, for the answer has already been stated. Now, if you think: "If space is without spatial divisions, then by that..."

298.09. In that case, since all sounds would occupy the same location, every sound would be perceived by everyone; however, it is not so perceived. Therefore, sounds have distinct locations, because they are not apprehended by all [hearers], just like the form of a finger or similar objects.
298.11. This [objection] is not valid, because the answer has already been stated. This has already been answered in the same manner as [the case of] conjunction.
Because of this reason, those who maintain that sound, conjunction, and so forth are pervasive—just like the form of a finger—should be asked as follows:
What is the meaning of "pervasiveness"? If pervasiveness means existing in its substrate (*āśraya-vṛttitva*), then nothing is contradicted.
But if it means something else, such [a thing] does not exist. We, however, hold that the pervasion of the form of a finger consists in its being perceived whenever its substrate is perceived.

We reply: sound and the other [sensory objects] are not perceived when their substratum is perceived; therefore, like the color of a finger, they are not pervasive. Thus, for those things that exist as a collection, their perception or non-perception when a single constituent of the collection is perceived constitutes pervasion or non-pervasion, provided they share a single substratum, given that their substratum has been perceived. Now, as for those...

298.19–20. Among the conjunctions of corporeal things with space, some are produced while others are unproduced. In that regard, the conjunction of an effect-substance [with space] is produced, because it is a conjunction born of conjunction (*saṃyogaja*).
This is because the conjunction of the effect with its causes occurs at the very moment it arises.
299.01 However, some do not accept that [conjunction] is produced by action, because conjunction, being inseparable, exists as long as the substance exists.

299.02 [They argue: "There is no [action-produced] conjunction in space; thus, there is no conjunction in space produced by action. 299.03 Yet, they maintain that the conjunction of an atom with space is something produced. In that regard, first, concerning the conjunction of an atom and space:

299.04 Regarding its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), the inference is as follows: the atom (*paramāṇu*) is related to space through a relation of being produced, because it possesses corporeality (*mūrtimattva*) and so forth, like a jar or similar objects. The conjunction of the effect with space, which is the subject of dispute, does not endure for as long as the substance exists, because—while existing in a substance that possesses motion—it is not the opposite of non-attainment (*aprāpti*) in a substrate that is indestructible.

Because [ether] is not possessed of form, like the conjunction of that which is other than corporeal; therefore, the conjunction of ether with an effect-substance is produced by conjunction, whereas the conjunction of an atom is produced by action. Regarding the object of dispute:
ether and the others are partless, because they are conjoined with substances possessing action, like an atom.
299.10 Just as the conjunctions of atoms with active substances do not exist in inactive substances, so too [is the case] with that which possesses conjunction.
299.11 Like sound and cognition, etc., [these qualities] are non-pervasive in the self (*ātman*), because conjunction has a non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) within the self.
299.12 It has been explained that "region" (*pradeśa*) means a part; and [the self] is one, yet it relates to substances that possess multiple forms and regions.
The meaning of "region" (pradeśa) is as follows: or rather, that which constitutes the state of being related to many things possessing regions, while space itself is a single entity;

this is the commonality of substances possessing regions, such as a jar and so forth. But why is no sūtra heard from the author of the sūtras regarding this point? [It is because] in what sense is space without regions (niṣpradeśa), and [why is it said] "space is without regions"?

299.16 [The opponent argues: "Because this meaning is understood from the sense (*arthataḥ*), it is not a *sūtra*; for since this meaning is understood from the sense, it is therefore not formulated as a *sūtra*.
Or, [it is argued that] it is not a *sūtra* because it does not establish a verbal sequence (*śabda-santāna*) through understanding from the sense.

299.18 Or, its understanding [comes] from the established tenets of the treatise (*śāstra-siddhānta*); however, the established tenets of the treatise are many, being designated as "reasoning" (*nyāya*).

299.19. Since inference (*anumāna*) is a branch [of grammar], that which is not explicitly stated [in the *sūtra*] is understood through it; therefore, it is not formulated as a *sūtra*. Furthermore, there is this: "This exists" (299.20). The commentary states: "It does not exist. What is the subject matter of this inquiry (*paryanuyoga*)? [The answer is: those who postulate the eternity of a word based on its existence are the ones to be questioned thus: "Is it perceived or not? (300.01).
Those who imagine the eternity of a word because it exists are the ones to be subjected to this inquiry.
"How do you gentlemen understand this: 'this exists' and 'this does not exist'? When questioned thus, they reply:
"By means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), through apprehension and non-apprehension. [If that is so,] then sound (*śabda*) does not exist.
300.05 [2-2-18(19)] Because of non-perception prior to utterance, and because of the non-perception of obstructions and so forth;

300.06 "Because of non-perception prior to utterance, and because of the non-perception of obstructions and so forth"—and that which is admitted by both parties, 300.07 namely, the impermanence of jars and the like, and those things to be questioned as such: this which is impermanent, such as a jar.

300.08 “How do you establish that it is impermanent? When thus questioned, if they establish the principle of impermanence regarding jars and so forth [as being due to their destruction], then [the same applies] to sound; this is the meaning of the Sūtra. [The Sūtra states: “Because there is non-perception of an existing thing when the causes for its non-perception are absent, sound is impermanent. The rest [is as follows].

In the Bhāṣya: [Objection: "If it is argued that there is no perception because of the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), [we reply: No, for the answer has already been stated. 300.12 The utterance of sound is its manifestor; since that is absent, it is not perceived. Thus, the qualification ‘because of non-perception’ is unestablished, as there is an absence of the cause [of perception]. 300.13 What is this so-called ‘utterance’? It is [an action] produced by the effort born of the desire to speak."
300.14. The striking against the locations such as the throat by the abdominal air when it is impelled [is not the cause], because the answer to that has already been stated.

300.15. Striking is the conjunction of the air with the palate and so forth, which depends on the momentum inherent in the air; [this is] conjunction. 300.16. That [conjunction] is the manifestor [of sound] has already been refuted. And thus, the truth is not covered by dust.
300.17 He said this: what is its meaning? When the truth has been stated, one objects by means of a *jāti* (fallacious sophistry), and that is the *jāti*.
300.18 [2-2-19(20)] Because that non-perception is itself unperceived, the existence of an obstruction is established.
300.19 “Because that non-perception is itself unperceived, the existence of an obstruction is established. What is the meaning of this statement?

300.20 The meaning is that there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to the non-perception of obstructions and so forth; for example, just as the non-perception of obstructions and so forth remains unperceived itself.
300.21 Furthermore, [the claim] that "there is likewise an obscuration" is inconclusive; for if there is non-apprehension, then that which is not being apprehended does not exist.
301.01 Because of its absence, apprehension exists; and it is established that there is no apprehension of that which is non-existent.
301.02 [This refers to] the obscuration. But how do you know that the non-apprehension of the obscuration is not itself apprehended?

301.03 Thus, what is there to be known here? Since it is to be personally realized (*pratyātma-vedanīya*), one realizes for oneself alone the non-perception of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-anupalabdhi*) and 301.04 the perception of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-upalabdhi*). This being the case, the subsequent statement has its subject matter already removed (*apahṛta-viṣaya*). 301.05 "Its subject matter is removed" means that there is no further arising for it; this is stated by way of a concession (*abhyanujñāna-vāda*).
And it is said: 301.06.
301.07 [2-2-20(21)] Even from non-perception, just as there is the existence of non-apprehension, there is no impossibility of an obscuration;
301.08 because of non-perception;
301.09 even from non-perception, just as there is the existence of non-apprehension, there is no impossibility of an obscuration, because of non-perception.
301.10 Thus, the meaning of this sūtra is that non-apprehension is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
301.11 [2-2-21(22)] Because non-apprehension has the nature of non-apprehension, it is not a valid reason (ahetu).

301.12 Because non-apprehension has the nature of non-apprehension, it is not a valid reason; for there is an opposition based on what is not of that same class. 301.13 "It is not an answer"—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Just as sound is of such a nature that it is impermanent, so too is that which is of that same nature...

301.14 “Nothing eternal has been observed. And what was said in this regard? It was stated: “Eternality is the connection with the existence of an entity that is not delimited by either end [of time]. Therefore, because it is a counter-position based on an incorrect understanding, this is trivial. [The argument] “Sound is impermanent, because, while being a quality, it is perceived by the sense organs of us and others... [is thus refuted].

301.17 Because it is an object [of cognition], like cognition (*buddhi*). Because, while not being all-pervasive, it inheres in an all-pervasive substance, it is perceptible, like pleasure (*sukha*). The reason for the absence of spatial parts (*niṣpradeśatva*) in space (*ākāśa*) is: "Space is without spatial parts because it is all-pervasive, like the self (*ātman*). Since it is a substance that is always formless, it is all-pervasive, just like the self.
Precisely because of that [being eternal], it possesses the quality of being uncreated and all-pervasive; for as long as it exists as a substance-pervader, it is always formless (*amūrta*).
By this, space (*diś*) and time (*kāla*) are explained. Thus much is established by the persistence of its own proof:
"Sound is impermanent."
302.01. "Now, one who asserts the eternity of sound," so says the Bhāṣya.
302.02. Since a dispute is rooted in authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is an inquiry into the reason (*hetu*). Dispute (*vipratipatti*) is defined as follows: 302.03.

It is the apprehension of contradictory properties regarding a single object by two [parties]. And a dispute is not possible without an authoritative means of knowledge; therefore, an authority for permanence must be stated. Hence he says: "It is permanent."
302.05 Sound [is not a substance] because it lacks tangibility.
302.06 [2-2-22(23)] Because it is intangible.

302.07 [2-2-23(24)] It is not [the case that] action is impermanent. 302.08 The application [of the reason] "like space" for one whose counter-example (vipakṣa) is not perceived in even a single part is subject to deviation (vyabhicāra).
The sūtra is for the purpose of demonstration; it is not because of the impermanence of karma. The remainder of this is in the Bhāṣya.
302.10 [2-2-24(25)] Not so, because atoms are eternal.
302.11 [2-2-25(26)] Because of transmission.
302.12 This is another reason for the eternity of sound: because of transmission; for nothing whatsoever is eternal [in that sense].

"Being handed over" [is a reason] that is contradictory because there is no positive example (*anvayin*); for there is no instance where something is both handed over and eternal. Now, if this thesis-meaning is established as "sound is [eternal] because it is handed over, like a jar and so forth," even so, its eternality is not proven.
302.16 [2-2-26(27)] The non-perception of that interval is not a valid reason. 302.17 [2-2-27(28)] There is no refutation because of the act of teaching.
302.18 The non-perception of that interval is not a valid reason; for while the giver and the recipient remain [in their respective positions],...
302.19 “It would be perceived in the interval”—this contradicts the meaning of the Sūtra. [Response: There is no contradiction, because of inference (anumāna).
302.20 Perception does not negate the existence of that which is not perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa) by means of its perception through inference.
303.01 What is the inference? It is teaching. What is this so-called teaching? It is the giving of what is being imparted to a recipient.
303.02. [The opponent argues: "There is a sound existing in the interval between the giver and the receiver, because it reaches [the ear], like an arrow and so forth.
303.03. [The response: There is no refutation, because in either of the two positions, one [of the two] is being taught.
303.04 [2-2-28(29)] There is no refutation because the teaching of either one of the two positions is being taught.

303.05 It is not the word (*śabda*) itself that is prohibited from being taught, but rather its impermanence, just like the instruction in dancing. 303.06 Regarding "teaching": as for this [objection] that the word exists in the interval between the giver and the receiver...

"This is a proof of what is already established," [the opponent says]. We too say that the sound uttered by the giver reaches the recipient through the process of a continuous series (*saṃtāna*); therefore, the recipient is not the cause for its persistence.
What, then, is the cause?
303.10 [2-2-29(30)] From practice (abhyāsāt). 303.11 "From practice, like the lute and so forth"—this refers to jumping, filling [gaps], and other such [skills] which are indeed impermanent.
303.12 "Practice" is contradictory [to permanence]. Furthermore, if stability were to be established through practice, even then, it would apply only to things that are unstable.
303.13 Thus, [the reason] "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and it is unestablished (*asiddha*) because the essential nature of repetition has not been determined.
303.14 For repetition consists either in the production of multiple cognitions regarding a single object, or in having a single form as its object.
In this regard, 303.15 this [reason]—whether repetition has a single object or a single form as its object—is unestablished due to doubt (*sandigdhāsiddha*). Repeated practice...

303.16. In the case of [the reason] being unestablished (*asiddhi*), the proof is provided by way of its being the object of repeated practice (*abhyāsa-upacāra*), for the purpose of making known its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
303.17 [2-2-30(31)] Even if there is difference, because of the figurative application of repetition. 303.18 This sūtra is for the purpose of negating difference.

303.19 [2-2-31(32)] Because one thing is not different from another, it is not non-different; thus, there is an absence of otherness. 304.01: "Because one thing is not different from another, it is not non-different"—this implies the absence of otherness. Regarding this which is called "other," 304.02:
you may think that this must be either different from or non-different from another; if it is other, it cannot be non-different, just as...

304.03 "One who is other than a brahmin is not a brahmin. Now, if he is non-other, even so, he does not become other, because of his non-otherness. How can that which is non-other become other? 304.04 [This is] because of its being non-other; how will that which is non-other become other?

304.05 [2-2-32(33)] In the absence of that, there is no non-difference between the two, because their establishment is mutually dependent. 304.07 The meaning of the sūtra is: "In the absence of that, there is no non-difference between the two, because their establishment is mutually dependent.
304.08 [This constitutes] non-contradiction. That non-difference which was accepted is thereby set aside. How is it set aside? By means of the negation.

304.09 Because it has another word as its object; for when there is no other, there is no "non-other," just as a non-Brahmin is not established in the absence of a Brahmin. 304.10 This, then, is the reason: because of recognition. Recognition is not observed in the case of [reflected] jewels and the like, yet recognition does exist in the case of sound; therefore—

"Sound persists because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). What is this recognition? It is the state of being the object of that cognition (*tat-pratyaya-viṣayatva*). [Objection: This is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for even when there is difference, there can be the state of being the object of that cognition. [Response: Recognition is the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the object of that cognition; for in the case of sound, there is never [a lack of] the state of being the object of that cognition.

304.15 There is indeed a deviation: that cognition which occurs with respect to what is similar ceases upon the perception of a distinction. Therefore, 304.16 the non-exclusion of that cognition from the word is not "recognition" (*pratyabhijñāna*); thus, the non-exclusion of that cognition [from the word] is unestablished (*asiddha*). For this cognition of "that" (*tat-pratyaya*), while occurring in one person, ceases in another person.
304.18 It has been observed that when a specific difference is perceived, the notion of identity regarding what is similar ceases.

304.19 If you think this is so, then in the case of sound, is the notion of identity due to the non-perception of a specific difference in what is similar, or is that notion [of identity] due simply to the absence of that [specific difference]? Thus there is doubt. Furthermore, recognition [occurs] because of the existence of that [identity].
Even if this position—that [the word] exists—is accepted, another reason must still be stated. Why? Because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

[Objection: It is because it functions as a specific qualifier through dependence. Furthermore, there is no non-exclusion of the cognition "this is the word 'go' (cow)," namely, "this is the word 'go'. Nor is there any deviation in the word 'go' being the agent of the cognition of a cow.

305.03 This too is doubted: for what purpose, by what cause-in-common (*kāraṇa-sāmānya*), does the cognition of "cow" not cease in the word "cow," or rather, is it because of the existence of that [cause]? By this, its status as the agent of that cognition is explained. However, it is logical that in the word "cow," there is a cognition of the word "cow" due to the cause-in-common.

305.06. Non-exclusion. How so? In the cognition of a cow, the cognition of "cow" does not cease, nor does its status as the producer of that cognition cease from this cognition of the word "cow. Therefore, when it serves as the cause for that cognition, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
305.08. And as for that which ceases precisely because no specific difference has been perceived, with respect to that thing, [it is] the non-cause.

305.09 Whether there is a distinction or not, you yourselves must be asked. If there is a distinction, [the argument] that "the non-exclusion of the condition is not a reason" is inconclusive (*anekānta*). Or, if there is no distinction, it follows that a single entity has a dual nature.
Because this is contradictory, the non-exclusion of the condition is not a reason, since it would apply to all persons without exception.
[The reason] is unestablished; furthermore, because it has as its object merely the person [as a subject], it is inconclusive—this, then, is the reason.
305.13 [2-2-33(34)] Because no cause of destruction is perceived (vināśa-kāraṇa-anupalabdhi).
305.14 Because no cause of destruction is perceived: whatever is impermanent has a cause of its destruction perceived;
305.15 for example, the disjunction of the constituent parts of a clod of earth [is the cause of its destruction], but such is not the case for sound; therefore, it is eternal.
305.17 [2-2-34(35)] Since no cause for non-hearing is perceived, there follows the consequence of constant hearing.
305.18 “Since no cause for non-hearing is perceived, there follows the consequence of constant hearing”: the rest is in the Bhāṣya.
305.19 [2-2-35(36)] Furthermore, since non-perception is absent when there is perception, it is not a valid reason (anapadeśa).

305.20 Furthermore, since non-perception is absent when there is perception, it is not a valid reason. By means of inference, a cause for the destruction of sound is perceived; and that which is perceived by inference does not fail to exist. Why?

306.02. "Inference is the occurrence of a continuum. Therefore, this [argument] regarding the non-perception of a cause of destruction is not a valid reason (*anapadeśa*). For example, [the argument]: "Because it has horns, therefore it is a horse. Now, what is it that is absent here: the horn, or the connection with a horn? He says: both, when [one refers to] a horned animal.
306.05 When one establishes the object by means of its being a horse, then the horn certainly exists; it is not the horn that is being negated.

306.06 Because of the absence of a relationship between the horse and the horn, it is rightly said that the inference is non-existent; because of its non-existence, it cannot serve as a probans (anapadeśa). 306.07 Thus [it ends]. If it is argued that [the inference] exists because of its being an action (karmatva), we say no, because its substratum is impermanent. Now, if you think:
306.08 Even that which is eternal and yet perceived is seen to be absolutely ungraspable, as is the case with the nature of action (*karmatva*).
306.09 And this [ungraspability] does not arise because the substratum is impermanent; rather, since the substratum is eternal, there is no possibility for a cause of non-hearing [or non-perception].
306.10 Thus we say: furthermore, the cause for the non-grasping of the nature of action is the impermanence of its substratum.

"Therefore, there is no such consequence. When a bell is struck, there is a loud sound, a louder sound, a soft sound, and an even softer sound; because of this difference in audition, a series of distinct sounds is indeed heard without interruption. In this regard, the following is considered: that which is the cause of the manifestation of a sound being manifested resides in the bell.
306.14 Or rather, does it have another mode of existence? If it resides in the bell, is it stationary or does it exist as a continuum (santāna)?

306.15 Even if it has another mode of existence, is it stationary or does it exist as a continuum? If it resides in the bell and is stationary, then a difference in sound (*śruti-bheda*) would not occur. Alternatively, if it resides in the bell [as a] continuum—

306.17 There would follow the consequence of perceiving multiple sounds simultaneously. Whatever sound is manifested by that which resides in the bell—whether it exists as a static entity (avasthita) or as a continuous process (santāna)—that much alone of the sound should be perceived at one time.
Furthermore, it must be explained how the cause of manifestation residing in the bell manifests a sound existing elsewhere.
306.20 Now, if you consider that the cause of manifestation is something else that has arrived, or that which resides within the continuum (saṃtāna), or that which functions [within it];

306.21 then, when a single bell is struck, it manifests sounds [only] in those [bells] situated nearby, and not in other bells situated in distant places. 306.22 Therefore, a reason for this restriction must be stated, since there is no difference between the sounds themselves.
If it is argued that a distinction must be established—namely, that what is called "high" (*tāra*) or "low" (*manda*) is actually the sound (*nāda*)—we say no.

Because it is perceived as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "sound," this term "high" or "low" functions as coreferential with the word "sound," and not as coreferential with the word "sound-quality" (*nāda*); therefore, it is the sound itself that is being designated.

307.04 And in the absence of sound being its object, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word [‘sound’] would not be logical, as in the case of ‘blue lotus. 307.05 If it is argued that this is a cognition based on delusion (*vyāmoha*), we say no, because no cause for such delusion has been stated. Now, 307.06 suppose you think that the cognition “high” or “low” is a delusive cognition that is coreferential with the word [‘sound’].

It occurs, as for example: "the sound is long" or "the sound is great. It is not [the case that this is so] because of a lack of a specific cause; nor is it a delusive cognition, for there is no reason [to regard it as such]. If this were a delusive cognition, then the cause of that delusive cognition would have to be stated, just as in the case of the expression "the sound is long."
307.10 When there is a perception of sound as a continuous, uninterrupted stream, the cognition of "long" arises;

for indeed, those substances which are long possess the quality of being objects of a continuous perception due to the accumulation of their parts, and it is by virtue of that commonality [that the term is applied]. 307.11–12 The cognition of "long" applies to sound, yet for one who maintains that sound is eternal, there is no basis for such a cognition being an error.
307.13 This is improper. If it is argued that this is the same [as the previous case], we say no, because its cause never exists.

307.14 Now, if you think that even for one who holds that the continuum (*santāna*) is eternal, there must be stated a cause of production—whether residing in the bell itself as a state of the continuum or residing elsewhere as a state of the continuum—[we reply: 307.15 [this is not so].

307.16 The cause of production residing in the bell sometimes produces sounds and sometimes does not; thus, there is the consequence that it must be permanent. 307.17 This is not a consequence, because the cause of the production of sounds exists only at certain times. 307.18 That [cause] functions as a state of the bell at certain times; when it exists, it functions as a continuous series (*santāna*).
Therefore, sounds conform to the diversity of their causes; because they function within a continuum, they produce a sound that conforms to various forms such as "weaker" or "weakest.
And the cause of that is *saṃskāra*. From what does its production arise? It arises from [the air] depending upon contact with the hand.
307.22. From the conjunction of the action with the bell and the dependence on the momentum residing in the hand, there is an action in the bell.
308.01. That action, depending upon the impact of the hand, produces a *saṃskāra* (dispositional force) at the same time as the disjunction [from the hand].
308.02. And that [force] grasps an internal wind that is without end; and it, being struck by the wind, [moves] again.

308.03 One performs an action; from that action, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises; by means of the latent impression, again an action, and again the grasping of the wind (*vāyu-upagraha*), and so forth—by such a principle, the latent impression is produced. In that process, because the final [moment] is extremely weak, 308.05 there is an absence of the power to disturb the great elements (*mahābhūta*) in the bell; consequently, the grasping of the wind is cut off, and from that...

"308.06 [It is] the destruction of the formative forces (saṃskāra). If you think, "There are no formative forces because they are not perceived," then indeed there are no formative forces because they are not perceived, and that [non-existence] is non-existent.
308.08 [2-2-36(37)] Because the cause, the hand, has ceased, there is no non-perception due to the absence of sound.
308.09 "Because the cause, the hand, has ceased, there is no non-perception due to the absence of sound. This sūtra has already been explained.
308.10 If you do not accept that the *saṃskāra* (impression/disposition) is the cause for the production of sound, then [the sound would arise] from the contact with the hand.

The continuity [of sound] would not be cut off. Now, if it is argued that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the bell ceases due to contact with the hand, even so, how is the continuity of the sound cut off? We do not say that the contact with the bell cuts off the sounds;
rather, due to the contact between the hand and the bell, the latent impression governing its operation—which possesses the quality of touch—is destroyed.
Because it is opposed by the conjunction of substances, it ceases; when the cause has ceased, there is an absence of the effect. Thus is the cutting off of the continuum.
308.16 [2-2-37(38)] Furthermore, because no cause of destruction is perceived, there follows the undesirable consequence that it is eternal while it persists.
308.18 Because no cause of destruction is perceived, there follows the undesirable consequence that it is eternal while it persists. Regarding this which is stated:
"Sound is eternal because no cause of its destruction is perceived"—if for something there is no cause of destruction...

No cause for [the destruction of] that which is eternal is perceived. As for these perceptions of sound, no cause for their destruction is established by you; because no such cause is established and because they persist, they are eternal.
Now, even if the causes for their destruction are not perceived, these perceptions of sound are nonetheless impermanent with respect to the sound.

309.03. Even so, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). Now, if the causes for the perception and destruction of sound are understood through inference, then it is not at all contradicted that "sound is [known] by that means of valid cognition" (*tat-pramāṇaḥ śabdaḥ*). 309.04–05. If you say it is improper because of a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*), and you think: "How can sound have a different locus? [we reply: 309.05. [It is established] because of its connection with the substratum (*āśraya-sambandhāt*). Just as the color and other qualities of a cloth are perceived when the cloth itself is perceived, so too is sound perceived when its substratum is perceived. Therefore, it is not the case that sound is not perceived. Thus, the objection regarding the difference in locus is refuted. 309.06. Furthermore, if one were to argue that sound is not perceived because it is imperceptible (*parokṣatvāt*), that too is incorrect. For sound is indeed perceived, since it is apprehended by auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). 309.07. Moreover, if one were to argue that sound is not perceived because it is momentary (*kṣaṇikatvāt*), that too is incorrect. For sound is perceived, since it is apprehended by auditory consciousness. 309.08. Furthermore, if one were to argue that sound is not perceived because it is non-eternal (*anityatvāt*), that too is incorrect. For sound is perceived, since it is apprehended by auditory consciousness. 309.09. Furthermore, if one were to argue that sound is not perceived because it is produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), that too is incorrect. For sound is perceived, since it is apprehended by auditory consciousness. 309.10. 315.01 Nor can a sentence be rendered meaningless simply because it expresses a universal (*sāmānya*). 315.02 This is because a universal is not the object of specific worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*). 315.03 Every instructor utters a word for the purpose of conveying a particular (*viśeṣa*). 315.04 There is no command regarding a universal, nor is there any agreement upon it; therefore, [the word] is a word (*pada*).
"It is indeed non-expressive," [some might say]. This is not so, because when there is a general subject matter (*sāmānya-viṣaya*), the specific hearing (*viśeṣa-śruti*) acts as a restrictor.

If a word were non-expressive, the general meaning would not be understood from the hearing of the word. That which is non-expressive—neither the general nor the particular is understood from it; yet from the word, both are understood just as they are understood from the object (*artha*).
315.07. A general term is restricted by a specific term; for example, [the general term] "cow" [is specified]. 315.08.
When there is a cognition of the general [term], it is understood through the specific term as "it stands" or "it moves.

315.10 However, because it is the cause for the cognition of a specific [meaning] in dependence upon a preceding word, the verbal testimony (*śruti*) is called "specific verbal testimony" (*viśeṣa-śruti*).
315.11 Or, let both [the action and its means] be understood from the word itself; indeed, both are understood from this very word "cow" (*go*).
315.12 Both the action and its instrument [are understood] when this word "cow" occurs without a fixed rule regarding the status of primary and subordinate.

315.13 When [the word] "cow" has "cowness" (*gotva*) as its cause because of its connection with cowness, then from the word "cow," the primary factor (*pradhāna*)—the means (*sādhana*)—is understood as "cow. But the action (*kriyā*), being subordinate (*aṅga-bhūtā*), is understood because it serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaka*). "Primacy belongs to 'cowness' (gotva). Thus, because there is no fixed rule regarding the relationship between the primary and the subordinate, both "cowness" and "cow" are understood from the two words "go-tvam" and "goḥ," respectively.

315.18–19. In that regard, based on the relationship of primary and secondary status (*pradhāna-upasarjana-bhāva*), there arises a doubt concerning the application [of a word] to those objects (2.2.59), because the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the universal (*jāti*) are all present together. 315.21 Therefore, it is not known whether the individual (vyakti), the form (ākṛti), or the genus (jāti) is the meaning of a word.

316.07 Because the form (*ākṛti*) is inactive, it does not indeed go, stay, or come into being;

thus it is in all cases. And the word "cow" is capable of denoting that which is connected with these specific qualities such as staying and so forth. Why? Because the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) has a single object. If...

316.13–14: "Otherwise it would not be so"—for the substance (*dravya*) and the individual (*vyakti*) do not exist as distinct entities. 316.15 [2-2-61(62)] "Not so, because of the lack of finality" (na tad-anavasthānāt) is the sūtra. By this word "cow" (go-śabda), it is not merely the individual (vyakti-mātra) that is expressed;
[if it were,] it would be pure [individuality]. If this [word] were an expresser of mere individuality, then in whichever [individual]...

The meaning of the sūtra is that the cognition would occur with respect to some particular individual (vyakti). If the individual were not the referent of the word (padārtha), how could there be such usage as "the cow stands" and so forth? [Response: This is a metaphorical application (upacāra) of the term based on a causal basis (nimitta), even when the thing itself is not present. 317.02. For the purpose of establishing that, there is the sūtra beginning with "concomitance" (sahacaraṇa) and so forth.
317.03 [2-2-62(63)] Metaphorical designation (upacāra) occurs on account of association, location, purpose, activity, measure, support, proximity, connection, instrumentality, and sovereignty;
as in the cases of a Brāhmaṇa, a bedstead, a mat, a king, groats, sandalwood, the Gaṅgā, a cloth, food, and a man— despite the absence of that actual state, there is the figurative application of it.

"Metaphorical designation (upacāra) occurs even when something is not that [thing] itself. Metaphorical designation is the expression of a word denoting one thing by means of a word denoting another; for example, just as a particular object is designated by the word "staff" (*yaṣṭikā*), yet through association (*sāhacarya*), a particular Brahmin is designated by the word "staff"—as in the case of "the staff-bearers" (*yaṣṭikāḥ*).
"Bring him in. This applies everywhere. But what, then, is the basis for this figurative usage (*upacāra*) [where] "staffs" refers to "Brahmins"?
