For a figurative usage cannot be established without a basis for that usage. Has it not been stated that it is "association" (*sāhacarya*)?
Association means a constant connection with the staff; and because of the connection with the staff, one is called "possessing a staff" (*yaṣṭikāvān*).
317.12 Thus it would be [the case that] "it is not a stick," whereas this word "possessing a stick" (*yaṣṭikāvān*) is primary (*mukhya*).

317.13 It must be so; therefore, another basis for metaphorical usage (*upacāra-bīja*) must be stated. First, regarding the stick, this word "stick" (*yaṣṭikā*) has a genus as its cause (*jāti-nimitta*); the genus is "stickness" (*yaṣṭikātva*), and that [genus] resides in the stick.
317.15 Through that stick, which is characterized by the state of being a "stick-ness," there is a connection (*yoga*) with the Brahmin due to their association (*sāhacarya*).

317.16 Having superimposed upon the Brahmin the genus (*jāti*) that is inherent in what is conjoined [with the stick], one says, "The Brahmin is a stick. In this way, 317.17 the remaining seeds of metaphorical usage (*upacāra-bīja*) are to be inferred by oneself.

317.18 [2-2-63(64)] The form (ākṛti) [is the meaning], because the establishment of the existence [of an individual] depends upon it. 317.19 If, then, the individual is not the meaning of the word "cow," let the form be the meaning instead.
317.20 Because the establishment of the existence [of an individual] depends upon it. Why is the form the meaning of the word?
318.01 Because it depends on that, the determination of a being—such as "this is a cow," "this is a horse," or "this is a person"—is established.

318.02 The generic form (*ākṛti*) is established in dependence [on something else], and that upon which the establishment of the determination of a being depends is the object of the word "cow. Even here, that same [objection] arises; it is not because of an infinite regress.

And that which possesses a connection with the genus (*jāti*) is the referent of the word "cow," not the configuration (*ākṛti*), because the configuration lacks a connection with the genus. Now, what is it that possesses a connection with the genus? It is the whole (*avayavin*) whose constituent parts have a fixed arrangement; the fixed arrangement of the constituent parts belongs to that which has such an arrangement.
That whole, which possesses a fixed arrangement of constituent parts, is [denoted] by the possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) "that which has a fixed arrangement of parts" (*niyatāvayavavyūha*).
It is thus explained.

318.08 [2-2-64(65)] Even though the individual and the form are present, sprinkling and other such rites do not apply to a clay cow; therefore, let the universal (jāti) be the referent of the word, since there is no such application even when the individual and the form are present.

318.09–318.10 Let it be, then, that the universal is the meaning of the word, because of the non-application of sprinkling and so forth to the clay cow, despite the presence of the individual and the form.

318.11 The genus (*jāti*) belongs to the clay cow, because both the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*) exist in the clay cow, yet sprinkling and other such rites are not performed upon it. For there is neither a command nor an understanding [of the command] regarding a clay cow when one says, "Bring the cow" or "Give the cow. That which, in its absence, results in the lack of comprehension in that case is the meaning of the word "cow" (*go*).

318.14 Because of the absence of what is there no conviction regarding "birth" (jāti) [as a universal]? Furthermore, why is "cowness" (gotva) not a birth [i.e., a universal] in the case of a clay cow?

318.15 Because a clay cow is not a cow; and that which is not a cow does not possess cowness therein, just as in the case of a horse. Furthermore, why is a clay cow not a cow? For this very reason it is not.
Because it is a clay cow. And this question—"Why is a clay cow not a cow?"—is not logical. Why?

Because it is contradicted by common understanding (*pratipatti-bādhita*). You yourself also understand this matter [to be so]: "This is not a cow. And thus the question is contradicted by that very understanding. Now, regarding the clay cow...

"The word 'cow' [applies] because of the commonality of form, like a painting and so forth. If it is argued that [the universal] is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), then you might think: "The universal is omnipresent; just as it becomes connected with a cow that is being born, so too it is connected with a clay cow. Therefore, the nature of 'cowness' (*gotva*) exists in the clay cow. This is not so, because it is not admitted by whom? By no one.

319.03–319.05. Although the universal (*jāti*) is accepted as being omnipresent (*sarvagata*), it nevertheless exists everywhere within its own domain; thus it is said to be "omnipresent. What, then, is the specific domain of "cowness" (*gotva*)? It is that wherein cowness exists. And where does cowness exist? Wherever there is a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*) caused by cowness.
[The universal] exists. But where does the universal "cowness" (gotva) reside such that it would be its means of proof?

Furthermore, what is the purpose of proving a permanent entity like a cow, since it is manifested by that [means]? For there is no manifestation of cowness apart from the object possessing the dewlap and other [characteristics]. Indeed, there is no distinct entity separate from the individual bodies.

319.09. Some say that "cowness" (gotva) does not exist in the intervals between individual bodies because it is not perceived there. This is not so, because conceptualization would otherwise be impossible. 319.10.

One who asserts that it is due to its non-perception in the intervals between bodies must be questioned regarding what this "interval between bodies" is: is it space (ākāśa), or rather non-existence (abhāva), or perhaps another substance (dravyāntara)?
319.11. [If you say it is space,] then one must ask: is this interval between bodies space, or is it non-existence, or is it some other kind of substance?

319.12 If space were not present there, then "cowness" would not be perceived there, for space is not a cow. By this, non-existence (abhāva) [as a distinct category] is explained. Furthermore, because specific cognitions cannot be without a cause, this cognition—which is distinct from the cognition of the individual body—arises from another cause.

319.15 Indeed, it is observed that for those conditions which partake in a distinction from the causal aggregate (piṇḍa), their arising occurs from another cause. For example, the cognition of "blue" with respect to cloth, leather, or woolen blankets [is not due to the aggregate itself].
319.16–17 If you argue that this is so because of a commonality of form (ākṛti-sāmānya), then you might think: let it be true that this [cognition] arises from a cause distinct from the aggregate.

There arises a conforming cognition (*anuvṛtti-pratyaya*). However, its genus (*jāti*) is not the cause; rather, it is because of the commonality of the shape (*ākṛti*) of the head, hands, and feet that the conforming cognition arises. Nor is it [caused] by the individual body (*piṇḍa*), because the shape is unique (*asādhāraṇatva*); for just as individual bodies do not subsist in other individual bodies.

Likewise, the configuration (*ākṛti*) also, because it resides in a single individual (*piṇḍa*), does not reside in other individuals. [Objection: It is admitted that the configuration resides in other individuals; there is no dispute regarding the name, nor regarding the fact. However, even if a universal (*sāmānya*) distinct from the individual is not admitted, nevertheless, by the refutation of a single universal, [the same result follows].

320.03 Another seed for the uniform cognition must be stated; for we do not observe a uniform cognition in the absence of a universal (sāmānya). If it is argued that a uniform cognition is observed even when a universal is absent—320.04–320.05 suppose you think that just as a recurring cognition is observed among universals even in the absence of another underlying universal—

[The opponent argues: "In the case of 'cowness' (*gotva*) and so forth, there is the cognition 'this is a universal,' 'this is a universal. Therefore, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the recurring cognition (*anuvṛtti-pratyaya*) does not prove that [the object] is caused by something other than its own nature. [Reply: This is not so, because we do not accept [your premise].
For I do not maintain that the cognition of a universal regarding cowness, potness, and horseness is without a cause.
320.09. Therefore, this [objection] is not a valid refutation. If you think: "There is a contradiction with the Sūtra," [we reply:

if you consider that there is a universal within universals, is that not indeed a contradiction with the Sūtra? For it is stated [in the Sūtra] that "there is no universal or particular within universals and particulars; from those very [particulars] alone arises cognition. This is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra.

320.12 This is the meaning of the sūtra: just as the cognition "this is a substance" occurs with respect to a substance due to the qualifier "substance-ness" (dravyatva), and not, however, with respect to universals (sāmānya) and particulars (viśeṣa); so it is not the meaning of this sūtra that the conforming cognition (anuvṛtti-pratyaya) is without a cause (nirnimitta). If you should think, "What is its cause?"—then consider this: [text continues].
320.15 What is the cause of the recurring cognition (*anuvṛtti-pratyaya*) with respect to "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, by virtue of which it is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*)?

320.16 From what does it become a universal? It becomes a universal because of its inherence (*samavāya*) in multiple objects. Just as cowness inheres in multiple objects, so too do horsehood (*aśvatva*) and the like; thus, there is a commonality regarding their inherence in multiple objects.

[Objection: "Because [of this], there is a recurring cognition (*anuvṛtti-pratyaya*) with respect to 'cowness' (*gotva*) and so forth. [If you say] "like words such as 'cook' (*pācaka*)," [then we reply:

Now, if you think that just as words such as 'cook' give rise to recurring cognitions, yet there is no specific universal (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) called "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*), so too is there a recurring cognition with respect to cows and the like.

320.21 [This is] not so, because of the lack of thorough knowledge regarding the meaning of the reason, since the specific cognitions would be accidental; this is the meaning of that reason. 321.01 [The meaning is: the production of a cognition distinct from the cognition of the composite whole arises from another cause.
321.02 It is not the case, however, that every inclusive cognition (anuvṛtti-pratyaya) arises solely from a universal (sāmānya). This being so...

321.03 That which is the primary instrument (*sādhana*) in the act of cooking is denoted by the word "cook" (*pācaka*). And since that primacy exists even in another cook, there is no fault. If the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) subsists in many individuals, does it exist by being fully present in each individual (*piṇḍa*), or by means of a single part? What follows from this?

321.06 If [the universal] exists by being fully present in each individual object (*piṇḍa*), then because it would be non-common (*asādhāraṇa*) like the individual objects themselves, it cannot logically be a universal (*sāmānya*). 321.07 On the other hand, if it exists by way of its parts (*ekadeśena*), even so, a single thing does not exist in many places; for how could that which is one exist in many? Therefore, it is the locations (*pradeśa*) of the universal that exist [in the individuals]. Those...

321.09 Those parts of the universal reside individually in each individual object (*piṇḍa*). Are they of the nature of the universal, or not? If they are of the nature of the universal, it follows that the one resides in many; yet it is not logical to say that the universal is one while residing in many. Or else...
321.12 Those [particulars] which do not have a common nature are empty; the designations for the universal exist in each of its parts as partial locations.

321.13 Thus, by means of those locations as well, the universal exists as before; hence there is the same aforementioned consequence (*pūrvavat-prasaṅga*). And there is no other way [to avoid this]. Therefore, the universal does not subsist in many [locations], because one does not admit the alternative [of its being a single entity].

321.15 This alternative does not exist: that the universal "cowness" (gotva) exists by being fully present in each individual body, or else it exists only partially. Therefore, because this alternative is not accepted, this question is invalid. Why?
Because the universal "cowness" is not accepted as being either a composite whole (avayavin) or a collection (samudāya). It is neither a composite whole nor a collection.

321.18 When the word "part" (*ekadeśa*) refers to a portion of a collection (*samudāya*), and the word "whole" (*kṛtsna*) refers to the entirety of the possessor of parts (*avayavin*) without excluding anything, then the word "whole" is used in relation to the parts of the possessor of parts. 321.19–20 And the word "collection" is used in relation to the members of the collection. Furthermore, "cowness" (*gotva*) is neither the possessor of parts nor a collection.

321.21 Therefore, the terms "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) and "part" (*ekadeśa*) do not apply; and since these two terms do not apply there, [the universal] is "cowness" (*gotva*). 322.01 Is it that [the universal] exists by way of its entirety or by way of a part? Such a question is not tenable. And it has been said in this regard:
322.02 One who asserts that "the one exists in many" should not be questioned. Why? Because [it exists] in both ways.
"Because of contradiction. How, then, does "cowness" (gotva) subsist in cows? By way of the relationship between substratum and superstratum (āśraya-āśrayi-bhāva).

What, then, is this relationship of substratum and superstratum? It is inherence (samavāya); it is in that [relation] that "cowness" has its subsistence. Subsistence is inherence, because it is the cause of the notion "it is here," as has been stated; for "cowness" does not subsist in a cow or a non-cow.

322.06 Now, if you think: "That which is this 'cowness' (*gotva*), the cause of the recurring cognition among cows—is that [cowness] present in a cow or in a non-cow? If, first of all, it is in a cow, then that [cow] is already a cow even prior to its connection with cowness;
thus, cowness is redundant. On the other hand, if it is in a non-cow, then even a horse or the like would become a cow through its connection with cowness."
[The cognition] occurs; yet there is no other possible state [of affairs]. Therefore, the recurring cognition does not arise from "cowness" (gotva).

[Objection: It is not so, because conceptual construction (vikalpa) is not admitted. There is no "cowness" in a cow prior to cowness, nor is it in a non-cow; thus, it is neither a cow nor a non-cow. What is the reason? Because both of these are cognitions of the qualified object (viśeṣya-pratyaya).
322.12–14. Without a connection to a qualifier, [the thing] does not exist; nor does the entity exist prior to its connection with "cowness" (gotva).

That which is non-existent cannot be designated as "cow" or "non-cow. At the very moment the entity exists, it is connected with cowness; thus, this conceptual construction (vikalpa) is groundless. By this, [the same argument applies] to the connection with "Being" (sattā).
The conceptualization of existence and non-existence has been explained: there is no connection with existence for that which exists, nor for that which does not exist.

Since that very object is connected with existence at that very same time, the fault of relying on both existence and non-existence is untenable. Therefore, the universal (jāti) is logically established. Furthermore, it is not the case that [the universal] is absent in a clay cow, because of the absence of which [the cognition] would not occur therein.
That category of object is characterized by lack of conviction.
322.19 [2-2-65(66)] It is not so, because the manifestation of the genus depends upon the form and the individual.

322.20–21: "Because the manifestation of the genus depends upon the form and the individual"—the manifestation of the genus depends on both the form (*ākṛti*) and the individual (*vyakti*). Since it is understood that it depends on both the individual and the form, the word "form" is placed first because of its predominance. Why, then?

323.01 Since the universal (ākṛti) is the qualifier of the individual (vyakti), and it is by means of the individual that the universal is qualified, 323.02 the universal is the mark of the genus (jāti); therefore, the universal is primary. Furthermore, when the universal and the individual are not being apprehended, 323.03 only the pure genus is understood from the word; therefore, even the genus [is not the primary denotation].
323.04. It is not the case that a word-meaning cannot exist in accordance with its object. What, then, is the word-meaning?
323.05. The word-meaning consists of the individual (vyakti), the form (ākṛti), and the genus (jāti).
323.06 [2-2-66(67)] The individual (vyakti), the form (ākṛti), and the genus (jāti) are the meaning of a word (padārtha).
323.07 The word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of specification; what is specified? The lack of restriction regarding the status of primary (pradhāna) and subordinate (upasarjana).
323.08 When the status of being the meaning of a word involves the intention to express distinction and the comprehension of a particular, as in "the cow stands" or "the cow sits."

323.09. Then the individual (vyakti) is the word-meaning, while the genus (jāti) and the configuration (ākṛti) are subordinate; for [actions such as] standing or moving do not exist in the genus or the configuration. 323.10. That in which these are possible is the word-meaning. Furthermore, when distinction is not intended to be expressed, 323.11.
and there is a movement toward the universal, then the genus is the word-meaning—as in "A cow must not be touched with the foot," where it refers to the configuration.
323.12 And it should be inferred that the state of being primary [belongs to the *ākṛti*]; thus, "having inferred for oneself" means this: where, then, has the primacy of the *ākṛti* been observed?

For example, as in the case of "Let cows made of flour be made. This very relationship between the primary and the subordinate is frequently inferred for oneself in practical applications; therefore, it is not [the case that] the individual (*vyakti*) and the *ākṛti*...

Some maintain that the referent of a word is the universal (*jāti*). Why? Because the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) [of "existent"] would otherwise be untenable. Since the term "existent" (*sat*) is pervasive, it is considered in relation to its basis; furthermore, by this very word "existent," the universal is denoted.
Is the referent the individual (*piṇḍa*), the relation (*sambandha*), or the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*)? Among these, first of all, the universal is not what is denoted.
323.18–19. If this word *sat* denotes a genus (*jāti*), it would be a word denoting a genus because it possesses non-different case endings with words denoting particulars (*bheda*).

323.19–20. [Otherwise,] there would result grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dravya*, which denotes a particular, as in the expression “existent substance” (*sad-dravyam*); for we do not observe coreferentiality between words that denote different objects. Indeed, not...

323.21: Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed in the case of "cow-horse" (*go-aśvam*). Now, since existence (*sattā*) resides in substances and so forth, 324.01 it indeed possesses co-referentiality with words such as "substance"; nevertheless, because existence is dependent (*pāratantryāt*), 324.02 co-referentiality is not observed between the word for "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and words denoting both a quality and its possessor.
324.03 Thus, as in the case of "the whiteness of a conch shell," by this the relationship (*sambandha*) has been explained. The word *sat* (existent) [is used].

324.04 It is not logical that it should be the designator (*vācaka*) of individual objects (*piṇḍa*), because individual objects are infinite; for it is not possible to declare the relationship of a single word with the manifold expansion of substances and qualities, nor can there be a cognition [of them] when the relationship has not been declared.

324.06. It is logical that the comprehension of an object from a word occurs through the relationship between word and object, because there is deviation [from the object] when there is merely the cognition of the word's own form.
324.07. Furthermore, upon hearing the word "existent" (sat), the intellect remains wavering among substance, quality, and action.
324.08. And it is not tenable to say that the designation from which the intellect wavers is the very designation [of that object].

Therefore, the word "existent" (sat) is not a denoter of particulars. Furthermore, the word "existent" does not even denote merely that which possesses a universal (jātimat), because it is not independent. For particulars such as jars and the like are not understood from the word "existent" alone; thus, since it does not imply those particulars such as jars, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

324.12 Non-existence. Alternatively, because it is not independent, the word *sat* (existent) primarily refers to *sattā* (being). 324.13 While referring to that [being], it is applied metaphorically to that which possesses it (*tadvat*). And when a word, while referring to one thing, is applied metaphorically to another, it is not the designator of that [other] object, just like the word "platform" (*mañca*). And it has been said in this regard:

324.15–16: It was stated that because the possessors of qualities (*tadvat*) are infinite, it is not logical for them to be denoted by the word "existent" (*sat*). Furthermore, there is no transfer of cognition [from the quality to the possessor] based on similarity of qualities, as in the case of the word "master" being applied to a servant;
nor is it due to the coloring of qualities, as in the case of "the crystal is blue," because such a sequential process does not exist and simultaneous occurrence is impossible.

And because it would follow that there is the production of knowledge that does not correspond to reality (*ayathārthajñāna*). Therefore, it is not logical that [the word], while denoting merely that which possesses a universal (*jātiman*), should also denote the unique particular (*asādhāraṇaviśeṣa*).
Furthermore, because it would follow that there is no cognition [of the object] elsewhere. And since there is no other alternative, [the word must denote] the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
324.21: "The word 'kṛt' (having done) is a term that, while excluding other referents of other words, brings about a specific meaning;

325.01: it is said that it 'denotes' [that meaning]. Here, by us, the individual, the configuration, and the universal have been established as the referent of a word through an unrestricted relationship of primary and subordinate status; 325.02: and these [proponents] are indeed proponents of extreme views."

"These are the faults. And as for how these are not faults: first, regarding the claim that the word "existence" (*sattā-śabda*) is not expressive of existence—that is not so, because it involves a contradiction.

To say "the word 'existence' is not expressive of existence" is a contradictory statement. Or else, if it were not expressive of that [existence], how could it be designated as "the word 'existence'"?

325.06 If it is argued that [the term] is being stated according to your own intention: then you might think, "In our system, there are no words for 'existence' (sattā); rather, you employ the convention by conceptualizing words for existence as being words for substance, quality, and action. Therefore, we too [respond] according to your intention—

325.09–325.10: It is argued that words for "existence" (sattā-śabda) are metaphorically designated as denoters (*vācaka*) because they conform [to existence]. This is not a contradiction, because there is no cessation [of their application]. Both parties investigate in what meanings such words as "existent" (*sat*) and so forth, which are well-known in the world, operate. We, however, say that the word "existence" operates in the sense of existence itself.
Furthermore, you say that the word "existence" (sattā) does not [denote] existence itself. Speaking thus, I confront you with a contradiction;

and since you have neither stated nor resolved this contradiction, by asserting that "I am stating the sequence according to your own doctrine," you do not escape the inconsistency. Moreover, as for this which is said by you—that [these things] are merely conceptual constructs—
325.15 [The claim that] "words denote existence" (sattā) is also not tenable, because there is no denotation of an imagined object;

for the object of what is imagined is not such [as it appears], since there is a superimposition of those properties upon a universal that does not possess them, as in the case of perceiving a person in a post. And if these words...

325.18 They are conceptual constructions (*parikalpita*); for their primary referent (*pradhāna*) must be expressed, since that which lacks a primary referent cannot be conceptually constructed. 325.19 As for the argument that "the distinction [between substance and existence] is due to the non-difference of their case endings," that is not so, because it stems from a failure to understand the identical meaning [of the terms]. We do not say that the word *sattā* (existence) stands in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dravya* (substance).
325.21–326.01: Rather, by the word *sat*, which denotes the primary means of existence (*sattā*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) are expressed.
326.01–326.02: Thus, here too, by the words *guṇa* and *karman*, which have entered into a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified, those very same [categories] are denoted.
And this being so, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of both the word *sat* and the word *dravya* is logical, as they share a single object.

326.03–05. Furthermore, when this word *sattā* denotes the property of existence (*sattā*) itself as the primary element and [the substance] as a subordinate means (*sādhana*), then there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "the substance is existence. Therefore, the impossibility of coreferentiality is not a fault, because of the rule regarding the difference in case endings for those words that denote a quality and its possessor.

326.06–07. By this, the objection that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "existent" (*sat*) and "substance" (*dravya*) is unestablished has been refuted. By this, the relation (*sambandha*) is also explained. How so? The relation is not denoted by the word "existent," but rather the relation is denoted only by a word for the relatum; furthermore, the relation is a quality (*guṇa*), whereas the word "existent" is not a quality.
326.09 Furthermore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a word denoting a quality and a word denoting a substance.

326.10 As for this argument that "because of infinity, a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*) is not a designator of particulars"—who says that a genus-word is a designator of particulars? You yourself are refuting a logical argument (*vāco-yukti*) that you have yourself employed.

326.12 If, then, [the word] denotes particulars (*bheda*), how is it that substances, qualities, and actions are denoted by the word "existent" (*sat*)? 326.13 [Reply: This word "existent," sir, is not a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*), but rather a particular-word (*bheda-śabda*).
326.14 Since this very [word] is a particular-word, and a particular is indeed denoted by a particular-word, nothing at all is contradicted. How so?

326.15 When the word "existent" (*sat*) does not exclude [particulars], the infinity of those particulars remains exactly as it was. Furthermore, it is impossible to express the relation of a single [word] with many [particulars]; and if the relation is not expressed, the comprehension of the word's meaning is not tenable.
Thus, [the word] does not denote [particulars] alone, because those which are unqualified by the word "existent" [cannot be denoted].

326.18 This fault applies to one who maintains that substances (dravya), qualities (guṇa), and actions (karman) are denoted [by words]. For us, however, 326.19 substances, qualities, and actions are denoted as qualifiers of existence (sattā). Wherever existence is perceived, there the word "existent" (sat) is employed; and since existence is one, the cognition of it persists. Therefore, [the word denotes] the particulars (bheda).

327.01 Infinity is not a fault. And what is this relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhya-sādhana-bhāva*) that you thus maintain regarding the word? 327.02 You are taking the property of a real entity (*vastu-dharma*) as the logical reason (*hetu*), on the grounds that [the particulars] are infinite. Alternatively, if the individuals themselves are made the subject (*pakṣa*) as the denotable objects of a generic term (*jāti-śabda*), even so, they possess neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

327.04. "The example exists" is not a valid reason because of infinity. Furthermore, even if one part [of the whole] is made the subject (*pakṣa*), [the claim that it is] "because of infinity"—327.05—that "the reason is a single part and the example is a single part" is also not [valid] due to contradiction. And this being so, there would be no object whatsoever to be expressed, nor any word whatsoever to be expressive; thus, regarding the expressible—327.06—
When the state of being a signifier has ceased, the qualification "these are not the signified" and "these are not the signifiers" is redundant.

Furthermore, as for the argument that this is due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it arises from a failure to understand the scope of deviation. For that which is called "deviant" is indeed that which, while existing in its own object and in things of the same class as that object, [does not exist in other things].
327.10 Otherwise, this word "existent" (sat) does not apply to what is non-existent apart from its own object.

327.11 Therefore, the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is misplaced, and because the status of being a reason (*hetu*) is not admitted. Furthermore, what is stated here as the reason—namely, that "substance, quality, and action [are real] because they exist" (*sattvāt*)? Therefore, this too is incorrect.

327.13 Because the denotation of difference is negated, it cannot be said that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word for a substance (*dravya*) and the word for "existent" (*sat*), due to contradiction. Furthermore, no word whatsoever denotes a substance; thus, the claim that there is coreferentiality between the words "substance" and "existent" is contradictory. As for the argument that [the substance] possesses those [qualities], that is not so, because it lacks independence.

327.16–18. Thus, it is said that the particulars such as the jar are not understood by the word "existent" (*sat*), because, like the jar and so forth, they do not imply those particulars; consequently, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is not so, because the answer has already been stated: it has been stated that the words "existent" (*sat*) and "substance" (*dravya*) possess coreferentiality because they have the same object.

327.19–21. Likewise, it is not logical that the word *sat* (existent) should imply the specific distinctions of jars and so forth, because it implies substances, qualities, and actions through its proof of existence (*sattā*). Substances, qualities, and actions are not implied by the word *sattā*; furthermore, it cannot be said that even by the word *sattā*, those things which have become subordinate are understood.
328.01. Regarding this word "existent" (*sat*), what is its denotation (*abhidheya*) which is understood from it?
328.02. What is its meaning (*artha*)? It is analyzed as threefold: existence (*sattā*), its connection (*tadyoga*), and a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). 328.03.
Among these, when the relationship of primary and subordinate is intended to be expressed, the primary factor is understood as the means (*sādhana*), while the other is the auxiliary.

328.04 And [the question arises: by what is the state of being primary or secondary between existence (*sattā*) and its connection [to a specific object] determined? It is determined by the purpose (*artha*). When existence performs some function, it does so by taking up a particular category of entity (*padārtha*) as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

In that case, existence is secondary and [the entity] is primary, because existence is the cause for the cognition of the primary [entity]. This is because the category of entity [depends] upon existence.

328.07 It is distinguished [from others] because the cognition [of existence] ceases in that which lacks a constituent part; for where that constituent part—such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth—is absent, there the cognition "it exists" does not arise. Thus, it is incorrect to say that [the word *sat*] does not imply distinctions such as the jar and so forth which possess that [existence].
Furthermore, regarding the claim that the word *sat* primarily denotes existence (*sattā*), when it occurs in that sense, it [denotes] that which possesses it (*tadvat*).

328.10 It is said that [existence] is metaphorically designated; this is not so, because of a failure to understand the referent of the word "existent" (*sat*). You have not understood the referent of the word "existent. Who has ever said that the word "existent" applies primarily to "being-ness" (*sattā*)?
And just as substances, qualities, and actions are the referents of the word "existent" by virtue of being the means for establishing being-ness, [so too is the case here].

And so it has been said: "By this, the infinity of particulars is refuted; the object of the word 'existent' (sat) is [the universal] existence. The object that establishes existence is one and the same as that which constitutes the means of establishing existence.

Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no transfer of cognition [from the particular to the universal] based on a similarity of qualities—such as the case where the word "master" is applied to a servant—that is not so.

328.16 The meaning of this is that the word "master" is applied to the servant because the servant conforms to the master. However, we do not understand this [claim] that there is a "transference of cognition" (pratyaya-saṅkrānti). If it means that the servant becomes the object of the cognition of the master, that is not a transference of cognition; for the cognition of the master does not actually arise with respect to the servant, but rather [the servant merely possesses] a state of being an object (gurutām).
328.19 Or, perceiving that [the word] "master" (svāmin) has become coextensive [with the servant], one applies it there simultaneously.

Just as a servant, 328.20 because he imitates his master, is figuratively designated as "master," yet the word *sattā* (existence) is not like that; it never at any time refers to substances (*dravya*) and so forth. But when [it is said] "existence is the state of those things that exist" (*satām bhāvaḥ sattā*), then...

329.02 Because they are qualifiers (*viśeṣaka*) of the existent things that constitute their qualities (*guṇa*), the term "existence" (*sattā-śabda*) denotes them; this state of being a qualifier is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

329.03 By this very [argument], the claim that [the crystal appears as blue] due to the coloring by a quality—such as "the crystal is blue"—is refuted. Furthermore, 329.04 the meaning of the statement "because there is no sequential occurrence and because simultaneous occurrence is impossible" is as follows: the word "existence" [applies] to existence...

329.05 It is said that because it exists as a substrate (*vartin*), it exists in that which possesses it (*tadvat*). But we do not observe this to be so; even simultaneously, 329.06 the cognition of existence (*sattā-pratyaya*) and the cognition of substance (*dravya-pratyaya*) cannot occur together. This too has not been stated [as a valid objection], because an answer has already been given. An answer has already been given to this: there is neither a sequence nor a simultaneous cognition here regarding the cognition of "being" (*sat*).
Because it is the object of the means of proof (*sādhana*). By this, the consequence that there would be the arising of a cognition not corresponding to the object (*ayathārtha-jñāna*) is refuted.

Thus, since the primary [status of] the cause has been rejected, it is established that the referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the genus (*jāti*).
It is not the case that a genus-word denotes particulars; therefore, [the objection regarding] the uselessness of the qualifier does not hold, for no one...

329.11 Sound is accepted by you as the designator of particulars, [serving] as a qualifier for the qualified (viśeṣya). 329.12 But since there is no cognition of a universal (sāmānya), it has no qualified object at all; nor is any referent of a genus-word (jāti-śabda) admitted to be expressed. Therefore, the qualifier is useless.

329.14 Furthermore, due to contradiction: if this were a genus-term (*jāti-śabda*) denoting particulars (*bheda*), then it would not even be a genus-term at all; for it is impossible for words denoting other categories of objects to possess the status of that [genus] term. Or how could it be called a "genus-term" while denoting particulars? And as for what...

It is said: "A genus-term (*jāti-śabda*) is not a denoter of particulars (*bheda*). In that case, what person of sound mind would accept particulars as being denotable by genus-terms? Furthermore, if particulars are not denotable by genus-terms, then they must necessarily be denotable by other terms. Now, if [they are] by other terms—
They are not expressible even [by words]; they are not expressible by genus-words (*jāti-śabda*), nor are they expressible by other words.

Thus, if both are inexpressible, what is the efficacy of this qualification? [The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that the genus-word is the designator (*vācaka*) of the particulars (*bheda*)? Therefore, it must be stated thus: the particulars are not expressible, and the words are not designators.

330.02 Thus [it is said]. Now, if you think that this is stated with reference to the opinion of another—that the genus-term (*jāti-śabda*) is not the designator (*vācaka*) of particulars—[we reply] no, because that is not admitted. For there is no systematizer (*tantrika*) who understands particulars as being denotable by a genus-term; for even if the genus were non-denotative, there would be a contradiction regarding the genus-term.

330.05 Thus, it cannot be said that whatever does not denote something is the word for that thing; nor can it be said that a genus-word (jāti-śabda) denotes particulars (bheda). Whom, then, does it denote? Since the denotation of particulars has been negated, the implication is that it denotes something else. If, moreover, denoting anything else is also not accepted, then [the argument] is futile.

330.08–330.10: [The opponent argues: "A genus-term (*jāti-śabda*) is not a denoter of particulars (*bheda*); therefore, it is logical to say that all words whatsoever are not denoters of objects. Now, if words are non-denoters and objects are non-denotable, this is also incorrect because of contradiction: for words would both be non-denoters and yet possess the state of being non-denoters.
330.11–12: "That words are communicated by means of words alone" implies that words are non-expressive; thus, there is a contradiction regarding the thesis and the reason.

For the thesis—that a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*) is not expressive of particulars (*bheda*)—and the reason [given as] "due to infinity" (330.12–13) are both of the nature of speech. Since both are of the nature of speech, there is a contradiction because they would themselves be non-expressive.

330.14 And for one who accepts that words are non-expressive, some other means of communication must be stated for the world. 330.15 If it is argued that they are accepted otherwise—that is, if you think: "I do not accept that words are non-expressive, nor do I accept that objects are inexpressible; rather, [it is] your own logic of the expressible and the expressive [that is at fault]."

330.17 That [universal] is accepted by us; it is what is being refuted. However, for us, it must be stated specifically that the universal, characterized as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), is denoted by the word. Otherwise, if words were denoters of objects [without such a qualification], it would have to be stated specifically [otherwise]. [This refers to] the universal as conceived by us.

330.20–331.02: Apart from [the universal] itself, words such as "universal" (jāti) and so forth do not denote universals and the like, because their own form (svarūpa) is not denoted. Furthermore, the nature of a universal cannot be specified apart from its being the cause of a uniform cognition; nor can the cognition of recurrence (anuvṛtti-pratyaya) be rejected; nor can the particular...
331.03 Since it is impossible for this condition to exist without a cause, there is no dispute that this condition is that universal (*jāti*).

This much is the fault in the statement as it was heard. Now, if the particulars (*bheda*) are also made the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of being denotable by words for universals, then regarding this very meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*), however many of these...

331.06 All those faults of speech likewise follow even when a partial position is adopted, because the relationship between qualifier and qualified is untenable; thus the previous fault persists. Furthermore, as for what is said—that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words "substance" (*dravya*) and "existent" (*sat*)—that too is not so, because it involves a contradiction. And yet, there is grammatical coreferentiality between the words "substance" and "existent."

331.09 And it is not contradictory to say that words do not denote difference. [Objection: There is no contradiction because [the terms] are used figuratively (upacārataḥ). 331.10 If you think this, then you consider that these two words, "existent" (sat) and "substance" (dravya), are expressed figuratively. 331.11 How so? By the word "substance," there is the exclusion of non-substance; by the word "existent," there is the exclusion of non-existence.
331.12 These two, functioning by way of the exclusion of non-existent substances, express a single object; thus they are said to be in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

331.13 It is said [thus] from a primary standpoint, but in reality, no word whatsoever is expressive through positive affirmation (*vidhāna*). 331.14 Since a primary [expression] is impossible, when a word for an existent substance is used primarily, it is [connected] with that through generality (*sāmānya*).
It is not logical to say that this is a figurative usage (upacāra) applied to something that is not actually so; for those who speak thus, there is no primary substance (pradhāna).

Furthermore, a figurative usage is not possible without a primary substance, nor is it tenable in the theory of exclusion of others (anyāpoha), because both [the primary and the secondary] would then be designated by the word "primary" (pradhāna). Just as the word "lion" applies to an actual lion and to what is not a lion—

331.19 Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, as for this claim that the meaning of a word is the exclusion (*apoha*) of the meanings of other words, that too is untenable. 331.20 If there is the possibility of a positive word-meaning, then the initial cognition—if it is a positive word-meaning—occurs first. 332.01 Therefore, when there is the cognition of the positive word-meaning being enjoined, its negation occurs elsewhere.

332.02. A negation is applicable only when the object being affirmed does not exist; for one who [affirms] that, how can there be a negation without first having an initial cognition? 332.03. As long as one does not cognize the one, so long does one not [cognize] the other. 332.05.

As long as one does not cognize the one, so long is it not reasonable to have a manifold misconception regarding the other, just as one does not [have such a misconception] regarding a cow as long as one does not cognize it.

332.06–332.08: To that extent, there is an absence of comprehension of both [the positive and the negative]. Furthermore, regarding this exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) which is "not non-cow"—that which is the meaning of the word "cow"—is it a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*)? If it is a positive entity, is it a cow or a non-cow? If it is a cow, there is no dispute; but if it is a non-cow, then the meaning of the word "cow" would be a non-cow. Alas! This is the meaning of the word!

[This is] skillful [reasoning]. However, non-existence (*abhāva*) is not tenable, because it is not the object of either the injunction (*praiṣa*) or the comprehension (*sampratipatti*). For, upon hearing the word "cow," there is neither an injunction toward non-existence nor a comprehension of it; and the meaning of a word is understood through comprehension. Furthermore, no one understands non-existence from the word "cow"; therefore, the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

332.12 Thus, [the objection] is improper because it is not comprehensive (*avyāpaka*). Where there is a duality of categories, there the one is understood through the negation of the other, just as in the word "non-cow" (*ago*), the cow is understood while the non-cow is being negated. 332.13 However, this is not the case for every word; for there is no such thing as "non-all" (*asarva*) that could be excluded by the word "all" (*sarva*).
332.15 If it is argued that [the term "all"] is pervasive because it excludes "one" and so forth— should you think that "non-all," such as one and so on,

is what is excluded by the word "all"— that is not so, because it would entail the fault of contradicting its own meaning. For if this were the case, the word "all," functioning by excluding "one" and so forth, would [exclude] the whole (aṅgin) distinct from the parts (aṅga) due to the negation of the parts.

Because [the collection] is not admitted [as something distinct], it would be meaningless; thus, all words denoting a collection (samudāya-śabda), when functioning by way of negating a part, become meaningless because a collection distinct from its constituents (samudāyin) is not admitted. Furthermore, since words such as "two" and so forth have conjunction (samuccaya) as their object, when there is a negation of "one" and so forth...

333.01 Because there is no combination of things being negated, words such as "two" and so forth would be meaningless; furthermore, since exclusion (*apoha*) has the nature of an action, its object must be stated. Is this exclusion—"it is not a non-cow"—an exclusion whose object is the cow, or is it an exclusion whose object is the non-cow? If its object is the cow, how can the absence of a cow be the cow itself? Or [if its object is the non-cow]...
333.04 You think that it has "non-cow" as its object; how can there be a cognition of something other than a non-cow through an exclusion (*apoha*) that has a different object?
For indeed, when a *khadira* tree is being cut, the cutting does not occur in a *palāśa* tree. Now, regarding the negation of the non-cow as "cow":
by what means was "non-cowness" ever attributed to a cow such that it must now be negated in the statement "the cow is not a non-cow"? How [can this be]?

Or, [in the case of] "cow" (*go*), there can be no negation without the prior cognition of the cow; for one does not perceive a negation without the prior cognition of the referent of the subsequent term. And it has been stated in this regard that the initial cognition would not be possible.
Furthermore, since there is no negation without the initial cognition, for this reason as well, Apoha is not tenable.

333.10 Because conceptual construction is untenable: Is this exclusion of the non-cow (*agoh-apoha*) which is the cow distinct from it, or is it 333.11 not distinct? If it is distinct, is it dependent or independent?
333.12 If it is dependent, then because it is dependent, it is a quality (*guṇa*); thus, by the word "cow," a quality would be denoted, not the cow itself.

The cow stands; grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not attained. Now, by what meaning is it "unreliant"? [If one says] "the sixth case [is used]: 'the exclusion (*apoha*) of the cow,'" then, if it is non-distinct, that is just the cow itself, and nothing has been accomplished. Furthermore, it must be stated whether this exclusion is one or many with respect to each object. If it is one...

333.16 Then, is "cowness" (gotva) that which is related to many individual cows? Or is it [the cows] themselves, being many? In the latter case, because they are infinite like individual material bodies (piṇḍa), [the universal cannot be established]. 333.17 Because of the impossibility of its designation, the cognition of the object is not tenable. Furthermore, you must first be asked this: is this exclusion (apoha) expressible by words or inexpressible? If it is expressible, then the meaning of a word is non-exclusive (anaikāntika).

333.19 "The meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha). [If this is so,] there is an infinite regress; for if exclusion is expressed by way of the exclusion of non-exclusion, 333.20 then that exclusion too would require another, resulting in an infinite regress. Alternatively, if it is not expressible, then the claim that it effects the exclusion of the meaning of other words is contradictory. Furthermore, if exclusion is not the denoted meaning of a word...

334.01 One must state its own meaning (svārtha) as distinct from the meaning of the denotable object (abhidheyārtha). Now, if that [exclusion] itself is its own meaning, even so, 334.02 it is contradictory to say that "a word, while effecting the exclusion of the meanings of other words within its own meaning, denotes [that meaning].
334.03 At that time, the meaning of that sentence becomes this: "it denotes while not denoting another."

334.04 Furthermore, since the term "many" (aneka) refers to objects such as two or more, a specific distinction must be resorted to for the comprehension of the general [meaning]. For, in the absence of resorting to a specific [distinction], it is not logical for a specific [object] to be understood from a word expressing a general [property]. 334.05–06 Thus, because the words "blue" and "lotus" are primary [in their own meanings], the relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva) between them would otherwise be untenable; therefore, [the specific distinction of the qualifier] must be [resorted to].

334.07. Regarding the rule of "prior placement" (*pūrva-nipāta*), because both [terms] are primary, [the required order] is not obtained. By this, the words *rāja-puruṣa* and so forth are explained. Furthermore, the meaning of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) must be stated by the proponent of exclusion of others (*anyāpoha-vādin*).
And for one for whom the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), how can the exclusions of "non-blue" and "non-lotus" be coreferential?

Thus it should be said: for one, however, for whom the word-meaning is being positively enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*), there is [the denotation of] a substance qualified by genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*).

By the two words "blue" (*nīla*) and "lotus" (*utpala*), a substance is expressed, and the genus and the quality reside in that substance; they do not, however, denote the exclusion of the non-blue and the non-lotus. Therefore, the meaning of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) does not exist [in this view]. Thus, in this way, it is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) [that is established].
In whatever way it is conceptualized, in that very way it contradicts the functioning of valid cognition.

334.14 But how is it known that there are distinct individuals (*vyakti*), forms (*ākṛti*), and universals (*jāti*)? If it is argued that the question is untenable because they have already been understood—namely, that individuals, forms, and universals have been understood through the sūtras beginning with "the word 'cow' and so forth"—then, since they have been understood, the purpose of the question is untenable. [This is not so,] for even when the threefold nature of the cause exists, there remains a need for its specific distinction.

334.17 Because the purpose of the question is to make known the specific object [of the term], the word *go* (cow), when being uttered, indicates [the referent] solely by way of the relationship between the primary and the subordinate; such is the meaning of the sūtras beginning with *yāśabdādibhyaḥ*. This being the case, it is appropriate that the question has the purpose of making known that specific object: "Among those, which is the individual (*vyakti*)? Which is the..."

334.20 What is *ākṛti*? It is the genus (*jāti*). Thus, there is a distinction between the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the genus (*jāti*) based on the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

334.21 But what, then, is the characteristic of the individual? For the purpose of explaining the characteristic of the individual, [it is said]: "The individual is the substratum of specific qualities and is corporeal"—this is the aphorism (*sūtra*). 334.22–23.
335.01 [2-2-67(68)] An individual (vyakti) is a substratum of specific qualities (guṇaviśeṣa); it is a corporeal form (mūrti).
335.02 In this context, that which is manifested is an "individual" (vyakti), meaning a substance (dravya) perceptible by the senses.

335.03 That which is the substratum of qualities beginning with color and ending with touch—provided they have reached the conditions for perception—is called "corporeal form" (mūrti) because it possesses parts and has a defined shape.

And it is also called "individual" (*vyakti*). However, we do not understand this: is this the definition of the composite substance (*avayavidravya*), or is it the definition of the individual that serves to exclude [the other two] among the three categories—genus (*jāti*), configuration (*ākṛti*), and individual—that have been introduced? We, for our part, say: here, the composite substance is not what is to be excluded; rather, it is the genus...

335.07. It must be stated what the meaning of the word "individual" (*vyakti*) is as distinct from the words "genus" (*jāti*) and "form" (*ākṛti*). And that individual, which is neither genus nor form, is included by this sūtra as follows: "The individual is the substratum of specific qualities (*guṇa-viśeṣa*); it is a material body (*mūrti*).
Here, due to the elision of the word *tad*, [the compound] "substratum of specific qualities" (*guṇa-viśeṣāśraya*) refers to the qualities, the specificities, and their substratum.
335.10 By means of a word, a substance (dravya) is expressed, and action (karman) is also obtained from a word that qualifies a quality (guṇa-viśeṣa-śabda); for distinctions arise from qualities.

335.11 Regarding "distinctions of quality" (guṇa-viśeṣāḥ): for what purpose is the mention of "distinctions of quality" [made], since [action] is already included within the category of quality (guṇa-padārtha)?
335.12 It is for the purpose of excluding the "form" (ākṛti). Form is a particular kind of conjunction (saṃyoga-viśeṣa), and it is excluded by the inclusion of "quality."

335.13–15. Since [the qualities] have already been included [in the definition], the term "specific qualities" (guṇaviśeṣa) is mentioned in order to exclude those [other qualities]. Regarding the expression "specific qualities," there are two ways of analyzing the compound: either as "those which are both qualities and specific" (guṇāśca te viśeṣāśca), or as "specifics that are distinct from qualities" (guṇebhyo viśeṣāḥ). The word "mūrti" is used here in grammatical apposition with the word "substratum" (āśraya); it refers to a substance (dravya), in the sense that it "coalesces" (mūrchati).

335.16 A substance is expressed by means of a word; and in this way, the definition is established for each individual term. And in this way, [the inclusion of] form—335.17 space and so forth—is subsumed. If this were the definition of the individual, then form and the rest, as well as space and the rest, would be encompassed; otherwise, the definition would not be all-inclusive.
Alternatively, "the substratum of specific qualities" (*guṇaviśeṣāṇām āśrayaḥ*): qualities (*guṇāḥ*) and particularities (*viśeṣāḥ*) together constitute "specific qualities.
Their substratum is substance (*dravya*). It is called "form" (*mūrti*) because it coalesces (*mūrchati*) therein.
336.01 [2-2-68(69)] *Ākṛti* is that which expresses the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of the genus (*jāti*).

336.02 *Ākṛti* is that which expresses the genus and its characteristic marks; for it is through this that the genus and its characteristic marks are made known. 336.03 One should understand that *ākṛti* is that [configuration], and it is not something other than the fixed arrangement of the parts of a substance (*sattva*). 336.04 That [arrangement] is fixed.

336.04 Indeed, the constituent parts (*vyūha*) of the limbs infer the genus (*jāti*). By means of the commonality of form (*ākāra-sāmānya*) characterized by having a head, hands, and so forth, 336.05 the state of being a cow (*gotva*) is manifested. Thus, either through the head, hands, and so forth, or sometimes through the perception of a specific whole (*avayavin*), this configuration (*ākṛti*) [is established]. But where does this configuration ever abandon its status as the referent of a word (*padārthatva*)? It abandons it wherever the configuration and the individual (*vyakti*) [are not perceived together].

336.07 Just as clay, gold, and silver do not constitute the genus [of "metal"], there is a restriction regarding the configuration (ākṛti). 336.08 Not every configuration indicates the genus; nor, conversely, does every genus indicate the configuration.
336.09 It is indicated [by the configuration].
336.10 [2-2-69(70)] *Jāti* is that which has the nature of producing a common cognition.

336.11 *Jāti* is that which has the nature of producing a common cognition. Just as various distinct entities, by being the cause of a recurring cognition (*anuvṛtti-pratyaya*) with respect to one another, are established as such; that is *jāti*. For example, these... 336.12 ...are established as such by being the cause of a recurring cognition with respect to one another; that is *jāti*. For example, these...
336.13–14: These [cognitions] follow as "pots" and do not exclude them as "not these pots"; that is the single real cause (sat-nimitta).

336.14–15: That which is the cause of recurrence (anuvṛtti-kāraṇa)—namely, the universal-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa) or the genus (jāti)—is the genus (jāti), because it is the cause for the arising of a uniform cognition (samāna-pratyaya-utpatti-kāraṇa). Thus, the rule regarding the genus is that it is the genus itself, and not that the arising of a uniform cognition depends upon the genus.
336.16 Because it is observed even in the absence [of a universal]. A common cognition is observed even in the absence of a genus (*jāti*), as in the case of 336.17 cooks and the like;

therefore, it is established that the referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the genus (*jāti*). 336.18 In the case of cows and the like, the recurring cognition is observed to arise from a mark (*liṅga*) distinct from the individual body; thus, it possesses a specific characteristic.

Because [the cognition of "cow" arises] from the individual cow, like the cognition of blue and so forth. Cowness is a different entity from the individual cow, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, like the cognitions of color and touch. Cowness is a different entity from the individual cow, because it is the object of a designating term, like Caitra and a horse. The recurring cognition of "cowness" in various cows has a distinct cause, because it is specific, like [the cognition of] a particular [object].
337.03 It is like the conditions for form and so forth.
337.04–05: Doubt, the examination of the means of valid cognition, their establishment, the true nature and authority of verbal testimony, and the categories (padārtha) are proclaimed here.
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the second chapter in the Nyāyavārttika by Uddyotakara.
337.08 And here the second chapter concludes. 338.01 In the Nyāyavārttika, the third chapter begins.
338.04 That object regarding which the knowledge of reality becomes the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra is examined immediately thereafter.

338.05 And since that [self] begins with the "self" (ātman), the self is now investigated. What, then, is to be investigated regarding it? Is it distinct from the body, the sense organs, the mind, and the intellect, or is it not? [This cannot be determined] because the subject (dharmin) is unestablished; for distinction and non-distinction are properties (dharmas) of the self only when a subject exists, and the subject here is unestablished. Nor can [the investigation proceed] when the subject is unestablished.
338.08–09: An investigation into two properties is appropriate only when there is a subject (*dharmin*); therefore, let the subject itself be established first. [Objection:

No one has any disagreement [regarding this], because the existence of the self (*ātman*) has already been established in the *icchā-ādi-sūtra*. Since it has been established, the subsequent investigation is appropriate. 339.01: [The opponent replies: No one... [has any disagreement].

339.02–04. The disputants disagree regarding the existence of the self (*ātman*), but they disagree regarding its specific nature: whether the self is merely the body, or the collection of intellect and so forth, or something distinct from the self, or the self itself. Furthermore, this disagreement concerning the specific attributes (*dharma-viśeṣa*) of the self would not be possible for those who have not yet accepted the existence of the self; therefore, an investigation into these attributes is appropriate.

339.05 And because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the non-existence of a self (*ātman*). Nor is there any means of valid cognition that establishes the non-existence of the self;
therefore, one does not disagree with its existence. Some say it does not exist because it is unproduced (*ajātatvāt*);
others say it does not exist because the self is unproduced, like the horn of a hare. In that regard, the two terms "it does not exist" and "self" are mutually contradictory.
This word "self" (ātman) is not in grammatical apposition with the word "non-existent"; it does not establish the non-existence of the self.

What is the reason? The term "self" denotes existence, and "non-existent" is its negation. Furthermore, that which is negated exists elsewhere than where it is negated, just as [the property] in grammatical apposition with "non-existent" [implies the existence of the thing itself].
339.11 The word "jar" is not capable of conveying the absence of the jar; rather, it negates [its existence] in respect to a particular place and time.
339.12 It negates it by saying, "the jar does not exist," [implying a specific location]; or the negation refers to a specific place, as in "it does not exist in the house";
or the negation refers to a specific time, as in "it does not exist now," "it did not exist previously," or "it will not exist hereafter."

339.14 Furthermore, this entire negation is not tenable for one who does not accept the existence of a jar. Likewise, regarding the statement "the self does not exist" (339.15), is this negated with respect to a particular place or with respect to a particular time? If it is first negated with respect to a particular place, that is not tenable in regard to the self, because the self is not a location, nor is it a location.
339.17 By the negation of the particular, the self (*ātman*) becomes negated. Now, if this is your intention:

339.18 "The body is not the self"—to whom does the body belong such that there is a negation with respect to it? 339.19 If you say the negation is "the self does not exist in the body," then to whom does the self belong in the body such that [it is negated]?
339.20 Where, then, is this negation? Nowhere is there a self. Is it that this self does not exist at all?
340.01 No; for there is a specific negation. What is the meaning of this statement: "It is neither in the body nor elsewhere"?
340.02 It is not that this [self] does not exist; rather, this statement is made because that which is as it is, is described accordingly.

And since this self does not exist anywhere [as a substance], for that very reason such a designation is made; nor is the negation of a specific time appropriate with respect to the self, because the three times are not manifested in the self.
Indeed, the three times are not manifested in the self because it is eternal; that "the self is eternal" will be explained further below.
340.06 We shall establish this in the previously discussed sūtra; therefore, there is no refutation of a specific time [for its existence].

340.07 Furthermore, by one who rejects the self (ātman), the referent of the word "self" must be stated. For we do not perceive a single word to be devoid of meaning. Even if you were to maintain that the word "self" has the body and so forth as its referent—

Even so, the contradiction remains unresolved. How so? Regarding the statement "there is no self," at that time its meaning would be that the body and so forth do not exist. Now, as for that self which you postulate, it does not exist; we do not postulate a self, nor is there any conceptual construction [of one].

340.12 Indeed, it is by means of a superimposition of its properties—based on a similarity with things that possess such qualities—that something which is not actually of that nature becomes an object of cognition; yet we do not apprehend the self as being of such a nature, regarding which you say, "you postulate this self. Thus, you must be asked: how do we postulate the self?

340.15 Thus [it is asked]: is it by way of existence (*sattva*) or by way of non-existence (*asattva*)? If it is by way of existence, how can there be a similarity (*sādharmya*) between the non-existent and the existent, by means of which you—who assert that the self (*ātman*) is the object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-viṣaya*) and that the commonality of self (*ātma-sāmānya*) belongs to the non-self (*anātman*)—would have the self accepted [as real]? For indeed, there is no commonality between the non-existent and the existent. Or if...

340.18–340.20: Having imagined the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which has the body and so forth as its object, to be the self (*ātman*), one is thus deluded. Since one accepts the existence of an ego that is distinct from the body and so forth as its object, the contradiction remains unresolved. Now, if you think that a single word does not necessarily have a corresponding referent—just as in the case of [the words] "void" (*śūnya*) or "darkness" (*tamas*)—[we reply: ...

341.01. Therefore, because the contradiction is not resolved, this is not the meaning of the word "empty" (*śūnya*): namely, that for which there is no protector of the substance [is empty]. 341.02. That substance does not exist; because it is beneficial to dogs, it is called "empty. Regarding the word "darkness" (*tamas*) as well, its object consists of substances, qualities, and actions that have reached the condition of non-perception (non-apprehension), wherever there is an absence of light. 341.03. Wherever there is an absence of light, those substances, qualities, and actions characterized by non-perception constitute the object of the word "darkness."

In various instances, substance and so forth are denoted by the word *tamas*. Furthermore, one who asserts that the word *tamas* is meaningless contradicts his own established tenet, because darkness (*tamas*) possesses the nature of being a perceptible object among the four [categories].
Therefore, no word is meaningless.

341.07. Furthermore, by saying "there is no self," one contradicts the established tenet. How so? "Venerable sir, am I not form? "No, bhikṣu, I am not feeling, nor mental formations, nor consciousness. "Venerable sir, am I not form? "No, bhikṣu, I am not feeling, nor mental formations, nor consciousness; thus it is. "Are you not feeling, nor mental formations, nor consciousness? "No, you are not. These aggregates are form—
341.10 The first [instance] was refuted as having the "I" as its object; furthermore, this is a specific negation, not a general negation.

341.11 And by one who does not admit a self (*ātman*), only the general [notion] should be negated, namely: "neither I, nor you. 341.12 If it is argued that the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) has the aggregate as its object because of the individual negations such as "you are not," even so—

341.13 A collection distinct from the five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*), must be stated as the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*); [otherwise,] it would be something other than those [aggregates]. 341.14 Furthermore, for one who accepts that the collection is the object of the notion of "I," there is a contradiction in terminology regarding the self (*ātman*). 341.15 If it is [the collection], then it is called a "collection"; however, if it were not distinct [from the aggregates], the singular cognition "I" would not be possible. For indeed—
341.16 We observe the same word applied to many things; yet the aggregates (skandhas), such as form and the rest, neither individually nor collectively [constitute] the self.
341.17 Therefore, the notion of "I" is a cognition that takes for something what it is not; let it be a false cognition.
341.18 What is there for us to lose? How could it not be sublated, since it merely imitates a correct cognition?

341.19. These are false notions; and for one who does not admit a self, the vision of the Tathāgata cannot be established as meaningful. 342.01. Nor is it the case that this statement does not exist in the *Sarvābhisamaya-sūtra*, because it is explicitly mentioned therein. Therefore, one who says "there is no self" contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

342.03–05. Likewise, monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, and the bearer of the burden. The burden is the five aggregates; the bearer of the burden is the person (*pudgala*). He who says that there is no self (*ātman*) holds a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Thus says the Sūtra.

Furthermore, this reason—"because it is unborn"—is also contradictory (*viruddha*), because it functions as a reason for excluding [the subject] from a different category. For "born" and "unborn" are both properties of real entities (*vastu-dharma*). What, then, is born, and what is unborn?
That which possesses existence through having a cause is "born"; that which possesses existence without a cause is "unborn."

342.09 Why is that [the unborn] not [existent]? Because the negative particle (*nañ*) has birth as its object of negation. Indeed, this negative particle, when functioning, performs the negation of birth, as in: "There is no birth for this.
342.10 Therefore, this statement "it is unborn" does not constitute a negation of the self, just as [in the case of] "a water-pot without water."

342.12 Thus [it is said]. Now, if this entity is indeed a negation, namely "the unborn," even so, there is a contradiction between the thesis and the reason. 342.13–14 Furthermore, the property "unborn" and this [subject] are one; yet it is not logical for a property to exist independently.
342.14 Apart from inherence (*samavāya*), that upon which this property depends is its self (*ātman*); thus [the position] is contradictory. Or, if it is a property...
Even if one says that there is no substratum (*dharmin*), the contradiction remains unresolved because an independent property (*dharma*) is not observed.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "because of being unborn" (*ajātatvāt*)? If this means that there is no birth for it, then [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), for the self possesses birth.
Moreover, what is the birth of the self? It is [birth] characterized by a specific class of body and sense-faculties.

342.18 [There is] a connection with unprecedented cognitions and feelings. Now, if "unbornness" means "causelessness," it is not so. 342.19 Someone objects that the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because for that which is causeless, there is permanence; thus, while proving non-existence, it results in [the subject] being established as permanent. Therefore, the reason is contradictory. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason. 342.20 [The reason] brings about permanence; thus, the reason is contradictory. And there is no contradiction between the proposition and the reason. Regarding the proposition:
342.21. Regarding the two [propositions]: "The object exists" and "The self exists"—the object [of the first] is absolute existence (*sattā-sambandha*).

These two, the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), are contradictory because their objects are respectively non-existent and existent. By this, [arguments such as] "because it is without a cause," "because it does not depend on a cause for its birth," "because it is not an effect," and "because it is not a cause," are refuted as having the same fault.
343.03 Furthermore, this which is stated—"like the horn of a hare"—is also an unestablished example.

343.04 Why? Because the word "hare's horn" has as its object a relationship; therefore, it is the relationship that is negated, not the horn itself. 343.05 Since the relationship between the hare and the horn will serve as the illustrative instance, that too [is unestablished].
343.06. It is never logical for a connection with a horn to be possible for a rabbit, [if you argue] that this contradicts worldly consensus (*loka-virodha*).
343.07. If you think: "If there were a horn on a rabbit, would it not contradict the world? 343.08.
It does not contradict [the world], because worldly activity proceeds by way of negating the relationship of cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*). For the world, first of all...

343.09–11: One negates that there is neither an effect nor a cause for a rabbit's horn, just as one does for a cow's horn; yet there is no relationship of cause and effect between a rabbit and its horn. Nor does its non-existence follow from the negation of a causal relationship, for it is not the case that if something has no effect [or cause], it must therefore be non-existent.

343.12 There is no such cause as there is for saying "Devadatta’s pot. And regarding this "hare’s horn," 343.13 one who says "it does not exist" should be asked: is this a negation of the general [term] or a negation of the particular?
343.14 If it is a negation of the general, that is not tenable because it is impossible; [for example,] the horn of a hare.
343.15 It follows that since [the horns] do not exist, the horns of cows and so forth do not belong to a rabbit either;

and this is untenable, for it is not the case that those [horns] do not exist. 343.16–17 Now, if there is a specific negation, then some particular horn is being negated for the rabbit—that which has the rabbit as its effect, and which is not the cause of the rabbit.

343.18 Thus, it is precisely this relation between cause and effect that is being negated. 343.19 Since the relation between cause and effect is observed elsewhere and is here negated, it does not serve as an example for establishing absolute non-existence.
343.20 By this, the non-existence of things such as a sky-flower should be understood as explained.

344.01 If it is argued that "the self does not exist because it is unperceived," here too there are faults such as those regarding the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, as well as faults regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), as before. Furthermore, the claim that "because it is unperceived" is also untenable. The non-perception [of the self] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the self is an object of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). First of all, the self is perceived through direct perception.

344.04 How can the cognition "I am," which does not depend on the recollection of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), conform to the distinction of the object's own nature?

344.05 Just like the cognition of form (rūpa) and so forth, it would be perceptual (pratyakṣa). Furthermore, as for that perception which you yourself accept as being accompanied by doubt, from what source does its status as perception derive? Therefore, you must necessarily [accept] that consciousness itself [is the means], such as the mark and so forth.

344.07 [If you think: "It should be understood as self-cognizable, independent of any external relation; for there exists this notion 'I am,' yet the Self is not its object"—well then, let the object be specified. If you say that form (*rūpa*) and so forth are the objects, and you think that form and the rest alone are the objects of the ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*), then it is thus: [end of fragment]

And it has been said that the self (ātman) is so called because it is the cause for the arising of the object of the notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra). That is not so, because of its non-existence and because of its refutation. The notion of "I" has been refuted: regarding form and the other [aggregates], one does not say, "I am form," nor does a physician say, "This is your form.
Therefore, form and the others are not the objects of the notion of "I," nor are they...
