344.13 This ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*) is never observed with respect to form (*rūpa*) and the other [aggregates]. For it never occurs that "I am form" or "I am feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth. [Objection: But does it not occur that "I am fair" or "I am dark"? [Reply: We say it does not. Why? Because this is not the case for the seer (*draṣṭṛ*): "This is my form," or "This fair [form] is I."

344.16 Thus, there arises the notion "I am fair" merely by eliding the possessive suffix *matup*; it indicates the sense of the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī-artha). 344.17 [The opponent asks: Why is it said that this is not so in reality? 344.18 If you think that this designation of the genitive sense occurs through the elision of *matup*, and yet it is not real in its true nature—what is the reason for this? [The answer is: Because of the notion of "mine" (*mama-pratyaya*).

344.19 Because of the indication of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), in whatever object the notion "mine" (*mama-pratyaya*) occurs for someone, 344.20 this very same [notion] is also "I" (*ahaṃkāra*); thus, by virtue of its coreferentiality with the notion "mine," it is understood that there is an elision of the possessive suffix *matup*.
345.01 Thus, this notion of "I" is seen to be coreferential with the notion of "mine" even when [the referents] are distinct, as in the case of something that provides assistance.

345.02–345.04: Because [the self] is the beneficiary, the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is observed to have the same locus as the notion of "mine" (mamapratyaya) with respect to the entity that provides assistance.

It has been stated in this regard: "This which is 'I' is seen," and "The notion of 'I' occurs with respect to the aggregates (skandhas) such as form (rūpa), even though it is not that [self]. Furthermore, it is said: "The notion of 'that' (tatpratyaya) [occurs with respect to what is not the self]. Thus, because it is the object of the notion of "I," the self is, for its part, perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa).

345.05 It has also been stated in the *icchā-ādi-sūtra* how the self (*ātman*) is apprehended through inference (*anumāna*). There is also scripture (*āgama*). These three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being connected as having a single object, establish the self; nor is there any other means of valid cognition that serves as a cause for contradiction.
345.08 Therefore, because of this non-perception, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) and doubtful (*sandigdha*), since there are three causes for non-perception.

345.09 The three causes of non-perception are: the perceiver (*upalabdha*), the act of perception (*upalambhana*), and the object to be perceived (*upalabhya*). 345.10 In that regard, when this non-perception occurs, it is doubted from whose absence it arises. If you say:

345.11 “Because of the non-existence of that which is to be perceived”—is this not indeed the very meaning of your proposition? And a proposition does not subvert a proposition. Thus, non-apprehension is not a valid reason. Furthermore, as for this non-apprehension that is employed to establish the non-existence of the self (ātman), what is its locus? If you [maintain that] it apprehends the self...
345.14 This becomes contradictory: that there is a substratum and yet it does not exist. Now, if it is without a substratum, what is the purpose of the proof?

For a property (dharma) that lacks a substratum cannot establish what is to be proven. Furthermore, if non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) itself does not exist, 345.15–16 what is the purpose of the proof by means of non-apprehension? Indeed, it cannot be a non-proof. Now, if...

345.17–19. Since "non-perception" is the property (*dharma*) of the imagined (*kalpita*), how is it to be stated that [it belongs] to the imagined? Is it by way of existence (*sattva*) or by way of non-existence (*asattva*)?

If it is by way of existence, then non-perception cannot be its property; for the properties of a post (*sthāṇu*) do not appear as the properties of a man (*puruṣa*) imagined [in its place]. Now, if it is by way of non-existence, [then... the imagined...

Non-apprehension is established as a property; however, the conceptualization of non-apprehension as a property is futile. What is the reason for this conceptualization? Because it does not correspond to reality. For conceptualization, by its very nature, is that which does not correspond to reality. Since the self is conceptualized as being non-existent, it does not exist by way of non-existence. If it does not exist by way of non-existence, then [the conceptualization] is futile.

346.03. [This is] a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). And for what purpose is this self (*ātman*) postulated as being non-existent? If it is for the sake of a reason (*hetu*), that reason is not established. For if one were to point to something as a reason by superimposing the properties of a post (*sthāṇu-dharma*) onto a person, that thing would not thereby become a post. Therefore...

Even so, non-perception is also not a valid reason. [The argument is: "The word 'self' has an object distinct from the objects denoted by the words for the aggregates such as form, because, while being different from the words for form and so forth, it is a single word, like the word 'jar'. By this, the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is explained. If it is argued that the example is unestablished (asiddha):

346.09. Here it has been stated that the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is distinct from the qualities (guṇa). [If you argue] that this is inconclusive because of the word "darkness" (tamas) and others—346.10. If you think: "Just as the word 'darkness' (tamas), despite being different from words such as 'form' (rūpa) and having the status of a single word, does not have another object as its referent, so too it is with the word 'self' (ātman)," that is not so, because of contradiction. 346.11. [For] while being different from words such as 'form' and being a single word, the word 'darkness' does indeed have another object as its referent. Thus, the example is not established. Furthermore, there is a contradiction: if the self were non-distinct from the qualities, then the self would be impermanent, just like the qualities. Therefore, the self is distinct from the qualities. This is established. 346.12. Moreover, if the self were non-distinct from the qualities, then upon the destruction of the qualities, the self would also be destroyed. But since the self is eternal, it must be distinct from the qualities. This is established. Furthermore, if the self were non-distinct from the qualities, then just as the qualities are manifold, the self would also be manifold. But since the self is unitary, it must be distinct from the qualities. This is established. One who asserts that the word "darkness" (*tamaḥ*) is without an objective referent contradicts our established doctrine, because darkness possesses derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*). Furthermore, we do not accept the claim that the word "darkness" is without an objective referent.
If the word "darkness" does have an objective referent, it would contradict the Sūtra [which states]: "Because of its dissimilarity to the production of substances, qualities, and actions."

"Non-existence is absence; it is darkness. This is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra. Substances, qualities, and actions that have lost their connection with light are designated by the word "darkness"; therefore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra. Others, however, taking the body—though it possesses life—to be the subject (pakṣa) on the grounds of its being soulless, [advance arguments] such as "because it exists," and so forth.
346.18 They state that [the argument] is not a valid reason because the conceptual construction is untenable. What is the meaning of "selfless" (*nirātmaka*)?

If it means "that which does not benefit the self," then there is no supporting example, for nothing whatsoever exists that does not benefit the self. If, on the other hand, it is a negation of the self—meaning "the body is not the self"—then of what [is it the self]?

347.01. Furthermore, because the word *ātman* is the subsequent member (*uttara-pada*) of the compound, one must state whether the body qualified by the negative particle (*nis*) is "with a self" (*sātmaka*).

347.02. For we do not observe the use of the negative particle without a subsequent member, as in the case of *nirmaśakam* ("free from mosquitoes"). Now, 347.03. if it is intended that the self is denied in relation to the body, you are proving what is already established; for whose body, indeed, is there a self?
347.04 [The body] exists. Now, if the body does not belong to the self, then there is no further example.
347.05 And all these are negations of particulars; and from the negation of particulars, a generality is admitted.
347.06 This being so, that which was intended to be negated becomes permitted. Now, as for the word "self" (ātman)—

347.07. The object [of the term "self"] is impermanent because it consists of the nature of phonemes; nevertheless, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the word "eternal," because [words such as] "body" (*śarīra*) and so forth are also designated by the word "self. If, on the other hand, the object of the word "self" is distinct from the body and so forth, even so, the object of the word "self" distinct from the body and so forth—[is impermanent].

347.10 There is a contradiction in [its] acceptance. Thus, in whatever way the non-existence of the self is investigated, in that very way it cannot withstand logical reasoning. 347.11 Therefore, it does not endure under analysis.
347.12 [The opponent argues: "The eyes and other [senses] exist for the sake of another, because they are composites, like beds, seats, and so forth; thus, they are for the sake of another composite.

347.13 [The proponent replies: If you say they are for the sake of an object, and you think it is true that composites exist for the sake of another, yet those [objects] are for the sake of another composite—just as beds and so forth are [for the sake of a person]—that is not so, because there is a contradiction in the acceptance of a composite [as being for its own sake].

347.15 For you do not admit a composite that is distinct from the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; nor, in the absence of another composite, can there be the state of one composite serving the purpose of another composite. If you should admit [such a thing], it would be contradicted and result in an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*). If you think: "No... [the response follows].

347.18 [The opponent argues: "It does not follow that it enters into another composite; rather, when this cause exists, this undesirable consequence follows, because for the sake of another, it is invariably concomitant with another composite, until it serves the purpose of another.
All of that is seen to be for the sake of another composite. [Response: No, because there is no contradiction and because it is not admitted. It is not so.

348.02 For indeed, according to some proponents of a distinct self (*vyatirikta-ātma-vādin*), a composite (*saṅghāta*) acts for the sake of another composite. 348.03 Since this is accepted by both parties, no undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa-āpādana*) is observed; moreover, it would involve a contradiction. 348.04 If, apart from the intended object, the object of inference were also unintended, then surely in this case—

348.05 If [the reason] were a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), all inference (*anumāna*) would be undermined. How so? That which is intended as an inference would not even attain the status of an inference. For example, regarding the impermanence of sound, what is the reason? Just as this "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), being inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with impermanence, establishes impermanence; [if it were a conceptual construction, it could not do so].

In this way, it establishes [the property] of being suffering, empty, and non-self; and just as it establishes [the property of] being suffering, empty, and non-self, it will also establish the property of not being perceivable by the ear. Consequently, sound is not perceivable by the ear because it is produced, like a pot. Thus, this meaning of the proposition is sublated by inference. Therefore...

348.11 It is not a valid reason. Is it not the case that this [argument] is also contradicted by scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*), which state that the eye and other [senses] have as their object another composite (*saṅghāta-antara*)? 348.12 Furthermore, whatever other composite you postulate, in that too the nature of being a composite (*saṅghātatva*) has not ceased; therefore, that too must have another composite as its object, and thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). 348.13 Thus, because the nature of being a composite persists even there, it must likewise have another composite as its object, and in this way, an infinite regress results.

348.14 And no one is able to bring it about, because it ceases [to exist]. 348.15 If that [entity] were uncomposite, then there would be no such thing as the uncomposite; for if the uncomposite is not admitted, a composite cannot be established. 348.16 This is a contradiction, for a composite is never established when the uncomposite is denied.

348.17 Now, if the opponent maintains that inference does not exist at all, one must ask him: "How is it that he does not understand? 348.18 If [he says] inference does not exist because it is sublated by inference, that is an extreme impropriety; for if inference is sublated by inference, yet inference does not exist, how then can there be the comprehension of objects beyond the senses? 349.01 And if [inference does not exist], how is there the comprehension of supersensible objects?

349.02. If inference does not exist, how can an object beyond the senses be known? It is not tenable that the comprehension of supersensible objects will occur through scripture (*āgama*), because the scope of inference is distinct from that of scripture.
Why? Because the scope of inference is distinct from scripture, as in the case of the cause of the sound of thunder; for [inference] does not [function there].

349.05 Therein, perception is not scripture; thus, it is established that the self exists. Regarding that [self], there is doubt because its designation is established in two ways. What, then, is this "designation"? It is the expression of the relationship between an action and an instrument with an agent. Seeing is the action, and the eye is the instrument. Of the instrument...

349.08. There is a relationship between an action and its agent, as in "one sees with the eye. And this designation occurs in two ways: [first] by means of a part for the whole, as in "the tree stands by its roots," where the word for the whole, "tree," denotes the possessor of the parts; and [second] by means of one part for other parts.
349.11 For when something is produced by elements of different classes, one perceives the other parts through the observation of a single part.

349.12 Furthermore, there is a designation [of the whole] by means of another, such as "the palace is supported by pillars," where one thing is designated by another. 349.13 And there is a designation of one thing by another: "he cuts with an axe"; here, the axe is the instrument (*karaṇa*) and cutting is the action.

349.14 Action is the connection of the agent with those two [instrument and object], as in "he cuts with an axe. And this designation exists here as well: "one sees with the eye. Is this a designation of one thing by means of another?
Or rather, is it that the whole is designated by its part, or that one part is designated by another part? Thus is action [designated].
349.17 Or, the designation [of relation] is the connection of the instruments and the objects with the agent, as in "he sees the tree with his eye.
349.18 There is a connection between the action, the instrument, and the object with the agent, and this designation exists here as well:
349.19 "He experiences pleasure and pain by means of the body"; in that case, it is not known what the reality is.
349.20. The truth is that this is a designation of one thing by means of another. How so? 350.01.

[3-1-1] Because a single object is apprehended through both seeing and touching. 350.02. "Because a single object is apprehended through both seeing and touching": that by which one sees is "seeing," namely, the eye.
350.03 Because one touches an object that is to be touched by means of this [organ], it is called the tactile organ (*sparśana*), namely the sense of touch (*tvag-indriya*).

350.04 Through sight, one recognizes through touch an object previously seen, thinking, "I am touching that which I saw," or "I am seeing that which I touched. These two cognitions, having a single object, are joined together; this joining is *pratisandhāna*.

And indeed, there is a state of having a single object for both [cognitions] together with memory. If it is argued that there is no connection because the conditions of seeing and touching have objects such as a jar, etc., and [thus] differ; if you think that these two conditions of seeing and touching have objects such as a jar, etc., and do not indicate a distinction from the self because they belong to different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), [we reply: ...

350.09 Thus [it is said]. This is not due to a lack of understanding of the meaning of the Sūtra. The meaning of the Sūtra is that the two conditions of seeing and touching have a single agent (350.10). And if you prove that even the distinctness of qualities has a single object by means of their connection, there is no fault whatsoever. If it is argued that the distinctness of qualities is unestablished, this has already been addressed regarding how the quality— [is established].

[The opponent claims: "It is distinct from the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*). [The reply: "If it is argued that there is a recognition [of identity] because of a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), this has already been answered in the *icchādi-sūtra*. Furthermore, regarding the recognition of things that do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). Or rather, the meaning of the sūtra is: 'Because an entity (*bhāva*) depends upon an agent (*bhavitṛ*). This is the view."

350.15–350.17: "Seeing" (*darśana*) and "touching" (*sparśana*), as well as "the act of touching" (*sparśana*), are these two cognitions of the nature of an action (*bhāva-rūpa*) that establish an agent (*bhavitṛ*). For we do not perceive an action that is without a substratum, just as [we do not perceive] an arising without an object.
It is not logical to say that there will be a substratum for the action; for seeing occurs even when the object of action (*karman*) is absent.

351.01. The state of existence arises from action (*karman*). And it is not logical that a destroyed action should be the substratum (*ādhāra*) of that state of existence. 351.02. Therefore, that which is the substratum of the state of existence is the self (*ātman*). Because seeing and touching have as their objects form (*rūpa*) and so forth, they do not have a jar or the like as their object; for when form and touch are not perceived, that [object] characterized by them— 351.03. ...is not perceived. Thus, the self is established as the substratum of the state of existence. Furthermore, because the self is eternal, it is not subject to destruction. Since it is not subject to destruction, it is not produced. That which is neither produced nor destroyed is permanent (*nitya*). That which is permanent is inactive (*niṣkriya*). That which is inactive does not possess motion (*gati*). That which possesses no motion does not undergo transformation (*vikāra*). That which does not undergo transformation is without change (*avikārin*). That which is without change is without distinction (*aviśeṣa*). That which is without distinction is without difference (*nirviśeṣa*). That which is without difference is without cause (*ahetuka*). That which is without cause is without effect (*akārya*). That which is without effect is without support (*anālamba*). That which is without support is without dependence (*anapekṣa*). That which is without dependence is independent (*svatantra*). That which is independent is the self. That which is the self is the agent (*kartṛ*). That which is the agent is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). That which is the enjoyer is the experiencer (*vedaka*). That which is the experiencer is the knower (*jñātṛ*). That which is the knower is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*). That which is the seer is the hearer (*śrotṛ*). That which is the hearer is the smeller (*ghrātṛ*). That which is the smeller is the taster (*rasayitṛ*). That which is the taster is the toucher (*spraṣṭṛ*). 351.04–06. Because of the observation of a condition (*pratyaya*), when one perceives an object whose form and other qualities are not being perceived, then a cognition characterized by that [object] arises for him, just as there is a cognition of a crystal situated over something blue and so forth;
and [this occurs] when the form and other qualities are unperceived, as in the case of a crane at night.

351.07. Because it is not apprehended [as such], the cognition of a bird [is distinct]; therefore, the cognition of a jar is distinct from color and touch, and because of recognition (*pratisandhāna*).
351.08. It does not have a distinct cause, for two cognitions having different objects are not recognized [as one].
351.09. And there is indeed recognition: "I touch that which I saw," and "I see that which I touched."

351.10 Thus, it is not logical that the two cognitions—seeing and touching—which have a composite as their agent should have a single object, because the plurality of the composite is not sublated. 351.11–12 A composite is dependent upon the things being combined; and those things being combined are multiple, and the synthesis [of them] is also multiple.

351.13 It is not logical that [the sense-faculties] are the cause of cognition, because cognitions produced by different agents and having different objects do not connect with one another. 351.14 If it is argued that they are "cognitions of a single sense-faculty," then you must think as follows:
351.15 That very same sense-faculty which is the cause of the cognition of seeing is also the cause of the cognition of touch.

351.16 That is not so, because it is not its object. Indeed, the eye is capable of connecting [the perception] with its own object, [thinking], "This very object which I saw is this one," but it cannot connect it with touch, because that is the object of another sense faculty. 351.17–18 Or else, there would be the uselessness of the other sense faculties; for each single sense faculty alone would then effect the connection of the grasping of multiple objects.
The arising of another sense faculty would be purposeless.
352.01 [3-1-2] Not so, because of the determination of objects. 352.02 It is not the case that the sense-faculties are conscious, because of the determination of objects.
352.03 Regarding the phrase "because of the determination of objects," its meaning is this: due to the restriction of the objects of the instruments [of cognition]. This being so...

352.04 When the eye exists, the apprehension of form occurs; when it does not exist, it does not occur. And when something exists, [something else] occurs, and when it does not exist, that [other thing] does not occur; therefore, that belongs to it. Since the apprehension of form occurs when the eye exists, the apprehension of form belongs to the eye. The same applies to the remaining [senses]. This being so, what is the use of another [entity called] volition (*cetanā*)?

352.07 If this is argued, it is not a valid reason because it is doubtful. Is this restriction of the objects of the sense-faculties [due to] 352.08 their being conscious, or rather due to their being instruments of consciousness? It is thus doubted. Even if they are instruments of consciousness, this [restriction] may belong to the sense-faculties, just as the perception of form occurs when a lamp exists.

When [the cause] is absent, [the effect] does not exist. Furthermore, the perception of form is not a proof for the contrary regarding the lamp. And this reason—“because of the determination of the object”—is intended to make known its capacity to prove the contrary.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: “There is no refutation [of the self], because the self exists precisely through that determination.”
352.13 [3-1-3] Precisely because of that determination [of objects], the self exists; therefore, there is no negation [of it].

352.14 Since these sense-faculties have determined objects, for that very reason, there must be another [faculty] whose object is not determined. For if even one sense-faculty were determined to grasp multiple objects—

352.16–18: Who could possibly infer another conscious being [as the cause] on the grounds that there must be an object? Furthermore, since consciousness belongs to the self, and because if the self were independent there would be no fixed order—just as in the case of the eye and other sense organs—the self is not unconscious.

[If it were unconscious,] the consequence of its lack of independence would follow, just as with the eye and so forth. If you argue that this is incorrect because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then...

352.19 You think that for the proof of the sentience of the self, there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor [negative concomitance]; 353.01 [you argue] that the reason is established even without [concomitance]. This is not so, because there is no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) in the case of a relationship of contrariety (*viparyaya*). 353.02 Furthermore, this is not a reason characterized by positive concomitance (*anvayin*), but rather a reason characterized by negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*); and in that case, regarding the relationship of negative concomitance—
353.03. Non-deviation is capacity. Furthermore, it is observed that whatever is insentient has a fixed object.

353.04. If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the property of] possessing odor and so forth being used to prove the eternality of earth and other elements—should you think that if a reason is negative (*vyatirekin*), it functions even without positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then [regarding] the eternality of earth and so forth...

If "being eternal" is the probandum (*sādhya*), why is "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*) not a logical reason (*hetu*)? It is not a reason because it lacks presence in both [the similar and dissimilar instances], since possessing odor is excluded from both the eternal and the non-eternal; however, lack of determination (*avyavasthāna*) is not excluded in this way.
Therefore, lack of determination is the reason, and not possessing odor.
353.09 Furthermore, the self is distinct from the body and so forth; it is not merely the collection of the body and its constituents.
353.10 [3-1-4] Because there is no sin when the body is burned.

353.11 Because there is no sin when the body is burned. By the mention of the "body," the aggregate consisting of the body, the sense organs, cognition, and feeling, which has become a living being, is understood. For one who burns a body that has become a living being, there would be the [sin of] harming a living being.

353.13 What has been done as evil is called a transgression (*pātaka*); its non-existence [is the case] for one who is not the agent, while there is a connection with the fruit for the agent. 353.14 And there is no such connection [for the other]. Why? Because for one who does not accept a self distinct [from the aggregates], there is another—the aggregate of body, sense-faculties, intellect, and sensation—who is the agent, and another who is the enjoyer of that fruit. Thus it is.

353.16–17: Furthermore, the undesirable consequence of the faults of [the self] undergoing what was not done and [the self] losing what was done would follow; therefore, that which is the agent and the enjoyer is the self. This sūtra is intended to demonstrate the fault for one who holds that the self does not exist, and not to provide a proof [for its existence], because it is like memory due to the relationship between cause and effect.
353.19 The conventional usage of "agent" and "experiencer" [is established] just as in the case of a continuum (*santati*) that is determined by the relationship between cause and fruit.
354.01 Just as memory arises in that very same continuum in which the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) was produced, so too:
354.02 That action (*karman*) which originates from the continuum of body and mind has its fruit originating from that very same continuum of body and mind.

354.03 There is no consequence of [the fault of] encountering what was not done or the destruction of what was done. How could that be? If an action performed in one continuum were to yield its fruit in another continuum, and if you were able to establish this point—that "he who acts is the very same one who experiences"—then both [faults] would not exist. But neither is the case.

Therefore, there is no fault such as the "attainment of what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama) and so forth, because this has already been answered; nor does the [doctrine of] continuity (saṃtāna) contradict the diversity [of things], for this has already been answered regarding the claim that [it is so] because [the effect] is not seen in a single [moment]. Furthermore, regarding the point that it is "due to the reconnection of cognitions having a single cause," it is like the case of the seeds of rice and other grains.

354.09 If you think as follows: just as a sprout arises from a rice seed—after the rice seed has been moistened and its husk removed—it manifests through the stages of the stalk, the stem, and so forth, by virtue of the assistance of the elements; and yet, there is no single underlying cause attached to it, and nevertheless...

354.12–13. The restriction [of the result] follows from a rice seed through a rice sprout; thus, by way of the relation of cause and effect, [the result arises] when the continuum is established. 354.13–14. [The result arises] from an action that has reached a specific transformation within the internal mind. [Objection: That is not so, because the parts of the seed do not persist, as in the case of a rice seed; therefore, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

354.15. There too, those parts of the seed, by abandoning their previous configuration, undergo another configuration. 354.16. And upon undergoing this other configuration, the earth element is taken up by the water element and, being internally heated by fire, it, while being cooked, produces a substance of sap. That sap, together with its former parts, attains the state of a sprout and so forth.

354.18 It follows [from this]. Therefore, because the parts of the seed persist, it is said that this is unproven—namely, that just as a sprout arises from a destroyed rice seed and yet there is a reconnection [of the continuum]—if you think that because the parts of the seed exist in the state of atoms, the aforementioned fault would apply. Or, if you further consider: [354.20]...

355.01 The parts of the seed abandon their previous arrangement and undergo another arrangement; since that [arrangement] also exists in the state of atoms, only the atoms of the seed remain. Furthermore, no further distinction of genus exists among the atoms, nor is there any difference between the atoms of a barley seed and a rice seed.

355.04 [Objection: There is a distinction; for example, atoms that have not yet produced a particularity bring about a rice sprout because of the necessity of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on their preceding that [particularity]. Likewise, for me as well, there is a necessity due to the causal relation. [Reply: No, because we do not accept that seeds exist in the state of atoms.
We do not accept this [claim] that [the seed exists] in all states,
because from the beginning state of swelling until the penultimate effect of the rice seed,
it never at any time exists in the state of atoms; for if it did so exist, it would never be perceived.
355.10 In that case, there would be no division down to the level of atoms, and thus there could be no production at the beginning of a kalpa, because the world would exist in the state of atoms;

and while the world is in the state of atoms, there is no manifestation of the species of rice and so forth. Therefore, it must be admitted that at the time of renewed production, the atoms themselves are the causes of the manifestation of the species, just as...

355.13 And [this applies] at the beginning of a kalpa, as well as when the seed is in the state of an atom (*paramāṇu*). This has already been answered by what was stated previously. 355.14 By this very [argument], it has already been answered that there is perception of all states; for at the beginning of creation, there is a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) which is the cause of the manifestation of the rice species, by means of which, for the sake of the experience of living beings, rice and so forth [are produced].

355.16–355.18: Depending upon that specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), the Lord (*īśvara*) causes those various atoms to be produced and combines them in such a way that the manifestation of each species, such as rice and so forth, occurs. By this, the baking of jars and other objects is explained. There is no destruction down to the level of the atoms, because [the object] is perceived in all its states.

355.19 Thus [it is said]. If it is argued that "cooking is impossible due to the state of being raw" (*āmadhyāt*), and you think: if the causal substance and the effect-substance were both cooked, then cooking would not occur because of the state of being raw, owing to the lack of contact with the heating fire (*pācaka-tejas*).
This fault would not arise if there were no obstruction, provided that the fire penetrates the composite whole (*avayavin*). 356.01 [This is the case] if...
But that [wind] does not obstruct it; rather, it enters the unobstructed fire.

Thus, because there is no cause for saying "it does not obstruct," it is not the case that there is no flow and so forth for a jar, since the obstruction of fluidity occurs in a jar that possesses such flow.
356.05. It is observed that liquidity, through its unimpeded nature, causes seepage, and this is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

356.06. If the entry of parts were the destroyer of the substance, then a jar possessing seepage and so forth would not be perceived; because it would be leaking, there would be no retention of the water contained within the vessel.
Furthermore, regarding the destruction of effect-substances, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving both the obstructed and the unobstructed at the same time;
for if one substance, having entered another, were to interpenetrate it, then because the visual ray has entered [the medium],
[the object] such as crystal would be destroyed, and thus [it would be perceived] both when obstructed and when unobstructed.

356.11 Equal perception would follow; therefore, the rice seed is not a valid example. Furthermore, for one [who holds] that other aggregates arise at the very same time as the cessation of the previous aggregates, 356.12 the production of those other aggregates would not have karma as its cause. [It would be] without a causal basis in karma.

356.14–16. [Objection: "Action for the sake of attaining the auspicious and the inauspicious does not occur through the creation of sentient beings. [Response: If you think that action is performed by oneself with the thought, "May I be happy" or "May I not be miserable," that is not so, because [the result] has not been experienced. For one by whom happiness has been experienced [possesses] the means to happiness...

Furthermore, one who possesses the recollection of the connection [between means and ends] adopts the means for achieving that end; however, for one whose mental formations (*saṃskāra*) perish moment by moment, there is an absence of the recollection of the connection between the means and happiness. Consequently, the activity [expressed as] "may I be happy" is untenable, and the exertion for the sake of liberation is likewise untenable without effort.
Because [liberation] is already accomplished, this person is liberated as soon as he is born; thus, the practice of celibacy for the sake of liberation is useless.
Furthermore, the formal inquiry would not be possible: the Tathāgata asks the monks, "Have you been disciplined by me?
and they reply, "We have been disciplined. [This would apply to] the past and the future...

357.03 Furthermore, because those that are present cannot be assisted, first, those conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) which are yet to come and are to be modified do not receive assistance because they are non-existent. Those that are past are likewise [non-existent]. As for those that are present, it is impossible to deposit a modification (*saṃskāra*) within them, because that which is characterized as present cannot be assisted; indeed, there is no persistence of it.
357.06 There is a time when assistance (upakriyā) would occur, because the object to be refined (saṃskārya) and the refiner (saṃskāraka) arise simultaneously.

357.07 If it is argued that this is logical, [we reply: no, for if the object to be refined and the refiner arise simultaneously, a restriction (niyama) is untenable. 357.08 [The restriction] is: "this is the refiner" and "this is the object to be refined."
357.09 It is not tenable; for if it acts while depending on a conditioning factor (*saṃskāraka*), it produces an effect that is distinct from what is to be conditioned (*saṃskārya*).
357.10 And the production of a distinct effect is called "conditioning" (*saṃskāra*). [But this is not so] because there is no designation of what is to be conditioned.
357.11 How could one say, "this is the conditioner" and "this is the conditioned"? For there is no distinction [of the agent] belonging to that [action].

357.12 It cannot be designated that "he" is the one who conditions nor that "this" is the conditioned object. Furthermore, 357.13 even if it is argued that through instruction the non-arising of future conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) is brought about, [it is not so], because 357.14 there is no such thing as the non-arising of future things. That which is the non-arising of future conditioning factors is not [an entity].
357.15–16: "If it is sometimes non-existent, what can be done with it? Therefore, the purpose of living in celibacy (brahmacarya) is for the sake of liberation.
This is untenable; thus, this is a fault [only] for one who does not accept that the self is something other [than the body].
357.17 [3-1-5] Its absence [of sin] would follow even when that which possesses a self is burned, because of its permanence.

357.18 Its absence [of sin] would follow even when that which possesses a self is burned, because of its permanence. For one for whom the self is permanent, 357.19 for him too, the two results of violence do not accrue; first of all, violence does not accrue, because of its permanence.
358.01 Even the result is not logically [produced] by itself, because it cannot be assisted; and regarding this point, they cite a verse (kārikā) as an illustration: 358.02 [The verse follows].
358.03 What can rain and heat do to the sky? Does the sky have any fear of them? 358.04 If it were like skin, it would be impermanent; if it were equal to space, it would yield no fruit.
358.05 Thus, in one view, violence is fruitless; however, in the other position, it is untenable.
358.06 And so, this violence is fruitless; this [violence] is possible in the Sāṃkhya position because the intellect (*buddhi*) is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).
Due to this state of transformation, the relationship of cause and effect is severed, and that very [intellect] produces those fruits.

358.09 [The opponent argues: "Because it does not abandon its state, no result is admitted there; likewise, cognition (*buddhi*) also does not abandon its prior state because of its permanence. [The proponent replies: "If you think that it abandons its prior state, then its permanence is contradicted.
By the relinquishing of its prior state, the permanence of cognition is contradicted. Furthermore, as for the state..."

If you think that [the entity] is divided [from its states], even so, the contradiction remains unremoved; for the possessor of states is not different from the states themselves. Since the possessor of states is not other than the states, when there is a difference in the states, the possessor of states is divided. Whatever fault applies to the Buddhist regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which perish at every moment, that same [fault] applies here.
358.15 [The same applies] even to those things that undergo transformation at every moment. If it is argued that they are like straightness and curvature:

if you think that, 358.16 just as the substance of a finger is not divided by the difference between straightness, curvature, and so forth, and these states are not other than the finger, 358.17 so too there is no difference in the cognition despite the difference in its states—this is not so, because they are indeed other. Straightness and curvature are other [than the finger], and this is logical.

358.18–19: That there is non-difference of one thing when another is different does not, however, imply that here the possessor of states (avasthāvat) is something other than the states themselves. Therefore, the example is not comparable. Furthermore, is curvature or straightness a quality produced by contraction?
Curvature is produced by contraction, and straightness is produced by expansion; and it has been established that qualities and the possessor of qualities are distinct entities.

359.01. If it is argued that this is also the case for cognition (*buddhi*), and you think: "Those two states of cognition are indeed distinct, yet cognition itself is not distinct from them"—that is not so. Because it contradicts your own tenet (*siddhānta-virodhāt*), for in your position there is no distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), even though you nevertheless accept their distinction.

The established tenet (siddhānta) would be abandoned. Therefore, just as the fault of not experiencing pleasure and pain exists in the case of the eternity of the self, and thus pleasure and pain are not attributed to it, so too, because of the eternity of cognition (buddhi), they should not be attributed to cognition either; for eternity is common to both. Now, [if one objects]:

359.07 What is produced for the eternal self by merit and demerit? By those two, what pleasure and pain are produced? 359.08 [Response: The cognition [of] pleasure and pain; the cognition having that as its object arises in the self. 359.09 Thus, only this much is produced, and that cognition is experience (*bhoga*). Furthermore, what is produced by rain and heat?

359.10 Regarding "the sky" (*vyomana*): that which is affected by rain and heat on the part of the hide is what is meant by "the sky. Now, 359.11 what is the connection with the hide? If it is argued that just as the hide is connected with rain and heat, so too is the sky;

and that because of its connection with rain and heat, the sky is impermanent like the hide—if you think thus, [then consider] as with the hide... 359.12 ...[the sky would likewise be impermanent]. If you maintain this view, then [it follows that] the sky is like the hide.
359.13 Just as the sky is modified through its connection with rain and heat, so too will [the atom] be subject to modification through its connection with rain and heat.

359.14 If this is argued, it is not so, because of the lack of exclusivity (anekānta): the atom, though connected with rain and heat, is nevertheless eternal. 359.15 Thus there is a lack of exclusivity. Furthermore, is the impermanence of leather due to its connection with rain and heat, or rather due to its cause?

[The opponent says: "Destruction occurs either through disjunction or through the destruction of the substratum. We, however, say that destruction is logical for that which possesses a cause, because of its disjunction from that [cause]; but for space (*ākāśa*), there is no cause, and thus both [conditions for destruction] are absent. Furthermore, since those things possessing [the cause] persist, the relation [between them] is not the cause of destruction; for if this relation were the cause of destruction, [it would contradict their persistence].

359.19 If [destruction] were not [the cause], there would be no persistence of those things that possess it; however, entities do persist as long as the collection of causes for their destruction has not occurred. Thus, [it is said]: "The contraction and expansion of leather occur due to rain and heat, but not so for space. If you think this, it is not so, because the alternative [explanation] is untenable.

360.03 Regarding the contraction and expansion of a hide, what is the meaning? Is it first of all smallness and largeness, or rather conjunction and disjunction? It is not that contraction and expansion are smallness and largeness, because dimension (parimāṇa) exists as long as the substance exists; for as long as the substance persists, its dimension remains, and while that substance exists, [it does not cease].
"It ceases. Now, [the opponent argues] that the contraction and expansion of the hide are conjunction and disjunction.
That too is not tenable, because of its unity; for conjunction and disjunction are not possible for a single entity.
How then is it said, "contraction of the hide," "expansion of the hide"? [It is said] with respect to the hide—
360.09–360.11: Those contacts among the parts of causes whose effects are not yet destroyed, which arise from contact with heat, do not initiate a new substance;
rather, through their mutual proximity, they subsist in the parts and are figuratively attributed to the hide as inhering in that same object, and this [statement] is with reference to that.

It is said that there is a contraction of the skin, but the skin itself does not contract. By this, [it is meant] the mutual disjunction of its constituent parts, which depend upon contact with water and whose effects are not yet destroyed;
this is "expansion. Furthermore, since there is no example for change [in the case of a substance], that very entity [the skin] undergoes change without being destroyed.

360.15 There is no such example as "it undergoes [change]. However, transformation (*vikriyā*) is the arising of a different entity; for instance, when the previous form and so forth cease and another form arises, the jar is said to be "transformed.
360.16–17 If such a transformation manifests even in the self (*ātman*), then [upon the cessation of pleasure] there too—

360.18 "The manifestation of suffering" means that when the conditions for pleasure cease, there are conditions for suffering; therefore, 360.19 it is established that the eternal self experiences pleasure and pain. Because the self is eternal, 360.20 the fault of violence is unavoidable, as it cannot be accounted for otherwise even if the self were eternal. Otherwise, [it would not be possible].
360.21–22: "Violence does not occur in this case because of the killing of the object, the locus, or the agent"—this is the sūtra for the purpose of making this meaning known.
361.01 [3-1-6] Not [is it killing] because of the destruction of the effect, the substratum, or the agent.

361.02 We do not say that the killing of an eternal being is violence; rather, [it is the destruction] of the body and the means for experiencing pleasure belonging to a being whose nature is indestructible. 361.03 [End of section].
361.04 The sense faculties are unique [to each being]; their affliction, impairment, or destruction constitutes violence (*hiṃsā*).

361.05 From what should this be understood? Because both the act of violence and the experience of its fruit are admitted by both parties; for both the violence and the experience of its fruit are admitted by both sides, and thus this is indeed violence.
361.07. In one view, for one who holds that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish at every moment, 361.08.

what indeed is destroyed? Since destruction is causeless, whose activity could there be? Or, if it is argued that another [agent] destroys by being established as the cause for the arising of a dissimilar [moment], [we reply:]...
361.10: "But surely this is a mere metaphorical designation (*upacāra*); for you, there is no *pradhāna* (primordial matter) by which the producer of the body could be metaphorically designated.

361.11–12: "It is not so, because of the equality [of the case]; for according to your own position as well, the *pradhāna* is not what is being harmed. 361.12: "True; for me too, violence (*hiṃsā*) consists in the killing of an agent who is the substratum of the effect, and thus it is equal [for both sides]. However, this is the distinction:"

361.13 Since, in this one position, that very same self which performs the action by means of the body and other instruments enjoys its fruit, there is no fault of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*).

For you, however, there is both the attainment of what was not done and the loss of what was done; therefore, by process of elimination, if the self were eternal, [the doctrine of] violence [would follow].

361.16 Thus it is established there that by the term "substratum of the effect" (kāryāśraya), the body is denoted, because enjoyment has that as its cause; the sense organs are the agents, because they are the instruments thereof. Alternatively, through a coordinate compound (samānādhikaraṇasamāsa), the body alone is denoted by both the terms "substratum of the effect" and "agent. Thus, [the body] is the agent.
And [the soul is] the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Furthermore, what is this so-called agency (*kartṛtva*) or enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*)?

Agency is the inherence (*samavāya*) of knowledge, desire to act, and effort; enjoyership is the inherence of the experience of pleasure and pain. However, this [enjoyership] does not reside in the body; rather, because it is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), the body is said to be the agent.
362.02 Furthermore, the self is distinct from the body and so forth.
362.03 [3-1-7] Because of the recognition by the other of what was seen by the left eye.

362.04 Because of the recognition by the other of what was seen by the left eye: "What was seen by the left eye, one recognizes by the other"—this is the aphorism. And that synthesis is recognition, which is preceded by memory.
Because recognition and synthesis exist, the fact that cognitions have a single agent is established.
Since this is already established in the section [beginning with] "Because one and the same object is grasped by both seeing and touching," there is no need to begin [this discussion];
thus, the distinction from the self is established, and because it is established, this section should not be commenced. [The opponent says: "The sense organs..."

"Some say it is for the purpose of making known the exclusion [of the self from the senses]. Some explain this section as being for the purpose of making known the exclusion of the self from the sense-faculties (*indriya*). That is not so, because that [exclusion] is already established; for by the preceding section alone, the exclusion of the self from the sense-faculties and the body has already been established. 362.15. It is impossible for [the mind] to have simultaneous contact [with multiple objects], because the atom-sized mind is not manifold, nor is the eye atomic. 362.16. "It will function even without being presided over"—thus the mind would be rendered useless, for it has been established that [the mind] is not presided over.

Rather, among many composite wholes (*avayavin*), that whose constituent causes have been separated is destroyed; that whose [causes] have not been separated is what is perceived. The rest is in the *Bhāṣya*.

364.10 [3-1-12] From the transformation of another sense organ (indriya-antara-vikārāt) / 364.11 And this conscious self (cetana ātmā) is inferred to be distinct from the body and so forth, because of the transformation of another sense organ / 364.12 When someone, having perceived the color or fragrance associated with a certain sour fruit by one [sense], [perceives it again by another].

364.13 When a visible object is being perceived by the sense-faculty [of sight], what is the modification of the gustatory faculty? Furthermore, what is this "modification"? It is the recollection of taste.
364.14 Greed for taste is set in motion; greed is thirst (*tṛṣṇā*). That which is set in motion by thirst for taste is the overflow of water from between the teeth.
364.15 This flooding, that is, the contact of the gustatory faculty with those waters, is called "modification."

364.16 And this memory would not be possible if the senses were conscious; nor [is it possible] in the case of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) that perish moment by moment, because one person cannot remember what was experienced by another. 364.17–18 How can a modification of one sense organ, which is a property of that other sense organ, establish the existence of a self distinct from them, given that they have different loci?
364.19 The modification of the sense-faculties is not the cause for the realization of a self distinct [from them], but rather memory (smṛti).

365.01 For memory would not be possible without a single experiencer; and memory, being an entity, 365.02 requires an agent, just like its own arising—this is the logical principle. Furthermore, there is no modification of the sense-faculties without memory.

365.03–365.04: "It is possible" refers to the perception of a change in another sense faculty [of one who has not experienced the taste], because there is no change in the sense faculty [of one who has]. This is a negative reason (*vyatireka-hetu*).

365.05 [3-1-13] It is not [the case that memory is a separate faculty], because memory has as its object that which is to be remembered (smartavya). Memory is a specific mental factor (dharma); its object is that which is to be remembered. Since this [memory] arises from the presence of the object to be remembered, its capacity [to perceive independently] is not observed.

365.08 It will not cause the rememberer to apprehend [the object], for a sprout produced from the presence of its own causes does not cause one to apprehend an object such as a jar whose capacity is unperceived. 365.09 [The sprout] does not cause the apprehension of an object like a pot, whose efficacy is not observed.
365.10 [3-1-14] There is no refutation because of the existence of that quality within the self (ātman).

365.11 There is no refutation because of the existence of that quality within the self. Memory does not arise from the mere object to be remembered. When one remembers a past object, memory would then follow as being without a substratum, and it cannot be without a substratum.

365.13 It is joined [to something] because it is a quality (*guṇa*); for no quality is ever observed to be without a substratum. 365.14 Nor does this [quality] reside in the sense organ, because it is not perceived there; nor in the object, because that [object] is non-existent [at the time]; nor in the body, 365.15 because bodily qualities are perceptible to both oneself and others, and this [quality] is not without a substratum.

It has been stated that [memory] is because it is a quality (*guṇa*). Nor is it the case that this [quality] does not exist; for if the self (*ātman*) were non-existent, its existence would not be logical.

To the question, "How is it understood that the capacity for its production belongs to something other than those [mental states]?"—this has already been answered by the very same [argument]: the self possesses the capacity to serve as the substratum (*ādhāra*) of memory, and this [memory] is not without a substratum.
"Because it is an effect, every effect is seen to have a substratum, like milk and so forth. By this [it is shown]:
"It is not in the eye, nor in the form, nor does it abide in the interval between the two.
It neither exists nor does it not exist, wherein it might be established."

Thus it was replied: "It is not that it exists, nor is it that it does not exist"—this is a contradiction. Furthermore, the state of being a support for consciousness cannot be refuted by this verse. Why?
Because it is a specific negation; there is a specific negation such as, "That eye is not [the support] of our form," and so forth.

366.06–366.08. Now, if consciousness were indeed without a basis, the statement "it is not the eye [that sees] in regard to form" would be purposeless. For whom does consciousness exist, either in the eye or in form, such that this negation is directed against them? Furthermore, when this negation of the support of consciousness is examined, it establishes the existence of a self (*ātman*).
366.09 For this sentence does not establish its meaningfulness without the existence of a self for consciousness.
366.10 Alternatively, the connection of the apprehension of multiple objects by a single [subject] is demonstrated by this very aphorism.
366.11 Thus is the stated method; the rest is in the commentary (bhāṣya).
366.12 [3-1-15] And because the objects of memory are innumerable.
366.13 [3-1-15(16)] Because the causes for the cognition of the self are not possible in the mind.
366.14 Because the causes for the cognition of the self are not possible in the mind—those which have been [posited] by you as the self...
All these reasons taught as proofs are possible only in relation to the mind;
and thus, a self distinct from the mind is not established.
366.17 [3-1-16(17)] Because the knower possesses the means of knowledge, there is merely a difference in designation.

366.18 Because the knower possesses the means of knowledge, there is merely a difference in designation; just as one who accepts a knower acknowledges the eyes and other organs as the means of knowledge, so too one who accepts a thinker [must acknowledge the means of thought].
367.01. One must accept a means for producing cognition; and that which is the means for producing that cognition is the mind (manas). 367.02.

[If you say this is merely a difference in terminology, we reply: if the cognizer produces cognition without a means, then in this way the knower will produce knowledge without a means, which entails the undesirable consequence of the abolition of all sense organs.

367.04 [3-1-17(18)] And the restriction is without inference. 367.05 And this restriction which is relied upon—that "cognition (mati) is not a means of proof, but rather it is the making known (jñapti)"—is without inference; for if cognition were a means of proof, it would be like the making known.
367.07. There is an inference that pleasure and so forth are objects distinct from form and so forth, because they have those [latter] as their objects.
367.08. There must be an instrument for perception; indeed, no cognition whatsoever has an object without an instrument.

367.09. It is observed to be like the cognition of form and so forth; thus, the restriction [that all cognitions require an instrument] is not without inference regarding the cognitions of pleasure and so forth.

367.10–12: [If it is argued that] "let all cognitions (*vijñāna*) be without means (*niḥsādhana*), so that they do not have objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth," then [if] cognition is said to be the means, the mind (*manas*) would also require another instrument, because it too is an object. 367.12–13:
If it is said, "Yes, there is an instrument for the mind," then what is that by which the mind is apprehended?

367.13 And by what is the mind apprehended? [It is apprehended] by the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions; for one for whom the mind is a direct perception (pratyakṣa), 367.14 the conjunction of the self and the mind, assisted by the dharma born of yoga (yogaja-dharma), is the instrument (karaṇa) for the yogis' dharmas.
367.15 Furthermore, because its object is inconceivable (acintya-viṣayatva), the question of how they perceive the mind is not to be investigated.
367.16 By this, the [existence of] the self (*ātman*) has been refuted, on the grounds that the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*) is the cause [of cognition].

Thus, first, the existence and distinctness of the self are established, as well as its plurality; for this very reason, through seeing and touching, [it is known that] because one object is grasped by both, one person does not remember what was seen by another. Therefore, [the soul is not destroyed] upon the burning of the body, nor is there [sinful] demerit (*pātaka*).
"Because of non-existence": this entire systematic arrangement is possible only when there is a difference of bodies.
Furthermore, regarding the question of whether this [self] is distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth, and whether it is eternal or non-eternal—

because it is observed in both ways, he establishes a doubt; yet this doubt is untenable in form, since by means of the reasons for the existence of the self, [it is shown that] the self remains non-different even upon the dissolution of the body.

368.04: [The opponent argues: "Since the perfected one (siddha) is already perfected, this treatise (*prakaraṇa*) need not be commenced. [The author replies: It is not that it need not be commenced. How so? From birth until death, from this [state], one attains perfection; however, it does not occur after the destruction of the body. Thus, for the purpose of making known this meaning—that there is a continuity of memory (*smṛti-anubandha*) due to what was practiced in a previous life for one who is born—[the treatise is commenced].
368.07. "The occurrence of joy, fear, and sorrow" is the aphorism.
368.08 [3-1-18(19)] Because of the continuity of memories practiced in a previous life, there is the manifestation of joy, fear, and sorrow in one who has been born.

368.10 The meaning of this is as follows: Indeed, this newborn infant, while his sense faculties are still incapable of perceiving external objects, is observed to experience joy, fear, and sorrow, which are to be inferred by his smiles, tremors, and weeping.

368.12 And these arise from the continuity of memory; furthermore, the continuity of memory does not exist without a previous body. 368.13 Thus, in that context, "birth" is the connection with a specific class [of beings] characterized by body, sense-faculties, cognitions, and feelings. 368.14 "Joy" is the experience of pleasure upon attaining the desired object through longing for it.

368.15 Fear (*bhaya*) is the inability to abandon that which one desires to avoid when it encounters the means of attaining an undesirable object. 368.16 Sorrow (*śoka*) is the longing for the attainment of something when there is separation from a desired object; its experience is the realization [of that loss].
368.17 Habitual practice (*abhyāsa*) is the arising of multiple cognitions regarding a single object, or a single form as an object.

Just as [one says], "these rice grains were cultivated by him," when direct perception has ceased, the cognition whose object is the synthesis of that [past experience] is memory (*smṛti*). The cognition whose object is the synthesis of that [past experience], supported by that [memory], is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which has the existence of that [object] as its object. The connection is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) called cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which is the cause of memory.
369.01. From the recollection of a desired object, there is clarity of the eyes and so forth, and smiling. From the recollection of an undesired object, 369.02.
there is the characteristic of the desire to abandon its cause and the performance [of that abandonment], consisting of the movement of the hands and so forth, accompanied by the shedding of tears.
369.03. A particular sound [arising] together with these is weeping. Since smiling and weeping have different loci, they do not constitute a valid proof.

369.04 Now, if you think that smiling and weeping occur during the state of childhood, and that this state of childhood does not belong to the self—and therefore, because they reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), [the reason] is not a valid means of proof—[we reply: no, because the state of childhood is established as possessing a self subject to sorrow and so forth; that is, it possesses a self characterized by sorrow and the like.

369.07 The state of infancy is the probandum, because it possesses smiling, crying, and so forth. The state of infancy is a property of age, like the state of youth. By this, the possession of a self—which is preceded by memory, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and experience, and which involves a connection with a previous body—is explained. How so? Just as [the existence of a self] is established through the presence of smiling and crying.

369.10 The state of childhood is established as possessing a self characterized by sorrow and so forth, by virtue of its possessing a self characterized by sorrow and so forth. 369.11 The state of childhood is to be established as possessing a self characterized by memory, by virtue of its possessing a self characterized by memory.

369.12 The state of childhood is to be established as possessing a self characterized by mental formations (*saṃskāra*), by virtue of its possessing a self characterized by mental formations, [just like] a previous experience.
369.13–14. "Possessing a self" means possessing a self by virtue of having the nature of previous experience—that is, possessing a self through connection with a previous body.

369.14–15. The state of youth is to be established as the universal example (*dṛṣṭānta*), for it is observed to possess both smiling and weeping; thus, it must be stated in all cases that [the subject] possesses a self characterized by sorrow and so forth.

369.16 [3-1-19(20)] Its modification is like the modifications of opening and closing in lotuses and the like; 369.17 even though they are impermanent, 369.18 because modification is observed, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika). This is the meaning of the Sūtra. But what is this "awakening" (prabodha), and what [is it]?
369.19. Regarding "closing": awakening is the non-destructive causal disjunction of the parts of the lotus petals.

369.20. Furthermore, the mutual contacts of the lotus petal parts that have already begun their causal activity [constitute the state]; that is "closing. This is not due to the impossibility of conceptualization, for in lotuses and the like, there is both awakening and closing.

370.02–04. Is the example "its modification is like that of a transformation and so forth" a case for proof (*sādhana-pakṣa*), or is it a case of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika-pakṣa*)? If it belongs to the side of proof, then since it is merely an example without a logical reason (*hetu*), it is not a proof;
thus, the example is non-probative. Alternatively, if it is a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), then what [is its basis] other than the observation of a cause?

370.05–370.07: Is it a rejection [of the cause], or the production of another reason, or an inference regarding the causes of its own arising and cessation, or its being accidental? If, first of all, it is a rejection of a perceived cause, that is incorrect, because [the cause] is specified by what is perceived during states such as youth and so forth.

It is observed that [the infant] possesses smiling and crying, as well as possessing a self characterized by sorrow and so forth. Since the possession of a self characterized by sorrow and so forth in the state of infancy is understood through the observed presence of smiling and crying, there is no fault. Furthermore, the proposal of another cause is also not tenable for this very reason.
370.11 Because it is qualified by what is perceived. Now, [if you argue] that there is an inference for the cause of the self’s arising and cessation:

370.12 That is not tenable, because that which exists as a substance is always formless; therefore, the self has no cause, like space and so forth. 370.13 Furthermore, by one who maintains that the self is produced, a cause for it must be admitted.

370.14 Why must it be stated? Because every effect possesses a cause; for it is observed that every effect has a cause. [Objection: This is not so, because the transformations consisting of the five elements have as their causes the seasons of heat, cold, and rain.
370.19 [Response: The meaning of the Sūtra is that this transformation—the opening and closing of lotuses and the like—is not accidental.
371.01 And this being the case, nothing is negated by the example regarding the transformations consisting of the five elements.

371.02 Thus [it is said]. It is not that the lotuses consist of the five elements; rather, they are called "fivefold" because they exist when there is the assistance of the five great elements (bhūtas). However, in reality, nothing whatsoever consists of the five [elements], as we shall explain further below.
371.05 [3-1-21(22)] From the desire for breast milk caused by the habitual practice of seeking food in a previous life;

371.06 from the desire for breast milk caused by the habitual practice of seeking food in a previous life. 371.07 The desire for breast milk in a newborn calf is understood through its activity; in that case, the desire for breast milk is inferred from the activity. By this—
371.08. Memory, as well as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), [proves] experience, and through that, a previous body; thus the application [of the argument] is as before. 371.09.
But for what purpose is this sutra commenced, when this matter has already been understood from the previously studied sutra? 371.10.
There is no fault, for the sutra is intended to make known the specific details of that which was understood only in a general sense. This is the commencement.

371.11–12: "The approach [of the soul] toward that [body] is like the movement of iron toward a magnet; this is for the purpose of making known that [the reason] 'being composed of matter' (mātratva) is inconclusive.
Thus is the aphorism.
371.13 [3-1-22(23)] Its approaching that [object] is like the movement of iron toward a magnet.

371.14 Not so, because conceptual construction is untenable. Is this movement of iron toward a magnet caused by a motive, or is it without a motive? If it is caused by a motive, by what is that known?

371.16 By necessity, iron pieces approach only a magnet, and not clods of earth or other such objects; nor do clods of earth and the like approach [the magnet]. From this restriction regarding the effect, a restriction regarding the cause is understood.
371.18 By this, the occurrence of things by chance is refuted. Is this movement of iron pieces caused by a visible cause?
372.01. This has been proposed either for the purpose of refutation, or for the purpose of demonstrating another reason, or [regarding] the self—372.02.
the inference of arising and cessation; thus, there is the same consequence as before.
372.03 [3-1-23(24)] Not so, because there is no occurrence elsewhere.
372.04 And the sūtra "because there is no occurrence elsewhere" is for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of causelessness (ākasmikatva).
372.05 [3-1-24(25)] Because the birth of one free from passion is not observed.

372.06 The self is eternal, because one who is free from passion is not seen to be born. For no one is born who is free from passion immediately upon birth; since those who are free from passion are not seen to be born, it is understood that one is born possessed of passion. Birth has already been explained. What follows from this? [That] passion is something previously experienced...

The source [of passion] is the mental preoccupation with sense objects, and passion does not arise when the sense faculties are incapable of perceiving those objects. Furthermore, such preoccupation with sense objects is not possible without memory.
If it is argued that this "volition" (saṃkalpa), which is the longing for an object previously experienced, arises from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)—if you think thus—then...

372.12–14: "The connection with a previous body is understood from passion; moreover, passion [arises] from the unseen (adṛṣṭa). This is not so, because of a failure to understand the intended meaning. The intended meaning is not that passion is restricted by its cause [in such a way], but rather that the purpose of the Sūtra is to demonstrate the connection with a previous body. And it is not by one who says that passion arises from the unseen [that this is established].
That is refuted; it has been stated that passion arises from being "composed of that" (*tanmaya*), meaning from the repeated practice of sense objects.

Indeed, this cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause [of passion], and what is called "being composed of that" refers to a specific type of birth (*jāti-viśeṣa*). Furthermore, it is said that a specific type of passion arises from a specific type of birth.
Now, this karma is the producer of the specific type of birth; because it serves that purpose, it receives that designation.
Like vīraṇa grass and so forth.

372.19 [3-1-25(26)] "Its production is like the production of a substance possessing qualities" (saguṇa-dravya-utpatti-vat tad-utpattiḥ). This is a sūtra regarding the inconclusive (anaikāntika) position. It was not stated [as a fault], because it has already been answered; this is an answer to what was previously stated.

373.03 [3-1-26(27)] "Because passion and the like have volition as their cause" (na saṃkalpa-nimitta-tvāt rāga-ādīnām). Here too, as before, the properties of being the self—namely, having volition, memory, latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), prior experience, and a prior body—should be applied. Thus...
And since it is established that beginningless saṃsāra ends in liberation (apavarga), it follows that this self exists as something distinct [from the body] and eternal.

373.08 Immediately after the self (*ātman*), the body (*śarīra*) is examined as it has reached its proper occasion. Alternatively, since the connection of the conscious being with a body is beginningless, the body is examined. While that is being examined, the section concerning the self is brought to completion. What, then, is to be examined regarding this [body], and what is it?

373.11 There is doubt arising from conflicting views as to whether [the sense organs] have a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) like the olfactory organ and so forth, or diverse primordial natures. Indeed, a conflict of views is heard regarding this matter; therein lies the truth.
373.13 [3-1-27(28)] The human body is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), because other qualities [of earth] are perceived in it. 373.14 Why is it specified as "human"?
373.15 It is rightly specified so that the bodies of other worlds are not considered to be composed of earth, since [the human body] possesses the quality of odor (*gandhavattva*).
373.16 Just as an atom possessing fragrance is observed to have a single nature, so too is the body possessed of fragrance.

373.17 Therefore, it has a single essence and a single intrinsic nature; however, this [body] is not composed of earth alone, unmixed with water and the other elements. 373.18 And since it is conceived as the basis for the sense organs and their objects, the conjunction of the primary elements (*bhūta*) is not contradicted.
“In that case, [the body] consists of earth, water, and fire, because their qualities are perceived” (3-1-29); “because inhalation and exhalation are perceived”;
[it is] composed of the four elements (3-1-30); “it is composed of the five elements because of smell, moisture, digestion, expansion, and the provision of space”—thus it has been refuted.
374.03–04: "Because those qualities are perceived in what is present therein"—this [body] has multiple elements as its material cause (prakṛti).

374.04–05: "The body would be without taste, without smell, without color, and without touch, because it conforms to its material cause"—this is the commentary (bhāṣya). Its explanation is: when [the body] is produced from earth and water, it would be odorless, because the cause...

374.06 Because a single odor does not initiate [a new substance]. That which is initiated by earth and fire would be without odor and without taste. 374.07 Because the odor and taste of the causes alone do not initiate [a new substance]. That which is [initiated] by earth and fire is without odor;
374.08 and it is without taste and without form, because wind lacks odor, taste, and form. [That which is initiated] by earth and space is without odor.
374.09. It is without taste, without form, and without touch; because of the absence of odor and so forth in space (*ākāśa*), the same principle applies everywhere.
374.10. This is because a solitary quality of a cause does not initiate [an effect]. Water and fire are without odor and without taste. 374.11.
Water and air are without odor, without taste, and without form; water and space are without odor, without taste, and without form.
And it is without touch, being distinct from fire and wind; it is without odor, without taste, and without form, being distinct from fire and space.
It is without odor, without taste, without form, and without touch, being distinct from wind and space; likewise with earth, water, and fire.
It is without odor, [without taste, without form, and without touch] by means of earth, water, and wind; likewise by means of earth, water, and space; likewise by means of earth, wind, and fire.
374.15 It is without odor and without taste by means of earth, fire, and space; likewise, it is without odor and without taste by means of earth, wind, and space.

374.16 It is also formless by means of water, wind, and fire; it is without odor and without taste by means of water, fire, and space; likewise, it is without odor, without taste, and formless by means of water, wind, and space;
likewise, it is without odor, without taste, and formless by means of fire, wind, and space; likewise, [it is so] by means of earth—
374.18 By means of water, fire, and wind—by earth, water, fire, and space—it is likewise without odor; by earth, water, fire, and space, it is likewise without form.
374.19 By water, wind, fire, and space—it is likewise without odor and without form; by water, wind, fire, and space, it is likewise without odor.
375.01 By earth, water, fire, wind, and space—it is likewise without odor, [due to] the single quality of its cause.
