It must be stated that [the effect] does not originate [from it] because it lacks a beginning; however, if it were to have a single cause, then—as has been stated—the impossibility of constant production and the consequence of its being eternal would follow.

375.04 [3-1-31(29)] And because of the authority of scripture (śruti). 375.05 And because of the authority of scripture: at the end of this mantra, "I fortify your eye with the sun," 375.06 [it says] "your body on the earth. This is a traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding the production of an effect from a cause. As it has been said:
375.07–08: “The sun is the cause of the eye, and the earth is [the cause] of the body”—this is the mantra at the time of the final sacrifice.

375.08: “May your eye go to the sun; may your body go to the earth. The meaning of this mantra is as follows: 375.09: Whatever has arisen from something, that returns to dissolution into that very same thing; for a modification dissolves back into its primary source (*prakṛti*).

375.10 [This is] the designation. By the word "pralaya" (dissolution), the cause devoid of its effect is expressed; it is not, however, 375.11 that the dissolution of the effect into the cause is "pralaya. And thus, the meaning stated is: "the non-existent arises, and the existent ceases.
375.12 This is the sense that has been explained.
375.13 [3-1-32(30)] Because there is perception when the black pupil (kṛṣṇasāra) is present, and because there is no perception when it is removed, 375.14 there is doubt.
375.15 Now, the sense organs are being examined according to the sequence of the objects of knowledge (prameya): are they unmanifest (avyaktika)?
375.16–17: "Are they derived from the ego (āhaṃkārika) or are they elemental (bhautika)? This is the aphorism intended to demonstrate the cause of doubt.

375.18 Because perception occurs when the pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*) is present, and because perception occurs even apart from it, there is doubt. 375.19 The pupil is composed of the elements (*bhautika*); for as long as it is unimpaired, there is the perception of objects. 375.20 Apart from the pupil, there is the perception of an object situated at a remote location; this perception occurring apart from it is [evidence that the sense organ] is not composed of the elements (*abhautika*).

376.01. Thus, because both properties are perceived, there is doubt. [The opponent argues: "The eye is indeed the black pupil (kṛṣṇasāra), because the perception of form occurs when that exists; for this perception of form occurs when the black pupil exists and does not occur when it does not exist.
And whatever occurs when something exists and does not occur when it does not exist, [that belongs to it]."

"That" [is the subject]; for example, as with the color and other qualities of an effect-substance (*kārya-dravya*). It is not so, because there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to lamps and the like. When a lamp exists, the perception of form occurs, yet the lamp itself is not the perception of form; thus, there is no inconclusiveness. For one whose eye has a black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*), [the perception of] near and distant objects [occurs].
It follows that there would be an equal perception [of both]. The black pupil (kṛṣṇasāra) does not reach the object, because there is no distinction in reaching it.

It follows that there would be an equal perception of what is near and what is distant, because [both would equally] be objects. If you think: "The near one is its object, while the distant one is not an object."
And thus, it is not the case that there is no equal apprehension, because this has already been answered in the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*.
Others say they are non-material (*abhautika*),
[because] of the perception of both the large and the minute.

376.13 Because it perceives both the large and the minute: "large" refers to that which is larger or largest, and "minute" refers to that which is more minute or most minute. 376.14 These two, being perceived by the eye, establish its material nature (bhautikatva).
376.15 For the eye obstructs [objects]; indeed, as long as something is material, it occupies space, whereas that which is non-material does not.
376.16 However, because it is all-pervasive, it is connected with everything; this is not so in the case of material things such as lamps, because [the property] is observed in them.
376.17 Material things such as lamps illuminate both the large and the minute; thus, [your reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

376.18 Alternatively, if lamps and the like are not accepted, then the illumination of the large and the minute belongs to the eye alone; thus, [the reason] would be an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) [inconclusive] one.

Therefore, [the reason] is not a valid probans (*ahetu*) for the exclusion of both the elemental (*bhautika*) and the non-elemental (*abhautika*). But surely, in the case of non-elemental cognition (*jñāna*), the capacity to illuminate the large and the small is observed? It is not so; for it is not the case that the large and the small are illuminated by the intellect (*buddhi*).
Rather, it has been established that cognition is illumination itself, and not the object of illumination. Thus, there is the abandonment of the determined object.

377.02–03: Since the intellect (buddhi) is the means for the apprehension of grasping (upādāna), equanimity (upekṣā), and cognition (buddhi), it is not composed of the elements; it is neither gross nor subtle, and it is illuminating.

377.03–04: Is it not true that the mind (manas) exists? Truly it does, yet it is neither elemental (bhautika) nor non-elemental (abhautika). By this, the self (ātman) is also explained: it is neither elemental nor non-elemental, if [it is so defined].

377.05–377.07. As for what was stated—that the sense faculties are derived from the primary elements (*bhautika*) while the mind (*manas*) is not derived from them—that remains unrefuted. For "not derived from the primary elements" is a synonym for having a non-existent nature (*abhūtātmaka*); thus, when it is said that the mind is "not derived from the primary elements," it means that the mind has a non-existent nature. However, in the primary sense, the mind is not derived from the primary elements.
377.08–09: It is not non-material (*abhautika*), because the same [reason] applies to the sense-faculties (*indriya*) as well; thus, the sense-faculty is non-material. 377.09–10:

To the extent that it is said to be "non-substantial in nature" (*abhūtātmaka*), one who maintains that the sense-faculty is both non-substantial in nature and pervasive (*vyāpaka*) must be questioned: why does the apprehension of an object not occur when it is obstructed? What [is the reason]?
377.11–12. [The opponent says: "Because the sense organ is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), walls and such things do not have the power to obstruct it"—this is the [opponent's] position.
377.12–13. [The author replies: If you think that this is being refuted—[we say] it is true that the sense organ is all-pervasive;
however, when it is stirred by the cause of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), its [faculties] emerge like bubbles from a great lake. They are thus [the means of perception].
377.14–15: Since [the senses] are obstructed by walls and the like, there is no proof for the existence of the sense-faculty (indriya) apart from its function (vṛtti).

377.15–16: Apart from that function, which consists in the grasping of objects, what proof is there for an "indriya" distinct from it? Furthermore, an object that lacks a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) cannot be established.

377.17 And it is not possible to establish the identity of that which is being negated and that which is not being negated; for if there were identity, then either [the negation] would be purposeless, or the operation (*vṛtti*)—expressed as "it operates" and "it issues forth"—would be negated. 377.18–19 Furthermore, because of non-distinction (*avyatireka*), if the sense organ (*indriya*) is non-different from its operation, then like the operation itself, the sense organ would possess the properties of arising and perishing.

In this way, both arising and destruction would apply to the sense organ as well. If it is argued that the manifestation of the function is not its origination, [we reply: cessation is indeed destruction, rather than mere concealment; therefore, manifestation is not distinct from origination. Now, if you think:
"I do not admit that there is an origination of the function, but rather that it is a manifestation," [we reply:
cessation is indeed destruction, rather than mere concealment; therefore, manifestation is not distinct from origination.
378.03. [This concerns] the distinction regarding origination. How so? Because there is no manifestation of that which has not acquired a distinction.

Now, if you think that what has not acquired a distinction is manifested, then manifestation would have to be eternal. By this, destruction is also explained. As for "concealment," it is not the case that something existing is obstructed.
378.06 For there can be no non-perception of that whose specific difference has not ceased. Nor is perception [possible] for one who maintains that everything is eternal;
378.07 since neither perception nor non-perception is logical, because there is no arising of a specific difference, and because there is no production of a specific difference.
378.08 Thus, for one who accepts that the sense organ is eternal and all-pervading, the meaning of "cause" is lost.
378.09. What is called a "cause" (kāraṇa) is that which exists immediately prior to something else; and if both cause and effect are eternal, [how can there be a sequence]?
378.10. Thus, what could exist immediately after what? And how could there be a relationship of cause and effect between the two, given their eternity?
378.11. Furthermore, the meaning of the word "cause" must be stated. Is it not true that a "causal agent" (kāraka) is so called because it "acts" (karoti)? Indeed, it acts.

Furthermore, for the proponent of eternalism (nityavādin), there is no agent (kāraka) whatsoever, nor is there anything to be produced; and when there is nothing to be produced, we do not perceive the purpose of an agent. If it is argued that the purpose of the agent lies in manifestation (vyakti), then the same applies to manifestation.

Since manifestation is also eternal—just like that which is manifested—there is no purpose of an agent even in relation to manifestation, because [the object and its manifestation] would exist simultaneously and in manifold ways.

Furthermore, because of the consequence of [multiple] cognitions: if the activity (*vṛtti*) is not distinct from the possessor of activity (*vṛttimat*), then because the activities persist, the possessor of activity would also persist; thus, there is the consequence of multiple simultaneous cognitions due to the multiplicity of activities. Moreover, if the activities are not distinct from the possessor of activity, it follows that a single sense-faculty (*indriya*) would become multiple, because it is non-different from its activities. Now, suppose this were not so...

378.18–20: [Objection: If it is argued that there is a distinction between the sense-faculties (*indriya*), then it follows that the functions (*vṛtti*) would be one, because the function and the possessor of the function (*vṛttimant*) are non-different. Alternatively, if both [the distinction and the identity] are not accepted so that this fault does not arise, then there is no other possibility regarding the distinction between the function and the possessor of the function. Therefore, a pervasive and eternal sense-faculty is untenable.

And [the phrase] "and so forth" [is used]. Furthermore, the apprehension of the large and the small is established otherwise; thus, this reason—namely, that "the sense organs are non-material because they apprehend the large and the small"—is established otherwise. It is not possible to understand the non-material nature or the pervasive nature of the sense organs merely from the apprehension of the large and the small. Why is this? [Because...]
379.04 Because, due to a specific proximity between the ray and the object, there is the perception of both the large and the minute.
379.05 [3-1-34(32)] Its apprehension is due to a specific contact between the ray and the object.
379.06 Because of a specific contact between the ocular rays and the object, there is the apprehension of both the large and the minute.
And that—379.07—the apprehension of the universal occurs from mere contact, while the apprehension of the particular occurs from a specific contact. What [is this]?

379.08. The distinction of contact (*sannikarṣa*) consists in the assistance provided by the contact with more [of its] parts (*bhūyo’vayava-sannikarṣa*), because this contact (379.09) is the cause for the apprehension of the particularity (*viśeṣa*). That which is assisted by the conjunctions with more parts—this contact between the sense organ and the whole (*avayavin*), which depends upon the conjunctions with other parts—is called a "distinction of contact" (*sannikarṣa-viśeṣa*); and that...

379.11–12. The specific nature of the contact between the ray and the object is the same for both the minute and the large; otherwise, the perception of the large and the minute would not be established. Furthermore, the contact of the ray with the object is evidenced by obstruction, because objects screened by walls and the like do not manifest their form [to the sense organ]. If [the sense organ] were to act without reaching its object, then walls and the like would lack the capacity to obstruct. Thus, it exists.

379.14–15: "Just as the ray of the eye [is like] the ray of a lamp"—this was said because [the ray] is to be inferred from its obstruction. 379.16: "The non-perception of that is not a valid reason. 379.16: "The non-perception of that is not a valid reason"; the meaning of the Sūtra is that the visual ray does not exist. How so?

379.17 Thus [it is said]. Because it has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), inference is untenable. For indeed, that which has reached the conditions for perception but is not perceived does not exist, such as a jar or the like. Since jars and the like possess largeness, being composed of multiple substances, and color, they are perceived; likewise, [the subject] possesses largeness, being composed of multiple substances, and color.
379.20 Why is the visual ray not perceived through direct perception? First, it is because of its minuteness (mahattva).

380.01 [The magnitude of a substance arises] from the magnitude of its causes, from plurality, and from accumulation; furthermore, the possession of multiple constituent substances (anekadravyavattva) [also leads to perceptibility], which likewise results from the plurality of causes.
380.02 Since fire possesses both color and touch, it is not devoid of color; thus, when all the conditions for perception are present, [it should be perceived].
380.03 When something exists but is not perceived, it is understood from that [non-perception] that it does not exist.
380.04 [3-1-36(34)] The non-perception by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of that which is being inferred is not a reason for its non-existence.

380.05 It is not the case that the non-perception by direct perception of that which is being inferred is a reason for its absence. 380.06 That which is not perceived by direct perception does not mean it is non-existent simply because it is being perceived by inference; just as in the case of the moon.

380.07–380.08: Furthermore, the far side of the earth and its lower part, even though they have attained the characteristics of being perceptible, are not perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Nor are they non-existent, since they are apprehended through inference (anumāna). What, then, is the inference?
It is the cognition of both [sides], just as in the case of the near side; likewise, the obstruction by walls and the like of the visual ray is an inference.

"It is possible," [they say]. Others, however, maintain that perception occurs because of largeness (*mahat*), the possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and the possession of color-form (*rūpavattva*).
Regarding this perception, they describe a restrictive rule (*niyama*): "It is not the case that whatever is being perceived is necessarily so. What is meant by this?
It is not logical to say that wherever largeness, the possession of multiple substances, and color-form exist, that very thing must be perceived.
380.13 However, in whatever [object] is perceived, there exist therein largeness (*mahat*), the state of being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and color-form (*rūpa*).
380.14 If that is so, then this Sūtra does not establish perception as having existence (*sat*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
380.15 for when largeness, the state of being composed of multiple substances, and color-form exist, perception does not fail to occur—therefore, these are not the causes of perception.
380.16 Thus [3-1-37(35)]: "And because of the distinction between substance, quality, and property, there is a restriction regarding perception.
Regarding the statement, "And because of the distinction between substance, quality, and property, there is a restriction regarding perception," the rest is in the Bhāṣya. Why?
380.19: "In that case, the visual ray is not perceived because of the absence of the causes for perception.

381.01: "The causes for perception are not merely these [large size and being composed of multiple substances]; rather, it is a specific quality of color (rūpa-viśeṣa) that is designated as such, on account of the apprehension of color, and not color alone—thus says the Sūtra. 381.02: "It is not only these that are the causes for perception, namely large size, being composed of multiple substances, and color; rather, it is a specific quality of color that is denoted by the term 'perceptible,' based on the apprehension of color, and not color in its mere generality. And thus is the Sūtra."
381.03 [3-1-38(36)] The perception of color occurs due to its inherence in multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color.

381.04 Regarding the statement "the perception of color occurs due to its inherence in multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color," here, by the mention of "specific quality of color" (*rūpa-viśeṣa*), the property of color known as "manifestation" (*udbhava*) is denoted, not the universal "color-ness" (*rūpatva*). 381.05 [End of section]
381.06. Internal form is distinguished; however, because it is that which brings about manifestation (*udbhava*), it is called a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*). Just as 381.07.

"a specific Brahmin" does not mean that Brahminhood itself is the specific Brahmin, so too, that which serves to distinguish among things of the same class is called a "distinction. And this manifestation is to be inferred from its effect, for in the absence of which [manifestation], [the cause] remains unattached.

381.09 A substance consisting of the watery constituent is perceived in winter, and that of the fiery constituent in summer; because of the absence of which [the latter], 381.10 the ray of a lamp and the ray of the sun are perceived—that is the specific quality called "emergence" (udbhava). 381.11 Since there is no such specific quality of form in that solar ray, it is therefore not perceived by the eye.
Furthermore, a distinction in the properties of fire is observed. Fire is of four kinds: that which has manifested color and touch, such as the rays of the sun;
that which has manifested color but unmanifested touch, such as the rays of a lamp;
that which has both manifested, because the color is manifest to perception; and that which has manifested touch but unmanifested color, such as [fire] situated within water.
381.15 Fire [is an example where] both [color and touch] are imperceptible, such as ocular fire, which has unmanifest color and touch; this is because of the non-manifestation of its color.
381.16 [This is so] because of the non-manifestation of its form (rūpa).
381.17 [3-1-39(37)] Furthermore, the arrangement of the sense organs is brought about by karma and is dependent upon the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha).
381.18 Furthermore, the arrangement of the sense organs is brought about by karma and is dependent upon the purpose of the person; the rest is in the Bhāṣya.
Regarding form—381.19—and the non-manifestation of touch: if the visual ray were not one whose touch is manifested, it would serve no purpose in worldly transaction (vyavahāra).
382.01. Therefore, when there is a specific visible object and multiple rays of light are present, the substance would be burned. 382.02.
Furthermore, when multiple rays converge, because the substance is obstructed, it ought not to be perceived.
382.03. Now, if you think that just as the visual ray is not obstructed by an object connected with the rays of the sun, so too [is it here].

382.04 “Even when there is a convergence with another ray [of light],” [it is argued]. That is not so, because it does not grasp the object by piercing through [the obstruction]; rather, 382.05 the solar ray becomes connected with a substance connected to it, provided that [the substance] possesses manifest color and tangibility.
382.06 For one whose eye has previously converged [with an object], even if that object is separated from the eye by something else, [the eye] does not [grasp it].

One might [object]: "When many rays converge, a distinct substance called a 'ray' (raśmi) arises from homogeneous substances. If this were so, it would follow that there would be an identical perception by both those whose eyes are complete and those whose eyes are incomplete;
yet this is not accepted because [the ray] is unperceived. Furthermore, [the eye] is [postulated as] ocular [light] for the sake of establishing conventional usage.

382.10 [The opponent argues: "Light possesses the nature of having non-manifest color and touch. [The reply is: "The universal manifestation of all substances is for the sake of the Person (puruṣārtha). And action, consisting of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma), is for the sake of the experience of the conscious being."
382.12 [3-1-38] Furthermore, because it is non-deviant, resistance is a property of material things.
382.13 Resistance, being non-deviant, is a property of material things; the eye is material.
382.14 Because resistance is observed by walls and such, like a jar and so forth; [therefore], due to the absence of resistance, it is not material.

382.15 If you think thus: "If [the visual faculty] is material (*bhautika*) because of its resistance (*pratighāta*), then it is non-material (*abhautika*) because of its lack of resistance"; 382.16 for a lack of resistance is observed, since perception occurs through glass, clouds, mica, and crystal.

382.17 This is not so, because of the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of the reason; there is a lack of resistance even in that which is material, just as in the case of the rays of a lamp. As with the rays of a lamp, there is no resistance in what is material.
Thus, because the fire that cooks does not encounter resistance within the cooking pot and other such vessels,
its non-perception is established due to a difference in the nature of the cause.
383.01 [3-1-40(39)] Its non-perception is like the non-perception of the light of a meteor at midday.

383.02 Its non-perception is like the non-perception of the light of a meteor at midday; just as there is a non-grasping of the light of a meteor at midday, which has reached the conditions for perception, due to a cause, namely because it is overwhelmed.
383.04 Likewise, there is the non-perception of the visual ray—which has reached the conditions for perception—due to the cause that the visible form (*rūpa*) has not manifested.
383.05 Thus, the light of a torch at midday is not perceived because of the light of the sun.
383.06 To say it is "because of being overwhelmed by the light of the sun" is incorrect, as it would entail the consequence that [the sun] possesses rays in all directions.

This being the case, it would follow that everything, such as clods of earth and so forth, possesses rays like [the sun]. Now, if one were to ask why clods of earth and the like do not have their rays perceived, and one were to say—without it having been stated—that it is because they are overwhelmed by the rays of the sun, that would be incorrect.
This [sūtra] is the response to that door.
383.10 [3-1-41(40)] Nor is there non-perception at night.
383.11 Nor is there non-perception at night. If clods of earth and the like possessed rays, they would be visible during the day due to the light of the sun;
[but] because they are overwhelmed [by it], they are not perceived. Therefore, they should be perceived at night. At night, too...

383.13 If it is argued that [the light] is not perceived due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), [we reply: no, for that which is an obscurer of something cannot be its manifestor. How then does it not follow that clods of earth and the like would be perceived by means of their rays?
Furthermore, from the word "also" (*api*), it is understood that a clod’s ray is not perceived even through inference (*anumāna*). Thus, in this way:
Because all means of valid cognition have ceased to function, the ray [of light] from a clod of earth does not exist; furthermore, the visual ray is not non-inferential in this way.

[This is because] it is obstructed by walls and the like. Since that [visual ray] exists externally, its non-perception is due to its lack of manifestation, even though there is perception of the object through the assistance of external illumination.
383.19 [3-1-42(41)] Because the apprehension of an object occurs through the assistance of external light, there is non-manifestation;
383.20 therefore, there is non-apprehension.
383.21 This sūtra is situated precisely as an illustration; what, then, has been stated? Namely, that which is external light...

384.01 Its non-perception depends on the non-manifestation of its form, that is, on its non-emergence (*anudbhūti*), just as in the case of [an object] that is attached—384.02 even here, a constituent part of a substance is not perceived due to the non-emergence of its form. Likewise, the visual ray depends upon the assistance of external light; therefore, its form is also not perceived due to its non-emergence.
Why, then, is it not said that the non-perception of the visual ray is due to its being overwhelmed?
It is not so stated.
384.06 [3-1-43(42)] And because of being overwhelmed during manifestation.

384.07 And because of being overwhelmed during manifestation: that which possesses manifest form and receives the assistance of external light, 384.08 does not depend [on it] and is thus overwhelmed, just as the light of a firebrand at midday, or that which lacks manifest form.
The visual ray requires the assistance of external light; that which has unmanifest color-form (*anudbhūta-rūpa*) is not overwhelmed.

For example, just like that same watery substance whose constituent parts are closely joined; and that which requires the assistance of external light, even if its color-form is manifest (*udbhūta-rūpa*), it is not overwhelmed—just like a substance such as a jar. Thus, this is both...
384.12 The point of contention is the contradiction that the conquest [of objects] by the ocular ray (*nāyana-raśmi*) is untenable. 384.13 [The thesis is:

"The black core [of the eye] possesses rays, because, while being a substance, it is the cause for the perception of form as a necessary factor of the means of proof, like a lamp. Alternatively: "The eye possesses rays, because, while being a substance..."
And because, while being determinate, it illuminates objects obstructed by crystal and the like, it is like a lamp.
384.16 [3-1-44(43)] And because the rays from the eyes of nocturnal creatures are observed.

384.17 "And because the rays from the eyes of nocturnal creatures are observed" is the aphorism providing an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The human eye possesses rays, 384.18 because, while having the nature of not reaching its object, it is the cause for the perception of form and so forth, like the eye of a nocturnal creature.

384.19 [Objection: "The distinction of the sense organs arises from the distinction of their genus (*jāti*). If you think that, just as the state of being a cat (*viḍālatva*) is a genus residing in a cat and not in a human, so too the eye will belong only to a radiant cat and not to a human; [Response: No, because of the capacity for obstruction. Even when this distinction of genus exists, just as in the case of a cat—
Just as the rays of light from lamps and such are obstructed by walls and other barriers, so too are those of humans;
thus, it is exactly the same. Furthermore, for this reason, the sense organs are composed of material elements (*bhautika*), because they possess resistance (*pratighāti*), like a jar.
Likewise, the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is composed of a primary element (*bhūta*), because, while being a substance (*dravyatva*), it manifests objects that have reached its external location.

385.05 [Objection: Like the sense of smell and so forth, its apprehension is untenable because it would require the contact of the ray with the object; for otherwise, apprehension occurs even without such contact. 385.07 [Response: There is apprehension without reaching [the object], because things obstructed by glass, clouds, films, or crystal are perceived. 385.09 [There is] apprehension without reaching [the object], because grass and other things [obstructed by these media] are perceived.

385.10 All substances are obstructed by glass or a layer of cloud. If the visual ray were to illuminate an object only upon reaching it, it would not be able to illuminate an object separated by glass or a layer of cloud.
385.11–12 But since it does so, the eye does not function by reaching its object. For this very reason, [the visual faculty] is non-material (abhautika) and does not reach [its object].

Since the property of being produced [by effort] (kāritva) is a quality of derived matter (bhautika-dharma), the non-perception of something obstructed by a wall does not constitute a refutation [of the argument].
385.14 [3-1-46(45)] There is no refutation [of our position] based on the non-perception of what is obstructed by a wall.
385.15 It has been stated that if the sense organ functions without reaching its object, then obstacles such as walls have no power [to block it].
385.16 The remainder is in the Bhāṣya.
385.17 [3-1-47(46)] Because it is non-obstructive, contact is established.

385.18 Because it is non-obstructive, contact is established. Neither glass nor a layer of clouds 385.19 obstructs the ray; being unobstructed, it penetrates through and becomes connected with the object.

And as for the thought that there is no non-obstruction for what is derived from the elements (*bhautika*), since all that is derived from the elements possesses the nature of obstruction— that is not so.
386.03 [3-1-48(47)] Because the rays of the sun are not obstructed even when the combustible object is separated by a crystal.

386.05 [It is] not [the case that there is no burning], because the rays of the sun are not obstructed, because they are not obstructed even when separated by a crystal, and because they are not obstructed even with respect to the combustible object.

386.06 [It is] not [the case that there is no burning]. Because the rays of the sun are not obstructed, because they are not obstructed even when separated by a crystal, and because they are not obstructed even with respect to the combustible object.

386.07. Because of the connection with the word "non-obstruction" (*avighātāt*), there is a division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*). A single sentence does not have multiple meanings; rather, there is a distinct meaning for each sentence—this is the remainder [of the argument] in the Bhāṣya. 386.08. [End of section].

386.09 What is this "non-obstruction"? It is the entry [of one substance] into another substance whose constituent parts are not being displaced. Of that substance whose parts are not displaced, the connection with those internal parts which are themselves not being displaced—that is "non-obstruction. Or, it is the state of a substance situated within, or of a substance whose parts are not being displaced.

The perception of external substances is observed in the case of water contained within a jar, where one perceives the cold touch on the outside; for it is not logical that a quality which is dependent should go outside without its substratum. In this context, *parispanda* refers to lateral movement, while *parisrava* refers to flowing out or falling.
386.15 [3-1-49(48)] No, because of the consequence of mutual dependence.
386.16 No, because of the consequence of mutual dependence. The property of one would be applied to the other, and the property of the other to that one.
386.17 And if there were no obstruction of the visual rays by crystals and the like, they would also [pass through] walls and the like.
It would encounter resistance from walls and the like, and it would also encounter resistance from crystals and the like; this is not a fault.
387.03 [3-1-50(49)] Just as there is the perception of form due to the inherent clarity of a mirror or water, so too is that perception;
387.04—that is, the perception of that—due to the inherent clarity of the mirror or water, just like the perception of form. Mirror... 387.05...mirror.

387.06. The clarity of water is a particularity of form (*rūpa-viśeṣa*), and it is its own [property] by necessity. What, then, is this particularity of form? It is either an inherence in a substance not conjoined with another substance, or 387.07–08.
it is the capacity for the perception of that form; this is its own property (*sva-dharma*), and its existence is due to its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).

387.09–11. In water and other such media, that same nature [of light] exists because of its translucent (prasāda) nature. In mirrors, water, and so forth, the ray of the eye is obstructed; being thus obstructed, it is reflected back and becomes connected with one's own face and the like. And because of its connection with the tip [of the ray], that which faces the tip faces the face and so forth.

387.12–14: “He sees” is like the case of a person standing directly in front [of a mirror]; the perception of the face in the mirror occurs sequentially. 387.13–14: That too is not perceived as distinct because of its extreme rapidity; rather, due to the simultaneous apprehension of the form of the mirror, the cognition is colored by it. The rest is in the Bhāṣya.
387.15 [3-1-51(50)] For there is no possibility of injunction or prohibition regarding things that are perceived or inferred.

387.16 For there is no possibility of injunction or prohibition regarding things that are perceived or inferred, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has reality as its object; indeed, these properties of substances, being perceived or inferred, exist exactly as they are.
387.17 Because the means of valid cognition has reality as its object, these perceived and inferred properties of substances exist in accordance with how they truly are.

387.18–19. Only real entities (bhūta) are established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), yet these two—your injunction (niyoga) and prohibition (pratiṣedha)—have been taught; in what objective domain could they possibly function? Nor is this logical, for just as there is the apprehension of fire through smoke, so too should there be the apprehension of water [through it]. Furthermore, the apprehension of water does not occur by means of smoke.
388.01 Thus, even the application [of the term] "fire" is not tenable; for you, who are employing it based on the object, must be disregarded.

388.02 Indeed, perception and non-perception are the determinants of resistance and non-resistance respectively. 388.03 Non-resistance is inferred by means of the perception of objects through crystal and the like, while resistance is inferred by the non-perception of objects that are obstructed.

388.04 And there is obstruction by walls and the like. If the eye functions by reaching [its object], 388.05 then why is it that the ointment-stick and such are not perceived? It is because they are not in contact with the sense organ.
388.06 Objects are perceived when they are connected with the sense organ, and the ointment-stick and such are not connected with the sense organ.
388.07 [It is] connected because the physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not the sense faculty (*indriya*); the ray (*raśmi*) is the sense faculty, not the physical basis.
388.08 [Therefore,] the collyrium-stick is connected with the ray.

388.09 Thus far it has been established that the sense-faculties are derived from the primary elements (*bhautika*). But are they one, or are they many? Some, however, [hold as follows]: 388.10 [They are one.]
388.11 [3-1-52(51)] There is doubt because of the multiplicity [of parts] when there is a difference in location, and because the whole occupies multiple locations.

388.13 There is doubt because of the multiplicity [of parts] when there is a difference in location, and because the whole occupies multiple locations. However, some [hold that] multiplicity is observed when there is a difference in location, as in the case of many jars; and [there is multiplicity] of a single [thing].

"388.15 [The objection: 'Just as there is multiplicity of location for a whole (*avayavin*). But this doubt is logically untenable. How so? 388.16 If it is formulated thus: 'Because multiplicity and unity are observed when there is a difference of location,' then, since a difference of location is not observed in the case of unity, it is not a common property (*samāna-dharma*). Alternatively, if [it refers to] multiplicity of location..."

"Since both unity and multiplicity are observed, there is doubt. To this we reply: when a substance occupies multiple locations, it is not seen as anything that is truly manifold. That which is manifold, such as a jar and so forth, does not occupy multiple locations; rather, its "manifoldness" consists simply in the diversity of its locations. Thus, this doubt is untenable in either case.
389.02 But regarding the sense-faculties and their locations, is it that they have various locations or a single location?
389.03 Regarding the sense-faculties, however, it is not possible [to say] "due to the diversity of locations" nor "due to the non-diversity of locations.
389.04 Because they are distinct from the body and yet exist, there is doubt; being distinct from the body, they are in both ways.
389.05–06. One thing is seen as both one and many, just as space and a jar, for example. Being is also seen in both ways—as one and as many.
389.06–07. Thus, because the senses are observed in both these ways—both as distinct from the body and as existing—their nature is subject to doubt.
389.07. Is the sense-faculty one? And what, moreover, is it?
389.08 [3-1-53(52)] Because of non-distinction from the skin (tvag-avyatirekāt).

389.09 Because of non-distinction from the skin. What, then, is this "non-distinction"? It is the connection with all substrates. 389.10 For there is no sense organ whatsoever that is not reached by the skin; nor is there any existence when it is absent.

389.11 There is some apprehension of objects through the skin; therefore, the skin is the single sense organ. [Objection: It is not so, because other objects are not perceived [by it]. Thus, one who asserts that there is only one sense organ contradicts common experience. 389.12–13 If the sense organ of the skin were present, it would follow that there would be perception of touch [alone], and [there would be no perception of] other objects by the sense organs.

389.14 The objects such as form and so forth, which exist in between [the sense organs], would be perceived by those who are blind and so on; however, they are not so perceived. Therefore, the sense organ is not one. 389.15 As for the argument that it is so because there is no distinction (*avyatireka*), that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For all the locations of the sense organs are reached by the non-sensory earth and so forth, despite their being many; thus, the reason is inconclusive.

389.17 If it is argued that [the perception of color and so forth does not occur] because of the impairment of a part [of the sense organ], then this might be the case: some part of the skin is impaired, and due to that impairment, color and other objects are not perceived by those who are blind and so forth.
389.18–19 Just as the perception of smoke occurs specifically through a particular part of the skin, so too there is a particular part of the skin in the eye; that—

390.01 [Objection: "There is no perception of the touch of smoke because it has ceased. [Reply: No, because that would involve a contradiction. 390.02 For one who asserts that the perception of color and so forth occurs through a specific part of the skin—just like the perception of smoke—it follows that the claim "there is only one sense organ" is contradicted; for having previously accepted that the skin is the single sense organ, one now [speaks of] a part of the skin... 390.03 ...[which is inconsistent].

390.04 One who asserts that "the particulars are the perceivers of form and so forth" admits the very thing to be negated, namely, that the parts are not distinct from the whole. 390.05 Furthermore, regarding those parts which you consider to be the perceivers of form and so forth through the sense of touch—do they consist of the sense organ itself, or do they not? And what follows from this? If they are the sense organ...

390.07–390.08: [If] they consist of the self, then they are not a single sense-faculty; furthermore, if they do not consist of sense-faculties, then form and the other [objects] would not be graspable by the sense-faculties—this is the connection with the Sūtra.
390.09 [3-1-54(53)] Not so, because of the non-perception of objects simultaneously.

390.10 Not so, because of the non-perception of objects simultaneously. For one who possesses only a single sense organ, the perception of all objects simultaneously would follow as a consequence. How so? The self is connected with the mind, and the mind is connected with the sense organ.

390.12 “The sense-faculty [is the cause of cognition] because all objects are present. [If this were so,] cognitions would arise simultaneously from the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the objects. 390.13 This is not the case, because it would follow that there would be simultaneous perception of things perceivable by a single sense-faculty, just as for one who maintains the theory of a single sense-faculty, when multiple objects are present simultaneously, [cognitions of them would arise] simultaneously. 390.14 [This is not observed.]

390.15 Just as perception is a fault for one who maintains that there are multiple sense-faculties (*aneka-indriya*) with respect to objects graspable by a single sense-faculty, 390.16 so too would there be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of simultaneous perception [for you]. Whatever rebuttal (*parīhāra*) is offered here, that same rebuttal will apply to me as well.
390.17 Thus, if this position is not faulty, then this consequence of simultaneous perception should not be pointed out.
390.18 Thus [it is said]. Regarding this, some offer a rebuttal: "Because there is a distinction in the desire to know (*bubhutsā*), there is no simultaneous perception.

390.19 [The opponent replies: "In my case as well, if simultaneous perception is not obtained because of a distinction in the desire to know, 390.20 then for me too, the distinction in the desire to know cannot be prevented by a staff. And when there is indeed a desire to know...

391.01. "Another principle must be determined regarding non-simultaneous perception. Others say: "Because it is an instrument (karaṇa). But others state the following rebuttal: "Because it is an instrument. The nature of an instrument is such that, even when presided over [by a conscious agent], it cannot perform multiple actions simultaneously, nor can it do so when not presided over.

And since it does not function [simultaneously], the case is the same. Even for one who holds that there is only a single sense-faculty (*ekendriya*), its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is not denied; therefore, the argument that "objects are not perceived simultaneously" is not a fault.
One who speaks thus, a proponent of a single sense-faculty, should be questioned after having made this distinction: what is that single sense-faculty?

391.07 You think [the sense organ] grasps all objects; does it then act by reaching [its object], or not? And what follows from this? If it acts by reaching, it must be stated what that [reaching] is. If it is the skin, then there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that forms (*rūpa*) reached by the skin would not be perceived. Alternatively, if it perceives a form without reaching it, then the same undesirable consequence would apply to touch (*sparśa*) and the other [objects] as well.

391.10 Now, if the sense-organ (*indriya*) possesses the capacity for action, it would grasp some [objects] that are reached and others that are not reached; thus, there would be a transgression of the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*). 391.11 Let there be a transgression of the nature of an instrument; what is it to us? It does not harm us. 391.12 Thus, regarding this position, the Sūtra states: "Because there is no consequence of simultaneous perception. Just as:

391.13 For one who maintains that there are multiple sense-faculties, [the objection] arises that there would be simultaneous perception of objects graspable by a single sense-faculty, because [all faculties] possess the nature of being instruments (karaṇatva). 391.14 This is not a valid rebuttal for him, because it transgresses the defining characteristics of an instrument;

moreover, this is contradictory, since an instrument is both "that which acts by reaching its object" and "that which acts without reaching its object. Furthermore, there is no concomitance [of the skin with all other faculties], for the skin does not possess such concomitance.
If that which has one apprehension of an object is [identical to] its second [apprehension], it would follow as an absurd consequence that there is no such thing as being blind or deaf.
391.17 [3-1-55(54)] And because of contradiction, the skin is not one.

391.18 And because of contradiction, the skin is not one; the remainder is in the Bhāṣya. If there were destruction of that [skin] upon the injury of one [part], 391.19 there would follow the non-perception of everything. Now, if the sense organ were one, then upon its impairment or destruction, [there would be non-perception of all].

392.01 There would follow the consequence of the non-perception of everything, because an obstruction is impossible [if the skin were the sole sense organ]. If the skin were the only sense organ, 392.02 there would be no efficacy for an obstruction. Consequently, there would follow the perception of things situated at a distance. Furthermore, there would be no conformity to the proximity or remoteness of objects regarding their perception or non-perception, since the skin does not act by reaching its object.

392.04. There would be no such thing as the perception [of an object] when the sense faculty is near and the non-perception [of it] when it is far away. Furthermore, because of the refutation: 392.05. Even if a probans for establishing multiplicity (*nānātva*) is adduced, multiplicity is not established because of that refutation. 392.06. We do not understand how, if the establishment of unity (*ekatva*) cannot occur due to refutation, multiplicity could possibly be established.
392.07. Thus, since an action cannot be without a means of accomplishment (*asādhanā*), how can unity be refuted? [It cannot be refuted] because of the very act of refutation (392.08).
The inference that establishes unity is set aside, but neither unity nor plurality is thereby set aside (392.09).
How, then, is this passage to be understood? [The answer is: "And because of the refutation, plurality is established immediately thereafter."
The probans for establishment (*sthāpanā-hetu*) is also employed because of the fivefold nature of the sense organs and their objects; or else, it is [employed] because of negation (*pratiṣedha*).

When the negation of unity has been effected by means of the probans of negation—namely, "because of the proof of plurality"—plurality is established by implication. What, then, is this probans of negation? It is "the simultaneous perception of objects."

392.13–14: Because [the opponent's position] leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*), unity is thereby refuted by this [argument]. Thus, this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the *vīta* [inference] within the establishment of the *avīta*.
392.15 [3-1-56(55)] "Because of the fivefold nature of the sense-faculties and their objects" (indriya-artha-pañcatvāt).
392.16 "Because of the fivefold nature of the sense-faculties and their objects"—this is the sūtra. "Object" (artha) means purpose (prayojana), and so forth, as stated in the Bhāṣya.
392.17 But this sūtra is not connected to the Nyāya system in any way whatsoever. How so?

392.18. To argue that the object being established is the "five sense-faculties" because there are five objects of the sense-faculties is incoherent. 392.19. If, on the other hand, the "fivefold nature of the purposes" is intended, that too is exactly the same. If, furthermore, the acts of apprehension are made the subject of the proposition, even then there is no conclusive reason (*aikāntika-hetu*). By this, the objects [of the senses] are also explained.
393.01 But this sūtra should be as follows: "Regarding color, taste, odor, touch, and sound, there is an agent whose actions are accomplished by various means.
393.02 Because, when one object is determined, there is a dependence upon another instrument for the establishment of another object;
393.03 for that agent who has multiple objects, when there is the determination of any one object, [there is a need for another] for the establishment of another object.

393.04 It is observed that there is a dependence on other instruments, as in the case of a person who has mastered many arts. 393.05 Just as there is a dependence on other instruments for an action following from the determination to act, so too, when there is a determination regarding one object such as form (*rūpa*), there is a dependence on another means of accomplishment for the establishment of another object.
Therefore, with respect to visible form, taste, odor, tangible objects, and sound, there are agents who perform various instrumental actions.
393.08 [3-1-57(56)] Not so, because there is a plurality of objects.

393.09 Not so, because there is a plurality of objects. The objection arises according to the literal reading, and its meaning is that there is a contradiction regarding the fivefold nature of the sense organs. One who asserts that there is a multiplicity of sense organs due to the multiplicity of objects, rather than due to contradiction, [is refuted by the following].

393.11. [The opponent claims: "It is accepted that there is only one sense-faculty (*indriya*). [The author replies: That is not refuted by me, because it is not established by proof (*asādhanāt*). It is not because of the multiplicity of objects (*artha-bahutvāt*) that the multiplicity of sense-faculties is being proven by me, such that there would be a contradiction;
rather, a contradiction is pointed out by me regarding what was stated by you as a proof—that there are five sense-faculties because there are five types of objects (*pañcatvāt*).

393.14 If the sense-faculties are five because there are five sense-objects, then [it would follow that] there are many sense-faculties because there are many sense-objects. 393.15 Thus, [the opponent's position] results in an infinite number of sense-faculties. The sūtra provides the resolution for this.
393.16 [3-1-58(57)] There is no negation of odors and the like, because they are not distinct from "odor-ness" and so forth.

393.17 There is no negation of odors and the like because they do not differ from "odor-ness" and so forth. Odors and the like are established by means of universals such as "odor-ness"; they do not have other instruments apart from their own respective instruments.

393.19 Since all those things in which the nature of odor exists are to be accomplished by a single means, [the sense organ is one]. Furthermore, other distinctions of genus—such as being desirable, undesirable, or indifferent—do not necessitate another instrument; this applies everywhere. The rest is in the Bhāṣya. If the universal (*sāmānya*) is the unifier...
394.03. Unity is attained [for the senses] because they do not differ from their objects.

394.04 [3-1-59(58)] Unity [of the sense-faculties] follows from the non-difference of their objects. 394.05 The meaning of this is that there is indeed no contradiction, because the answer has already been stated [in the previous sūtra], namely, "because of the fivefold nature of the sense-faculties and their objects. 394.06 This has already been answered by the [previous] statement regarding the object; and for the purpose of making this meaning known, it is not [necessary to state] the basis characterized by cognition.
394.07. "Because of the fivefold distinctions of destiny, form, and birth," so says the aphorism.
394.08 [3-1-60(59)] Not so, because of the fivefold nature of cognition, its characteristics, its substrata, its movements, its forms, and its classes.
394.09 In this context, the meaning of "the characteristics are indeed the cognitions" has been explained as being due to the fivefold nature of the sense objects.
394.10 Thus, the sense organs are manifold because their substrata are distinct; that whose substratum is distinct is manifold.

394.11 Just as multiplicity is observed in the case of jars and other objects due to a difference in their substrates, so too there is a difference in the substrates of the sense organs; therefore [they are] manifold. 394.12 If it is argued that the difference in substrates is unproven, we say no, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and others. Furthermore, for one who holds that there is a difference [of the sense organs] based on a difference in substrates, when there is a destruction of a single substrate, [the organ located in] that substrate—

394.14 There is no fault in [the argument] that there is a persistence of the internal substratum (*antara-āśraya*). Regarding the phrase "because of the difference in movement" (*gati-bhedāt*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) is "because its movement is distinct," which is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) as before. "Configuration" (*ākṛti*) means size (*parimāṇa*) or dimension (*iyattā*).
The olfactory, gustatory, and tactile organs have their own respective locations and dimensions. The visual organ, however, extends outward; having gone out, it reaches the object.

That [auditory organ] is all-pervading and great; however, the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) functions by being restricted to its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), namely the ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*), which serves as the means for perceiving sounds—whether desirable, undesirable, or indifferent—in accordance with the conjunction of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). That connection of the auditory faculty with space (*ākāśa*) follows the nature of that [substrate]; space does not exist apart from the cavity.
395.02 By this [statement], "only here," he indicates the sound and not anything else, because of the distinction between its assistance and its counteraction (upakāra-pratīkāra).

395.03 Or rather, it is assisted and countered; however, space (*ākāśa*), being eternal, is neither assisted nor countered. 395.04 Thus, the distinction between superior and inferior auditory organs arises from this very [fact]; it is the universal (*jāti*).

395.05 Thus they declare the source (*yoni*). Indeed, these five—the elements beginning with earth—are the sources of the sense-faculties (*indriya-yoni*). "Source" here means identity (*tādātmya*), not the state of being its effect (*tad-kāryatva*).
[For example,] it does not arise from space because of its eternity. How, then, is it known that the sense-faculties have the elements as their material cause (*prakṛti*)?

395.08. It is not the case that the sense-faculties have the unmanifest as their material cause, because this has already been answered; it has already been answered that the sense-faculties do not have the unmanifest as their material cause.
395.09. This has already been answered.

395.10 [3-1-61(60)] Identity [is established] from the perception of specific qualities of the elements (bhūta). 395.11 Identity from the perception of specific qualities of the elements: the specific qualities of the elements are smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; they are called "specifics" (viśeṣa) because they are distinguishing characteristics. For example, by means of possessing smell and so forth...

395.13 [The opponent argues: "Water and the other elements are distinguished from earth and the others by their tastes and other qualities; for this is observed among external things. 395.14 [The response: Indeed, a restriction regarding the manifestation of their own specific qualities is observed among the primary elements (bhūtas), such as earth and the rest, which are admitted by both parties. 395.15 And there exists a restriction regarding the manifestation of odors and so forth by means of the olfactory organ and the others; therefore, [this is] a quality of the elements.

395.16 Because of the perception of specific qualities, the sense organs have the elements as their material cause (*prakṛti*). As for what their respective natures are: that by which a particular quality is manifested [is its nature]. Among these, the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), because it is the cause for manifesting odor, just like an external earthly substance. The same applies to the remaining [organs] as well.

395.19 It has been stated that smell and the others are the qualities of earth and the rest; and this statement is common to [the modes of] restriction (*niyoga*), option (*vikalpa*), and 396.01 conjunction (*samuccaya*). Among these, restriction is the state of having each quality individually; option is that some have one [quality], some two, and so forth; and conjunction is when all [qualities] are present everywhere. Therefore, [the following] is for the sake of specification.
Of odor, taste, visible form, touch, and sound, those ending with touch belong to earth; [those ending with] touch belong to water, fire, and air, respectively.
Having excluded the former [elements], the latter [sound] belongs to space; this is for the sake of restriction in the sūtra.
396.05 [3-1-62(61)] Of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound, those ending with touch belong to earth.
396.06 [3-1-63(62)] Having excluded each preceding one among water, fire, and air, the latter belongs to space.
396.07 There are four [qualities] in earth; in each subsequent element, there is a reduction by one, ending with touch.

396.08. There is a change of grammatical case (vibhakti-vipariṇāma). What is accomplished by this? [It serves] for the final members of the series ending with "contact" (sparśa) that have been assigned.

396.09. That which is "subsequent" (uttara) belongs to space; thus, sound is subsequent to space. 396.10. This indication by means of the suffix -tarap is not appropriate, because it is observed here between two things, whereas in this context it should express superiority (prakṛṣṭa).

[Objection: It would follow that [the suffix] *uttama* should be used. [Response: This is not an indication of the *tarap* suffix; rather, this is a designation for "another" (*para*). What is meant by "another" is what is meant by "subsequent" (*uttara*). Or, because the contact is intended to be expressed according to the system (*tantra*), let there be the indication of the *tarap* suffix. [Objection: But was it not said that the form *uttama* would result? [Response: No.
396.14 Because touch is intended [to be specified], it is said that "touch is beyond smell and the others," and "this is beyond touch.
396.15 To the extent that this has been stated, it is as much as to say "the subsequent one"; it is not because of the non-perception of all qualities.
396.16 [3-1-64(63)] Not so, because not all qualities are perceived.

396.17 This application of [the sense organs] to their respective qualities is not correct; why? Because, by means of the earth-based organ of smell, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving earth-based odors and the other qualities [such as taste and color]. Likewise, by means of the water-based organ of taste, there would be the perception of the three [qualities].
396.19 Regarding the statement "by means of the fiery eye, [one perceives] both": how, then, should the qualities of the self (ātman) be applied?
397.01 [3-1-65(64)] Because each subsequent [element] possesses a quality that exceeds the preceding one, there is a non-perception of those [qualities] in the subsequent ones.
397.02–397.03: Because each subsequent [element] possesses a quality that exceeds the preceding one, there is a non-perception of those [qualities] in the subsequent ones; for this reason.
397.04–05. Each of the elements possesses a single quality; therefore, there is the apprehension of a single quality, as in the case of "each individual hawk" (ekaika-śyena).
[Question: How then is it that the elements are perceived as possessing multiple qualities? [Answer:
It is through their combination (saṃsarga) that there is the apprehension of multiple qualities; for the earth is combined with water and the other elements. Therefore...

"Many qualities are perceived"—thus [it is said] regarding the remaining [elements]; however, their mutual association is not prohibited. Regarding the phrase "and of the five": if that were so, the restriction would not apply, namely that there are four [qualities] in earth and none in the others.
[Objection: Because the association is unrestricted. [Reply: It is not that it does not apply; why? Because one [element] is indeed permeated by the other.
397.10 [3-1-66(65)] "The posterior is indeed pervaded by the anterior.

(397.11) The posterior, such as water and so forth, is pervaded by the anterior, such as earth and so forth; it is not the case that the anterior, such as water and so forth, is pervaded by the posterior, such as earth and so forth.
(397.12) This state of being pervaded is a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*). It is not [the case] for earth and water [in general], because they are perceptible (*pratyakṣatvāt*).
397.13 [3-1-67(66)] "No, because the earthy and the watery are perceptible.

(397.14) With this, he refutes the three preceding sūtras. For one who holds that the elements possess only single qualities, (397.15) in his view, only a fiery substance would be perceptible because it possesses color.

397.16 It is neither earth nor water, because it is formless (*arūpa*). Regarding this sūtra, the commentary explains that its meaning is conceived through various alternatives (*vikalpa*), and thus manifold. 397.17 That very [explanation] is refuted as a mere popular opinion (*pravāda*) contrary to logic.
397.18 Having rejected [the objection] that "it is not so because all qualities are unperceived," that [point] is now established.
398.01 [3-1-68(67)] Because of the progressive excellence of qualities in each preceding one, each respective [organ] is predominant.

398.02 Because of the progressive excellence of qualities in each preceding one, each respective [organ] is predominant; therefore, there is no perception of all qualities by the sense organs beginning with the olfactory organ. 398.03 Among the sense organs beginning with the olfactory organ, each preceding organ is more predominant than each succeeding one.

398.04 What is primacy? It is the possession of four qualities and so forth; what is the excellence of a quality? It is the capacity for the manifestation of its own specific quality. 398.05 By whichever quality a substance is excelled, that quality is considered superior because it manifests a member of its own kind, just as is the case with external substances. And such [excellence] exists in the sense-faculties as well, in their own...

398.07 There is a rule regarding the manifestation of qualities; therefore, there is no perception of all qualities. Furthermore, for one who asserts that the sense of smell perceives odor because it has odor as its quality, there follows the undesirable consequence of perceiving all qualities. Why then is it not established that every sense of smell is composed of earth? It is for the purpose of making known the rule governing this specific determination.
The sūtra states: "But their establishment [is determined] by the majority."

398.11 [3-1-69(68)] But its determination is due to abundance (bhūyastva). 398.12 What, then, is this "abundance"? It is the conjunction of distinct substances that are capable of accomplishing a purpose, brought about by human refinement; for the word "abundance" is observed to be used in the sense of excellence.

398.14 Just as in the world a preeminent object is called "abundant," and just as substances such as poison, medicinal herbs, and gems—which are capable of distinct causal functions—are produced through the influence of human refinement;
[if it is asked: why do the sense organs not perceive [their objects] by means of their own qualities? 398.15–16 [The answer is: because they are brought about [in that way].
398.17 For what reason do one's own sense faculties, such as the olfactory faculty and the others, not perceive themselves?
398.18 [3-1-70(69)] Because the sense-faculties exist as possessing qualities (saguṇa).
399.01 Because the sense-faculty exists as possessing qualities, it exists together with its quality; however, that which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) is not a sense-faculty.
Therefore, it does not perceive. Furthermore, if odor were the auxiliary cause (sahakārin) of the sense-faculty...
And it would also be that which is grasped.

399.04 [3-1-71(70)] And because it cannot be perceived by that very same [organ]: 399.05 If the sense organ were to perceive its own odor, then that odor of the sense organ would not be perceivable by the sense organ; and while perceiving the odor, the sense organ would also perceive itself.

399.07 For its odor belongs to the self (*ātman*). And since there is no instrument for establishing the self, there is a contradiction with the illustrative example (399.08). Nor is this [the self] perceptible in the same way that the nose is the perceiver of odor through the nose (399.09). Why, then, is it not taught: "How is the nose perceived by the nose? and "Why is it not grasped?"

399.10 It is not taught because it is not seen; the nose does not perceive the nose itself, and therefore it is not taught. 399.11 The same applies to the statement that the nose does not perceive its own odor; this too should not be untaught. 399.12 Why the sense organs do not perceive their own qualities is the same [as the previous case].
399.13 For, in both cases, there is an absence of a logical reason.
399.14 [3-1-72(71)] Not so, because of the perception of sound as a quality. 399.15 It is untenable to say that the sense organs do not perceive their own qualities;
for one's own quality, namely sound, is perceived by space (ākāśa), yet the ear is not itself possessed of sound.
399.17 “It is not a sense organ” means that space is not like the other sense organs which possess qualities.

399.18 Why? Because sound differs from the qualities of the others, and because space differs from the other substances; for the purpose of making this point known, there is the aphorism: “The perception of that [space] is due to its difference from the qualities of the others. 399.19–20.
399.20 [3-1-73(72)] Its perception is due to the difference in properties from one another.

400.01 Sound is not the manifester of sound, nor is space the sense organ possessed of qualities. What, then, is this auditory organ? It is space, by process of elimination. Among these, the self is certainly not the auditory organ, for it is the agent.
Because it belongs to the listener, the ear is not the self. Nor can it be that the mind is the ear;

for if the mind were the ear, there would be no such thing as deafness and so forth, since the mind has all things as its object, and thus the ear would necessarily have all things as its object. Furthermore, earth and the other elements cannot be the ear, because they are assigned to the functions of the nose and the other senses.

400.06–400.08: Earth and the other elements, which are employed as the nose and so forth, would [then] constitute the nature of the ear; and in the absence of those [nose and so forth], there would be the consequence of the non-perception of sound. Furthermore, if the skin were the nature of the ear, there would be no such thing as deafness and the like; and if it were destroyed in its entirety, death would follow. Moreover, if space and time were the nature of the ear, then since sound is a quality of something else, [it would not be perceived].
400.09. There would be the consequence of non-apprehension. If it is argued that sound is a quality (*guṇa*) of that [space], there is a dispute over the name;
for you, that which has sound as its quality is space (*ākāśa*), while for us, those two are direction (*diś*) and time (*kāla*). Thus, only the designation differs. 400.10–11.
Or else, there is the rejection of space, because sound would have something other than space as its quality; for if sound were a quality of direction and time, [space would not exist].
400.12 In that case, space (ākāśa) would be rejected; for there is no mark (liṅga) for the existence of space apart from sound.

400.13 Just as "prior," "posterior," and so forth are the marks for the [existence of] direction and time, and yet no other substance remains [as their substratum], nor is it logical that qualities (guṇa) constitute the auditory organ (śrotra), nor that actions (karman) do.
400.15 Furthermore, because no causal capacity is perceived in universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), or inherence (*samavāya*), this [ear] is not any of those.
400.16 There remains no other mark for the perception of sound than space (*ākāśa*); therefore, the ear is space.
Thus ends the first daily lesson (*āhnika*) of the third chapter in Uddyotakara’s *Nyāyavārttika*. Now begins the second daily lesson of the third chapter.
401.03 Homage to the Supreme Self.

401.04 The sense organs and their objects have been examined; now follows the sequence for the examination of cognition (*buddhi*). Regarding that [cognition], there is an inquiry into its nature as to whether it is impermanent or permanent, since the existence of the self has already been established and [the inquiry] depends upon it.
It establishes doubt.
401.07 [3-2-1] Doubt arises from the commonality with action and space.

401.08 Doubt arises from the commonality with action and space. The commonality with both is the quality of being intangible (*asparśavat-tva*). 401.09 The distinction is that [action] possesses the nature of arising and passing away, whereas the opposite is observed in the case of cognition; therefore [doubt arises].

401.10 Doubt. This doubt is indeed untenable, because it is to be personally experienced by all embodied beings; for this—that is, that "intellect is impermanent"—is to be personally experienced by all embodied beings. Furthermore, since intellect is manifest throughout the three times, its manifestation across the three times is observed: "I know," [I knew, I shall know].
"I shall know" and "I have known"—and yet, there is no manifestation of the three times (past, present, and future) without the occurrence of arising and passing away.

For, in things whose nature is devoid of arising and passing away, such as space and so forth, the three times are not manifested; nor is it logical for doubt to arise when a specific characteristic is perceived. Therefore, the process of doubt is untenable. The remainder [is as follows].

In the commentary: this treatise is for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of [wrong] views; it is not intended to establish the impermanence of cognition (*buddhi*), but rather to overturn the position of the opponent. For it is with this perspective that the Sāṃkhyas proclaim, "Cognition is eternal," and they set forth the proof regarding the object—
Because of recognition.
402.04 [3-2-2] Because of the recognition of the object.

402.05 "That which I previously knew, this is what I know now"—this synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of two cognitions regarding the same object is possible only for one who possesses a persisting intellect (*buddhi*). If there were a plurality of intellects, recognition would not occur.
There is no logical possibility [of its occurrence], just as in the cognitions of other persons.

402.08 [3-2-3] It is not a valid reason because it is equivalent to the point to be proven (sādhyasama). 402.09 It is not a valid reason because it is equivalent to the point to be proven. Just as the eternity of cognition is the point to be proven, so too is the recognition of cognition a point to be proven. Why? Because the property of a conscious being is not possible in an instrument, [and thus it must belong to the person (puruṣa)].

402.11 This dharma is indeed knowledge, vision, apprehension, and awakening. For it is the conscious [self] that recognizes an object previously known; therefore, for this very reason, its permanence is logical. Since an instrument has no substratum for its activity—402.12–13 for an instrument is not the substratum of an action—the apprehension [belongs to the self].

And that action cannot reside in the instrument. If it is argued that this is incorrect because [the instrument] is the locus of its own action— meaning, if you think that every causal factor (*kāraka*) is the locus of its own action,
and therefore it is incorrect to say it is not the locus of action— it is true that it is the locus of its own action.
Furthermore, the designation "instrument" (*karaṇa*) does not arise from its own action; for in its own actions, every factor of action (*kāraka*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*).

Since the investigation regarding the intellect (*buddhi*) is based on its status as an instrument, it is therefore incorrect [to claim] that this would entail the consequence that everything is an agent. If, however, the designation "agent" were caused by its own action, then everything...
402.20. It is true that the agent (*kartṛ*) has been established as the causal factor (*kāraka*); however, it is not merely the [opponent's] admissions (*abhyupagama*) that are pointed out as faults.

402.21. Furthermore, how is the designation of "agent," "instrument" (*karaṇa*), and so forth dependent upon the primary action? 403.01. That action for the sake of which the instrument is employed is the primary action; and in relation to that [action], there exists the state of being a means (*sādhana*).
Whether the distinction is intended or not intended, the agent and so forth are expressed by this term "kāraka.
However, when the distinction is intended, they are denoted by the words "agent," "instrument," "object," and so on.
Thus, even when the kārakas are designated by the general term "kāraka," [the specific distinctions are understood].
403.05. An object that is internal and mutually distinct is designated [as such] because of the absence of anything else.

403.06. However, the designations of "agent" (kartṛ) and so forth for the factors of action (kārakas) depend upon the primary action. In this regard, that which is not prompted by another and is the prompter of other factors is indeed the agent; likewise, the terms for the remaining factors [are applied].

403.08. These points should be stated as before. If agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in not being prompted by another factor (*kāraka*), then surely this [agent] too is prompted by the adoption of a factor; it is not so prompted, because it is the prompter of the result. The result prompts the agent, but not the instrument (*karaṇa*) and other factors; and the result is not itself a factor (*kāraka*). Thus they [the opponents] argue.

That [instrument] is invariably concomitant with its material cause (*upādāna*). For an action (*kriyā*) is not possible without the material cause of the agent (*kāraka*), such as the instrument (*karaṇa*); thus, because of this invariable concomitance, the factors of action (*kārakas*) are employed.

Therefore, having accepted that the property of consciousness (*cetana-dharma*) is not possible in the instrument, [one concludes that] recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) resides in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

403.14 Its uniqueness consists in its exclusion from both the one and the many; for recognition is not observed in the case of unity, nor in the case of plurality. Thus, when there is a determination of the essential nature through recognition, it is contradictory [to claim otherwise]. And when this recognition is examined, recognition establishes a distinction between cognitions.

Indeed, when there is a contradiction with the first perception upon seeing a second [instance], and when there is the manifestation of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) previously deposited, the third perception occurs preceded by memory. Furthermore, for one who maintains that there is no difference in cognition, even a second perception does not exist; how then could there be a third? Thus, there is a difference in the cognitions.

404.01. Now, if you think that while the intellect (*buddhi*) remains constant, its conditions (*pratyaya*) disappear and then manifest; and that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) occurs when the first perception disappears and another perception appears—that is not tenable. This is because, apart from those [perceptions], the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the intellect cannot be determined. [For one would have to point out] that [intellect] which is distinct from the perceptions.
404.04 You must state what the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that cognition (*buddhi*) which you postulate is.

404.05 For us, however, cognition is merely a condition (*pratyaya-mātra*); for cognition is the grasping of an object. Because there is recognition through touch of what was seen by sight, recognition occurs despite multiplicity; thus, [your position] is contradicted by the example of a lamp.

404.07 [The opponent says: "It is like seeing what is between by means of another lamp.
