If the intellect (*buddhi*) determines [the object], then what does the conscious being (*cetana*) do with the present cognition? Who is it that perceives? If that which possesses the determination is the one who perceives, this is contradictory. Or, if the self (*ātman*) perceives, how [is that so]?
The self perceives by means of a cognition residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), for it does not [perceive] by means of an action residing elsewhere.
Otherwise, one thing would possess the nature of another. Now, if it is said that "the person perceives" and "the intellect knows," this is not so;
for as long as it is said that "it perceives," so long is it said that "it knows"—[the two] are not distinct from knowledge.

404.13 [Objection: "It is *buddhi* that makes known. If you think thus, [we reply: then you hold that *buddhi* makes the self (*ātman*) know; yet it is the person (*puruṣa*) who truly knows, while *buddhi* merely makes it known. Furthermore, you must state the difference in essential nature between determination (*adhyavasāya*) and consciousness (*cetana*), and you must also state their identity in terms of place and time.

404.16 Because there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the self (*ātman*) determines for itself that which has been determined by cognition (*buddhi*) as being without difference of place and without difference of time.

404.17 If it is argued that the non-difference of intrinsic nature is unproven (*asiddha*), and you think: "It is true that the self determines what has been determined by cognition as being without difference of time and without difference of place; however, [it does not determine] those things which are insentient..."
404.19 “The self alone is the determiner”— this is not so, because it would entail the consequence of multiple persons for each body. If there were another who is the cognizer (cetayitṛ),

404.20 and another who is the determiner (adhyavasātṛ), and another who asserts, another who sees, and another who hears or reflects— then in such cases, these would indeed be distinct persons, namely the seer, the hearer, and so forth.

405.01. Regarding the term "cognizers" (*mantṛ*), you must state whether these properties belong to a single entity. Are these words—“one who has non-different objects,” “these words,” and so forth—synonymous? Indeed, they are such words. 405.03. Even here, if the object is not distinct, then the conscious one, the determiner, the cognizer, and the perceiver [are the same]; therefore, [your position] is untenable.

405.04 This intellect determines: "The self cognizes. If, however, this recognition [were to serve as] 405.05 a proof for the permanence of the mind, it would not be logical for it to be so; for 405.06 the permanence of the mind is already accepted by virtue of its being admitted as permanent. In that regard, [this is] the proof: [text fragment].
405.07. It is useless [to argue] because of the lack of certainty; the oneness of the instrument is not established by recognition, for it is observed that 405.08.

there is recognition even when the instruments differ, due to the oneness of the knower, as in the case of what was seen by sight being recognized by touch; or as in the case of what was seen by one lamp being recognized by another lamp. As for this which is thought:

When the intellect (*buddhi*) is present, its functions (*vṛtti*) manifest according to their respective objects; and the function is not distinct from that which possesses the function. Furthermore, this is not so because they are not perceived simultaneously.
[3-2-4] Because they are not perceived simultaneously.
The meaning of the sūtra is that because there is an abiding of that which possesses activity, there is an abiding of the activity itself.
405.14 [3-2-5] And if there were no recognition, it would follow that there is destruction;

405.15 for when there is no recognition, it follows that there is destruction of the functions, and consequently the possessor of the functions is also destroyed—this is the meaning of the sūtra. Furthermore, the single mind (*manas*), being non-omnipresent, connects with the sense organs in succession.
405.18 [3-2-6] Because of its sequential occurrence, there is no simultaneous apprehension;
405.19 because of its sequential occurrence, there is no simultaneous apprehension. This is due to the difference between the function (*vṛtti*) and that which possesses the function (*vṛttimat*).
405.20 This is the meaning of the sūtra: if the function and that which possesses the function were one and the same, there would be an absence of manifestation and disappearance.
406.01 [3-2-7] And non-recognition [of an object] occurs due to preoccupation with another object;

406.02 "And non-recognition occurs due to preoccupation with another object"—this is possible only if there is a distinction between the function (vṛtti) and that which possesses the function (vṛttimat). 406.03 For if they were identical, preoccupation would be purposeless; and this is so because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is all-pervading (vibhu).
406.04. There is a conjunction with the sense-faculties by way of succession.

406.05 [3-2-8] Not so, because of the absence of movement. 406.06 "The sense organs have reached the internal organ"—this is the meaning of the sūtra. Furthermore, if they were all-pervading (vyāpin), there would be the fault of the consequence that multiple sense organs would be connected simultaneously, resulting in simultaneous perception. If they were atomic (aṇu)...

406.08 If it is argued that there would be the consequence of simultaneous perception even regarding objects graspable by a single sense-faculty, [we reply: no, because of its being an instrument (*karaṇa*). There is no simultaneous grasping [of all objects] because of this instrumental nature. Why is this not also a refutation for my position? Because it is observed that when there is a difference in instruments, [simultaneous action does not occur].
Indeed, those instruments which are non-distinct are governed by a single presiding agent.

It is observed that things presided over [by a single agent] operate simultaneously, just as two axes operated by both hands function at once. Likewise, since the sense organs are presided over by the pervasive internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), simultaneous activity would necessarily follow; and if that were to follow, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous perception.

And because there is no motion, since for an all-pervading internal organ (*antakaraṇa*) there is no going for the purpose of reaching [an object], there is no proof for the non-simultaneity of cognitions;
by what means of knowledge could one establish that non-simultaneity of cognitions which has already been refuted? For how could something be established even if it has been refuted?

406.17–18. Likewise, the motion of the eye has been refuted by someone on the grounds that it perceives both near and distant objects at the same time; for one perceives with the eye a nearby hand and the distant moon simultaneously. Therefore, the eye does not possess motion—thus it is refuted. 406.19. Even though this is contested...

406.20 [Objection: An existent movement is inferred by means of obstruction and resistance. Nor is there a simultaneous cognition [of all objects]. 407.01 There is no proof for its arising; thus, this dispute is not regarding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), nor regarding its eternity.

407.02 From where, then, does the dispute arise? It is regarding its omnipresence (*vibhutva*). And that [omnipresence] does not exist, because it is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). No.

407.03 For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [such as to claim] that "the internal organ is one, and these various functions (*vṛtti*) consisting of visual consciousness and so forth are many. Furthermore, this [distinction] is untenable if the function and the possessor of the function are identical; however, for one who holds that the function and the possessor of the function are distinct, the [omnipresence of the] internal organ— 407.04–05 ... [is not required]. And these various functions, consisting of visual consciousness and so forth, are not possible if the internal organ were not omnipresent. Therefore, the internal organ is omnipresent. But its omnipresence does not entail that it is eternal, because it is produced by the conjunction of the self, the mind (*manas*), and the sense organs. Thus, the internal organ is both omnipresent and non-eternal. It is also manifold, because it is divided into the auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory, and visual organs. This is established by the fact that the functions of hearing and so forth are restricted to their respective locations. Moreover, the internal organ is not a single entity, because its various functions are observed simultaneously. If the internal organ were one, then all its functions would have to occur at once, since there is no distinction between the parts of a single substance. However, we observe that the functions of hearing and so forth occur sequentially. Therefore, the internal organ is manifold. Furthermore, it is not the case that the internal organ is merely the mind (*manas*), because the mind is a single substance while the internal organ is manifold. Nor is it the case that the mind is the internal organ, because the mind is atomic (*aṇu*) while the internal organ is omnipresent. Thus, the internal organ is distinct from the mind. It is also distinct from the sense organs, because the sense organs are external while the internal organ is internal. Furthermore, the internal organ is distinct from the self (*ātman*), because the self is eternal while the internal organ is non-eternal. It is also distinct from space (*ākāśa*), because space is eternal while the internal organ is non-eternal. It is also distinct from time (*kāla*), because time is eternal while the internal organ is non-eternal. It is also distinct from the directions (*dik*), because the directions are eternal while the internal organ is non-eternal. It is also distinct from the atoms (*paramāṇu*), because the atoms are eternal while the internal organ is non-eternal. It is also distinct from the qualities of color and so forth, because those are qualities while the internal organ is a substance. It is also distinct from the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*), because those are categories (*padārtha*) while the internal organ is a substance. Therefore, the internal organ is a distinct category from the mind, the sense organs, the self, space, time, the directions, the atoms, the qualities, and the other categories. It is established that the internal organ is a substance distinct from all others. Its nature is that of a substance, because it possesses qualities such as number and so forth. Its existence is inferred from the perception of objects through the eyes and other senses, which would not occur if the internal organ did not exist to connect the self with the senses and the objects. It is logical that the self, having the eyes and other [senses] as its instruments, perceives objects; by this, the objection regarding distraction toward another object is refuted. As for the claim that "the person (puruṣa) knows, not the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)," what indeed is this intended "distraction"? It is the production of multiple cognitions regarding desired objects, and that—

407.09–11. Furthermore, this distraction of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), characterized by its presence and absence [with respect to various objects], belongs to the person and not to the internal organ; thus it is permitted. That "the internal organ is one, but its functions (*vṛtti*) are manifold"—one who seeks to perceive things according to reason ought not to accept this, just as the internal organ is indeed one.

“If it is argued that such a modification [of the internal organ] contradicts what is observed, and you think: ‘If [the modification] does not differ from the internal organ, then surely it contradicts what is observed—namely, form, taste, smell, and touch’—[we reply:
this perceived difference in cognition would not exist; yet it would not be non-existent, because it conforms to the difference in its objects.”
The modification (*vṛtti*), though undivided, appears as if divided by conforming to the difference in its objects,
just as a substance such as crystal appears as if divided by conforming to the difference in the colored objects placed near it.
And for the purpose of making this point known, there is the conceit of its being something other [than itself], just like the conceit that the crystal is something other [than its own nature].
Thus ends the Sūtra.
407.19 [3-2-9] The misconception of its being something else is like the misconception of a crystal being something else.

407.20 This is not so, because it is inconclusive; for this misconception of difference is observed in both ways: among various things such as odors and the like, and also in a single, undivided crystal—as stated in the sutra according to the literal text, there is thus an absence of a probans.
407.22–408.01: Because it is merely an illustration, this is just an illustration; there is no logical reason (*hetu*) here. This is because the alternative possibilities (*vikalpa*) are untenable.

Regarding this illustration, "like a crystal," what is the alternative? Is this crystal differentiated by the difference in the objects placed near it, or not? And what follows from this? If it is differentiated, then it is not a valid illustration.
408.03. Now, if it is not divided, how can there be a designation of multiplicity? If [you say] it is divided because of the difference in the substrates (*upadhāna*), [we ask:

how do you understand this? If [you claim] the occurrence (*vṛtti*) is undivided while there is a contradiction due to the difference in the conditions (*pratyaya*), then there is a contradiction in saying "the condition is divided," because occurrence is synonymous with condition. Or else, for you...

408.06 What is the proof for the distinction between the modes of activity (*vṛtti*)? It is the observation that cognitions arise and perish in succession. 408.07 Cognitions are seen to arise and perish in succession; and because they possess single or multiple objects, there is the designation of their plurality. How is there the apprehension of single and multiple objects within a single [cognition]? 408.08 Regarding the cognition of a single object...

408.09. A perception of diversity is observed in a crystal, and a perception of diversity is also observed among various things such as odors and so forth. 408.10. Because this conceit of diversity is seen in both ways, the notion that "this is one" or "this is many" is not tenable. Furthermore, regarding this undivided crystal:
408.12 That cognition of difference is also not tenable without a difference in the cognitions themselves.

For one who maintains non-difference, a difference in the cognitions of blue and so forth in a crystal is not tenable; thus, in the case of the crystal, 408.14 the cognition of blue and so forth is not tenable because of the lack of connection, for the substance blue is not in contact with the eye.

[Objection: "It is thus: that very [object] which is proximate is blue, not the crystal. [Response: A cognition of blue in the crystal is not tenable as being co-referential with the crystal. [Objection: It is not so, because of the perception of their contiguity. [Response: When the substances—the crystal and the blue [object]—are situated in contiguity, they both come into contact with the eye; from that contact [the cognition arises].

Just as there is a false cognition that "the crystal is blue" due to the superimposition of the quality of blueness upon it; likewise, because the intervening space is not perceived among things that have intervals, there arises the cognition of conjunction. For one for whom this cognition does not differ [from the cognition of non-conjunction], the scriptural teaching that "there are three means of valid cognition" (pramāṇas) would be contradicted, for it is not so.

408.21. [Objection: A distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible even when there is no difference in the cognition itself. If it is argued that there is a threefold nature [of the means of cognition] due to the difference in objects (*viṣaya*), [we reply: 409.01.
Now, if you think that the object is divided into three kinds, and therefore the cognition colored by it is likewise threefold—409.02.

that is not tenable, because when there is no difference in the means of valid cognition, the difference in objects cannot be established. For indeed, [without a difference in the means of cognition,] there is no...

409.03 [Objection: It is possible to apprehend [the object] even without a distinction between the object and [its cognition]. If you say this is because of identity with the object (viṣaya-tādātmyāt):
409.04—then perhaps you think that the object itself is established in such a way that, due to its identity [with the cognition], it appears in that manner.

409.05—That is not so, because of the futility of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). If this were the case, the means of valid cognition would be useless; for the means of valid cognition does not [establish] a distinction between objects.
409.06–409.08: [The opponent argues: "Difference (bheda) causes [the object] to be understood, but the object itself is established as such through identity (tādātmya), just as one determines it;
thus one intends it accordingly. [Response: This is a contradiction, because that which possesses a mode (prakāravat) cannot [be identical to] that which lacks a mode (aprakāravat).
Furthermore, it is illogical for that which lacks a mode [to be so]; and there is a contradiction in saying that the cognition perceives that very representation (pratyaya).

409.09–10. Since there is no difference between the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and that which is contained within it (*ādheya*), the cognition (*pratyaya*) [of the latter] is itself the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus, there is non-difference between the locus and that which is contained within it. And this being the case, the claim that "one perceives the cognition residing in the intellect" is contradictory.

Not tolerating the claim that "the misconception of its being something else is like the misconception of a crystal being something else," the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin) says: "Even in the case of a crystal, because individuals arise one after another due to their momentariness, [that example] is not a valid reason."
409.13 [3-2-10] Even in the case of a crystal, because individuals arise one after another, they are momentary.
409.14 This is not a valid reason.
409.15 [3-2-11] Since there is no cause for restriction, one must accept things as they are observed.

409.16 It is incorrect to claim that there is a misconception of difference regarding a crystal that exists without distinction, because individual entities are momentary (kṣaṇika). Their momentariness is established by the observation of a continuous process of accumulation and decay. For, in the case of the body and so forth, the substance of *rasa* produced by digestion is accumulated or diminished at every moment.

409.19 From accumulation there is the arising of manifestations, and from diminution there is the cessation of manifestations; and those two, arising and cessation, 409.20 are observed by him at different times. Therefore it is understood that [the body] accumulates and diminishes at every moment.
410.01 And so it is with the body; indeed, its accumulation and diminution occur at every moment, not—
410.02–04. Even over a period of time, no two instances of that [body] are identical, just as there is no identity in the case of the earth when it is being cooked.
This refers to things produced by cooking (*pākaja*); and just like the qualities produced by the cooking of the earth while it is being heated, there is a distinction at every moment.
The formal argument for this is: at every moment, the body becomes something else and yet another, because external conditions do not differ.

410.05 Since there is an end [to the body], because a distinction is observed— just like that which is produced by the ripening of the earth while it is being cooked, and just like that which is produced by the ripening of the earth while it is not being cooked— it follows that this observation of the continuity of increase and decrease, being seen in the body, establishes the distinctness of the body; however, it does not establish the distinctness of those specific increases and decreases that are not perceived.

410.08. [The argument] that "the distinctness of crystals and the like is established from this" is not a valid reason. Regarding that in which perception occurs, 410.09—if you think that "distinctness" is what is meant—then we do not establish the momentariness of all entities by observing a continuous process of increase and decrease; rather, it is established in that case where such [momentariness] exists. 410.10. 410.11 Regarding "momentariness": it is true that for whatever a continuous process of accumulation and decay (*upacaya-apacaya-prabandha*) is perceived, there is a difference in that [thing] from itself; however, this is not momentariness. Furthermore, the observation of a continuous process of accumulation and decay is the manifestation of change (*anyathābhāva*).
410.13 Thus, [the presence of such a process] is no reason for momentariness. How else could the previous constituent parts [be replaced] by the constituent parts of food?

410.14–410.16: "If you argue that a distinction [between the two states] is logical because, by abandoning the previous configuration (*vyūha*), they, being joined together, undergo another configuration and produce another body—this is not a valid reason. For the proposition regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) is the same. If you think that when there is a connection with the accumulation of the parts of the previous food, the parts of the body..."
410.17 They initiate another body by abandoning the previous configuration; it is not [a different body] because of momentariness.

410.18 Regarding this, what is the reason for saying "it has been born"? It is not because of a lack of proof, nor because I have established the difference of the body through its connection with the increase and decrease resulting from food; rather, [the difference is established] by you through the observation of specific characteristics of the body.

410.20. "Otherness" was asserted, and from that [otherness], "momentariness" follows; thus, the perception of difference (*viśeṣa-darśana*) is the proof of momentariness. 411.01. That perception of difference, as it occurs otherwise, is by us established as the proof for [the property of] momentariness.
411.02. Only this much is being stated; it is not being called a formal "proof" (*sādhana*). Now, if it must necessarily be a proof...
To this we say: this must be stated—that [the self] does not [exist], because the causes of its arising and destruction are not perceived.
411.04 [3-2-12] Not so, because the causes of origination and destruction are perceived.
411.05 The causes of origination and destruction—namely, accumulation and decay—are observed in the case of anthills, jars, and the like.
411.06 Since both of these are seen, they would not exist if things were momentary; furthermore, "accumulation" means increase.
"Accumulated" means "increase," while "diminished" means "decrease"; thus, "the cow is diminished" refers to both.

Furthermore, this concerns an existing entity, for it is not said that something previously non-existent arises and increases, nor is it said that what is perishing is "accumulated," because we perceive the causes for increase, decrease, arising, and destruction.
411.10 This is the meaning of the Sūtra. Alternatively, "cause" (kāraṇa) is designated as the substratum (ādhāra), and [the term] "effect" (kārya) refers to that which is supported (ādheya).

411.11 Furthermore, the relationship between substratum and supported is not possible if things are momentary (kṣaṇika). Nor, without the state of being a substratum and supported, can there be a causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva). Therefore, [this is established] from the perception of the causal relationship.
411.13 “The state of being non-momentary”: the formal argument for this is that cause and effect are experienced at one and the same time.

411.14 Because they stand in the relation of container and contained, like milk and a bowl. Milk exists in the bowl, and it experiences the time of the bowl; likewise, the effect exists in the cause, and therefore it too [experiences the time of the cause].

If it is argued that [the effect] experiences the time of the cause because the relationship of container and contained (ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva) is unestablished— [that is,] if you think that the relationship of container and contained between cause and effect is unestablished because the effect has no container— for indeed,
we do not observe any effect whatsoever to possess a container— [we reply: no, because [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
411.19 This is not an absolute rule that every effect is without a substratum (*anādhāra*). For instance, as is agreed upon by both parties:

color (*rūpa*) is an effect and possesses a substratum, while touch (*sparśa*) is its support; thus, there is a contradiction [if one were to deny this]. If color were indeed without a support, then the claim that touch is its support would be contradicted. And by this...

412.01 By means of the analogy of form (*rūpa*), it is established that whatever is proven to exist through simultaneity is experienced at one and the same time; thus, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established. If it is argued that even in the case of momentary things, destruction and arising are simultaneous, like the rising and falling of the two ends of a balance scale; 412.03 if this is the case—
Because the effect exists at the same time as the destruction [of the cause].

When the cause perishes, the effect arises; thus, the perishing cause exists simultaneously with the production of the effect, just as, for example, the lowering and raising of the two ends of a scale. This is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason.

412.08 We do not say that the relation of cause and effect does not exist in the case of momentariness; rather, 412.09 because the cause and the effect belong to different times, the relation of container and contained (*ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva*) is not tenable. Thus, the effect is without a container. There is no such example [to the contrary] in our position, for in our view, the effect possesses a container.

The example is "form and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the operation of the support of the scale, [the simultaneous occurrence] is not established because of the acceptance of rising and falling; this is due to its being a single entity. If you speak with reference to the scale, then there is simultaneous occurrence because the single action called "swinging" is one.

412.14 It is not logical, for two [actions] do not exist simultaneously. Now, regarding the two actions of the parts (*avayava-karman*), since their relationship as cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*) is not admitted, what is connected with what? Or, if it is intended merely to express simultaneous existence, then simultaneous existence [occurs] due to the simultaneity of causes, in as many objects as there are.
412.17–18. The simultaneous existence of causes means that there is the arising of that many [effects] at one and the same time.

[Objection: Rising and falling are unconnected; however, the simultaneity of causes consists of gravity, effort, and conjunction. [Response: Regarding rising and falling, there is also the conjunction of a rope with a scale-beam, which is assisted by the conjunction of a substance possessing gravity. Even so, it is not [the case that they are unconnected].

412.20. An opponent may propose that action (*karman*) is either a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) or a conjunction (*saṃyoga*); the response to that has already been stated. 413.01. Just as conjunction is a distinct entity, so too is action a distinct entity by virtue of being the cause of conjunction. For example, 413.02.
while a cause for the production and destruction of entities is perceived, such is not the case for the crystal. Nor...

And it is possible to accept that which is not perceived, just as there is the non-perception of a cause upon the destruction of milk, and just as there is the production of curd; thus its existence is established.
413.05 [3-2-13] Just as the cause of the destruction of milk is unperceived, and just as there is the production of curd; 413.06 that [destruction] is established.
413.07 Just as the cause of the destruction of milk is admitted even though it is not perceived, so too is that of the curd.
And since the cause of production is thus perceived for individual instances such as crystals, the causes of their destruction must likewise be admitted to exist.
413.10 [3-2-14] Because it is apprehended through a mark (*liṅga*), it is not non-perception (anupalabdhi).

413.11 Because it is apprehended through a mark, that which is so apprehended does not exist as "non-existent. 413.12 And the contrary is seen in the case of crystal and the like; for there is no [perceptual] difference among the successive individual instances (*vyakti*) of crystals and such things.

413.13 [Objection: There is a mark for [the existence of] production; it is not the case that there is no [mark], because the distinction between cold and hot touch exists when there is multiplicity (nānātva).

413.14 [Response: Because it serves as a means of proof, the distinction between cold and hot touch is observed in cases of multiplicity, such as in fire and water. 413.15 This distinction between cold and hot touch exists in the crystal; indeed, it exists, but it arises from another cause.

413.16 Furthermore, how could there be an entry of the constituent parts of water and fire? [If it is argued that] it is cold due to the entry of the constituent parts of water, 413.17 and hot due to the entry of the constituent parts of fire—such an entry of the constituent parts of water and fire is not logical, 413.18 because there is no cause for an entry of fewer or more numerous parts. For in winter, when things have been left exposed in the open air...

413.19 Just as a progressively greater degree of coldness is observed in wood, earth, stone, and iron, so too, 414.01 when these very same things are heated by the summer sun, a progressively greater degree of heat is observed. Indeed, we do not perceive any cause for a lesser or greater penetration [of heat] within them; therefore, they depend upon the specificities of the primary elements (mahābhūta) inherent within themselves, while being conditioned by external causes.

414.03 It is logical that the elements themselves arise in such and such a manner; it is not logical that [the nature of the elements is negated]. For, by the entry of the parts of water and fire, the nature of the elements is not set aside;
thus, because the nature of the elements is common to both positions, the nature of the elements is not a valid proof, and this reason is contradictory if [it refers to] the parts.

414.06–07: You do not admit the mutual penetration [of the elements], asserting that the primary elements (bhūta) consist of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. This is contradicted. How so? Because that which is solid is at one and the same time also hot, and that which is hot moves toward what is solid; thus, it is a single entity possessing a single intrinsic nature (eka-svabhāva).

It would follow that [the object] possesses two natures or three natures. However, for one who maintains that there is an entry into the parts, this fault does not exist, because heat is perceived as it exists elsewhere, conjoined and inherent [in the substance].
Thus, this reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), since one accepts a single particularity; how can [it be] one?

414.12 A single entity at one time is hard, hot, and moving; thus it possesses three natures. Therefore, 414.13 because this reason—"on account of the perception of distinct qualities"—is accepted [by you] as a tenet, it is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it contradicts that very tenet.
414.14 Thus it is contradictory. Now, if you think that the mere perception of distinct qualities does not establish plurality...

414.15 [The opponent claims: "But a contradictory particularity (*viśeṣa*) is the proof for plurality. [We reply: No, because of a failure to understand our intention. 414.16 We do not say that a mere particularity is the proof for plurality; rather, it is a contradictory particularity. 414.17 One that is mutually excluded and established as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is contradictory; if it were not contradictory, it would not be so.
If the three characteristics were to reside in a single entity, what would that object be called?

If it were earth, that would not be correct, because heat is observed [therein]. If it were fire, that too would not be correct, because solidity is observed. By this, air is also explained. This is the reason regarding the elements (*bhūta*).

The proof of plurality does not contradict the characteristic of the elements, nor is it non-existent. By this, the perception of heat in water is refuted; for even there, heat, moisture, and motion exist simultaneously. However, the consequence that the form of fire would be perceived in water is not tenable due to suppression [by the water]. Therefore, this [objection] is not [valid], because of a lack of understanding of our established doctrine.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the form of fire is overcome by the form of water; however, because light (*tejas*) is fourfold, there is no perception of its form therein—this has been proven in the section on the sense faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, as for this proposition that "one crystal is different from another," [it is refuted].

415.06 And what is the meaning of this? If it means merely "otherness," then it is a case of proving what is already established (siddha-sādhana), since crystal is indeed other than jars and the like. If it means "other than another crystal," that too is exactly the same. If it means "other than the previous crystal," then which one is that "previous crystal"?

415.09. "This is another" [is not established], because exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is impossible; thus there is no designation. For example, 415.10: it is not logical to investigate whether things such as a jar are other than or non-other than those forms and so forth that are admitted by both parties.
Furthermore, in this case, there is no prior crystal admitted by both parties from which the present one could be distinguished as being other.

415.12 If it is being proved that the previous crystal-moment, which is admitted by both parties, is different [from the present one], then the proof is redundant. Or, 415.13 if, having accepted the present crystal, it is being proved that the past crystal-moment is "other" than it;
415.14 in that case, the difference between the sensations of cold and heat would not be a property of that present crystal.
415.15 Since it possesses the nature of a phenomenon (*dharma*) and because it is present, who would not accept that the past is other than the crystal?

415.16 Now, if you claim that it is the very same thing yet other, there is a contradiction: "it is the very same" and "it is other. In this way, however one examines its otherness, it results in proving what is already established and contradicts your own tenet (*siddhānta*).
415.18. Now, the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that crystal is not the objective support (*ālambana*) of cognitions occurring at non-simultaneous times.

415.19. Even regarding this meaning of the proposition, there is no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). [Objection: A lamp is the illustrative example; a lamp [is not the support of non-simultaneous cognitions]. 415.20. [Response:
There exists an illustrative example, namely, properties such as existence (*sat*) and so forth, which are not the objective support of cognitions occurring at non-simultaneous times.
415.21 [Objection: This is unproven because it is unestablished that cognitions occurring at non-simultaneous times do not have a lamp as their objective support.

416.01 First, regarding the lamp: since it persists for multiple moments, there is first the time of its connection with the existence of its own causes, 416.02 the time of the manifestation of the universal (sāmānya), and the time of the motion of its parts; immediately following that is the time of disjunction (*vibhāga*).
416.03 Time [is defined as] the moment immediately following that, which is the time of the destruction of that conjunction; from that follows the destruction of the substance.

416.04 Just as with a lamp, so all entities perish by conforming to their own causes, existence, connection, manifestation, and the destruction of their contrary substratum. There is no destruction of that which is causeless.
Because we do not accept it; for nothing whatsoever perishes for us without a cause.

[If you argue that] this would be like the destruction of a substance or an action, [we reply: that is not so, because there is a contradiction in accepting [the existence of] action, and because we do not accept it. If you say, "Because there is no cause of destruction," and you think that there is no cause for destruction—
Therefore, this entity perishes as soon as it has arisen; thus, there is no logical inconsistency in this [position].

One who asserts that "there is no cause for destruction" should be questioned: "Is destruction non-existent because it lacks a cause, or is it eternal because it lacks a cause? In your own system, that which is causeless is of two kinds: the eternal and [the non-existent].

416.12 But for us, [destruction] is indeed eternal. If destruction were eternal because it is causeless, 416.13 then the arising of an effect would not occur, and there would be the fault that an arisen entity would persist simultaneously with its destruction. 416.14 Furthermore, since destruction is not incompatible with entities, they would persist eternally.

Thus [it is argued]. Now, if destruction (*vināśa*) were non-existent, then everything would be eternal because of the absence of destruction. Furthermore, if destruction were non-existent, the cognition "it is destroyed" would not occur when destruction is absent; for there is no such thing as "one goes" when there is no going. Alternatively, since it would be indestructible, destruction would be causeless.
416.18–19. You think that destruction does not perish; why is this so? Because those things that have perished do not arise again.

416.19–20. If you think: "If destruction were to perish, then what has perished would arise again"—this is not tenable, because there is no absence of the absence of destruction from which its [re-]destruction could occur.

Furthermore, even if an entity were to possess a cause, its arising would occur at the time when that cause exists; however, destruction possesses no cause and thus does not perish, because it is a non-entity (*abhāva*).
This is the nature of entities (*bhāvadharma*): that which possesses a cause perishes; but a non-entity, being causeless, does not.

417.04 It perishes, just as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), though possessing a cause, does not perish, as does posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). If destruction possesses a cause, then surely that which produces [an effect] would become its destroyer;
for that very same contact with fire which is the producer of the qualities born of cooking (*pākaja*) is itself the [destroyer] of those qualities born of cooking.

417.07. "In the case of intermediate production, one cuts off those things produced by prior cooking"; thus, that which is the producer becomes the destroyer. 417.08. [The opponent replies: "No, because there is no restriction; you have not understood this view of the Kāśyapīyas. For it is not our position that the very same conjunction with fire which produces the things produced by cooking also destroys them; rather, it is the fire—"
The subsequent conjunction destroys the preceding form and so forth, and immediately thereafter it initiates the [subsequent] forms and so forth.
Therefore, because one [conjunction] initiates those and another [conjunction] initiates yet others, there is no consequence that the producer is the destroyer.
Now, if you think that even that which is similar in nature to the producer cannot be the destroyer—[we reply: it is not so.
For it is observed that the production of a sprout occurs through its conjunction with water and other factors; yet that very same conjunction with water and other factors becomes its destroyer.
Thus, there is indeed nothing impossible in what is observed. Furthermore, the fault regarding the destruction of something without a cause is unavoidable.
Therefore, it is said in this way: "the destroyer is of the same nature as the producer. So much for this point.

The fault has already been stated regarding the proof of otherness. However, for those who seek to prove momentariness on the grounds of observing specific differences and because of the absence of a cause for destruction, this is said in response to them: "Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary. One who asserts this must be asked about the meaning of the word "momentary": what is it that is meant by "they are momentary"?

417.19 If [the opponent means] "those which are perishable," this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*). If, on the other hand, they mean "those which perish quickly," then that qualification contradicts one's own tenet (*siddhānta-virodhin*). If they mean "those which perish as soon as they have arisen" (*utpanna-pradhvaṃsin*), this too is exactly the same. To say "arisen and perishing" is *siddha-sādhana*. If, however, they mean "that which has arisen..."

"Destroyed" refers to a single time; thus, arising and destruction would be simultaneous. Consequently, it follows that just as there is the arising of what has not yet arisen, so too there would be the destruction of what has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, even on the position that "what has already arisen perishes," destruction, like arising, would possess a cause.

418.06 Just as origination, because it is an action and because it occurs only occasionally, has a cause, so too does destruction experience a cause of destruction; therefore, it perishes [only] from that. Thus, the fault in the case of causeless destruction has been stated. 418.07 And as for this possessive suffix in the words "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) and "non-momentary" (*akṣaṇika*), how could it be [justified] if [the term] were etymologically derived...

418.09. [The opponent argues: "Momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) means that which possesses a moment (*kṣaṇa*), where a moment is defined by destruction (*kṣaya*) according to logic; this is not tenable. 418.10.

Because of the difference in time, when there is destruction, the destroyer does not exist; therefore, the possessive suffix (*matu-artha*) cannot apply to two things existing at different times. 418.11. Furthermore, it is observed that an entity itself, being characterized by immediate destruction, is "momentary."
Thus it is said; nevertheless, since that very thing does not exist in that same way by virtue of that [property], the possessive suffix (*matu-artha*) is not appropriate.

Furthermore, if it is argued that "momentary" means those things which abide for the duration of the time of a moment—that is, having established the final limit of all time as a "moment," those which abide therein are "momentary"—this too is not tenable.

Because time is accepted as being merely a designation (*saṃjñā-mātra*). [The opponent claims: "The five aggregates are merely a difference in designation," according to the treatise. However, it is not logical for a mere designation to serve as a qualification of a real entity (*vastu-viśeṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, having made the proposition that things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), it was stated that there is no supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*), such as a lamp-flame and so forth.
Because they are unestablished (*asiddha*). Even those reasons such as "because of the perception of a distinction" (*viśeṣa-darśanāt*) and so forth are likewise unestablished;

they are either established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or, even if one grants that there is a distinction, they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the presence of a distinction in the single present moment, which is admitted by both parties. As for whichever [reason]...

419.02. The moment (*kṣaṇa*) is present; it possesses specific qualities and is one—thus, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because of the observation of a specific quality at the end" (*ante viśeṣa-darśanāt*), the qualification is redundant because the meaning of "end" (*anta*) has not been stated. It must be specified: "because of the observation of a specific quality at which end? For if "end" means destruction (*vināśa*), that is not the case here.

419.05 There is the perception of a distinction; now, if the final object itself is what is denoted by the word "end," then, in this case, the reason "perception of a distinction" is contradictory. Furthermore, regarding this reason "because of perception and non-perception" (419.07), its meaning is said to be the production of a substance such as a lamp in another location while it is being carried away.
419.08. Cessation occurs in another location; seeing and non-seeing are caused by that. Therefore, as Devadatta and others move, 419.09 there is seeing and non-seeing.

From this, it follows that even for him [Devadatta], there is arising and destruction at every moment. This is not logical, 419.10 because the seeing and non-seeing of Devadatta and others are due to other causes, being produced by conjunction and disjunction.

419.11 Visibility and invisibility are not caused by arising and destruction; for in whatever place a conjunction has ceased, in that place the conjoined object is not perceived, whereas in whatever place it has arisen, in that place it is perceived. 419.12–13 This is because the cognition of "it exists here" (iha-buddhi) occurs with respect to a substance when that [conjunction] is present or absent, owing to its being possessed of that [quality]. Now, as for conjunction—
419.14 Neither disjunction (*vibhāga*) nor conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is perceived [as distinct entities]; furthermore, it has been established that conjunction is a separate entity (*arthāntara*).

419.15 By this, disjunction is also explained. Thus, through the production of conjunction and disjunction, there occur the perception and non-perception of a substance; it cannot be otherwise. Furthermore, as for this production of a lamp in another location—

419.17 We do not understand this either. How so? First, according to your position, that entity which has arisen perishes right where it arose. Since that which is about to arise possesses no deposited latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it is incapable of arising in another location due to its non-existence [there]. Or, if there is an arising in another location even for that which possesses no deposited latent impression—[then we ask: how could it reach that other location? It would have to go there by means of motion (*gati*). But motion is not perceived; nor is it logical, because it is momentary. Therefore, since the entity does not persist until it reaches another location, it is not possible for it to be perceived there. Consequently, the perception of the object in another location is not established. Thus, the claim that "the object is perceived in another location" is merely a false assertion. Furthermore, if one were to say that the object itself moves to another location, that too is incorrect, because the object is momentary and cannot endure until it reaches another location.
