419.20 No entity whatsoever arises in a location distinct from itself; furthermore, if the cause is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then by virtue of that which is deposited within it, the effect also arises as being exactly of such a nature. Thus, it is the same for the effect.
Just as it is impossible to deposit a conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*) in the effect, so too is it impossible in the cause; thus, they are equal.
420.03. In your view, it must always arise either from a cause located in a different place or from one located in the same place.
420.04. By this very [argument], the "falling at unequal times" is explained. It is not, however, because of falling at unequal times that momentariness is established;
for indeed, in the case of a clod of earth or similar objects falling through the air, there is no obstacle whatsoever whose conformity [to the time of fall] would [account for the delay].
420.06 Some things, such as clods of earth and the like, fall slowly, while others fall quickly; therefore, due to their momentariness (kṣaṇikatva),
certain states arise that lack the capacity for the production of a downward continuum, whereas other similar states arise that do possess it— this too [is established].

420.09. Otherwise, it would be established as redundant that for substances of equal weight, the causes of one's falling are gravity, effort, and projection, while for another it is gravity alone, and for yet another, gravity and effort. Thus, substances possessing gravity conform to differences in their causes and thereby exhibit falling that is either slow or rapid.

420.12 "It happens" is not a valid reason, as it is an unequal application. Furthermore, regarding this [objection] that "the arrow would continue to fall," this fault of the proponent of a single [homogeneous] formation (*saṃskāra*) is also refuted by the non-acceptance of the oneness of formations.
And how there are multiple formations has been explained in the *Pāṇinimittapraśleṣasūtra*.

420.15 Furthermore, a single conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra), depending on the difference in its causes at various times, performs its functions either intensely or 420.16 weakly; this should be understood as being like gravity. Just as a single instance of gravity produces a slow fall due to the presence of a concurrent conjunction, yet produces an intense one when that obstruction has been removed.
For it is observed that the fall of a stone released in the air is rapid, whereas that of water is slow;
thus, even such unequal falling is not a valid reason [for non-momentariness]. Now, what proof has been stated regarding the absence of momentariness? [It is argued:
because of the relationship between support and supported, cause and effect are experienced simultaneously, like a jujube fruit in a bowl.
421.01 Therefore, cognitions that are not simultaneous, though divergent, have a single object and do not deviate [from it].

421.02 This is because, while sharing the same substratum as that cognition, they are denoted by the same word, like the multiple cognitions of various persons regarding a single present moment. Just as, for example, the cognitions of many persons whose objects are the present moment— 421.03 [are one with respect to that object].
421.04 When there is a non-deviation from those cognitions in their coreferentiality with those cognitions, [it follows that] those which are denoted by the same term,

421.05 possess the state of having a single object; and likewise, those cognitions which are coreferential with those non-deviating cognitions, 421.06 and which are denoted by the same term, though they are contradictory and do not occur simultaneously, they too are one— [object].

421.07 Regarding the objects [of cognition], the cognitions are not produced by multiple agents for each individual, because that would entail the consequence of a lack of synthesis [of experience], just like the cognitions of Devadatta and others. 421.08 Thus, the cognitions of form, taste, smell, and touch have a single or multiple cause.
421.09 This is because of the synthesis [of them] as "by me," as in the case of many people who have made an agreement regarding the various [objects] existing in a single present moment.
421.10 Like consciousness: the consciousnesses of tomorrow and today within a single continuum have both single and multiple causes.

421.11 Because of the synthesis "by me," as in the previous case, the cognitions of the meaning of a treatise have both single and multiple causes. 421.12 Because of synthesis, as before, there are cognitions of various objects and cognitions produced by various agents.
"Because there is no reconnection" (apratisandhānāt)—the reasoning is exactly as before.

421.14 [3-2-15] It is not [the case that milk ceases to exist], because of the appearance of other qualities through the transformation of the milk. 421.15 It is not that the milk perishes in this way;
nor is curd produced [as something entirely new]. Rather, when the previous properties of the persisting substance cease, [new] properties [arise].

421.17 Some explain that another [quality] arises. Others, however, [hold that] when there is the cessation of a quality of a persisting substance, another quality arises. This indeed is the position of one school.
What is the meaning of the analogy? In both cases, the substance persists; for one [quality], there is disappearance and manifestation.
421.20. "The destruction and appearance of one [thing]" is the meaning of the analogy; the answer in both cases is that [it arises] from another arrangement (*vyūha*) of substances. 421.21.
The observation of the production of a subsequent substance is the inference of the cessation of the preceding substance.
422.01 [3-2-16] The observation of the production of a different substance from a different configuration is an inference for the cessation of the previous substance.

422.03 The remainder is in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, as for the claim that the disappearance and manifestation of one thing are the destruction and appearance of another, that is not so, because there is no abandonment of the previous state. If there were destruction and production...

Whether it be the disappearance and appearance [of qualities], or their manifestation and non-manifestation, in every case the substance abandons its prior state. For manifestation and non-manifestation do not occur for that which has not departed from its prior state;
nor do destruction and appearance. Therefore, it is illogical that there is transformation of a persisting entity.
And having permitted both the causeless destruction of milk and the causeless production of curd.
422.09 [3-2-17] Because the cause of destruction is unperceived in some cases and perceived in others, there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).

422.11 Because the cause of destruction is unperceived in some cases and perceived in others, there is inconclusiveness. Like milk and curd, the destruction and arising of individual crystals are without cause; however, this is not the case for jars.

422.13 “Like the first [example], these two possess a cause”; there is no reason for this here, and thus the statement of the example is without a basis (*niradhiṣṭhāna*). What is the meaning of "basis"? It means a support (*āśraya*). What is meant by saying it is "without a basis"?
It means that the subject of the property (*dharmin*) does not exist. For indeed, there is no arising of a crystal...

Since destruction is perceived at every moment, this reflection arises: "Are these two [origination and destruction] with a cause, or rather without a cause? Just as someone might say to one who has not accepted the true nature of sound, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; this case is similar," [the argument fails] due to the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

And the [argument] that it is "non-existence" is the same. Furthermore, having admitted the arising and destruction of the crystal, since you have admitted the proof for this, there is no refutation. Both of these examples—like milk and curd, and like a jar and so forth—are present; in that case, let either the jar and so forth be the example, or else milk and curd.
423.03 Thus [it is said]. In this regard, the argument "like a jar and so forth" is appropriate because the causes for the production and destruction of jars and such things are observed.

423.04 However, the argument "like milk and curd" is not appropriate, because [the latter] is apprehended through inference. Thus it is established that cognition is impermanent. Furthermore, cognition is impermanent because, while being a quality (*guṇa*), it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). 423.05 [This is established] by its being directly perceptible.
Because it inheres in a pervasive substance, like sound; because, while possessing a genus, it is perceptible by people such as ourselves, [like sound];
because it is dependent, like sound; and because, while being an instrument, it is perceptible by those who are not yogis, just like sound.
423.08. However, it is now considered whose quality this cognition is; for its status as a quality has not yet been established.
423.09. Since it is impermanent and not perceptible by the eye, its status as a quality is doubtful because it arises from sense-contact.
423.10. Thus, in this regard, there is this distinction.
[3-2-18] It is not [the case that cognition arises from the contact of the sense organ and the object], because even when those two have perished,
cognition persists. Indeed, when both the sense organ and the object have perished,
there occurs the cognition "I saw," namely, "I saw"— this does not arise from the contact of the sense organ and the object.
423.14 Because it is memory, this is memory; it cannot arise from the contact of the sense organ with its object.

Memory also—423.15—is similar [in this regard]: just as knowledge does not occur without a knower, so too memory is untenable without an experiencer who has perished. 423.16 Let it be, then, that cognition is a quality of the mind (*manas*).

[3-2-19] Because objects of cognition are not perceived simultaneously, [cognition] does not belong to the mind (*manas*). Indeed, it is established that the mind is characterized by the non-simultaneous perception of objects; therefore, cognition is not an attribute (*guṇa*) of that [mind], because [the Sūtra] specifies a qualification [of the instrument] as being an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of plurality— should you think that because the mind is established through the non-perception of objects of knowledge simultaneously, cognition is not a quality of that [single] mind— then by speaking thus, you would be admitting multiple internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*); for without a plurality of internal organs, such a qualification would not be possible.
424.02. "It is meaningful," [one might say], because not every sense organ is the cause of mental reflection (*manana*); therefore, not every sense organ is [the mind]. 424.03.

Because it is the cause of mental reflection, it is called the "mind" (*manas*). This being the case, the qualification [of the definition] is appropriate. 424.04. Since the mind has been established through the non-perception of simultaneous objects of cognition, knowledge is not a quality (*guṇa*) of that [mind].

Even so, the qualification is useless because nothing else is admitted. If that internal organ [is not the locus], then it follows that knowledge is a quality of some other means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Because nothing else is admitted, there is no refutation of another [means] being possible, due to the lack of a fixed limit for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

424.08 When this yogi discerns one person from another person—that is, when he discerns a distinct person—then, in that discernment of another person, the other person is the means (*sādhana*). Thus, it is logical that [the cognition] possesses the quality of knowledge of reality; therefore, it is a qualification. Consequently, cognition is not a quality of that [person]. Of what, then, is it a quality?
424.11 In that case, because the knower is one who possesses mastery (*vaśitva*), the instruments must necessarily belong to the master, the knower; yet this [mind] is not a knower.

424.12 This restriction—that only a master who is a knower is the possessor of mastery—is not absolute, for even one who is a knower can also be subject to mastery. For the restriction applies only to non-conscious things.
424.13 Indeed, everything non-conscious is subject to mastery; the mind is subject to mastery because it is non-conscious, like the sense of smell and so forth.

Or, if [the internal organ] possesses the quality of cognition (*jñāna-guṇatva*), there is merely a difference in terminology, namely that "the mind" (*citta*) is the internal organ and it possesses the quality of cognition. Only the designation differs. Just as the sense organ is the instrument of cognition for the knower, so too must there necessarily be an instrument of thought (*mati*) for the thinker. Since both are conscious, the distinction between their respective cognitions is established through inference.
If the internal organ were all-pervasive and possessed the quality of cognition, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous perception through all the sense organs.
424.19 [3-2-20] Even if it were a quality of that self, the same [objection] would apply.
424.20 [3-2-21] Because of the absence of contact between the mind and the sense organs, there is no production of that [cognition].
424.21 Even if it were a quality of that self, the same [objection] would apply; for one who holds that the self is omnipresent and has cognition as its quality, the same [problem] follows.

425.01. Since there is no prohibition against the connection with all the sense-faculties, it would follow that there is simultaneous perception. [Reply: This is not a necessary consequence, because of the existence of other causes; just as the contact between the sense-faculty and the object is a cause, so too is the contact between the sense-faculty and the mind (manas) a cause. [Objection: That [contact] is not simultaneous because the mind is atomic (aṇu). [Reply: But if, moreover, [the mind were to connect] the self, the sense-faculty, and the object—
425.04. Knowledge would arise from contact alone; what [harm] would there be if it were so? 425.05.
[3-2-22] Not so, because no cause for its arising has been specified.
425.06. "Not so, because no cause for its arising has been specified": let it arise from this very [contact]; there is no [other] cause [stated].

The meaning of the sūtra is that [cognition] is pointed out [as arising] from the contact of the self, the sense organ, and the object; thus, "knowledge arises from the contact of the self, the sense organ, and the object.

Alternatively, when there is no simultaneous production, no other cause is pointed out; or rather, when the sense organ is connected with an object situated externally, there is no production of cognition in the absence of a body (videha).
425.10 It must be explained why, since the connection with the self also exists there, there is no cognition of the "incorporeal" (videha).
425.11 Furthermore, if the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is rejected, the self alone would be the cause of memory and so forth.
425.12 Why, then, do memories not arise simultaneously when both the sense organ and the self are in contact with the object at once?

425.13 When [the cognition] has arisen, is the cause the contact between the sense organ and the object, or the contact between the self and the object, or the contact between the self, the sense organ, and the object? This is a failure to specify the cause. Furthermore, since no cause for its destruction is perceived, it follows that it must be eternal if it were to persist.
425.16 [3-2-23] Furthermore, because no cause for destruction is perceived, there follows the undesirable consequence that it would persist eternally.

425.18 Even if it were a quality of the self (*ātman*), the same [consequence] applies; this is what is being joined by this [argument]: if cognition (*buddhi*) is a quality of the self, then because of the absence of a cause for its destruction, its eternity would follow. How so? 425.19 [It is asked: "How [does this follow]?"
426.01. There are two causes for the destruction of qualities: the disappearance of their substratum and the manifestation of a contradictory quality.
In that regard, [the first] is impossible because the self is eternal; furthermore, there is no contradictory quality, as that would entail the consequence of [the self] being non-eternal.
426.04 [3-2-24] Because its impermanence is perceived, the destruction of a cognition occurs through another cognition, just like sound.

426.05 Because its impermanence is perceived, the destruction of a cognition occurs through another cognition, just like sound; it has been established that cognition is impermanent. In that regard, its destruction occurs either through another cognition or through a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

426.07 Thus it should be understood. If you think that two cognitions do not exist simultaneously—that is, if you consider that two cognitions do not arise together—because the former is sublated by the latter, [we reply: that is not so, because simultaneous arising is what is being denied, not coexistence. For there is no contradiction whatsoever in two cognitions existing at the same time.
It is contradictory because one accepts the destruction of the cause by means of the effect once that effect has acquired its own nature.

And when the effect has acquired its own nature, it then destroys the cause, just like sound. Just as the effect, sound, having acquired its own nature, wipes out the causal sound, so too is the case with cognition.

Regarding the word *api*: if you think that [destruction] would not occur in the case of the final two, then consider this: if the preceding cognition and sound [are destroyed by subsequent ones], how can there be a cause for the destruction of the final cognition and sound in the absence of those subsequent ones?
Just as the final cognition and sound perish without an external cause, so it is with the others.

426.16–17: Nor can it be said that [the final sound] arises from conjunction with a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat-dravya-saṃyoga*). For by conjunction with a substance possessing touch, the final sound is obstructed. Those conjunctions of the cause with walls and the like obstruct the sound which is inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*); therefore, there is a total non-hearing of the sound.
426.19 Thus: the final cognition perishes due to the absence of a cause for its persistence, either because of time or because of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

427.01 How [is it] because of time? Since merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the causes for the persistence of the final birth, are absent, the final cognition perishes. Why, then, is it said thus, and not otherwise? 427.02 Because of the absence of those two. Why is it said thus, and not otherwise? [Because]...

427.03 It is not accepted that destruction is causeless, because of the faults already stated. Regarding causeless destruction, the fault has been stated by those who refute momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). If [it is argued] that because causes are not simultaneous, cognitions arise non-simultaneously, then where there is simultaneity of causes—
In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous production, as in the case of memories. Regarding this, first, there is one rebuttal:

because a single instrument has the capacity to accomplish only a single action; for an instrument is not able to bring about multiple actions at one time, and because memories are [individually] distinct.
427.09. [The question arises: "Is there simultaneous production of cognitions, or non-simultaneous production? Others, however, seeking to establish the non-simultaneity of causes, state:
427.10–11. "Because memory arises from the contact of the mind with a specific region of the self (*ātman*) in which cognition is inherent, there is no simultaneous production. Thus he says.
[3-2-25] Because memory arises from the contact of the mind with a portion of the self conjoined with cognition, there is no simultaneous production [of cognitions].
To demonstrate that this [objection] is not correct, he says: "Not [because it] functions within the body..."
Because of the nature of the mind.
427.16 [3-2-26] Not so, because the mind functions within the body.

427.17 What is the meaning of "functioning" (*vṛtti*) when it is said that the mind functions within the body? It cannot mean "being supported," for the mind is not supported by anything; nor does it mean "activity," for its own activity— 427.18 —is not [the same as its functioning].

427.19–20. Its capacity [is established] because it is observed to have external effects; the eye, presided over by the mind, goes forth and grasps color-form (*rūpa*) and so on. Since there is no other possible explanation for the activity of the two eyes—which are themselves prone to dispersal—given that [the activity] occurs only when the mind is present, it follows that the mind does not function within the body. In this regard:
We reply: the function (*vṛtti*) of the mind is neither the relationship of support and supported (*āśraya-āśrita-bhāva*), nor is it the attainment of an effect (*kārya-pratilambha*).

However, since there is no effect for a mind that is bodiless, this is the meaning of the mind's "function. For a mind that is not embodied does not perform any purposeful action for the person (*puruṣa*). [Your argument] is not a valid reason (*ahetu*), because it is yet to be proven (*sādhya*).

428.05 [3-2-27] "It is not a valid reason because it is itself yet to be proven. 428.06 "The claim that 'the mind, being bodiless, is incapable of accomplishing the purpose of the person' is itself something to be proven; therefore, for one who remembers this, there can be no refutation on the grounds that the maintenance of the body is possible. 428.07–08. No negation [of the mind's capacity] is established.
428.08 [3-2-28] There is no refutation [of the soul's existence] because the maintenance of the body is possible for one who remembers;
428.09 it is observed that remembering and the maintenance of the body occur simultaneously, and this is observed by everyone;
428.10 furthermore, when the mind has been projected outward for a long time, the maintenance of the body by one who remembers cannot [otherwise be accounted for].
It might be so; yet it is not, because of the mind's rapid movement.

[3-2-29] It is not so, because of the mind’s rapid movement. Both [memory and retention] are established; it is not [the case that memory alone is established], because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of memory.
[3-2-30] Not so, because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of memory.

428.15 The time of recollection is not fixed; therefore, this [position] is untenable. 428.16 Furthermore, for one who asserts that the conjunction of the self and the mind—without depending on the conjunction with the body—is the cause of recollection, the status of the body as the locus of experience would cease to exist. 428.17 Consequently, upon the cessation of that [status], the production of a body would be rendered purposeless.
428.18 [3-2-31] Nor is there a specific conjunction [of the soul with the mind] due to self-impulsion, chance, or knowledge.
429.01 Others, however, state the following rebuttal: "Nor is there a specific conjunction due to self-impulsion, chance, or knowledge. 429.02 Thus they offer their refutation.
[3-2-32] It is the same as the case of a person whose mind is distracted [from a foot], who experiences a foot injury through a specific type of contact.
[3-2-33] Because cognitions of objects such as an intention (*praṇidhāna*) or a sign (*liṅga*) do not occur simultaneously, there is no simultaneous recollection.
[3-2-34] However, just like intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*), if recollection were independent of intention and so forth, it would follow that multiple recollections occur simultaneously.
This is equivalent to the case of a person whose mind is distracted [by something else] and who suffers a pain in the foot due to a particular contact.

Thus, it is not a valid refutation. It is not tenable to say that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) acts as a regulator for the sake of experience, because [the same logic would apply] equally. Therefore, the previous refutation alone stands: [it is not so] because [the mind] functions within the body.

429.11 Regarding the phrase "of the mind": if it is argued that [simultaneous cognitions do not arise] because of the non-simultaneity of the contact between the self and the cognition-inherent [in the self], 429.12 the following rebuttal is reached: the simultaneous arising of memories would follow, since their cause is simultaneous.
429.13 This is not so, because the auxiliary causes do not exist simultaneously.

429.14 Since that which is the auxiliary cause for the conjunction of the self and the mind— such as volition (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth— does not exist simultaneously, there is no simultaneous arising of memories. If the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on volition and so forth, is not the cause of simultaneous memory, then those memories [arise] when volition and so forth are present.
429.17 There could be simultaneity among them in the interval [between cognitions], but this is not so because it is not admitted.

For there is no recollection independent of the mental application (*praṇidhāna*) and other factors, since for one who exists, recollection arises from a cause of memory, namely, a prior experience. 429.19 If you say, "This [recollection] has the same nature as intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*)," then let it be intuitive; in that case, it would occur simultaneously.
430.01. It is not tenable; for it has not been stated that its cause is absent, since this has already been answered.
430.02. This has already been answered: for a cause does not possess the capacity to bring about multiple effects. 430.03.
And if intuitive cognition (*prātibha*) were manifold knowledge, would it arise with respect to a single object or with respect to multiple objects? First of all, it is not [the former].

430.04 [Cognition occurs] in one [body] because [in many] it would be redundant; nor does it occur in many [bodies] because of the absence of capacity. Nor is there this restriction—that cognitions do not occur simultaneously—because for a knower whose nature is subject to modification, cognitions do occur simultaneously when there is a plurality of bodies. And if [it is argued that cognition arises] from contact with a portion of the self inherent in knowledge...

430.07–08. There is no simultaneous arising of memories; for those mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) which reside in specific locations within the body, [if they were to arise simultaneously], there would be a simultaneous recollection of multiple objects in a single location due to the co-inherence (*samavāya*) of multiple cognitions in one part of the body. But this is not the case; therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal. The mental impressions belong to the body as it remains in its state.

It is incorrect to say that [mental states] occupy the same location, because the locations of the self are not distinct substances. This being the case, if all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) occupied the same location, the unavoidable consequence would be the simultaneity of cognitions. If it is argued that there is no simultaneity of memory due to the proximity of the mental formations (*saṃskāra*), what constitutes this proximity? It is none other than [the proximity of] the substratum (*āśraya*). However, since the self is a single entity, how can there be a distinction between proximity and non-proximity? Furthermore, if the self were omnipresent, it would follow that it is in contact with everything; thus, all objects would be perceived simultaneously. Moreover, since the self is eternal, it would always be in contact with its objects, and therefore the simultaneous perception of all objects would be unavoidable. Consequently, the self is not omnipresent. Nor is it unitary. Since it is established that the self is neither omnipresent nor unitary, it follows that it is not a substance. Therefore, the self does not exist. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for an agent," this is not so. For the activity of an agent is merely the arising of a specific transformation (*vikāra-viśeṣa*) in the continuum of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*). Thus, the agent is nothing other than the aggregates themselves. Furthermore, if the self were a substance, it would have to be either permanent or impermanent. If it were permanent, it would be incapable of performing actions, just like space. If it were impermanent, it would be a mere collection of momentary entities, and thus could not be an agent. Therefore, the self is not a substance. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for an experiencer," this is also not so. For the experience of pleasure and pain arises from the conjunction of the sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness; there is no separate experiencer. Furthermore, if the self were the experiencer, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of experiencing anything. Therefore, the self is not the experiencer. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a knower," this is also not so. For the act of knowing is simply the arising of cognition; there is no separate knower. Furthermore, if the self were the knower, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of knowing anything. Therefore, the self is not the knower. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a mover," this is also not so. For movement is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate mover. Furthermore, if the self were the mover, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of moving. Therefore, the self is not the mover. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a controller," this is also not so. For control is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate controller. Furthermore, if the self were the controller, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of exercising control. Therefore, the self is not the controller. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a thinker," this is also not so. For thinking is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate thinker. Furthermore, if the self were the thinker, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of thinking. Therefore, the self is not the thinker. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a rememberer," this is also not so. For remembering is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate rememberer. Furthermore, if the self were the rememberer, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of remembering. Therefore, the self is not the rememberer. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a doer," this is also not so. For doing is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate doer. Furthermore, if the self were the doer, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of acting. Therefore, the self is not the doer. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a perceiver," this is also not so. For perception is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate perceiver. Furthermore, if the self were the perceiver, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of perceiving. Therefore, the self is not the perceiver. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a speaker," this is also not so. For speaking is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate speaker. Furthermore, if the self were the speaker, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of speaking. Therefore, the self is not the speaker. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a hearer," this is also not so. For hearing is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate hearer. Furthermore, if the self were the hearer, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of hearing. Therefore, the self is not the hearer. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for an enjoyer," this is also not so. For enjoyment is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate enjoyer. Furthermore, if the self were the enjoyer, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of enjoying. Therefore, the self is not the enjoyer. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a sufferer," this is also not so. For suffering is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate sufferer. Furthermore, if the self were the sufferer, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of suffering. Therefore, the self is not the sufferer. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a seer," this is also not so. For seeing is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate seer. Furthermore, if the self were the seer, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of seeing. Therefore, the self is not the seer. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for an agent of action," this is also not so. For the agency of action is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate agent of action. Furthermore, if the self were the agent of action, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of acting. Therefore, the self is not the agent of action. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a knower of the truth," this is also not so. For the knowledge of the truth is merely the arising of a specific transformation in the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate knower of the truth. Furthermore, if the self were the knower of the truth, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of knowing the truth. Therefore, the self is not the knower of the truth. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a liberator," this is also not so. For liberation is merely the cessation of the continuum of the aggregates; there is no separate liberator. Furthermore, if the self were the liberator, it would be subject to change, and thus it would be impermanent. If it were not subject to change, it would be incapable of being liberated. Therefore, the self is not the liberator. As for the claim that "the self exists because there is a need for a means of liberation," this is also not so. For the means of liberation is merely the path consisting of morality, concentration, and wisdom; there is no separate means of liberation. Furthermore, if the self

430.13 For there exists a state of proximity and distance among the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*s), because they occupy the same location. We do not say that proximity is mere spatial closeness; rather, for a latent impression, proximity is the convergence of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), just as it is with sound—for example, all sounds exist within a continuum (*saṃtāna*).

430.16 Just as in the case of space, even though they occupy the same location, that for which there are causes of perception is perceived, while others are not; so it is also with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). 430.17–18 Regarding the view held by some that "the knowledge belongs to the Person (*puruṣa*) and the desire, etc., belong to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*"), that is refuted [on the grounds] that desire and aversion have the wise one as their cause.
Because of the commencement and cessation [of activity].
430.20 [3-2-34(35)] Because the commencement and cessation [of action] have desire and aversion as their cause, [desire and aversion belong to the knower].

431.01 The meaning of the sūtra is that desire and the rest belong only to the knower (*jñātṛ*). If desire and the rest belonged to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), 431.02 they would not be perceptible; for desire and the rest, when residing in one thing, cannot be perceived by another.

[The qualities] ought to exist [in the self]. Furthermore, desire and the other qualities would never be imperceptible if they were attributes of the mind, because the mind is beyond the senses. Moreover, since the commencement and cessation [of activity] are observed in one's own self, there is an inference [of their existence] in another [self].
431.06 [3-2-35(36)] Because desire and aversion have that as their mark, there is no denial of them in earth and the other elements.
431.07 Because desire and aversion have that as their mark, there is no denial of them in earth and the other elements; [this is known] through activity and cessation.
431.08 "Because of their co-inherence, there is no over-extension to the body and so forth"—this is the meaning of the sūtra.
431.09 [3-2-36(37)] Because we observe the commencement and cessation of activity in relation to axes and the like,
431.10 the meaning of the sentence is not inconclusive (anekānta) due to the observation of the commencement and cessation of activity in axes and the like.
431.11 [3-2-37(38)] Restriction and non-restriction, however, are its qualifiers.

431.12 Restriction and non-restriction are its qualifiers. The state of having as their object past entities that are being employed is the restriction regarding engagement and withdrawal; regarding those past entities that are employed, there is engagement and withdrawal.

431.14 [Objection: "They do not belong to all of them. 431.15 [Reply: If, moreover, the activity and cessation of beings were to occur because of their being-knowingness (*jñatva*), they would occur in mere beings (*bhūta-mātra*)—just as [gravity and other properties occur] in those beings which possess gravity and so forth. 431.16 Furthermore, a rule is observed such that those beings fall due to their own quality; therefore, it is not [the case that activity and cessation are caused by being-knowingness].
431.17–18: "The elements are sentient" implies that within a single body there would be a plurality of knowers, which is without logical proof.

431.18–19: For one who holds that the elements are sentient, since there are many elements in a single body, there would be many sentient beings. If it is argued, "Let there be many sentient beings; what harm does that do us?"—no.
431.20 There would be an inference based on the establishment of cognitions if there were multiplicity; however, we observe a lack of such establishment.

432.01 Because cognitions are linked together, every cognition being so linked is seen to occur within a single aggregate of cause and effect. 432.02 Furthermore, because it is described otherwise, [it follows that] there is the attainment of the beneficial and the harmful.
432.03. [The opponent says: "Motion (*parispanda*) has the purpose of avoidance; for you, however, activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) are merely action (*kriyā*).

432.04. [The author replies: "And by relying on the cessation of action, because they are the marks (*liṅga*) of that [cessation], there is no prohibition [of desire and aversion] in earth and the other elements.
432.05. Thus it has been stated: "In whatever manner activity and cessation are employed, they have as their substratum (*ādhāra*) the elements being acted upon."
"Since [the qualities] exist in that which has become thus, merely as an entity," this is a common refutation regarding the elements, the sense organs, and the mind;
the mind, however, is mentioned merely by way of illustration.
432.08 [3-2-38(39)] Because of the aforementioned reasons, because of dependence, and because of the arrival of what was not done, it is not [the case] of the mind.
432.09–432.10 Because of the aforementioned reasons, because of dependence, and because of the arrival of what was not done, it is not [the case] of the mind. As stated—
432.11 "Because of being a cause" refers to such reasons as "because the same object is apprehended through both seeing and touching.
432.12 [This is] because there is no refutation [of these]. "Because of dependence" means that the body, the senses, and the mind are dependent;
432.13 they function in the activities of supporting, propelling, and expanding by virtue of effort, whereas in the case of consciousness, they are independent.

[If the body and so forth were] insentient, there would be the fallacy of the arrival of the unperformed and the destruction of the performed, because the action performed by a person would be experienced by those [insentient things], due to the consequence of the arrival of what was not done and the loss of what was done.
However, if they are sentient, there is the experience of the fruit of one's own performed karma as the means for achieving that [result]. This is the summary of the established conclusion.
432.17 By way of elimination and because the aforementioned reasons are established.
432.18 [3-2-39(40)] By the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), because the aforementioned reasons are established;
432.19 [3-2-40(41)] memory, however, belongs to the self (*ātman*) because of its nature as a knower.
432.20 Knowledge is a quality (*guṇa*) of the self; this is the subject under discussion, because the aforementioned reasons are established.

433.01 Because there is no refutation of the reasons that establish the self (*ātman*); [it is established] by elimination (*pariśeṣāt*). Since the body, the sense faculties, and the mind have been refuted, and since nothing else remains possible, and because the self is what remains, its quality is knowledge (*jñāna*). Or, "by way of logical proof" (*upapattyā*) is used independently.
433.04: "The reason for the eternity of the self is for the sake of what? [It is] for the sake of the possibility of both saṃsāra and apavarga;
thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya. It was said that because the causes of memory do not occur simultaneously, there is no simultaneous recollection.
Now, [the question arises]: from what does memory arise? This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the causes of memory do not occur simultaneously.
433.07 The Sūtra on the Vow and so forth.
433.08 [3-2-41(42)] From the causes of: resolve, connection, repetition, characteristic mark, similarity, acceptance, substratum,
433.09 that which is supported, relation, immediate succession, separation, common effect, opposition, excellence, attainment, 433.10 intervention,
pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, fear, seeking, action, passion, merit, and demerit.
Thus it is established that cognition is impermanent.

433.13 Regarding the impermanent nature of cognition (*buddhi*), there arises a doubt because it both perishes upon arising and persists for a period of time. Is cognition that perishes upon arising like a sound, or does it persist for a period of time like a jar? It is logical that it perishes upon arising; what, then, is the meaning of this?

433.16 “Perishing immediately upon arising” means that it perishes more rapidly than other perishable things; however, this does not mean that it is destroyed immediately after its production. What, then, is the logic here? [The argument is:

cognition perishes more rapidly [than others] because, while possessing the quality of being born (*jātimattve*), it is perceptible to persons such as ourselves, and [because] substance is pervasive— 433.18 [and thus cannot be the cause of such rapid destruction].
Because it manifests each object individually while functioning as an instrument for the production of something new at every moment— just like sound—

it is observed that whatever functions as an instrument for manifesting objects produced anew at every moment is extremely perishable, such as a lamp which [manifests] objects produced anew at every moment.

The intellect (*buddhi*) manifests perishable objects according to their respective determination; therefore, this [intellect] also perishes very rapidly. Alternatively, the intellect is something that perishes very rapidly because, while being a quality (*guṇa*), it is not perceptible by the external senses, just like pleasure (*sukha*). For the purpose of making this point known, [the author states] "action" (*karma*).
"Because of the apprehension of that which is non-abiding," so says the Sūtra.
434.07 [3-2-42(43)] Because of the apprehension of non-abiding karma.
434.08 If, then, the cognition is not stable with respect to non-abiding objects,
then when a jar or the like is perceived as being established in cognition, at that time, does it abide for a period of time just like the jar?
"Or is it that [the cognition] perishes instantly? Even when [an object] such as a jar is perceived as persisting, there is the cessation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
When one perceives a persisting jar or the like, even then, cognitions cease only by way of a continuum (*santāna*).
Why? Because direct perception ceases with respect to what is obstructed; if time were like a jar...
If cognition were to persist for an interval of time, it would remain as a direct perception even with respect to an object that has been obstructed.

However, it does not so persist; therefore, it does not abide for another duration of time. [Objection: If it is argued that [cognition] persists because of memory—if cognition were perishable, memory would not exist—for indeed, memory is not [of something other than cognition].

434.16–17: "We observe memory even in the case of difference, as in the cognitions of different persons; and yet memory exists [in a single person]. Therefore, cognition persists. This is not so, because of this very lack of persistence; for memory is not possible while cognition remains present. Memory, by definition, occurs when a perceptual cognition has ceased, being preceded by that [perception].

434.19–434.21: The reconnection with an object, such as "I saw this," is not tenable while a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa-buddhi*) remains present. Furthermore, since that [reconnection] occurs from another cause, memory (*smṛti*) is not a logical mark (*aliṅga*). This memory which is admitted as a mark for the persistence [of the self] in cognition is not a valid mark, because it persists due to its existence from another source.

435.01. [The opponent says: "The mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is born from cognition (*buddhi*); therefore, memory arises depending on causes such as focused attention (*praṇidhāna*). 435.02. [The proponent replies: "If you think that memory arises from the mental formation and not from cognition, [we ask: what is the reason for its persistence? If memory itself persists, then cognition would be memory. 435.03. [The opponent says: "There is an absence of a cause. 435.03. [The proponent asks: "What is the reason for this? If memory alone persists, then cognition is not [distinct from] memory.
It may be so.
435.05 [3-2-43(44)] Because it is non-persistent, the perception of form during a flash of lightning is like the perception of something indistinct.
435.07 [3-2-44(45)] By the employment of a reason, there is the admission of that which was to be negated.
435.08. The perception of the unmanifest occurs because of its non-abiding nature, like the perception of form when lightning flashes.
435.09. If cognition is non-abiding, it follows that there would be a perception of the unmanifest, just as there is a perception of the unmanifest [forms] illuminated by lightning.
435.10. This is not so, because of the contradiction; since there is a perception of the unmanifest, cognition must be abiding.

435.11 By saying "cognition," you [implicitly] admit that which is to be negated—that cognition is non-abiding (momentary). 435.12 And because you admit that, what was stated—that cognition abides for a period of time—is refuted; furthermore, it is not [the case that there is no perception of the unmanifest], because the apprehension of the unmanifest has another cause.

435.14 The non-abiding of the intellect (*buddhi*) is established because of the apprehension of the unmanifest (*avyakta*). That which is manifest and that which is unmanifest—there is no such thing as an "apprehension" [of these].
435.15 Rather, it is because of the difference in the causes of apprehension, due to both the abiding and non-abiding of the intellect; and because that [unmanifest] is impossible.
435.16 There is no such thing as an "apprehension" called "unmanifest. Why? Because the intellect consists merely in the apprehension of an object (*artha*), and [the unmanifest] is not an object.
Cognition is merely the grasping [of an object]. And that grasping of the object occurs both generally and specifically.

That which has the universal as its object is manifest with respect to the universal; likewise, that which has the particular as its object is manifest with respect to the particular, and that which has the possessor of the attribute (*tadvat*) as its object is manifest with respect to the possessor of the attribute. Thus, how can this unmanifest grasping be taught in relation to a single [object]?
If it is argued that there would be a contradiction with common experience (*loka-virodha*) because cognition would not be established regarding its object, then [we reply]:

in that case, the apprehension of the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) would not occur; for how could this worldly convention—"I see something manifest in these few things"—be possible otherwise? This is not [a matter of] the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*).

436.03–05. Furthermore, the distinction between the apprehension of the manifest and the unmanifest occurs in relation to things possessing those qualities; rather, it is the apprehension of the unmanifest that arises through the desire to perceive the specific details of a subject (dharmin) already known in a general way. Moreover, because this is not invariably so, it is not a universal rule that there is an apprehension of the unmanifest whenever there is a failure of the cause for apprehending the object or a lack of stability in the object to be grasped.
436.06 [3-2-45(46)] Its apprehension is not like the apprehension of a lamp-flame made manifest by its continuity; for even though it is non-enduring,
just as in the case of lamp-flames existing in a continuous series, there is no instability in the object of apprehension.
And there is no stability in the perception; rather, the perception is clearly manifest, just as in the case of a flame.
As it is with flames, so it is elsewhere; thus it is established that cognition is momentary. [Regarding] the quality of the body:
consciousness exists when the body exists and is absent when it is absent. And whatever [exists] when something else exists...
436.13 It is understood that "this belongs to that" when [the latter] exists and does not exist when it is absent, as in the case of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
436.14 Thus, consciousness (*cetanā*) is not established as a quality of the body merely because it exists when the body exists.

436.15 For we observe that something may exist when another thing exists even though it is a quality of something else. This is not the case for conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), or the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

436.16 Furthermore, the qualities of action (karma-guṇāḥ) are such that when action exists, they exist, and when it does not, they do not. 436.17 And although sound exists when conjunction, disjunction, and [other] sounds exist, it is nevertheless not their quality (guṇa).
436.18 Moreover, its status as a quality is established there through perception, provided that what is present therein is perceived, just like color (rūpa).

436.19 [The opponent says: "That [consciousness] is its quality. Now, if one were to claim that consciousness is perceived in the body on the grounds that it exists when the body exists, that too suffers from the fault of being unproven (*asiddha*), for consciousness is not perceived in the body.
437.01 Rather, only consciousness itself is perceived; and that is doubtful, as to whether it belongs to the body or to something else.

437.02–03. Having approached [the body], there is the perception of consciousness in the body. Is consciousness a quality of the body, or is it a quality of some other substance? Since there is doubt regarding a substance due to the perception of its own qualities and the qualities of others, the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated.
437.04 [3-2-46(47)] There is doubt regarding a substance because of the perception of its own qualities and the qualities of others.
437.05 Consciousness is not a quality of the body, because it persists as long as the substance exists, like color and other such qualities; this is the illustrative example.
437.06 Sūtra.
437.07 [3-2-47(48)] Because color and the other qualities persist as long as the substance exists (yāvad-dravya-bhāvitva).

437.08 By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): those which are qualities of the body persist as long as the body exists, such as color and the rest; however, consciousness does not persist as long as the body exists, therefore it is not its quality.
437.10 Or, by way of analogy, it is not a quality of that [body], just as heat is not a quality of water.

437.11 If you think: "Just as the *saṃskāra* (formative impression) is a quality of the body but does not persist for as long as the body exists, so too is consciousness," [we reply: no, because the cause of the *saṃskāra* is not cut off; it is not [a quality] of the body.

437.13–15: [The opponent argues: "Only that [material cause] is the cause; for when causes such as impulsion (*nodana*) are present, [the effect] occurs, and when they are absent, it does not—this is logical. But this is illogical for that which possesses a cause in the form of a conscious agent (*cetanā*), because even that [conscious agent] would be absent.
If you think thus—that just as the cause of the *saṃskāra* is absent, so too [is the conscious agent]—then...

437.16–17: It is also incorrect to claim that consciousness (*cetanā*) is the cause [of the body], because such a conceptualization is untenable. Regarding that which is the cause for the arising of consciousness in the body: does it reside in the body or in some other substance?
Even if it resides in the body, does it persist as long as the body exists, or is it adventitious (*naimittika*)? If it persists as long as the body...

437.19–20: A body devoid of consciousness would never be perceived, because the cause [of consciousness] is always present. Now, if it is argued that the cause for the production of consciousness in the body is a specific efficient cause (nimitta) residing in another substance, 438.01: then in that case too, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that [that other substance] must itself possess consciousness. Or, if it is claimed that the efficient cause resides in one substance while operating upon another substance...

438.02 Regarding the claim that [consciousness] produces sentience in the body but not in other substances, a restrictive cause must also be stated here. 438.03 Furthermore, [if it were inherent], would that which resides in another substance be permanent or impermanent? Even if it were impermanent, would it persist for a period of time or perish in a single moment? In either case, the same undesirable consequence as for consciousness itself would follow. And if one should think [it is like] the dark color...

438.05 Furthermore, a substance possesses its initial quality, yet blackness does not persist as long as the substance exists; and that is not so because of the arising of another quality produced by heating (pākaja). 438.06 [End of section].
438.07 [3-2-48(49)] Not so, because of the production of another quality born of cooking (pākaja).
438.08 It is not that there is an absolute cessation of blackness followed by the production of another color; however, the cessation of consciousness (cetanā) is absolute.
438.09 Thus, for this reason as well—as the establishment of the opposite case—the denial of qualities produced by cooking is not valid.
438.10 [3-2-49(50)] There is no prohibition regarding the qualities produced by transformation (*pākaja*) on the grounds that their opposites are established.
438.11 In as many substances as there is the negation of the prior quality, in those same [substances] there is the perception of another, opposing quality.
438.12 As is seen, for example, when blackness ceases, redness and so forth [appear]; however, this is not the case with the body.
438.13–14: If it is argued that another quality contrary to consciousness is perceived, yet the absolute cessation of consciousness alone [is what is meant], then [we reply]:

438.14–15: Now, if you think that even in the body there is a distinct quality called "unconsciousness," that is not so, because it cannot be defined in its own nature. As for this thing called "unconsciousness," is it a real entity existing as a property that is the opposite of consciousness?
438.16 Or, if it is merely the negation of consciousness, then that which is perceived would be the opposite of possessing consciousness.
438.17 If it were merely the negation of consciousness, then it would not be a quality.
438.18 [3-2-50(51)] Because of its pervading the body.
438.19 For this reason as well, consciousness is not a quality of the body, because it pervades the body, just like the body itself.
439.01 The parts of the body are pervaded by the arising of consciousness. What is the meaning of "pervasion"? It is that there is no part of the body [that is not so pervaded].

439.02 [The opponent argues: "If it were devoid of consciousness (*cetanā*), then because everything has consciousness as its cause, the limbs of the body would, like the body itself, possess consciousness. [The proponent replies: "Let the limbs of the body possess consciousness; however, this does not entail a confusion of the conditions [for perception].
For if the limbs of the body possessed consciousness like the body itself, there would be a confusion of the conditions for perception."
439.05. "The members of the body are not sentient, because they are not perceived [as such] in hair, nails, and so forth"—this is the aphorism of the illustrative example.
439.06 [3-2-51(52)] It is not [the case that the self is non-existent] because of its non-perception in the hair, nails, and so forth.
439.07 [3-2-52(53)] Since the body extends only as far as the skin, there is no application [of the definition of the body] to the hair, nails, and so forth.
Because the body extends only as far as the skin, there is no application [of the definition] to the hair, nails, and so forth; the hair is a substance that is conjoined [with the body].

"Starting with the nails," [it is argued], "but not the limbs of the body; therefore, this undesirable consequence does not apply. Furthermore: "Consciousness is not a quality of the body, because it possesses characteristics different from the qualities of the body."
439.11 [3-2-53(54)] Because of its dissimilarity to the qualities of the body:

439.12 Qualities of the body exist in two ways; those such as color (rūpa) and so forth are perceptible by external sense organs, whereas heaviness is supersensible (atīndriya). However, consciousness (cetanā) is a different category altogether, for it is not perceptible by external sense organs due to its being directly self-evident (susaṃvedyatva).
439.14 They are not supersensible because they are objects of the mind; therefore, they are not qualities of the body, unlike color and so forth, because of their mutual dissimilarity.
439.16 [3-2-54(55)] It is not so, because of the mutual heterogeneity of color and the other qualities.
439.17 Just as color and the others, though mutually heterogeneous, do not transcend the status of being qualities of the body, so too,
439.18 even when there is a heterogeneity from color and the others, consciousness will not lose its status as a quality of the body.
439.19 [3-2-55(56)] There is no refutation of form and the rest because they are perceptible by the senses.
439.20 Form and the rest are perceptible by the senses; therefore, there is no refutation [of their existence]. There are two kinds of qualities belonging to the body.
Thus the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated. The mutual dissimilarity of form and the rest, as well as their non-conjunction and non-exclusion, [are established].

440.02 And thus, this is merely a case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-mātra*); however, it does not constitute a proof through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*) that consciousness is a quality of the body.

Therefore, this is unequal [to our position]. As for the reasons obtained by this method, their formal application (*prayoga*) is as follows: consciousness is not a quality of the body, because no other cause is observed and no contrary quality is seen.

440.05 And [if it were argued that consciousness exists] because it persists as long as the substance [of the body] exists, like heat in water, [we reply: no, because [consciousness] pervades the entire body.
440.06 However, this is not a proof; rather, for one who asserts that consciousness resides in the body, there follows the fault of the consequence that there would be multiple conscious entities.
440.07 Consciousness is not a quality of the body, because it is not perceptible by the external senses, like pleasure and so forth. Now, this...

440.08–09: Why should this treatise, whose subject matter has already been determined, be undertaken again? Even when reality is examined in many ways, it becomes even more firmly ascertained; therefore, it is commenced. Thus, the intellect has been examined.
440.10 The mind, having reached the point of examination, is now scrutinized: is it one or many with respect to each body?
440.11 Upon investigation, because cognitions do not occur simultaneously, the mind is one.
440.12 [3-2-56(57)] Because cognitions do not occur simultaneously, the mind is one.
440.13 That cognitions do not arise simultaneously is a matter of direct perception, and this establishes the oneness of the mind.
440.14 How so? If there were many minds, there would be a connection of the mind with each sense organ individually.

440.15 Thus, when multiple objects are present simultaneously, there would have to be multiple cognitions at once; however, the fact that cognitions do not arise simultaneously with respect to objects perceivable by the senses is not a proof for the singularity of the mind (manas). 440.16 For it arises from another cause; otherwise, it has already been stated that [the non-simultaneity] occurs because of its being an instrument (karaṇatva).

440.18 [3-2-57(58)] "Because multiple actions are not perceived simultaneously" (na yugapad-aneka-kriyā-upalabdheḥ). The remainder is in the Bhāṣya. This is the sūtra concerning the subsequent door. 440.20.

441.01 [3-2-58(59)] Its perception is like the sight of a whirling firebrand, due to rapid movement. 441.02 Just as in the case of a whirling firebrand, its existing sequence is not perceived; so too, because cognitions occur with such speed, their existing [sequence] is not perceived.
No sequence is perceived, nor does simultaneous production exist as admitted by both parties,
by which we might establish the multiplicity of the mind.
441.06 [3-2-59(60)] And because of the reason already stated, the mind is atomic (aṇu).

441.07 Because of the reason already stated, that very reason which was stated for the oneness of the mind is also the reason by which the mind is to be understood as atomic. Indeed, sir, the activity of the mind occurs within the body endowed with sense organs.
441.09 When the body is being investigated, the mind itself has already been investigated; therefore, the body is investigated again.

441.10 Is this creation of the body initiated by the elements independently of karma, or rather, dependent upon it? Because of these conflicting views, there is doubt. Indeed, a conflict of opinions is heard in this regard.
In this regard, the truth is this: its arising occurs due to the connection with the fruit of what was previously done.
441.13 [3-2-60(61)] Its production is due to the connection with the fruits of previously performed actions.

441.14 That which was previously performed is the activity in a former body, characterized by the initiation of speech, intellect, and the physical body. 441.15 Its fruit consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) produced thereby; their "connection" (*anubandha*) is their continued persistence as inherent in the self (*ātman*).

Because the time of ripening is not fixed, the time of ripening is indefinite; it may occur in this life, in another life, or in the interval between them. Therefore, from those primary elements (*bhūta*) that have been set in motion by that [karma] which remains, there is the production of that body, and not from independent elements. Why, then, does karma—designated as merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*)—not produce its fruit at the very same time as its own arising?
442.01 It gives. Who says that it does not give? Because the time of ripening is indefinite.

When there is the presence of all causes without exception, and when those causes are unimpeded even in their presence, then it certainly gives. But when it does not give, then [it is because] while it is ripening—
442.04 Due to the obstruction by an excellence of karma (*karmātiśaya*), that which is undergoing maturation becomes an excellence of karma.

442.05 That which is designated as merit or demerit (*dharma-adharma*) and whose fruit has not yet been experienced—due to the obstruction caused by that, even though the fruit of karma exists, it does not yield its result. Or rather, [there are] other living beings for that karma...
442.07–08. Those [results] that would have been experienced equally [do not manifest] because they are obstructed by the ripening of other karmic latencies (*karmāśaya*).

Nor do those other living beings who were entitled to share in the fruit of that karma [manifest it], because they are obstructed by their own respective karmas. Alternatively, for that karma, the causal condition characterized as merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*) as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*) does not exist.
442.10 Thus, for this reason, there is no production of the fruit, either because of an obstruction to that [dharma] or its auxiliary conditions, or due to the actions of other beings.
442.11 Or, due to an obstruction of the auxiliary conditions, dharma and adharma do not yield their fruit at all times.
442.12 Thus, the course of karma is difficult to discern; it cannot be determined by one who possesses only human attributes.
442.13 Only the general form has been stated. But what is the reasoning here [regarding] the systems of karma?

442.14 That the elements (*bhūta*) initiate the body and do not act independently—this reasoning is now set forth: 442.15 The body is preceded by elements impelled by the specific qualities of the person (*puruṣa*), because it is an effect that performs actions for the sake of the person’s purpose.
442.16 By virtue of its capacity: that which is capable of fulfilling a human purpose is seen to be preceded by elements impelled by the specific qualities of a person.

442.17 Just as chariots and the like, being produced from elements impelled by the specific quality of a person—namely, effort—are seen to be capable of performing functions for a person, so too is the body; therefore, this [body] also [is produced] from elements that depend [on such a cause].

442.19 It is argued that [the body] is produced because it possesses pleasure and pain as its causes, like a jar and so forth; and for this reason also, because it is an effect, like a chariot and so forth; and because, while being perceivable by external organs, it possesses form and other qualities, just like a jar and so forth. 442.21 Here, the nihilist says: its material cause is derived from the primary elements (*bhūta*), just as the production of a physical form is derived from them.
443.01 [3-2-61(62)] Just as the taking up of material forms occurs from the elements, so too does that [taking up] [occur from them].

443.02 Just as material forms—such as sand, gravel, chalk, and gold—are produced from the elements independently of karma, 443.04 so too is creation; thus, the reason "because of the capacity for purposeful action" is subject to the fallacy of being inconclusive (anaikāntika).

443.05. [This is] the sūtra. On the side of the proof (sādhana), it is unestablished because it is merely an example (dṛṣṭānta). Now, the thesis (pakṣa) is: "The elements (bhūtāni), independent of action (karman), initiate a body because they possess the capacity for purposeful activity (puruṣārtha-kriyā-sāmarthya), like sand and so forth. And this is not [valid], because it is equivalent to the point to be proven (sādhyasama).

443.08 [3-2-62(63)] Not so, because it is equivalent to the point to be proved (sādhyasama). 443.09 Just as the production of the body is to be proved as being initiated by the elements independent of karma, so too the production of sand and the like is to be proved as being not caused by karma; for even in the case of sand and the like...

443.11 Creation has karma as its cause; it is for this very reason that [the doctrine] is established. Furthermore, just as the example of chariots and the like—which is accepted by both parties—is preceded by elements impelled by the specific qualities of a particular person (puruṣa), 443.12 there is no such example in the case of the position that creation is not caused by karma. Thus, this presentation is inconsistent.
443.14 It is not like the acquisition of a physical form from the elements, because the mother and father are merely the causes of its birth.
443.15 [3-2-63(64)] Not so, because the mother and father are the cause of its birth.

443.16 By the words "mother and father," the blood and semen, which constitute the seed, are understood; therein, the two karmas of the parents—which are to be experienced as the fruit of a son—and the karma of the sentient being to be experienced as dwelling in the womb, together with the mother... 443.17-18.

It brings about the production of the body within the womb; and having been produced there, it conforms to the seed. And because of this conformity to the seed, one comes to be of the same kind as those who are its parents.
443.20 [3-2-64(65)] Likewise, regarding food:

443.21 "Because food is the cause of production"—this is the subject under discussion. Furthermore, this very point of heterogeneity is stated by means of sand and so forth: that which is eaten and drunk is food; from its digestion, the substance of nutrient-fluid (*rasa*) arises.
444.02 It is brought forth; it develops within the mother’s body and is deposited within the fetal body.
444.03 Developing through the stages of the *kalala* and so forth, it attains the state of hands and other limbs by means of the primary elements (*bhūta*) which are dependent upon karma.
444.04 If, however, the primary elements were independent of karma, [the fetus] would be like food placed in a cooking pot.
It would follow that [the cause] would ripen [independently], but this is not the case; therefore, [causes] are dependent, because there is no fixed rule regarding their attainment.

444.06 [3-2-65(66)] And because there would be no restriction regarding acquisition (prāpti), the elements (bhūta) would initiate the body independently of karma; thus, every union of husband and wife would result in offspring and other such fruits. However, when the elements are dependent upon karma, this lack of restriction is not applicable.

444.09 Thus, because of its connection with all selves, there would follow the undesirable consequence that [the body] possesses a common physical form for all. 444.10 If it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of a cause for restriction— should you think that the body is connected with all selves through a conjunction produced by [prior] conjunction or by action— then in that case, there is no cause whatsoever for restriction residing in the body and so forth.

444.12 Thus, by which [reason] the body itself would belong to that self, and yet no specific distinction pertaining to the person exists, by which the body could become the instrument of experience for one particular person. 444.13 And since there is a restriction [of experience], therefore the cause of that restriction must be stated. This is the aphorism that provides the answer to this: [4.2.20].

Action is the cause for the production of conjunction, just as it is the cause for the production of the body. (3-2-66) By that very action by which the body is produced, that same [action] determines the conjunction.

444.19 But if the production of the body were caused by non-action (*akarma*), then the aforementioned defect would follow; from what, then, would its stability arise? 444.20 If you think: "If action (*karman*) is the regulator of the production of the body, then from what does the regulation of that action arise? [The answer is: It is not so, because the regulation arises from the specific conjunctions produced for each individual self (*ātman*). 445.01 For whichever self it belongs to...

445.02. "Conjunction; therefore, whatever action arises from it belongs to that [self]. From what [source] does this restriction regarding conjunction arise? 445.03. Just as the objection regarding action does not cease, so too it applies to conjunction.
445.04. It is not so, because of the mind being the cause of the restriction: whichever mind belongs to whichever self, the conjunction is with that [mind].

445.05–445.06: "That which is produced belongs to him"—this is equally applicable even to the mind (*manas*). If it is argued that [the mind] would then belong to all souls because of its connection with them, what is the restrictive factor? It is action (*karman*) alone;

that mind which is bound by the action of a particular soul belongs to that soul. If it is asked how this is so at the beginning of creation (*sargādau*), it is because we do not accept a beginning of creation.

445.08. It cannot be pointed out; it has been established in the previously cited sūtra that saṃsāra is beginningless (anādi). 445.09. [The opponent argues: "If saṃsāra had a beginning, this could be pointed out; it is not so in the case of what is beginningless."

450.04 [4-1-1] "Activity (pravṛtti) has been explained as stated. The meaning of the sūtra is that activity has been examined in accordance with how it was explained. What, then, is activity?

450.07. In that regard, activity (*pravṛtti*) is twofold: it consists of the form of the cause and the form of the effect. Because it is restricted by all-pervading time, because it inheres in the self, and because it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), it is non-eternal, as seen from [the occurrence of] death and so forth. 450.13–14: Birth has its cause in the connection with the fruits of past actions; from that, its arising occurs. Thus it is stated that [the elements] are the causes of saṃsāra and apavarga: when they exist, there is saṃsāra; when they do not exist, there is apavarga, and so forth.
"In that case, let the faults (doṣas) which immediately follow from [the theory of] activity be stated"; therefore, he says: "Likewise, the faults."

455.14 "He is separated from feelings. 456.10–12. [The claim] that "the production of things possessing color and so forth arises from what possesses color and so forth" is not a definitive rule (ekānta) because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

It is not a definitive rule that the production of things possessing color and so forth arises only from things possessing color and so forth, because we observe that jars and the like, as well as cows and the like—which possess color and so forth—are produced even from conjunction (saṃyoga), which is itself devoid of color. "Because [the qualities] are grasped by two [senses], such as touch and [sight], like a jar, or like sound; this is the point of dissimilarity (vaidharmya). This is the reality.

An entity arises from non-existence, because it manifests without having been destroyed.
457.15 Thus, some hold this view; regarding this, they state the reasoning: "Because [the effect] does not arise without having destroyed [the cause].

457.16 It is said that an effect arises only when the cause has not yet perished. For example, the sprout manifests at a time subsequent to the destruction of the seed. that which destroys must exist, for that which is non-existent cannot be a cause of destruction; and that which arises does not exist, for [if it did], it could not be destroyed.

[Therefore,] it does not destroy [itself].

458.05 [4-1-16] It is not so, because the term "agent" (kāraka) is applied to the past and the future. 458.06 Because the term "agent" is applied to the past and the future; for instance, the term "agent" is seen to function even with respect to the past, as when one laments, "The jar is broken. 458.07 The term "agent" is observed to be employed regarding that which is past, such as: "He grieves over the broken jar."
