When a jar has been broken, one says, "The jar has become shards. Even regarding a son who has not yet come into being, one says, "A son will be born," and one rejoices at the son who is about to be born;
one gives a name to the son who is about to be born, and it is common to say, "Unborn sons cause distress to their elders."
"The applications are figurative. Thus it is said that "this sprout, about to appear, destroys [the seed].

What, then, is the meaning of "destruction" (*upamarda*)? It means "immediate production" by virtue of its immediate succession, because this [sprout] appears immediately after the destruction of the seed. Regarding this, it has been stated: "Because of contradiction."

There is no destruction by that which is unborn, nor does that which is capable of destruction arise. Furthermore, regarding what is said—that terms for an agent (*kāraka*) are employed with respect to the past and the future—this is not intended to prohibit such usage; rather, it is because arising from a non-existent cause is illogical, and yet the terms for an agent apply across the three times.
The formal argument (prayoga) has been stated in the *Prāmāṇya-sāmānya-cintā*: "It is just as when one says, 'The tree stands.
Furthermore, as for what is said—that [the sprout] arises having destroyed [the seed] by virtue of its immediate succession—this is not the case;
the destruction of the seed is not the cause of the sprout, but rather, it is the prior [state] of the seed's parts whose arrangement has been disrupted.
When one configuration ceases, another configuration arises; thus, the sprout manifests from that other configuration.

Furthermore, since it is not possible for a subsequent configuration to exist while the preceding configuration has not yet perished, "immediacy" (ānantarya) is the meaning of "manifestation. In this way, the seed is rightly established as the material cause (upādāna). And of this point...
The sūtra is for the purpose of making this known.
459.05 [4-1-17] Not from those that have perished, because there is no production. (459.06) "Not from those that have perished" means: for the destruction of the seed is not the cause of the sprout;
rather, it is the parts of the seed by virtue of their abandoning their previous configuration—this is the meaning of the sūtra. (459.07)

459.08 [4-1-18] Because of the sequential instruction, there is no negation. 459.09 Because of the sequential instruction: first the destruction of the seed, afterwards the arising of the sprout—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. 459.10 If non-existence were the cause of the arising of the sprout, then everything would arise from everything.

459.11 Because non-existence (abhāva) is devoid of any specific distinction; for when a rice seed has perished, there is no persisting capacity (*anvaya-śakti*) whatsoever. 459.12 And if the effect were unconnected [to its cause], it would have to arise from all capacities whatsoever; however, what is observed is that it is connected. 459.13 Therefore, non-existence is not the cause—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Now, another says:
459.14 [4-1-19] God is the cause, because human action is seen to be fruitless.

459.15 God is the cause, because human action is seen to be fruitless; this person, though exerting effort, 459.16 does not necessarily obtain the fruit of that effort; therefore it is understood that human action is dependent on another.
459.17 Regarding "the determination of the fruit": if the person were independent [of causes], he would be capable of experiencing the fruits of his actions.
460.01 No action whatsoever would be fruitless, nor would anyone ever experience suffering. 460.02 Both of these are observed; therefore, God is the cause.

460.03 [4-1-20] Not so, because the fruit is not produced in the absence of human action. 460.04 "Not so, because the fruit is not produced in the absence of human action"— if God were the sole cause,
460.05 then the experiences of pleasure and pain would occur even without human action, and consequently, there would be the nullification of *karman*.

And there would be no liberation [from bondage], because the Lord, being of a single nature, would possess only a single form of activity. Furthermore, if the Lord brings about an effect by conforming to a diversity of causes, it follows that he does not perform that which he requires [but lacks].
For a potter does not create his own staff and other tools; likewise, if the Lord were dependent upon karma for the world, [he would not be its independent cause].
If God were the cause of the production of action, He would not be the Lord.
460.10 [4-1-21] Because it is caused by that, it is not a non-reason.
460.11 Because it is caused by that, it is not a non-reason. We do not say that Īśvara is the cause independently of karma and so forth.
460.12 Thus. Rather, Īśvara favors the karma of persons. What is the purpose of this favoring?
Whatever [karma] is of such a nature, for whom it belongs, and at what time its maturation occurs, that he assigns accordingly at that time.

Thus, for one who instead regards Īśvara as the cause while disregarding karma, there are faults such as the impossibility of liberation and so forth; however, if Īśvara is regarded as dependent [on karma], there is no fault as previously stated. The remainder is in the Bhāṣya.
By stating that [the world] is produced by Him, it follows that Īśvara is accepted as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

And whatever is the efficient cause is the supporter (*anugrāhaka*) of the other two causes—the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)—just as the shuttle and so forth are for the threads and their conjunctions. This being the case, if Īśvara...

460.19 What has been stated as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the world and the direct material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world? [It is] earth and so forth, or else the substance known as the supreme subtle atom (*paramāṇu*). However, when the acceptance of manifest causes is maintained, there is a dispute regarding the specific efficient cause; for it is in regard to the efficient cause that the system of the Lord (*īśvara*) is proposed.
461.03 Some dispute [the cause], saying it is Time; some say it is God; others say it is Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*).

Thus, regarding this disagreement concerning the specific efficient cause (*nimitta-viśeṣa-vipratipatti*), what is the logical principle (*nyāya*)? The logical principle there is that it is God (*īśvara*), for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operate therein without contradiction. If it is argued that its existence is not established:

461.06. Now, if you think that once the existence of God (*īśvara*) is established, the exclusion of other causes and the status of [God] as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) would be established, and therefore [the argument for His existence] is not improper because it is already established in reality—[we reply: no, for that is not the case, since by the very same logic by which God’s causality is established, [the existence of other causes is also established].

461.09 Therefore, it exists; for that which does not exist cannot be a cause. Furthermore, what is the logic regarding the causality of Īśvara? This logic is stated: prior to their activity, the primary matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and karma proceed when presided over by an intelligent cause (*buddhimat-kāraṇa*), because they are insentient (*acetanatva*), like an axe and other such tools.

461.12–14. The word "like" (vat) means that just as an axe or similar tool functions when presided over by an intelligent carpenter because it is insentient, so too do the primary matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and karma function while being insentient;
therefore, these too must be presided over by an intelligent cause. In this regard, first, those who hold primary matter to be the cause [argue as follows].

They describe the *puruṣārtha* (the purpose of the *puruṣa*) as the presiding factor over *pradhāna*; impelled by the *puruṣārtha*, the *pradhāna* proceeds. And the *puruṣārtha* is twofold: the perception of sound and so forth, and the vision of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. Since both of these do not exist without the activity of *pradhāna*, they [do not exist] prior to that activity.

461.18 Because of non-existence: as long as the *pradhāna* does not transform into the state of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, there is no perception of sound and the rest, nor is there perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*; thus, due to the absence of a cause, the activity of the *pradhāna* is untenable. Furthermore, that which exists attains its own nature as existent; that which is existent is not ceased.
462.01 And this being so, it is not the case that the existent *puruṣārtha* (the purpose of the Self) sets the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) in motion;

for the activity of the *pradhāna* is not for the sake of the *puruṣārtha*. Indeed, in the world, that which already belongs to someone does not require that person to strive again for its sake. Furthermore, [if the *puruṣārtha* were the cause], continuous activity would result, because the cause would be ever-present.

462.04 Thus, the purpose of the *puruṣa* (*puruṣārtha*) is the cause of activity (*pravṛtti*). Since the purpose of the *puruṣa* is eternal, activity must occur constantly. 462.05 Now, if [the *pradhāna*] does not act even though the [purpose] exists, then the purpose of the *puruṣa* is not the cause—[that is,] that in the absence of which the *pradhāna* does not act, and that in the presence of which it does.

462.07–462.09: [The opponent argues: "That cause operates because of its existence. Or, if it exists but does not operate due to an obstruction, then because the removal of that obstruction is impossible, there would be perpetual non-operation. Furthermore, since the person who is the cause of the obstruction cannot remove that object of obstruction—because one cannot abandon what possesses an existent nature—the obstructing factor remains.

Because it is eternal, there ought to be a constant non-functioning. When you describe *prakṛti* as the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, it must be explained from where that [equilibrium] ceases.
Furthermore, as long as the state of equilibrium has not ceased, it is impossible for there to be disequilibrium.
462.13 Now, since there is no fixed rule regarding the relationship between the parts and the whole (*aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva*), a discrepancy arises here as well; we shall therefore question you further:

462.14 How can that which exists in a state of equilibrium become superior or inferior, given that there is no prior accumulation? 462.15 There is no prior increase, nor is there a prior loss, [in the case] of those sounds and so forth whose own nature was previously unperceived.
The person perceives, and the intellect causes [the object] to be perceived; do these [factors] possess a produced distinction, or are they without a produced distinction?

If they are perceived while possessing a produced distinction, it is contradictory, for that which lacks an existent nature cannot be perceived. On the other hand, if they are perceived while indeed lacking a produced distinction...
Even so, the contradiction remains unresolved: [the opponent claims] that "Pradhāna impels [the world] for the sake of the Puruṣa.

To whatever extent this doctrine of Pradhāna is examined, it contradicts the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for those who hold that atoms, presided over by the karma of the Puruṣa, are the cause of the world...

Regarding those who describe [the process] as such, this is said: "Atoms proceed" implies they must exist in a state of constant activity. Alternatively, if they proceed while depending on a specific time, then time has already been explained; for atoms, being insentient, require an intelligent supervisor.
463.03 Just as [the cow and so forth] depend [on causes], time also [depends on them]; thus, its lack of sentience (*acetanatva*) is not removed there.

463.04 [End of quote. If it is argued that activity occurs even for that which is insentient, like milk and the like—for instance, just as milk and so forth act for the sake of nourishing offspring—so too atoms, though insentient, [act] for the sake of the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).

[The opponent says: "They will proceed [of their own accord]. That is not tenable, because it is equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*). Just as it is to be proven that atoms proceed independently, so too is it claimed that insentient things such as milk proceed independently.
If milk and the like were to proceed independently, they would proceed even among the dead; however, they do not.
Therefore, it is understood that [the world] proceeds as being presided over by an intelligent cause; yet this reason is not [conclusive].

Consequently, it does not proceed in such a way. Thus, for as long as anything insentient proceeds, all of it is presided over by a sentient [being]. This is another reason [for asserting] that it is presided over by an intelligent cause.

463.12 The manifest, beginning with the great elements (*mahābhūta*), becomes the cause of pleasure, pain, and so forth, because it possesses form and other qualities, like a lute and such instruments. 463.13 Virtue and non-virtue, presided over by an intelligent cause, bring about experience for the person (*puruṣa*), because they are instruments, like an axe and such tools. The self (*ātman*) alone is the presiding agent.

If it is argued that [the soul] will exist as the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of merit and demerit, such that "he to whom these two, merit and demerit, belong shall be the presiding agent," this is not tenable;
for prior to the production of the body and the sense organs, that [agency] is impossible.
As long as the aggregate of the body and the instruments has not arisen, this ignorant person does not perceive even those things that are perceptible.
463.18 To that extent, one does not perceive form and the other [sensory objects]; how then, in the absence of perception, could one perceive merit and demerit?

463.19 If the person were to act independently, he would not cause suffering; for no one desires suffering for themselves. And as for [the acts] such as the mutilation of one's limbs or the cutting off of one's head—[which one performs against oneself]—[they would not occur].
If it is argued that [the atoms] act when there is a deficiency [of merit], or that a mind intent on welfare proceeds at the time of death— if, on the other hand,
the atoms were to proceed governed solely by merit and demerit, this would not be logical;
for nothing insentient is ever observed to be independent or an autonomous governor, having accepted this as a premise.
Furthermore, the capacity for the activity of atoms belongs to merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), not to the instrument alone;

for an instrument by itself lacks the capacity to bring about action, and indeed no instrument is ever observed to produce an action independently. Rather, it is produced by merit and demerit in dependence upon the atoms.

That too is not tenable because it is unobserved; for nowhere do we ever see an action being produced by means of an instrument of action [apart from the agent]. Thus, the claim that "the self will be the agent" is stated out of ignorance.
Furthermore, the view that there is production without a cause is not tenable, because it is unobserved. It is not so.

464.11 And since there is no other possibility, atoms and actions proceed only when presided over by an intelligent cause (buddhimat-kāraṇa). [Objection: If you think that they are not causes because action does not enter into them—[Reply:
Indeed, those who are agents are possessed of action, such as potters and others; thus, action...
464.14 And since the Lord is devoid of that [activity], He is not the cause; for it is not because of the impossibility of conceptualization that the Lord is inactive.

464.15 With reference to what kind of activity is this stated? For our activity is of two kinds: that consisting of throwing upward and so forth, and that which is denoted by verbal roots (ākhyāta-śabda). If it is stated with reference to that which is denoted by verbal roots—

464.17 Then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because of the admission of independence (*svātantrya*). For independence exists eternally in the Blessed One. What, then, is independence? It is the state of not being prompted by other causal factors (*kāraka*) and the state of not prompting other causal factors. This has been stated by those describing the causal factors. Now, [regarding] throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth...
464.20 It is said with reference to this that [the cause] is "devoid of action" (*niṣkriya*); in that case, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*), for a cause is also seen to possess action.
465.01 And it is "devoid of action" in the sense that sometimes substances, having ceased their activity, initiate another substance.
465.02 When the action has ceased due to conjunction, substances that have conjunction as their instrument initiate a substance.

465.03 Thus begins the discussion of those things that are inactive (*niṣkriya*). And when many substances (*dravya*) are conjoined simultaneously, 465.04 then, from conjunctions that are excluded from having non-common effects, only a single substance is produced.
465.05 But when there is a disjunction of a single part, upon the cessation of the [original] substance, the remaining other substances produce another substance.
465.06 Thus begins the discussion of those [substances] that are inactive. However, some [substances] possess activity.

465.07 When they begin from an internal class of action, once the action in the other substance has ceased due to conjunction, 465.08 and the substance arises at the very same time as the cessation of the action, then [the process occurs] because of the initiation by a substance possessing activity.
465.09. There would be the undertaking of those who possess activity and contradiction, because activities such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth are not admitted [by you].

465.10. Thus, God is not the cause, because the conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are untenable. If God is an agent, does he act dependently (*sāpekṣaḥ*) or independently (*nirapekṣaḥ*)? And what follows from this? If he acts dependently, by what...

If he acts as a non-agent (*akartṛ*), then this same consequence applies elsewhere as well: that by which he acts would also be a non-agent. Or, if he acts without depending on anything at all, then the same consequence follows for other things too. Furthermore, if he acts entirely independently of everything, then human action would be fruitless, and there would be no liberation.
And that fault which would attach to a creation not caused by karma would also attach here;
[this is not so] because we do not admit an independent agency, and thus there is no fault such as the fruitlessness of merit and demerit,
nor is there the fault of a creation not caused by karma— [the question remains] by what he acts.

If it is argued that he is not its agent, we say no, because of non-exclusive exclusivity. Since there is no such exclusive rule that "he who acts by means of a certain instrument does not act when that instrument is absent"— just as a man perfected in many arts makes a handle and so forth when employing a tool like an axe,
but makes a staff and so forth when employing a tool like an axe— [the same applies here].
466.02 One who possesses that [material cause] produces things such as a jar; however, agency does not consist in being an agent of a successive transformation (*paryāya*).

466.03 Likewise, God (*īśvara*) also possesses merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) as his material causes for the body, pleasure, pain, and so forth, through the conjunction of the self and the mind. 466.04 Merit and demerit are the means for pure and impure intentions, and they depend upon pleasure, pain, and memory, as well as their respective means.
466.05 And with regard to the initial [intention], there is both a pure and an impure intention. When one acts, then [there is the agent].

466.06 If it is argued that he is a non-agent (*akartṛ*), and you think: "When this person brings about some perceived object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then it follows that he is a non-agent of that by which he accomplishes it," we do not say this.

466.08–466.10: [Objection: Does he perform all purposes at one time? Or rather, does he do so successively? If it is argued that there is no fault in his being an agent who acts successively, [we reply: if you think that when he acts for the first time, his production occurs without a cause—namely, if you consider that his agency regarding the body and so forth depends upon merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), and the like, then, at the very beginning...
How could he be the first creator? Since that is not admitted, this [objection] cannot be stated; for saṃsāra is beginningless.
Thus it has been established that dharma and adharma are efficacious, provided that saṃsāra is beginningless.
Furthermore, there is dependence on a creator; in this way, there is the efficacy of the dharmas and adharmas inherent in other living beings.

466.14 Now, for what purpose does this Lord act when acting? For those who are agents in the world, 466.15 they proceed toward something with a specific aim, thinking, "I shall obtain this" or "I shall abandon this.

But for the Lord, there is nothing to be discarded because he is free from suffering, nor is there anything to be acquired because he possesses mastery. [If it is argued that he acts] for the sake of sport— 466.16 [we reply: no.
466.17 Thus some say: "The Lord creates for the sake of sport. But is this not improper?

466.18 For sport, by its very nature, exists for the sake of pleasure; and for those who do not find pleasure without sport, the Blessed One would not seek pleasure, because he is free from suffering. [On the contrary,] it is for the sake of attaining happiness for those who suffer.

“They sport. Others say it is for the purpose of manifesting his majesty (*vibhūti*). “The manifold nature (*vaiśvarūpya*) of the world must be manifested,” so others think. But this too is exactly like that; for no excellence whatsoever is gained by manifesting one’s majesty, nor is anything lost by its manifestation. For what purpose [then]?
467.03. In that case, [the objection] that "it acts because it possesses that nature; thus it proceeds" is not faulty, just as the earth and other elements. 467.04.

Just as they perform actions such as supporting [things] due to their own nature (*tad-svābhāvya*), so too does the Lord proceed due to his own nature. 467.05. Thus, reality has the nature of activity; it proceeds constantly due to that very nature.

If you think that [the ultimate] proceeds, and if you consider that if reality has activity as its intrinsic nature (*pravṛtti-svābhāvaka*), then activity and cessation would not be possible— for indeed, cessation is not tenable in a reality whose intrinsic nature is activity—
then gradual arising would not be possible because reality would possess a single, uniform form; thus, this [should] now be, and this [should] not.

467.09. Now, it is not logical to say "let it not be," for we do not observe a diversity of effects arising from a cause of a single form. This is not a fault, because [the cause] is qualified by being intelligent (*buddhimat*). That it is intelligent has already been established. And being qualified by intelligence, it is dependent; nor is it...

467.12 It proceeds at all times, yet it does not produce everything simultaneously; that for which the collection of causes is present comes into being, while that for which the causes are absent does not. Furthermore, there is no simultaneous presence of causes for everything; therefore, the simultaneous production of all things is not logical. Indeed, as it proceeds...

It depends upon the time for the ripening of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), the production of other auxiliary causes, the presence there of those sentient beings who are destined to experience that [result], the non-ripening of the merit and demerit of those sentient beings who are not destined for it, and the absence of any obstruction. As for that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of Īśvara— is it eternal or non-eternal?

467.18 If [sovereignty] is impermanent, its cause must be stated; and for one whose sovereignty is impermanent, there exists a distinction of causes regarding the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth. Thus, the same applies to others as well, and it follows that there would be many Īśvaras.
468.01 Now, if there were multiplicity, what would be contradicted? [It is the fact that] two [beings] with conflicting desires cannot exist toward a single object.

468.02–04. The activity of two lords is not possible; if one surpasses the other, he who surpasses is the lord, and the other is not. Furthermore, if sovereignty were eternal, there would be the fault of the futility of *dharma*, for that [sovereignty] does not arise from *dharma*.
To this we reply: it is eternal. And the fault of the futility of *dharma* does not apply, because his *dharma* is [eternal].

468.05 [Objection: Does he not exercise sovereignty over the Lord (īśvara) in that case? [Reply: No; rather, he favors the individual mental states consisting of the accumulations of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). 468.06 And it is not to be questioned why there is no merit in the Lord, because his essential nature has not been definitively determined. 468.07 There is doubt as to whether the Lord is a substance (*dravya*) or one of the others, such as a quality (*guṇa*); [the answer is: he is a substance.

468.08 [Objection: Since it possesses the quality of intellect (*buddhi*), it must be a distinct substance (*dravya-antara*), like other substances; therefore, because it possesses intellect, it must be another self (*ātma-antara*). [Reply: It is not another self because of the difference in its qualities (*guṇa-bheda*). Just as when there is a difference in qualities, earth and the other elements are not [identical] selves, so too the Lord (*Īśvara*) is distinguished by his qualities; therefore, he also is not another self. But who, then...
468.11 This is its distinction. First, some say that dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty possess excellence (atiśaya).
468.12 "In that [state]" means that permanence is the excellence. However, we do not understand this in the same way as [the claim] regarding the possession of intelligence.
468.13 There is valid evidence for the existence of God; but there is no such evidence for the permanence of dharma and the other qualities. Nor is there any evidence for their permanence.

And it is not possible to establish [the existence of God] on the basis of invalid means of knowledge; rather, the excellence [of the argument] lies in the eternality of His intellect and the distinction of His qualities.

For in that system, intellect is eternal, and there are six general qualities beginning with number, such as the six qualities of space; thus, the Lord is like space. Now, what is the proof for this eternality of His intellect? Is it not this very [argument]?

468.17–18: "Atoms function when presided over by an intelligent cause"—this is the proof for [the existence of] intelligence. But how is it that this [intelligence] is eternal? Because of the impossibility of a restriction to specific objects; for those distinct cognitions which are restricted to specific objects arise only when the causes such as the body are present.

But this [cognition] is not restricted to each individual object, because we observe the simultaneous production of multiple effects, just as there is the simultaneous production of many distinct stationary things. And that [simultaneous production] is not possible for the Lord in the case of distinct cognitions restricted to each object,
such as the cognitions of number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction.

His qualities: Now, if one maintains that God possesses intelligence, one must also admit His connection with a body. By one who admits this, the body and so forth must necessarily be accepted as either eternal or non-eternal.
If they are non-eternal, the existence of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) must be admitted; and once that is admitted, [the system] is dependent upon them.

Because of that, the Lord would not be the Lord. Now, if you postulate that the body and so forth are eternal, even so, what has been postulated is contrary to what is observed; for one who adopts a position contrary to observation, cognition must be understood as being eternal. Or, [if you say] it is a plurality of cognitions existing in a continuum...
469.09 Even if one accepts [the existence of] an *īśvara*, it does not follow that stationary objects and the like arise simultaneously.

469.10 Now, if those cognitions (*buddhi*) exist as part of a continuum (*santāna*), even so, what is imagined contradicts what is observed. And by imagining it in this way, one must necessarily accept the eternity of cognition itself.
469.12 And this much would be the case: [the self] would be either eternal or existing as a continuum.

469.13 [But it is] not tenable. If difference arises from the difference of qualities (*guṇa*), then that which has non-different qualities would follow as being one, just like space and time. 469.14 We do not say that there is multiplicity due to the difference of qualities because of the lack of certainty; rather, we do not say it is so because of the non-difference of qualities.

469.15 “Unity” [is asserted] because, for example, jars and other such things possess non-different qualities; whereas 469.16 “multiplicity” [is asserted] because direction and time possess different qualities despite having no difference in their effects. Furthermore, 469.17 the production of the world by Īśvara is not possible without his being intelligent; and that intelligence [comprehends] all objects, past and future.
469.18 Perception has the present as its object; it is not inferential, nor is it based on scripture, for there is no inference therein.
469.19 Nor is there scripture, because consciousness is eternal; thus, the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvara*) is eternal.
470.01 Since no impression (*saṃskāra*) exists therein, and because there is an absence of impressions, there is no memory, due to the eternity of the intellect (*buddhi*).
470.02 And because there is no memory, there is no inference; because there is an absence of demerit (*adharma*), there is no suffering, and for that very reason, there is no dispassion (*vairāgya*).
470.03 Thus, because there is an absence of suffering, one does not become dispassionate; and for that very reason, there is no aversion, as suffering is absent.
470.04 However, desire exists—unafflicted and unimpeded with respect to all objects—just like cognition (*buddhi*). Now, [the opponent asks]:...

470.05. "Is this one bound or liberated? It is not bound, precisely because of the absence of suffering; it is not liberated, because of being unbound. 470.06. Thus, one who possesses bondage is liberated; yet since there is no bondage in the Blessed One, he is therefore not liberated. If it is argued that, due to the lack of connection with other selves, his status as a controller is untenable— 470.07. [then we reply: ... [it is not so].
470.08 Now, if you think that those dharmas and adharma which inhere in a different substance are directly connected with the Lord,
rather than through a succession [of intermediaries], and that it is not logical for the operation of dharma and adharma to occur when they are not presided over [by Him]—
that is not so, because an eternal connection is untenable. Some maintain that there is an eternal connection of other selves [with the Lord].
470.11–12: "They desire this, and it is not refuted here"; thus, because it is not refuted, it is accepted.
470.12–13: They, however, establish through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the unborn [Lord] is connected with pervasive entities such as space (*ākāśa*), [arguing]:
"The Lord is connected with corporeal substances, because he is related to corporeal substances, like a jar. Just as a jar and the like are related to corporeal things...
470.14 Just as [the self] is connected with ether and so forth, which are the pervaders of the relation possessed by jars and the like, so too is the Lord.
470.15 Because he is related to that which possesses form, therefore he too is connected with the all-pervading ether and so forth.
470.16 Thus, as for that connection between the self and the Lord, whether it is pervasive or non-pervasive, there is no purpose [in determining this].

470.17 This relationship between the self (ātman) and the Lord (īśvara) is indeterminable; it can only be said that it exists. 470.18 Furthermore, whether that [self] pervades the Lord or does not pervade him is not determined. Even for those who do not accept a conjunction (saṃyoga), there is a relationship because of the occurrence of the conjunction between atoms and the mind.

Those internal mental faculties (pratyātma-manas) are all connected to the Lord (īśvara); therefore, by virtue of the establishment of a connection with that connection, he presides over other selves. Just as, through the conjunction and effort of the self and the hand, action occurs in the hand;
once the action has arisen, the hand becomes connected with tongs or similar instruments, and through that connection [it performs its function].
471.02 He presides over the iron ball and so forth. If, then, this logic has been stated regarding God’s causality at the beginning of creation, it follows that God is not the cause now as well;
for even now, that same logic applies to the merit and demerit of those possessing dead bodies, which [merit and demerit] have an intelligent cause.

The same logic applies to the term "presided over" (*adhiṣṭhita*). The great elements, ending with air, proceed toward their respective functions such as supporting, because they are insentient, like an axe and so forth; this is presided over by an intelligent cause.
Likewise, taking grass and other things as the subject (*pakṣa*) on account of their being effects, [they are seen to be] perceived and touched...

It should be stated that [the reason] is "because it is an object. Thus, wherever there is a disagreement and [the subject] possesses the nature of being an effect, each such case should be established by means of this very logic or by using this example of the axe and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*). Furthermore, from scripture (*āgama*) also, it is heard that God is the cause.
471.11 This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain;
471.12 impelled by the Lord (Īśvara), it may go either to heaven or to its own destruction.
When that God is awake, then this world moves and acts;
when He sleeps, His self being at peace, then everything closes its eyes.
471.15 [4-1-22] The arising of entities occurs without a cause, as seen in the case of the sharpness of thorns and so forth.

471.17 Now another says: The arising of entities occurs without a cause, as seen in the case of the sharpness of thorns and so forth; for example, the sharpness of thorns and the like possess neither a cause nor a material substrate (*upādāna*).
In the same way, the creation of the body and so forth is also [subject to this principle]; this is the aphorism regarding the illustrative example. What, then, is the logic here?
"The specific arrangements of the body and so forth are not without a cause, because they possess a particular structure, like thorns and the like.
Thus, for those whose causes are not perceived, the cause is not apprehended through inference. Whose [is it]? It belongs to one who...

The cause is not perceived through direct perception; how then can it be understood through inference? [It is understood] from the commonality of substances possessing a cause. Indeed, those substances which possess a cause and have specific shapes—such as jars and the like—and that body which has a specific shape, as well as thorns and so forth.
"Therefore, they possess causes. And it has been said in this regard: "What has been said? [It was said] that their arising is due to the connection with the fruits of previously performed actions.
Furthermore, it is not observed that anything possessing a specific configuration—which is accepted by both parties—is without a cause. Others, however, say: [as follows].
472.07 They describe the resolution.
472.08 [4-1-23] Because that which is signless is itself the sign, it does not arise from the signless.
472.09 Since that from which an arising occurs is the sign, and because that which is signless is itself the sign, 472.10 arising does not occur from the signless; and this is not the sign.
472.11 There is no refutation [of the argument] because the two "signless" states are distinct entities.
472.12 [4-1-24] There is no negation because the cause and the non-cause are different things.
472.13 The cause is one thing and the negation of the cause is another; thus, it is not a negation at all.
472.14 That which is to be negated is the cause; therefore, "non-cause" is an admission of the object.

The refutation of that [position] is as follows: it is illogical for both affirmation and negation to be identical. Indeed, this doctrine—that the creation of beings is without a cause—is not distinct from the [previously discussed] view that "the birth of thorns and such things is without a cause. Since there is no difference between them, it should be understood that by the very refutation of that [latter view], the present one is also refuted.

One who asserts this must be questioned: Is the birth of thorns alone causeless, or is that of everything [causeless]? If it is the case that the birth of thorns alone is causeless, then it can be established by the remaining examples that [all things] possess a cause. On the other hand, if this position is held that everything is causeless, even so, there is a contradiction.

473.02–03. Because you accept the principle of the communicator and the communicated (*pratipādya-pratipādaka-nyāya*), yet you maintain that everything is without a cause (*animitta*), there is a contradiction (*vyāghāta*). Furthermore, there is a contradiction because of the employment of this very sentence: "The arising of entities occurs without a cause, like the sharpness of thorns and so forth. This sentence is employed as a communicator, yet it asserts that there is no cause.

473.05 There is a contradiction in saying "it exists. If you understand there to be a difference in meaning between the two statements—"the arising of an entity is without cause" and "the arising of an entity is with cause"—then because of this difference in sentences, the understanding of a difference in meaning results in a contradiction regarding the claim that "the arising of an entity is without cause. Now, if...

473.08–473.10. You do not understand the difference in meaning through a difference in sentences; thus, your employment of specific sentences is contradicted by one who maintains that whatever sentence is adopted [proves] the causeless arising of entities. By asserting that the arising of entities is causeless, all worldly convention is cut off.

By taking "mere existence" as the subject (pakṣa), the example [of a pot] is established. Alternatively, if you take a single part of the body and so forth as the subject, even then the example lacks the property of one of the two [reasons]: because while "possessing a specific configuration" exists [in the example], "being without a cause" is absent. Others, however, think that everything...
473.14 It is impermanent because its nature is subject to arising and destruction.
473.15 [4-1-25] Everything is impermanent because it possesses the nature of arising and perishing.
473.16 What is called "impermanent"? That whose existence occurs at some time is impermanent; it possesses the nature of arising.
473.17 That which has not arisen does not exist, and that which possesses the nature of perishing, having perished, no longer exists. What, then, is "everything"?

473.18–20: It is understood that both the material, such as the body and so forth, and the non-material, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, possess the properties of arising and perishing. Therefore, because the Sūtra [statement] "all is impermanent" is intended as an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntārtha*), and because everything is included therein, there is no further example; all is impermanent.

474.01. If you say this, there is an absence of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because everything has been made the subject (*pakṣa*); therefore, the thing to be proven (*sādhya*) cannot serve as an illustration. 474.02. Furthermore, this reason (*hetu*)—"because of having the nature of arising and perishing"—is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). If you take "having the nature of arising and perishing" as the reason after making everything the subject, [it fails] in the case of atoms (*paramāṇu*), space (*ākāśa*), and so forth.
Furthermore, since certain qualities belonging to those [entities], such as generality (*sāmānya*) and so forth, do not possess the nature of arising and perishing,
the reason [you have provided] is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), because impermanence is not universal.
[4-1-26] Not so, because impermanence is not eternal.

One who asserts that "everything is indeed impermanent" must be asked: Is this impermanence of everything permanent, or is it impermanent? If impermanence is permanent, then not everything is impermanent;
if impermanence is impermanent, then because of the absence of impermanence, the reason that "everything is impermanent" is contradicted.
474.10 [4-1-27] That impermanence of fire is like the destruction following the destruction of the combustible object.

474.11 That impermanence of fire is like the destruction following the destruction of the combustible object. Just as fire, having destroyed the combustible object, is itself subsequently destroyed, so too impermanence, having destroyed everything, is itself subsequently destroyed.
Moreover, this very doctrine that "all is impermanent" explains permanence.
474.14 [4-1-28] There is no denial of the eternal, because its existence is established according to how it is perceived.

474.15 It is not logical to deny the eternal, because its existence is established according to how it is perceived; wherever this cause is perceived, there we understand impermanence through the efficacy of that cause. 474.16 Wherever this cause is perceived, there, by the power of the cause, we realize impermanence. Where...

Furthermore, this reason [of yours] does not exist; how then is their impermanence to be understood? Or, if it is causeless, then you are asserting that which is impermanent; thus, the reason "because of having the nature of arising and perishing" is contradicted.

By one who says "it is impermanent," permanence must necessarily be admitted, whether through the negation of the absolute (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) or the exclusionary (*paryudāsa*) sense of the negative particle.

475.01 Because it has negation as its object, this negative particle (*nañ*), when employed, functions either as a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) or as an implicative negation (*paryudāsa*). 475.02 Thus, if it is not eternal, it is "non-eternal" (*anitya*), which is established by means of the subsequent word (*uttara-pada*).
475.03 That which exists elsewhere is negated elsewhere; thus the subsequent word is established. Now, if...

475.04 Even so, there must be a subsequent term [to express] "the impermanent from the permanent"; for if the referent of the subsequent term does not exist, its distinctness cannot be established. And since there is no such thing as "impermanence" [as a separate entity], the claim that "everything is impermanent" is without fault.
475.06 For that which is called the property (dharma) "impermanence" does not exist in the absence of a substratum (dharmin); and this being the case—

475.07 [The opponent argues: "There is no fault in [the claim that] everything is impermanent. Furthermore, [if one were to argue that] what is established as impermanent by virtue of having the property of arising—475.08 [namely,] the remaining [things] whose impermanence is doubted and those whose permanence is [erroneously] inverted—are impermanent because they exist (sattvāt), 475.09 [then we reply: even for him, since the subsequent term is established, the permanence [of the subject] is established; thus, due to the defect in the thesis (pratijñā-doṣa), the statement [is invalid].
"It ceases"—this is another extreme view.
475.11 [4-1-29] Everything is eternal because the five elements are eternal.

475.12 Everything is eternal because the five elements are eternal. All this is merely the elements, and they are eternal because the destruction of the elements is impossible; therefore, everything is eternal.

475.14 [4-1-30] Not so, because the causes of arising and destruction are perceived. 475.15 Not so, because the cause of the arising of entities is perceived, as is the cause of their destruction; both of these would not exist if there were permanence, for that which is called "permanent" does not [arise or perish].
"It is born; it perishes."
475.18 [4-1-31] There is no refutation because it is included within that definition.

476.01 There is no refutation because it is included within that definition. As for this [notion] that "it arises" and "it perishes," 476.02 you think that nothing is perceived as lacking the characteristics of the elements (*bhūta*), because everything is included within the characteristics of the elements; therefore, all is eternal.

476.03 Thus, one who asserts that "everything is impermanent" does not admit that "anything is born or perishes. 476.04 And if that were admitted, his physical exertion for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful would become purposeless. Furthermore, because everything [would be included] within the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), there would be an absence of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); thus, the formulation of the statement [of the syllogism] would be undermined.

And this statement, which is employed for the purpose of communicating to another—namely, "everything is eternal because the five elements are eternal"—what does this sentence accomplish? Does it establish what is unestablished, or does it negate what is already established?
If, first of all, it establishes what is unestablished, then what is this...

476.09. If accomplishment (*siddhi*) is established by means of a statement, then cognition (*vijñāna*) would be contradicted, because [the statement] asserts that "everything is eternal" and yet "cognition arises. Alternatively, if no such comprehension is produced, what then is this accomplishment? It is that which, when it proceeds, necessarily causes an agent to bring about some previously non-existent thing (*apūrva*).
476.12 Because of its non-origination, either its status as a causal agent (*kārakatva*) is precluded, for there is nothing whatsoever to be done by that which is eternal;

or else, if the position is adopted that it causes what is already established to cease, even in this position there is a contradiction, namely that it is both eternal and ceases. Or, if it is said that it "becomes hidden" (*tirobhavati*), then regarding this concealment...

Furthermore, one must necessarily accept either the arising of something previously non-existent or the destruction of a previously existing entity; thus, in every way, you do not escape contradiction.

For when a form that was previously unperceived is later perceived, one must necessarily accept either the arising of something new or the destruction of a prior entity; therefore, you cannot avoid contradiction in any case.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "everything is eternal" because it is subsumed under the characteristics of the primary elements (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), this is not otherwise [than false]. For that logical proof—that the conjunction with the characteristics of the primary elements is possible in another way—is untenable.
477.01 [4-1-32] Not so, because of the perception of origination and its cause.

477.02 Because origination and its cause are perceived, and the production of qualities similar to those of the cause is observed; 477.03 and this [production] is observed, yet neither of these two pertains to the eternal, for there is no origination of that which is eternal, nor...

477.04 Since there is a cause for that which is eternal, and since both [cause and effect] exist, therefore the effect produces that which possesses qualities identical to those of the cause; thus, the effect arises possessing qualities identical to those of the cause. And when there is the production of that which possesses qualities identical to the cause, the inclusion within the characteristics of the nature of the effect is established. This is the logic of the distinction.
And this [point], namely that there is no intention to speak of the manifest and the unmanifest because of their authoritative status, is contained in this sūtra.
Furthermore, this reason—that "the five elements are eternal"—is non-pervasive (avyāpaka); for how could there be non-pervasion regarding action and so forth?
Action, cognition, sound, and the like are known by the knower to be pervaded by the statement: "because the five elements are eternal."
Furthermore, because effort is observed, there is a contradiction; for effort is seen to belong to a cognizer who is subject to arising and destruction.

Moreover, if everything were eternal, [effort] would not be logical, yet it is well-established that the whole (avayavin) possesses those properties, namely the properties of arising and destruction. Since the existence of the whole has been demonstrated, this [argument] is untenable. How, then, can that which is non-pervasive be an inconclusive reason (anaikāntika) regarding the thesis?

477.13 Because it abides in two extremes, the position [that] "everything is indeed eternal" is [refuted]; for that "everything" possesses the characteristic of being produced (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) and otherwise. 477.14 Because it abides in those two extremes of the position, it is not the case that everything possesses the characteristic of being produced; thus, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). If it is argued that this is a false perception, like the conceit regarding objects in a dream—then...
477.16. That which arises and perishes in the human realm does not exist in reality; it exists only as a non-entity. 477.17.

Regarding this [non-existent thing], there arises the conceit that "it has arisen" or "it has perished," just as objects do not exist in a dream, yet there is a conceit of objects therein. This is because there is no means of valid cognition [to prove its existence]. 477.18. As for this [conceit], it lacks any basis in valid cognition.

477.19–20: Regarding the production and destruction of things such as cows or jars, it is observed that this [non-existence] is logically consistent; however, the statement "it does not exist" is not asserted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes non-existence.
Furthermore, it is impossible to apprehend what lacks a basis in valid cognition, just as we shall explain later that objects do not exist apart from the mind. If [you argue that] dream-objects—
478.02. Furthermore, the perception of the elements would result in being merely a misconception, just like the misconception regarding the objects of a dream.
478.03. If it is argued that "in the absence of earth and the other elements, all worldly transactions would be abolished," and if you think:
478.04. "The elements such as earth do not exist; surely, worldly transaction is based upon earth and the other elements."

478.05 That [objection] would be refuted; the same applies elsewhere. If you accept the existence of real entities (bhūta) out of fear that conventional usage (vyavahāra) would be destroyed, then for that very reason you must also accept arising and destruction. For no conventional usage whatsoever is established without arising and destruction. Thus, [the claim] that eternal substances are beyond the reach of the senses...
Because origination and destruction are beyond the scope [of perception] and lack an object, that which is eternal is supersensible and lacks an object;
therefore, it is incorrect to say that there is a misconception regarding that [eternal entity], just as there is a misconception regarding the objects of a dream.
By one who asserts a "misconception of origination and destruction," the object of that origination and destruction must be stated.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that everything is eternal, there is no object for arising and destruction; and by one who denies such an object, the erroneous cognition that conforms to it must be abandoned. Others, however, explain "everything is eternal" in another way: when that material cause is established, it is merely a property [of it].
Only the phenomenon (dharma) ceases; and that which manifests, even when it has ceased, continues to exist. Furthermore, that which manifests exists even prior to its manifestation.
478.16 [4-1-33] Not so, because the non-establishment of the fixed order [is untenable].

478.17 "Not so, because the non-establishment of the fixed order"—the rest is in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, you who assert that "that which ceases still exists even after it has ceased" must be asked: what is meant by this?

478.19 If you say that what was previously perceived is not perceived later, then [you must explain] on what basis there is this non-perception of an existing thing. 478.20 If it is caused by an obstruction and so forth, then that obstruction and so forth should be perceived; and it has already been stated in this regard that when something previously unperceived is perceived later, there is the production of a new quality and the disappearance of a previous quality.

479.02 It must be accepted; and if that is accepted, there is a contradiction. Furthermore, as for what was said—that whatever manifests exists even prior to its manifestation—that is not a contradiction; it manifests and yet exists.
Now, if manifestation means becoming manifest (*abhivyakti*), even so the previous fault is not avoided, for [the definition of] manifestation...
"It becomes non-existent"—this is another extreme view.
479.06 [4-1-34] Everything is distinct because of the distinctness of the characteristic of being.
479.07 Everything is distinct because of the distinctness of the characteristic of being. The characteristic of a thing (*bhāva*) is the word (*śabda*), by which the thing is characterized.
479.08 Every thing is designated by a term for a thing; every such term has multiple referents, just as, for example, the word "jar" (*kumbha*).
The word that expresses an entity (bhāva-samākhyā-śabda) applies to a collection of many parts, just like the word "jar" (kumbha).

Other words are also like this. The formal argument for this is: the word "jar" has multiple objects because it is a single word, just like the word "army" (senā); for from the hearing of a single word, there is the comprehension of multiple meanings.
479.12 From the hearing of a word, multiple meanings are understood, as for example in the case of the word "army" (*senā*).

479.13 [4-1-35] Not [is there a single entity], because a single entity is not produced by multiple characteristics. 479.14 “By multiple characteristics” (*aneka-lakṣaṇaiḥ*) is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyapadalopin*), meaning “by characteristics of various kinds. And [these are] by qualities such as odor (*gandha*) and so forth, and by bases (*budhna*) and so forth.

479.16 And because a single entity arises as connected with its parts, when there is the cognition of one from that word, the remainder is understood as being concomitant; thus, the possessor of qualities is distinct from the qualities, and the whole is distinct from the parts. This is the established principle of differentiation. Furthermore, because it consists of a single word, a term such as "jar" has multiple objects [as its referents].
479.19 Thus, that [argument] is not [valid] because of the absence of an example; for there is no word whatsoever that has multiple objects.

479.20 Because words such as "army" (*senā*) and so forth are not established as having multiple objects—just as it was stated how a word such as "army" has a single object—and because everything is made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is an absence of an example due to the relationship between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*).

480.02–03. Because there is the apprehension of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are interconnected, as well as the whole (*avayavin*), the negation (*nañ*) is not established otherwise. 480.03–04. Furthermore, because it exists as having both the scope of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and relative negation (*paryudāsa*), this [reason] "manifold" (*aneka*) is contradictory. 480.04.
This application of the negation occurs because it negates by way of having both the scope of absolute negation and relative negation.

480.05 It is conceptualized [as follows]: if it is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), then "it is not one" means that what is negated in one place exists elsewhere; and in this way, there is a contradiction. Now, regarding the position of exclusion (*paryudāsa*): "other than one is many"—even so, "one" is thereby admitted, for if "one" does not exist, [the term "many"] cannot exist.

Therefore, something other than that is established as manifold. And for this reason as well: [4-1-36] There is no refutation precisely because of the establishment of its definition. Because of the very establishment of that definition, there is no refutation; for there is no such thing as a single entity.

480.11 Why is this position untenable? Because of the establishment of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-pravyavasthāpanāt*). For when "pot" (*kumbha*) is uttered, 480.12 a plurality of objects is not understood. How is it not understood? Because it ends in the singular number;
480.13 this word "pot" ends in the singular. It is not appropriate for the singular number to apply to many things, [given] the correspondence between the command and the understanding.

480.14 Because they share a single object, the command "Bring the jar" has a single object. The other [person] also, having understood [the meaning] from the word "jar," brings a single jar. These two—the command and the comprehension—make known that they have a single object, indicating that a single referent is denoted by the word "jar. As for those [qualities] such as form (rūpa) and so forth...
480.17 You accept the parts; that is not the meaning of the word, but rather it is a secondary implication (*anuṣaṅga*), because [the whole] is inseparable from them.
480.18 And since there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding the distinction of the collection (*samūha*), that wherein it comes to rest is the single [entity], such as a cow or a jar.
481.01 By one who accepts the substances (*dravya*) such as a cow and so forth as they are combined, a collection (*samūha*) is admitted; and this very [collection]—

481.02 A collection [is defined as] "these many substances existing in the form of a jar and so forth"—this distinction does not hold for it, because of its being more or less minute. That which is the ultimate minimum is indivisible; from that, [the notion of] this distinction ceases.
And that from which this distinction ceases is one. By one who denies the one...
Even a single [atom] must be rejected because it is a collection of many [factors]. Now,
if you think that the indivisible atom which you postulate is a collection of form and so forth—
namely, the four substances such as earth and the others combined— or if you think that the atom is these [substances] themselves in combination, in this case...

481.08. Regarding the view that those [elements] such as form which have come together constitute an atom (*paramāṇu*), it must be stated: of what is that form in the atom a collection? The same applies to the remaining qualities; for one who asserts that the four substances (*dravya*) in their combined state are atoms, because they are the cause of the conjunction of the fourfold set.

If that which is a single entity, such as earth and so forth, is [the atom], it must be stated of what it is an aggregate. Or, if you maintain that it is infinite, and you assert that an atom is an aggregate of eight substances combined, then the treatise is contradicted; for the statement that "an atom consists of the desired number of substances" would be untenable if there were only one [substance].

481.14 “There is no manifold arising”—this is what must be abandoned. And as for this reason: “because the word ‘entity’ (bhāva) is applied to a collection” (481.15)—thus, because there is a contradiction on both sides, nothing whatsoever [is established], nor in any way; on neither side is there any single entity (481.16).
There is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason in the statement: “an entity exists in a collection because the word ‘entity’ is applied to it. Since—

481.17–19: Since a collection is not tenable if a single object is untenable, for one who denies the "one" while relying upon a "collection," that very collection becomes denied. Thus, this is a doctrine of nonsense (*yad-kim-cana-vāda*) due to contradiction on both sides. The rest is in the *Bhāṣya*.
482.01 Now, there is this other extreme view.

482.02 [4-1-37] All things are established through mutual non-existence among things. 482.03 Whatever constitutes the totality of existing things, all that is [established as such]. 482.04 Why is it that all things are established through mutual non-existence among things? Because of the negation of the notion of "non-existent" and because of [the establishment of] negation.

482.05 Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting existence (*bhāva*), everything is non-existence (*abhāva*), like a cloth that has not yet arisen or one that has already perished.

482.06 Every word denoting existence is coreferential with "non-existent" and coreferential with negation, like a cloth that has perished; for example, in the case of "the cloth does not exist," how [is it non-existent] and when [is it non-existent]?
482.07 Just as in the case of "the cloth does not exist. How does it not exist? And at what time does it not exist?

482.08–09: "Not being produced in the form of a pot-sherd and so forth, and yet having perished"—this very word "pot" (ghaṭa), being in grammatical apposition with the notion of non-existence (asat-pratyaya), establishes the absolute non-existence of the pot. And thus, since all entities are in apposition with the notion of non-existence, everything is non-being. This is the proposition (pratijñā).

482.11. There is a contradiction between the two terms, namely the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the possession of non-different case endings—this being because one accepts that "having a single case ending" means the utterance of a single inflection, and because one accepts that [the word] *tat* [refers to that very thing]. 482.12–13.
[This is a case of] affirmation (*vidhi*). If you think that "whatever is everything" is "non-existence," [that cannot be so], for there can be no cognition of that [non-existence] when it is absent.
It is possible [to say] that non-existence is not existence by means of the suffix of existence (*bhāva-pratyaya*), and thus existence is negated.

Since the negative particle (*nañ*) is not employed when the meaning of the subsequent word (*uttara-padārtha*) is absent, there are the two types of negation: absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*).

As before, the same contingency applies: just as in the case of the word "non-eternal" (*anitya*) consisting of multiple words, so it is with all words and even with the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*).

The contradiction is to be inferred; the remainder is in the commentary. It must be stated that there is a determination of the intrinsic nature of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) even when all things are non-existent.
Furthermore, if everything is non-existence, it must be stated what the intrinsic nature of the case-ending is. This is so:
and in the absence of a case-ending, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in having an undifferentiated case-ending.

Thus it is contradicted. You claim that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the negation of a non-existent object; yet you also exclude [the view] that "everything is non-existence," for a non-existent thing cannot be a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*).
The connection with the aphorism is this: that which exists in a certain locus is called a substratum, and such a thing does not exist in the case of non-existence.

483.03 [4-1-38] "There is no establishment of things by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva). This means that things do not exist by virtue of their own being; this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Furthermore, what is accomplished by this Sūtra? It is raised as an objection against the contradiction with the preceding Sūtra. How so?

483.06–08. Thus, because the mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) of entities is established, "non-existence" is designated as the state of being non-existent (*abhāvatā*). Furthermore, by asserting this, you accept non-entities (*abhāva*) as having an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the qualification [“mutual”] is redundant regarding entities, since their mutual non-existence is already established. Indeed, if all things were non-existent, one would have to say exactly this: "Entities do not exist."

Furthermore, it is not logical to say that "the one is not the other," for this term "vidhāna" (prescription/affirmation) does not apply when everything is non-existent; nor is there any entity being prescribed that could be denoted by the word "other. And having accepted that [something] is denotable as "other," [one might claim] "the one is in the other."
"It is being negated. Thus, the establishment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is accepted. And what is this intrinsic nature?

It is the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "existence" (*sat*) and so forth, and the particular (*viśeṣa*) such as "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*) and so forth, belonging to entities (*bhāva*) such as substance (*dravya*) and the rest; as well as the infinite individual distinctions (*bheda*) of earth and the other elements, extending up to tangibility (*sparśa*), as well as [the categories of] universals, particulars, inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth.

There are general, particular, and internal subdivisions of non-existence that are infinite. Since this [non-existence] is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), there could be no differentiating nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) capable of conveying its meaning; yet such a differentiation does exist.

Therefore, everything is non-existence. Alternatively, if it were established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-siddhi*), then when the term "cow" is applied, [it would follow that the cow is non-existent].

483.18–19. It is not non-existence that is perceived; rather, it is a substance qualified by its genus (*jāti*). If everything were non-existence, then when the word "cow" is employed, non-existence would be understood. Therefore, not everything is non-existence.
Alternatively, because of the establishment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-siddhi*), a cow is non-existent in the form of a horse, and a non-horse is a cow; thus, "non-cow" is a cow.

484.02 Why is it not stated? Because it is not stated that "the non-cow is a cow," it would be a contradiction (*vyāhata*) if one were to say so. 484.03 If, for fear of contradiction, one does not say "the non-cow is a cow," then, alas, the negation (*abhāva*) is established! How then is this negation expressed as "the non-cow is a horse"? It is through the negation of difference (*vyatireka-pratiṣedha*).

484.05–484.07: [The opponent argues: "There is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the term 'non-existence' (*asat*) and its object, just as in the case of the expression 'there are no jujube fruits in the bowl' (*kuṇḍe badarāṇi na santi*), where the relationship between the bowl and the jujubes is negated, but it is not the case that the bowl and the jujube are themselves non-existent.
[Reply: No, there is no establishment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-siddhi*), because [existence] is relative (*āpekṣikatvāt*). [4-1-39]

484.08 There is no establishment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is dependent. Since that which is established dependently has no establishment by way of its own self, it is like long and short, or prior and posterior.
484.10 [4-1-40] It is untenable because it is contradictory.
484.11 It is untenable because it is contradictory. If "long" is produced in dependence on "short," then "short" is relative;
484.12 or if "short" is produced in dependence on "long," then "long" would be non-relative. And as for those two which are mutually dependent...
484.13–14: "The other arises through dependence; that which is independent [of it] does not exist. Thus, there is the non-existence of both because of the non-existence of one. 484.14–15:
Whether there is dependence or independence between two substances, there is no difference; they remain exactly as much substance as they were. 484.15–16:
While they are dependent, they are exactly as much [substance] as when they are independent; for there is no difference in either case.

484.16 How can there be the apprehension of a distinction (*atiśaya*) if there is no difference between two substances, whether they are mutually dependent or independent? 484.17 In that case, the cognition of "long" and "short" would not occur; indeed, it would not occur if there were only the apprehension of the two [substances] themselves.
484.18 Because of the apprehension of the distinction, however, there are indeed two cognitions corresponding to each respective object regarding those two substances.

Therefore, [the observer] perceives the excellence existing in one [object] and the shortness existing in the other; having perceived both, he synthesizes them. From this synthesis arises his cognition: "This is long compared to that, and that is short compared to this. However, there is no production of a new entity.

485.02. Regarding the phrase "non-arising": if intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were not established, dependence (*apekṣā*) would not be possible. If, even in the absence of an established intrinsic nature, distinctions such as long and so forth were to arise due to differences in dependence, then everything would be perceived as such in relation to everything else; however, there is no capacity for dependence in the cognitions of form, taste, odor, or touch.

485.05 There is no one who perceives the spherical atoms (*paramāṇu*) as such that, depending upon one atom, [he] would produce the cognitions of "long," "short," and so forth in another atom; therefore, these cognitions are not produced through dependence. Thus, the claim that "everything is non-existent" is in every respect a contradictory doctrine.

485.08 Why is there a contradiction? First, regarding the arising or non-arising of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the opponent claims] "everything is non-existent" (485.09). One who speaks thus must be questioned concerning the means of valid cognition. If he says [something], it becomes contradictory;
if he does not state [anything], his point is not established due to the absence of a means of valid cognition. [This applies to] the statement "everything is non-existent."

If that [sentence] conveys its expressed meaning, there is a contradiction as before; if it does not convey it, then the mere utterance of syllables is meaningless. Furthermore, regarding the statement "everything is non-existent," if it conveys [its meaning] to both the speaker and the listener, there is a contradiction as before.

If one perceives a difference in meaning between these two statements, "everything is non-existence" and "everything is existence," they are contradictory; but if one does not perceive such a difference, the specific qualification [of "everything"] is redundant. Thus, this doctrine of universal non-existence, to whatever extent it is investigated, fails to withstand logical scrutiny.

485.17 Now, these are the doctrines of numerical monism (*saṃkhyā-ekānta-vāda*), such as "everything is one because there is no distinction," and so forth, as stated in the *Bhāṣya*. 485.18 The following *sūtra* serves as the refutation of them.
485.19 [4-1-41] The absolute [monistic] nature of number is unestablished, due to the impossibility and possibility of a cause.

486.01 The absolute [monistic] nature of numbers is unestablished because the cause is excluded from the meaning of the proposition; for instance, the proposition that "everything is one. 486.02 [The unestablishment follows] because the cause is distinct from the meaning of the proposition, "everything is one."

486.03 If, having made [the proposition], one states a means of proof (*sādhana*) that is distinct from the thing to be proven (*pratijñeya*), the absolute [monism] is not established. 486.04 And since there would be both that means of proof and the object of the proposition, there is duality; and this applies likewise to dualism and so forth. Alternatively, 486.05 if there is no means of proof distinct from the thing to be proven, even so, his absolute [position] is not established.
Because there is no means of proof, that which is to be proven is not the means of proof.
486.07 [4-1-42] Not so, because the cause is a constituent part [of the probandum].

486.08 "Not so, because the cause is a constituent part" means that since the cause is a constituent part of the probandum (sādhya), this is the meaning of the sūtra. And in this case, the proof of the constituent part of the probandum is a proof distinct from the probandum itself.
It has not been stated that there is no proof without a means of proof.
486.11 [4-1-43] It is not a valid reason because it lacks constituent parts.

486.12 It is not a valid reason because it lacks constituent parts; since only that which possesses constituent parts can be a cause, this is not a valid reason. 486.13 Because the subject of the proposition lacks constituent parts, in this case regarding the proposition "everything is one," [it is not a valid reason].

486.14–16. Something is excluded by that which is not excluded; thus, everything is made a "subject" (*pakṣa*). Consequently, for that which is partless (*niravayava*), because it has been made a subject, there is no reason (*hetu*) and no probandum (*sādhya*). A reason cannot function as a reason [for itself]. Furthermore, action upon oneself is contradictory; it is not logical that that which is to be established (*pratipādya*) is itself the establisher (*pratipādaka*). Nor is it [logical].

"An action must have an instrument. Now, these extremist numerical doctrines—if they proceed by rejecting the distinction of objects produced through specific causal efficiency—are false doctrines, because they contradict perception, inference, and scripture. This distinction between cows and the like, or pots and the like, is perceptible; [it is also established] through inference.

486.20 Furthermore, one thing is understood by means of another; it is also understood through scripture (*āgama*). One who has already realized [the truth] is the instructor, while one who has not yet realized it is the recipient of instruction. Now, if they proceed by way of mutual consent, even so, they abandon their absolute [distinction]. Or, if there is non-difference produced by the universal (*sāmānya*), as opposed to the particular (*viśeṣa*)—

Even if it is understood that difference is produced, nothing is thereby contradicted. Furthermore, since a universal finds no scope without difference, one who accepts a universal must necessarily admit difference; and by one who denies difference, the universal must also be rejected.
Since a universal that lacks a specific substratum cannot be an object [of cognition], these indeed are the one-sided views regarding number;
they have been examined for the sake of discerning the knowledge of reality.
Immediately after the state of rebirth (pretyabhāva), the fruit was indicated;
regarding that [fruit], there is a doubt as to whether its production occurs immediately or at a later time.
There is a doubt concerning the production of the fruit—whether it occurs immediately or at a later time. Some action...

487.11 Just as [the expressions] "it ripens immediately" (*sadyas-phalā*) or "she milks" (*dogdhi*) have immediate results—namely, the eating and the milk respectively—487.12 so too there is that which occurs immediately after the action, according to you. On the other hand, some [action] has a result at a later time, such as "he ploughs" (*kṛṣati*) or "he sows" (*vapati*); its result occurs at a later time, and the harvest is not obtained immediately after the action.
487.14 And there is this action, namely, "one should offer the Agnihotra"; regarding its fruit, there is doubt:
487.15 Does this have its fruit immediately, such as heat and so forth, or does it have its fruit at another time?
487.16 [ (4-1-45) ] Not immediate, because it is to be enjoyed at another time. 487.17 Heaven is heard in scripture as the fruit [of action] by means of the enjoined rite;
it cannot be [the fruit] of a purposeless action, nor is this person desirous of suffering and the like.

488.01 One performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice; by this it is understood that [the merit] arises from the connection between the self and the mind, supported by a pure intention (*abhisandhi*), in dependence upon those actions such as the offering (*havana*). 488.02–03 Thus, dharma is produced in the self.
And that [dharma], its power unobstructed at a later time and assisted by place and other factors, [produces its fruit].
488.04 That fruit is bestowed, and it occurs when that body has fallen, for one who has entered another body; therefore, [the result is said to be] "immediate.
488.06 [4-1-45(46)] There is no production at a later time because the cause has perished.

488.07. [Objection: There is no production at a later time because the cause has perished. Since the oblation has ceased and the previous body has ceased, it is not logical that the fruit should be heard of in another body arising from a cause that has already perished.
488.09. [Response: Prior to its production, it would be like the fruit of a tree.
