488.10 Before its completion, it would be like the fruit of a tree. We do not say that the effect arises from a cause that has already perished; rather, [it arises] through an action characterized by the Agnihotra oblation and so forth. 488.12 As it was stated according to the aforementioned method, "it is Dharma," therefore it is called "the fruit," just as [in the case of a tree].
488.13 One who desires fruit performs actions such as watering the root of a tree; yet it is not from the root that has perished due to the watering [that the fruit arises].
488.14 Rather, it is endowed with fruit because of the action performed, such as watering the root, by the enjoyer.
488.15 Depending upon the action, he favors the elements such as earth; being thus favored, [the tree] internally [produces fruit].
Being cooked by heat, it produces a sap-substance; that sap-substance pervades the tree immediately from [the root] up to the fruit.

From this, the leaves and so forth, as well as the fruit, are produced. This being the case, the production of the fruit results from the watering of the roots even though [the water] has perished, and yet the watering of the roots and so forth is not rendered useless.
This [is the case] prior to its completion.
489.01 [4-1-47(48)] It is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent.

489.02 Prior to its production, that which possesses the nature of arising is neither non-existent, because there is a restriction of the material cause; for if it were equally non-existent, there would be no restriction regarding the material cause.
489.03 It is not non-existent, because of the restriction of the material cause; since non-existence is equal [in all cases], there would be no restriction of the material cause.
Even if it were to attain [existence], it would not come to be; for the arising of that which already exists is contradicted.

Thus, [the claim] "it exists" and "it arises" are contradictory. That which is existent is not non-existent, because there is a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) between the existent and the non-existent.
"Existent" implies the admission of an object, while "non-existent" is its negation; thus, there is a contradiction between admission and negation.

Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is untenable. Therefore, an effect that is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor even the opposite of both is not logical, because its own-nature (*svarūpa*) cannot be specified. Indeed, its own-nature cannot be specified. Prior to its production, it is certainly non-existent, being characterized by the property of arising. This is true.
Why?
489.11 [4-1-48(49)] Because of the observation of arising and passing away.

489.12 Because of the observation of arising and passing away: the subsequent apprehension of a thing that was previously unapprehended in its form; 489.13 that which is the arising of what was non-existent is logical, as is the destruction, which is the non-apprehension again of that which had been apprehended in its form.

489.14 Thus [it is said]. And this is not the case for one who maintains that everything is eternal; for production is not a real category, nor is destruction. 489.15 Furthermore, by one who denies both production and destruction, the world must be abandoned.
489.16 Now, for what purpose does this world proceed? Indeed, it proceeds.

489.17 "I shall attain this" and "I shall abandon this"—it is only in this way that [action] proceeds truly; however, for the proponent of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*sat-kārya-vādin*), there exists nothing whatsoever to be rejected or accepted. Furthermore, the employment of the members of a syllogism, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, is useless, because of the denial of arising and passing away; nothing at all is born, nor does anything cease.

490.03 If something perishes, the employment of constituent parts is useless; for if it is the case that the effect pre-exists (*sat-kārya*), since the cognition [of the effect] already exists, the employment [of causes] is useless. For in the world, one does not employ a material cause for something that already exists. Alternatively, [it might be argued that the cause is employed] for the purpose of removing ignorance or obscuration.

"Appropriation" (upādāna) is likewise of that same nature; for it is not logical that there should be a cessation of ignorance for that which has not undergone a specific transformation. Now, if appropriation is for the sake of manifestation, what is this so-called "manifestation" that is produced by appropriation? If it is the effect itself, then [the theory of] the effect being pre-existent is contradicted. Or, if it is a property of the effect...

Even so, the contradiction remains. If "manifestation" (abhivyakti) is the production of the effect's object, then it is not freed from the contradiction. If, on the other hand, manifestation is the persistence in the form of the effect of that which was already established in the form of the cause—even so, the contradiction regarding the form of the effect does not cease.

490.12 The subsistence [of the effect] would be non-existent. Now, if manifestation is a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) of the cause, 490.13 then since that particular configuration comes into being where it did not previously exist, there is a contradiction. Alternatively, if it already exists, the material cause (*upādāna*) is useless.
490.14 Now, if manifestation is the nourishment of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the cause, [then] there is no acquisition of what was previously non-existent.

We see that the inclusion of the phrase "for the sake of strengthening the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa-puṣṭi*) is redundant; furthermore, the strengthening of the specific characteristic [is untenable], because you do not escape the contradiction that something which did not previously exist comes into being later. Thus, by whatever means the manifestation of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is expressed, it subverts the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*sat-kārya*). As for what was further...
490.18 This is not so, because there is a restriction regarding appropriation.
490.19 [4-1-49(50)] But that which is established by cognition is non-existent.
490.20 But that which is established by cognition is non-existent. This restriction of the material cause is not due to [the object's] existence, but rather due to capacity (sāmarthya);
for instance, "this sentence is to be produced by this [cause], and not this [sentence] by this [other cause]"—thus the effect is established by cognition.
491.02 Having established that whatever is capable of producing something is what is appropriated for it, and not everything for everything;

491.03 since it is not observed that everything arises from everything. Now, if one establishes the restriction between cause and effect through the restriction of arising—that is, by the restriction of the effect—then, by that [means], regarding the two terms "effect" and "cause":
What is the meaning of "to be expressed"? What do you mean by "the cause," and what do you mean by "the effect"?

Now, is it not the case that the "cause" is that which acts (*karoti*) and the "effect" is that which is acted upon (*kriyate*)? If you mean manifestation, then the same objection as before applies. Or, do you think that the sense of "acting" is observed even in the case of things already existing?
491.08 Just as when one says, "Arrange the hair; arrange the back," there is no difference in the speech regarding those things that already exist;
491.09 whereas for the hair, something non-existent is being produced, and later, for the back, the removal of dirt—which was non-existent—is performed.
491.10 Thus, we never perceive a cause for something that already exists; therefore, this [argument] is invalid.

491.11 If indeed that which is non-existent is produced, why is the horn of a donkey not produced? Who says that it is not produced? That which is the horn of a donkey—that very thing is produced. 491.12–13 Now, we do not know why the donkey does not serve as the cause for the horn.

491.14 Why does it not occur? It is not because a horn is never seen being produced from a donkey. 491.15 Therefore, it is concluded that by this [example], the hare’s horn is explained: it is not because of its non-existence that it is not produced, but rather because of the absence of a cause. Furthermore, non-existence is not the cause for production.
491.17–19. But since that which exists does not arise, [you claim] that what is non-existent arises; however, because it is non-existent, a donkey’s horn does not arise.
One who speaks thus contradicts his own tenet, for according to your position, a donkey’s horn does not exist.
Since existence and non-existence are equal [in this regard], that which has a cause arises; thus, the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkārya*).

And thus it has been said by the proponent that the worldly transaction of all people would be destroyed [if one held that] "what was not previously existent is not born" and "what was previously existent does not perish. Now, what is the proof for the theory that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production]? There is neither inference regarding existence nor regarding non-existence, because there is no disagreement concerning the locus (*dharmin*). Where, then, is the dispute? It is over that which is already agreed upon by both parties.
Regarding his doctrines, the weavers who have accepted both positions debate them with him. Some first say that the cloth is merely the threads;
others, however, say that the threads exist in a particular configuration; still others say that it is the very threads themselves that persist in the form of the effect.

492.06 Thus [it is said]. For others, it is the manifestation and disappearance of dharma and adharma. Yet others say that the cloth is the threads characterized by a specific capacity (*śakti*). Thus, among these various positions, the distinction from the mere threads must be established, and that has been demonstrated. As for those who...

Regarding those who describe a cloth as being [merely] threads existing in a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*), the proof against them is as follows: "Prior to the time of perception, the threads are devoid of any particular configuration, because they are its causes, like the shuttle and other such tools. By this, it is explained that [the threads] do not exist in the form of the effect; likewise, [the argument applies].

492.12–14. Since the manifestation and disappearance [of things] consist merely in the appearance and disappearance of other properties (*dharma*), for this very reason threads remain in a state of specific potencies (*śakti-viśeṣa*).
One who asserts this does not invalidate anything at all; therefore, no formal proof (*sādhana*) is stated against them.
Thus, that very object which is established by cognition is what is non-existent; that same object remains in a state of specific potencies.
492.15–16: In all these positions, the cognition of a cloth cannot occur without the production of something previously non-existent;

thus, a contradiction is unavoidable. 492.16–17: Since the threads are for the purpose of manifesting what already exists, they are invariably taken up by one who desires that [cloth], just like a spade and other tools used for manifesting what is already present. If it were non-existent, there would be no manifestation.

492.18 Just as in the case of manifestation (*abhivyakti*), the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) applies to the effect (*kārya*); and all of this has already been answered. Furthermore, regarding the point [stated at] 493.01—that "because of the restriction of the material cause" (*upādāna-niyamāt*)—the material cause is the cause, and we do not perceive any purpose for a cause when [the effect] already exists; thus, the logical consequence remains as before. As for the argument that it is "like a shovel and so forth," there is no shovel... [text fragment].
493.03 It is not taken for the sake of water and so forth, but rather for the sake of the removal of an obstruction; and that removal of an obstruction—493.04—is disjunction (*vibhāga*).

Since that [disjunction] comes into being after having not existed, the illustrative example is unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, if one does not admit disjunction, then even one who does not admit disjunction must be questioned regarding the cause for the arising of the cognition of disjunction.

493.06 Now, if one understands the notion of separation from mere non-attainment (*aprāpti*), is that non-attainment (1) the absence of attainment (*prāpti*), or (2) something other than attainment? And what follows from this? If non-attainment is the absence of attainment, it must be stated from where that non-attainment arises. If it is caused by opposition to attainment...

493.09. That is its division; thus, it is not the case that there is no division. For when something is negated in one place, it exists elsewhere—this has been stated. Furthermore, non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is twofold: the conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) of those already joined and the division (*vibhāga*) of those joined.
Among these, that which is the division of those joined is "division," and tools such as a spade [bring about] that.

[They] perform [this]. Now, if there were a non-possession (*aprāpti*) distinct from possession (*prāpti*), that too would be twofold; in that case as well, the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before would apply.

(493.13) Now, if one were to maintain that disjunction (*vibhāga*) consists in arising in different locations—thinking, "these two have arisen in different locations"—(493.14) because of the employment of this qualification, it follows that arising in different locations is not itself disjunction. When [the things] have arisen...
493.15 "Produced" means "divided" by virtue of being in different locations; [and] from that division, it is "separated.

493.16 These are the causes for the notion of difference, which are to be inferred from the difference in the cognitions themselves. For these—namely, "divided," "produced," and "separated"—are not synonymous terms. Furthermore, production in different locations has already been refuted.

[Objection: Since [the action] exists, disjunction is not the production in a different location; because disjunction is momentary, the arising of the cognition of disjunction is not tenable. [Response:
No, because the arising of that cognition is experienced at the very time of the manifestation of the universal and the destruction of the conjunction, following first from its own cause.

The disjunction that has arisen manifests the universal; after the manifestation of the universal, it produces the cognition of disjunction and destroys the conjunction. After the destruction of the conjunction, [the substance] perishes due to that conjunction which consists of two parts. Thus, because it is experienced over multiple moments, it does not perish at the very moment of its production.
The claim that "division perishes" is unproven. Thus, it is established that what is non-existent arises.

[4-1-50] The argument that "it is like the production of fruit from a tree because of the distinction of its substratum" is not a valid reason; for there is also the watering of the roots and so forth.

494.07. Furthermore, both the action and the fruit, such as leaves and so forth, depend upon the tree; however, in this case, the action is in one place and the fruit of the action is elsewhere. 494.08. Thus, because of the difference in their substrata, like the production of a fruit from a tree, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

494.09 [4-1-51(52)] "There is no prohibition because pleasure has the self as its locus" (prīter ātmāśrayatvād apratiṣedhaḥ). Regarding this: "The separation from the locus is unestablished"—this is the meaning of the sūtra. That is to say, wherever there is action, right there is the fruit of that action.
494.12 [4-1-52(53)] Not so, because of the mention of results such as sons, wives, cattle, attendants, gold, food, and so forth.
494.14 Not so, because of the mention of results such as sons, wives, cattle, attendants, gold, food, and so forth.
Sons and the rest are 494.15 mentioned as being the results; it is not that sons and the rest exist within the Self.
494.16 [4-1-53(54)] Because the fruit is produced through connection with them, there is a metaphorical designation of them as "fruit.

494.17 Because the fruit is produced through connection with them, there is a metaphorical designation of them as "fruit. Due to the connection with sons and so forth, 494.18 the fruit—namely, joy—arises; because they are the cause of that, sons and so forth are designated by the word "fruit."

495.01 Just as life is accomplished by food, one says, "Life is indeed food. This is a metaphorical usage (upacāra) employed because of the absence [of life] when [food] is absent, following the common expressions used in the world. 495.02–03 Immediately after the result, suffering has been both mentioned and defined; suffering is characterized by affliction (bādhanā-lakṣaṇa).

495.04 "Is this a total rejection of the happiness of all the world, or is there another way? [He] replied: "There is another. [The questioner asked: "How so? Indeed, it is not possible to reject the happiness witnessed by the entire world.
495.06 "But this [rejection] belongs to one who is weary of the suffering caused by the experience of the continuous succession of birth and death."

495.07. The instruction on the cultivation of suffering: How indeed should one cultivate the thought that "all is suffering"? And by cultivating it, how might one become dispassionate, and being dispassionate, be liberated? Furthermore, how does one cultivate the thought that "all is suffering"?
[One does so by reflecting that] all classes of sentient beings, all renewed existence, and all places of birth are suffering.
495.10 Because it is accompanied by suffering, it is called "suffering" by the seers; therein the cultivation of suffering is taught, and 495.11 no other cause is accepted.
495.12 [4-1-54(55)] Because it is associated with various afflictions, birth (*janma*)—its arising—is indeed suffering (*duḥkha*).

495.13 "Because it is associated with various afflictions, birth—its arising—is indeed suffering. In that context, 495.14 "birth" refers to the body, the sense faculties, and the intellect; it is used as a designation for the manifestation of the body and so forth.

495.15 Arising (*utpatti*) means birth; arising-birth refers to various types of affliction (*bādhanā*), namely the inferior, 495.16 the middling, and the superior. The rest is in the commentary (*bhāṣya*). With this intention, suffering (*duḥkha*) was taught, and pleasure (*sukha*) was not rejected.
495.18 [4-1-55(56)] Nor is there the production of pleasure in the interval, because pleasure arising in the interval between afflictions is directly perceived; and for this reason as well:

496.01 [4-1-56(57)] There is no refutation [of the opponent's position] because the seeker of the cessation of affliction experiences [pleasure], due to the fault of seeking; for pleasure is [pursued] with the aim of [removing] suffering. From the context, since this person, while experiencing, [thinks]: "This is a means to my pleasure," "this is my..."

496.04–06. Thinking, "This is a means to suffering," one strives to obtain the means to happiness and to abandon the means to suffering. And while he is striving for the attainment of the means to happiness, various kinds of afflictions assail him.
Therefore, because of the experience of these afflictions, it is said that "all is suffering" and not because of the manifestation of happiness.
And this very same meaning has been described by the Sage in a verse:
"When the desire of one who longs for pleasure is fulfilled, another desire quickly assails him. And so forth.
[4-1-57(58)] This is because of the conceit of happiness regarding what is actually a variation of suffering.

496.11 And because of the misconception of pleasure within the conceptualization of suffering: when one who strives for the sake of pleasure experiences what is actually a conceptualization of suffering, they mistakenly conceive it as pleasure because it is a subordinate factor of pleasure. Grasping that again and again, they return repeatedly; thus, due to that perception of pleasure, they do not transcend saṃsāra.

496.14 This teaching is presented as an antidote, namely: "All is suffering. If this is so, why is it not stated that "birth is suffering"? Since he ought to have said this, the fact that he says instead "suffering itself" (duḥkham eva) indicates by that the absence of pleasure; even that pleasure which arises in the interval between [birth and death] is [ultimately suffering].

497.01–497.03: "Suffering indeed [arises] from the attachment to suffering, not from its non-existence. For one who desires the cessation of birth, this very word "suffering" teaches the cessation of birth by means of [the realization that] "all is suffering. By contemplating [this], one does not take up the means to suffering; not taking them up, one is liberated.
497.04. Immediately after the enumeration of suffering, liberation (apavarga) is now being explained.
497.05 [4-1-58(59)] Because of the persistence of debt, suffering, and worldly activity, there is no liberation.

497.06 By this sūtra, "because of the persistence of debt," 497.07 there is no liberation. The remainder is in the Bhāṣya. Persistence means that which must always be performed; it is not merely the persistence of debt.

497.08–09: "At some time, from birth until death, one is liberated"—this is because of the continuity of afflictions (*kleśa*). There is no liberation; for this person is born indeed bound by afflictions, and dies indeed bound by afflictions. 497.10: Because of the continuity of activity (*pravṛtti*), there is no liberation; at no time does this person not perform karma.
497.11 As for the statement that "he acts because of the persistence of debt":

497.12 [4-1-59(60)] When there is an impossibility regarding the primary term (*pradhāna-śabda*), there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) by means of a secondary term (*guṇa-śabda*) for the sake of censure (*nindā*) or praise (*praśaṃsā*). 497.13–497.14: "When there is an impossibility regarding the primary term, there is a restatement by means of a secondary term for the sake of censure or praise."

497.15 This word *pradhāna* (primary) is not [applicable here], because of the impossibility of there being a "giving of what is to be returned" (*pratyādeya*) or a "taking of what is to be given back" (*pratideya*). For indeed, 497.16 where one person gives what is to be returned and the other takes what is to be given back, 497.17 there this word *ṛṇa* (debt) is primary; elsewhere it is figurative. Therefore, this [word] is used as a quality-word (*guṇa-śabda*).

498.01. Regarding the term "metaphorical designation" (*anuvāda*), as in the expression "the boy is fire," there the word "fire" refers to a specific kind of light (*tejas*) characterized by the capacity for burning and so forth. While it applies to that [specific light], it is applied to the boy—who does not possess those qualities—on account of a commonality [between them]. Thus, one says "the boy is fire"; however, the word "fire" is not in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the boy.
It does not, however, designate the boy as being capable of burning and so forth;
rather, it designates the boy as one who possesses those properties (dharmas) such as tawny color and the like which belong to fire.
And this word, when employed by means of that [connection], is secondary (gauṇa) because it functions through the mediation of a quality (guṇa).
498.07 And thus the word "debt" (*ṛṇa*) is employed; furthermore, this sentence, "one is born with a debt," is an analogy.
498.08 Here, the comparison must be understood as being elided [in the form] "one is born with a debt. What is the meaning of the comparison?
498.09 Just as one who has a debt is not independent, so too this one being born is not independent regarding his actions.
"He exists as one who is not independent," and this term "being born" (*jāyamāna*) is indeed a secondary (*guṇa*) word;

it cannot be used in its primary sense, for when a boy is being born from his mother, there is no possibility of the performance of actions such as studying while he has blood on his hands, feet, and mouth. Therefore, [the phrase] means "when one is being born as a householder."
498.13 But how can there be a connection with the common action for one who is being born as a householder?

[It is] through the commonality of the connection with the sacrificial act of the *agnihotra* and so forth that "the householder is born. Just as a young boy, being born from his mother, is connected with a body and so on, so too is the *agnihotra*— 498.14–15—[connected].

[The cognition] arises through a commonality of connection with actions such as sacrifice (*havana*) and so forth. Why? Because [only] one who is capable [is entitled]. Since only one who is both capable and desirous is authorized by ritual acts (*karma*), and because neither capability nor desire exists in a newborn infant, both [are required]; however, these two exist in a householder.

Therefore, it is said that one who is being born is called a "householder" while being born. Furthermore, since there is no cessation of desire (*arthitva*), the scriptural statement regarding "living until old age" (*jarā-marya-vāda*) is established; and as for this Brāhmaṇa passage which teaches the connection with ritual actions "until old age," that would otherwise be impossible if desire were not present. Thus, there is no cessation of desire.

499.03 The establishment of the doctrine of old age and death: when there is a transformation of desire, and when desire has been transformed, 499.04 then one should properly set aside the *agnihotra* sacrifice and, having renounced for a fourth part of one’s life, go forth [into homelessness].
499.05 He spoke what is improper regarding "old age," for as long as there is connection with life, to say "by means of old age" is indeed meaningless.

499.06–08: Because this external power of one who is capable is prescribed when there is a desire for [the results], there is the offering of oblations by another. Furthermore, when that desire has undergone transformation, then renunciation (sannyāsa) is taught. Why, then, is it said in the injunction regarding ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) that "when there is a desire, there is the offering of the *agnihotra*"?

499.09 Because the scriptural injunction regarding desire is heard in respect to every ritual action, [it is said] "desire for heaven" (svarga-kāma). 499.10 Just as the instruction is given for the sake of the taught meaning, and the one who understands the taught meaning is the subject of the instruction—499.11 the instruction is directed toward him; it does not apply to a singer among the deaf, nor...
499.12 A dancer is blind; furthermore, a child lacks the knowledge resulting from instruction. Therefore, instruction is not intended for him.
499.13 Nor is the worldly [instruction] distinct from what is already worldly; at least, even a worldly person who has not yet investigated would not say this.
499.14 One would not say to a newborn infant: "Study! Sacrifice! Lead the life of a religious student (brahmacarya)! Why?

Thus the sage, having established himself as one who speaks what is faultless, would say this. Furthermore, either that which has been enjoined is restated, or else a meaning is postulated according to desire; in that case, the restatement of what has been enjoined is logically untenable.

For the expression of a matter that lacks authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would have to be postulated according to whim—that matter which [actually] exists by virtue of authoritative means of knowledge.
499.18 As long as a designation for that [subject] is not possible, there is a voluntary conceptualization of a designation for it.

500.01 For example, it is possible to say, "the newborn infant is in debt"; this is a statement following upon a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), namely, the word "newborn" applied to a householder. 500.02 [This is] an explanatory restatement (*anuvacana*). Just as the word "newborn" refers to a householder.

How is it understood that he is a householder? Because of being a means for sacrifice (*yajña-sādhana*); for he is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). In the case of a means, an effortful activity is observed, but not in the case of the fruit; just as [effort is directed] toward firewood and such things which are the means for cooking, but not toward the cooking itself, nor toward clods of earth and such things which are not means. The rest is in the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

But how, again, is it understood that this Brāhmaṇa passage is intended for one who desires the fruit? [Sūtra 4.1.61: And because of the injunction based on the substratum, it is like another knowledge.
[Sūtra 4.1.60(62): There is no prohibition against its being superimposed upon the Self.
Because there is superimposition upon the self, there is no negation [of the self]. For superimposition occurs when the desire for [objects] has ceased.
[4-1-61(63)] Since the final destruction of the vessel is untenable, there is an absence of fruit.

500.12 There would be an absence of results because the limit of the collection of alms-bowls would not be reached; for when the desire [for worldly life] has ceased, actions ending with the collection of alms-bowls are no longer performed by those who have gone forth. And if this Brāhmaṇa [text] were to apply without distinction, then it would follow that actions ending with the collection of alms-bowls must be performed everywhere.

Thus [ends the section]. The rest is in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, as for this [objection] that [liberation is impossible] because of the non-interruption of the continuity of the afflictions (*kleśa-santati*):
[4-1-62(64)] Liberation is like the absence of afflictions in one who is in deep sleep and sees no dreams. Just as there is an absence of dreams for one in deep sleep—

500.18–501.02: "In the state of non-perception (*adarśana*), the persistence of afflictions (*kleśa*) is severed, as is the persistence of the means for pleasure and pain; such is the case for the liberated one.
Furthermore, they describe this as the form of the liberated yogi. This is because [otherwise] there would be a persistence of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*).
Thus it is said.

501.03 [4-1-63(65)] There is no activity for the sake of rebirth in one whose afflictions have been diminished. 501.04 Even though activity exists, 501.05 it does not lead to rebirth in the absence of afflictions; thus, it does not constitute the cause of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).

501.06 Thus, it has been stated that "rebirth (pratisandhi), however, occurs when the previous birth ceases and there is a new birth; and that is brought about by craving. And this was stated in the Sūtra: "Because one does not observe the birth of those free from passion. If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of the fruitlessness of karma, we say no, because the experience of the maturation (vipāka) of karma is not denied.
501.09 We say that one is liberated while karma still exists; however, 501.10 [it is] at the end of [this life] that karmas ripen in a future birth.
501.11 [This is so] because the continuity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is not inherent (*svābhāvika*).

501.12 It is not [the case that the continuum of afflictions ceases], because the continuum of afflictions is intrinsic. The cessation of the continuum of afflictions is not possible. 501.13 Why? Because the continuum of afflictions is intrinsic. This continuum of afflictions is beginningless.
501.14 Since it has proceeded by way of its own nature, it cannot be severed. Regarding this, some offer the following rebuttal:
501.15 They explain:
[4-1-65(67)] Just as there is impermanence in the non-existence prior to arising, so too is there impermanence in that which is innate;
just as there is impermanence in the non-existence prior to arising, so too is there impermanence in that which is innate. For example, prior—

502.01 Non-existence arises from production, yet it is terminated by existence; likewise, the beginningless continuum of afflictions for one who does not know reality will be opposed by the knowledge of reality.
502.02–03 Or, it is like the permanence of the blackness of an atom. [4-1-66(68)]

Or, like the blackness and impermanence of an atom—just as the blackness of an atom is beginningless yet impermanent—so too is the continuum of afflictions (*kleśa-santati*). Indeed, for an existing entity (*dharma*), there are the two states of permanence and impermanence.

Those who determine [the status of] permanence and impermanence have stated that [these terms] are used figuratively (*bhākta*) with respect to the nature of reality (*tattva-bhāva*). What, then, [is this nature]?

502.07 Here, devotion is eternal and without cause, whereas antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), being non-eternal, having come into being, 502.08 does not [persist], nor does it exist when the antecedent non-existence has ceased; this is the general rule.
Furthermore, 502.09 this "beginningless blackness of atoms" is improper as something characterized by non-arising and non-eternal, because of the absence of a cause.
502.10 There is no cause for this; rather, this is a meditative absorption (samādhi).
502.11 [4-1-67(69)] Furthermore, because passion and the like have conceptualization as their cause...
502.12 ...because passion and the like have conceptualization as their cause, and because they have karma as their cause, they are mutually dependent.
"And because it is the cause" (nimittatvāt) is the meaning of "and" (ca). It has been stated that [desire] is the conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*) that longs for an experienced object.
From false conceptualizations—those which are provocative of passion, anger, and delusion—passion and the other [afflictions] arise.
Furthermore, karma, which brings about rebirth in a particular class of beings, produces passion and the rest in dependence upon conceptualization.
For a certain class of beings is observed to abound in passion, such as pigeons and the like;

another abounds in anger, such as snakes and the like; and another abounds in delusion, such as pythons and the like. If karma were to produce passion and the other [afflictions], then [beings] would always [possess] passion and the rest.

[If it were so,] there would be the consequence of no liberation (*anirmokṣa-prasaṅga*). [This is not the case] because of the deficiency of causes; for karma depends upon volition (*saṅkalpa*) and other factors, and desire (*rāga*) and so forth are its causes, not something independent. In that case, pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest would also not have karma as their cause, because [pleasure and so on] are not independent when karma is to be performed in relation to pleasure and the like.

503.04 It does not depend on volition (*saṅkalpa*), but rather produces pleasure and so forth depending on the proximity of its own causes. 503.05 Just as an action such as lifting depends on impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth to produce a formative force (*saṃskāra*), but is independent [of them] regarding conjunction and disjunction (*saṃyoga-vibhāgau*). 503.06 Furthermore, it is observed that passion and the other [afflictions] are mutual causes; for one who is impassioned...

503.07 One who is attached becomes deluded; one who is provoked becomes deluded; and one who is deluded becomes attached and provoked. 503.08 Regarding the statement that "the continuum of afflictions is beginningless," that is not so, because there is no distinction.
Just as the continuum of afflictions is beginningless, so too are all internal phenomena beginningless.
503.10 They proceed as a continuous stream; nothing whatsoever that has not previously arisen ever arises.

Nor is it the case that anything characterized by non-arising is asserted [to arise]. 503.11 However, the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), which has not previously arisen, 503.12 arises alone; no other internal entity whatsoever arises.
Thus ends the first daily lesson (*āhnika*) of the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyavārttika* by Uddyotakara. The second daily lesson of the fourth chapter begins.
Homage to the Supreme Self.

Now, as this knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) arises, does it pertain merely to the object in general, or rather to a specific aspect of the object? First of all, it is impossible for there to be knowledge of reality regarding the mere object; why is that?

504.06–504.08: Because objects are infinite, even regarding a specific object, that which remains as an object of the knowledge of reality must be explained by way of distinction. In this regard, since other objects—those distinct from the objects of cognition such as the self and so forth—are excluded, because the Sūtra has as its scope specific objects of cognition, that Sūtra concerning the self and so forth does not [apply] to them.
504.09 Only the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is being denoted; for if only the object of knowledge were denoted, the mention of "the self" (*ātman*) and so forth would be redundant.

504.10 Rather, it is a specific object of knowledge which, by being established as the domain of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), becomes the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra; whereas that which, because it is the domain of delusion (*moha*), extends saṃsāra—that [specific object] is [the object of knowledge] in its true sense.

Regarding the term "to be known" (*jñeya*): concerning this, the following question arises—does the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) arise with respect to each and every object that exists, or does it arise only in some instances? It cannot be the former, because [the objects] beginning with the self (*ātman*) are infinite. What is this infinity? It is the state of being beyond the scope of any cognition of measure (*iyattā*).
504.15 Now, if true knowledge (*tattva-jñāna*) arises in some place where it had not previously arisen, then delusion (*moha*) has not been eliminated there.

504.16 Where there is delusion, there are passion (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*); thus, since passion, aversion, and delusion constitute bondage, the consequence would be that liberation is impossible. 504.17 Now, if you think that true knowledge, having one object, eliminates delusion which has a different object—
And this being the case, liberation would follow for every living being;

for there is no living being whatsoever who does not [possess] the truth or the lack thereof regarding some object, because it is not from the non-cognition of the meaning of delusion that the cognition of reality arises.
Delusion is not merely the non-occurrence [of cognition], but rather false cognition is delusion; and that false cognition exists in relation to that [object].

505.03 That which functions toward an object becomes the seed of *saṃsāra*; that object should be known according to reality (*tattvataḥ*). What, then, is that false knowledge? It is the notion of a self (*ātma-pratyaya*) with respect to what is not-self (*anātman*). The rest is in the commentary (*bhāṣya*).
505.05 [4-2-1] The cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) results from the knowledge of reality regarding those things that have the defects as their cause.

505.06–07: The cessation of the ego-sense results from the knowledge of reality regarding those things that have the defects as their cause. Everything from the body up to suffering is the object of the defects, because false knowledge has that as its object; therefore, the knowledge of reality has that as its object.
505.08 It eliminates the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) that has arisen toward that object, because of the contradiction between the two when the object is the same.
505.09 And all of this has been stated in the second sūtra:
[4-2-2] "The objects, such as form and so forth, which are caused by defects, are produced by conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*)."

505.11–12. The objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are the causes of faults, are produced by conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*). These objects are called "desires" (*kāma*) and "sense-objects" (*viṣaya*). Among them, those objects, when falsely conceptualized, give rise to passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions]. What, then, is their false conceptualization? It is that which is not common [to all].

The determination that "these are mine alone" arises from the perception of them as the cause of their own origination. One should regard them as non-common [to others], thinking: "These are not mine, for they are non-common due to fate, thieves, fire, or heirs.
For one who regards them in this way, the delusion regarding the object of that determination ceases.

505.17 Thus [it is said]. Upon its cessation, one should contemplate internally the body and so forth. Furthermore, what is this "contemplation" (prasaṃkhyāna) regarding the body and so forth? It is the contemplation that consists in the perception of their distinction [from the self], namely: "These are not the self. 506.01 One who dwells thus, with a mind detached both internally and externally, is called "liberated. And this...

506.02 They say that the wise man is liberated from both joy and weariness even while still living. Beyond this, it is taught that some notion is to be cultivated and some is to be abandoned; there is neither the rejection of the object nor the appropriation of the object, but rather, regarding the subject as it actually exists, what exactly is to be cultivated?
506.05 Something must be refuted.
506.06 [4-2-3] However, the misconception of a whole (avayavin) is caused by that; however, the misconception of a whole has those defects as its cause.
506.07 However, the misconception of a whole is caused by them; it has those defects as its cause.
506.08. The conceit of a whole (*avayavin*). In that regard, the designation "whole" should be cultivated, while the designation "woman" should be abandoned.

506.09. A man together with his requisites—his requisites being a bond—is the designation "man. 506.10. Regarding "together with his requisites": therein, moreover, there are two designations—the designation of signs (*nimitta*) and the designation of meaning and phrasing (*artha-vyañjana*).
506.11 And: the perception of signs (*nimitta-saṃjñā*)—such as "these are teeth and lips"—is based on the nature of being teeth and so forth in relation to the teeth and other parts.
506.12 Perception of meaning and phonemes (*artha-vyañjana-saṃjñā*) is likewise: "the teeth are thus," "the lips are thus.
506.13 Such a perception, when expressed through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), is delusion (*moha*); and that is the cause of passion and the other afflictions.
506.14 It is that which is to be abandoned; however, the composite whole (avayavin) is not to be rejected, because it exists as such according to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
506.15 Now, at this point, by one who intends to refute the object (*artha*), the existence of the whole (*avayavin*) is established.
506.16 [4-2-4] Doubt arises from the twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance.
506.17 Doubt arises from the twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance; it is twofold because of the perception of both the existent and the non-existent.

506.18 Knowledge (*vidyā*) consists in the non-apprehension of both the existent and the non-existent; thus, ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed twofold. And so, if the whole (*avayavin*) is apprehended—507.01—or if it is not apprehended at all, one is by no means released from doubt.
Regarding this, it has already been stated that the twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance is not the cause of doubt, [but rather] the apprehension and non-apprehension [of the object].
507.03 Because it is a qualifier of the preceding term.

507.04 [4-2-5] There is no doubt regarding that, because the previous reason is well-established. 507.05 There is no doubt regarding that; there is no doubt concerning that composite whole (*avayavin*).

507.06. [The position is] logical, because the previously stated reasons have not been refuted; for those reasons that were indicated regarding the existence of the whole as a distinct entity (arthāntara) cannot be refuted.
507.07–08. [Objection: Even so, there is no doubt [regarding the non-existence of the whole], because its subsistence (vṛtti) is untenable.

507.09 Furthermore, there is no doubt [regarding our position] because the occurrence [of the whole] is untenable. He analyzes this by stating: "The whole does not exist. 507.11 [4-2-7] Because the parts do not subsist either in their entirety or in part, there is an absence of the whole.
507.12 Because the parts do not subsist either in their entirety or in part, there is an absence of the whole; [for] the parts [cannot reside] in the whole.
507.13. Do wholes reside in their parts, or do parts reside in the whole?

507.14. Regarding those residing in the whole, do they reside by way of their entirety or by way of a single part? In that regard, first, parts do not reside in the whole by way of their entirety, because of the difference in dimension between the part and the whole; [the part] has a small dimension.

507.16 The part (*avayava*) is of great dimension (*mahā-parimāṇa*), and the whole (*avayavin*) [is also of great dimension]; thus, there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the great dimension by the small dimension. It follows that the part would consist of a single substance (*eka-dravya*), because it subsists in a single whole. 508.01 Furthermore, there is no substratum (*ādhāra*) consisting of a single substance that remains without perishing, nor does the whole subsist in its parts by way of occupying only a portion (*ekadeśena*). 508.02 Nor does it subsist [in its entirety], for then it would follow that the whole is nothing other than the parts themselves. Thus, the whole is not established. Therefore, the whole is non-existent. Consequently, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) do not exist. Since they do not exist, the external object (*bāhyārtha*) does not exist. Because the external object does not exist, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is without an object (*anālambana*). Thus, all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty (*śūnya*). This is the meaning of the statement "all phenomena are empty. This is the second chapter on the refutation of the whole (*avayavin*). 508.03 [Question: Why is it said that the whole is not established? [Answer: Because the whole is not perceived apart from the parts. 508.04 [Objection: Even if it is not perceived separately, it exists as something distinct from the parts, just as a forest exists as something distinct from the trees. 508.05 [Response: That is not so. For the forest is merely a conceptual construction (*prajñapti*) based on the trees; it is not a real entity (*dravya*). If the forest were a real entity, then when one tree is removed, the forest would remain. However, in reality, when one tree is removed, the forest is no longer perceived. Therefore, the forest is not a real entity. Similarly, the whole is not a real entity. 508.06 Furthermore, the whole is not perceived because it is obstructed by the parts, just as a jar is not perceived when covered by a cloth. 515.05 This is logical. What is the reason?
