515.18 [4-2-18] Because of the interpenetration with space, that is untenable;
515.19 because of the interpenetration with space, that is untenable. An atom is interpenetrated by space.
515.20 Because it is subject to disintegration, [the self] is impermanent, like a jar.
516.01 Or else, [it follows that the self] is not omnipresent, like space.
516.02 [Or else,] because internal and external causes of a produced substance are mentioned, [it follows that the self] is not unproduced.
516.03 Its absence;

516.04 or else, space would not be all-pervading. If there is no internal space within atoms, then it follows that space is not all-pervading, because there would be no connection between the internal atoms due to the lack of interpenetration by space. Because of the non-interpenetration by space, [atoms would be discrete].
516.06 One who asserts that "the atom is impermanent" must be asked for the sake of clarification: what was said [to be the cause]?

516.07 [The opponent replies: "It is because of the interpenetration (*vyatibheda*) with space. 516.08 If this "interpenetration" means a connection of the atom with space, then nothing here is contradicted; for [impermanence] does not follow from a connection with space.

516.09. It follows that there would be either permanence or impermanence in the atom (*paramāṇu*). Now, if one were to say that the mere relation itself is the cause of impermanence, even so, the mention of space (*ākāśa*) is useless, because the mere relation establishes impermanence; for it is not the case that when "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) functions as a probans, [the example] such as Devadatta’s being produced is required.

516.12 What was stated is appropriate, and it is merely the conjunction that is reiterated by the subsequent sūtra for the sake of completing the argument, since the occurrence of conjunction has already been established.

516.13 Thus, this very point is being stated once again; therefore, this does not mean "interpenetration" (vyatibheda). 516.14 Now, if interpenetration were the connection between atoms, that too is not tenable, because it would result in [atoms] having no further effects.

516.15–17. To speak of "inside" or "outside" in relation to an atom is merely a way of referring to the causes of an effect; however, the atom is not an effect. Therefore, it has neither inside nor outside. Furthermore, as for the connection of the atom's parts with space—that too is exactly the same, because the atom is not an effect and thus possesses no parts.

516.18 Now, as for the division or disjunction of the parts of an atom, that too is refuted by the very fact that [the atom] is not an effect (akārya). 516.19 For it is the parts of an effect that are divided, whereas the atom is not an effect.
516.20 Therefore, there is no division of parts; having approached the atom, there are no parts, nor is there space for their division.

517.01 For separation is produced by action (*karma*), and space (*ākāśa*) is not its cause; such is the logical principle (*nyāya*). Furthermore, if space were admitted as a cause of separation, it would follow that all entities (*bhāva*) are non-abiding; for when space exists as the cause of separation, entities [would never cease from it].
517.04. Abiding is logical. Even though space exists, it depends upon another cause;

for apart from that [cause], 517.05 there is no proof that space possesses the capacity for its own production. Furthermore, 517.06 if you claim that "interior" means a cavity or a separation, this is also not the case, because for that which is entirely enclosed, there is nothing in its middle.

517.07 There are no parts; that void is not [composed of] atoms, for how could atoms have parts? 517.08 "Void" (*śuṣira*) means interpenetration (*vyatibheda*). Since there is no other possibility, it follows from this interpenetration with space (*ākāśa*) that [space itself is the void]. 517.09 Thus, the designation "void" is established. Furthermore, if this were the case, it would follow that space is not all-pervading (*asarvagata*).

517.10 Because there is no connection with the intermediate atom (*paramāṇu*), [it is not the case that] this is due to a lack of thorough knowledge of the meaning of "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*). 517.11 This is not the meaning of "all-pervading," namely, that there is no connection with that which does not exist; rather, the meaning of being all-pervading is that there is a connection with everything that possesses form (*mūrtimat*). 517.12 And since there is no middle [space] for atoms, therefore it is not [the case].
517.13 Because of that lack of connection, it would follow that space is not omnipresent.
517.14 [4-2-21] And because of the pervasion of all conjunctions and sound, it is omnipresent.
517.15 And because of the pervasion of all conjunctions and sound, it is omnipresent; for [space] is connected with all things possessing form.
Conjunctions manifest in space; sounds, having that as their substratum, arise from the proximity of their own causes.
Since all [sounds] depend upon space as they are produced, space is omnipresent.
518.01 [4-2-22] Non-obstruction, non-resistance, and omnipresence are the qualities of space (ākāśa).

518.02 Non-obstruction, non-resistance, and omnipresence are the qualities of space. 518.03 Space is not obstructed by a moving, active substance; rather, it is the quality that serves as the cause for the motion of a moving, active substance.

518.04 Why does it not obstruct? Because it is intangible (*asparśatvāt*). Whatever possesses tangibility is subject to displacement (*vyūhyate*); 518.05 space, however, does not possess such properties and thus does not obstruct; therefore, you [should admit that] it is non-obstructive (*apratighāti*).
518.06 It is stated that one ought not to suspect a property contrary to what is observed in a composite substance (*sāvayava*) that possesses tangibility. Thus it has been said.

518.07 And here, if the atom were to be divided, it would no longer be an atom. What is the reason? 518.08 Because, in the process of division, there follows the consequence of something even smaller; since nothing smaller than that can exist there [as a limit]. Furthermore, regarding the destruction of the atom, it would have to be conceived as occurring either from the destruction of its causes or from the disjunction of its causes; both [possibilities] apply.

And it has been stated that the atom does not exist because it would lack any effect; therefore, impermanence does not result from the penetration of space. [4-2-23] Furthermore, because the formation of shape is possible for things possessing form, the existence of parts is established.
518.13 And because the occurrence of configuration is possible for things possessing form, there exists the state of having parts (*sāvayavatva*). Atoms are not partless.

518.14 Because they possess form—that is, because they possess configuration—they have parts. 518.15 Like that which possesses configuration; for example, jars and the like are seen to have parts. Therefore, atoms possess configuration; therefore [they have parts].
518.16 "They possess parts. 518.17 [4-2-24] Because conjunction is possible.
518.18 [4-2-25] There is no refutation [of the argument], because it would lead to an infinite regress, and because an infinite regress is untenable.

518.19 [The meaning of the sūtra is: "Because of the occurrence of conjunction; it possesses parts because it is conjunct. Now, is this sūtra not already rendered superfluous by the [previous] statement "because it has shape" (saṃsthānavattvāt), since a particular kind of conjunction is designated by "having shape"? No, it is not rendered superfluous, because "having shape" refers to a particular kind of conjunction of parts.

519.02 Because it is so designated, that which is merely a conjunction is expressed by the word "conjunction"; thus, there is no fault. 519.03 In this context, "figure" (*mūrti*) refers to the sixfold dimension of non-pervasive substances: minute, large, long, short, extremely short, and the atom (*paramāṇu*). "Configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to conjunction known as accumulation (*pracaya*). Conjunction...

519.05 [Objection: "Attainment (*prāpti*) is preceded by non-attainment. As for the claim that "because they possess form (*mūrtimat*), they must have parts," 519.06 that is not so, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). That which is a part of an atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses form and yet is partless;
thus, there is an inconclusiveness. If, on the other hand, it is argued that because it possesses form, it too must have parts, then in that case—

It has been stated that the atom (truṭi) becomes immeasurable in terms of weight, number, and dimension. Now, as long as that which possesses form is divided until its end, it must be said that the ultimate [atom] is partless.
Furthermore, if there were a division at the end, that would not be tenable, because division is impossible without something being divided.

519.11 Thus it would be; and this much is the [proper] method (*kalpa*). The division [of matter] must end in the atom (*paramāṇu*), whether that [division] is finite or infinite. 519.12 If it ends in the atom, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*), and a contradiction (*vyāghāta*) arises: "The atom possesses form (*mūrtimat*) and yet is not composed of parts (*sāvayava*). What, then, is the contradiction here?

519.14 You maintain that the atom is partless (*niravayava*) and yet possesses form (*mūrtimant*), and you also assert that it has parts (*sāvayava*). 519.15 This position is contradicted by its own logical implications; for if it were infinite, there would be a contradiction at the point of dissolution, and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the atom being immeasurable (*ameya*).
519.16 Furthermore, there would be the consequence of disjunction (*vibhāga*) having no substratum; thus, the thesis (*pratijñā*) that "the atom has parts" is undermined.

519.17 [This is] a contradiction. How so? The meaning of the term "possessing parts" (*sāvayava*) is that which is produced from things of the same class, which rests upon things of the same class; these "parts" (*avayava*) are its substrata. Thus, by one who asserts that "the atom possesses parts," it is stated that the atom is a particular kind of effect (*kāryaviśeṣa*). That the atom is a particular kind of effect...
[This is] contradictory. Now, if you maintain that an atom has a single atom as its antecedent, then an atom would not be partless;

it would have parts. However, an atom is not [produced], because it is preceded by [another] atom. And this is not so, because there is no example [of such a case], and because a single [atom] is the cause.
520.03 There is an example: a single atom being initiated does not depend upon a causal totality (kāraṇa-sāmagrī).
520.04 Since it exists, prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is not tenable; and for that which has no prior non-existence, there can be no arising.
520.05 This is not tenable. Now, if one maintains that sound and so forth are preceded by a single [prior] sound, then one would have to admit their prior non-existence and so on.

That too is unproven. Even if one were to maintain that there is no single cause, but rather that sound, depending on its substratum and other factors, produces another sound, [one must still explain] what the nature of a single atom is, how it precedes [another] atom, and what the meaning of "having parts" (sāvayava) is—what therein constitutes the part and what constitutes the whole? Furthermore, what is the cause?
520.09 Thus, since it is a part, there is no causal atom at the time of the effect-atom;

520.10 therefore, the meaning of "having parts" must be stated. One who asserts that "the atom has parts because it possesses form" (mūrtimat) 520.11 should further be questioned through an alternative analysis: what is this "form" (mūrti), by virtue of which [the atom] is possessed of form?

520.12 Regarding the term "atom" (*paramāṇu*): since there is such a thing as form (*mūrti*), is the atom something other than that form or not other than it? 520.13 If "form" refers to specific qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, then according to your position, there is no entity possessing form (*mūrtimān*) by means of such a form; nor does one apprehend an atom through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as distinct from color and the other qualities.

520.15–17. When all [qualities] such as color (*rūpa*) have been subtracted, that which remains is the atom (*paramāṇu*); yet it is not the case that the atom possesses color and so forth by means of those qualities. Nor do we observe the derivation of the possessive suffix *-mat* (*matup*) when there is no distinct entity [between the possessor and the possessed]. But is it not observed that the possessive suffix occurs even when there is no distinct entity, as in the expression "an army possessing elephants" (*hastimatī senā*)?

520.18 We say that [the atom] is not seen. And it has already been stated how an army is not a separate entity [from its parts]. 520.19 Furthermore, since there is no atom existing as a separate entity and no corporeality (mūrti), atoms possess parts.
520.20 The meaning of the statement "because they possess corporeality" is that form and the other [sensory qualities]—namely, those possessing form and so forth—are possessed of form and so forth.
"By this [statement], it is refuted that 'the cloth has parts because it is not incorporeal' (amūrtimattvāt).

For you do not admit a cloth distinct from color and so forth, yet you maintain that it is corporeal; moreover, you assert that 'the cloth has parts because it is corporeal. If you accept this distinction, there is a contradiction."

521.02 If it is not accepted, the intended meaning is not established; because the property of both [the subject and the example] must be established in the example, [the property of] having parts is not [established] in the cloth. 521.03 [Therefore,] "having parts" does not mean "possessing corporeality. By this, the argument that "atoms have parts because conjunction is possible" has been explained. If conjunction is accepted, there is a contradiction; if it is not accepted, [the reason is unestablished].
The meaning of the reason "because of being an atom" (paramāṇutvāt) is that it possesses a specific configuration (saṃsthānaviśeṣavattva); however, this is unestablished (asiddha).

That very same meaning which is expressed by "because of having parts" (sāvayavatvāt) is the same meaning as "because of possessing a specific configuration. Now, if you were to understand configuration as the dimension (parimāṇa) of a substance that is not all-pervading, then, in that case, [it would follow] by virtue of its corporeality (mūrtimattva).

521.08. That [atom] possesses shape (*saṃsthānavattva*) because its purpose has been fulfilled; this must be stated separately from "possessing form" (*mūrtimattvāt*), because it possesses a specific configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣavattvāt*).
And it has been said in this regard concerning division: since there would be the consequence of something even smaller, that which is not smaller does not exist there.
Because of the persistence [of the atom], and because it would follow that the atomic part would be even more minute, the existence of an effect that is an atom is negated.

Furthermore, regarding this [argument]: if an atom, existing in the middle of a conjunction and arising from it, were to be connected with those preceding and following [atoms], then it would possess parts. This very point is expressed by the verse: "When six [atoms] are joined simultaneously, the atom has six parts."

"If the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom," because the locations of the relations [of conjunction] are identical. Now, if all the conjunctions of the six atoms occupy the same location, it follows that the aggregate would be the size of a single atom. This would be the case if two substances [conjoined] at a time.

521.17 It is stated with reference to that; therefore, it is not the case that multiple conjunctions occupy the same location with reference to the atom which is related to those [conjunctions]. 522.01 Nothing is contradicted by this. Furthermore, as for this [claim] that atoms occupy the same location:

522.03 That is not so, because it is not admitted that atoms themselves do not exist in space; how then could they [the objects] occupy the same location? Furthermore, there is no substance whatsoever that occupies the same location; thus the example is unestablished. But surely cause and effect occupy the same location through conjunction, as for instance a jar with a cloth?

"It is connected by means of the thread and that fiber, which has its own substratum," and so forth. This is refuted by the non-acceptance [of such a view]. One must state that the conjunctions therein occupy the same location; thus, they are neither cause and effect, nor are the conjunctions two each with respect to [the parts], because all six occupy the same location.

522.09 A substance does not remain fixed in a common location, nor in a location common to its conjunctions. 522.10 As for this [objection]: "For that which possesses a distinction of direction and location, unity is not tenable"—who says such a thing? 522.11 [The response is:
There is a distinction of direction and location; and these distinctions of direction and location are directions and conjunctions that are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).

522.12 Having imagined spatial divisions [in] atoms, a spatial division is accepted as primary; however, 522.13 there is neither a spatial division nor a division of the atom itself, for an atom is not connected with space. 522.14 Thus, only this much exists, and this does not contradict anything regarding shadow and obstruction.
522.15 In that case, [shadow and obstruction] do not apply to atoms because they lack spatial extension (*adeśatvāt*). It is not because of having spatial extension that shadow and obstruction occur.

522.16 What then? Because they possess form and tangibility (*mūrtimat-sparśavattvāt*), a substance possessing form and tangibility obstructs another substance. 522.17 What does this obstruct? It obstructs the connection of the other by virtue of its own connection.
"It negates [light]," he says. Shadow, however, arises from the obstruction of light-atoms by a material atom; where a light-atom is obstructed by a material atom, there is shadow.
Everywhere, substances, qualities, and motions associated with a rarefied connection with light are designated as "shadow."

But those things which possess a connection with excluded light are designated as "darkness" (*tamas*). Thus, because shadow (*chāyā*) and concealment (*āvṛti*) are established otherwise, [the reason] is not a valid probans (*ahetu*). By this, [the arguments] based on possessing action (*kriyāvat*), possessing touch (*sparśavat*), being the originator of another substance (*dravyāntarārambhakatva*), being the causal condition for the formative force of action (*kriyākāraṇasaṃskārapratyayatva*), and [possessing] priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatvavat*)—are also refuted.

The [objections] beginning with "because of being so" (523.04) have already been refuted. How so? Just as in the statement, "They possess parts because they are corporeal" (523.05), there are defects of the proposition (*pratijñā-doṣa*) and defects of the reason (*hetu-doṣa*), so too in all these positions accepted by the opposing party, there are—according to the circumstances—the contradictory (*viruddha*), unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and other such [fallacies].

523.07 The distinctions among defects must be stated; the remainder is in the Bhāṣya. As for those who seek to prove the impermanence of atoms by means of their possession of action (*kriyāvat-tva*) and so forth, they must necessarily admit that this possession of action is either a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) or a producer (*kāraka*). If possession of action were the producer of impermanence, then that which is without action— [is it not eternal?]

In that case, it would follow that [the atom] is eternal. Alternatively, if "birth" (janman) is defined as "action" (kriyā), then atoms would be non-eternal because they possess birth; this is the meaning of the reason (*hetu*). However, the possession of birth is unestablished (*asiddha*) for atoms.
Or, if it is argued that "possessing action" is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), even if it is a manifestor, the non-eternality of atoms would still [be established] by means of something else.

It must be said: this is not a property of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) that it should produce an unmanifested thing; rather, [the manifestor] manifests what has already come into being from another cause. Indeed, a lamp does not illuminate an object by first producing it if it does not already exist.
[The reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*) if one accepts actions such as "lifting" (*utkṣepaṇa*) established by others. By this, [the same applies to] jars and so forth.

The example has been explained. Furthermore, "possessing action" (*kriyāvat-tva*) means the inherence (*samavāya*) of action; if this is accepted, it is contradictory [to the probandum of permanence]; if it is not accepted, the meaning of the reason—"the atom is impermanent because it is an atom"—is contradicted.
Moreover, since the suffix *-mat* is seen to have meanings other than [mere] possession, it is contradictory; if it does not have another meaning, there is an absence of an example.
In this manner, the remaining statements should be analyzed, and their faults stated according to what is applicable.

Now, if one accepts these [reasons] as established by the opponent's school, how can they be established by the opponent's school? Or if not, how can a property that has not been perceived by oneself be employed for the purpose of convincing another on the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
524.03–05. As for this thought that you hold, based on the intellect (*buddhi*), that objects exist: these are false cognitions.
For if these were cognitions of reality, then when the intellect performs its analytical discernment, the true nature of the objects of cognition would be perceived.

524.06 [4-2-26] However, through the analytical discernment by the intellect (*buddhi*), the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of entities is not perceived; just as when threads are removed, the existence of a cloth is no longer perceived, so too is that [true nature] not perceived through the analytical discernment by the intellect of entities.
524.07–524.08 Through the analytical discernment by the intellect of entities, their true nature is not perceived, just as when threads are removed...

524.09 Just as there is no perception of the existence of a cloth [when its parts are analyzed], so too is there no perception of that [whole]. These things such as cows and so forth, which are objects of cognition—524.10 as well as jars and the like—do not exist in reality. Why? Because when they are being analyzed by cognition into their distinct components, 524.11 they are apprehended [as separate]; just as, for example, when threads are being analyzed by the cognition "this is a thread, this is a thread," [the cloth is no longer perceived].

524.12 There is no cloth whatsoever that could be the object of the cognition "cloth"; likewise, by means of the cognition [of the cloth], one analyzes the threads, and so on, until one reaches the atoms. 524.13 Even the atoms, when analyzed part by part, are analyzed down to their dissolution. Thus, since everything is non-existent, [the cognition is baseless].
The cognitions of "cow" and so forth, the cognitions of "jar" and so forth, are false cognitions.
524.16 [4-2-27] It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory (vyāhata).
524.17 Because it is contradictory, it is not a valid reason. [The opponent claims: "Because things are distinguished by the intellect (buddhi), all things are non-existent.
524.18 This is incorrect. Why? Because of contradiction (vyāghāta). What is the contradiction? It is the impossibility of coexistence (saha-asambhava).

525.01 If the analysis of entities is by means of the intellect, then it is not the case that all entities are non-existent; for if all entities were non-existent, there would be no analysis of all entities by means of the intellect. One who asserts that "there is the non-existence of all entities" must be questioned regarding his authority (*pramāṇa*), should he claim to have such authority.

525.04 It becomes contradictory; or, if he does not speak, his purpose is not established due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). 525.05 Now, if establishment occurs without a means of valid cognition, why is the arising of all things not established? And as for this doctrine that "the non-existence of all things exists within things because their establishment is mutually dependent," there is a fault in this position.

525.07 It has been stated that this [argument] should also be seen here. Furthermore, if this [cloth] were a substance distinct [from its parts], such as the cloth and so forth, it would be perceived separately when the threads are being mentally distinguished. 525.08–09 This is the point.

525.09 [4-2-28] Because it has that as its substratum, there is no separate apprehension. 525.10 Because it has that as its substratum, there is no separate apprehension. An effect, which is dependent upon the causal substance, is not perceived separately from it; thus, in the contrary case, if there were separate apprehension where there is a relation of cause and effect—
Furthermore, there is no relationship of support and supported therein, nor is there a separate apprehension [of them].
525.13 [4-2-29] And because the apprehension of an object occurs through the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

525.14 And because the apprehension of an object occurs through the means of valid cognition: whatever exists and in what manner it exists, and whatever does not exist and in what manner it does not exist—all that is established by the perception [of the object] through the means of valid cognition. The rest is in the Bhāṣya.
525.16 [4-2-30] By means of the non-establishment and establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
525.17 [4-2-31] This conceit regarding the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition (prameya) is like the conceit regarding the objects of a dream.
525.18 This conceit regarding the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition is like the conceit regarding the objects of a dream; just as in a dream...

Objects do not exist, yet there is the conceit of objects; likewise, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) do not exist, yet there is the conceit of the means and objects of valid cognition.
Or, it is like an illusion, a city of Gandharvas, or a mirage.
526.02 [4-2-33] Non-establishment due to the absence of a cause.
526.03 [4-2-34] And the conceit regarding the objects of a dream is like memory and mental construction.
526.04 Or it is like an illusion, a city of Gandharvas, or a mirage; it is not [real] because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of the end of a dream.
526.05–06: "In this regard, no reason is stated for the conceit [of existence] toward objects that do not exist.

526.06–07: "And what is the reason that objects are non-existent at the end of a dream? If it is argued that it is because they appear [as such], then [this applies to] the non-existence of those objects perceived in the waking state which are distinct from the mind."

526.08. The reason—that appearances are like dreams—is not valid because the example is equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*). As for those objects that appear during the state of dreaming, what is the reason for the claim that they are not distinct from the mind? If you think they do not exist because they are not perceived by one who has awakened, then...

526.11 Because they are not perceived by one who has awakened, it does not follow that they do not exist, since a qualification has been employed. 526.12 It would follow that those things which are perceived by one who has awakened do exist; thus, the qualification "because they are not perceived by one who has awakened" is either redundant or [implies] that the object being perceived during the waking state [is non-existent]. 526.13 If [it were so], then the object perceived in the waking state...

526.14–15: Furthermore, regarding the statement "you consider the mind to be non-existent; what is the reason for this claim that it exists?"—if [the opponent argues] that the non-perception of the waking state is not a valid reason because of a lack of capacity, [we reply]: if perception were the means of proving existence, then non-perception would prove non-existence, for its capacity is observed in the case of the opposite.

526.17 Objects are not distinct from the mind, because they are objects of apprehension, like sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth. Just as sensation and the rest—which are objects of apprehension—are not distinct from the mind, so too are objects; [otherwise], since the mind is knowledge (*jñāna*), and knowledge is distinct from pleasure and pain, the example would be unestablished (*asiddha*). 526.18–19 Sensation and the rest, which are apprehended, are not distinct from the mind; likewise, objects are also [not distinct]. Pleasure and pain are the mind, and knowledge is distinct from pleasure and pain. Thus, the example is unestablished.

527.01. Pleasure and pain are the objects of apprehension (*grāhya*), and cognition is the act of apprehension (*grahaṇa*); thus, because of this state of object and subject, there is a difference between them. 527.02. Now, if consciousness is non-different from feeling, even so, the object of apprehension and the act of apprehension would be one and the same.
527.03. There is no such example; for it is never observed that the action and the agent of the action are one and the same. Or else...
527.04 Even if you were to accept oneness without disregarding the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would still be "four aggregates" (*skandha*).

527.05 This would contradict the treatise (*śāstra*). Alternatively, if you do not accept the fourfold nature and instead maintain that only what is perceived is consciousness (*vijñāna-mātra*), 527.06 then you must also account for the observed distinctions between external and internal consciousnesses.

Because there is no cause for the differentiation of consciousness [in that case], how can there be a differentiation of consciousness? If one maintains that there is a differentiation of consciousness—as in a dream—that too must be established as a differentiation of consciousness through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding things previously seen or experienced. Now, in the case of dreams, [the appearance of] things occurs by virtue of mental cultivation.

He too would have to admit a distinction between consciousnesses; furthermore, he must stand opposed [to this] by means of the distinction between the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) and the producer (*bhāvaka*).

It is not the case that the object to be produced and the producer are non-distinct. And as for these cognitions in dreams and so forth, which conform to distinctions such as cities, palaces, gardens, and vehicles—they are false cognitions. Thus, regarding false cognitions...

527.13 And one who says, "Because they share the commonality of being cognitions of the waking state, all my cognitions will likewise be false," should be questioned regarding the primary cause (*pradhāna*). For we do not perceive a cognition of error that is devoid of a primary cause; thus, he fails to establish an object distinct from the mind.
One must inquire into the nature of the proof and the refutation: if [the object] has an external nature, there is a contradiction;
527.17 if, on the other hand, it has the nature of consciousness, the point that "another person is not apprehended by means of consciousness" is not established.
527.18 For one person does not perceive another's dream without it being told to them. If, then, consciousness has the form of a word...
528.01. Therefore, one must also explain the meaning of "aspect" (ākāra) in the statement that "the mind takes on the aspect of sound.
528.02. For an "aspect" is indeed a cognition of something as being what it is not, based on a commonality with a primary object.
528.03. And since, according to your position, sound does not exist [as a real entity], the claim that "the mind takes on the aspect of sound" is devoid of referential meaning.

Not perceiving an object distinct from consciousness, one must be questioned regarding the distinction between the waking and dreaming states: "In the waking state objects do not exist, just as in the dreaming state.
From what [source] is this established—that "this is the dreaming state" and "this is the waking state"—such that there would be no confusion regarding the determination of merit and demerit?

Just as in the state of dreaming, no demerit arises from approaching those who should not be approached and so forth, so too it would not arise in the waking state either. If, however, one were to maintain that the distinction between the impairment and non-impairment of a perfected being (*siddha*) produces a difference [in the result], that too would be exactly the same; for the impairment of a perfected being is likewise [subject to the same conditions]. Thus, there is a transformation (*vaikṛtya*).

How is it understood that [consciousness] has a cause? Now, if one were to perceive a distinction between consciousness being clear or unclear, then in the absence of an object, the emptiness or lack of clarity of the cognition must be explained.
If you argue that a distinction in cognition is observed even when the object does not exist—just as in the case of similar [cognitions]—then...

528.13 Pretas born from the ripening of karma see a river filled with pus, yet no such river exists there. 528.14 There is neither pus, for a single entity cannot possess multiple forms; moreover, a difference in consciousness is observed.
528.15 Some see that very same [river] as filled with water, while others see it as filled with blood; therefore, it is concluded:
528.16 Just as in the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), consciousness arises in such a manner even when there is no external cause, so too [is it here].

528.17 [Objection: This is not so, because of contradiction; for one who asserts that "even in the absence of an external object, consciousness itself arises in such a manner," he must be asked: "How does it arise in such a manner? If [you say] consciousness has the form of blood...
528.19 Then it must be stated: what is blood? It must be explained as having the appearance of water or the appearance of a river.
528.20 And the words of the sentence, "they see [it] filled with pus," must each be examined individually.
529.01 The aggregates (skandhas) such as form and so forth become devoid of objective referents through these entities, and there is a restriction regarding location and so forth.
529.02 One does not perceive a river full of pus in one location while perceiving it in other locations.

529.03 Since the object does not exist, a reason for this restriction must be stated; however, for that which exists and is established in a certain form, it is logical that the remaining [perceptions] are false cognitions. And these are indeed false cognitions.
529.05 "Sirs, since they do not contradict the primary [cause], the primary cause of the perceptions of pus and so forth must be stated.
529.06 "Just as it is with the perceptions of pus and so forth, so it is with illusions, cities of the Gandharvas, and the water of a mirage.
529.07 "Thus, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an action is imagined to be in one place, while its fruit is imagined to be elsewhere"—this is the meaning of this [statement].

529.08–10. It is said that wherever the action (*karman*) occurs, there alone the fruit (*phala*) must occur for one whose objects (*viṣaya*) are distinct from the mind (*citta*). For such a person, the action is in one place and the fruit of the action is in another; thus, the action and its fruit would have different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*). This is not so, because it is not accepted; I do not accept that the action and its fruit have different loci.

529.11 There is no fault in [the position] that the action resides in the self and the fruit likewise resides therein. [The objects] are distinct from my own mind because they possess both generality and particularity, like the mind of another continuum (santānāntara), and because they are cognizable by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because they are effects, because they are impermanent, and because they are preceded by [moral] qualities (dharma).
And this being so:
529.15 [4-2-35] The destruction of false perception occurs through the knowledge of reality, just as the delusion regarding the objects of a dream is destroyed upon waking;
529.16–17 the destruction of false perception occurs through the knowledge of reality, just as the delusion regarding the objects of a dream is destroyed upon waking.

Upon awakening, the determination that "this is a person" regarding a post is a false perception; it is sublated by the knowledge of reality. That false determination ceases, but the object characterized as either a post or a person does not [cease], for it is not the case that the post does not exist.
Just so, those determinations regarding things perceived in a dream are [sublated] by the perception of the waking state.
530.03. [The cognitions] are turned back, but not the object characterized by the general nature of the sense-field. The rest is in the Bhāṣya.
530.04 [4-2-36] And likewise, because the existence of a cause is perceived for cognitions;

530.05 and because the existence of a cause is perceived for cognitions, the cause of a false cognition—530.06 what indeed is that? It is the perception of a commonality and the superimposition of a non-existent particularity.
530.07 Thus. One who maintains a false cognition must state its causeless nature, and one who maintains [a true] cause must accept the object. 530.08 And so it is.

530.09 [4-2-37] Furthermore, the twofold nature of false cognition is established due to the distinction between the real (tattva) and the principal (pradhāna). 530.10 Regarding the statement "the real is a post" (sthāṇu), and "the principal is a person" (puruṣa): when there is no elision of either the real or the principal, a false cognition arises. The remainder...
In the Bhāṣya it is stated: "From the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna), the cessation of egoism (ahaṅkāra) occurs through [the removal of] the causes of defects.
Now, how does this knowledge of reality arise?
530.14 [4-2-38] From the practice of a specific concentration (samādhi).

530.15 From the practice of a specific concentration. The remainder is in the Bhāṣya. If it is argued that withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is not appropriate because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is all-pervading—should you think that the internal organ is pervasive—then [the answer follows].

530.17–18: How is that [objection] refuted? Because the answer has already been stated. It has been explained above that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not all-pervading. 530.18–531.01: If it is argued that "the observation of the movement of one's own limbs is possible," then you must consider this: even for one who holds that the internal organ is atomic (*aṇu*), the observation of the movement of one's own limbs would likewise be impossible.

531.02 Because of their simultaneous proximity to the hand or the eye, due to the simultaneity of the conjunction of the body, the self (*ātman*), and the mind; 531.03 because of the simultaneous arising of effort and vision, there occurs simultaneously the connection of the self with its own body and the connection of the self [with the external object].
531.04 In that case, from the connection of the self, the mind, and the body, there arises the movement of one's own limbs and the [movement] of the self and the mind.
531.05–06: It is observed that the movement of the eye results from a connection [with the mind], and likewise, the movement of one's own limbs occurs through effort.

531.06–07: This is because of the proximity of the ocular rays and the object; furthermore, since there are no spatial parts (*pradeśa*) of the self (*ātman*), this is not to be questioned. Moreover, if the self possessed spatial parts, the mind would be connected with one part of the self by one means and with another part by another.

531.08–09: Regarding the [objection that] "the body" implies defects such as movement and vision in one's own limbs, for one who holds that the self is indeed without spatial parts (*niṣpradeśa*), this defect does not arise; thus, there is a connection of the mind with the self that is related to the body.

531.10 [4-2-39] Not so, because of the intensity of the specific object. 531.11 It is not the case that the practice of a specific meditative concentration is impossible for one who does not wish to know; for cognition arises even [in such a person], as in the case of the sound of thunder and similar phenomena. 531.12 Even for one who does not desire to understand, the arising of cognition occurs, just as it does with respect to the sound of thunder and other such things.
531.13 [4-2-40] And because of being impelled by hunger and so forth.
531.14 Because of being impelled by hunger and so forth; for even one who has not ceased from hunger and thirst, 531.15 cognitions arise—thus, this specific meditative concentration is not tenable.
531.16 [4-2-41] Its arising is due to the connection with the fruit of what was done previously.
531.17 Its arising is due to the connection with the fruit of what was done previously. "Done previously" means practiced in a previous body.
532.01 A specific state of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viśeṣa*), its fruit which is merit (*dharma*), and the further specific state of meditative concentration produced by that [merit].

532.02 And because of a particular state of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viśeṣa*), there is the overcoming of external objects. Even for a worldly person established in a particular state of concentration, cognitions do not arise when external objects present themselves; how much more so for a yogin? If, however, object-cognitions were to manifest upon the presentation of external objects, [then...]

532.05. This same contingency would apply even in the case of liberation (apavarga); moreover, it is logical that in liberation there should be the occurrence of contact with specific external objects.
532.06. [If this were so,] there would be the contingency of the arising of the cognition "it exists."
532.07 [4-2-42] Instruction on the practice of yoga in forest retreats, caves, riverbanks, and similar locations.
532.08 [4-2-43] Even in the case of liberation (*apavarga*), such a contingency would arise.
532.09 [4-2-44] No, because that which has been accomplished is necessarily destined to occur.

532.10 Not so, because [the object] is not necessarily established [prior to cognition]. When the body exists, the external object is the cause for the arising of cognition; it is not otherwise. This is the meaning of the Sūtra.
532.12 [4-2-45] And its absence occurs upon liberation (apavarga).
532.13 And its absence occurs upon liberation; that is, upon liberation, there is the absence of that [set of causes for perception], such as the body and so forth.
532.14 Thus, liberation is the release from all suffering, because it is the seed of all suffering.
532.15 And suffering is severed in liberation; therefore, liberation is freedom from all suffering.
532.16 [4-2-46] For that purpose, there is the purification of the self through *yama* and *niyama*, and through yoga by means of the methods of the inner science (*adhyātma-vidhi*).
533.01 For that purpose, there is the purification of the self through *yama* and *niyama*, and through yoga by means of the methods of the inner science.
For the attainment of that liberation, there is the cultivation of the practices of *yama* and *niyama*.

533.03 [4-2-47] The repeated practice of grasping knowledge and conversing with those who possess that knowledge; 533.04 because of the repeated practice of grasping wisdom (*prajñāna*) and conversing with those who possess it, the "grasping of knowledge" (*jñāna-grahaṇa*) refers to the grasping of the scriptures (*śāstra*).
They understand the effort toward that knowledge as the means; thus, the term "those who possess that knowledge" (*tad-vidya*) is a statement whose meaning is not yet fully differentiated.
533.06 [4-2-48] One should approach him with a student, a teacher, a fellow-student, or those seeking a distinguished excellence, provided they are free from envy.
533.07 One should approach him.
533.08 This sūtra, beginning with "with a student, a teacher, a fellow-student," and so forth, is as follows.
The meaning has been established by the very [text of] the Nigada.
533.10 [4-2-49] Or, even if it lacks a counter-position, one may accept it if there is a purpose and a need for it; "one may accept it" is understood to carry over from the previous context.
533.11 Or, even if it lacks a counter-position, one may accept it for the sake of a specific purpose when there is a need for it. "One may accept it" is supplied from the preceding rule.

[4-2-50] Disputation (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, just as one uses a fence of thorny branches to protect the growth of seeds. [Disputation and cavil are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, like a fence of thorny branches used to protect the growth of seeds.]

"Like a barrier of thorny branches": this should be done by one who has not yet produced the knowledge of reality; such is the meaning of the sūtra. And [it applies] to one who is being treated with contempt by others due to their learning, world-weariness, and so forth.
[4-2-51] Speaking after having engaged in debate with those two.

534.02–03. By means of those two—cavil (jalpa) and wrangling (vitaṇḍā)—one engages in debate "with the desire for victory" and not with the desire to know the truth; 534.03. and this is for the purpose of preserving one's learning, not for the sake of gain, honor, or fame.
The connection between activity and defects, as well as rebirth after death, have been explained in detail;
the result, which is suffering, and liberation are proclaimed in the fourth [chapter].
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyasūtravārttika* by Uddyotakara.
The fourth chapter is completed.
